subject: US Week Ahead: July 13 - July 19
summary:
# US Week Ahead: CPI and Retail Sales Headline a Fed-Heavy Calendar

**Theme:** Softening core inflation and cooling consumer spending, against a crowded slate of Fed speakers  
**Markets:** US macro (inflation, consumer, activity)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jan Hatzius, 12 July 2026  

### Landscape
- Q2 GDP tracking at +2.2% (quarter-over-quarter annualized), with the June Current Activity Indicator at +2.5%.
- US MAP index of economic surprises sits at 0.0 — data broadly in line with expectations.
- Last core CPI ran +0.2% MoM and +2.9% YoY; headline last printed +0.5% MoM and +4.2% YoY, still well above target.
- Last core PCE-relevant reads and last retail sales were firm: headline retail +0.9%, core +0.7% MoM.
- Consumer sentiment (UMich) last at 49.5 and long-run inflation expectations anchored at 3.3%.

### Drivers
- **Disinflation in core, led by shelter and autos:** [REDACTED] sees June core CPI at +0.17% MoM, trimming YoY to 2.8%; used cars -0.5%, new cars -0.1%, OER +0.23%, rent +0.17% as underlying shelter trend keeps slowing.
- **Energy pulling headline down:** [REDACTED] estimates headline CPI -0.11% MoM on a 4.4% drop in energy, cutting YoY to 3.87% from 4.25%.
- **Core PCE running hotter than core CPI:** [REDACTED] forecasts +0.24% core PCE for June, lifted by a large financial-services contribution that reflects May's equity gains flowing through with a lag.
- **Consumer spending decelerating:** [REDACTED] sees headline retail sales +0.1% (gasoline drag) with core +0.4%, a step down from the prior firm reads.
- **Fed messaging in focus:** Chairman Warsh's semiannual testimony (House Tuesday, Senate Wednesday) plus a dense speaker lineup, with the Beige Book watched for how firms and consumers respond to higher energy prices from the Middle East conflict.

### Unpacked
**The week's signal is a softer inflation trend colliding with a Fed that is not uniformly convinced.** June core CPI is expected at +0.17% MoM, enough to round YoY down to 2.8%, with soft autos and benign shelter doing the work. Airfares (+1.5%) and hotels (+0.3%) rise more moderately on alternative-data signals, while potential residual seasonality weighs on communication and new cars. Headline falls 0.11% on lower energy, pulling YoY to 3.87%.

The CPI-PCE wedge matters this month. **[REDACTED]'s +0.24% core PCE estimate runs above core CPI, driven by another large financial-services increase tied to May equity gains that reach the component with a lag** — a reminder that the two gauges can diverge on non-consumer-facing inputs.

On the consumer, Thursday's retail sales are expected to cool: headline +0.1% held down by gasoline, with core (ex-autos, gas, building materials) at +0.4% on a still-solid alternative-data signal. Other Friday activity data are steady — industrial production +0.2% on strong autos and electricity but weak natural gas, capacity utilization unchanged at 76.2%, and a sharp housing-starts rebound (+12.5%) after the prior slump.

**The Fed commentary spans the full hawk-dove range, which is the real reason to watch the week.** Dallas's Logan (voter) has flagged that higher rates could be needed later this year; Kansas City's Schmid frames inflation creeping toward 3.5% and openly asks whether to hike a quarter or two; Goolsbee sees the problem clearly on the inflation side of the mandate; and Warsh strikes a softer note, citing lower inflation expectations and AI's potential to expand supply. Williams reiterated an oil-prices-lower baseline over 6–12 months.

The note offers no explicit trade idea; it is a calendar preview with [REDACTED] forecasts attached to each release.

subject: Global Rates Trader: Energy Speedbump
summary:
# Energy Speedbump: Oil Reclaims the Rates Driver's Seat, But Long-End Valuations Are Merely Fair

**Theme:** Oil eclipses AI-issuance as the near-term vol driver; front-end risks the swing factor across G10  
**Markets:** G10 rates  
**Source:** [REDACTED], George Cole, 10 July 2026

### Landscape
- US 10y and 2y yields traded in near-lockstep with Brent through mid-week after renewed US-Iran escalation; long-end forwards have rebounded from "slightly rich" to "about fair."
- ~45bp of Fed hikes priced through early-2027, with Fed uncertainty premium already embedded in upper-left vol.
- 1-month bills remain rich on low seasonal supply and MMF AUM growth, while 3m/6m bills have cheapened vs OIS as money-fund WAM skewed shorter.
- ECB: Z6 pricing oscillating around one more hike (September base case); ~15bp of hikes priced Oct-to-June.
- Foreign official UST demand soft — both TIC and NY Fed custody data show continued net selling, tracking a stronger Dollar.
- JGBs: 10y and 30y rallied ~10bp on Finance Minister Katayama's pension-investment comments; GPIF holds 26.9% domestic bonds vs a 25% target.
- Antipodes: RBA has delivered 75bp of tightening this year; RBNZ delivered its first hike with ~22bp priced for September.

### Drivers
- Oil has re-emerged as the common global rates factor after Iran strikes, tightening the correlation between energy prices and front-end/forward rates across the US, Europe, UK and AUD — the report expects this correlation to weaken where energy passthrough to core inflation stays limited.
- AI-related capex and corporate issuance remain the structural bid for higher yields, but the absence of a clear dislocation between long-end yields and macro/fiscal fair value argues against issuance playing an outsized role right now.
- Dollar strength is a persistent drag on foreign official Treasury demand; FX strategists have revised Dollar forecasts stronger, suggesting the drag continues, though a low-vol Dollar keeps outright selling contained.
- Euro-area liquidity is draining toward a "money market crunch," with more bidders at ECB tenders and reserves nearing preferred levels — but pressure on money-market rates and bases is expected to build only gradually.
- In Japan, fiscal-dominance concerns keep loading risk premium into the long-end; 2s10s and 10y traded inflation have begun to decouple, signalling broader (not just inflation) risk premium is still rising — watch the Basic Policy release this month.

### Risks
- **Downside (to long positions):** stalling disinflation on sticky energy — the European and UK front-end sell-off is flagged as the warning; higher oil leaves markets vulnerable to a firmer US CPI print.
- **Upside (to hike pricing):** re-escalation in Iran would pull forward ECB and precautionary RBA hike pricing.
- **Two-sided (JGBs):** the analyst sees FX intervention as likely and warns it could amplify JGB volatility, since capping JPY depreciation forces rates to act as the pressure-release valve.
- The note frames near-CPI risk as asymmetric — skewed to a firmer print if oil stays elevated — but expects a benign print to compress front-end risks.

### Unpacked
**The week's core message is that recent rate volatility was more about oil than about issuance.** Renewed US-Iran conflict restored energy as the common global factor, with US yields tracking Brent through mid-week. Although a debt-financed investment cycle should push yields up over time, the rebound in long-end forwards from slightly-rich to fair, plus the lack of a clear gap between yields and fundamentals, undercuts the idea that corporate borrowing is currently driving Treasury valuations. Next Tuesday's June CPI is the focus: economists project a 0.17% core increase and a 0.11% headline decline, which should compress front-end risk and erode hike pricing — making limited-downside structures that position for an on-hold Fed sensible carry expressions.

**At the very front, policy uncertainty is the swing factor for bill valuations.** 1m bills stay rich on low supply and MMF growth, while shorter money-fund WAM has cheapened 3m/6m bills — one day shorter WAM richens 1m by ~0.3bp and cheapens 3m/6m by ~0.1bp vs OIS. Heavier summer supply is a headwind, but growing money-fund AUM and a patient SOMA stance should keep cheapening pressure contained.

**In Canada, the USMCA annual-review decision removed the worst escalation fears without clarifying the outlook**, likely keeping the BoC on hold through the year (normalization expected only in 2H27). This should steepen the CAD curve as markets look to eventual normalization. The 2s5s steepener is closed for a potential 9bp gain including carry and rolled into a 2s10s steepener (entry 53bp, target 80bp, stop 40bp), with underperformance expected to be led by 5y5y.

**Europe's front-end rally stalled abruptly as Iran pushed energy higher, cutting against the "ECB may pass on hikes" narrative.** Front-end flatteners are preferred and work across scenarios — re-escalation pulls hikes forward, while gradual disinflation erodes cumulative hike pricing — but they should be paired against short 2y2y to neutralise bear-steepening risk from elevated long-end yields (equivalently, EUR OIS 2y2y vs 1y1y steepeners). On France, OAT weakness on election fears looks premature: the 3y BTP/Bono/OAT long vs OIS was stopped out and closed for a small carry gain, but with the presidential election distant, imprecise polls, and small policy differences between RN candidates relative to France's fiscal scale, risk-reward for OAT shorts is judged poor and carry should dictate returns.

**In the UK, the front-end repriced on energy but is expected to rally back**, with the sell-off likely exacerbated by long positioning. The curve should keep steepening since the bar for BoE hikes is unlikely to be met while fiscal challenges persist; sticky risk premium is better expressed in curve trades than in Gilts on asset swap. Leverage-ratio changes free up ~£150bn of bank balance-sheet capacity but only ~£2-3bn of direct Gilt buying — the indirect extension of leverage to the broader system offers more support, with long-Gilt asset-swap carry reasonable in 5y and 10y.

**Japan stands apart from G3: its curve keeps steepening on fiscal-dominance concerns while others flatten.** GPIF greater demand could support JGBs from an NIIP angle, but this year's cheapening looks macro-led rather than supply-driven — 30y bonds cheapened even as long-end swap spreads widened on Lifer buying. A GPIF shift would therefore more likely help 30s than the belly, where macro volatility now dominates. With JPY weakening and intervention likely, rates remain the release valve, and the market seems set to keep adding long-end risk premium.

**In Australia and New Zealand, the oil-driven rise in forward rates is seen as an opportunity rather than a signal.** With limited energy passthrough and 75bp of RBA tightening already delivered, the oil/forward-rate correlation should weaken; the receive AUD 2y1y vs pay Aug RBA trade was stopped out, but energy-driven sell-offs are viewed as a chance to re-add longs further out and to pay near-term meetings. In New Zealand, the RBNZ began a two-hike mini-cycle; at 22bp priced, paying September is poor risk-reward, so the preference is fading hike premium above one hike, and the NZD 2s10s steepener is maintained.

subject: US Daily: June CPI Preview
summary:
# June Core CPI to Undershoot Consensus on Soft Autos and Cooling Shelter

**Theme:** Below-consensus core print as autos, shelter, and travel all decelerate  
**Markets:** US inflation  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jessica Rindels, 9 July 2026  

### Estimates
- **+0.17% m/m core CPI** in June (vs. +0.3% consensus), taking the y/y rate to **+2.76%** (vs. +2.9% consensus).
- **-0.11% m/m headline CPI** (vs. -0.1% consensus), with food +0.3% and energy -4.4% on lower retail gasoline; y/y **+3.87%** (vs. +3.9% consensus and +4.25% in May).
- **+0.24% m/m core PCE** implied for June, lifted by a sharp rise in the financial services component (+0.04pp) as May's equity gains feed through with a lag.
- **Autos:** used cars -0.5%, new cars -0.1%, auto insurance -0.1%.
- **Shelter:** OER +0.23%, rent +0.17%.
- **Travel:** airfares +1.5% (vs. +2.8% two-month average), hotels +0.3% (vs. +1.7%).
- **Path:** core CPI near +0.2% m/m over the next couple of months.

### Outlook
- Core inflation should hold around 0.2% m/m near term, on continued shelter deceleration and the reversal of jet-fuel and World Cup pressure in travel services.
- Risks skew to the upside if oil-market disruptions and higher oil prices prove more persistent than assumed.

### Unpacked
The June call sits well below consensus on core, driven by broad-based softness rather than a single category. **Weak autos anchor the forecast — used car auction prices point to a 0.5% drop, rising incentives pull new car prices down 0.1%, and online data show insurance premiums easing.** The headline decline is a separate, energy-led story, with a 4.4% fall in energy offsetting firmer food prices.

**Shelter is expected to normalize after two noisy months**, with OER at +0.23% and rent at +0.17%. April's spike reflected the unwind of last year's government-shutdown bias, and May's above-trend reading was concentrated in the Northeast — likely statistical noise rather than a genuine reacceleration in the underlying trend.

Travel services are the swing factor. **Airfares and hotels both moderate this month, but the drivers point in opposite directions going forward.** Airfares still carry some passthrough from higher oil since the start of the Iran war, while hotels are already coming off their World Cup boost, which shows up early because rates are measured at time of booking. Residual seasonality adds a further drag, with new cars and communications having averaged declines of 0.1% and 0.2% in recent Junes.

**The near-term picture is one of a softer trend, with the main upside risk external: a more persistent oil shock.** Beyond that, the read-through to core PCE is higher than the CPI print alone would suggest, since the financial services component tracks equity prices with a lag — worth watching for readers focused on the Fed's preferred gauge.

subject: USA: Existing Home Sales Decline
summary:
# USA: Existing Home Sales Slip on Affordability Sensitivity, With Thin Inventory Still Pointing to Price Risk

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US existing home sales, June 2026  
**General comment:** Neutral data read-through; a soft print but growth tracking left unchanged.

### Context
June existing home sales came in against expectations for a modest gain, feeding the ongoing debate over how sensitive US housing demand is to small moves in mortgage rates and how tight supply shapes prices.

### The case
- **Sales fell 2.4% to a 4.09mn annualized rate, missing both the [REDACTED] call (+2.5%, 4.27mn) and the median forecast (+1.0%, 4.20mn), even as May was revised up 0.5pp to +3.7%.** The decline was broad: single-family (-2.4%) and condos/co-ops (-2.7%) both fell, and three of four regions dropped — South (-3.6%), Midwest (-3.0%), West (-1.3%) — with only the Northeast up (+2.1%). The report frames this as evidence that the month-to-month swings, driven by mild fluctuations in mortgage rates, show how sensitive buyers are to affordability.
- **Prices remain firm and supply-demand balance is unchanged, keeping upside price risk in play.** The median price rose 0.1% m/m (SA by [REDACTED]), an +1.8% y/y pace, while months' supply held at 4.3. The key distinction drawn is that without consistent gains in inventory, prices can accelerate — thin supply, not demand strength, is the pressure point.
- **The macro read-through is muted.** The soft print does not shift the growth picture: the Q2 GDP tracking estimate is left at +2.2% (q/q annualized) and Q2 domestic final sales at +2.0%.

### Implications
- Housing activity stays hostage to affordability; further volatility should be expected as mortgage rates wobble.
- The binding constraint on prices is inventory, not demand — a risk of renewed price acceleration if supply fails to build.
- No signal for the broader growth trajectory: Q2 tracking is unchanged.

subject: USA: Jobless Claims in Line With Consensus Expectations
summary:
# US Jobless Claims Land on Consensus, Signalling a Steady Labor Market

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US weekly jobless claims  
**General comment:** Neutral data readout; a non-event that matches consensus and points to no change in labor-market conditions.

### Context
A routine post-release note on the Department of Labor's weekly jobless claims for early July 2026. The prints matter only as a high-frequency read on whether the labor market is loosening.

### The case
- **Initial claims came in essentially flat and on consensus.** They ticked down 2k to 215k in the week ended July 4, from a prior week revised up 2k to 217k. That was close to the median forecast of 217k and slightly below [REDACTED]'s own 225k call. The four-week moving average — the smoother read — fell 4k to 219k, consistent with no deterioration in layoffs.
- **Continuing claims edged up but also matched expectations.** They rose 8k to 1,814k in the week ended June 27, hitting the median forecast exactly, from a prior level revised down 8k to 1,806k. The small offsetting revision leaves the underlying level of people collecting benefits broadly unchanged.

### Implications
- Nothing in the data shifts the labor-market picture: both series landed on consensus, so the release carries no new signal for the Fed or rate expectations.
- With claims low and the moving average declining, there is no sign of rising layoffs or of a stalling in re-employment for those already on benefits.

subject: USA: FOMC Minutes Note Participants Would Support Unchanged or Lower Rates if Inflation Dissipates “Soon” but Higher Rates if Inflation Remains Elevated
summary:
# FOMC rules out cuts for now and signals the next step hinges on whether inflation comes down "soon"

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** Federal Reserve / US monetary policy  
**General comment:** Reading of the June FOMC minutes; base case stays for rates on hold in 2026, in line with consensus, but flags two-sided risk skewed toward hikes.

### Context
The June FOMC minutes were released while the fed funds rate sits at 3.5–3.75%, with core inflation still well above target. The debate is whether the Fed's next move is a cut or a hike — and the minutes frame that explicitly as conditional on the inflation path.

### The case
- **The Fed held unanimously in June, but the committee is no longer uniformly patient.** "All" participants backed keeping the rate at 3.5–3.75%, yet "a few" judged there was already "a case" for a hike — a hawkish tail within an otherwise unanimous hold.
- **The next move is explicitly state-contingent on the inflation path, and symmetric.** In scenarios where inflation dissipates and returns "soon" to 2%, "almost all" participants would maintain or eventually lower rates; in scenarios where inflation stays elevated — driven by AI-related demand, the Middle East conflict, or tariffs — "almost all" would favor "some policy firming." The reaction function is thus two-sided, with the trigger being how quickly inflation fades.
- **The inflation read has broadened and firmed, which underpins the hawkish contingency.** Participants saw inflation "increased further and remained well above" 2%, with "several" flagging that pressures had become more broad-based (transportation, airfares, petrochemicals, agricultural inputs) and that non-housing services inflation "remained high." Above-potential growth from strong AI-related investment was seen by "most" as a source of more persistent pressure.
- **The labor market is not the problem.** Activity is growing at a "solid" pace on AI-driven business investment, and "many" participants explicitly noted the labor market is "not currently a source of inflationary pressures." Consumer spending has been supported by higher equity prices and earlier tax refunds, concentrated among higher-income households — so the inflation concern is not a wage-price story.
- **Fed staff see inflation as sticky near-term, easing only later.** The staff raised its inflation forecast versus April on incoming data, higher energy prices, and AI effects, expecting core to "change little" this year, step down next year, and reach "about 2 percent" only in 2028, with unemployment near its longer-run rate until edging slightly below in 2028.

### Implications
- Base case: the FOMC keeps the policy rate unchanged through 2026, though there is genuine risk of hikes this year given the hawkish tail and the elevated-inflation contingency.
- The [REDACTED] forecast is more constructive on disinflation than the staff's: core PCE to 3.0% by December 2026 (from 3.4%, partly on BEA methodological changes) and core CPI to 2.6% (from 2.9%), with tame monthly core CPI prints expected near-term.
- Watch the coming inflation prints as the pivotal variable — a fast enough deceleration keeps cuts on the table, while persistence flips the committee toward firming.

subject: USA: [REDACTED] Economic Indicators Update
summary:
# US: Financial Conditions Marginally Tighter, Activity Stable at +2.6%

**Theme:** weekly reading of proprietary indicators; economy showing no inflection  
**Markets:** US macro  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jan Hatzius, 8 jul 2026  

### Landscape
- The nominal FCI tightened 2.3bp on the week, to 98.45, driven mainly by a higher 10-year Treasury yield.
- The real FCI tightened 1.2bp, to 98.17.
- The June Current Activity Indicator stood at +2.6%, stable versus May's +2.6%.
- Q2 GDP forecast at +2.2% (quarterly annualized).
- The MAP index of economic surprises fell on net to +0.1, close to neutral.

### Drivers
- The tightening in financial conditions comes entirely from the rates side — the 10-year yield rose on the week, while the real and nominal components moved in the same direction, a sign that the impulse is coming from rates rather than credit or FX.
- Current activity remains flat: the CAI repeated +2.6% from May to June, with neither acceleration nor deceleration in the latest data.
- Economic surprises have essentially flatlined (+0.1 on the MAP), indicating data coming in line with consensus and little pressure to revise forecasts.

### Unpacked
This is a periodic update of the bank's proprietary indicators, with no central thesis — the value lies in the current scoreboard. **The aggregate message is one of stability: growth around 2%-2.6%, financial conditions nearly unchanged, and data coming in line with expectations.**

**The Q2 GDP forecast of +2.2% annualized is consistent with the June Current Activity Indicator of +2.6%, both pointing to moderate expansion with no sign of inflection.** The slight tightening in the FCI, concentrated at the long end of the yield curve, is too small to alter this reading.

The report also includes a set of trackers — capex, labor-market slack and job creation, ISM manufacturing and services surveys, wages, core inflation, and social-media economic sentiment — presented only as exhibits, with no values or commentary in the text. There is no explicit trade idea and no risks flagged; it is a monitoring document, not a recommendation.

subject: USA: Trade Deficit Slightly Below Expectations
summary:
# US: trade deficit widens in May, but comes in below expectations and doesn't alter the GDP trajectory

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US trade balance, May 2026  
**General comment:** Neutral read-through; a wider headline deficit that [REDACTED] treats as GDP-neutral, leaving its Q2 tracking unchanged.

### Context
Commentary on the May US trade data released 7 July 2026. The headline deficit widened sharply but came in slightly narrower than the consensus and [REDACTED] forecasts, so the piece focuses on what the move means for Q2 growth tracking.

### The case
- **The deficit widened by $23.0bn to $77.6bn, still slightly below expectations.** The gap came in narrower than the $78.4bn median forecast and [REDACTED]'s own $78.5bn, though the prior month was revised to a much smaller $54.6bn deficit. The widening was driven by goods: imports rose $12.3bn to $317.0bn — the highest level outside Q1 2025 — on broad-based gains across industrial supplies, capital goods and consumer goods, while goods exports fell $11.3bn, mostly on lower nonmonetary gold and computers/electronics. The services surplus edged up $0.6bn.
- **The headline move overstates the hit to growth once gold and oil are stripped out.** US oil exports have risen notably since the start of the Iran war, but much of that increase reflects drawdowns of commercial inventories and the Strategic Petroleum Reserve rather than new production — which implies a broadly neutral GDP impact. Excluding gold (which is not counted in GDP) and the recent oil-export rise, the underlying deficit actually widened more, to $99.3bn in May from $84.3bn in April.
- **Growth tracking is unchanged despite the wider gap.** Because the distortions net out for national-accounts purposes, the data did not move [REDACTED]'s estimates: the Q2 GDP tracking forecast stays at +2.2% annualized and Q2 domestic final sales at +2.0%.

### Implications
- No signal for the Q2 growth call: the report is treated as neutral, leaving the +2.2% GDP and +2.0% final-sales tracking intact.
- Headline trade figures are being distorted by gold flows and war-driven oil exports; the cleaner underlying deficit is both larger and deteriorating, worth watching for later-quarter net-export drag.

subject: US Economics Weekly Update 7/6/2026
summary:
# Labor Market in Balance, Fed's Eyes Turn to Inflation

**Theme:** Neutral jobs data clears the path for an inflation-driven Fed decision  
**Markets:** US macro / economics  
**Source:** [REDACTED], David Mericle, 7 July 2026  

### Landscape
- Wage growth ran at 3.4% over the past year, below the 4% pace seen as compatible with 2% inflation given above-2% productivity this cycle.
- Three-month average payroll growth stood at 111k, with underlying trend job growth estimated at 74k — above the 60k breakeven rate.
- Q2 GDP tracking was cut 0.1pp last week to 2.1%; full-year growth is now pegged at 2% / 2% / 2.1% / 2.1% across Q1–Q4.
- Factory orders fell 1.3% in May, core capital goods shipments rose 0.1%, and real construction spending rose 0.2%.

### Drivers
- The labor market reads as neither too hot nor too cold, leaving Fed officials little reason for concern in either direction and free to focus on incoming inflation data — which is expected to come in cooler than recent months.
- Chairman Kevin Warsh signaled that inflation expectations and inflation risks have come down, and framed AI's near-term inflationary pressure as outweighed by its potential medium-run disinflationary supply-side effects.
- Housing is set to cool: residential investment is expected to fall a bit more than 3% Q4/Q4 in 2026, with home prices up just 0.8% this year and rent growth slowing from 3.2% now to 2.2% by end-2027.
- AI's productivity payoff is building but gradual, with first gains expected in information, professional services, insurance, and finance.

### Risks
- Upside (rates): Dallas Fed's Logan previously said higher rates "could be necessary later this year" to restore price stability — but the note flags this view is over a month old and predates the US-Iran agreement, tempering its weight.
- The note frames the near-term Fed question as whether to hike, not cut, leaving the policy risk tilted toward tightening rather than easing.

### Unpacked
The week's central takeaway is a labor market in balance. With wage growth contained and job creation running above breakeven but not overheating, **the June employment report removes the labor market as a source of pressure in either direction, shifting the Fed's decision entirely onto the inflation data.** That data is expected to soften, which matters because the framing of the upcoming decision is whether or not to hike.

Fed communication reinforced a benign inflation read. Warsh's remarks that expectations and risks have both come down, together with his pivot toward AI's disinflationary supply-side potential, point away from near-term urgency. He also hinted the dot plot could eventually be phased out, with a task force reviewing the question. Among this week's speakers, Waller offered no signal, Williams has described policy as "well positioned" to return inflation to 2%, and Logan's more hawkish stance carries the caveat noted above.

On housing, the forecast is for a broad-based cooling. **Residential investment is expected to decline more than 3% Q4/Q4 in 2026, driven by weak demographics and strained affordability on the demand side, a more normal supply-demand balance reducing the incentive to build, and higher mortgage rates depressing turnover and brokerage fees.** Home prices are seen rising 0.8% this year and 2.3% next, with rent growth easing to 2.9% by end-2026 and 2.2% by end-2027.

The AI-productivity piece draws directly on the ICT experience. That earlier revolution took time to lift economywide productivity because component costs were high, network effects needed critical-mass adoption, and organizational change required investment in intangible capital. **AI's impact is expected sooner — costs are falling faster and network effects matter less — but reorganizing work processes will again take time.** As with ICT, which first showed up in the industries that invested earliest and reorganized most, a composite exposure-and-adoption index points to information, professional services, insurance, and finance as the first beneficiaries.

The note offers no explicit trade idea.

subject: Global Rates Trader: Oil Relief Gets Real
summary:
# Oil Relief Restores Duration's Hedge Role; Anchor Rate Longs Slightly Out the Curve

**Theme:** Falling energy prices ease inflation risk across G10, reshaping front-end positioning as central-bank uncertainty shifts from macro to reaction function  
**Markets:** Developed-market rates (US, Canada, Euro area, UK, Australia)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], George Cole, 26 June 2026  

### Definitive impacts
- BoC hike premium for this year has compressed to about 12bp, with a generalized reset across the CAD forward curve, as oil prices fell.
- RBA market pricing has moderated to less than 50% of a hike through the year-end peak in the curve; Australia's unemployment rate sits below the RBA's NAIRU estimate.
- The market now trades below [REDACTED]'s 3% end-2026 Bund yield forecast.
- US implied vol has settled above pre-conflict levels but sits toward the lower end of [REDACTED]'s fair-value range, with risk premium concentrated at shorter tails; 1y-tail vol is rich to macro and to [REDACTED]'s vol-surface PCA, while belly-tenor vol is low versus the wings.
- Most of the recent decline in 10y Gilt yields has come from term-premium compression rather than shifting rate expectations.
- US funding conditions are accommodative: money-fund AUM keeps growing, weighted-average maturity has shortened (1m Bills-OIS tightening), and levered-fund shorts are dwindling as Treasury futures basis opportunities compress.
- ECB facility usage remains low, at roughly EUR15bn under the MRO, consistent with abundant Euro-area liquidity.

### Opinative impacts
- **[REDACTED] favors US rate longs anchored slightly out from the very front end (1y1y or 2y1y), or around the 5y spot point** — firmer data likely front-loads hike risk while forwards stay stickier, giving better near-term asymmetry.
- **[REDACTED] expects July Fed pricing to decay absent clearly strong data**, and sees the Z6 probability mass building around an on-hold outcome; it warns against downgrading labor-market data despite the June FOMC's price-stability focus.
- **[REDACTED] sees scope to return to vol selling**, especially if moderating hiring and inflation data let hawkish momentum decay gradually; it expects a flatter tail curve as uncertainty shifts to the Fed's reaction function.
- [REDACTED] expects US swap spreads to stay wide, preferring 3y swap spreads for carry-to-vol and insulation from balance-sheet risk; a more serious Fed debate on the ample-reserves framework is a medium-term risk to belly/long-end spreads.
- [REDACTED] thinks remaining CAD hike premium should decay and front-end yields can fall toward pre-conflict levels, with a passed July 1 USMCA deadline keeping trade risk (and easing risk) in view.
- [REDACTED] expects European rate vol to fall rather than yield levels, and to underperform US vol; it prefers 5y EGB outperformance given the ECB's hawkish bias and a forecast September hike.
- [REDACTED] views the Solvency II review as a net tailwind for long-dated sovereign credit, boosting insurer demand and rate hedging past the 20y point.
- [REDACTED] prefers GBP steepeners (1y1y outperformance) as BoE-hold confidence builds and front-end real rates normalize lower; it expects term premium to persist ahead of the Autumn budget, with Andy Burnham the likely next PM.
- [REDACTED] keeps a bias to hold JGB pressure on the belly given unresolved domestic risks despite cheap valuations.

### At issue
Continued declines in oil prices — extended this week as shipping flows through the Strait of Hormuz recovered following the US-Iran deal — have curtailed inflation upside across G10. In the US, the hawkish front-end repricing has held despite the energy move, but near-term real rates are participating in rallies again, front-end skew has rotated back toward receivers, and Fed pricing has eased from hawkish extremes. The June FOMC signaled awareness of inflation risk without urgency to hike. This is the standing [REDACTED] Global Rates Trader publication, which pairs regional rate assessments with trade recommendations.

**Explicit trade idea:** receive 2y1y OIS vs pay August RBA (entry −18bp, target −35bp, stop −10bp).

### Backdrop
Since a geopolitical energy shock earlier in the year, elevated oil prices had lifted inflation risk premium and pushed G10 rates markets to price hawkish central-bank paths. An April ceasefire began decoupling European rates volatility from yield levels; the subsequent US-Iran deal and Hormuz normalization have extended that energy relief. European rates volatility and the ECB path are driven more narrowly by energy uncertainty than the broader macro drivers in the US, which conditions the relative-vol view.

The EU's Solvency II review — to be implemented by 31 January 2027 — aims to steer insurers toward the real economy (a rising equity allocation over time), but also revises risk-free-rate methodology, the Volatility Adjustment mechanism, and rate/credit-spread correlation parameters in ways relevant to sovereign-bond demand.

### Unpacked
The through-line is that lower oil has changed the *character* of rates risk more than its level. **With inflation and growth risks now co-moving rather than pulling against each other, nominal duration has recovered its role as a risk-asset hedge** — which is why receivers, real rates, and moderated Fed pricing all move together. The positioning conclusion follows from reaction-function uncertainty rather than a directional yield call: because near-term hike risk stays sticky after last week's signal, the cleaner expression is to sit slightly out the curve where forwards are stickier and firmer data front-loads the risk.

**The same logic reframes volatility as the more attractive variable than direction.** Front-end steepness historically lets implied vol undershoot macro fundamentals, and as supply-side risk and macro uncertainty fade, [REDACTED] expects the vol premium to keep compressing — favoring vol selling and a flatter tail curve as the locus of uncertainty moves to how the Fed reacts rather than to the macro itself.

Funding and supply dynamics reinforce the constructive carry backdrop. Easy Treasury funding — ample money-fund cash against subdued levered demand — gives the market a buffer to absorb rising cash demand without funding stress, though quarter-end repo pressure and eventual balance-sheet-policy debate are the caveats. In Europe, the analogous risk is that equity-IPO-driven funding pressure spills into Bund spreads, as it did in H2 2024 when Bund spreads cheapened ~15bp beyond fair value over six months; the context differs now (QT no longer accelerating, spreads cheaper), but it is flagged as worth watching as QT drains liquidity into 2027.

The regional calls share one structure but differ in curve expression. **The US and Euro area favor the belly; the UK favors steepeners as front-end real rates normalize lower; Canada and Australia carry residual hike premium that [REDACTED] expects to decay, tilting balance-of-risk toward eventual cuts.** Japan is the outlier — cheap but pressured by unresolved domestic risk. Across all, the message is that energy relief lowers volatility and hedging cost more than it lowers yields.

subject: Global Markets Comment: Market Stress Monitor — 7 July 2026
summary:
# Market Stress Benign, With Only a Marginal Uptick From Very Low Levels

**Theme:** Market function and microstructure across asset classes  
**Markets:** Global cross-asset (DM credit, rates, equities, EM)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], William Marshall, 6 July 2026  

### Landscape
- Broad market-stress measures have deteriorated very slightly over the past month but remain very benign versus historic norms, as of the 3 July snapshot.
- Rates microstructure has improved after a brief drop in market depth in April and May, with yield sensitivity to orderflow declining again.
- Funding costs have continued to ease, supporting wider swap spreads.
- Sovereign spreads have widened slightly from conflict-driven tights.
- Equity bid-ask spreads have moved broadly sideways in the US and Europe over the month; UK spreads have widened slightly from their tights.
- Equity funding spreads have reversed part of their recent widening but stay elevated on a longer lookback.

### Drivers
- Easing funding costs are the main supportive force in rates, feeding through to wider swap spreads.
- Recovering rates market depth has pulled yield sensitivity to orderflow back down after the spring dip.
- A modest widening in sovereign spreads reflects normalization away from conflict-tights rather than fresh stress.
- Equity funding pressure is partially unwinding but remains high relative to its longer history — a mixed signal rather than a clean improvement.

### Unpacked
**The overall message is one of calm: the aggregate stress index sits at very low levels by historical standards, and the small month-on-month deterioration does not change that picture.** The report constructs its indices by normalizing stress indicators within each market segment against full-sample averages, averaging across indicators in a category, and then averaging categories into an aggregate, all shown as 3-day moving averages with levels as of 3 July.

**In rates, the story is one of repair after a spring wobble.** Market depth dropped briefly in April and May, but microstructure measures have since improved and the sensitivity of yields to orderflow has fallen again. Alongside this, funding costs have kept easing, which has supported a widening in swap spreads, while sovereign spreads have edged wider from levels compressed during the earlier conflict episode.

**In equities, the picture is flatter and more mixed.** Bid-ask spreads have been broadly sideways in the US and Europe over the past month, with only the UK showing a slight widening from its tights. Equity funding spreads have given back part of their recent widening but remain elevated when viewed over a longer window, leaving that one measure as the notable outlier against an otherwise benign backdrop.

The note is a monitor built around charts and normalized indices rather than a trade recommendation, and it offers no explicit trade idea.

subject: USA: Trade Deficit Widens by More Than Expected in May; Lowering Q2 GDP Tracking Estimate to 2.2%
summary:
# EUA: déficit comercial de bens surpreende no mês e derruba o tracking do PIB do 2T para 2,2%

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US trade balance and Q2 GDP tracking  
**General comment:** Neutral data read; a modest, mechanical downgrade to the growth tracking, not a change in view.

### Context
Comment on the May Advance Economic Indicators Report. The advance goods trade balance came in at -$105.8bn, far wider than [REDACTED]'s -$84.0bn and the -$85.0bn median forecast, prompting a revision to the Q2 GDP tracking estimate.

### The case
- **The goods trade deficit widened much more than expected in May, driven by both sides of the ledger.** The seasonally adjusted deficit widened by $22.7bn to $105.8bn. Goods exports fell $11.8bn, led by declines in industrial supplies and capital goods, while goods imports rose $10.9bn, led by consumer goods, industrial supplies and autos. Wider net trade subtracts from GDP.
- **On net, the report's details came in softer than the prior tracking assumptions.** The combination of the wider trade gap and the underlying inventory/trade detail was enough to lower the Q2 GDP estimate, though domestic demand is treated separately (see below).

### Implications
- Q2 GDP tracking cut by 0.2pp to +2.2% quarter-over-quarter annualized.
- The Q2 domestic final sales estimate — a cleaner read on underlying demand, stripping out trade and inventory swings — stands at +1.9%, signaling the downgrade is driven by net trade rather than softer domestic demand.

subject: USA: ISM Services in Line With Expectations
summary:
# US: June Services ISM Comes in Exactly at Expectations, With Mixed Composition

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US services activity (June 2026 ISM/PMI)  
**General comment:** Descriptive and neutral reading of a print in line with consensus; no directional bias of its own.

### Context
Commentary on the release of the June 2026 services ISM and the final reading of the S&P Global US services PMI for the same month, both used to gauge the pace of the US services sector.

### The points
- **The services ISM index fell 0.5pt to 54.0, exactly in line with the house forecast, consensus, and the median projection.** The composition was mixed: declines in new orders (-2.2pt, to 55.1) and business activity (-2.3pt, to 55.4), offset by a rise in employment (+3.3pt, to 51.2). Supplier deliveries fell 0.8pt (54.4), new export orders rose 0.4pt (50.4), and imports fell 1.7pt (49.4). Prices paid fell 3.6pt, to 67.7 — still above the pre-war level of 63.0 in February, but in line with the H2 2025 range.
- **The release points to specific sectoral pressures and reliefs.** There were fewer reports of impact from petroleum-derivative prices and signs that "supply chains are stabilizing amid sustained activity," though "tariff impact" remains a theme. Supply pressures persist in AI-related commodities needed for data-center construction. The rise in employment was attributed, at least in part, to World-Cup-related hiring.
- **The final reading of the S&P Global US services PMI was revised 0.1pt lower, to 51.2.** The revisions were all marginally negative: new business (-0.1pt, to 51.2), employment (-0.1pt, to 49.4), input prices (-0.1pt, to 59.9), and output prices (-0.4pt, to 57.8).

### Implications
- The services sector remains in expansion (ISM above 50), but at a slightly weaker pace, with demand (new orders and activity) losing steam while employment surprises to the upside — part of this possibly temporary (World Cup).
- The decline in prices paid suggests cost relief, even though the level remains elevated; tariffs remain a source of pressure to monitor.

subject: USA: Core PCE in Line With Expectations; Q1 GDP Revised Up to +2.1% on Lower Imports and Higher Inventories; Core Durable Goods Orders Above Expectations; Lowering Q2 GDP Tracking Estimate to +2.4%
summary:
# US: Core PCE in line, Q1 GDP revised to +2.1% on imports and inventories, and capital goods beat expectations

**Theme:** End-of-month data dump — inflation with no surprise, GDP composition shifts to trade and inventories, capex firm  
**Markets:** US macro (activity, inflation, labor market)  
**Source:** [REDACTED] (Jan Hatzius), 25 Jun 2026

### Landscape
- Core PCE rose 0.32% in May (in line), with the year-over-year rate advancing to 3.41%; headline PCE rose 0.45% in the month and 4.07% over 12 months.
- Dallas Fed trimmed mean estimated at +0.23% in the month and +2.42% over 12 months.
- Q1 GDP (third estimate) revised to +2.1% annualized, from +1.6% previously and from [REDACTED]'s own estimate.
- Q1 personal consumption revised down to just +0.5% annualized, from +1.4% previously; real final domestic sales at +2.2%.
- May personal income (+0.7%) and personal spending (+0.7%) above consensus; the savings rate steady at 3.0% (revised up).
- Durable goods orders fell 4.5% in May, but ex-transportation (+1.3%) and core capital goods (+1.6%) surprised to the upside.
- Initial jobless claims at 215k (below expectations); continuing claims at 1,821k, slightly above.

### Drivers
- Q1 GDP composition shifted axis: imports revised down by 9.3pp (+11.8%) lifted net trade's contribution by 0.9pp, with another 0.1pp from inventories — a gain offset by weaker consumption.
- Consumption is weakening at the margin: real spending of +0.3% in May, but downward revisions to prior months pulled down Q1 consumption and lifted savings; real disposable income flat over 12 months.
- Capex resilient: core capital goods above expectations in May, with April revised up from -0.7%; Q1 business fixed investment revised up to +10.6%.
- May income was inflated by a temporary factor: 0.2pp came from the second round of the Farmer Bridge Assistance program.
- The labor market remains firm on the initial claims side, though the four-week average and continuing claims continue to drift slightly higher.

### Unpacked
The report is a data note, not a thesis: it consolidates various May releases and updates the Q2 tracking estimate. **On inflation, nothing changes the picture — core PCE came in line, and the acceleration in the annual rate to 3.41% reflects base effects, not a monthly surprise.** The April revision was minimal (+0.01pp, to 0.25%), and the Dallas Fed trimmed mean estimate of 2.42% suggests underlying core inflation remains well above target.

**The upward revision to Q1 GDP, to +2.1%, is low quality: the gain came from lower imports and higher inventories, not domestic demand.** Real final domestic sales were actually revised down 0.5pp, to +2.2%, with consumption cut 0.9pp — driven by travel and financial services — and residential investment down 1.5pp, to -7.8%. Offsetting that, business fixed investment rose to +10.6%, keeping capex as a bright spot.

May income and spending data came in above consensus, but with caveats. **Part of the strength in income is temporary, and the savings rate only held at 3.0% because consumption in prior months was revised down.** In real terms, spending advanced 0.3%, with goods outpacing services.

**On the industrial side, core orders surprised to the upside and reinforce the read of firm capex, despite the 4.5% drop in the durables headline.** That decline was concentrated in commercial aircraft, following a strong April gain — noise, not trend. Core capital goods rose 1.6% and had April revised up, even though shipments (+0.3%) came in below expectations.

On jobless claims, initial claims fell to 215k, a sign the labor market remains tight, but the four-week average and continuing claims rose marginally. **On balance, the Q2 GDP tracker fell 0.1pp, to +2.4% annualized, with final domestic sales at +1.8% — activity around trend, with no explicit trade idea in the note.**

subject: US Economics Analyst: Mid-Year Housing Outlook: Stabilizing but Subdued
summary:
# US Housing at Mid-2026: Stabilizing at a Subdued, Rate-Locked Equilibrium

**Theme:** High mortgage rates freezing turnover while supply-demand normalizes and shelter disinflation resumes  
**Markets:** US housing and shelter inflation  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Ronnie Walker, 6 July 2026  

### Landscape
- Residential fixed investment fell an estimated 5% annualized in Q2 after an 8% annualized drop in Q1, hit by poor weather and a rebound in mortgage rates.
- Mortgage rates sit at 6.43%, up sharply since March on the Iran War, higher oil prices, and Fed-hike fears.
- Almost 80% of mortgage borrowers hold rates below current market rates and nearly 60% are more than 2pp below — the core of the "lock-in" effect.
- Single-family starts are down 2% year-to-date but still average 4% above 2019 levels despite mortgage rates 3pp higher.
- The multifamily under-construction backlog has fallen 33% from its peak but remains 9% above 2019.
- New-lease rent growth has slowed to around +1% from a 2022 peak of +12–13%; the rental vacancy rate has risen from a 5.6% trough to 7.3%.
- PCE shelter inflation is 3.2% year-on-year, with the monthly pace already down to 0.23% in Q1 from a 0.76% peak in 2022.

### Drivers
- **Rate lock-in** is the dominant force and is stable: it holds existing home sales near 4.2mn in 2026 (22% below 2019), with only a modest lift to ~4.3mn in 2027 as rates edge down and the effect naturally decays.
- **The housing shortage** still supports single-family building but is fading as supply-demand balances normalize and builder margins compress back to pre-pandemic levels; starts are forecast at 0.92mn in 2026 (vs 0.94mn in 2025).
- **Housing demand** is tepid and roughly flat: supportive domestic demographics and improved purchase intentions are offset by weak income growth and reduced immigration, leaving household formation near 1.0mn/year, below trend.
- **Multifamily construction** is still contracting but decelerating, as developers clear the remaining backlog before starting new projects; the backlog should return to pre-pandemic levels next year.
- **Shelter disinflation** is resuming as elevated completions and softer demand push rental vacancies up and cap new-lease rents; watch new-lease growth, which the model sees running 2–3% annualized, somewhat below the pre-pandemic pace.

### Risks
- **Downside to supply:** the analyst flags immigration slowdown as weighing slightly more on demand than supply — states with larger immigration slowdowns saw weaker sales, building, and prices, though the price relationship has only borderline statistical significance and no meaningful link to vacancy rates was found.
- **Upside to shelter inflation persistence:** because official measures capture continuing leases and only a modest share of tenants move each year, the analyst notes the official rate cannot fully converge to the ~1% new-lease pace, keeping disinflation gradual.

### Unpacked
The forecast rests almost entirely on the mortgage-rate path. **Strategists expect rates to stay elevated near today's 6.43% through year-end before easing only to 6.3% by end-2027, reflecting a dovish Fed call** — not enough to unlock the frozen resale market. The lock-in effect matters for GDP beyond turnover itself, since existing home sales feed residential investment through brokers' commissions, which carry a 15% weight in RFI. A rebound in sales adds little to net supply, as households mostly swap between existing units.

On single-family, the improvement in available supply and the compression of builder margins have produced a measured slowdown rather than a slump, with starts ending the year around a 0.93mn annualized pace — a view broadly consistent with equity-analyst delivery expectations that proxy corporate guidance. **The combination of still-solid supply growth and slightly weaker demand should push the homeowner vacancy rate from 1.1% in Q1 2026 to 1.2% by Q4 and 1.3% in 2027, holding national home price growth to just 0.8% December-over-December this year and 2.3% next year.**

The immigration question receives extended treatment. The muted supply hit is less surprising than it looks: prior metro-level work found lower immigration puts downward pressure on rents because short-run housing supply is inelastic, and the shortage of residential construction workers has sharply eased over the last two years, blunting the labor-supply channel that once made the sector vulnerable.

Multifamily is the clearest drag. **With completions still near multi-decade highs and absorption poor, starts are forecast at 0.43mn in 2026 (vs 0.41mn in 2025), leaving total starts roughly flat at 1.35mn versus 1.36mn in 2025.** Softer demand and heavy completions keep pressure on rental vacancies and new-lease rents.

On shelter inflation, the mechanics turn on the gap between new and continuing lease rents, now estimated 2–3% narrower than pre-pandemic as continuing rents have more than caught up. **Monthly PCE shelter inflation is expected to average 0.19% for the rest of 2026 and 0.18% in 2027, pulling the year-on-year rate to 2.9% by December 2026 and 2.2% by December 2027 — the slowest since 2013 and below the pre-pandemic norm.** Because shelter carries an outsized weight in the underlying-trend measures the Fed watches, especially CPI-based ones, this feeds directly into resumed core disinflation.

Pulling it together, RFI is forecast at -1.5% then +1.5% annualized in Q3 and Q4 2026, as a homebuilding drag is offset by renovations spending and slightly firmer home sales — implying -3.2% on a Q4/Q4 basis for 2026, a touch worse than the prior -3.0% forecast but an improvement on 2025's -3.8%. The note offers no explicit trade idea; it is a forecast update across the housing complex.

subject: USA: New Home Sales Below Expectations; Lowering Q2 GDP Tracking Estimate to 2.5%
summary:
# US: New Home Sales Disappoint and Nudge Down Q2 GDP Tracking

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US housing data / Q2 GDP tracking  
**General comment:** Factual data-reaction note; marginal downward adjustment, with no change in thesis.

### Context
Commentary reacting to the May release of US new single-family home sales, which came in below expectations and prompted a small revision to Q2 GDP tracking.

### The case
- **New home sales fell far more than forecast.** In May they dropped 7.3% to 580k units (seasonally adjusted annualized rate), against an expectation of a rise — [REDACTED] had projected +3.6% (644k) and the market median +3.2% (640k). The prior month's figure was revised to -6.2% (626k).
- **The decline was geographically concentrated.** The drop came from the West (-26.9%) and the South (-4.1%), while the Midwest (+16.2%) and Northeast (+3.0%) rose. The magnitude of the West's decline accounts for most of the negative aggregate result.
- **The growth impact is marginal.** Q2 GDP tracking was lowered by just 0.1pp, to +2.5% (quarter-over-quarter, annualized), with the Q2 domestic final sales estimate at +1.9%.

### Implications
- The data cuts 0.1pp from Q2 GDP tracking, a small adjustment that does not alter the growth picture.
- On [REDACTED]'s surprise map, the result registers -4, signaling a below-expectations print, but without a broader reassessment of activity.

subject: USA: S&P PMIs Slightly Above Consensus Expectations
summary:
# US Flash PMIs Firm in June, but a Sharp Drop in Manufacturing Employment Clouds the Picture

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US S&P Global flash PMIs (June)  
**General comment:** Neutral data readout; prints came in slightly above consensus, but the note flags a soft internal detail on jobs.

### Context
Reaction to the June preliminary S&P Global US PMIs, released against a backdrop of recent Middle East tensions and their easing. Both headline indices topped consensus, but the report weighs the firmer top-line against a mixed manufacturing composition.

### The case
- **Services firmed with a broadly healthy composition.** The services PMI rose 0.6pt to 51.3, roughly matching the median forecast of 51.1 (prior 50.7). The gain was well-supported internally: new business rose 0.7pt to 51.5 and employment jumped 2.2pt to 49.5. Both price components edged higher (input prices +0.1pt to 60.5, output prices +0.4pt to 58.2), and the forward-looking future output index climbed 4.3pt to 63.2.
- **Manufacturing headline beat, but the detail was mixed.** The manufacturing PMI rose 0.5pt to 55.7 — against consensus for a small decline — reaching its highest level since May 2022 if the final reading confirms. Output (+1.2pt to 57.7) and new orders (+2.4pt to 57.5) drove the gain, but employment fell sharply (-4.6pt to 47.0), its weakest outside the Covid and financial-crisis periods (lowest since October 2009). Price pressures eased from May's multi-year highs, with input prices down 4.1pt to 71.2 and output prices down 2.2pt to 61.0; the future output index rose 1.1pt to 70.1.
- **S&P's read: confidence recovering, but growth still sluggish and jobs the worry.** S&P attributed some of June's improvement to "brighter news out of the Middle East" restoring business confidence, while cautioning that overall growth remains relatively soft versus earlier in the year, before the conflict. It singled out the further fall in employment — especially in manufacturing — as "most worrying," tied to doubts over whether the recent demand upturn is sustainable and to rising raw-material costs.

### Implications
- The firmer headlines point to still-positive but decelerating activity, consistent with S&P's "relatively sluggish" characterization rather than a reacceleration.
- The sharp manufacturing employment drop is the key soft signal, raising questions about the durability of the demand recovery even as output and orders improve.
- Cooling manufacturing price components after May's peaks tentatively ease input-cost pressure there, though services prices remain elevated.
