subject: US Economics Analyst: The Macroeconomic Spillovers From AI Electricity Demand
summary:
# AI Electricity Demand: A ~6% Power Inflation Wave With Small Aggregate Growth Drag

**Theme:** Electricity price outlook and spillovers to consumer/business inflation, spending and GDP  
**Markets:** US, developed markets  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Manuel Abecasis, 11 February 2026  

### Key findings
- Consumer electricity inflation is expected to hold near 6% in 2026-2027 and slow to about 3.5% in 2028 as natural gas prices ease — the answer to how AI-driven power demand feeds through to household bills.
- Data centers are projected to add roughly 1.2pp to annual power demand in 2026-2030, nearly half of total demand growth, while capacity grows only ~1.1% amid regulatory and supply bottlenecks.
- Regional wholesale prices will rise far more than the national average in tight markets — Midwest, California, Texas, Mid-Atlantic — because ~1% of counties hold ~70% of data center capacity.
- Higher power prices are estimated to lift headline PCE inflation by about 0.2/0.15/0.1pp in 2026/2027/2028, combining direct effects and indirect cost passthrough (led by medical, food and transportation services).
- The drag on consumer spending growth is put at roughly 0.2pp in 2026-2027, falling hardest on lower-income households and data center-heavy regions.
- Net GDP drag is only about 0.1pp in 2026-2027, as weaker consumption is partly offset by higher utility capex.
- The cost allocation is decisive but unsettled: in the baseline data centers bear ~two-thirds of excess capex, but if non-AI customers instead carry half, electricity prices rise ~8% in 2026-2027 and ~4% in 2028-2030.
- The GDP hit is small against the AI upside — the present value of these price-driven losses is under 3% of projected AI-induced GDP growth through 2035.

### Method & verdict
[Reasonable] The note stitches together the firm's own gas-price and demand forecasts, EIA scheduled-capacity data, and empirical hourly supply curves estimated for major ISOs/RTOs to map how tightening spare capacity lifts regional wholesale prices. Inflation passthrough is modeled by adapting a commodity-passthrough framework to BEA input-output tables for both electricity and capex costs, with capex trajectories anchored to utility capital plans, PJM capacity-auction clearing prices, and OBBBA tax changes. The framework is coherent and transparent about its assumptions, and it flags real limits: daily supply curves overstate short-run rigidity relative to annual flexibility, the cost-allocation split between data centers and other customers is an assumption rather than an observation, and outcomes hinge on regional regulatory choices the model cannot pin down.

### Unpacked
Electricity has been running hot — up 6.9% year-over-year through December 2025 versus 2.9% headline PCE — and the note asks whether the AI build-out turns that into a durable inflation and growth problem. The starting expectation is intuitive: a demand surge meeting slow supply should push prices up, and the interesting question is how much leaks from data centers onto everyone else.

**The core mechanism is a demand-supply squeeze made worse by geography.** Data centers, now about 7% of US power use, are set to drive nearly half of demand growth, while grid connection queues have stretched to 4½ years and turbine and labor shortages cap new supply. Because capacity is extraordinarily concentrated, the price pressure is regional rather than uniform, spiking where spare capacity runs thin.

**A second, slower channel runs through utility capex, which has become the dominant driver of electricity inflation.** Utilities earn a regulated return on invested assets financed through prices, so the investment needed to serve surging demand mechanically raises bills. Capacity-market auctions in PJM clearing at two-to-three times pre-pandemic levels underline how expensive meeting that demand will be.

**Who absorbs the cost is the swing factor in the whole forecast.** Regulators are pushing data centers to fund their own grid costs, but leakage to households and non-AI businesses is hard to prevent — policies are incomplete, siting is chosen partly for lenient passthrough, and attribution is murky. The baseline assumes data centers carry two-thirds of excess capex; the alternative where non-AI customers bear half lifts the price path from ~6% toward ~8%, showing how sensitive the numbers are to a single assumption.

**The macro damage is real but contained, and distributionally uneven.** The combined inflation lift erodes real disposable income enough to shave about 0.2pp off consumer spending, but higher utility capex offsets much of it, leaving GDP only ~0.1pp lower. Lower-income households and data center regions bear more, and because data centers employ few workers, local labor income does little to cushion the hit.

**The framing conclusion is that this is a manageable near-term cost, not a threat to the AI thesis** — the present-value losses are under 3% of expected AI-driven GDP gains. The main tail risk sits with reliability: outages cost roughly $8.4 per kilowatt-hour, nearly 50 times the residential price, so any rise in outage frequency from tight markets would dwarf the modest price effects modeled here. The note offers no explicit trade idea.

subject: USA: Payroll Growth Above Expectations, Partly Reflecting Methodological Changes; Unemployment Rate Declines
summary:
# January Payrolls Beat on a Birth-Death Model Change; Jobless Rate Slips to 4.28%

**Theme:** A methodological shift to net-business-formation estimates inflated the headline print and will raise monthly volatility; benchmark revisions cut the prior year's trend.  
**Markets:** US labor market / Fed policy  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jan Hatzius, 11 February 2026  

### Definitive impacts
- Nonfarm payrolls rose 130k in January, above the 65k median and [REDACTED]'s 45k; private payrolls rose 172k. Prior months were revised down 2k (December) and 15k (November).
- The new birth-death model added roughly 70k to January job growth versus December (SA by [REDACTED]), about 50k of it in healthcare and education.
- Healthcare and education payrolls jumped 137k — the largest monthly gain ever outside the 2020 Covid rebound. Federal government payrolls fell 34k (partly the deferred-resignation program); tech-related information employment fell 7k to its lowest since May 2022.
- Unemployment fell 10bp to 4.28%, with temporary-layoff workers down 83k and reentrants down 180k. Household employment rose 528k; participation edged up to 62.5%; U6 fell 0.4pp to 8.0%.
- Average hourly earnings rose 0.41% MoM; the YoY rate eased 0.02pp to 3.71%.
- The annual benchmark cut the March 2025 employment level by 898k; only ~117k (~10k/month) came from the birth-death component. Business-formation contribution for April–December 2025 was revised down 240k (27k/month).
- The payrolls diffusion index rose 0.8pt to 55.0.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] suspects the birth-death methodology change boosted the January print and will increase monthly job-growth volatility going forward — arguing for smoothing payrolls over a longer horizon.
- [REDACTED] estimates the underlying pace of job growth at +55k, blending the payroll and household surveys.
- [REDACTED] attributes much of the benchmark revision not explained by the birth-death model to the exclusion of unauthorized immigrants from the QCEW source data.
- [REDACTED] reads current wage growth (3.71% YoY, vs its 3.4% tracker) as still below the pace it judges compatible with the Fed's 2% inflation target.

### Backdrop
The BLS estimates net formation of new businesses — jobs at firms too new to appear in the survey sample — via a statistical "birth-death" model, which is periodically recalibrated. Separately, the annual benchmarking process realigns the payroll survey to the more complete QCEW administrative data, revising the prior year's level and monthly trend. Both processes were in play this month, alongside residual distortions from an earlier federal government shutdown that had inflated temporary layoffs and depressed reentrants.

### At issue
The January employment report carried three overlapping developments. First, a headline beat: nonfarm payrolls up 130k against a 65k consensus. Second, a methodological change to the birth-death model, which [REDACTED] estimates lifted the print by ~70k relative to December and concentrated gains in healthcare and education. Third, the annual benchmark revision, cutting the March 2025 employment level by 898k and trimming the April 2024–March 2025 trend by 75k/month — of which only ~10k/month was the cyclical business-formation component — plus a 27k/month downward revision to the birth-death contribution for April–December 2025.

### Unpacked
The report is harder to read than the headline beat suggests because the same methodological change that produced the upside surprise also undermines confidence in it. **The 130k print flatters the underlying trend: strip out the ~70k mechanical lift from the recalibrated birth-death model and the signal is far weaker.** The concentration of that lift in healthcare and education — a record 137k monthly gain outside the Covid rebound — is the tell that the model, not organic hiring, is doing much of the work.

The household side is cleaner and genuinely firmer. **The 10bp drop in unemployment to 4.28% rests on real improvement — a 528k rise in household employment and a higher participation rate — rather than people leaving the labor force.** Much of the move also unwinds shutdown distortions, as workers on temporary layoff and reentrants normalize, so the level is more informative than the monthly change.

For the reader, the practical takeaway is to downweight the payroll headline. **[REDACTED] pegs the true underlying pace near 55k and flags that noisier prints ahead warrant smoothing payrolls over a longer horizon.** Wage growth continues to cool toward a Fed-compatible pace, and the benchmark revision — largely traced to the exclusion of unauthorized immigrants from source data rather than to a weaker business-formation cycle — reinforces that last year's labor market was softer than first reported, without changing the read on its current momentum.

subject: [REDACTED] FX Morning Notes: Into Jan Payrolls
summary:
# January Payrolls: Benign Base Case, but Revisions Add the Real Volatility

**Theme:** A modally quiet print — unchanged 4.4% unemployment, sub-consensus jobs — but annual benchmark and birth-death revisions widen the risk  
**Markets:** US labour market, USD and FX  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Stuart Jenkins, 11 February 2026  

### Estimates
- **+45k headline jobs growth** for January payrolls, a slight miss to consensus, with the BLS business birth-death adjustment seen as a 30–50k drag versus recent months.
- **4.4% unemployment rate** (rounded, unchanged), off a low unrounded 4.38% starting point; risks skewed to the downside given slight negative residual seasonality in January.
- **-750k to -900k** for the BLS annual benchmark payrolls revision (April 2024–March 2025), versus the BLS's -911k preliminary estimate.
- **Negative** expected update to the birth-death forecast for April–December 2025, released alongside the report.

### Outlook
- Risks on the unemployment rate skew to the downside, per [REDACTED] economists, given the 4.38% base and January's negative residual seasonality.
- The modal outcome implies a limited Dollar impulse, but January releases historically drive larger Dollar moves than other months — partly from bigger past jobs surprises, partly from the extra volatility introduced by the various revisions.
- The FX playbook is unchanged from prior months: with the Dollar still trading procyclically, high-beta currencies should perform as well as safe havens on a weak print, and vice versa on a strong one.
- Note: the household survey annual population-control adjustment, usually bundled with the January report, has been pushed to the February release this year.

### Unpacked
Incoming data ahead of the print has been mixed. **Alternative jobs-growth metrics have been subdued, but the pace of layoffs has stayed resiliently low** — leaving the headline near consensus rather than pointing to a clear break in either direction. The birth-death model, now updated monthly as of this report, is the specific factor pulling the January estimate down relative to recent months.

What makes this release unusual is not the point estimates but everything arriving alongside them. **This report carries two sets of annual revisions on top of the monthly print — the benchmark payrolls revision and an updated birth-death forecast — both expected to be negative.** That bundle of new data, rather than the headline itself, is where the surprise potential sits.

That framing carries into the market read. Recent payrolls — September, the combined Oct/Nov, and December — all moved the Dollar TWI less than 20bp in the first 30 minutes, helped by prints landing near expectations, the unemployment rate consolidating after earlier focus on its uptrend, and lingering data-quality concerns from the government shutdown. **January is the historical exception: it tends to generate higher-magnitude Dollar reactions than other months, so a quiet modal call does not mean a quiet tape.**

For the cross-market view, the procyclical Dollar continues to shape the response. Over the past year, high-beta EM currencies such as BRL and ZAR have performed at least as well as traditional safe havens like JPY in response to jobs-growth misses — the reason [REDACTED] expects high-beta FX to hold up on a weak report and lag on a strong one. The note offers no explicit trade idea beyond this directional playbook.

subject: US Daily: January CPI Preview
summary:
# January Core CPI: +0.33% m/m, a Touch Above Consensus as Tariffs and January Resets Bite

**Theme:** Core CPI running slightly hot on seasonal resets, tariffs, and firm travel, offset by softer autos  
**Markets:** US inflation  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jessica Rindels, 10 February 2026  

### Estimates

**January CPI (release under preview):**
- **+0.33% m/m core CPI** (vs. +0.3% consensus), taking the y/y rate to **2.52%** (vs. +2.5% consensus).
- **+0.24% m/m headline CPI** (vs. +0.3% consensus), for a y/y rate of **2.44%** (vs. +2.5% consensus); driven by higher food (+0.45%) and lower energy (-1.3%) prices.
- **+0.31% m/m core PCE** implied by the CPI forecast — a modestly lower reading than core CPI. December PCE releases 20 February; January PCE on 13 March.

**Key component forecasts (January, m/m):**
- Communications **+0.4%** and private transportation **+1.5%**, both lifted by residual seasonality.
- Medical care commodities **+0.7%**, reflecting start-of-year price resets.
- Tariff-exposed categories add **+0.07pp** to core: apparel +0.5%, household furnishings +0.7%, recreation +0.4%, education +0.2%, personal care +0.2%.
- Airfares **+2%**, hotels **+1%** — firm travel services.
- Used cars **-1.5%**, new cars unchanged, car insurance **+0.4%** — softer autos overall.

**Forecast path:**
- Monthly core CPI of **0.2–0.3%** over the next few months, then **0.1–0.2%** thereafter.
- **+2.1% y/y core CPI** and **+2.1% core PCE** by December 2026.

### Outlook

- Tariffs remain the near-term upside driver, keeping monthly core in the 0.2–0.3% range before the pace eases as housing rental, labor-market, and tariff contributions shrink.
- January's initial print risks being revised lower: annual seasonal-factor revisions pull elevated monthly readings toward the annual average, and roughly 20% of a month's relative strength has historically been revised away in the first annual revision.

### Unpacked

The forecast rests on a handful of identifiable, largely mechanical drivers rather than a broad-based acceleration. **Seasonal distortions and the "January effect" — start-of-year price resets in categories like medical care commodities — account for much of the above-consensus core reading**, alongside firm travel services inflation that [REDACTED] reads off equity analysts' online airfare tracking and Smith Travel Research hotel data. Tariffs add a smaller but concrete +0.07pp, concentrated in exposed goods such as apparel and household furnishings.

Pulling the other way is autos. **A 1.5% drop in used car prices — signalled by Manheim auction data — plus flat new car prices soften the goods side**, as tariff pressure on new vehicles is offset by richer sales incentives. Car insurance continues to rise modestly.

The wrinkle this month is methodological. **The BLS releases recalculated seasonal factors reflecting 2025 price movements, plus updated weights, which could dampen the seasonal swings that drove much of last year's month-to-month core volatility.** Because annual revisions tend to push readings toward the yearly average, January 2025's unusually strong print (23bp above the 2024 average) and the soft March–May prints (8bp below) are the kind of extremes most likely to be reshaped — worth keeping in mind when reading the headline number.

Looking further out, the disinflation case leans on fading contributions from rents and the labor market, with tariffs as the swing factor keeping near-term prints firmer before the trajectory settles toward roughly 0.1–0.2% monthly and 2.1% year-over-year on both core CPI and core PCE by end-2026.

subject: Global Markets Daily: Treasury Demand in 2026: Absorption Not Too Challenging
summary:
# Treasury Supply in 2026 Looks Digestible — the Fed Turns Buyer and Bank Balance Sheets Reopen

**Theme:** Whether the market can absorb 2026 UST net supply, and which buyers do the work  
**Markets:** US Treasuries / US rates  
**Source:** [REDACTED], William Marshall, 10 February 2026

### Definitive impacts
- **The Fed swings from passive net seller (QT) to a source of net demand**, buying Treasuries to offset MBS runoff and rebuild reserves — mechanically absorbing $575bn of bills supply to the private sector, exclusively in bills for now.
- **2026 Treasury net supply is put at $1.2tn of coupons and $932bn of bills** (after buybacks), the base the market must digest.
- **SLR changes announced last year free up significant balance-sheet capacity**, leaving large banks bound by CET1 alone, having previously been constrained by a mix of CET1 and SLR.
- **Dealer inventory has risen $70bn YTD (FR2004 data) and, as a share of bank assets, is at record highs** — occurring alongside wider swap spreads.
- **Observed 2025 flows through Q3:** foreign private +$455bn, banks +$187bn, pensions/asset managers +$153bn/+$123bn, 'households' (largely levered funds) +$229bn; foreign officials turned modest net sellers in Q2 and Q3.
- **Chinese regulators are advising banks to limit UST purchases** — a fact cited as part of ongoing reserve diversification.

### Opinative impacts
- **[REDACTED] sees 2026 absorption as less challenging than 2025**, despite elevated fiscal deficits — the Fed's shift is the biggest swing factor.
- **[REDACTED] pencils in only ~$155bn left for the 'household'/levered-fund sector, down from a 2025 estimate of $300bn**, and judges this stepdown manageable given stable funding conditions and more constrained net coupon supply.
- **Foreign official demand stays tepid at ~$50bn net**, on structural diversification and a demand base now less sensitive to FX moves; [REDACTED] does not expect pronounced selling but flags it shifts clearing toward more price-sensitive buyers.
- **Foreign private demand ~$500bn — still firmly positive but the slowest pace since 2022** — supported by [REDACTED]'s baseline for a steeper Treasury curve (vs Gilts and JGBs) and a weaker USD, partly offset by episodic erosion in Treasuries' hedge value.
- **Money-fund demand decelerates modestly to ~$250bn**, as a steeper curve and resilient risk assets slow inflows while Fed buying lightens the bill-absorption burden.
- **Bank buying accelerates modestly to ~$250bn** (from ~$200bn in 2024–25), with [REDACTED] judging swap-spread carry and roll sufficient to clear leverage- and VaR-based return hurdles.
- **Dealer demand slows to ~$150bn** as the regulatory-easing adjustment peaks early in the year.
- **Pensions and insurers add only ~$100bn, roughly half their recent pace** — a structurally diminishing source as DB plans immunize, freeze, and compete with rising long-dated IG issuance from M&A and AI capex.
- **Asset-manager demand holds ~$150bn**, within recent ranges.
- **Compressed dispersion along the curve and wider swap spreads should persist**, given stable funding and a lighter coupon-supply need for outsized levered-fund appetite.
- **Idiosyncratic risk flagged:** Japan's MoF could sell foreign-currency assets, including USTs, if it taps FEF FX gains to fund tax cuts.

### Backdrop
Treasury financing runs through a familiar cast of buyers whose relative weight has been shifting for years: away from foreign official reserve managers and toward domestic and price-sensitive private buyers. Over 2025 the Fed was running gradual quantitative tightening, acting as a passive drain on demand; foreign officials edged toward net selling; and the incremental clearing increasingly fell to banks, money funds, and levered "household" accounts. That price-sensitive base, plus regulatory constraints on bank and dealer balance sheets (SLR), set the conditions the 2026 outlook now revises.

### At issue
The note assesses whether 2026's UST net supply can be absorbed and maps expected demand buyer-by-buyer. The defining new element is the Fed's turn from QT to outright Treasury buying (bills) to offset MBS runoff and lift reserves, which removes a supplier and adds a buyer at once. Around it sit last year's SLR changes now feeding through to bank and dealer capacity, early-2026 data showing surging dealer inventory, and headlines on Chinese official diversification — combined into group-level demand estimates (Exhibit 7) against $1.2tn coupons and $932bn bills of supply.

### Unpacked
The starting worry is straightforward: deficits are large and net issuance is heavy, so who buys it all? **The answer the note builds is that the demand math is easier this year mainly because the Fed flips sides** — no longer shrinking its holdings but adding to them, and doing so in bills, precisely where private absorption pressure is greatest.

The through-line is a market that clears at the margin through more price-sensitive hands, and the note reads recent regulatory easing as enlarging those hands rather than signaling stress. **The record dealer inventories alongside wider swap spreads are interpreted as improving intermediation capacity, not building constraints** — a distinction that matters, because the same data could otherwise look like balance sheets choking. That framing is what lets [REDACTED] raise bank and dealer estimates even as spreads widen.

The offsets are structural and long-end. **Traditional long-duration buyers — chiefly pensions — are fading as a demand source just as IG duration supply rises**, so the belly and front-end carry more of the load. Foreign demand splits: officials stay quietly absent, while private foreign buyers keep coming for the curve and FX, though at the weakest pace in years.

**Netted out, only a modest slice is left for levered funds, and that stepdown is the crux of the "not too challenging" call** — less reliance on outsized levered appetite, stable funding from Fed reserve purchases, and a lighter coupon path together argue for compressed curve dispersion and persistently wider swap spreads. For a reader, the actionable implication sits in that spread and dispersion view rather than in a direction-of-rates trade; the note itself advances no explicit trade idea tied to its thesis, and the daily's standing trade list is a separate book unrelated to this analysis.

subject: USA: Core Retail Sales Below Expectations; Employment Cost Index Slightly Below Expectations; Lowering Q4 GDP Tracking to +1.6%; Estimating 0.36% for December Core PCE
summary:
# US Q4 Growth Tracking Cut to 1.6% as December Consumer Spending Disappoints

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US economic data (December retail sales, Q4 ECI, import prices, PCE)  
**General comment:** Marks-to-market on incoming data; net dovish read — softer consumption and contained wage growth, both consistent with the Fed's inflation goal.

### Context
A same-day reaction to the December retail sales, Q4 employment cost index, and December import price releases, updating GDP and inflation tracking estimates ahead of the corresponding PCE report.

### The case
- **Consumer spending was materially softer than expected in December, and prior months were revised down.** Core retail sales (ex-autos, gasoline, and building materials) fell 0.1% against an expected +0.3%, and headline sales were flat versus +0.4% expected. Compounding the miss, the November level of core sales was revised down 0.4%, reflecting 0.2pp downgrades to growth in each of October and November. Even so, using PCE and CPI details, real retail sales are estimated to have risen at a 1.9% three-month annualized pace through December.

- **Wage growth remains contained and below the pace judged consistent with 2% inflation.** The ECI rose 0.7% in Q4 (not annualized), a touch below the 0.8% consensus. The key underlying gauge — private wages and salaries excluding incentive-paid occupations — rose 0.8%, leaving the internal wage tracker at 3.4% on both a quarterly annualized and year-over-year basis, in line with the ECI and below the target-compatible pace.

- **Import prices firmed at the margin, but the input that feeds core PCE softened.** Ex-petroleum import prices rose 0.4%, slightly above consensus, while headline import prices rose 0.1% as expected. More relevant for inflation tracking, the international airfares component — source data for the foreign travel piece of core PCE — declined 0.7%, nudging the December core PCE estimate down.

- **Inflation tracking is little changed and just below 3% year-over-year.** Core PCE is estimated to have risen 0.36% in December (from 0.37% pre-report), a 2.97% year-over-year rate; headline PCE is put at 0.36% (2.86% y/y) and market-based core PCE at 0.35%.

### Implications
- The softer December spending and downward revisions cut the Q4 GDP tracking estimate by 0.4pp to +1.6% annualized, with domestic final sales at +1.1% and private domestic final sales at +2.3%.
- Wage growth running below the target-compatible pace, alongside sub-3% core PCE, points to continued disinflation progress on the labor-cost side.

# Commodities Comedown: Equity and Bond Inflows Stay Robust as USD Demand Cools

**Theme:** Broad risk-on flows persist even as commodities and gold soften  
**Markets:** Global cross-asset fund flows  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Isabella Rosenberg, 9 February 2026  

### Landscape
- Global equity funds drew +$35bn in the week ending February 4, a sharp reversal from -$15bn the prior week, led by global benchmark funds.
- Global fixed income funds saw strong inflows, driven by very large flows into Agg-type bond funds.
- Money market fund assets rose $87bn on the week.
- Commodities funds kept positive but slower net inflows despite a selloff in gold — the week's featured "Chart of the Week" theme.
- Cross-border FX flows stayed firm overall, but foreign inflows into USD slowed markedly.

### Drivers
- Equity demand is concentrated in global benchmark funds rather than single-country vehicles, with Western Europe ex-UK a strong regional inflow point and US inflows positive but subdued.
- Sector rotation favors energy (largest sector inflows) and technology, which kept drawing inflows despite the software selloff.
- Within EM equities, Korea remained the strongest inflow destination; Japan turned slightly net negative ahead of its election.
- Fixed income demand skews toward the belly/short end: short-duration bond funds saw positive flows while long-duration funds saw outflows.
- USD demand is fading at the margin — cross-border FX flows held up but foreign inflows into the dollar slowed sharply.

### Unpacked
**Equity flows rebounded hard, but the strength was broad-based rather than country-specific — global benchmark funds, not concentrated national bets, did the heavy lifting.** Within the G10, the US attracted positive but muted flows, while Western Europe ex-UK stood out on the strong side. Japan was the notable soft spot, turning slightly net negative with an election approaching. In EM, Korea continued its run as the top inflow destination.

**At the sector level, the flow picture cut against the week's equity price action: technology funds kept drawing money through the software selloff, and energy led all sectors.** Commodities funds tell the "comedown" story in the title — inflows continued but slowed, and did so even as gold sold off, the relationship the note highlights in its Chart of the Week.

**On the fixed income side, the inflow was large but positioned defensively on duration** — Agg-type funds saw very large inflows and short-duration funds drew positive flows, while long-duration funds bled. EM debt was uniformly weak, with negative flows across both hard-currency and local-currency bond funds. The $87bn jump in money market assets rounds out a week where cash and core bonds both attracted substantial demand.

The note is a flow-reporting product built around EPFR data and positioning exhibits; it carries no explicit trade idea, and none should be inferred. The clearest signal to carry forward is the marked slowdown in foreign USD inflows against otherwise firm cross-border FX activity.

subject: US Economics Weekly Update 2/9/2026
summary:
# Delayed January Payrolls Set to Undershoot, Plus a 750–900k Benchmark Markdown

**Theme:** Soft January jobs from big-data weakness and a birth-death overhaul, alongside the annual benchmark revision  
**Markets:** US labour market and US inflation  
**Source:** [REDACTED], David Mericle, 9 February 2026  

### Estimates
- **+45k** nonfarm payrolls in the delayed January report (Wednesday), below **+69k** consensus.
- **4.4%** unemployment rate, unchanged, with risks skewed toward a small decline.
- **-750k to -900k** cumulative payroll revision (April 2024–March 2025) from the annual benchmark revision to the establishment survey; a further downward revision is likely for April–December 2025 as the BLS updates net birth-death forecasts using QCEW and monthly payrolls.
- **+0.33%** m/m core CPI in January (consensus +0.3%), leaving the y/y at **2.52%**.
- **+0.24%** m/m headline CPI, y/y at **2.44%**.
- **7,067k** job openings in December (average of JOLTS, Indeed, LinkUp), down 110k m/m; job-workers gap now **-0.5mn**.
- **231k** initial jobless claims, up 22k, back near 2025H2 levels.
- **-3%** annualized Q1 residential fixed investment, cut on winter-storm effects.

### Outlook
- Payrolls should come in soft because big-data indicators were weak and the updated birth-death model could subtract 30–50k jobs per month; fewer-than-expected January layoffs in a low-turnover market are a modest offset, and Snowstorm Fern hit too late to matter.
- The birth-death model change — using payroll growth at businesses in the current sample to estimate openings and closings — should improve real-time accuracy and shrink annual revisions but may raise monthly volatility.
- Core CPI is lifted by seasonal distortions (communications +0.4%, private transportation +1.5%), start-of-year resets, and tariffs (+0.07pp); headline is held back by energy (-1.3%) despite firmer food (+0.4%).
- College-graduate unemployment has risen more than usual (+0.7pp to 2.8% since January 2023, vs 2.1% in 2019), driven by low turnover for new grads and sharper hiring pullbacks in information, finance, and professional/business services; AI is not yet judged a meaningful contributor but could disproportionately affect this group later.

### Unpacked
This is a heavily front-loaded data week: the delayed January jobs report lands Wednesday and carries far more than a single month's read. **Alongside the point estimate, it brings the annual benchmark revision to the establishment survey, which [REDACTED] expects to cut cumulative payroll growth over April 2024–March 2025 by 750–900k, with a further downward revision likely for the rest of 2025 once the BLS refreshes its net birth-death forecasts against QCEW and monthly payrolls.**

The report also debuts a rebuilt birth-death model. Rather than relying on historical patterns, the BLS will infer business openings and closings from payroll growth among firms already in its sample. **The trade-off is cleaner real-time estimates and smaller annual revisions in exchange for potentially noisier month-to-month prints** — a structural change worth keeping in mind before over-reading any single figure. Last week's data leaned soft in support of the low payroll call: job openings fell sharply in December and claims bounced 22k back toward second-half-2025 levels.

On prices, the January CPI is shaped by the usual start-of-year mechanics — seasonal jumps in communications and private transportation, annual price resets, and a small tariff contribution — partly offset by a used-car decline and slightly slower shelter inflation. **The same report also refreshes seasonal factors and category weights, which tends to pull monthly changes back toward the annual average, another reason to treat the headline move cautiously.**

Two cross-currents round out the week. **Snowstorm Fern's main mark will be on housing, where [REDACTED] now sees Q1 residential investment contracting 3% annualized, while effects on spending, manufacturing, and surveys should be milder.** Separately, the note flags a widening in college-graduate unemployment — a mix of weak turnover for new entrants and retrenchment in the white-collar industries that employ them — with AI a possible future pressure rather than a current cause.

subject: US Daily: Why Has the Unemployment Rate of College Graduates Risen More Than Usual?
summary:
# Why the college-graduate unemployment rate has risen more than usual: weak hiring in degree-intensive sectors

**Theme:** Why the college-graduate unemployment rate has risen disproportionately, and how much of it is entry-level dynamics, sector hiring, or AI  
**Markets:** US labor market  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jessica Rindels, 9 February 2026

### Definitive impacts
- The college-graduate unemployment rate rose 0.7pp since January 2023 to 2.8% in December 2025, above the 2019 average of 2.1%, and stands more elevated than other education levels on a standardized basis (relative to its own cycle norm and volatility).
- Unemployment rates for young workers rose more, on a standardized basis, than for older age groups in both education groups; within each age group, college graduates rose disproportionately.
- Job growth in industries that employ the largest shares of college graduates (information services, finance, professional and business services) averaged -9k/month over 2023-2025, down from +44k/month over 2017-2019.
- Job growth in industries employing the smallest shares of college graduates (construction, transportation, retail trade) averaged +12k/month over 2023-2025, down from +31k/month over 2017-2019.
- Both the hiring rate and the layoff rate sit below their 2019 averages, with the hiring-rate decline especially pronounced.
- Among unemployed workers aged 16-35, those in states with the largest declines in labor-market turnover saw larger increases in unemployment-spell length than peers in states with smaller declines.
- AI adoption correlates only slightly positively with rising college-graduate unemployment across industries so far; the same pattern holds for young workers aged 20-30.
- College-graduate employment share correlates strongly and positively with AI adoption at the industry level, and graduates are disproportionately in occupations with higher shares of potentially automatable tasks.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] reads the rise as driven jointly by two effects — being a new labor-market entrant and being a college graduate — rather than by either alone.
- [REDACTED] attributes the older-graduate increase mainly to sharper hiring pullbacks in graduate-intensive industries, a reversal of the 2017-2019 and 2021-2022 pattern when those sectors outgrew non-graduate ones.
- [REDACTED] sees the low-hire, low-fire regime as raising the risk that young unemployed workers get increasingly "locked out" of the labor market as spells lengthen.
- [REDACTED] is not convinced AI has meaningfully driven graduate unemployment to date, noting that headwinds are confined to a few exposed subindustries and that young tech-worker unemployment, elevated in 2024, has since normalized.
- [REDACTED] sees AI as a larger future risk to graduates given their concentration in high-adoption industries and automatable occupations, but expects displacement to be partly offset by AI-related job gains and by graduates' higher rate of transitioning to other occupations when displaced.

### At issue
[REDACTED] revisits its mid-2025 work on graduate labor-market outcomes, asking again whether college graduates are struggling to find work and why. It decomposes the graduate and non-graduate unemployment rates by age (young/new entrants vs. all others) on a standardized basis, tracks industry-level hiring by graduate employment share, links young workers' unemployment-spell length to state-level declines in turnover, and tests the correlation between AI adoption and graduate unemployment across industries.

### Unpacked
The note reframes a single headline number into two overlapping stories. **The graduate unemployment rate is elevated not because of one force but because two coincide: new entrants face a market that has stopped churning, and graduates specifically depend on industries that have stopped hiring.** Separating age from education is what lets the analysis assign weight to each.

For young workers, the mechanism is the low-hire, low-fire market. When turnover collapses, the people hurt most are those trying to enter for the first time, since they rely on new hiring rather than on holding an existing job. The state-level evidence — longer unemployment spells where turnover fell most — is the concrete link, and it carries the warning that a stagnant market can trap entrants rather than merely delay them.

For older graduates, the driver is compositional. **The industries that concentrate graduates — information, finance, professional and business services — have swung from leading job growth to shedding jobs, while lower-graduate sectors kept adding at a reduced pace.** This is a reversal of the prior regime, and it explains why the graduate premium in employment outcomes has eroded.

On AI, the note is deliberately two-sided: little measurable damage so far, but a structural setup for more later. The reassurance is that observed AI effects are narrow and that the 2024 spike in young tech unemployment has faded. The caution is that graduates sit precisely where adoption is highest and task-automatability greatest — tempered by the point that adoption can augment rather than replace labor, and that graduates historically re-transition faster when displaced. The note offers no explicit trade idea.

subject: [REDACTED] FX Morning Notes: Parsing the Supermajority
summary:
# Japan's LDP Supermajority Sets Up a More Fiscal Government — Yen Weakness Still the Base Case

**Theme:** Election result reinforces proactive fiscal policy; near-term Yen reaction diverges from the medium-term view  
**Markets:** Japan FX and rates; US Dollar  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Stuart Jenkins, 9 February 2026  

### Landscape
- USD/JPY traded a leg lower on net after the result despite its prior positive beta to prediction-market pricing of an LDP majority, and sits close to pre-Jan 23rd rate-check levels.
- JGB yields rose and domestic equities saw an initial bounce, both consistent with markets pricing in more fiscal spending.
- The Dollar was broadly weaker this morning, contributing to the move in USD/JPY.

### Drivers
- The LDP won a two-thirds supermajority in the Lower House on its own, wider than expected, and with coalition partner JIP can push through most legislation — including fiscal policy — despite lacking an Upper House majority.
- The result raises the likelihood of a consumption tax cut and reinforces prospects for proactive fiscal policy under PM Takaichi, though the clearest boost to domestic spending is not expected until FY2027 (April 2027 – March 2028).
- Elevated intervention risk is the main force holding USD/JPY down near-term, with the pair close to pre-rate-check levels; FM Katayama's comments on potentially using FX reserves to fund state spending add to the counter-move.
- A heavy US data week — January payrolls and CPI — is the near-term Dollar driver; January reports historically produce larger-than-usual FX reactions, especially for payrolls, due to year-start technical factors and backward data revisions.

### Risks
- Upside to USD/JPY (Yen weakness) is the baseline as fiscal spending is priced further in, with the pair seen moving through 160.
- Downside to USD/JPY near-term from intervention risk given proximity to pre-Jan 23rd rate-check levels — the analyst frames this as the foremost reason for the initial move against the medium-term view.

### Unpacked
The election outcome hands PM Takaichi's coalition control over the legislative agenda well beyond what a Lower House majority alone would imply. Because the supermajority lets the government pass most bills — fiscal measures included — without an Upper House majority, the constraint on spending ambitions is materially loosened. **The economists read the result as reinforcing proactive fiscal policy and significantly raising the odds of a consumption tax cut, though the strongest impulse to domestic spending is not expected before FY2027.**

The cross-asset reaction split along an informative line. JGB yields and domestic equities moved as if more spending is coming, but USD/JPY went the other way despite having tracked LDP-majority odds positively into the vote. **The medium-term call is unchanged — further pricing of Japanese fiscal spending is expected to weaken the Yen and carry USD/JPY through 160 — but the note treats the initial opposite move as credible rather than noise.** The pair sitting near pre-Jan 23rd rate-check levels puts intervention squarely in view; broad Dollar softness and Katayama's remark about tapping FX reserves for state spending round out the explanation.

**The week's US calendar is the other axis, with January payrolls and CPI the two prints that matter most.** The economists look for a 33bp core CPI reading and +45k headline NFP. The note flags that January releases tend to generate outsized Dollar reactions — the payrolls print especially — because year-start technical factors and backward revisions add volatility beyond a typical month, so the reader should size event risk accordingly.

subject: Global Markets Daily: Macro and Equity Returns—Cycle Dominates Valuations, But Tension Could Fuel Volatility
summary:
# Cycle Beats Valuation in 2026 Equities — But the Gap Fattens the Downside Tail and Argues for Owning Volatility

**Theme:** Whether a friendly macro cycle can keep pushing US equities higher despite historically stretched valuations, and what that tension implies for volatility  
**Markets:** US equities / US macro  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Vickie Chang, 9 February 2026  

### Definitive impacts
- US equity valuations sit at historically high levels and, per the macro models, run above what the macro backdrop would normally justify — even after crediting the favorable conditions of recent years (Shiller CAPE vs. model-predicted P/E).
- In the macro scenario framework, a 60bp growth upgrade (market moving to fully price the Q4/Q4 2.5% growth forecast) plus an offsetting dovish policy shock that pulls 10y yields to year-end targets lifts the S&P 500 by ~6%.
- Cyclical factors alone — lower core inflation, range-bound yields, stable-to-slightly-higher unemployment — add roughly +2pp to one-year real returns in the models.
- The high starting level of "macro valuation" subtracts roughly 7pp from one-year real returns.
- Netting valuation and cycle against a baseline real return, the full model implies modestly positive one-year nominal returns of ~5%.
- Longer-dated equity volatility has not risen in a sustained way and remains below long-term averages.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] expects continued equity upside this year: it sees strong growth and falling inflation dominating high valuations, consistent with its Portfolio Strategy team's 7600 S&P 500 year-end target (~10% upside).
- [REDACTED] treats the ~5% model estimate as illustrative, not a forecast it would lean on — it flags the number as possibly too optimistic (if the assumed baseline return is too high) or too pessimistic, and prefers it to a firm point call.
- [REDACTED] leans toward the model understating next year's macro tailwind: with growth composition tilted toward productivity, the unemployment rate (its cycle proxy) likely shows more labor-market softness per unit of GDP than usual, biasing the return estimate low.
- [REDACTED] judges the measured overvaluation may itself be overstated, because the 10-year-earnings CAPE cannot capture AI-driven future earnings the market is pricing up front — though it stresses significant AI benefit is already embedded in prices.
- [REDACTED] argues high valuations do not block positive returns while the cycle stays friendly; the bill for rich valuations comes due only when the macro backdrop turns unfriendly, which fattens the downside tail if recession risk returns.
- [REDACTED] expects volatility to persist and can rise even as equities climb (its vol models tie higher valuations to higher volatility), citing the late-1990s pattern of rising vol and credit spreads alongside rising stocks.

### At issue
Since April, US equity valuations have kept climbing to historically high levels while early-2026 price action has been caught between improving growth data and the vulnerability of expensive markets to AI and policy headlines — a tension that has already lifted volatility. The note applies [REDACTED]'s macro valuation and return models to this setup to gauge 2026 equity returns and volatility, alongside its Portfolio Strategy team's separate 7600 target.

### Backdrop
[REDACTED] frames equity valuations the way it frames bonds: relative to the macro environment rather than to long-run averages. Its model explains broad S&P 500 valuation shifts with three macro variables — the 10-year Treasury yield, the change in unemployment, and core inflation — plus a slow-moving demographic factor. The gap between this "macro-consistent" valuation and actual valuation is its measure of whether equities are rich or cheap versus their usual macro relationship, and it argues this measure combined with a forward view of those variables predicts returns better than valuation alone. AI optimism has been a central pillar of the strong US returns of the past two years.

### Unpacked
**The note's real message is not the ~5% number but the structural tension it exposes: a cycle strong enough to justify further upside sitting on top of valuations rich enough to make any cyclical disappointment unusually costly.** The two [REDACTED] approaches bracket the outcome — Portfolio Strategy's 7600 target implies ~10% upside, while the macro model, dragged down by its 7pp valuation penalty, lands nearer 5%. [REDACTED] deliberately does not reconcile them, presenting the macro model as a cross-check that surfaces the trade-off rather than a competing forecast.

**Much of the discussion is about why the valuation drag might be smaller than it looks.** The CAPE denominator uses trailing 10-year earnings, so if AI is leading investors to capitalize future earnings before they arrive, the metric overstates richness. Separately, the productivity-led growth mix means the labor market may look softer per unit of GDP, causing the unemployment-based cycle proxy to understate the macro tailwind. Both arguments push the same way — toward returns being better than the mechanical model output — without asserting the overvaluation is illusory.

**The operational takeaway is to pair long risk with long longer-dated volatility.** The late-1990s analogy is the anchor: stocks kept rising while volatility and credit spreads reset higher as risk premium rose. Because longer-dated vol is still below average, protective options and longer-dated call structures — capturing further upside while capping downside — are cheaper and more viable than in 1998–2000. [REDACTED] frames positioning for higher longer-dated volatility as sensible even if the macro backdrop stays benign and AI optimism holds, since the fatter downside tail is a property of the valuation level itself, not a call that the cycle is about to turn.

subject: US Daily: January Payrolls Preview
summary:
# January Payrolls +45k: Below Consensus as Birth-Death Reset and Benchmark Revision Land

**Theme:** Soft nonfarm payrolls into a report reshaped by the annual benchmark revision and a birth-death methodology change  
**Markets:** US labour market  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Ronnie Walker, 8 February 2026  

### Estimates
- **+45k** nonfarm payrolls in January, below consensus of +70k and the two-month average of +53k.
- **+45k** private payrolls, below consensus of +75k and the two-month average of +44k.
- **0k** government payrolls: a −10k federal decline (hiring freeze, possible year-end deferred resignations) offset by +10k state and local.
- **4.4%** unemployment rate, unchanged from December (unrounded 4.38%), with risk skewed toward rounding down to 4.3%.
- **+0.35% m/m** average hourly earnings, helped by positive calendar effects.
- **−750k to −900k** estimated final annual benchmark payrolls revision for April 2024–March 2025, smaller than the BLS preliminary −911k because QCEW job growth has since been revised up.

### Outlook
- **Unemployment risk skews down, not flat.** The bar to round to 4.3% is low, and the January rate shows modestly negative residual seasonality — the unrounded rate has fallen in each of the last three Januarys.
- **Layoffs stayed low, but the seasonal offset is muted.** Subdued end-of-year layoffs would normally lift seasonally adjusted January hiring, but seasonal factors have adapted to expect smaller January declines, limiting the boost.
- **The birth-death methodology change adds forward volatility.** Incorporating current sample information each month should shrink future annual revisions, but at the cost of greater month-to-month payroll swings.
- **A downward post-benchmark revision (April–December 2025) is likely,** reflecting the QCEW slowdown and weak establishment-survey private payrolls.
- No explicit trade idea is offered; this is a data preview.

### Unpacked
This is an unusually noisy report because two structural changes land on top of the monthly print. The headline call of +45k sits below consensus, and the drivers pulling it down are largely mechanical: **the birth-death model — updated with this report — could add 30–50k fewer jobs than in recent months, and the alternative "big data" indicators [REDACTED] tracks averaged just 39k, pointing to a subdued private-sector pace.** Government hiring is expected to net to zero, with the federal freeze and lingering deferred resignations offsetting modest state and local gains.

The main upside argument is layoffs, which matter more in January than in any other month. Initial claims averaged 206k in the payroll month versus 218k in December, and the Business Trends survey showed far fewer firms cutting staff than in recent years. Challenger announced layoffs jumped 73k on a raw basis, but only 8k seasonally adjusted — near the bottom of the past year's range. **The catch is that low January layoffs no longer buy much: because end-of-year layoffs have been light for several years running, the seasonal factors already expect smaller January declines, raising the bar for any seasonally-adjusted boost.** Retail and construction should rebound — retail because weaker-than-usual holiday hiring means fewer January cuts, construction because poor December weather depressed the prior month — and the end of worker strikes adds 1.5k.

A few factors wash out. Winter storm Fern formed roughly a week after the reference week, so most workers would have been counted as employed regardless, and it is not expected to drag on payrolls. Employer survey trackers stayed in contraction (manufacturing −1.1pt to 48.7, services flat at 49.7), but [REDACTED] gives them little weight given their unreliable post-pandemic signal.

**The bigger story is the benchmark and methodology overhaul, which will dominate how this report is read.** The annual benchmark revision is set to be the largest since at least 2000, cutting the March 2025 employment level by roughly 800k; [REDACTED] sees the final number landing at −750k to −900k rather than the preliminary −911k. Alongside it, the BLS updates net birth-death forecasts for April–December 2025 — a downward revision looks likely — and switches the model to incorporate current sample information each month. Going forward, that change is the one to watch: it should dampen future annual revisions but make individual monthly prints jumpier, so month-to-month payroll swings deserve more caution than usual.
