subject: USA: Factory Orders Well Above Expectations but Roughly in Line With Our Expectations; Capex Orders and Shipments Revised Down; Lowering Q4 GDP Tracking to +2.0% on Wider Trade Deficit
summary:
# US Q4 GDP Tracking Cut to +2.0% as a Wider Trade Deficit Offsets an In-Line Factory Orders Beat

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US factory orders and Q4 GDP tracking  
**General comment:** Routine data comment; the headline beat is discounted as already anticipated, and the net read is a modest downgrade to growth.

### Context
A reaction to the November factory orders and trade balance releases (published 29 January 2026), used to update [REDACTED]'s running Q4 GDP tracking estimate.

### The case
- **The factory orders beat is less impressive than the headline suggests.** Orders rose 2.7% in November, well above the 1.6% consensus, but essentially matched [REDACTED]'s own +2.4% call, so the surprise was to the market, not to the house view. Stripping out transportation, orders rose only 0.2%, and the prior month was revised down 1.2%.
- **The capital goods details softened on revision.** Core capital goods orders growth was revised down 0.3pp to +0.4% and core capital goods shipments down 0.2pp to +0.2% — the components most relevant for business investment moved the wrong way. Durable goods orders were unrevised at +5.3%, but the ex-transportation cut (down 0.1pp to +0.4%) points the same direction.
- **Trade, not factory orders, drove the GDP downgrade.** The details of the same-day trade balance report came in weaker than prior tracking assumptions, implying a wider trade deficit and a larger drag from net exports. With factory orders roughly as expected, the trade miss is what moved the estimate.

### Implications
- Q4 GDP tracking is cut 0.4pp to +2.0% (q/q annualized), with domestic final sales at +1.4% and private domestic final sales at +2.5%.
- The gap between the soft headline GDP figure and the firmer +2.5% private domestic final sales reading suggests trade and other volatile components, rather than underlying private demand, account for the markdown.

subject: USA: Trade Deficit Widens by More Than Expected; Initial Claims Remain Low; Productivity Growth and Unit Labor Costs Unrevised
summary:
# US Data: Trade Deficit Blows Past Estimates While Productivity Holds and Labor Claims Stay Low

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US macro data (trade, productivity, labor)  
**General comment:** Neutral data readout; the trade miss is the notable surprise and a downside signal for Q4 GDP tracking.

### Context
A same-day roundup of three US releases on 29 January 2026: final Q3 productivity and unit labor costs, the November trade balance, and weekly jobless claims. The trade figure is the outlier versus expectations.

### The case
- **Productivity and unit labor costs came in exactly as expected, with no revisions.** Nonfarm productivity held at +4.9% annualized in Q3 (+1.9% year-over-year), leaving the post-2019Q4 trend at 2.0% annualized. Unit labor costs were unrevised at -1.9% annualized, though the year-over-year rate was nudged up 0.1pp to +1.3%. Compensation per hour rose +2.9% annualized (+3.2% year-over-year), and the wage tracker sits at +3.4% on both an annualized and year-over-year basis.
- **The November trade deficit widened far more than forecast, and the details are weak.** The gap widened by $27.6bn to $56.8bn — well beyond the -$44.0bn median and [REDACTED]'s own -$37.0bn — as imports rose $16.8bn (pharmaceuticals, computers, semiconductors) and exports fell $10.9bn (partly a $4.2bn drop in gold). Stripping out gold, which is excluded from GDP, the deficit was wider still at $69.8bn, versus $46.9bn in October. These details run below prior GDP tracking assumptions, and Q4 estimates will be revised after the mid-morning data.
- **Labor market data stayed firm.** Initial claims ticked down 1k to 209k, slightly above expectations but off an upwardly-revised prior week; the four-week average edged up to 206k. State moves were mixed (increases in New York, Nebraska, Illinois; declines in Michigan, Kentucky, South Carolina). Continuing claims fell 38k to 1,827k, somewhat below consensus.

### Implications
- The wider goods deficit points to downward pressure on Q4 GDP tracking; the piece defers the actual revision pending later data.
- Steady productivity alongside negative unit labor cost growth keeps the labor-cost backdrop benign for inflation.
- Low initial and falling continuing claims signal no deterioration in the labor market.

subject: US Daily: January FOMC Recap: Some Signs of Stabilization
summary:
# FOMC on hold as labor market shows "some signs of stabilization"; [REDACTED] pushes next cut to June

**Theme:** Better growth and a stabilizing labor market keep the Fed patient; the path back to cutting is slow.  
**Markets:** US monetary policy  
**Source:** [REDACTED] (David Mericle), 28 January 2026

### Definitive impacts
- The FOMC held the policy rate unchanged at this meeting.
- The statement now says the unemployment rate has shown "some signs of stabilization" and dropped the prior reference to risen downside risks to employment.
- Per the December dot plot, 15 of 19 participants anticipate additional normalization.
- The projected terminal rate under [REDACTED]'s cut path is 3–3.25%, roughly the middle of participants' estimates of the appropriate terminal rate.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] pencils in the next 25bp cut in June and a final cut in September, mainly because inflation improvement will be slow to build a strong FOMC consensus to normalize.
- [REDACTED] expects the labor market to stay stable this year, with unemployment moving sideways in the mid-4s — a view it shares with the FOMC but does not treat as settled.
- [REDACTED] sees inflation progress as gradual: even on its own forecast (core PCE falling to 2.1% by year-end, more optimistic than the FOMC's and the consensus), year-over-year core PCE stays closer to 3% than 2% until mid-year.
- [REDACTED] reads Powell as not treating labor-market stabilization as definitive, citing his caveats about "continued cooling" — a view [REDACTED] explicitly endorses.

### At issue
At its January meeting the FOMC left rates on hold and softened its labor-market language, citing "clear improvement in the outlook for growth" and "evidence of stabilization" in employment. Powell called the Committee "well-positioned" (a word he used five times) to stay on hold while assessing incoming data. He described the stance as "loosely neutral" or "somewhat restrictive," said inflation is running "just a bit above 2%" excluding tariffs, and indicated that once tariff effects fade "we can loosen policy." He qualified the stabilization signal — "some signs of stabilization" but "wouldn't go too far with that," pointing to the latest decline in the Conference Board's job-availability measure as continued cooling. Powell declined to address questions on the Governor Lisa Cook court case, the DOJ investigation into him, and whether he will remain a governor after his term as Chair ends.

### Unpacked
The meeting's signal was one of patience rather than a turn. The trigger for cutting is explicit and asymmetric: Powell said "clearly a weakening labor market calls for cutting," but with both the Fed and [REDACTED] expecting unemployment to hold in the mid-4s, that trigger is not expected to fire. **Absent renewed labor-market weakness, the bar for the next move is an inflation story that takes months to play out, not a growth or jobs shock.**

The constraint is the composition of the Committee, not just the aggregate forecast. Some participants prefer to read official core PCE as reported and, largely for that reason, remain reluctant to cut. **Because year-over-year core PCE stays near 3% into mid-year even on [REDACTED]'s optimistic path, a strong consensus to normalize cannot form until the data visibly improve** — which is why the next cut is pencilled in for June rather than sooner.

The note offers no explicit trade idea; it is a policy-path call. For the reader, the operative takeaway is a data-dependent hold with two cuts back-loaded into June and September to a 3–3.25% terminal rate, and a labor market whose stabilization is the swing variable — firm enough to keep the Fed on hold, soft enough that a downside surprise would pull cuts forward.

subject: USA: FOMC Leaves Fed Funds Rate Unchanged, With Dissents by Waller and Miran; Post-Meeting Statement Notes “Solid” Growth and “Stabilization” in the Unemployment Rate
summary:
# USA: Fed holds at 3.5–3.75% as statement turns more upbeat on growth and jobs, drawing two dovish dissents

**Source:** [REDACTED], Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US monetary policy — FOMC January decision  
**General comment:** Neutral readout of a hawkish-leaning hold; the dissents came from the dovish side, favoring a cut.

### Context
The FOMC held the federal funds target range steady at 3.5–3.75% at its January 2026 meeting, in a statement that upgraded its read on the economy while two governors pushed for easing.

### The case
- **The Committee kept rates unchanged, but not unanimously.** The target range stayed at 3.5–3.75%. Governors Waller and Miran dissented, both preferring a 25bp cut — signaling a dovish minority against the decision to hold.
- **The statement's economic characterization turned firmer, especially on growth and the labor market.** Growth was described as "solid," an upgrade from "moderate." On jobs, the Committee said the unemployment rate had "shown some signs of stabilization" — even while noting job gains "remained low" — and dropped its prior language about rising downside risk to the labor market. Inflation was still called "somewhat elevated," left unchanged.

### Implications
- The combination of a firmer growth and labor-market assessment with removal of downside-risk language reads as a step back from a near-term easing bias, despite the two dissents.
- The split vote marks a dovish faction on the Committee willing to cut now, a divide to watch at coming meetings.

subject: Global Markets Daily: EUR Curve Steep But Stable
summary:
# EUR 10s30s: Steep, Stable, and Still a Reasonable Carry Trade

**Theme:** Whether the EUR long-end curve has more room to steepen, and why steepeners remain a good expression despite limited upside  
**Markets:** Euro-area rates (long-end curve)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], George Cole, 28 January 2026

### Definitive impacts
- Dutch pension reform (DB-to-DC transition, eligible from the start of 2026) is estimated at 20–30bp of 10s30s steepening, benchmarked against the reduction in DB liabilities.
- Up to half of the total 2025 10s30s steepening is attributed to foreign spillovers rather than domestic euro-area drivers.
- The macro curve model shows 10s30s currently sits modestly too steep versus its macro-fitted value; adjusting the model for Dutch DB pension liabilities flips this to roughly 10bp too flat.
- Each percentage point of government bond free-float (debt stock less central bank holdings) steepens 10s30s by about 1bp in the macro model.
- Early-2026 supply is being absorbed smoothly: strong syndication demand (bid-to-cover), record issuance volumes, new 20y syndicated bonds in France and Italy, and stable Bund spreads.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] sees EUR long-end curves (e.g. 10s30s) remaining steep but stable, arguing the baseline macro outlook is well-priced and leaves only modest room for further steepening.
- [REDACTED] keeps 10s30s steepeners as a recommended trade, citing a favourable carry-to-vol profile and cheap tail-risk hedging given low implied volatility.
- Near-term risks are seen as skewed toward steeper curves: a re-emergence of European trade risks would anchor the front end and likely trigger further fiscal expansion, and shifts in global long ends could add steepening pressure.
- [REDACTED] expects little follow-through from the front end to the long end, since the ECB is on hold and the back end trades less directionally with near-term rate expectations outside acute hiking/cutting cycles.
- [REDACTED] views the JGB curve as too steep (with ongoing volatility risk) and sees Gilt risk-premium reduction, on an improving UK backdrop, as the main bullish spot in the G4.

### Backdrop
Through 2025 the back end of the EUR curve steepened notably, with 10s30s among the most profitable vol-adjusted curve trades in European and global rates. This reflected a broader G4 rebalancing of supply and demand for duration: elevated deficits and central-bank QT raised government bond free-floats, while higher rates cut pension and insurance liabilities and shifting retirement-savings mixes structurally reduced long-end demand. Two macro forces overlapped with the Dutch story — inflation normalisation allowing ECB cuts from above-neutral levels, and German fiscal expansion pushing up European duration risk premium. The note judges these macro factors as now well-priced.

### At issue
The Dutch pension reform lets funds transition from defined-benefit to defined-contribution schemes from the start of 2026. This lowers hedging demand for long-dated liabilities and reduces duration holdings relative to equities and other real assets — a structural flow supporting long-end steepening. The note assesses how much of this is already in the price and whether further steepening is warranted, concluding the fundamental flows offer only limited remaining room.

### Unpacked
The steepening of 2025 invites a simple question: is the Dutch pension trade played out? **The answer is largely yes on the macro picture, but not entirely on the flows.** The EUR move was not an outlier within the G4, and the similar performance of bond and swap curves argues against a purely fiscal, spread-widening story — pointing instead to broad, shared supply-demand drivers.

**The reform's fundamental flows still leave some room, but only a little.** Headlines around the reform have produced short-lived curve reactions, suggesting the market is roughly correctly positioned; price action this year does not indicate the flows are fully behind us, yet the model-implied gap is small. With the ECB parked and the long end trading independently of front-end pricing, the residual steepening impulse from macro is modest.

**The stronger case for staying in steepeners is carry and cheap optionality, not directional conviction.** The carry-to-vol profile is favourable, and low implied vol makes steepeners an inexpensive hedge should growth disappoint. Persistent supply — especially German and EU borrowing needs, with slower WAM reduction than the UK or Japan — should keep the long end steep, though markets may prove unusually sensitive to long-end issuance given the duration-demand backdrop and a high bar for adjusting ECB QT.

The note carries an explicit house trade to stay in 10s30s steepeners, alongside a broad cross-asset trade list unrelated to the EUR thesis.

subject: Global Markets Analyst: Japan's Equilibrium Rate Check — A Framework for JGBs and JPY
summary:
# Japan Nears an Inflection Point: With Inflation Heading to 2%, Intervention Without Tightening Only Buys Temporary Relief for the Yen and JGBs

**Theme:** FX intervention risk vs. a shift in the domestic policy mix  
**Markets:** Japan rates and FX (JGBs and JPY)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], George Cole, 28 January 2026
### Landscape
- Japanese inflation swaps are approaching 2%, with long-dated JGB forwards at levels similar to other G10 rates markets.
- 2-year JGB yields at 1.2%, above the 1% threshold beyond which the correlation pattern between the curve and rates tends to shift.
- Long-end real rates have already been rising alongside inflation since 2024, but front-end real rates, while off their lows, remain deeply negative.
- Inflation volatility in Japan is higher than rate volatility, unlike in the G3, where the central bank's reaction function reverses that relationship.

### Drivers
- Rising inflation expectations are the central force: with nominal rates pinned near the effective lower bound (ELB), real rates are determined by inflation, which weakens the Yen and favors equities via lower real rates.
- Asymmetric fiscal risk skewed toward more stimulus: the upcoming election tilts the balance toward additional stimulus, and news of more spending weakens the Yen rather than strengthening it — the opposite of what standard models would suggest.
- Signals of coordinated intervention: the NY Fed's "rate check," alongside signals from the MoF and the BoJ, have raised intervention risk; the US Treasury is reported to have acted to strengthen the JPY.
- An incipient shift in the correlation regime: since 2024, real rates at longer maturities have started rising with inflation, moving Japan closer to the "DM" pattern — the metric to watch is 2-year yields, where a rise from here tends to flatten the curve.
- Macro data as a stabilizing factor: if inflationary pressure in Japan eventually moderates or the USD weakens broadly, rate and FX volatility could ease — which is why JGB yields are seen as too high relative to the macro forecasts.

### Risks
- Downside (for JPY/JGBs): if the policy preference is intervention without monetary or fiscal tightening, relief for the Yen and JGBs tends to be temporary, with a risk of transmitting volatility to other assets.
- Upside (for JPY/JGBs): intervention accompanied by fiscal restraint, faster BoJ tightening, and a focus on upside inflation risks would have a more durable effect.
- The report judges fiscal policy as the fastest route to durably support JGBs and the JPY, whether via a tighter election outcome or a policy shift.

### Unpacked
Since Abenomics began in 2012, Japan's policy mix has aimed to raise inflation expectations and keep real rates low. Under Ueda, the BoJ has raised rates gradually, but cautiously given fragile inflation. **The central thesis is that the recent volatility in Japanese rates and FX is a consequence of rising inflation expectations, not a pricing error to be corrected by intervention.** With inflation now heading toward 2%, the question is whether the dynamic that prevailed near the ELB will persist.

Within a liquidity trap and with inflation below target, it makes sense that higher inflation weakens the Yen and supports equities via lower real rates — and that fiscal stimulus weakens, rather than strengthens, the currency. **This is the inverse of the usual G10 pattern, where stronger inflation lifts front-end real rates via the central bank's reaction function, generating a positive correlation between real rates and inflation.** Since 2024, however, this relationship has begun to change at longer maturities, even though the market still operates as if policy will remain behind the curve.

The signal to monitor is the correlation between the level of 2-year yields and the slope of the 2s10s curve. Over the past 30 years, higher 2-year yields have come with a steeper curve — consistent with being near the ELB. **Restricting the sample to periods with 2-year yields above 1%, the correlation turns low or negative, and with the current 2-year at 1.2%, the risk skews toward a flatter curve if rates rise — the typical G10 pattern.** The same shows up in the analysis of G4 markets: when inflation is well below target, higher inflation steepens the curve; once it reaches or exceeds target, the correlation falls and can turn negative.

The assessment of policy options starts from the ability to contain not just market volatility but also inflation risk. The standard response to reduce upside inflation risk would be to raise rates enough to tighten financial conditions, or to tighten fiscal policy — both of which reduce growth expectations. **Isolated intervention, in the Yen or in JGBs, reduces volatility in the directly affected asset, but, absent other changes, risks transmitting volatility to other assets or having only a temporary effect.** Bilateral intervention would be more potent and credible, but would require additional policy commitments from Japan.

**Mapping the policy choices shows the market's reaction to the current mix is broadly correct:** fiscal expansion combined with gradual rate hikes should produce a weaker currency, higher yields, a steeper curve and strong equities — a normal reflation dynamic, not a fiscal-risk episode in which all domestic assets sell off together, as seen in the UK. That is why the gap between the Yen and the [REDACTED] model — based mainly on nominal rate differentials and risk sentiment — does not represent a pricing error, but reflects the fact that such models rely on correlations that do not hold in every regime.

Recent actions expose the tension between the prevailing framework and policymakers' revealed preferences: US officials voiced concern over JGB volatility, the BoJ suggested adjusting bond purchases to contain the long end, and Japanese officials said they were uncomfortable with a weak Yen. **Reducing rate and FX volatility at the same time, without changing the policy mix or the macro backdrop, is a difficult task — and unless the BoJ accelerates hikes or fiscal policy becomes more restrictive, intervention alone should not durably stabilize inflation risk.** The BoJ's framework includes more oversight and coordination with the government than that of other Western central banks, as the FX response after Prime Minister Takaichi's victory in the LDP leadership race demonstrated.

That is why fiscal policy stands out as the fastest route to durably support JGBs and the JPY, whether through a tighter election outcome or a policy shift. There are signs in that direction, with Takaichi emphasizing that a potential food-tax holiday would be temporary and without new debt issuance — rhetoric worth watching. **The unusual prospect of combined MoF and US Treasury intervention should reduce the odds of a weaker Yen in the near term and contain JGB volatility for now, but without fundamental disinflationary policies to reinforce it, relief for USDJPY and long-end JGBs is likely to be short-lived.**

subject: USA: Consumer Confidence and Labor Differential Decline Sharply
summary:
# US Consumer Confidence Collapses in January, With the Labor Differential at a Near Five-Year Low

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US consumer confidence and labor-market sentiment  
**General comment:** A descriptive data comment flagging a sharp, worse-than-expected deterioration in sentiment and jobs perceptions.

### Context
Reaction to the January release of the Conference Board consumer confidence index, which came in far below both [REDACTED]'s own estimate (90.5) and the median forecast (91.0), and well under the upwardly revised December reading.

### The case
- **Confidence fell sharply and broadly, to its weakest level since March 2014.** The headline index dropped 9.7pt to 84.5, missing expectations by a wide margin even as December was revised up 5.1pt to 94.2. The decline was not concentrated: both the expectations component (-9.5pt to 65.1) and the present situation component (-9.9pt to 113.7) fell hard, and the Conference Board noted that all five sub-components deteriorated, describing confidence as having "collapsed."
- **The labor differential dropped to its lowest since February 2021, pointing to a softer read on the jobs market.** The gap between respondents saying jobs are "plentiful" (-3.6pp to 23.9%) and those saying jobs are "hard to get" (+1.7pp to 20.8%) narrowed by 5.3pt to 3.1, from an upwardly revised December level of 8.4. Both sides of the measure moved in the weaker direction — fewer see jobs as plentiful, more see them as hard to get.
- **Pessimism was tied to prices, even as the survey's inflation gauge stayed roughly flat.** Twelve-month-ahead inflation expectations edged up 0.3pp to 5.7% from a downwardly revised 5.4%. Write-in responses skewed toward pessimism, with elevated references to prices and inflation, oil and gas, and food and grocery costs.

### Implications
- Signals weakening household sentiment across both current conditions and forward expectations, with the price backdrop cited as the main driver of pessimism.
- The drop in the labor differential is a soft signal on labor-market perceptions, notable given it now sits at a near five-year low.
- Note the timing caveat: preliminary results had a January 16 cutoff date.

subject: Global Markets Daily: One, Big, Beautiful Refund
summary:
# One, Big, Beautiful Refund: A Bigger Tax-Season Dip in Subprime Delinquencies

**Theme:** How a larger 2026 tax refund flows through to lower-income consumer credit and ABS delinquencies  
**Markets:** US consumer ABS (subprime auto, consumer unsecured)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Ben Shumway, 27 January 2026  

### Definitive impacts
- +$1,000 to the average household tax refund this year per the Treasury factsheet — a ~31% rise over last year's $3,230 average per filer, driven by retroactive 2025 tax cuts without a matching adjustment to withholding rates.
- Serious (90+ day) delinquencies fall on average by 2bp in Q2 versus a 1bp rise in other quarters (2003–present, broad consumer lending), with credit card, mortgage and "other" debt all showing average Q2 declines.
- Subprime auto ABS 30+ day delinquencies fall on average 1.3% from March to April, versus +14bp in other month-to-month transitions — against a generally rising delinquency trend over the period.
- Consumer unsecured ABS 30+ day delinquencies fall on average ~19–20bp from March to April, versus +2bp in other transitions.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] expects this year's seasonal delinquency dip to be somewhat larger than usual: roughly 1.7% for subprime auto and ~26bp for consumer unsecured, versus the typical 1.3% and ~20bp.
- The benefit will concentrate in subprime auto — where delinquencies are at record highs — and to a lesser degree in consumer unsecured, the segments most weighted toward lower-income borrowers; credit card ABS skews prime and is expected to benefit little.
- [REDACTED] rejects any parallel to COVID-era stimulus: the ~$1,000 refund is far smaller than the $6,400+ a lower-income dual-adult household received then, and today lacks that period's unique backdrop, so the effect should be muted and short-lived rather than a prolonged dampening of delinquencies and losses.

### Backdrop
Tax refund season already produces a modest, recurring improvement in consumer credit performance each spring, as filers use refunds to catch up on payments. That effect is uneven across products: it is strongest where lower-income borrowers concentrate — unsecured personal loans (part of "other" debt) and subprime auto — and weakest in prime-skewed segments like credit card ABS, which carry structurally lower delinquency rates than the broader credit card population.

The 2026 setup sits against a "K-shaped" economy debate: benign hard data (stable unemployment, solid GDP, stretched valuations) alongside weak consumer sentiment and stress in pockets such as record-high subprime auto delinquencies. In response, the administration has pushed a series of affordability measures — largely targeting mortgage affordability, plus a proposed 10% cap on credit card interest rates.

### At issue
The 2026 tax filing season opened officially on 26 January. The earlier One, Big, Beautiful Bill Act cut taxes for consumers retroactively for 2025, but withholding rates were left unchanged — mechanically producing larger-than-normal refunds. A newly published Treasury factsheet estimates the average household refund will run about $1,000 higher than last year, framing this spring as a checkpoint for the affordability agenda.

### Unpacked
The note starts from a simple observation and pushes it one step further. **Because refunds already lower delinquencies every spring, a refund that is ~31% larger should deepen that seasonal dip — but only at the margin, not on a stimulus-era scale.** The whole analysis is an exercise in sizing: take the historical seasonal move, scale it modestly for the extra cash, and land on 1.7% for subprime auto and ~26bp for consumer unsecured.

**The mechanism matters more than the headline number: the refund bump exists only because withholding was never adjusted to the retroactive 2025 cuts, so it is a one-off timing effect rather than a durable increase in take-home pay.** That framing is what justifies the "muted and short-term" call and the explicit distancing from COVID — the payment is a fraction of pandemic transfers and lacks the surrounding economic conditions that made that episode's credit improvement so pronounced and persistent.

The targeting logic ties the pieces together: the benefit lands where lower-income borrowers cluster, which is why subprime auto — the segment currently under the most stress — is flagged as the primary beneficiary, with consumer unsecured second and prime-heavy credit card ABS largely unaffected.

The note offers no explicit trade idea tied to this thesis; the standing "Best Trade Ideas" list is a separate cross-asset appendix unrelated to the tax-refund analysis. For the reader, the practical takeaway is a modestly better-than-seasonal Q2 for subprime auto and consumer unsecured ABS delinquencies, with the improvement expected to fade rather than mark a structural turn.

subject: Global Rates Notes: 1Q26 Treasury Refunding Preview
summary:
# Treasury to Lift Q1 Borrowing to $640bn; Coupon Sizes Held, Guidance Likely Unchanged

**Theme:** 1Q26 refunding — higher near-term borrowing, no coupon size change, and three watch-items (forward guidance, SOFR FRN, buyback switches)  
**Markets:** US Treasury supply / rates  
**Source:** [REDACTED], William Marshall, 26 January 2026  

### Estimates
- **$640bn** marketable borrowing for Q1, up from the **$578bn** projected at the November refunding; estimate to be released 3pm Monday, February 2.
- **$290bn** marketable borrowing for Q2, assuming an **$850bn** TGA target.
- **No change** to nominal coupon, FRN, or TIPS auction sizes at the February 4 decision (documents released 8:30am).
- **$326bn** net bill supply in Q1 and **$2bn** in Q2, assuming a stable liquidity-support buyback envelope and $85bn of cash-management buybacks in Q2.
- **Fed bill purchases** to absorb **$184bn** in Q1 and **$151bn** in Q2.
- **Coupon auction size increases** still expected to begin **November 2026**, skewed to the front-end and belly, with no increases in 10s through 30s.

### Outlook
- **Forward-looking guidance likely little changed**, per the analyst: the "next several quarters" language probably stays, with a possible tweak from "has begun to preliminarily consider future increases" to "continues to consider." A November start to coupon increases argues for a more substantive change, but Treasury's apparently lower deficit assumption (vs [REDACTED] economists' $2.05tn FY26) supports a status-quo signal for now.
- **A 1y SOFR-linked FRN would see solid uptake**, in the analyst's view — it counts as 1-day maturity for money-fund WAM, compares directly to repo lending, and gives Treasury another front-end issuance point. Any decision is not expected quickly; the meeting may signal how seriously it is being explored.
- **Supply absorption is not a concern** given low vol, compressed dispersion, and wider swap spreads, despite episodic policy/geopolitical volatility.
- **No active adjustment to the issuance mix expected** to lower borrowing costs, despite the administration's affordability focus.
- The note offers **no explicit trade idea**.

### Unpacked
The immediate story is a modest upward revision to near-term funding, with the Q1 marketable borrowing estimate rising to $640bn from the $578bn pencilled in at November's meeting, and Q2 seen at $290bn against an assumed $850bn cash balance target. **The mechanics leave coupon, FRN and TIPS auction sizes untouched this quarter, so the adjustment falls almost entirely on bills** — net bill supply of $326bn in Q1 against just $2bn in Q2 — while Fed bill purchases absorb a meaningful share on the demand side. The market backdrop of low volatility, compressed dispersion and wider swap spreads is read as consistent with easy absorption of that supply.

Beyond the numbers, three questions frame what to watch on February 4. The first is the forward guidance. **The baseline is that Treasury sticks with a status-quo signal, softening its language only marginally even though coupon increases are expected to begin this November** — a restraint attributed to Treasury apparently working from a lower deficit assumption than the $2.05tn FY26 figure used by [REDACTED] economists.

The second is product design. A 1y SOFR-linked FRN is seen as attractive because it would register as a 1-day maturity for money-fund weighted-average-maturity purposes while its stated maturity governs weighted-average-life, and because it maps cleanly onto repo as an alternative. **The complication is that the existing 2y FRN is linked to T-bills and already faces liquidity challenges, so Treasury must decide how to run two FRN products in parallel** — a decision unlikely to come fast.

The third is the buyback program. Treasury has floated "exchange" operations that swap off-the-run securities into more liquid on-the-runs, which carries duration-neutrality and risk-management appeal but departs from current practice. **Unless auction sizes were cut in tandem, moving to switches would add duration to the market — manageable at the front-end and belly where issuance is set to rise anyway, but a likely surprise at the long end.** Also on the table is converting 7s from a monthly new issue to a quarterly cycle with two reopenings, akin to 10s, with potential benefits for market liquidity (fewer CUSIPs) and dealer balance-sheet efficiency weighed against on-the-run liquidity concerns.

Going forward, the concrete near-term catalysts are the February 2 financing estimates and the February 4 refunding documents; the medium-term signposts are the anticipated November start to coupon size increases and any firming of Treasury's stance on the SOFR FRN and buyback switches.

subject: Top of Mind: Americas First
summary:
# Top of Mind: The "Donroe Doctrine" and the Return of Hemispheric Power Politics

**Theme:** "America First" widening into "Americas First" — a more forceful US posture in the Western Hemisphere and its market fallout  
**Markets:** Latin American economies, oil, EM assets, US-Europe relations  
**Source:** [REDACTED] (Allison Nathan), 26 January 2026  

### Landscape
- The Trump Administration opened 2026 with a more forceful foreign policy framed as the "Donroe Doctrine", extending "America First" into an "Americas First" focus on the Western Hemisphere.
- Oil sits at the center of recent events, with Venezuela and the broader region named as the immediate flashpoints.
- The note's contributors agree the doctrine points to more US action across the hemisphere, with the rise in geopolitical risk seen as its most profound implication.

### Drivers
- Both Mauricio Claver-Carone (Trump's former Special Envoy for Latin America) and Hal Brands (Johns Hopkins SAIS) read the doctrine as a deliberate shift that portends further US intervention in the region.
- Regional economic implications are assessed by [REDACTED]'s Alberto Ramos; oil-market implications by [REDACTED]'s Neil Mehta and Daan Struyven.
- Ivan Krastev (Centre for Liberal Strategies) frames US-Europe relations as heading into a rocky period but not a "divorce".

### Risks
- **Geopolitical (both directions):** The analysts flag rising geopolitical risk as the doctrine's most profound implication; the specific scenarios and magnitudes are not detailed in the provided text.

### Unpacked
This note is the intro to a [REDACTED] "Top of Mind" survey; the provided text is a teaser, not the analysis itself. **The organizing idea is that "America First" is evolving into "Americas First" under what the report calls the Donroe Doctrine, and the panel's shared read is that this means more US action across the Western Hemisphere.** The substantive discussion — motives, economic and oil-market consequences, and portfolio implications — sits in the full report and is only named, not developed, here.

subject: US Economics Weekly Update 1/26/2026
summary:
# FOMC on Hold, Cuts Deferred to Mid-Year as Growth and Investment Outrun Consensus

**Theme:** Steady policy while the labor market stabilizes; growth momentum into 2026  
**Markets:** US macro & monetary policy  
**Source:** [REDACTED], David Mericle, 26 January 2026  

### Landscape
- Funds rate held unchanged at the January FOMC after three cuts already delivered; next 25bp cut penciled for June, a final cut in September to 3–3.25%.
- 2025 Q4 GDP tracking raised to 2.4%, with full-quarter real GDP now estimated at 2.5% Q4/Q4.
- Real personal spending up 0.3% in both October and November; saving rate down to 3.5%.
- Real construction spending rose 0.9% in October, unchanged in September.
- Core capital goods orders +0.7% and shipments +0.4% in November.

### Drivers
- **Labor-market stabilization** is the pivot: as it firms, the case for further easing weakens, and inflation is not seen falling fast enough to build a strong FOMC consensus for another cut before mid-year.
- **Business investment** is expected to be the fastest-growing part of GDP again this year, supported by firm core capital goods orders and shipments.
- **Consumer spending** remains solid heading into a tax-cut tailwind — roughly $100bn added to household refunds over the February–April filing season.
- **Fed leadership uncertainty**: prediction markets have cycled through three frontrunners for the next chair in three weeks; after a Trump comment, weight shifted away from Kevin Hassett toward Rick Rieder and Kevin Warsh.

### Risks
- **Downside (labor):** the 2026 baseline assumes labor-market stabilization; the analyst's own 2025 review notes the labor market softened somewhat more than expected, a trajectory that would keep cuts on the table if it persists.
- **Downside (AI displacement):** net job losses in the most AI-exposed industries are expected to increase meaningfully this year.
- **Policy path skew:** the analyst expects no meaningful further rise in the effective tariff rate and no major new fiscal stimulus ahead of the midterms — but flags tariffs as the key forecast miss of 2025, when the White House imposed far larger duties than expected.

### Unpacked
The January meeting is framed as a non-event. Only minor statement changes and few path hints are expected, with Powell likely to stress that three cuts already delivered should help stabilize the labor market, leaving the Committee well positioned to wait and assess their impact. **The logic for patience is that further easing loses urgency once the labor market steadies, and inflation is unlikely to fall fast enough to forge a strong cutting consensus before June.**

On activity, the picture is one of durable momentum. **Growth and business investment are both expected to beat consensus in 2026, with investment again the fastest-growing component of GDP.** The consumer enters the year with solid spending and a lower saving rate, and a February–April refund boost of roughly $100bn provides near-term support.

The note's centerpiece is its top-10 questions for 2026, a set of directional calls. Growth beats consensus, investment beats consensus, the Fed cuts again, core goods inflation falls at least 1pp, shelter inflation drops below 2.75%, and wage pressures stay compatible with 2% inflation. **The "no" answers are as telling as the "yes" answers: single-family starts do not rebound above 1 million, the effective tariff rate does not rise meaningfully further, and no major fiscal stimulus arrives before the midterms — while AI-exposed job losses do increase meaningfully.**

The retrospective on 2025 sharpens the confidence bands. Right: growth and spending beating consensus, three Fed cuts, a sharp immigration decline, and no meaningful primary-deficit reduction. **Wrong: far larger tariffs than expected, a labor market that softened a bit more, and a neutral-rate estimate that failed to rise further** — the same tariff and labor threads that shadow the 2026 baseline.

subject: US Economics Analyst: 10 Questions for 2026
summary:
# 2026 US Outlook: Above-Consensus Growth, Inflation Back to Target, Two More Fed Cuts

**Theme:** A calmer policy year in which fiscal tailwinds replace tariff drag  
**Markets:** US macro (growth, labor, inflation, rates)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], David Mericle, 26 January 2026  

### Landscape
- 2026 Q4/Q4 GDP growth seen at 2.5% vs 2.1% consensus (2.9% vs 2.4% full-year), above consensus for the fourth straight year; 2025 Q4/Q4 is tracking around 2.5%.
- Core PCE inflation ended 2025 near 3% and is forecast to fall to 2.1% by December 2026.
- Core goods inflation sits roughly 2pp above its pre-pandemic pace on tariff effects; shelter runs at an official 3¼% year-over-year (closer to 3½% adjusted for a missing October reading).
- The wage growth tracker is at 3.5%, down from a near-6% 2022 peak, with survey expectations at or below that rate; productivity growth is running at 2% this cycle.
- Fed policy rate stands above the 3-3.25% level [REDACTED] expects it to reach by September; the last cut was in December.
- The labor market is now somewhat softer than its pre-pandemic state, with AI-related net job losses so far only about 5-10k in the most exposed subindustries.

### Drivers
- Business investment is the strongest growth engine, seen up just over 5% (double consensus), pushed by AI spending, easier financial conditions, OBBBA tax incentives, and reduced trade-policy uncertainty.
- The net policy-and-financial-conditions impulse swings from a -0.2pp drag in 2025 to a +0.3pp boost in 2026; the OBBBA fiscal impulse averages roughly +0.5pp over Q1-Q3.
- Tariff passthrough is largely spent — most impact lands within five months of implementation, so core goods inflation should fall toward its modestly negative pre-pandemic pace.
- Shelter disinflation is intensifying: the catch-up effect is over and new-lease rent indicators (CoStar, Yardi, Zillow) are running at just 0.5% year-over-year, pointing to 2.3% shelter inflation by December.
- Residential investment stays the weakest component; single-family starts are unlikely to top 1 million, held back by rising vacancy, the lowest household formation in years (immigration at half its 2010s rate), stretched affordability, and construction-labor and land-use supply constraints.
- AI is turning from a minor to a more visible drag on employment — watch for net job losses of at least 20k per month in the most-exposed subindustries in 2026, partly offset by AI-related gains elsewhere.

### Risks
- Upside to growth: the mechanical shutdown swing (from -0.3pp to +0.3pp) plus the policy/financial-conditions impulse could imply faster growth than the 2.5% base case; [REDACTED] deliberately anchors on ~2% potential rather than last year's rate, flagging the risk skew as tilted up.
- Downside to tariffs/inflation: a Supreme Court ruling against the IEEPA tariffs is seen as more likely than not, which — with new deals and exemptions — tilts the effective tariff rate slightly lower rather than higher.
- Labor market: named as the most uncertain piece of the outlook, with the pace of AI-driven displacement the hardest variable to call.

### Unpacked
The through-line of the year is a handoff: the tariff drag that weighed on 2025 gives way to a fiscal and financial-conditions tailwind in 2026, without reigniting inflation. **[REDACTED] frames its above-consensus growth call as unadventurous rather than bold, arguing the arithmetic of the shutdown reversal and the policy impulse actually points higher than its 2.5% forecast.** The conservatism comes from anchoring to a potential growth rate of a bit over 2%, since 2025's GDP prints were distorted by pre-tariff frontloading and mismeasurement.

**Business investment carries the growth story, seen growing just over 5% — double consensus — on AI, tax, and financial-conditions tailwinds.** At the industry level, the revived OBBBA investment incentives cut the cost of capital most in manufacturing, mining, transportation and information, while the loss of green-energy credits hits the power sector; investment in manufacturing structures remains elevated on IRA and CHIPS subsidies whose boost fades further this year. The flip side is net exports, where [REDACTED] sits furthest below consensus, largely because AI equipment is imported.

**Housing stays the laggard, and the note pushes back on the intuition that a national shortage should spark a single-family rebound.** Even with a genuine shortage and policymaker interest in affordability, higher vacancy where building rose most, the weakest household formation in years on collapsed immigration, prices high relative to income against high mortgage rates, and entrenched labor and land-use constraints all cap new construction. Rate strategists expect long-term yields to hold roughly stable, since the two Fed cuts are already priced and builder teaser-rate discounts have likely run their course.

**The labor market is cast as the swing factor, with AI the central unknown.** AI has contributed little to the hiring slowdown so far, but the technology could eventually automate a large share of tasks and displace 6-7% of current jobs; adoption is rising fastest where tasks are most exposed and firms are keen to cut labor costs. The offsetting comfort is that the labor market starts from a soft footing — which is why the note downplays fears that fiscal stimulus revives wage and price pressure. With productivity at 2%, 3.5% wage growth implies unit labor cost growth below 2%, and still-elevated core-services inflation should catch down.

**On inflation, the 2025 stability in core PCE masked two offsetting moves — a falling services trend against a tariff-driven goods bump — and 2026 is where the goods bump unwinds.** With most passthrough behind (peaking around 70%) and no major new tariffs expected before the midterms, core goods should slow by more than 1pp toward its slightly negative pre-pandemic rate. Shelter, the statistically dominant Phillips-curve category, adds another 1pp-plus decline as the catch-up effect ends and leading rent indicators sit at 0.5%.

**The Fed cuts, but not with urgency: [REDACTED] pencils in 25bp in June and a final cut in September to 3-3.25%.** A stabilizing labor market makes further easing less pressing, and leadership will likely want a firmer consensus than backed December's cut, which takes time as the inflation data improve.

**Politically, 2026 is expected to be quiet, shaped by midterms and voter focus on affordability.** The White House is seen avoiding further tariff hikes — with the effective rate likely edging down via deals, exemptions or a Supreme Court ruling against IEEPA tariffs (any Section 122 replacement capped at 15%, possibly 10%; Section 301 alternatives slow and impractical to scale). No major new fiscal stimulus is expected either: Trump's proposed $2,000 per-person tariff rebate has gained no traction among congressional Republicans, held back by a wide deficit, a rising debt-to-GDP path, and GOP opposition to the tariffs that would fund it.

subject: [REDACTED] FX Morning Notes: Intervention intention
summary:
# JPY intervention signal strengthens as US joins the rate check; Canada trade risk resurfaces

**Theme:** Coordinated Yen-buying looks more likely; US-Canada tariff overhang returns  
**Markets:** G10 FX (USD/JPY, USD/CAD)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Lexi Kanter, 26 January 2026  

### Landscape
- Friday's USD/JPY move was large in scale, but its spillover to the broad Dollar was similar to the average response seen in actual MoF Yen-buying interventions over the past three decades.
- Canada's Q4 2025 Business Outlook Survey showed modest improvement in future sales and investment intentions, though most activity indicators remain weak.
- Canadian headline inflation surprised to the upside last week, but the BoC's preferred core measures slowed notably on both a year-over-year and sequential basis.
- CAD's sharpest weakness of 2025 came in January, after President Trump proposed a 25% tariff on Canada.

### Drivers
- The FRBNY reportedly ran a USD/JPY rate check last Friday on behalf of the US Treasury — historically an action that often precedes actual intervention, and here US participation makes the signal stronger than in 2022 or 2024, pointing to likely coordinated Yen-buying.
- Even if intervention occurs, direct operations tend to be only temporary when the macro backdrop justifies currency pressure, as it does now; they can slow the move and buy time for new catalysts rather than reverse it.
- US-Canada trade tensions have re-escalated on weekend reports of a possible 100% additional US tariff on Canada, contingent on Canada striking a trade deal with China.
- Fading tariff headwinds had recently supported improved Canadian domestic data, but the weekend headlines reintroduce uncertainty.

### Risks
- Downside (CAD): renewed US-Canada trade friction is flagged as a key near-term risk; ambiguity over what counts as a China "deal" triggering tariffs keeps the outcome open, though most Canadian exports remain USMCA-exempt and would likely stay so under any new tariffs.
- On JPY, intervention is assessed as likely to slow rather than reverse the move, given the broader backdrop supporting Yen weakness.

### Unpacked
The rate check follows FM Katayama's January 16 verbal intervention warning that Japan was "prepared to take decisive action, including all available options." Rate checks have often preceded actual operations, though timing varies: the last reported check came mid-way through the two-day July 2024 operations, while the September 14, 2022 check preceded intervention by about a week. **What sets this episode apart is the reported US Treasury involvement, which suggests a bilateral approach and makes coordinated intervention likely.** The degree of USD/JPY spillover to the broad Dollar and other majors, however, looks consistent with typical price action after past Yen-buying interventions.

On Canada, PM Mark Carney met President Xi Jinping earlier this month to agree a framework for easing existing trade barriers, but it is unclear whether this "strategic partnership" — or any other agreement — would qualify as a "deal" that triggers the threatened US tariff. **Carney has responded that Canada will honour its USMCA commitment not to enter free trade agreements with nonmarket economies, and has no intention of signing one with China.** Canada has been more exposed than most to US trade-policy uncertainty, with rising unemployment in some trade-intensive sectors and stickier domestic inflation following reciprocal tariffs. The recent data recovery had been encouraging, but the weekend developments show trade relations remain the dominant near-term swing factor for CAD.

subject: US Consumer Dashboard: January 2026: Spending Remains Solid Ahead of Tax Refunds
summary:
# US Consumer Dashboard: Solid Spending Into 2026 on Tax-Refund Tailwind, Even as Income Stays Weak

**Theme:** Resilient consumer spending despite soft income, carried by very strong balance sheets and incoming OBBBA tax cuts  
**Markets:** US consumer / household sector  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jan Hatzius, 26 January 2026  

### Landscape
- Headline retail sales rose 0.6% and core retail sales 0.4% (both nominal and real) in the November report; real PCE rose 0.3% on the month and 3.0% on a 6-month annualized average.
- Job growth was soft at 50k in December — underlying pace estimated at only 11k — but the unemployment rate ticked down to 4.4%.
- Real disposable income growth ran at just 1.0% year-over-year and 0.1% 3-month annualized through November.
- The saving rate fell to 3.5% in November, down from 4.1% in August and 4.3% at end-2024; the net worth-to-disposable income ratio sits near its all-time high on equity gains.
- Consumer credit growth edged up to 2.4% year-over-year (2.0% 3-month annualized), while home equity loans grew 5.0% (12-week annualized through January 14); leverage and debt-service costs remain low by historical standards.
- UMich sentiment rose 3.5pt to 56.4 in January; the Conference Board's confidence index fell 3.8pt to 89.1 in December.

### Drivers
- **Fiscal tailwind, intensifying:** OBBBA tax cuts add roughly $100bn to household tax refunds over the Feb–April filing season, supporting a forecast of 2.2% real PCE growth in 2026 (Q4/Q4, vs. 2.3% in 2025).
- **Income, turning up from a weak base:** real income growth is projected to accelerate to 2.5% in 2026 (from 1.4% in 2025) as job growth normalizes, tax cuts land, and the tariff inflation headwind fades.
- **Labor market, stabilizing but fragile:** a pickup in overall growth is expected to keep the market steady, with unemployment edging only to 4.5% by end-2026 on 64k/month average job gains.
- **Balance sheets, strong and stable:** near-record net worth, backed by equity appreciation, underpins spending even as the saving rate is expected to rebuild to 4.3% by end-2026 and 4.5% by end-2027.
- **Credit, benign but watch delinquencies:** delinquency rates, including autos, appear to be stabilizing but remain elevated versus pre-pandemic levels.

### Risks
- **Downside — renewed labor market weakening:** risks to the labor market outlook are skewed toward renewed softening, given the underlying job-growth pace of only 11k.
- **Downside — bottom-quintile squeeze:** cuts to Medicaid and SNAP benefits are expected to disproportionately weigh on real income growth for the lowest income quintile, even as middle-income households outperform.
- **Sentiment — geopolitical concerns:** timely daily sentiment measures (Morning Consult) have pulled back recently, possibly on geopolitical risk.

### Unpacked
**The report's core tension is a consumer that keeps spending even though income growth has been weak — the gap bridged by a falling saving rate and unusually strong balance sheets.** November spending data held up across retail sales and PCE, and the base case is for that resilience to carry into 2026 rather than fade.

**The near-term catalyst is the OBBBA tax package, which pushes roughly $100bn of extra refunds into households during the Feb–April filing season.** This underpins above-consensus 2026 spending forecasts and is expected to lift real income growth to 2.5% (Q4/Q4), a marked improvement on 2025's 1.4% pace, alongside normalizing job growth and a fading tariff inflation drag.

**The distributional split matters: the same tax cuts drive middle-income outperformance, while Medicaid and SNAP reductions weigh most on the bottom quintile.** The aggregate income improvement therefore masks divergent outcomes across the income distribution.

**On the labor market, the signals are mixed — headline job growth is soft and the underlying pace is very low, yet unemployment ticked down to 4.4%.** The baseline sees the market holding steady with unemployment rising only slightly to 4.5% by end-2026, but the analyst explicitly flags risks skewed toward renewed weakening.

**Household balance sheets remain the key source of support, with net worth near record highs on equity gains and leverage and debt-service costs low.** The saving rate has dropped to 3.5% but is expected to rebuild toward 4.5% by end-2027. Credit growth is modest, home equity borrowing is picking up, and delinquencies — including autos — look to be stabilizing while still sitting above pre-pandemic norms.

The report gives no explicit trade idea; it is a dashboard of the consumer landscape rather than a directional call.
