subject: US Daily: January FOMC Preview: Further to Go, but Not for a While
summary:
# FOMC on Hold in January; [REDACTED] Pencils in the Next Cut Only in June

**Theme:** An uneventful January meeting that sets up a slower, consensus-driven path to two more cuts  
**Markets:** US monetary policy  
**Source:** [REDACTED] (David Mericle), 24 January 2026  

### Definitive impacts
- No change to the fed funds rate, held at 3.5–3.75%, following three cuts already delivered (the most recent in December).
- Only minor statement edits expected: possibly dropping the December line that inflation "has moved up since earlier in the year" while keeping "remains somewhat elevated," and adding that the unemployment rate "remains low" alongside "has edged up."
- Just one expected dissent (Governor Miran, in favor of a cut) — down sharply from three statement dissents and seven soft dissents in the dots at the December meeting.
- 15 of 19 FOMC participants project one to four further 25bp cuts as eventually appropriate; only four see no further normalization.
- Core PCE inflation net of estimated tariff effects is already near 2%, while the official measure is likely to stay closer to 3% than 2% in the first half of the year.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] expects the next 25bp cut in June and a final cut in September to a terminal 3.0–3.25%, though it flags low confidence in the timing given uncertainty over the next Chair and possible participant departures.
- [REDACTED] sees rate risks over the next year or two as tilted to the downside: hikes look unlikely with the funds rate above the median neutral estimate and the labor market softer than late last cycle, while several scenarios could justify more cuts. Its probability-weighted forecast sits below both its own baseline and market pricing — a modestly dovish lean.
- [REDACTED] reads the leadership as wanting the next, less-urgent "normalization" cut backed by a stronger consensus than December's, which will require more convincing inflation progress and take time.
- [REDACTED] expects the labor market to stabilize this year, projecting the unemployment rate to hold at 4.5%, but judges job growth still a bit too soft to keep pace with labor supply and sees risks tilted to a worse outcome.
- [REDACTED] expects Powell to signal the Committee is "well positioned for now" while it assesses the impact of the three delivered cuts, offering little guidance on the path ahead.

### Backdrop
The Fed cut three times into December, bringing the funds rate to 3.5–3.75%. The December meeting was unusually divided — three dissents in the statement and a record seven soft dissents in the dots — reflecting disagreement over how urgently to keep easing. That divide traces largely to how participants read inflation: some, including Powell, look at the trend net of one-time tariff effects, which is already near target; others anchor on the official numbers, which remain elevated.

### At issue
The January FOMC meeting, at which the Committee is expected to hold rates and give little forward guidance. The note is a preview: it lays out the likely statement tweaks, the expected shift from a heavily divided December to a near-unanimous hold, and [REDACTED]'s read of what would have to change — chiefly clearer inflation progress — before cuts resume.

### Unpacked
The setup is a Committee that has just eased three times and now wants to pause and watch. **The central distinction is between cuts that address an immediate risk and cuts that merely normalize policy — and the next one falls in the second category, which raises the bar.** An urgent cut can pass on a split vote; a normalization cut, the leadership appears to feel, needs a firmer consensus, and December's fractured vote is the counterexample they want to avoid repeating.

What stands between now and that consensus is the inflation read. **Because participants measure progress differently, the same data can look like "near 2%" to some and "still near 3%" to others, and only time will close that gap.** Those who strip out estimated tariff effects already see target-consistent inflation; those anchored to the official series will need the first-half numbers to come down before they sign on.

The labor market is the other half of the logic. Stabilization would remove the urgency argument entirely, and [REDACTED] expects exactly that — unemployment holding at 4.5% on a modest growth pickup — even while conceding job growth still looks too soft and its slack tracker is drifting up. **If jobs hold, the case for near-term easing weakens, which is why the projected next move slips all the way to June.**

For the reader, the practical takeaways are a quiet January and a Fed whose reaction function now hinges on inflation convincing the skeptics rather than on labor-market rescue. **The risk skew is gently dovish: [REDACTED]'s probability-weighted path runs below both its baseline and market pricing, with hikes treated as remote and several plausible routes to more cuts.** Timing carries an extra layer of uncertainty from the unresolved question of who chairs the Fed next and whether current participants stay. The note offers no explicit trade idea.

subject: US Daily: A Retrospective on 10 Questions for 2025
summary:
# 2025 in Review: Growth Beat, Labor Softened, and Tariffs Masked Real Inflation Progress

**Theme:** Scorecard on 10 macro calls — what was right, wrong, and close  
**Markets:** US economy, inflation and Fed policy  
**Source:** [REDACTED], David Mericle, 23 January 2026  

### Landscape
- GDP grew 2.5% Q1–Q3 2025 and an expected ~2.4% in Q4 (Q4/Q4), beating the 2.0% consensus held at the start of the year, despite an estimated 1.2pp Q4 drag from the government shutdown.
- Consumer spending rose 2.2% Q1–Q3 and looks set for ~2.6% in Q4, a 2.3% Q4/Q4 average, versus 2% consensus.
- The unemployment rate rose to 4.4% from 4¼%, against a call for a slight decline to 4%.
- Core PCE inflation is tracked at 2.98% y/y for December, with tariffs estimated to contribute 62bp — leaving the underlying rate a hair below 2.4% net of tariff effects.
- The fed funds rate sits somewhat above the FOMC's median neutral estimate, which held at 3%.

### Drivers
- Labor demand cooled faster than labor supply: immigration and supply growth slowed sharply, but job growth slowed even more, pushing unemployment up rather than down.
- Underlying disinflation continued, driven by labor-market rebalancing and the exhaustion of catch-up inflation, as in 2023–24 — the headline overshoot is mostly tariff pass-through, not a stalled trend.
- Tariffs rose far more than expected: "reciprocal" and other measures hit nearly all countries, and the policies now in effect are estimated to eventually lift the effective tariff rate by ~10pp, versus the 3–4pp originally forecast.
- Net immigration fell from an annualized ~1.5mn early in 2025 to around 0.5mn by year-end, moderately below the 0.75mn forecast.
- Fiscal policy left the primary deficit roughly unchanged: higher tariff revenue offsets the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's tax cuts, while DOGE spending cuts came in far below the $2 trillion once debated.

### Risks
- Downside/uncertainty on tariffs: the 2026 effective rate is expected to fall slightly as new deals and exemptions apply, and any tariffs replacing ones the Supreme Court might overturn would likely be capped at 15%, below some current rates — the analyst notes this path is contingent on pending legal outcomes.
- Institutional risk to Fed independence: the analyst flags that the attempt to fire Governor Lisa Cook (so far blocked by courts, with prediction markets now expecting her to stay) and a criminal investigation into Chair Powell have encroached on the Fed, even though Powell himself has not been fired or demoted.
- Immigration estimates remain highly uncertain, given suspended State Department visa data and disagreement over voluntary departures.

### Unpacked
The retrospective grades ten calls made at the end of 2024. On growth, the team was right for the right reasons: **both its GDP and consumer-spending forecasts beat consensus, even after the whole forecasting community cut estimates in spring 2025 when tariffs briefly looked much larger and more disruptive.** The final outcomes landed close to the original above-consensus calls.

The labor market was the clearest miss. **The expectation that unemployment would edge down to 4% rested on reading 2024's softening as a temporary struggle to absorb surging immigrants rather than weak demand — but demand proved the binding constraint, and unemployment rose to 4.4%.** Slower immigration did materialize; it simply was not enough to offset an even sharper slowdown in hiring.

Inflation is scored a close call. The headline core PCE figure near 3% overshot the target, **but the team argues nearly all the overshoot is tariff pass-through, leaving the tariff-adjusted rate just below the 2.4% threshold the question set.** Its tariff-contribution estimate of 62bp sits close to or slightly below comparable figures from the Fed Board, the St. Louis Fed, and the Harvard Pricing Lab.

On the Fed, the dovish call paid off. **Three cuts were delivered at the year's final three meetings, vindicating a view — drawn from the 2019 insurance cuts — that the second Trump administration's policies were more two-sided for rates than markets assumed.** The companion call that the median neutral-rate dot would rise to at least 3.25% was wrong: it stayed at 3%, with individual estimates notably stable in the December dot plot.

The political-economy questions split. Trump did not fire or demote Powell, scored technically correct, though the summary above captures the surrounding pressure on the Fed. The universal-tariff call was judged incorrect on substance: no formal 10–20% universal tariff was imposed, but the effective outcome was broader and larger than the flat levy the question envisioned.

Fiscal policy closed the scorecard as forecast. **Full extension of the 2017 tax cuts plus modest new personal cuts passed in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, tariff revenue roughly offset the cost, and the primary deficit ended up little changed** — with the once-touted $2 trillion in DOGE spending cuts amounting to far less. The note offers no trade idea; it is a self-assessment of prior forecasts.

subject: Global Rates Trader: There and Back Again
summary:
# Global Rates Trader: Headlines Whipsaw the Curve, but Fundamentals Keep Yields Grinding Higher

**Theme:** Range breaks that don't stick — carry-friendly baseline plus selective tail hedges  
**Markets:** G10 rates (US, Euro area, UK, Scandinavia, Japan)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], George Cole, 23 January 2026  

### Landscape
- US longer-term yields have settled above the range that held since late 3Q25 heading into the January FOMC, though without a lasting rise in volatility.
- 3m 2s10s implied curve vol sits modestly below recent realized, which — despite an uptick — remains well below prior vol-spike episodes.
- Short-expiry implied vol has reached levels last seen in 2021, while long-end swap spreads touched their widest since early 2023.
- The inflation term structure is compressed, with 5y5y/10y10y forwards steepening steadily and overall curvature near lows last seen in the 2018-19 low-inflation period.
- Repo rates have normalized toward longer-run relationships with liquidity, bill supply and money fund assets after December reserve management purchases began.
- Bunds did not outperform on renewed tariff uncertainty to the extent seen in April 2025, whether outright, versus swaps or cross-market.
- French OATs now trade flat versus BTPs, with the idiosyncratic OAT premium largely unwound.
- Norges Bank held at 4% last week; the Riksbank meets next week with inflation still trending lower, broadly in line with its own projections.

### Drivers
- Headline-driven volatility (Greenland, the Fed Governor Cook case, tariffs) keeps producing sharp but short-lived rates moves, as participants — conditioned by 2025 — wait to see whether risks prove durable before repricing.
- The above-consensus US growth view remains a near-term upside risk to yields, particularly in the belly, keeping the bias toward selective positioning and hedges.
- Reserve management purchases of $40bn/mo (expected through April, then decelerating to $20bn/mo) have stabilized funding faster than expected; part of late-2025 volatility may have been temporary adjustment frictions, pointing to lower repo rates and further SOFR/FF widening.
- Compressed risk premia and broad appetite for carry are a common factor driving low vol and wide swap spreads together.
- In Europe, the tension between a resilient (improving in Germany) domestic economy and a challenging trade/external backdrop is the dominant force; rising geopolitical risk only strengthens the case for fiscal response.
- The rising probability of a successful 2026 French budget (deficit cut from 5.4% to 5.1%, censure motions expected to fail) supports EGB carry and sovereign-credit resilience.
- UK incoming data remains disinflationary; with geopolitics settling, focus should return to labour-market and inflation data that support Gilt risk-premium compression — watch upcoming releases against still-noisy political headlines.
- JGB long-end volatility drove global yields this week, with G3 responses closely matching long-run spillover estimates; MOF signals and a more tentative BOJ toward yen weakness unwound some risk premium, but a full unwind is unlikely before the early-February election.

### Risks
- Upside (yields): stronger-than-consensus US growth could reprice the currently narrow implied distribution, making a structural short-gamma stance uncomfortable — the analyst's stated reason for caution.
- Downside/curve tail: global spillovers or exogenous risk-sentiment shocks could drive sharper steepening, the scenario the recommended curve-cap hedge targets.
- For swap spreads, the analyst flags a possible negative shift in demand for US assets, but judges near-term supply and moderating funding volatility as supportive enough to stay in spread longs.
- In Japan, the analyst notes an asymmetric feedback risk: common risk factors (fiscal, geopolitical, institutional credibility) would amplify JGB spillovers, while any relief on risk-premium concerns would conversely amplify a rally in global long-end yields.

### Unpacked
The US section centers on a "range break" that failed to hold. Volatility around institutional worries and country risk premia flared and reversed within the week, and while vol did not stay elevated, longer-term yields have quietly settled higher. **The benign macro backdrop remains a moderating force, but the above-consensus growth call keeps the bias toward being selective and holding hedges rather than leaning fully into carry.** The January FOMC is expected to bring no rate change, putting the focus on the Fed's labour-market read and its assessment of the policy stance.

On curve positioning, the baseline is a modestly steeper curve, with sharp steepening only in tails. Playing that carry-efficiently is the challenge: further-out steepeners like 5s30s offer better carry but risk belly-led underperformance if growth surprises up. **The preferred route is the compression in curve vol — owning a 3m 2s10s A+10/A+25 curve cap spread (entry 2.3bp, target 10bp, stop 0bp) as an attractive risk/reward hedge against tail steepening.**

The inflation curve shows two features: forward breakevens stayed compressed even as risk assets priced better growth, and longer-dated forwards keep steepening, leaving very little curvature. **Forward inflation longs are favored as a cheap hedge against risks to an otherwise low-vol, risk-friendly outlook**, with the compressed shape echoing the 2018-19 low-inflation regime.

Funding markets get detailed treatment. Reserve management purchases have replenished reserves and cut the residual between where SOFR/TGCR set late last year and longer-run relationships imply. The overshoot had suggested the reserve demand curve shifted right versus the prior cycle, generating volatility at higher system liquidity than before. **The swifter-than-expected moderation raises the possibility that some late-year funding stress was temporary adjustment friction — implying repo could stabilize lower and SOFR/FF widen further.** On the vol-and-spreads co-movement, the note stops short of a valuation-only long-vol or short-spread trade, but prefers belly swap-spread longs — the 7y sector — for their carry-to-vol profile.

Europe turns on the idea that "Bunds ain't what they used to be." The week produced a steeper 2s10s, with front-end rates flat-to-lower on tariff fears and long-end yields dragged up by JGBs. **Bunds' muted safe-haven response reflects the view that rising geopolitical risk only intensifies pressure for German fiscal action, so curve steepeners are favored — they capture cyclical improvement and fiscal term premium while offering protection if ECB-cut expectations build.** The bearish EUR core view is retained, expressed as short 10y Bunds versus Gilts.

Sovereign credit is the preferred carry expression. The improving odds of a French 2026 budget support OAT carry in the 2-5y despite the idiosyncratic premium being largely gone, and the broader resilience of spreads to trade and Japan spillovers underpins a constructive view. **BTPs and Bonos are expected to benefit from further foreign inflows on diversification demand and fundamental improvement in Spain**, with sovereign credit favored over low EUR rate implied vol.

The UK read is that data says buy while politics distracts. Gilt yields rose against disinflationary data, partly on JGB spillovers consistent with historical beta. **As geopolitics settles, the expectation is for yields to decline and for 10y Gilt-Bund and Gilt-UST spreads to compress**, alongside further OIS-vs-Gilt widening, though near-term risk/reward there is becoming more balanced as reduced Q1 supply gets priced. In Scandinavia, the bias is higher belly and 10y rates: a firmer Swedish growth environment, German fiscal spillovers and heavy issuance point up, while contained inflation caps front-end tail risk; in Norway, sticky inflation skews path risks up, keeping front-end NOK rangebound pending clarity.

Japan closes the note as the swing factor. The long-end selloff extended before MOF signals and a more tentative BOJ pared back some risk premium. **Moderate headline inflation and a more front-footed BOJ are seen driving further risk-premium compression later in the year once fiscal uncertainty clears — but a full near-term unwind is unlikely before the early-February election**, and JGB spillovers will remain a key driver of global yields in both directions.

subject: G10 Inflation Monitor: Core Inflation Surprises to the Downside Outside of Japan
summary:
# G10 Core Inflation Cools Broadly — Japan the Lone Holdout

**Theme:** December core inflation surprises to the downside almost everywhere; Japan bucks the trend  
**Markets:** G10 core inflation  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Megan Peters, 23 January 2026

### Landscape
- [REDACTED] trimmed core year-over-year sits at +3.0% in the UK, +2.4% in Canada, +2.2% in the US and Euro area, and +1.6% in Japan.
- On a 3-month annualized basis, trimmed core rose in Japan (1.5% vs. 1.0%), the UK (3.2% vs. 2.8%), and the US (1.7% vs. 1.5%), but slowed in the Euro area (1.9% vs. 2.4%) and Canada (1.7% vs. 1.9%).
- December sequential trimmed core ticked up in the UK (3.7% vs. 2.6%), US (2.3% vs. 1.4%, [REDACTED] PCE forecast), Canada (1.2% vs. 0.7%), and Japan (1.1% vs. 1.0%), but fell in the Euro area (1.2% vs. 2.3%).
- Traditional core has fallen ~7pp from peak in the UK, ~5pp in the Euro area and Canada, and ~4pp in the US.
- The share of the basket exceeding an 8% annualized pace held at 11% in the US (vs. 6% in Q1) and remains below 10% elsewhere; the distribution of 3-month rates is close to pre-pandemic norms in most economies.

### Drivers
- Core goods reaccelerated on a 3-month annualized basis in Japan (3.7% vs. 2.1%), the UK (0.8% vs. 0.2%), and Canada (1.6% vs. 1.3%), but slowed in the US (0.2% vs. 1.1%) and the Euro area (-0.6% vs. flat).
- Core services inflation edged up across all developed markets.
- Rent inflation ticked up in the US (1.6% vs. 1.3%), held at 3.3% in the Euro area, and slowed in the UK (3.7% vs. 4.1%), Canada (6.3% vs. 6.4%), and Japan (0.7% vs. 0.8%).
- Energy inflation slowed everywhere except the UK; food inflation rose in most DMs but eased from an elevated pace in Canada.
- Breadth is narrowing: the share of the basket running above 4% on a six-month annualized basis fell in the Euro area, UK, and Japan and was flat in the US and Canada.

### Risks
- Downside to US and UK 2026 core: the forecast slowdown to 2.3% depends on tariff and special policy-related boosts fading — [REDACTED] treats these as fading but does not quantify the risk if they persist.
- Japan is the asymmetric upside outlier: it is the only economy where December core surprised above consensus and where trimmed core accelerated on both monthly and 3-month bases.

### Unpacked
December delivered downside core inflation surprises in the US, UK, Euro area, and Canada, with Japan the sole exception where new core CPI came in a touch above consensus. **The headline read is broad-based cooling outside Japan, though the underlying monthly and 3-month trimmed measures actually firmed in several economies, so the "surprise" is relative to expectations rather than a clean deceleration in the data itself.**

The Euro area stands out as the cleanest disinflation story: sequential trimmed core dropped to 1.2% from 2.3%, the 3-month measure slowed to 1.9%, core goods ran outright negative at -0.6%, and the weighted median monthly rate declined alongside Japan's. **Japan is moving the opposite way — trimmed core rose on every basis, and core goods jumped to 3.7% from 2.1% on a 3-month annualized basis, the fastest goods reacceleration in the group.**

Rent remains the persistent cross-country divide, ranging from 0.7% in Japan to 6.3% in Canada, differences the report notes partly reflect methodology rather than fundamentals alone. [REDACTED] also flags that its harmonized core — which strips a consistent item set across countries — runs below the central banks' preferred measures everywhere except Canada, where excluding owned housing (notably mortgage interest costs) and soft financial services pushes it well above the official read.

**On forecasts, [REDACTED] sees Q4/Q4 year-over-year core slowing to 2.3% by end-2026 in the US and UK, 2.2% in Canada, 1.9% in the Euro area, and 1.4% in Japan — generally below consensus.** Over the past month it nudged up the US and UK end-2026 numbers by 0.1pp each while trimming the Euro area by 0.1pp, with the US and UK slowdowns explicitly tied to fading tariff and policy-related boosts.

subject: Global FX Trader: Correlation Comeback
summary:
# Correlation Comeback: Cyclical Rotation Trumps Carry, Dollar Downside Capped by Hedging Flows

**Theme:** Cross-asset correlation shifts driving FX hedging flows; cyclical exposure over carry  
**Markets:** Global FX (G10 and EM)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Kamakshya Trivedi, 23 January 2026

### Landscape
- The Dollar depreciated this week, with its rolling correlation to US equities shifting higher after the week's price action (Exhibit 1).
- USD/JPY stayed largely rangebound through the week, but the Yen underperformed most majors and failed as a risk-off hedge on Tuesday, in contrast to April.
- EM currencies sit among both the top YTD performers and the underperformers, leaving carry as a weak differentiator of spot returns.
- USD/IDR broke above 16,900 for the first time on fiscal and BI-independence concerns.
- EUR/GBP completed a round-trip on the week; Sterling returned to laggard status across European currencies.
- SEK and NOK outperformance versus the Euro accelerated this past week (Exhibits 5–6).

### Drivers
- Tariffs weigh on the Dollar through multiple channels — terms of trade, policy uncertainty, foreign-policy response, and hedging flows — all judged to have played some role in this week's move; expected to be less prevalent in 2026 but still enough to cap Dollar upside.
- Solid global growth and more balanced global returns favour procyclical currencies and pressure the Dollar's high valuation over the year.
- Cross-asset correlation is the swing factor: a return of unfriendly FX-equity correlations could trigger another round of FX hedging and outsized moves — flagged as a risk to watch, not the baseline.
- FX policy is taking a larger role across NJA: the PBoC signals tolerance for CNY strength, Korea pushes back on KRW weakness, Thailand coordinates to weaken THB and de-link it from gold, and India's RBI allows more USD/INR flexibility under a tariff-driven external shock.
- Japan's Lower House election skews fiscal risk premium higher near-term, but a disappointing result for the ruling coalition could drive a sharp partial unwind.
- Cross-border flow shifts drive Scandi strength, as in Q2 2025, reinforced by expected higher European defence spending.

### Risks
- Upside to USD/JPY (analyst's baseline skew): benign risk backdrop and rising pre-election fiscal premium; intervention, a rate check, or faster BoJ hikes could limit but likely only temporarily reverse the move.
- Downside to USD/JPY over time: if consumption tax cuts fail to pass and the US-Japan rate differential compresses per baseline.
- Upside risk to the Dollar over coming weeks: mean-reverting FX environment sees it recover lost ground, especially in European crosses.
- Tactical risk to short ILS/CLP: a correction in CLP's recent outperformance.
- Tactical risk on the Scandis: regional crosses like EUR/SEK and EUR/NOK are prime candidates for a reversal after sharp moves.

### Unpacked
The through-line is a shift in what drives FX. **With cross-asset correlations moving, the analyst expects cyclical exposure — via equity and commodity linkages — to matter as much as carry for relative spot returns in the year ahead.** The Dollar view is modest depreciation, held back from anything stronger by the same tariff and hedging channels that made FX move more than other cyclical assets in 2025; the baseline remains a mean-reverting environment in which the Dollar recovers some ground near-term.

On the Yen, the stance is cautiously bearish tactically, with USD/JPY risks skewed to the upside. **Intervention keeps a lid on upside but is seen as working only temporarily when the backdrop justifies the pressure, as in 2022** — a Friday rate check raises the odds of actual operations, while faster BoJ hikes or a change in the administration's policy plans would be more durable fixes.

In EM, the note reframes the funder question around a procyclical mix. Lower-yielding but highly cyclical currencies (CLP, NZD, AUD) screen poorly as RV funders. **ILS stands out for overvaluation and tight correlation to tech stocks, making it a cheap hedge — the trigger for a new short ILS/CLP recommendation, target 260, stop 290,** supported by scope for domestic political noise to return around budget talks and an election due by October 2026. Against a long carry basket (BRL, COP, HUF, MXN, ZAR), the Dollar still scans as attractive on valuation and normalising risk beta, but under a shallower depreciation view the optimal mix adds GBP (overvalued, risk-neutral tilt, small carry cost), SGD (overvalued, +2pp carry), and CAD (carry plus resilience to oil downside); JPY funding offers carry but higher volatility. The short CAD/ZAR recommendation is maintained with a tightened stop and raised target.

NJA forecasts are lifted for USD/INR, USD/IDR and USD/PHP, with fresh highs seen as likely, while USD/MYR is lowered after a faster-than-expected MYR rally. **The core message holds: USD/CNY moves lower, and low-yielders — especially tech-export-linked currencies — outperform high-yielders.**

Sterling is placed back as the European laggard on a weakening labour and inflation trend, its poor positioning to benefit from hedge-ratio shifts, and residual fiscal and political risk premium that has receded but not fully cleared. **The short GBP/SEK recommendation is closed for a potential +2.2% total return, rotated instead into a tactical long EUR/GBP, target 0.8740, stop 0.8595.** The Scandi close-out reflects caution after sharp NOK and SEK outperformance and the reversal potential in regional crosses, even as the medium-term backdrop stays supportive for both.

subject: USA: S&P Services and Manufacturing PMIs Slightly Below Consensus Expectations
summary:
# US: January PMIs Point to Sustained Growth, but at a Cooler Pace with Hiring Stagnant

**Theme:** S&P Global flash January PMIs slightly below consensus; mixed composition  
**Markets:** US economic activity  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jan Hatzius, 23 Jan 2026  
### Definitive impacts
- Services PMI unchanged at 52.5 in January (preliminary), below consensus of 52.9 and matching the prior 52.5.
- Manufacturing PMI rose 0.1pt to 51.9, roughly in line with consensus of 52.0 (prior 51.8).
- In services, new business (+1.3pt, to 52.4) and employment (+0.4pt, to 50.4) advanced; input prices (-2.9pt, to 59.1 — the lowest level since April 2025), output prices (-0.5pt, to 56.9) and the future output index (-0.5pt, to 63.0, NSA) retreated.
- In manufacturing, output (+1.3pt, to 54.8), new orders (+1.8pt, to 50.8), input prices (+1.5pt, to 62.7), output prices (+2.5pt, to 58.8) and the future output index (+1.8pt, to 70.1, NSA) rose; employment retreated (-1.3pt, to 51.1).

### Backdrop
The S&P Global flash PMIs are among the first activity readings of each month. A value above 50 indicates expansion; below, contraction. The internal components (new business, employment, input and output prices, future output expectations) allow an assessment of headline quality beyond the level itself.

### At issue
Release of the preliminary January 2026 readings. The services headline held steady and the manufacturing headline rose marginally, both slightly below consensus, but with distinct compositions: in services, gains in new business and employment alongside price relief; in manufacturing, higher output and new orders, but a drop in employment and accelerating prices. S&P's commentary highlighted "sustained economic growth at the start of the year," but flagged a cooling in pace versus autumn and "disappointing" job creation, with payrolls nearly stagnant amid uncertainty, weak demand and elevated costs.

### Unpacked
The readings came in marginally below expectations at the headline level, but **the central message is in the composition, not the headline number**: services held their level with improved new business and employment, while manufacturing edged up at the headline level supported by output and orders.

The price contrast is the point that deserves attention. **In services, input prices fell to their lowest level since April 2025, while in manufacturing both input and output prices accelerated** — opposite signals of cost pressure between the two sectors.

Employment is the common thread of caution. **Despite sustained growth, hiring is weak — declines in the manufacturing component and S&P's own commentary pointing to nearly stagnant payrolls** — attributed to uncertainty, weak demand and high costs. The note carries no positioning recommendation or monetary-policy call; it is a data comment.

subject: USA: Personal Spending and Core PCE in Line With Expectations in November, Saving Rate Declines to 3.5%; Personal Spending Above Our Expectations in October; Boosting Q4 GDP Tracking to +2.4%
summary:
# US Consumer Held Up Through Late 2025 — Firm Spending and On-Target Core PCE Lift Q4 Growth Tracking

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US personal income, spending and PCE inflation (Oct–Nov 2025)  
**General comment:** Constructive read on US demand; data land close to consensus and nudge the growth call higher without altering the inflation picture.

### Context
A comment on the November personal income and outlays release (with October detail), read for what it says about consumer momentum, the inflation trend, and Q4 GDP.

### The case
- **Spending stayed firm while the saving rate fell.** Personal spending rose 0.5% in both October and November — October well above the analyst's own expectation — with real spending up 0.3% in each month, split between a 0.2% average gain in real services and a 0.5% average gain in real goods. Income was softer, up 0.3% in November and just 0.1% in October, both a touch below expectations; compensation and rental income rose 0.3% on average while asset income was flat and proprietors' income slipped. With spending outrunning income, the saving rate dropped to 3.5% in November from 4.0% in September — the mechanism behind the spending strength.
- **Core PCE ran in line, leaving the inflation trend intact.** Core PCE rose 0.16% in November and 0.21% in October month-over-month, holding the year-over-year rate at 2.79%, as expected; headline PCE was up 0.21% in November for a 2.77% annual rate. Prior months saw only marginal revisions (September core trimmed 1bp). Nothing in the print shifts the disinflation read.
- **Stronger consumption feeds directly into the growth upgrade.** Because spending came in above prior tracking assumptions, the Q4 GDP estimate was raised 0.3pp to +2.4% quarter-over-quarter annualized. Q4 domestic final sales are put at +1.3% and private domestic final sales at +2.4%.

### Implications
- The Q4 growth call moves up to +2.4%, driven by the consumer rather than by any change in the inflation outlook.
- A saving rate down to 3.5% funded the spending, raising the question of how durable that pace is if income growth stays soft.
- Core PCE holding near 2.8% and on expectations keeps the inflation backdrop unchanged for policy purposes.

subject: USA: Q3 GDP Revised Up Slightly to +4.4%; Initial Claims Somewhat Below Expectations
summary:
# US: Q3 GDP revised to +4.4%; jobless claims below expectations

**Theme:** Third estimate of Q3 GDP nudges growth higher on trade and inventories; weekly labor data comes in firmer than consensus  
**Markets:** US growth, inflation and labor market  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jan Hatzius, 22 January 2026

### Definitive impacts
- Q3 real GDP revised up 0.1pp to +4.4% (QoQ annualized), driven by exports (+0.8pp to +9.6%) and a smaller inventory drag (+0.1pp to -0.1pp contribution).
- Real private domestic final sales revised down 0.1pp to +2.9%, mainly on weaker housing investment (-2.0pp to -7.1%).
- Business fixed investment revised up 0.4pp to +3.2%, led by structures (+1.3pp to -5.0%); consumer spending (+3.5%) and government spending (+2.2%) unrevised.
- Q3 core PCE inflation revised up 0.01pp to +2.88% annualized (+2.87% Q4/Q4 YoY); headline PCE up 0.01pp to +2.78% annualized (+2.71% YoY, unrevised).
- GDP deflator revised up 0.01pp to +3.77% annualized (+2.98% YoY), reflecting higher federal government spending inflation (+0.46pp to +4.22%), partly offset by lower residential (-1.01pp to +3.53%), nonresidential (-0.14pp to +5.11%) and imports (-0.46pp to +0.22%) inflation.
- Initial jobless claims rose 1k to 200k in the week ended January 17, below the 209k median; four-week average fell 3k to 202k.
- Continuing claims fell 26k to 1,849k in the week ended January 10, against consensus for an increase.

### Backdrop
The GDP third estimate is the final revision to the quarterly national accounts, incorporating more complete source data on components such as trade, inventories and investment. Weekly jobless claims are among the most timely indicators of labor-market conditions; initial claims proxy new layoffs and continuing claims track the stock of workers on standard benefit programs. [REDACTED] tracks incoming data against its own forecasts and consensus through its US MAP scoring (here: initial claims 0, continuing claims +1).

### At issue
Two releases are covered. First, the third estimate of Q3 GDP: growth was marked up to +4.4% on stronger exports and a smaller inventory drag, with an offsetting downward revision to housing that trimmed private domestic final sales; price measures were nudged up by roughly 1bp across core PCE, headline PCE and the deflator. Second, weekly labor data for mid-January: initial claims edged up but stayed below expectations, and continuing claims fell where consensus expected a rise. State-level moves in initial claims were small (+2k each in California and South Carolina; -3k Ohio, -2k Georgia).

### Unpacked
The headline revision is cosmetic in size but its internal composition matters more than the top line. **Growth was revised up on trade and inventories — components that tend to be volatile and less indicative of underlying demand — while the demand-oriented private domestic final sales measure was revised down.** That divergence points to slightly softer core momentum than the +4.4% print alone would suggest, concentrated in a weaker housing read.

The inflation revisions are trivial in magnitude, on the order of a single basis point across the main gauges, and do not change the picture. **The one visible shift is in the deflator's mix — higher federal government spending inflation offset by softer investment and import prices — rather than in the aggregate.**

The labor data lean firmer than expected on both fronts: claims held at a low level and the continuing-claims decline runs counter to consensus for an increase. **Together the releases describe an economy still growing well above trend with a labor market showing no sign of loosening, even as the demand-side detail of GDP is marginally softer than the headline.** The note offers no explicit trade idea and confines itself to reporting the data.

subject: Global Markets Daily: Credit returns can withstand tight spreads
summary:
# Tight Starting Spreads Need Not Mean Negative Credit Returns in 2026

**Theme:** Why ultra-tight IG and HY spreads can still deliver positive excess returns, as in 2025  
**Markets:** US corporate credit (investment grade and high yield)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Spencer Rogers, 22 January 2026

### Definitive impacts
- Current sub-10th-percentile spread thresholds sit at ≤88bp for IG and ≤295bp for HY; USD IG and HY currently trade near all-time tights.
- 2025 delivered positive excess returns of +1.2% (IG) and +2.6% (HY) despite starting the year at spreads of 80bp and 287bp, both inside the 10th historical percentile.
- Across 25 years, mean and median 12-month forward excess returns are negative when spreads start below the 10th percentile — but outcomes split by macro regime (2007 and 2021 deeply negative; 2004/05 and 2024 still positive).
- IG and HY durations sit near 10-year lows (IG) and all-time lows (HY), mechanically reducing return sensitivity to any spread widening.
- All-in yields screen around their 60th percentile for IG and 30th percentile for HY.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] sees 2026 repeating 2025, with IG and HY posting positive excess returns despite tight starting valuations, resting on benign macro, low duration, strong fundamentals and yield support.
- [REDACTED]'s spread forecasts imply full-year excess returns of +0.1% (IG) and +1.1% (HY), assuming gradual spread widening driven by supply technicals.
- [REDACTED] argues the current backdrop resembles the 2004/05 and 2024 "goldilocks" episodes — above-trend real GDP, decent yield support — far more than the 2007 and 2021 episodes that ended in recession and sharp tightening, so spreads should stay range-bound.
- [REDACTED] continues to advise adding portfolio hedges to buffer against a sudden rebuild of risk premium; it offers no explicit long/short credit trade idea beyond this.

### Backdrop
Very tight starting spreads have historically skewed the distribution of forward outcomes toward widening, so periods of ultra-low spreads tend to precede negative 12-month excess returns to Treasuries. That average, however, blends distinct regimes: the same starting valuation resolved very differently in a credit-driven downturn (2007) or a sharp monetary-tightening cycle (2021) than in an environment of above-trend growth and supportive yields (2004/05, 2024). The starting spread level alone is therefore an incomplete guide; the surrounding macro determines whether tight valuations mean-revert painfully or simply persist.

### At issue
Entering 2026, USD IG and HY spreads are near all-time tights, prompting investors to ask whether they should brace for negative excess returns this year. The note frames the current setup against four prior sub-10th-percentile episodes and argues it most closely resembles the two benign ones. It pairs this with an accommodative macro read — above-trend US GDP, a Fed still cutting, cooling inflation — and with improving Q3 leverage and coverage metrics and subdued default risk.

### Unpacked
The starting point is a genuine tension: the base-rate signal from history is negative, yet the immediate precedent — 2025 — contradicts it outright, landing squarely in the middle of the historical return distribution for both IG and HY. **The resolution offered is that regime, not the spread level, drives the outcome, and the current regime lines up with the episodes that held up rather than those that broke.**

From there the argument leans on four mutually reinforcing supports. The macro read supplies the range-bound thesis; low duration limits the damage if that thesis is wrong; improving fundamentals and low defaults keep the loss drag minimal; and yields well off their tights keep total-return buyers engaged. **Duration is the quiet workhorse here — with IG near decade lows and HY at record lows, even a spread rebuild translates into a smaller price hit than in prior tight-spread episodes.**

**The forecasts are modest rather than bullish — +0.1% IG and +1.1% HY — a call for positive-but-thin carry, not spread compression, with widening the base case.** That is why the hedging advice sits alongside the constructive view rather than against it: the position is that returns hold up while the asymmetry stays skewed to the downside, so cheap protection against a sudden risk-premium rebuild remains warranted. For the reader, the practical takeaway is a stay-invested-but-hedged stance on US credit, with the whole thesis contingent on the goldilocks macro backdrop persisting.

subject: Fed Chatterbox: January Edition
summary:
# Fed Speakers Coalesce Around a January Hold, With the Bar for Further Cuts Rising

**Theme:** Post-December Fed commentary — a likely January hold and a split on how much more easing, if any, is coming  
**Markets:** US monetary policy  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jessica Rindels, 21 January 2026  

### Landscape
- The fed funds rate sits after 175bp of cuts since mid-2024 (75bp of it in 2025), which Jefferson views as having reached a range consistent with neutral.
- The unemployment rate stands at 4.4%, which Bostic characterizes as historically low even after recent labor-market cooling.
- Breakeven payroll growth is estimated at roughly 50k jobs/month by Schmid and 30k–80k/month by Musalem, with actual payrolls said to be running near that pace.
- Inflation remains above the 2% target but with improving underlying trend; Williams attributes about half a percentage point of current inflation to tariffs to date.
- Williams sees inflation peaking near 2¾–3% in H1 2026, averaging just under 2½% for the year, and reaching 2% only in 2027.

### Drivers
- Reaction-function caution is holding policy steady: most participants back Jefferson's "well positioned" framing to await data, pointing to a January hold.
- Fading tariff effects are pulling expected inflation toward 2%, cited by Jefferson, Bowman, Paulson, Musalem and Williams; Paulson sees a decent chance 3-month inflation hits 2% by year-end even if 12-month readings stay elevated.
- Labor-market fragility is the main dovish force — Bowman and Paulson weight downside employment risk heavily — but most expect stabilization near full employment this year, so it is a risk to monitor rather than an active easing trigger.
- A higher perceived neutral rate is muting the case for cuts: Schmid and Musalem judge policy roughly neutral, so further easing would risk moving into accommodative territory. Watch Musalem's point that lower 2026 inflation projections raised the real policy rate through Q4.
- Structural forces (AI adoption, immigration/demographic shifts) are reframing labor weakness as something Schmid argues monetary policy is ill-suited to address.

### Risks
- Upside inflation risk: Bostic flags that stronger 2026 growth could add price pressure, and Kashkari notes January is a natural point for firms to reset pricing and pass through tariff costs.
- Downside employment risk: Bowman warns the labor market has become more fragile and could deteriorate further; Jefferson sees downside risks to employment as having risen, though his baseline holds unemployment steady.
- The analyst frames these as two-sided, with Musalem explicitly casting a roughly neutral stance as the way to balance upside inflation risk against downside labor risk.

### Unpacked
**The dominant signal is that a January hold is broadly expected, but participants diverge sharply on what follows.** Jefferson's "well positioned" line anchors the consensus. Beyond January, Paulson allows for "some modest further adjustments" later in the year on his baseline, while Musalem sees "little reason for near term easing" and Schmid "little reason at this point to further lower the policy rate." Bowman stands on the dovish edge, urging readiness to move policy toward neutral and warning against signaling a pause without evidence the labor market has improved.

**The debate over further cuts turns largely on how restrictive policy actually is.** Bowman and Paulson call it "moderately" or "a little" restrictive, leaving room to ease; Jefferson, Musalem and Schmid see policy at roughly neutral, which sharply narrows that room. Schmid goes furthest, arguing the neutral rate has risen post-pandemic so that a stance that would have been restrictive before is no longer very restrictive now. Kashkari and Miran echo the theme from the resilience and deregulation angles respectively, questioning whether policy is as tight as assumed.

**On the labor market, weakness is acknowledged but most expect stabilization rather than deterioration.** Jefferson's baseline holds unemployment steady this year; Musalem sees payrolls near breakeven and unemployment near its neutral rate; Williams expects stabilization then some strengthening. The dissenting concern comes from Bowman, who stresses fragility and favors preemptive support. Schmid's structural argument matters here: if cooling stems from technology and immigration rather than a demand shortfall, rate cuts do little to fix it — a direct challenge to the case for easing on labor grounds. Barkin adds a process note that no single meeting carries much weight given policy's ~12-month lag.

**Inflation is the clearest point of qualified optimism, hedged by the tariff question.** Most agree underlying trend inflation has improved and expect convergence toward 2% as tariff effects fade. Schmid is the notable holdout, reluctant to step back until he sees more convincing evidence, and Bostic worries stronger 2026 growth could lift prices. Williams supplies the most explicit path — a near-term peak around 2¾–3%, a full-year average just under 2½%, and 2% only in 2027 — framing the tariff contribution as roughly half a point and describing non-tariff trends as favorable.

The note offers no trade idea; it is a survey of official commentary, not a recommendation.

subject: European Daily: EU—Retaliation Options in Response to Further US Tariffs
summary:
# EU's Retaliation Ladder If Trump's 10% Tariff Lands February 1

**Theme:** How the EU could respond to new US tariffs, and how far each option can go  
**Markets:** Euro area trade and macro  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Giovanni Pierdomenico, 19 January 2026  

### Definitive impacts
- Real GDP in the eight affected European countries falls 0.1–0.2% via lower net exports, if the announced 10% US tariff takes effect February 1.
- Ratifying the EU-US deal would have cut the effective tariff rate on affected EU imports from the US by 1.5pp, to 0%; stalling it holds that rate in place.
- Pausing the deal's implementation avoids the loss of roughly EUR 5bn in EU tariff revenue, with limited upside to inflation versus a deal-in-place counterfactual.
- The suspended EU counter-tariff list covers EUR 93bn of US goods imports (agricultural products, aircraft, cars), with suspension expiring February 6, 2026.
- Counter-tariffs at a 10% rate would add about EUR 0.06% to consumer prices (mechanical and temporary), a negligible GDP hit, and roughly EUR 8bn in incremental revenue.
- A flat 10% tariff on all EU imports of US services, available under the ACI, could mechanically raise about EUR 50bn.
- Activating the ACI requires a qualified majority in the EU Council (55% of member states representing ≥65% of population) within 10 weeks, after which the Commission has up to 6 months to deploy measures.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] sees retaliation as more likely than last year, reading the firm and uniform response of EU leaders as a signal they will act if Trump proceeds.
- The bank expects a gradual, multi-pronged sequence: first pause the deal, ready the counter-tariffs for shortly after any US increase, then activate the ACI only if the US escalates — and even then without immediate measures, to preserve room for negotiation.
- [REDACTED] flags a retaliation risk: if the EU withholds tariff elimination, the US could reverse the auto-tariff cut and take European autos back from 15% to 27.5% — and possibly respond more forcefully still.
- On services, the bank judges that US firms' market power, especially in digital, would leave European consumers bearing much of any services tariff, since substitution is hard.

### Backdrop
The EU and US agreed a trade deal last August: the EU would eliminate tariffs on all US industrial goods and grant preferential access to a range of US agricultural goods, while the US cut tariffs on European auto exports from 27.5% to 15%. The US side has already delivered its auto cut, but the EU's tariff elimination still needs European Parliament ratification. Parliament began vetting the deal last September and has moved slowly amid uncertainty over the US administration's stance.

Separately, during last year's trade dispute the EU drew up a EUR 93bn retaliation list whose implementation was suspended until February 6, 2026, as part of the deal. The EU also holds an untested instrument, the Anti-Coercion Instrument (ACI), designed to counter undue interference in EU policy — its broadest and potentially most powerful tool.

### At issue
President Trump announced a 10% tariff on imports from eight European countries, effective February 1. EU leaders responded firmly and scheduled an emergency leaders' summit for Thursday, January 22, to weigh retaliation. The note maps three escalating options: (1) pause implementation of the EU-US trade deal by freezing parliamentary ratification — the lowest hurdle; (2) let the EUR 93bn counter-tariff list take effect after a non-binding consultation with EU ambassadors; (3) activate the ACI, which permits tariffs on US services plus broader measures such as investment restrictions, a higher digital services tax, and "buy Europe" procurement clauses.

### Unpacked
The announcement matters less for its direct macro hit — a tenth or two of GDP in the exposed countries — than for what it triggers. **The note's organizing idea is a retaliation ladder ordered by procedural hurdle, where the EU's likely path is to climb it slowly enough to keep de-escalation on the table at every rung.**

Each rung trades reach for cost and complexity. Pausing ratification is nearly free procedurally and economically — it mainly protects EUR 5bn of revenue and keeps existing tariffs on US goods in place — but it invites the specific counterpunch of the US restoring the 27.5% auto tariff. The counter-tariff list is a step up in force yet still procedurally light, gated less by rules than by whether the main member states agree; its economic footprint is small and its inflation effect mechanical and temporary. **The ACI is the qualitatively different lever: untested, slow to fire, but able to reach services, investment, taxation and procurement where goods tariffs cannot.**

Its design is the point. The multi-stage timeline — a coercion declaration, a qualified-majority Council vote within 10 weeks, then up to six months for the Commission to deploy — is a feature, letting the EU signal intent while holding actual measures in reserve as negotiating leverage. **That is why [REDACTED] expects the EU to activate the ACI, if at all, without implementing anything immediately.** The catch on services is substitution: because US providers dominate, especially in digital, a services tariff would fall largely on European consumers — which is partly why the ACI's non-tariff options (a higher DST, investment curbs, procurement clauses) may prove more usable than services duties themselves. The note offers no explicit trade idea.

subject: US Economics Weekly Update 1/19/2026
summary:
# Core CPI Cools to 2.0% Underlying, but Core PCE Set to Print Near 3% for December

**Theme:** Shutdown-distorted inflation reads point lower while a December PCE bump lingers; Greenland tariff threat added as tail risk  
**Markets:** US inflation and activity  
**Source:** [REDACTED], David Mericle, 19 January 2026

### Landscape
- Core CPI rose 0.24% m/m in December and 2.64% y/y.
- On a three-month basis — which smooths most shutdown distortions — core CPI ran 1.6% annualized, or roughly 2.0% adjusting for a downward shelter bias that will not reverse until April.
- Core PCE is now expected at 2.98% y/y for December.
- Q4 2025 GDP tracking ended last week at 2.1%, well above consensus but far below the Atlanta Fed's GDPNow at 5.3% (GDPNow excludes an estimated -1.2pp shutdown drag).
- Industrial production rose 0.4% in December and manufacturing production 0.2%.
- Core retail sales rose 0.4% in November, with downward revisions to September (-0.1pp to -0.2%) and October (-0.2pp to +0.6%).
- New single-family home sales rose 1.8% on average across September and October.

### Drivers
- Underlying inflation is running near the 2% area once shutdown noise and the temporary shelter bias are stripped out — the clean signal is softer than the headline y/y prints suggest, with a shelter rebound not due until April.
- The year-end core PCE forecast moved higher last week on specific price jumps: software (+7%) in the CPI, medical and portfolio management prices in the PPI, and airfare import prices — worth watching whether these persist or reverse.
- The monthly PCE path is expected to steepen into year-end: +0.16% October, +0.20% November, +0.37% December, with October and November data due Thursday and December on February 20.
- Consumer spending is holding but decelerating: personal spending seen flat in October and +0.4% in November (vs. 0.5% consensus).

### Risks
- Upside/policy risk: Trump announced 10% tariffs on Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Finland, France, Germany, the UK, and the Netherlands from February 1, rising to 25% on June 1 unless a deal is reached on the "Complete and Total purchase of Greenland." [REDACTED] views implementation as highly uncertain.

### Unpacked
The central reading is that the December inflation picture is cleaner than it looks. **The headline year-over-year figures still carry shutdown distortions, but the three-month annualized pace of 1.6% — about 2.0% once the temporary downward bias to shelter is added back — is the more reliable gauge, and it sits close to target.** The shelter drag will not see an offsetting rebound until April, so the next few prints will continue to understate underlying momentum on that component.

The PCE side tells a less benign near-term story. **Core PCE is now tracked at 2.98% y/y for December, lifted by the +0.37% December monthly forecast that follows softer 0.16% and 0.20% readings in October and November.** The upward revision to the year-end forecast last week came from a handful of specific categories — a 7% jump in software prices in the CPI, medical and portfolio management prices in the PPI, and airfare import prices — rather than a broad-based pickup. The data calendar matters here: October and November PCE arrive Thursday, with December not published until February 20.

On activity, the quarter is tracking well but the signal is muddied by the government shutdown. **Q4 GDP tracking closed last week at 2.1% — above consensus yet far below GDPNow's 5.3%, a gap [REDACTED] attributes largely to GDPNow omitting a shutdown effect estimated at -1.2pp.** Industrial and manufacturing production both rose in December, home sales firmed across September and October, and core retail sales held up in November even as prior months were revised lower. Spending is expected to have been flat in October before recovering to +0.4% in November, just under consensus.

The tariff announcement is the main new wildcard. **A 10% tariff on eight European countries from February 1, escalating to 25% on June 1 unless the U.S. secures the purchase of Greenland, is flagged as highly uncertain to be implemented** — noted for awareness rather than built into the baseline.

The note also recaps [REDACTED]'s 2025 forecasting scorecard. Its week-ahead calls were 71% directionally correct versus consensus across 12 top-tier indicators, above the 64% average since 2017, with perfect marks on GDP (3 of 3), 90% on core CPI, 67% on retail control, and 60% on payrolls. **Markets in 2025 reacted far more sharply to inflation surprises (1.5x normal for stocks, 2.6x for bonds) than to growth surprises, and weighted unemployment-rate surprises well above payrolls surprises — likely reflecting uncertainty about the breakeven rate.**

The note gives no explicit trade idea.
