subject: US Economics Analyst: 2026 Inflation Outlook: Traveling Toward Target
summary:
# Core PCE Back Near 2% by End-2026 as Tariff, Shelter and Wage Pressures Fade

**Theme:** Why disinflation resumes in 2026 after stalling in 2025, and why [REDACTED] sits 30–60bp below consensus  
**Markets:** US inflation  
**Source:** [REDACTED] (Ronnie Walker), 4 January 2026  

### Definitive impacts
- Core PCE forecast to fall to 2.1% year-over-year by December 2026, from 2.8% in September 2025 — driven by smaller contributions from goods (−0.3pp), housing (−0.2pp) and nonhousing services (−0.2pp).
- Estimated tariff contribution to year-over-year core PCE is 0.5pp now, implying ex-tariff inflation has already reached 2.3%.
- Shelter inflation forecast to fall from 3.7% year-over-year (September 2025) to 2.3% by December 2026, below its pre-pandemic pace; the new-vs-continuing-lease rent gap is 1–2pp narrower than pre-pandemic and alternative new-lease measures rose just 1% over the past year.
- Health care services (ex-insurance) forecast to accelerate from 2.6% (2025) to 2.9% (2026) — the last major case of "catch-up inflation," with the Medicare Economic Index up 22% since 2020Q1 vs 16% for consumer prices.
- Headline CPI forecast at 2.0% for 2026, 0.1pp below the 2.1% headline PCE forecast — reversing the historical norm of CPI running ~0.3pp above PCE, due to CPI's larger shelter weight and declining CPI-unique insurance categories.
- Monthly prints distorted near-term: December core PCE 0.25% / core CPI 0.28% (an ~11bp core-CPI boost as delayed November data collection unwinds); January core PCE 0.27% / core CPI 0.26% (~8bp "January effect" boost). A ~0.24pp monthly shelter jump is expected in April 2026 from unwind of shutdown-era carry-forward imputation.
- CPI data quality degraded: monthly prices collected fell ~20% across 2025; the CPI monthly standard error nearly doubled versus its 2015–2019 average (90% interval widening to ~20bp from ~10bp); 20 CPI-U series were deemed inadequate for publication on average in Q3 vs 3 in 2019Q4; BLS prices-program headcount set 7% lower this fiscal year.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] sees disinflation resuming in 2026 on three grounds: a fading tariff boost, soft shelter inflation, and a cooler labor market with wage growth already at target-consistent levels.
- [REDACTED] expects the tariff boost to rise to 0.8pp by mid-2026 before falling to 0.2pp by December — resting on assumptions that the effective tariff rate declines ~2pp in 2026 (staying 9.5pp above early-2025) and that the consumer-borne share peaks at 70%.
- [REDACTED]'s 2026 core PCE call (2.2% Q4/Q4) sits 30bp below Bloomberg consensus and the FOMC median; its headline CPI call (2.1% Q4/Q4) is 60bp below consensus and 30bp below market pricing — but the firm frames a 0.3pp miss as well within normal forecast-error bounds.
- [REDACTED] judges 2026 risks as more balanced than last year, with tariffs now two-sided: upside from higher rates or a longer-lagged pass-through beyond 70%; downside if exemptions spread or the Supreme Court strikes the IEEPA tariffs without meaningful replacement.
- [REDACTED] expects residual seasonality to be a smaller problem in 2026 (seasonal factors normalizing) but data-collection shortfalls to persist as a source of monthly volatility.

### Backdrop
US core PCE inflation peaked at 5.6% three years ago and had retraced most of the way to the 2% target by 2024. Progress then stalled in 2025, with core PCE forecast at 2.7% for December 2025 versus 3.0% a year earlier. Official shelter inflation moves with a long lag driven by the gap between rents on new and continuing leases, so a narrowing of that gap signals slower shelter inflation ahead. Nonhousing services inflation tracks wage growth, which has now cooled to target-consistent levels. CPI and PCE differ in construction — CPI weights shelter far more heavily and includes insurance categories with source data unique to it — which normally leaves CPI running above PCE in a strong economy.

### At issue
This is [REDACTED]'s 2026 inflation outlook. The central claim: the roughly 0.3pp upside surprise to its year-ago 2025 forecast and most of the residual overshoot reflect the one-time impact of larger-than-expected tariffs, not firmer underlying cost pressures. The note lays out the forecast path for core PCE, headline CPI and the CPI–PCE wedge, the tariff pass-through assumptions behind it, the near-term monthly distortions from the government shutdown and start-of-year repricing, and a survey of data-quality issues at the BLS.

### Unpacked
The framing question is whether 2025's stalled disinflation signals stickier inflation or a transitory shock. **[REDACTED]'s answer is that the overshoot is mechanical and fading — a tariff bulge working through the data rather than a broadening of cost pressures — which is what lets the firm forecast near-target, below-consensus inflation into 2026.** The strength of that call rests entirely on the tariff assumptions: a ~2pp decline in the effective rate this year and a consumer-borne share peaking at 70%, with the year-over-year boost cresting at 0.8pp mid-year before collapsing to 0.2pp by December.

The disinflation story is then reinforced by two forces less dependent on policy. Shelter is the larger of them: a new-vs-continuing-lease gap 1–2pp narrower than pre-pandemic, near-flat new-lease rents, heavy multifamily supply and rising vacancies point to shelter undershooting even its pre-pandemic pace. **Because shelter carries a much heavier weight in CPI than PCE, this same slowdown is what flips the usual CPI–PCE relationship, pushing headline CPI slightly below PCE against its normal pattern.** The one holdout is health care — long contracts and government price-setting leave it as the last pocket of catch-up inflation, and its larger PCE weight partly offsets the CPI-side insurance declines.

The near-term wrinkle is that the next two prints run hotter than the benign trend. **December and January readings are pushed up by one-off distortions — the unwind of shutdown-depressed November collection and a residual January repricing effect — so a reader should not mistake those prints for a change in trend.** The firm is explicit that these are calendar and measurement artifacts, and even flags a specific April shelter jump from the reversal of shutdown-era imputation.

Underlying all of it is a caution about the data itself. **A ~20% drop in monthly price collection has nearly doubled the CPI's monthly standard error and multiplied the number of unpublishable subseries, meaning 2026 inflation surprises may owe as much to measurement noise as to genuine price moves.** For a reader whose main use of this note is calibrating Fed expectations, the takeaway is a sub-consensus inflation path with genuinely two-sided tariff risk, delivered through data of degraded and worsening precision — so individual monthly beats or misses deserve less weight than usual.

subject: US Daily: December [REDACTED]: Rising Through the Snowfall
summary:
# [REDACTED] Jumps to 61.4 as New Orders Surge, Even as Broader Surveys Soften

**Theme:** Analyst index strengthens on orders and hiring while price components cool; 2026 special questions point to more headcount and capex  
**Markets:** US economic activity  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jessica Rindels, 4 January 2026

### Landscape
- Headline [REDACTED] rose 1.9pt to 61.4 in December, well above the 50 line that [REDACTED] reads as consistent with trend growth.
- New orders jumped 10.6pt to 68.4 and employment rose 5.1pt to 51.2, while shipments held flat at 55.5.
- Exports rebounded 12.5pt to 51.2 after November's lowest reading since November 2022; inventories fell 3.4pt to 67.3, lifting the orders-less-inventories gap 14.0pt to 1.1.
- Both price components fell: materials prices down 13.3pt to 66.7 and output prices down 12.0pt to 48.2.
- [REDACTED]'s manufacturing survey tracker slipped 1.6pt to 49.9 and its nonmanufacturing tracker fell 0.7pt to 52.2, both softer on net.
- Survey employment components were roughly flat: manufacturing down 0.2pt to 49.7, services up 0.6pt to 49.5.

### Drivers
- Order flow is the main lift — the double-digit rise in new orders drove the headline and reopened a positive orders-less-inventories gap, a forward-looking positive.
- Hiring firmed at the margin, with the [REDACTED] employment component crossing back above 50, though the separate survey trackers show employment stuck just under 50.
- Pricing pressure is easing, with both [REDACTED] price components down sharply and output prices back below 50.
- AI adoption is broadening but not yet displacing labor on net: 67% of Dallas Fed firms now use AI (vs. 59% in May), and 76% report no impact on their need for workers.

### Unpacked
The December [REDACTED] reading combined a stronger headline with a healthy composition. **The advance came from the components that matter most for direction — new orders and employment both rose while shipments held — and the drop in inventories alongside rising orders pushed the orders-less-inventories gap back into positive territory.** Exports also recovered from a multi-year low. Set against this, the price components moved the other way, with materials and output prices both falling by double digits and output prices slipping below 50.

The [REDACTED]'s strength sits against softer readings elsewhere. **[REDACTED]'s own manufacturing and nonmanufacturing survey trackers both edged down, leaving the month's business-activity signals mixed but softer on net.** The employment components of those trackers were essentially unchanged and remain just below 50, a more cautious read on labor than the [REDACTED] employment component implies.

**The Dallas Fed special questions show AI use spreading without broad labor displacement so far:** adoption rose to 67% of firms, and most report no change to their workforce needs, though 8% say AI has already reduced headcount and 25% expect it to reduce their need for workers over the medium term. Where AI has affected employment, the burden falls on the least experienced: on net 26% of firms cut low-skill roles and 22% cut workers with little or no experience, while 10% on net added high-skill workers and 3% added workers with over a decade of experience.

**The [REDACTED]'s own special questions point to a firmer 2026 hiring and investment stance:** a larger net share of analysts expect companies to add headcount this year than last (33% increase, 44% unchanged, 22% reduce), 44% expect higher capex with none expecting a decline, and 78% expect price increases in line with the usual pace. The [REDACTED] weights new orders at 30%, shipments 25%, employment 20%, materials prices 15% and inventories 10%, mirroring the ISM's pre-2008 method; responses were collected December 18–29.

subject: US Consumer Dashboard: December 2025: Solid Spending Growth Expected in 2026
summary:
# US Consumer Dashboard: Spending Holds Up as the Labor Market Softens

**Theme:** Resilient consumption meets a cooling labor market  
**Markets:** US consumer / macro  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Joseph Briggs, 1 January 2026  

### Landscape
- Core retail sales rose 0.8% mom nominal and 0.7% real in October, though headline retail sales were flat.
- Real consumer spending ran at 2.4% on both a 6-month annualized and year-over-year basis through September, and 3.5% qoq annualized in Q3.
- The unemployment rate rose to 4.56% in the November employment report.
- November job growth rebounded to 64k after a 105k October decline, but the estimated underlying pace was just 32k, below the 70k [REDACTED] breakeven.
- Real disposable income grew 1.5% yoy and 1.8% on a 3-month annualized basis through September.
- The net worth-to-disposable-income ratio sits near its all-time high on strong equity gains.
- The saving rate fell to 4.0% in September, down from 4.1% in August and 4.3% at end-2024.
- Consumer credit grew a soft 2.2% yoy in October, while home equity loans expanded 6.7% (12-week annualized).
- University of Michigan sentiment ticked up 1.9pt to 52.9 in December; the Conference Board index fell 3.8pt to 89.1.

### Drivers
- Fiscal support is turning into a tailwind for spending — roughly $100bn in added household tax refunds is expected in 2026H1, underpinning a forecast 2.2% Q4/Q4 real spending growth in both 2025 and 2026.
- The labor market is still softening, with federal payrolls a 162k drag in October from the deferred resignation program; stabilization is forecast for 2026 at a 64k/month average pace, but risks are skewed to further weakening.
- Income growth is set to accelerate, from 1.7% yoy at end-2025 to 2.7% Q4/Q4 in 2026, driven by a job-growth pickup, new tax cuts, and a fading tariff inflation headwind.
- Balance sheets remain a stable support, held up by equity appreciation, with the saving rate expected to rebuild toward 5% by end-2026.
- Sentiment is low but improving at the margin — Morning Consult's daily measure has fully reversed its government-shutdown decline.
- Debt dynamics are benign overall, with leverage and debt-service costs low and delinquencies broadly stabilizing.

### Risks
- Downside: the analyst sees risks to the labor market skewed toward further weakening, which would undercut the income and spending baseline.
- Downside: auto loan delinquencies remain elevated, concentrated in subprime borrowers and 2022–2023 vintages, even as other delinquency rates stabilize.
- Distributional: Medicaid and SNAP cuts are expected to weigh disproportionately on real income for the bottom income quintile.

### Unpacked
**The central read is a two-speed consumer: spending and balance sheets are healthy while the labor market and lower-income households weaken.** Early holiday signals were consistent with a 0.4% mom rise in core retail sales for November, and the 2026 spending forecasts sit above consensus.

**The labor market is the main source of doubt.** November's 64k headline gain masks an underlying pace near 32k, well short of the 70k breakeven, and the October drop was distorted by the federal deferred-resignation program. The base case has the unemployment rate ticking down to 4.5% in December 2025 and holding there through end-2026, but the acknowledged risk is that it does not stabilize.

**Tax policy is the swing factor for income and its distribution.** The One Big Beautiful Bill Act's new cuts are expected to favor middle-income households in 2026, while Medicaid and SNAP reductions pull the other way for the lowest earners — leaving aggregate income growth stronger but more uneven across the distribution.

**Wealth and credit remain quiet supports rather than problems.** The net worth-to-income ratio near record highs reflects equities, and the low saving rate is expected to rebuild toward 5%. Credit growth is soft apart from rapid home equity borrowing, and while overall delinquencies are stabilizing, the auto segment stays a localized weak spot.

The report gives no explicit trade idea; it is a dashboard of the consumer landscape rather than a directional call.

subject: G10 Consumer Dashboard: December 2025: Improvement in the UK, Canada and Australia
summary:
# G10 Consumer Dashboard: Strong Balance Sheets and Jobs, but Weak Sentiment and Softening Incomes

**Theme:** Consumer health broadly stable to improving, led by UK, Canada and Australia  
**Markets:** G10 developed-market consumers  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jan Hatzius, 1 January 2026  

### Landscape
- Household net worth-to-income sits near or above P90 in the US, Australia, Euro area, Japan and Canada, and around P60 in the UK.
- Consumer sentiment remains below its historical average across all of the G10 (Exhibit 13).
- Unemployment is near historical lows in the Euro area (6.4%), Japan (2.6%) and Australia (4.3%); it stands at P55 in the US (4.6%), P45 in Canada (6.5%) and P25 in the UK (5.1%, 3mma).
- The saving rate is below its pre-pandemic level in the US but remains elevated in the other G10 economies (Exhibit 10).
- Debt service ratios are low by historical standards in the US, Euro area and Japan, but higher in Canada, Australia and the UK.
- Overall consumer-health proxy: ~P60 Australia, ~P55 Euro area, ~P50 Japan, P40 US and UK, ~P35 Canada — improved or flat everywhere since the last update.

### Drivers
- Real income growth improved in the UK (P55) and Australia (P45) but deteriorated in the US (P10), Japan (P35) and Canada (P45); UK private-sector pay slowed to 3.9% in October (from 4.2%), and Japan's nominal cash wages rose to 2.6% yoy though only 2.2% on a same-sample basis.
- Real spending growth improved in Australia (P60), the UK (P40) and Canada (P30), was flat in Japan (P40), and slowed in the US (P35) and Euro area (P35); Australia's 1.3% October jump was driven by discretionary spending on promotions and festival events.
- Labor markets diverged: unemployment fell 0.4pp in Canada but rose in the US and UK — though the US increase was ~2bp ex the rise in unemployed government workers tied to the deferred resignation program.
- Real net worth growth improved in Australia (P40), Japan (P55) and Canada (P45) but stayed at or below its historical average in the Euro area (P50), US (P45) and UK (P35).
- Housing is broadly flat across DMs but still falling in Canada; mortgage credit growth is subdued in North America and Western Europe but above pre-pandemic pace in Japan and Australia.

### Unpacked
The overall message is one of resilient fundamentals offset by soft mood. G10 consumers still draw support from healthy labor markets and strong balance sheets, but real income and net worth growth have softened and sentiment stays low. **The net improvement this month is concentrated in the UK, Canada and Australia, while the US shows the weakest income momentum in the panel.**

In the US, the sentiment picture is mixed under the surface: the UMich headline ticked up 2.3pt, yet its current-conditions component fell 0.4pt to 50.7 — a new historical low. Real personal spending was flat in September but year-over-year growth held at a solid 2.4%, and US real income growth slipped to P10, the lowest income reading across the G10. **The US remains the outlier on saving — the only economy where the saving rate sits below its pre-pandemic level.**

Australia stands out on the activity side. Spending accelerated to 1.3% in October, well above expectations, but the gain leaned on discretionary categories boosted by promotional discounting and major festival events — a composition worth discounting for durability. Sentiment there also retraced 9.0% after an unusually high November print, so the confidence signal reversed even as spending firmed.

**Canada's improvement is led by the labor market, where unemployment fell 0.4pp, even as consumer confidence stays weak and house prices keep declining.** Interest expenses remain elevated in Canada (Exhibit 15) and outstanding household debt climbed there while ticking down in the US, leaving Canadian consumers the lowest-ranked in the panel at ~P35 despite a high net-worth-to-income ratio.

The UK is the clearest weak spot on jobs: the labor market deteriorated further, with unemployment at 5.1% (3mma) ranking around P25, the softest in the group, even as real income and spending edged up. On methodology, note that from the June 2025 publication pension assets were stripped from the UK net-worth measures to harmonize with G10 peers, given their illiquidity and a persistent, outlier devaluation. **The composite weights real spending, the unemployment gap and consumer confidence at 20% each, real income at 15%, and debt-service, real net worth and net-worth-to-income at 10/10/5% — so labor and spending dominate the health scores.**

The report flags no explicit risk scenarios and offers no trade idea; it is a dashboard update, not a directional call.

subject: USA: Initial Jobless Claims Below Expectations on Christmas Week
summary:
# Jobless claims surprise lower over Christmas week, but holiday noise clouds the signal

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US labor market / weekly jobless claims  
**General comment:** Neutral read-through; flags the beat as possibly distorted by holiday seasonal noise rather than genuine labor-market strengthening.

### Context
Comment on the weekly US jobless claims release covering the Christmas week (initial claims for the week ended December 27, continuing claims for December 20), a period when seasonal adjustment is unusually difficult.

### The case
- **Both initial and continuing claims fell and came in below expectations.** Initial claims dropped 16k to 199k, well under the 218k median forecast and [REDACTED]'s own 235k estimate, with the prior week revised to 215k. Continuing claims fell 47k to 1,866k, also below the 1,902k median, with the prior revised down to 1,913k. On the surface this points to a still-tight labor market with limited layoffs.
- **The smoother trend measures are steadier than the weekly headline.** The four-week moving average of initial claims edged up 2k to 219k, so the sharp weekly decline sits against a broadly flat underlying trend. State detail was mixed and small in scale — declines led by Texas, Washington and Massachusetts, increases led by New York, Tennessee and Kentucky.
- **The beat should be discounted for holiday distortion.** Seasonal adjustment around the holidays is hard, which raises volatility in the claims data. The implication is that the low reading may reflect noise in the adjustment process rather than a real improvement in labor conditions — a point the piece flags twice rather than treating the number at face value.

### Implications
- The data reinforces a picture of low layoffs, but the holiday caveat argues against reading the beat as a fresh signal of labor-market strengthening.
- The steady four-week average, rather than the volatile weekly print, is the cleaner gauge for now.
- Expect continued elevated volatility in coming holiday-period releases, warranting caution before adjusting a labor-market view.

subject: G10 Inflation Monitor: Inflation Surprises to the Downside in the US, UK and Canada in November

### Drivers
- Core services disinflation continues in most DMs, but stalled in the UK at 3.2% (3-month annualized), keeping UK underlying inflation the highest in the group.
- Rent inflation is cooling in the US (1.3% vs. 2.3%) and Canada (6.4% vs. 7.8%) but ticked up elsewhere — a moderation in shelter also helped pull Canada's core lower.
- Core goods diverged: accelerating in Canada (1.2% vs. 0.2%) while slowing across other DMs.
- Energy inflation rose in Japan, the Euro area and Canada but slowed in the US and UK; food inflation accelerated in Canada and eased everywhere else.
- Tariff and special-factor boosts are set to fade — [REDACTED] expects the tariff impulse in the US and Canada, and UK policy-related factors, to diminish through 2026.

### Risks
- Data reliability, US and UK: [REDACTED] attributes the US downside surprise largely to methodological difficulties from the missing October CPI and later-than-usual November price collection, and flags core goods and volatile services behind the UK miss — meaning the softness may partly reflect measurement rather than a clean signal.

### Unpacked
**November brought downside core inflation surprises in the US, UK and Canada, but the cleanliness of the signal varies sharply by country.** In the US, the absence of October CPI forced [REDACTED] to assume a constant monthly growth rate for each component from September to November, and the November print itself was distorted by late price collection — so the soft reading (October/November trimmed core averaging 1.2%, and a PCE-based 3-month rate of 1.4%) should be treated cautiously. The UK miss was driven by core goods and some volatile services. Canada's slightly-softer-than-expected preferred core reflected certain volatile services plus easing shelter.

**Breadth measures confirm that the disinflation is genuine in most economies, even as a few countries buck the trend.** Extreme price movements remain contained almost everywhere, and the cross-item distribution keeps normalizing — Canada is the clear exception on dispersion, and the US ticked up on the above-8% share, though that partly reflects the same interpolation caveat. The share of the basket with rising year-over-year inflation ticked up only in Canada.

**[REDACTED] forecasts core inflation converging toward target across G10 by end-2026, on a Q4/Q4 basis, and generally below consensus.** The projections are 2.2% in the US and Canada (a fading tariff boost), 2.2% in the UK (special policy factors diminishing sharply), 1.9% in the Euro area (services disinflation on lower pay pressures, plus disinflationary impulses from a stronger Euro and Chinese export rerouting), and 1.4% in Japan (slowing food inflation and government measures, only partly offset by a weaker Yen). Over the past month [REDACTED] nudged end-2026 forecasts up 0.2pp in Canada and 0.1pp in the UK, and trimmed the US PCE forecast by 0.1pp.

**On a like-for-like basis, [REDACTED]'s harmonized core sits below central banks' preferred measures everywhere except Japan.** The gap outside Japan owes partly to excluding food away from home (UK, Euro area) and owned housing (US); in Japan, excluding owned housing pushes the harmonized measure above the BoJ's preferred core. The note offers no explicit trade idea.

subject: USA: FOMC Minutes Note “Most” Participants See Further Rate Cuts “Over Time,” While “Some” See Policy “Unchanged for Some Time” After December
summary:
# USA: December FOMC Minutes Show a Committee Split on Whether Cuts Continue or Pause After December

**Source:** [REDACTED], Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US monetary policy — Federal Reserve  
**General comment:** Neutral read-through of the minutes; flags a genuine divide on the Committee between further easing "over time" and a pause "for some time."

### Context
A note on the minutes to the FOMC's December meeting, at which the Committee cut the fed funds rate. The minutes clarify how much internal support that cut had and how divided participants are on the path from here.

### The case
- **The December cut had broad but not unanimous support, and it rested on a shift in the risk balance rather than on confidence about inflation.** "Most" participants backed the cut, citing increased downside risks to the labor market against upside inflation risks that were lower or unchanged. Dissent was real: "some" preferred no cut, worried that inflation progress had stalled or wanting more confidence in sustainable disinflation, and "a few" called their support "finely balanced" or said they could have supported holding.

- **The Committee is split on the path forward.** "Most" participants still see further cuts as appropriate "over time" if inflation slows as expected — consistent with October. Against that, "some" would likely favor holding "for some time" after December, which "a few" argued would let the FOMC assess the effects of this year's cuts and gain confidence that inflation is returning to 2%.

- **The risk assessment is asymmetric: employment risks to the downside, inflation risks to the upside.** "Participants generally" saw upside inflation risks as still elevated and downside employment risks as elevated and rising since mid-2025. On labor, most expect stabilization "under appropriate monetary policy" but call the outlook "quite uncertain"; "several" pointed to rising unemployment among demand-sensitive groups, potential layoffs in a low-turnover market, and job gains concentrated in a few sectors as signs of fragility.

- **Inflation is expected to ease only gradually, and cutting into elevated inflation carries a credibility risk.** Participants generally expect inflation to stay somewhat elevated near-term before declining to 2%, with "many" expecting tariff pressure on core goods to fade and "a majority" expecting housing-services disinflation. Notably, "several" warned that cutting while inflation is elevated "could be misinterpreted as implying diminished policymaker commitment to the 2% target" — even as "several" others judged upside inflation risks had decreased.

- **Balance-sheet policy: reserve management purchases (RMPs) began, framed as strictly technical.** Participants generally backed giving the New York Desk flexibility over the size and timing of RMPs, with debate over front-loading versus purchasing around periods of higher demand for Fed liabilities, and "several" favoring aligning bill holdings with TGA swings. They stressed RMPs are a tool for rate control and market functioning only, with "no implications for the stance of monetary policy."

- **Staff projections turned modestly more constructive on growth and slightly softer on inflation.** The staff saw moderately faster GDP growth through 2028 than in October — above potential, with declining unemployment — on easier financial conditions, stronger potential output, fading tariff drag, and fiscal support, alongside a slightly lower 2025–26 inflation forecast. Risks: growth and labor to the downside, inflation to the upside.

### Implications
- The minutes do not lock in a January move; the "over time" versus "for some time" divide leaves the next decision genuinely open and data-dependent.
- With employment risks skewed down and inflation risks skewed up, the reaction function hinges on which risk deteriorates first — labor-market softening would favor continued cuts, stalled disinflation would favor a pause.
- The RMP framing is meant to prevent markets from reading balance-sheet action as an easing signal; treat it as separate from the rate decision.

subject: US Economics Analyst: 2026 Capex Outlook: Adding Up the Tailwinds
summary:
# Capex Set to Outrun Consensus in 2026 on Fiscal, AI and Financial Tailwinds

**Theme:** Bottom-up tally of the fiscal, financial-conditions, AI and tariff impulses to US business investment  
**Markets:** US business fixed investment  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Manuel Abecasis, 30 December 2025

### Key findings
- Real capex is forecast to grow 5½% on average in 2026, well above the 3% consensus, driven by four converging tailwinds.
- The 2025Q1–Q3 headline pace of 6.5% overstates strength: stripping out an import surge in IP equipment and a volatile software deflator leaves "underlying" domestic capex growing only ~2.2%, in line with GDP but soft for an expansion.
- The OBBBA's investment provisions add about 3pp to 2026 capex growth by cutting the user cost of capital by just under 2%, then flip to a small drag in 2027 as IRA credits expire.
- Easier financial conditions than a year ago contribute about 0.8pp to 2026 capex growth.
- AI lifts actual capex growth by ~2pp and measured capex growth by ~1½pp, but most of it flows to imported equipment, so the net GDP boost is only 0.1–0.2pp.
- The tariff drag fades from ~1½pp in 2025H2 to ~½pp on average in 2026.
- Net, the four impulses add ~3.8pp to measured capex growth versus trend, of which ~1pp leaks to imports and is netted out in GDP.
- Risks are two-sided: tighter financial conditions or a weaker labor market to the downside; stronger AI demand or a larger OBBBA response to the upside.

### Method & verdict
[Reasonable] The note builds its 2026 capex forecast by quantifying four impulses separately and summing them. The fiscal channel runs OBBBA provisions through the CBO's CapTax model to get the change in user cost of capital, then applies an investment elasticity of 0.5 (drawn from a survey of studies, adjusted via Chodorow-Reich's methodology) and assumes three-quarters of the expiring-TCJA impulse was anticipated. Financial conditions use the firm's FCI impulse framework; AI relies on analyst consensus for infrastructure builders adjusted for national-accounts measurement gaps; the tariff drag is built from BEA input-output tables measuring supply-chain exposure by capex subcomponent, isolating domestically-produced capex. The approach is transparent and internally consistent, but rests on assumed elasticities, anticipation shares and a partly judgmental treatment of measurement distortions, and the additive framework assumes the channels do not interact.

### Unpacked
The starting motivation is that 2025's capex data are hard to read. A 6.5% headline masks two distortions pulling in different directions: a wave of imported information-processing equipment that mechanically inflates capex but nets out in GDP, and wild swings in the BEA software deflator that first suppressed and then flattered real growth. **Once both are removed, underlying domestic capex was running near 2.2% — respectable but unremarkable — which sets the bar the four 2026 tailwinds are meant to clear.**

Fiscal policy is the largest lever. The OBBBA restores full expensing of equipment and R&D, introduces bonus depreciation for manufacturing structures, and lifts semiconductor credits, while stripping out most IRA green subsidies. **Routed through the CapTax model, this lowers the user cost of capital by a bit under 2%, concentrated in manufacturing, and translates into roughly a 3pp capex boost in 2026 — though the effect reverses to a small drag by 2027.** Two things temper the impulse: much of the equipment/R&D expensing was widely expected and so already acted upon before 2026, and factory building as a share of output is still about five times pre-IRA/CHIPS levels, leaving less room to grow.

The other three channels are smaller and more mixed. Easier financial conditions than a year ago — higher equities, weaker dollar, lower rates, looser lending standards — add about 0.8pp. AI is the most nuanced: it may lift actual capex by ~2pp, but because semiconductors are treated as intermediate inputs and tech IP exports go largely unmeasured, only ~1½pp shows up in measured capex, and imports absorb most of the rest, leaving a negligible GDP contribution. **The AI story is therefore more a capex story than a GDP story — though the drag from imports should ease as buyers shift from individual chips to full server racks.** Tariffs, which weighed on the most import-intensive component of GDP in 2025, are expected to fade to about a ½pp drag as the shock ages and some frontloaded imports reverse.

Summed, the impulses imply a 3.8pp lift to measured capex versus trend, ~1pp of which leaks abroad and is netted from GDP, underpinning the 5½% forecast — front-loaded in 2026H1, decelerating but still strong in H2. **Timely indicators, notably the Dodge momentum index and core capital-goods orders, already point to firming investment, lending near-term support to a call that sits well above consensus.** The reader's takeaway is a directional overweight on the capex theme — particularly manufacturing and AI-linked investment — with the caveats that the gap to consensus rests on assumed elasticities and anticipation effects, and that a softening labor market or tighter financial conditions could quickly pull down the most cyclical part of GDP. The note offers no explicit market trade.

subject: US Week Ahead: December 29 - January 4
summary:
# US Week Ahead: Higher Bar for Cuts, and a Payrolls Number Running Negative

**Theme:** Post-December-FOMC read — minutes and jobless claims into a holiday-thinned week  
**Markets:** US macro / rates  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jan Hatzius, 28 December 2025  

### Landscape
- Current Activity Indicator at a preliminary +1.5% for December, down from 2.0% in November.
- US MAP index of economic surprises at -0.2, near neutral.
- Fed funds target range at 3.5-3.75% after the December 25bp cut.
- Initial jobless claims last at 214k; continuing claims last at 1,923k.

### Drivers
- **Fed policy — turning more restrictive at the margin:** the December statement and Powell's press conference raised the bar for further cuts; watch Tuesday's minutes for the extent of internal disagreement on the near-term path.
- **Labor market — softer than headline payrolls suggest:** Powell and the Fed staff estimate payroll growth is overstated by ~60k/month, implying actual growth is running negative on average; watch the minutes for staff detail on the overstatement estimate.
- **Housing — cooling:** pending home sales seen at +0.5% (consensus +1.0%) after +1.9%, and home-price indices (FHFA, Case-Shiller October) seen roughly flat to marginally positive.
- **Manufacturing — weak but off the lows:** Dallas Fed seen improving to -6.0 from -10.4 and Chicago PMI to 39.8 from 36.3, both still in contraction; S&P Global manufacturing PMI holds at 51.8.

### Risks
- **Upside (data noise) to claims:** initial claims estimated to rebound 21k to 235k (well above 215k consensus), which the analyst attributes to seasonal distortions from the Christmas holiday timing rather than a genuine labor-market deterioration.

### Unpacked
The week's calendar is thin and holiday-distorted — Thursday is a market holiday — so the signal concentrates in two events: Tuesday's FOMC minutes and Wednesday's jobless claims.

**The December meeting delivered a 25bp cut to 3.5-3.75% alongside an unusually divided committee** — two hawkish dissents in the statement and six hawkish soft dissents embedded in the 2025 dots. The minutes are expected to document ongoing disagreement about the appropriate near-term path, filling in the split that the statement and dots only signalled.

**The more consequential takeaway from December was the labor-market read: Powell and the Fed staff put the payrolls overstatement at roughly 60k jobs per month, enough to make underlying payroll growth negative on average.** The minutes are the next place to look for how the staff derived that figure — a detail that matters more for the policy debate than any single print this week.

Wednesday's claims number carries a caveat built in. The estimated jump to 235k sits above consensus but is read as a seasonal artefact of the Christmas week rather than fresh weakness, so a high headline print should not be taken at face value.

The rest of the docket is second-tier: soft-but-improving regional manufacturing surveys, a still-contractionary Chicago PMI, flat-to-soft housing prices and a decelerating pending-sales pace. Philadelphia Fed President Paulson, an FOMC voter, speaks twice on Saturday at the ASSA meetings, with text and Q&A expected.

The note offers no explicit trade idea; it is a calendar and preview.

subject: USA: Initial Jobless Claims Below Consensus Expectations

# US: Initial Jobless Claims Below Consensus, No Signs of Labor-Market Deterioration

**Focus:** US labor market (jobless claims)  
**General comment:** Descriptive, neutral read on the weekly data; constructive tone, no signs of weakening.
### Context
Comment on the weekly US jobless claims release, for the week ended 20 December, in a context where the market tracks the data as a high-frequency gauge of labor-market health.

### The case
- **Initial claims fell and came in below consensus, with no geographic concentration of weakness.** Initial claims declined 10k, to 214k, versus a median of 224k. ### Implications

- The rise in continuing claims warrants monitoring, but seasonal noise argues against drawing a conclusion about re-employment from this number.

subject: US Economics Weekly Update 12/23/2025
summary:
# US: Growth Surprises, but Weak Labor Market Keeps the Fed in Normalization Mode

**Theme:** Post-shutdown data dump sets up above-consensus 2026 growth with fading inflation  
**Markets:** US macro (growth, labor, inflation, Fed policy)  
**Source:** [REDACTED] (David Mericle), 23 December 2025  

### Landscape
- Q3 GDP grew 4.3%, beating consensus, with consumer spending up 3.5% and net trade adding 1.6pp; smoothing Q1–Q3 to strip tariff-driven trade and inventory swings leaves an average 2.5% pace this year.
- Q3 private domestic final sales rose 3.0% and gross domestic income rose 2.4%.
- Underlying trend job growth is estimated at 32k/month, below the 70k breakeven rate.
- Unemployment rose to 4.6% in the Oct/Nov report, but the true starting point is judged to be 4.4–4.5% once a temporary shutdown effect on government workers unwinds in December.
- Core CPI rose just 0.08% on average across October/November, with shelter at 0.09% and airfares down 3.4% (shaving 4bp off monthly core).

### Drivers
- Growth momentum is being supported by reduced tariff drag, tax cuts, easier financial conditions, and a 0.3pp bump from the shutdown ending — feeding a 2026 US GDP call of 2.6% (2.5% Q4/Q4), above 2.0% consensus.
- The soft Oct/Nov inflation prints are partly artefacts: later-than-usual price collection during heavy holiday discounting and an assumption of zero shelter inflation in October — a December payback is expected as these biases reverse.
- Disinflation is set to continue as tariff pass-through fades and wage and shelter inflation fall, taking core PCE to 2.1% by end-2026.
- Hiring is expected to pick up on stronger final demand, stabilizing unemployment at 4.5%, but it starts from a weak base.
- The effective tariff rate is expected to decline by 2pp, though still leaving it 9.5pp above the start of 2025.

### Risks
- **Downside (largest):** further labor market softening — the analyst flags this as the biggest risk to the forecast, since hiring is starting weak and the promise of AI could restrain it further.
- **Downside (Fed path):** while the base case is two more 25bp cuts to 3–3.25%, the analyst sees risks tilted lower, with a probability-weighted Fed forecast more dovish than market pricing.
- **Policy-contingent:** if the Supreme Court blocks the IEEPA tariffs, new Sec. 122 tariffs would be capped at 15%, below some current rates — a potential downside to the effective tariff rate.

### Unpacked
The October/November employment report is framed as a threading-the-needle print: **not strong enough to signal labor-market stabilization, but not weak enough to force a January Fed cut.** The reported rise in unemployment to 4.6% is treated as largely mechanical, driven by a shutdown effect on government workers set to reverse in December, which is why the forward starting point is placed at 4.4–4.5%.

On inflation, the message is to look through the softness. The unusually low core CPI reflects specific measurement quirks — price collection delayed into a period of holiday discounting after the late-November reopening, and a methodological decision to assume no shelter inflation in October when data could not be gathered. **Both are expected to produce a payback in December rather than signal genuine disinflation at that pace.**

The 2026 outlook is above-consensus on growth and constructive on inflation: global GDP of 2.8% (vs 2.5%) and US GDP of 2.6% (vs 2.0%), with core PCE slowing to 2.1%. **In this setup, further rate cuts are cast as normalization rather than risk management** — the FOMC is expected to compromise on two more 25bp cuts to 3–3.25%, with the balance of risks pointing to a lower terminal rate.

Politics runs through the policy section. With midterms ahead, the White House is expected to prioritize cost-of-living concerns, but the concrete levers look constrained: **Trump's proposed $2000/person tariff rebate has not gained traction among congressional Republicans, and the bar for another 2026 fiscal stimulus package looks high.**

The consumer outlook ties the threads together. Stronger job growth, a larger fall in inflation than in wages as tariff effects fade, and new tax cuts are expected to lift real income growth to 2.6%, supporting 2.2% consumption growth. **The gains are uneven — weaker at the bottom, where lower immigration and government spending cuts bite hardest, and firmer in the middle (income) and at the top (wealth effect).**

A final observation on layoffs marks a behavioral shift. Historically, stock reactions to layoffs depended on cause — underperformance when driven by falling sales, outperformance when driven by efficiency restructuring. **This year, companies announcing layoffs have underperformed across the board, even when the cuts were attributed to automation.**

subject: US Economics Analyst: 2026 Consumer Outlook: Solid Growth Supported by a Fiscal Boost
summary:
# US Consumer 2026: Fiscal Cuts and Equity Wealth Keep Spending Solid at 2.2%, Above Consensus

**Theme:** Why household consumption should hold up in 2026 despite a 2025 slowdown, and how unevenly the gains land across income levels  
**Markets:** US consumer / macro  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Elsie Peng, 23 December 2025  

### Definitive impacts
- Consumer spending slowed to 2.2% in 2025 (Q4/Q4), down from 3.4% in 2024, driven mainly by weaker real income growth.
- Real income growth fell from 2.2% year-over-year at end-2024 to 1.9% in September 2025, with slower job and real wage growth accounting for most of the decline.
- Recent job gains have run at just 32k per month.
- Tariff effects have added an estimated 0.5pp to inflation so far, with another 0.3pp expected over the next six months as passthrough continues before fading.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] forecasts consumption growth of 2.2% in 2026 (Q4/Q4), above the 1.9% consensus, and stronger in H1 on frontloaded fiscal and wealth effects.
- [REDACTED] expects job growth to rebound to 70k per month in 2026, premised on a diminished tariff drag and a fiscal boost lifting GDP growth.
- [REDACTED] projects real labor income growth of 2.3% in 2026 (up from ~1.9% in 2025) and real wage growth a little over 1%, as inflation falls slightly faster than wages.
- [REDACTED] estimates the One Big Beautiful Bill Act tax cuts add ~0.4pp to household income growth and +0.2pp to consumption growth in 2026, frontloaded in H1; combined with labor income, real income growth is seen rising from 2.0% to 2.6%.
- [REDACTED] sees equity-driven wealth effects adding a further ~0.2pp to consumption growth over the coming year.
- [REDACTED] expects a modestly K-shaped 2026: softest growth at the low end (hit hardest by government spending cuts and lower immigration's drag on aggregate job/income growth), strongest real income for middle-income households, and strongest spending among middle- and upper-income households via the equity wealth effect.
- [REDACTED] argues the 2025 K-shaped narrative was overstated: inflation and real income evolved similarly across quintiles, and weak low-end store spending reflects fewer low-income households (falling immigration) rather than individual households faring worse.
- [REDACTED] downplays rising consumer and auto loan delinquencies as a spending risk, attributing them to inadvertently risky lending years ago rather than weak finances; rates have stabilized and are normalizing on recent vintages.
- [REDACTED] flags two major downside risks: a labor market that fails to stabilize (possibly from hiring reluctance or AI-driven layoffs), which would hit low-income consumers hardest; and a fall in asset prices — a 20% equity and 4% home-price decline would subtract 0.7pp from 2026 consumption growth.
- The note offers no explicit trade idea.

### Backdrop
US consumer spending is the largest component of GDP, and its trajectory rests on real income growth (jobs, wages, inflation), fiscal transfers, and wealth effects from asset prices. Through 2025, two headwinds dominated: a cooling labor market and tariff-related goods-price inflation that eroded real purchasing power, with the pullback concentrated in tariff-exposed goods categories.

Immigration has fallen sharply, which weighs on aggregate — but not per capita — job and labor income growth, an effect felt most at the lower end of the income distribution. Equity holdings are concentrated among higher-income households, so any wealth effect flows disproportionately to the top.

### At issue
This is [REDACTED]'s 2026 US consumer outlook. It assesses whether the 2025 slowdown persists and lays out a forecast in which the two 2025 headwinds abate: tariff passthrough fades and the labor market recovers. The new element is the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, whose tax cuts are quantified as a household-income and consumption tailwind for 2026, concentrated in the first half of the year.

### Unpacked
The note reframes a decelerating 2025 as a soft patch rather than a turn. **The 2.2% pace of 2025 is diagnosed as a mechanical consequence of two temporary drags — a hiring slowdown and tariff-inflated goods prices — both of which the forecast expects to reverse over 2026.** That framing is what lets [REDACTED] hold a solid 2026 call even as growth decelerated through the year just ended.

The forecast is built additively from three legs: recovering real labor income, the fiscal boost, and the equity wealth effect. **The 2.2% 2026 number sits above the 1.9% consensus largely because [REDACTED] credits the tax bill and the lagged wealth effect with roughly 0.2pp each, on top of a labor income rebound others may not share.** The gap to consensus is therefore concentrated in judgement calls — the job-growth rebound to 70k and the durability of high asset prices — rather than in the current data.

Much of the note is devoted to distribution. **The K-shape is presented as real but modest, and crucially driven by different forces at each end: spending cuts and immigration compress the bottom, while equity gains lift the top.** The immigration point is subtle — it depresses aggregate low-end income by shrinking the number of households, not by making individual low-income families worse off, which is why 2025's headline low-end weakness overstated household-level distress.

The risk section is where the forecast is most exposed. **Both major downside risks — a labor market that never stabilizes and an asset-price correction — would hit low-income households hardest, meaning the same shock that breaks the central forecast would also sharpen the K-shape.** The quantified downside — 0.7pp off consumption from a 20% equity and 4% home-price drop — signals how much of the constructive call leans on elevated valuations holding. The reader's takeaway is that the outlook is solid conditional on two things going right, and both are judgement calls rather than settled facts.

subject: USA: Industrial Production Slightly Above Expectations; Consumer Confidence and Labor Differential Decline
summary:
# US: Firm Industrial Output but a Softening Labor Signal from Consumers

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US industrial production and consumer confidence data  
**General comment:** Neutral data readout; the standout is a labor-market signal weakening faster than the headline suggests.

### Context
A same-day readout on two November/December US data releases — industrial production (with October revisions) and the Conference Board consumer confidence survey. The releases feed the running debate over how much the US economy, and specifically the labor market, is cooling.

### The case
- **Industrial production came in modestly firm, but the underlying manufacturing picture was softer.** Headline output rose 0.2% in November, just above the 0.1% consensus, while October was revised to -0.1%. Manufacturing itself was flat in November (below the 0.1% expected) and fell 0.4% in October. Two weak spots stand out: motor vehicle assemblies dropped 8.9% cumulatively since September to 9.7mn, and the capex-sensitive business equipment category was unchanged on net over the same period. Capacity utilization was little changed, ending November at 76.0%.
- **Consumer confidence fell more than expected, driven entirely by the present situation.** The Conference Board index dropped 3.8pt to 89.1 in December, below expectations, even off an upwardly revised November. The split is telling: the expectations component held flat at 70.7, while the present situation component fell sharply by 9.5pt to 116.8 — so the deterioration is about how consumers judge conditions now, not their forward outlook.
- **The labor differential is the weakest signal in the data.** The gap between respondents saying jobs are "plentiful" versus "hard to get" fell 2.2pt to 5.9, its lowest since February 2021, and the prior November reading was revised down. Both sides moved the wrong way — fewer see jobs as plentiful, more see them as hard to get — pointing to a labor market cooling faster than headline payroll figures imply.
- **Inflation expectations remain elevated but stable.** The survey's 12-month-ahead inflation expectation edged down 0.1pp to 5.7%, off an upwardly revised November — high in level but not deteriorating.

### Implications
- The labor differential's drop to a near-five-year low, plus the downward November revision, is the piece's most consequential signal — a further data point for a softening labor market and, by extension, the case for Fed easing.
- Weakness concentrated in autos and business equipment suggests soft demand in cyclical, capex-linked sectors rather than a broad industrial downturn.
- Confidence erosion confined to current conditions, with expectations steady, tempers the read as a present-tense complaint rather than a signal of collapsing forward sentiment.

subject: USA: Q3 GDP Above Expectations on Strong Consumption and Lower Imports; Core Capex Orders Increase Sharply
summary:
# US Q3 GDP Surprises at 4.3% on Consumption and Net Trade; Core Capex Firm into Q4

**Theme:** Stronger-than-expected Q3 growth, driven by a services-led consumption revision and net trade, with capital-goods orders holding up in October  
**Markets:** US growth and activity  
**Source:** [REDACTED] (Jan Hatzius), 23 December 2025

### Definitive impacts
- Real GDP rose 4.3% annualized in Q3 (initial), above the 3.3% median and up from 3.8% prior; net trade added 1.6pp.
- Consumer spending rose 3.5% annualized, above the 2.7% median; monthly consumption growth was revised up to 0.51%/0.30%/0.11% for Jul/Aug/Sep (from 0.37%/0.27%/0.05%), with the July upgrade concentrated in services.
- Private domestic final sales rose 3.0% annualized; real GDI, a separate activity measure, rose 2.4%.
- Business fixed investment rose 2.8%: structures −6.3%, equipment +5.4%, and IPP +5.4%. Housing investment fell 5.1%; government spending rose 2.2%.
- GDP price index rose 3.8% annualized; core PCE prices rose 2.87% annualized, in line with expectations.
- Durable goods orders fell 2.2% in October (below the −1.5% median), driven by defense (−32.4%) and nondefense (−20.1%) aircraft; ex-transport rose 0.2%.
- Core capital goods orders rose 0.5% and core capital goods shipments rose 0.7% in October, both above consensus; September figures were revised up across all four durable-goods series.

### At issue
Two US data releases. First, the initial Q3 GDP estimate: 4.3% annualized growth, beating the 3.3% median forecast, with consumer spending (3.5%) and net trade (+1.6pp) the main upside sources. The consumption surprise largely reflects an upward revision to July services spending, tied to the BEA incorporating new Quarterly Services Survey source data. Second, October durable goods: headline orders fell 2.2% on a sharp drop in aircraft, but the core capex measures — orders (+0.5%) and shipments (+0.7%) — came in above expectations, with September revised higher.

### Unpacked
The headline growth number is strong, but its composition matters more than its level. **Net trade contributed 1.6pp — a large and typically volatile swing driven by lower imports — so the underlying pace of demand is better read from private domestic final sales at 3.0% than from the 4.3% headline.** That distinction keeps the print from being read as a broad acceleration in domestic activity.

Within domestic demand, the consumption beat is as much a measurement story as a spending one. **The July revision was concentrated in services and stemmed from the BEA folding in new Quarterly Services Survey data, so part of the surprise is better source data rather than a fresh pickup in household demand.** The monthly path — 0.51% in July fading to 0.11% by September — points to softer momentum entering Q4, even after the upgrade.

Investment was mixed beneath a firm business-fixed-investment figure: structures contracted while equipment and IPP each rose 5.4%, and housing extended its decline. **The October capex signal is the more forward-looking takeaway: core orders and shipments both beat and September was revised up, suggesting business equipment spending carried momentum into Q4 despite the aircraft-driven drop in headline durable goods.** GDI at 2.4% sits well below the GDP figure, a reminder that the two activity measures are not telling the same story this quarter. The note offers no explicit trade idea.

summary:
# Holiday Retail: Solid Online Start, Softer Stores — [REDACTED] Sees +0.4% Retail Control

**Theme:** Firm ecommerce over Black Friday/Cyber Week, softer brick-and-mortar, netting to a moderate November print  
**Markets:** US consumer spending / retail sales  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jessica Rindels, 21 December 2025  

### Estimates
- **+0.4% m/m SA** in Census retail control for November (nominal), the note's headline forecast.
- **+0.6% m/m** in nominal headline retail sales for November, driven by an auto-sales rebound and higher gasoline prices.
- **+0.4% m/m** in real core retail sales for November, after incorporating the November CPI report.
- **+0.5% m/m** in real headline retail sales for November.
- **+7.5% y/y** in Adobe-panel ecommerce spending over Black Friday weekend and Cyber Monday, decelerating from **+8.6%** last year and below the double-digit average pace of the 2010s.
- **+3.4% y/y** in ecommerce sales in the three weeks before Thanksgiving (vs November 2024).

### Outlook
- The signal is split by channel: online spending was solid, but brick-and-mortar — 70% of retail control — was mixed-to-soft, with Redbook implying a roughly unchanged reading and Second Measure suggesting an outright decline.
- The late Thanksgiving (November 27th) is judged a non-factor: seasonal adjustment in the retail sales report appears to almost fully offset the calendar timing, so no meaningful drag on November growth is expected.
- Official Census data are delayed by the government shutdown and will likely not arrive until January; the November report originally set for December 17th has not been rescheduled, raising the weight placed on private hard data for now.

### Unpacked
**With the Census release stalled by the shutdown, the forecast leans on hard measures of actual spending rather than sentiment surveys, mall traffic, or website visits.** The most-weighted input is Adobe Digital Insights, a panel of 4,500 retail websites covering 80 of the top 100 retailers, chosen for its high correlation (+0.72) with the official retail control category. For November 2025, the Adobe data alone would imply a moderate sequential increase in retail control.

**The brick-and-mortar picture pulls the other way, which is why the net call lands at a modest +0.4% rather than something stronger.** Redbook's seasonally adjusted department-store panel points to a roughly flat physical-store reading, while Second Measure indicates a decline. [REDACTED]'s own consumer spending tracker — built from private credit-card data and consumer-sentiment surveys — also moderated sequentially in November, reinforcing the softer store-side read.

**The late-Thanksgiving concern is addressed directly and set aside.** In principle a November 27th holiday could shift spending into December, but the report's seasonal factors appear to adjust for this almost fully; in past years with similar calendar configurations, November core retail growth showed no consistent acceleration or deceleration.

For what comes next, the January Census release is the item to watch, since it will be the first official read against these private-data forecasts, and the headline figure carries the added swing from autos and gasoline that lifts it above the core pace.

subject: Global Rates Trader: New Year Approaches Without Resolution

# G10 Rates Enter 2026 With the Core Questions Still Open

**Theme:** Disinflation priced, growth upside not — competing tails across G10  
**Markets:** G10 rates (US, Euro area, UK, Japan, Australia/NZ)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], George Cole, 19 December 2025  

### Landscape
- US front-end inflation pricing has compressed to close the gap between market-implied 2026 inflation and [REDACTED] economists' baseline, leaving near-term inflation risks balanced.
- The delayed US CPI came in well below expectations, the miss likely reflecting data-collection distortions; CPI swap-implied m/m fixings rose most for the December 2025 and April 2026 releases as payback is priced in.
- Short-expiry rate vol (3m10y vs 1y10y ratio) sits at the cheap end of its historical range after recent gamma underperformance.
- US repo behavior in December looks little different from prior months; SOFR spread to IORB shows no material year-end shift, with the TGA down about $140bn from its late-October peak.
- Euro area front-end has stabilised after recent steepening; the ECB raised GDP and core inflation projections but gave no clear policy read-across.
- UK 2y SONIA still sits ~50bp above [REDACTED]'s terminal forecast, with relatively little easing priced; long-end Gilts outperformed on the BoE meeting.
- Australian terminal rate (2y2y proxy) stands at 4.3%, near the ~4.6% post-pandemic peak that proved clearly restrictive.

### Drivers
- **US labor market (direction unresolved):** the "catch-up" data failed to settle labor questions; a weak early-January print would pull cuts forward, while a firm one shifts focus to cyclical acceleration — the key event to watch is the early-January release.
- **US cyclical firming (building):** abating tariff headwinds give way to tailwinds from easier financial conditions and front-loaded fiscal support in 1H26, a growth boost [REDACTED] expects markets to price as activity upside is realized.
- **Fed funding policy (compressing tails):** the rebranding of the Standing Repo operations and removal of "backstop"/operation limits signals an effort to encourage usage and compress funding tails into 2026.
- **German fiscal inflection (turning, gradual):** the 2026 funding plan lifts net bond issuance to ~€135bn and gross to €350bn (from ~€95bn/~€285bn), confirming fiscal easing is on track and pointing to higher Bund yields, though WAM adjustment stays gradual.
- **UK disinflation (intensifying):** continued softening in demand and last week's downside inflation surprise are the engine for lower Gilt yields across the curve, even as the BoE's hawks delay the next cut to March.
- **BOJ normalization (gradual):** the expected 25bp hike confirmed a path toward semi-annual hikes; belly yields pressed higher but the weak Yen kept FX markets unconvinced.
- **Nordic holds (stable to firming):** Riksbank and Norges Bank both held; Riksbank's growth upgrade tilts the next move toward a hike, while Norges guides to only modest easing (terminal 3.25% in 1H27).

### Risks
- **Upside (US yields):** if early-January data does not disappoint, [REDACTED] sees risk the market pivots quickly to cyclical acceleration, lifting inflation forwards that have lagged the rebound in cyclical assets.
- **Downside (US yields):** disappointing January labor data would open the door to pulling cuts forward; [REDACTED] frames the broader skew as tilted toward lower policy rates given disinflation and stagnant hiring.
- **Upside (JGB yields, near-term):** [REDACTED] flags tactical risk that yields overshoot its mid-year forecasts (5s/10s/30s at 1.50/2.00/3.45), driven by fiscal risks into the initial budget and the weak Yen.
- **Downside (AUD terminal pricing):** [REDACTED] views 4.3% terminal pricing as unwarranted on a sustained basis, citing downside labor risks and uncertainty over how much of the inflation overshoot is demand-driven.
- **Two-sided (Euro area front-end):** [REDACTED] sees balanced risks — German fiscal support pulling one way, traded inflation well short of hike-consistent levels the other.

### Unpacked
The late-year event risk resolved little but framed the early-2026 debate. **The US setup is a benign fundamental backdrop — disinflation plus stagnant hiring — sitting uneasily against a market that has priced the disinflation but not the growth improvement [REDACTED] economists expect.** That asymmetry is the core tension: front-end (Z6/Z7) steepeners are positioned to balance the two tails, and [REDACTED] leans toward long gamma into early 2026, favoring short- versus intermediate-expiry vol on the 5-to-10y curve after gamma's recent cheapening. The bigger-picture view is that growth ends up in the driver's seat, leaving Treasuries well placed as a risk hedge and a growth-driven selloff as an opportunity to add duration and lean back into carry.

The CPI distortions matter mainly for their echo. **The below-expectations print reflects collection problems — missing October data, late November price collection weighing on core goods, and a methodological shelter effect that could rebound in April 2026 CPI — rather than a clean disinflation signal.** Market pricing has already moved to reflect the December and April payback, and the compression in front-end fixings has largely aligned 2026 pricing with the baseline, so [REDACTED] looks to cyclical improvement to buoy lagging inflation forwards.

**On funding, the year-end turn looks manageable despite the calendar.** Reserve management purchases are too new to read, but the reclassification of the repo facility to "operations" and the dropped "backstop" language reinforce a policy shift toward compressing funding tails. Near-term, December 31 net coupon settlements of $88bn are comparable to December 1, and likely negative net bill settlements around those dates keep issuance benign; some upward repo pressure is possible but broad liquidity measures show little strain.

In Europe, the ECB package gave no strong steer — higher GDP and core projections, but Lagarde declined to opine on the risk skew, and an upside services-inflation revision was tempered by benign wage-tracker signals and geopolitical growth headwinds. **The clearer European story is German fiscal, where the 2026 funding plan confirms the inflection is on track and, combined with EU issuance for Ukraine, should push Bund yields higher via a belly-led selloff as cyclical firming plays out.** The UK runs the opposite way: **soft inflation, not the BoE's hawkish reaction function, is the dominant force, skewing risks to lower Gilt yields even though the next cut slips to March.** Long-end Gilt outperformance on the meeting reflects an ongoing risk-premium reduction tied to falling inflation, independent of the pace of BoE easing. The Nordics held, with Riksbank's next move biased up and Norges guiding to only modest easing.

Japan is hawkish enough for rates but not for the Yen. **Ueda's expected 25bp hike preserved optionality — flagging neutral-rate uncertainty while noting policy remains "some distance" from the range's lower end — enough to lift belly yields but not to support the currency.** [REDACTED] sees near-term risk that JGB yields overshoot its mid-year targets on fiscal uncertainty and a weak Yen that historically predicts front-end JPY underperformance, but eventual fiscal resolution and a benign 1.7% 2026 headline inflation forecast underpin a range-bound rather than bearish baseline.

In the Antipodes, Australian terminal pricing near restrictive levels looks overdone given downside labor risks and unclear demand-driven inflation, so [REDACTED] is comfortable long AUD forwards and sees 10y ACGBs rallying to 4.6% by end-2026. **New Zealand shows durable green shoots — including the Q3 GDP print — pointing to a return toward neutral and an RBNZ hiking cycle in 2H2026, with 10y NZGB yields seen near 4.5%.** With the two economies converging, the expressed trade is to stay received 5y5y AUD versus paid 5y5y NZD.

subject: Global FX Trader: That's A Wrap
summary:
# Dollar Sets Up Shallower in 2026 as FX Returns Turn Pro-Cyclical

**Theme:** Cyclical beta over pure carry; a shallow-Dollar year with balanced risks  
**Markets:** Global FX (G10 and EM)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Kamakshya Trivedi, 19 December 2025

### Landscape
- The broad Dollar is down 7% this year, and this week's marginally hawkish Fed and hawkish BoJ shifts left the Yen weaker.
- The BoJ hiked 25bp — its first move in nearly a year — but the statement and Ueda's comments underdelivered against pricing; economists see the next hike in July.
- EUR/USD is targeted at 1.25 over the next year, on a slower, shallower path than before; little valuation case remains after this year's move.
- The BoE cut on a narrow vote split, with Bailey flagging the policy rate as approaching neutral; economists now see three 2026 cuts (March, June, September), still more than markets price.
- Argentina's BCRA shifted its crawling band to track monthly inflation instead of a fixed 1% pace; USD/ARS forecasts were raised to 1,630/1,720/1,870 at 3/6/12 months (from 1,540/1,590/1,690).
- The Hungarian MNB pivoted more dovish this week.

### Drivers
- **Less US outperformance, fading negative US impulses** — the core case for a shallow-Dollar year, now with a more pro-cyclical tilt to returns as the drags that pushed the Dollar lower ease.
- **Cyclical beta rivals carry in EM** — as the Fed cuts, low-yielder EM carry keeps rising while high-yielders (Brazil, Hungary) cut, so cyclical exposure becomes as important as carry for relative spot returns.
- **CNY appreciation beyond forwards** — one of the highest-conviction calls; ZAR and CLP carry high betas to it and to cyclical pricing, plus cheap valuations.
- **Global macro dominates the Yen** — a baseline that typically produces Yen underperformance, with a reticent BoJ hiking cycle reinforcing it; front-end rate differentials still weigh on USD/JPY over time.
- **European growth and fiscal follow-through** — supportive for EUR and, with leverage, for the Scandis; SEK slightly the larger beneficiary.
- **Rising JPY intervention risk** — FM Katayama's language firmed ("respond appropriately to excessive moves"), capping USD/JPY upside; watch whether policymakers act after recent Yen weakness, though real TWI levels are less stretched than before 2022/2024 episodes.

### Risks
- **Downside to the Dollar (analyst):** a loosening US labor market and cooling inflation could drive more policy divergence and even less US outperformance, extending this year's trends.
- **Upside to the Dollar (analyst):** sturdy US growth could again set a high bar for the rest of the world; the Dollar's underperformance versus other cyclical indicators leaves idiosyncratic reversal risk, especially in European crosses. The analyst frames Dollar-depreciation risks as balanced overall.
- **Euro specifically (analyst):** having outperformed other cyclical indicators this year, EUR "has more to lose than most" if the US regains outperformer status.
- **Brazil (analyst):** elections raise local noise, but a less market-friendly outcome is better expressed as a lower probability that BRL's full risk premium unwinds, rather than sharp underperformance versus forwards.
- **CAD (analyst):** the USMCA review and unresolved US trade talks pose downside; labor and GDP details remain soft.

### Unpacked
The refreshed 2026 forecasts keep the shallow-Dollar core view but add a pro-cyclical tilt, which is why many small, open G10 economies are upgraded. **Carry still matters for total returns — more BRL outperformance is expected — but currencies like ZAR that pair cyclical beta with a carry buffer are flagged for greater attention.**

In EM, 2025 differentiated on carry; 2026 is expected to reward cyclical exposure roughly as much. **The high-carry outperformers of 2025 must now contend with local noise — elections in Brazil, Colombia and Hungary, and the USMCA negotiation in Mexico.** Brazil's real rates stay elevated relative to EM even with cuts. Hungary's short EUR/HUF recommendation is closed, as the dovish MNB pivot and the prospect of a closer EU relationship post-election are now better aligned for rate receivers. ZAR stands out as less exposed to domestic headline risk, backed by fiscal consolidation, a rating upgrade and a lower inflation target — the CAD/ZAR short is maintained. Within Asia, tech-related KRW, TWD and MYR are preferred over higher-yielders, while valuations become a growing constraint on otherwise pro-cyclical MXN and ILS.

On the Yen, the hike "is not enough": the global macro backdrop points to underperformance, especially versus EUR, though lingering US labor risk and already-elevated fiscal risk premia make this a lower-Sharpe expression. **Intervention would raise vol and dull tactical shorts, but has repeatedly failed to reverse direction when the macro justifies weakness — so JPY can keep underperforming on crosses.** For that reason the top tactical trades are instead short GBP/SEK and short CAD/ZAR.

Sterling's slight outperformance this week is read as a setback, not a trend change. The BoE's relatively hawkish read — narrow vote, "finely balanced" future decisions, a rate near neutral — provided the boost, but the broader UK data-weakening trend is expected to resume. **The core premise is unchanged: gradual UK data divergence from G10 Europe, overlaid on structural Sterling overvaluation, driving further underperformance on European crosses.**

Among small open G10s, above-consensus US, China and EM growth should help AUD, NZD and CAD over 12 months, but near-term the note prefers AUD and NZD to CAD, where growth risks are higher. The split traces back to 2022-23 tightening: Australia's gentler RBA path and lower peak rate left it more resilient, while faster tightening in New Zealand and Canada lifted unemployment more. **NZ's "green shoots" look genuine and anchor a long NZD trade, but Canada needs more evidence of a cycle bottom given volatile labor data, soft Q3 GDP internals and trade-policy exposure.** Policy convergence across the two is preferred via short AUD/NZD.

The Scandis face fragile, flow-sensitive price action — evident in SEK's outperformance and reversal this month — plus weak labor markets in both Sweden and Norway (Norges Bank could cut more sharply than priced, though economists dialed that back after hawkish guidance). **Still, SEK and NOK are seen as the best G10 Europe performers in 2026, just less outsized than in 2025, since H1's "perfect storm" — defense-spending surprises and record reallocation flows out of US equities — is unlikely to repeat.** The elevated FX risk contribution in equity portfolios that drove those hedging flows has normalized.

Finally, Argentina's move to an inflation-linked band is judged a step in the right direction — creating room for USD/ARS to depreciate and consistent with the BCRA's plan to accumulate about US$10bn of reserves in 2026. **But it is a crawl, not a step: the Peso is expected to keep trading near the upper band, implying only a moderately weaker real exchange rate over two years and stopping short of a competitiveness-restoring step depreciation.**

**This is a landing/podcast page, not the research itself — its substantive content is limited to the outlook's title and a list of topics the conversation covers.** The discussion features Jan Hatzius (Chief Economist) and Dominic Wilson (Senior Markets Advisor), moderated by Allison Nathan, and is described as spanning where growth is heading in the US, Europe, China, and beyond, and how to express that view across equities, credit, commodities, and bonds.

No figures, current levels, forecasts, or trade ideas are stated on this page. The 29-minute podcast and its underlying reports — the Global Economics Analyst "Macro Outlook 2026," the Markets Outlook "Some Like It Hot," the Equity Strategy "Tech Tonic," and the Commodities "Ride the Power Race and Supply Waves" — are where the actual data and positioning live. To respect fidelity, nothing beyond the theme above can be summarized from the material provided.
