subject: US Week Ahead: December 15 - December 21
summary:
# US Jobs, Retail, and CPI All Land in One Week — Payrolls Seen Recovering to +55k, Core CPI Easing to 2.9%

**Theme:** Delayed data floods in — November payrolls, October retail sales, and November CPI all print in a single week, with a soft-but-recovering labor read and cooling core inflation.  
**Markets:** US labour market and inflation  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jan Hatzius, 14 December 2025  

### Estimates

**November employment (Tue Dec 16)**
- **+55k nonfarm payrolls**, November (consensus +50k; last +22k in September); October estimated at **+10k**.
- **+50k private payrolls**, November (consensus +40k; last +83k September); October **+70k**.
- **Government payrolls: -60k October, +5k November**, reflecting the DOGE deferred-resignation drag (assumed 70k hit in October, +10k more in November) partly offset by state/local hiring.
- **+0.35% average hourly earnings m/m**, November (consensus +0.3%; last +0.2% September); October **+0.30%**.
- **4.5% unemployment rate**, November (consensus 4.5%; last 4.44% unrounded in September). No October rate — BLS did not collect the household survey.

**October retail sales (Tue Dec 16)**
- **Flat headline retail sales** m/m (consensus +0.1%; last +0.2%), on lower auto sales and gasoline prices.
- **+0.5% core retail sales** (ex-auto/gas/building materials; consensus +0.4%; last -0.1%).
- **+0.3% ex-auto** (consensus +0.2%) and **+0.4% ex-auto & gas** (consensus +0.4%).

**November CPI (Thu Dec 18)**
- **+0.20% headline CPI m/m**, two-month average across Oct–Nov (Oct +0.14%, Nov +0.27%); **+2.91% y/y** (consensus +3.1%; last +3.01% September).
- **+0.21% core CPI m/m**, two-month average (Oct +0.25%, Nov +0.16%); **+2.88% y/y**, rounding to 2.9% (consensus +3.0%; last +3.02% September). BLS will not produce a standalone October core print.

**Other [REDACTED] forecasts**
- Initial claims **225k** (week ended Dec 13; consensus 225k; last 236k); Philadelphia Fed manufacturing **5.0** (consensus 3.4; last -1.7).
- Existing home sales **+1.5%** November; UMich sentiment **53.6** final, 5–10y inflation expectations **3.2%**.
- Q3 GDP tracking **+3.5%** q/q annualized; November Current Activity Indicator **+1.9%** (vs +1.7% October); US MAP surprise index **0.3**.

### Outlook
- The note carries no explicit trade idea and no consolidated house forecast beyond the point estimates; its forward-looking content sits in the cited Fed-official remarks rather than in [REDACTED]'s own directional call for this week.
- Fed commentary skews dovish into the week: Miran (who dissented in favor of a 50bp December cut) reiterated the recent data "should push one in the dovish direction"; Waller framed December's cut as insurance against a weakening labor market. Williams sees downside employment risks rising and upside inflation risks easing. Bostic is the counterweight, calling the labor signal ambiguous and warning against feeding "the inflation beast."

### Unpacked

This week clears a backlog created by the government shutdown, stacking three major releases together. **The employment picture [REDACTED] sketches is weak in level but firming at the margin: private hiring runs at a moderate 70k/50k pace over October and November, while a large government drag from the DOGE deferred-resignation program masks it.** A surprisingly modest rise in federal separations in the latest JOLTS report led [REDACTED] to trim its assumed payroll hit, so the headline recovers to +55k in November from a depressed +22k September base.

The unemployment rate is a special case. **With no household survey collected for October, there is no October rate, and the November estimate of 4.5% clears only a low bar off September's unrounded 4.44%.** Rebounding continuing claims and furloughed federal workers not working during the reference week could nudge the count higher even though the shutdown had ended partway through that week.

On inflation, the same data gap means October and November core CPI can only be read as a two-month average, and month-over-month changes for those months are not recoverable. **The +0.21% average core pace pulls the year-over-year rate down to a rounded 2.9%, below both September's 3.1% and the 3.0% consensus.** The composition is granular: used-car prices rise on auction signals (+0.5%), new-car prices firm slightly on dealer incentives (+0.2%), car insurance dips (-0.1%), and airfares net higher (+1%) despite seasonal distortions. Shelter rebounds after an outlier-driven slowdown, with primary rent and OER both accelerating.

Two offsetting forces sit inside the core estimate. **Tariffs add about +0.08pp on exposed categories such as communication, household furnishings, and recreation, while delayed data collection subtracts -0.04pp by missing late-November holiday discounting in apparel, furnishings, and personal care.** Headline CPI reflects higher food prices (+0.3%) against lower energy (-0.1%).

Beyond the numbers, the calendar is dense with Fed speakers, and the quoted remarks matter for how these prints will be read. **The dovish contingent — Miran, Waller, Williams — is leaning toward continued easing, while Bostic's caution on inflation expectations marks the dissenting view the data this week will test.** Retail sales round out the picture: core spending rebounds 0.5% on improved alternative spending measures and slight residual seasonality, even as headline stays flat on autos and gasoline.

subject: US Daily: November Payrolls Preview
summary:
# US Payrolls Preview: DOGE Drag Fades, Private Hiring Holds a Moderate Pace

**Theme:** Federal deferred-resignation drag now looks smaller than feared, but the cleaner signal is steady private job growth  
**Markets:** US labour market  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Ronnie Walker, 12 December 2025  

### Estimates

**November employment report (delayed from Dec 5), to be released Tuesday Dec 16 at 8:30am ET; includes October establishment-survey data but no October household-survey data.**

- **+55k** total nonfarm payrolls in November (vs. consensus +50k; below the prior three-month average of +62k).
- **+50k** private payrolls in November (vs. consensus +50k).
- **+10k** total nonfarm payrolls in October; **+70k** private payrolls in October.
- **+5k** government payrolls in November and **−60k** in October, after netting state & local hiring against federal drags.
- **4.5%** unemployment rate in November (off an unrounded 4.44% in September); no October rate, as the household survey was not collected.
- **+0.30% m/m** average hourly earnings in October (neutral calendar effects); **+0.35% m/m** in November (positive calendar effects).

### Outlook

- **The DOGE deferred-resignation drag is now assumed smaller** — a 70k hit to October and an additional 10k to November, down from prior expectations, after a surprisingly moderate rise in federal separations in the latest JOLTS report.
- **The program's swing tells the reader little about labour-market health**, per the analyst — it does not touch private payrolls, which give the cleaner read on underlying job growth.
- **The Fed reads payrolls as more inflated than [REDACTED] does.** Powell cited staff estimates that payroll growth is overstated by ~60k/month, versus [REDACTED]'s 30–35k; on that basis the FOMC would interpret private payrolls in line with the [REDACTED] forecast as +10k in October and −10k in November.
- **Any November retail-hiring shortfall from a late Thanksgiving should reverse into December**, so the ~15k assumed drag is a timing shift rather than a level change.

### Unpacked

The report is unusual because of the shutdown: October establishment data were collected late and are folded into this release, while the October household survey — and therefore an October unemployment rate — was lost entirely and cannot be reconstructed. **The single largest source of forecast uncertainty is the federal deferred-resignation program, under which certain employees took paid administrative leave in exchange for resigning at a set date.** Earlier OPM reporting pointed to a larger payroll hit, but the muted rise in federal separations in the latest JOLTS softened that assumption; an ongoing hiring freeze still weighs on federal employment, partly offset by state and local hiring.

Set against that government drag, the private-sector signal is firmer. **Alternative "big data" measures pointed to moderate private job growth — averaging 62k in October and 38k in November, or 65k and 52k excluding ADP — and the broader [REDACTED] tracker improved to 64k and 67k after a stagnant summer.** The ADP figure is dragged down by a recent birth-death update that imposes roughly a 50k monthly hit not currently embedded in nonfarm payrolls, which is why the ex-ADP readings run higher. The end of worker strikes adds a small 3k boost in November.

Seasonal timing works the other way. **A late Thanksgiving (November 27) pushed back Black Friday and the holiday shopping season, and retail hiring has decelerated in six of the last seven late-Thanksgiving years — worth about 15k off November, to be recovered in December.** The mixed indicators carry less weight: initial claims fell (to 226k in October and 225k in November from 240k), the JOLTS layoff rate ticked up to 1.2%, and employer surveys stayed in contraction but have been an unreliable guide post-pandemic. Job openings are roughly flat to slightly lower on alternative measures despite a JOLTS jump, leaving the jobs-workers gap near −0.2mn.

Going forward, the private payroll figure is the number to anchor on, since it strips out the program noise that dominates the headline. **The gap between the Fed's larger overstatement estimate and [REDACTED]'s smaller one matters for how a given print gets interpreted at the margin** — the same headline can read as modest growth or slight contraction depending on which adjustment the reader applies.

subject: Global Rates Trader: Front-end Stress Test
summary:
# G10 Front-Ends Reprice From Cuts to Hikes — Steepeners Still Favoured Where Inflation Stays Benign

**Theme:** Cut-to-hike repricing across G10 front-ends; inflation as the swing factor for returns  
**Markets:** G10 rates (front-end)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], George Cole, 12 December 2025  

### Landscape
- G10 front-ends have sold off sharply in recent weeks, shifting the distribution from cuts to hikes in AUD, CAD, NZD, SEK and EUR — with echoes of the October 2021 vol shock.
- NZD and CAD 1y/1y1y curves screen at the steep end versus a fair-value model based on inflation, growth, spot inflation and the policy rate; AUD and EUR screen as more vulnerable.
- US front-end prices only ~20bp of cuts across the first three 2026 FOMC meetings; both US and UK front-ends skew hawkish versus [REDACTED]'s own economists' policy path.
- NZ 1y1y sits ~125bp above the spot policy rate, a move [REDACTED] reads as somewhat overdone.
- 6m T-bills are 4–6bp rich versus OIS, and [REDACTED]'s model expects that richness to persist over the next few months.
- CAD 2s10s screens ~10bp flat and 5y5y modestly rich versus macro fair value.

### Drivers
- **Growth improvement** is the fundamental kernel behind the hawkish shift — visible in data and market-based growth pricing — but it is more convincing in some curves than others.
- **Inflation is the key swing factor:** falling inflation with a positive 1y/1y1y slope favours front-end longs; rising inflation is the main risk to further steepening.
- **US Fed balance sheet:** reserve management purchases restarted in mid-December (earlier and slightly larger than expected); at $40bn/month through end-April, reserves rise ~$100bn versus the November level and settle at 12–12.5% of bank assets, shifting the TGCR anchor from ~3bp above IORB to at or modestly below it from Q2. Bill purchases of $223bn (Dec–end-March) largely offset $247bn of net bill supply.
- **ECB:** German cyclical momentum is turning up, but nominal repricing has outrun traded inflation — watch whether Lagarde endorses the hawkish skew at the December meeting; if she stops short, near-term consolidation is likely.
- **UK:** weak activity (October GDP contraction) keeps a BoE cut in view and supports Gilt outperformance, though belly underperformance reflects global spillover rather than domestic drivers.
- **Australia vs New Zealand:** Australia's hike premium is backed by sticky inflation and a hawkish RBA but with a stagflationary tilt (softening jobs, weak surveys); NZ's is cyclical green shoots. High return autocorrelation in both suggests a large systematic-strategy footprint at this turning point.

### Risks
- **Upside to yields (Europe):** the analyst flags that markets may still underappreciate cyclical acceleration in Germany, which could floor the inflation distribution and push EUR core yields higher.
- **Upside to yields (Australia):** a hot inflation print could make near-term RBA hikes more realistic, making hike risk hard to fade.
- **Upside to yields (US):** firmer early-2026 growth, plus a shifting investment/savings balance that can keep long-end yields sticky even under benign 2026 supply.
- **Two-sided in the Scandis:** strong Swedish growth forecasts and sticky Norwegian inflation cut against the case that these steep front-ends should flatten; NOK cut pricing stays vulnerable to better activity data.
- **Asymmetry, US/UK:** the analyst sees the skew as favourable to steepeners — clear labour-market weakness could trigger a sharp rally and impose a speed limit on selloffs, while better data only pares cut pricing.

### Unpacked
The report's organising judgement is that the directional shift from cuts to hikes is reasonable given better growth, but its durability depends on inflation. **The valuation model splits G10 into curves that have out-steepened their macro — NZD and CAD — and those still carrying vulnerability, AUD and EUR.** For NZD and CAD, negative output gaps and a benign inflation path leave investors reasonably compensated for "normalization hike" risk on a 1-to-2y horizon, so the bias is constructive despite caution around individual prints.

**In the US, the higher bar to cuts after a hawkish-leaning December FOMC still leaves a clear pathway to easing, and steepeners remain well positioned into the data** — though the stop on the SFRZ6/Z7 recommendation is tightened to 8bp after month-to-date steepening. [REDACTED] economists see about 20bp more disinflation than priced next year, with 3m annualised core PCE converging to 2% in 2H26; a still-clear skew toward cuts should cap selloffs while leaving room for a sharp rally on weakness.

**The Fed's balance-sheet adjustments read as friendly for front-end dynamics.** Starting RMPs earlier trims year-end funding tail risk (though the incremental liquidity is modest), and running them longer builds a buffer for TGA swings around the April tax date. Net bill issuance net of Fed purchases stays restrained near $270bn for 2026, keeping bills rich; the Fed left the door open to buying short coupons but would need more significant richening to shift composition. Higher reserves and an uncapped SRF should move funding onto a flatter part of the demand curve and attenuate episodic funding pressure.

**In Canada, the BoC's dovish tone reversed part of the post-payrolls selloff, which [REDACTED] had viewed as overdone.** Attention turns to inflation, the key ingredient for the constructive CAD view; with hike pricing backloaded into 2026, shorts in M6 can tactically hedge roll-down expressions, while a global rethink of the end of the cutting cycle may floor longer-dated forwards and support broader steepening.

**Europe centres on whether German cyclical improvement is convincing enough to shift the Euro-area inflation distribution.** [REDACTED] does not see 2y1y steepness as excessive, but the abrupt nominal repricing has outrun traded inflation; better data should floor inflation and drift core yields higher (they stay short Bunds vs Gilts), yet absent an ECB endorsement of hike pricing, near-term consolidation is the more likely path. On France, a narrow social-security budget agreement keeps election risk at a distance and supports modest OAT-Bund tightening, but the tight path to pass the main bill by 23 December caps OAT upside — [REDACTED] targets OATs at 75bp and BTPs at 70bp over Bunds. In the UK, the macro foundation still supports Gilts, with room for further Gilt-Bund and Gilt-OIS compression, though next week's labour and inflation data pose near-term two-way risk; stops are tightened on both long-Gilt positions.

**The Scandis screen steep but carry genuine two-sided activity risk:** SEK front-end pricing is judged fair given Sweden's expected top-tier G10 growth, while Norges Bank could cut faster than priced on weak activity even as above-target inflation keeps NOK cut pricing exposed to any upturn.

**In the Antipodes, a common global move masks diverging fundamentals**, with Australia's stagflationary tilt set against New Zealand's cyclical recovery and NZ's 1y1y move looking stretched. Expecting the two economies to converge as NZ activity and inflation catch up, [REDACTED] favours spread tighteners expressed further out the curve — received AU 5y5y versus paid NZ 5y5y.

subject: Global FX Trader: The Present of Payrolls
summary:
# Dollar Bending Not Breaking, With Risk Beta Back in the Driver's Seat

**Theme:** Fed easing bias vs resilient global data ahead of US payrolls; currency-by-currency reads  
**Markets:** Global FX (G10 and EM)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Kamakshya Trivedi, 12 December 2025  

### Landscape
- USD moved broadly lower after Powell kept the door open to further easing and confirmed the Committee's easing bias.
- CNY sits around 25% undervalued on a weighted average of [REDACTED]'s two valuation models — a degree of undervaluation comparable to the early- to mid-2000s "China Shock"; USD/CNY forecasts of 6.95 (3m) and 6.85 (12m) are stronger than both consensus and forwards.
- BRL and HUF have appreciated 15-20% versus the Dollar this year, with even higher total returns from positive carry, but both turned more volatile over the past week.
- USD/INR is trading close to all-time highs after INR underperformed other EM currencies over recent weeks; forecasts were revised to 89.50, 91 and 91 at 3, 6 and 12 months.
- The SNB stayed on hold in December, characterizing its inflation outlook as "virtually unchanged" despite a near-term downward revision, and slightly upgraded 2026 growth partly on lower US tariffs.

### Drivers
- Fed easing bias points to a weaker Dollar over time, but now with more risk beta than the Euro-led strength and carry returns that defined much of this year — trend durability hinges on US labor-market stabilization near current levels.
- Next week's US employment data is the near-term marker across most crosses; [REDACTED] economists do not expect it soft enough to trigger a January-style cut, leaving room for a slight USD correction if data land in line.
- BoJ is expected to hike 25bp on December 19, but one hike alone looks unlikely to end Yen underperformance; guidance is key, and reduced emphasis on the neutral-rate estimate could read hawkish only if paired with a focus on future hikes.
- Sustained modest CNY appreciation is functioning as an equilibrating mechanism — low inflation and high productivity lift [REDACTED] fair value while a large current-account surplus supports [REDACTED] appreciation — to limit protectionist pushback against booming exports.
- BoE is expected to cut next week; [REDACTED]'s view of deeper-than-priced cuts rests on inflation falling faster than the Bank projects, not on a dovish reaction function.
- INR weakness reflects subdued capital flows, reduced RBI intervention and a widening current-account deficit; a Q1 improvement plus tariff relief should stabilize rather than strengthen the Rupee as the RBI rebuilds reserves.

### Risks
- Downside for JPY shorts (i.e. Yen strength): a significant miss on US employment data could drive meaningful short-covering given stretched tactical short positioning, though the response may be muted after Powell flagged expected data volatility.
- Upside for USD near-term: [REDACTED] sees room for a Dollar correction if payrolls confirm labor-market resilience, with AUD, NZD and SEK the biggest movers in that outcome.
- The analyst still sees risks tilted toward earlier and deeper Fed cuts — and a weaker Dollar — than markets currently discount.
- EM political noise is a rising downside risk for BRL and HUF into 2026; for BRL this is framed as a lower probability of the full risk premium unwinding rather than sharp underperformance versus forwards.

### Unpacked
The Dollar view is one of gradual weakness with a changed character. **The move lower is expected to continue, but increasingly as a function of risk-on beta rather than the Euro strength and carry themes that led earlier in the year** — which fits the open recommendations to be long ZAR, SEK and NZD, currencies among the highest outright beta to risk. Near term, however, [REDACTED] economists do not expect next week's data to be soft enough for the FOMC to act, leaving room for a slight correction if payrolls come in as forecast.

On the Yen, the December 19 BoJ hike is widely priced, so guidance rather than the decision itself will set direction. **With one hike unlikely to end Yen underperformance, global macro and any domestic fiscal risk premium become the bigger drivers**, and benign US data should pressure JPY lower while supporting cyclicals. The preferred expression is short JPY versus EUR, chosen against lingering AI-related wobbles and downside growth risks; a large data miss is the main scenario that would flip this, given how stretched tactical short positioning has become.

The China call is a valuation story with a policy rationale. **The Yuan's ~25% undervaluation and strong exports argue for appreciation, and allowing it in modest, sustained form serves as an equilibrating mechanism against protectionist pushback.** Export strength spills over unevenly: low-yielding Asian currencies, the Euro area and CEE are vulnerable because their export mix resembles China's, while commodity exporters like CLP, IDR and ZAR are cushioned by the offsetting demand impulse from stronger Chinese intermediate demand.

Sterling remains a structural underperform on softer growth and inflation, but [REDACTED] advises scaling back downside risk into next week's BoE meeting. **The caution rests on a less near-term-restrictive Budget, a reaction-function point where some members may discount temporary Budget-driven disinflation, and pivotal inflation and labour data due that week.** The short GBP/SEK recommendation is kept (target 12.10, stop 12.80), just with dialed-down risk after a solid run for Sterling bears.

Among EM high-yielders, political noise is the new variable. In Brazil, Flavio Bolsonaro's candidacy for the October 2026 election is seen as too far off to extrapolate cleanly; **any market focus on a less friendly outcome is more likely to show up as a smaller unwind of BRL's risk premium than as outright underperformance**, with elevated carry sustained by a hawkish BCB — BRL has already retraced most of its initial weakness. In Hungary, reports of Orban eyeing the presidency weighed on HUF, but the prospect of closer EU ties and unlocked EU funds keeps appreciation pressure intact; the short EUR/HUF trade is maintained, with next week's MNB guidance in focus.

INR weakness is framed as part of an adjustment rather than a crisis. **External vulnerabilities remain far below prior episodes such as the Taper tantrum, and below-target inflation lowers the cost of letting the currency weaken and correct its 2023-2024 overvaluation.** Improvement is expected in Q1 as tariffs ease and equity inflows return, but the outcome is more likely stability than strength, since the RBI is seen using the window to rebuild reserves.

Finally, the Franc: the SNB's high bar to negative rates and its tolerance for inflation at the bottom of the range leave it on hold, with policy shifts likely only if clear currency pressure emerges. **Recent EUR/CHF strength is read as an overcorrection on trade headlines and idiosyncratic events including hawkish Schnabel commentary, leaving the cross rangebound near term but biased higher medium term** as resilient growth and a Fed easing cycle weigh on safe havens — CHF less so than JPY.

subject: Weekly Fund Flows: Rising Demand for Defensives
summary:
# Rotation into Defensives as Equity and Bond Inflows Cool

**Theme:** Broad slowdown in fund inflows, with a steady rotation from cyclicals into defensives and standout foreign demand for Brazil  
**Markets:** Global equity, fixed income and FX fund flows  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Isabella Rosenberg, 12 December 2025  

### Landscape
- Global equity funds took in +$6bn in the week ending December 10, down from +$8bn the prior week.
- G10 equity flows were neutral overall, with UK equity funds turning negative again.
- EM equity flows stayed firm on global EM benchmarks, and flows into Brazil were very strong.
- Utilities funds saw the strongest sector inflows on the week.
- Agg-type fixed income funds drew +$9bn, down from +$16bn the prior week.
- EM bond funds saw small net inflows across both hard-currency and local-currency funds.
- Money market fund assets fell by $8bn.

### Drivers
- The rotation into defensives is intensifying: flows into cyclical sector funds have fallen sharply in recent weeks while flows into defensives have steadily risen on average (Chart of the Week).
- Demand for core fixed income remains the main support for bond flows, with Agg-type funds still strong even as the overall pace slows.
- Foreign demand for Brazil is a clear standout, showing up in both very strong equity inflows and strong cross-border FX demand for BRL.

### Unpacked
**The dominant signal this week is not the headline slowdown in flows but the composition shift underneath it: money is moving out of cyclical sectors and into defensives.** Overall equity and bond inflows were subdued, but the steady multi-week drift toward defensive sectors — utilities led the week — is the report's featured theme.

Within equities, the G10 picture was flat, with UK funds the notable soft spot as they returned to net outflows. The strength was in emerging markets, where global EM benchmarks kept attracting firm inflows and Brazil stood out with very strong demand.

**Brazil is the cross-asset standout, drawing both very strong equity inflows and strong foreign FX demand for BRL.** On the fixed income side, the slowdown was broad but core exposure held up, with Agg-type funds remaining the strongest category; EM bond funds added modest inflows across both hard and local currency. The $8bn drop in money market assets rounds out a week of generally lighter, more selective positioning.

The note carries no explicit trade idea.

subject: US Daily: Shelter Inflation: Undershooting the Pre-Pandemic Pace in 2026
summary:
# Shelter Inflation to Fall Below Its Pre-Pandemic Pace Through 2026

**Theme:** Why cooling new-lease rents point to near-target inflation next year  
**Markets:** US inflation  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Ronnie Walker, 12 December 2025  

### Definitive impacts
- Official shelter inflation has slowed to +0.26% per month on average over the last three months, down from a +0.76% peak in late 2022 — back in line with its pre-pandemic pace.
- The gap between rents on new and continuing leases is now 1–2pp narrower than pre-pandemic, removing the "catch-up" pressure that had kept official shelter inflation elevated.
- Alternative new-lease rent measures have risen only ~1% over the past year, down from a 12–13% peak in 2022.
- The rental vacancy rate rose from a 5.6% trough to 7.1% in 2025Q3, while multifamily units under construction stand 14% above 2019 levels and starts run roughly at their 2019 pace.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] forecasts PCE housing inflation of 0.22% m/m (3.4% y/y) in December 2025 and 0.16% m/m (2.1% y/y) in December 2026 — well below the pre-pandemic rate — driven by subdued new-lease rent growth.
- Its new-lease rent model projects ~2% annualized gains over the next couple of years, below the 4% pre-pandemic rate, reflecting strong multifamily supply, a cooler labor market, slower immigration and rising vacancies.
- [REDACTED] sees shelter's contribution to core PCE shrinking from 0.7pp to 0.6pp by December 2025 and 0.4pp by December 2026 (vs 0.6pp average in 2018–19), reinforcing its call for near-target inflation in 2026.
- It expects shelter's contribution to core CPI — where the weight is roughly double — to fall from 1.5pp to 1.4pp by December 2025 and 0.9pp by December 2026, meaningfully narrowing the historical PCE–CPI wedge.
- [REDACTED] expects core PCE net of tariffs to reach 2% by H1 2026, and headline/core CPI at 2.2% y/y by December 2026; its one-year headline CPI forecast sits roughly 30bp below market pricing.
- The note offers no explicit trade idea beyond the below-market inflation forecast.

### Backdrop
US official shelter inflation in the CPI and PCE reports is measured from rents across all leases, most of which are continuing leases for existing tenants. These reset only gradually, so official shelter inflation lags market rents on newly signed leases. When a large gap opens between new and continuing lease rents, continuing rents keep rising as they catch up to market rates, keeping official shelter inflation elevated long after new-lease growth has cooled. Shelter carries roughly twice the weight in CPI as in PCE, and between 2000 and 2019 headline CPI ran ~37bp and core CPI ~30bp above their PCE counterparts.

### At issue
Several years ago [REDACTED] flagged that this new-versus-continuing lease gap would make official shelter inflation lag its leading indicators for longer than usual, as continuing rents caught up. The note marks that catch-up as complete: with the gap now narrower than pre-pandemic and new-lease rent growth around 1%, the dynamic has reversed, and shelter inflation is positioned to undershoot rather than overshoot its pre-pandemic pace going forward.

### Unpacked
The mechanism that once argued for persistently *high* shelter inflation now argues for persistently *low* shelter inflation. **The same lease-catch-up logic that kept official rents hot in 2022–24 has run its course, and with new-lease growth collapsed to ~1% the gap has closed to below pre-pandemic norms — so continuing rents no longer have market rents to chase.**

The forward case rests on supply. Despite rising vacancies and weak rent growth, multifamily developers keep completing units at a rapid clip, and the construction pipeline remains wider than in 2019. **A cooler labor market, slower immigration and a rising vacancy rate compound the supply glut, and [REDACTED]'s model reads all of this as ~2% new-lease rent growth — half the pre-pandemic rate — for the next couple of years.**

**The macro payoff is that shelter, long the stickiest obstacle to disinflation, becomes a modest tailwind toward target just as tariff pressure is expected to add only a tiny further increment.** Because shelter weighs more heavily in CPI, the effect is larger there and compresses the usual CPI–PCE wedge. **The actionable edge is the 30bp gap between [REDACTED]'s 2.2% one-year headline CPI forecast and market pricing — the note's clearest expression of where it thinks consensus is too high.**

subject: [REDACTED] FX Morning Notes: Another Negative GDP Print in the UK
summary:
# UK Growth Falters Again: Sterling Set as 2026's Regional Laggard, While the Real's Pullback Looks Shallow

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Teresa Alves  
**Focus:** FX strategy (GBP and BRL)  
**General comment:** Bearish on Sterling into 2026; relaxed on the Real's recent dip — both broadly in line with a carry-and-fundamentals framing.

### Context
The UK's monthly GDP contracted 0.1% against expectations of a 0.1% expansion, the second consecutive negative print after September, sharpening the debate over next week's Bank of England decision. The note also addresses BRL after a bout of underperformance.

### The case
- **The UK data mix points to a BoE cut and a weaker Sterling.** The GDP miss was driven by services, prompting a downgrade of the Q4 growth estimate to flat from 0.2% qoq. With unemployment forecast to rise to 5.1%, wage growth slowing, and inflation roughly matching the BoE's forecasts, the softer data argues for a rate cut at next week's meeting.
- **The combination of easing and fiscal restraint is a negative currency mix.** Monetary easing alongside fiscal tightening is read as a bad policy blend for GBP, making Sterling the expected regional laggard in 2026. The view is best expressed against European crosses, hence the open recommendation to be short GBP/SEK.
- **The Real's recent weakness is modest and its carry support intact.** BRL is down 1.8% versus last Thursday's close, but the cyclical model attributes only about 1% of underperformance relative to other fundamentals — small given strong year-to-date gains. Despite a pickup in volatility, elevated carry is likely to persist as the BCB keeps a hawkish tone.

### Implications
- Positioning favours short GBP against European currencies (specifically SEK) rather than the dollar, on a policy-divergence view running through 2026.
- The BRL pullback is treated as noise within a still-favourable carry story, implying limited concern about the Real's near-term trajectory.
- Next week's UK labour and inflation data are the key confirmation points for the BoE-cut and Sterling-weakness thesis.

subject: Global Markets Daily: AI Capex to Boost Yield Sensitivity to Debt Supply
summary:
# AI Capex Could Double the Sensitivity of Long-Term Yields to Public Debt

**Theme:** How the AI investment cycle reshapes the savings-investment balance and revives the link between fiscal supply and yields  
**Markets:** Developed-market rates  
**Source:** [REDACTED], George Cole, 11 December 2025  

### Definitive impacts
- The estimated sensitivity of G10 5y5y yields to public debt has fallen from 2-3bp per 1pp of debt-to-GDP in the early 1990s to near zero during the pandemic, and has since reversed to about 2bp on the latest reading.
- Under a baseline ~25pp rise in US debt-to-GDP over the next decade at the current ~2bp sensitivity, cumulative upward pressure on 5y5y yields is about 50bp — already embedded in the firm's yield projections.
- If sensitivity roughly doubled to 3-4bp (investment adjusting alone), that same debt path would lift cumulative pressure on 5y5y yields to 80-100bp.
- China's current account surplus is projected to reach close to 5% of Chinese GDP (about 1% of global GDP) by the end of the decade.
- Applying the historical China-surplus-to-savings relationship, that channel adds an estimated 1-1.2pp to the global savings-investment balance, offsetting roughly half of the 1.5-2pp rise in AI-driven global investment demand.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] sees the global savings-investment balance averaging 0-0.5pp over the next few years, down from a pre-pandemic 1-1.5pp, once AI investment and recycled Chinese savings are netted.
- On that basis it expects yield sensitivity to public debt to settle in the 2-3bp range last seen in the early-to-mid 2000s, keeping sustained upward pressure on long-term yields against structurally wide fiscal deficits.
- The firm judges that the aggregate savings-investment balance — not how capex is funded — is the primary driver of debt absorption, while flagging that debt-funded capex coinciding with heavy public supply would test the market's capacity to absorb duration.
- [REDACTED] argues the coming savings recycling will be bumpier than the mid-2000s "savings glut": with China's Treasury footprint much smaller and diversifying toward outbound FDI, clearing DM debt should require more intermediation, higher risk premia, and more flexible valuations, from a more price-sensitive buyer base.
- It notes countervailing forces — financial deregulation, possible productivity-led disinflation, and a shift in issuance mix away from the long end — that could partly offset the bearish yield impulse.

### Backdrop
Over roughly three decades, long-term G10 rates became progressively less responsive to public debt supply. [REDACTED] attributes much of this to a secular rise in global savings relative to private investment, which absorbed growing debt issuance without forcing yields materially higher. A reference point is the mid-2000s "global savings glut," when China's WTO-era current account surplus and other high-saving EMs were recycled into global markets — much of it into US Treasuries — expanding the market's capacity to absorb public debt.

The analysis rests on a panel regression of G10 5y5y forward yields on short-rate expectations, unemployment, long-term nominal GDP growth expectations, foreign yields, and debt-to-GDP excluding central bank holdings, with debt interacted by year dummies to trace a time-varying sensitivity.

### At issue
The note assesses whether the AI capex cycle will reverse the decades-long decline in yield sensitivity to debt. The global economics team takes prior large technological cycles — which lifted investment-to-GDP by 2-5pp — as a guide, with an AI cycle peaking near 2% of US GDP as a reasonable baseline. Absent offsets, that deterioration in the savings-investment balance would roughly double debt sensitivity to 3-4bp. Against it, the team sets an expected large expansion of China's current account surplus, whose recycling is estimated to neutralize about half of the added investment demand.

### Unpacked
The starting observation is that investors have begun asking whether AI-related capex will make private investment demand compete with still-elevated public debt supply for capital. **The regression update gives that concern empirical grounding: the sensitivity of yields to debt has already inflected higher, from near zero to about 2bp, and the recent rise is sharper than earlier estimates — read as heightened market attention to fiscal news rather than the depths of the pandemic.**

The forward case turns on two moving parts that do not have to move one-for-one. Investment is the more visible driver, and taken alone it would double the debt sensitivity. But history shows savings adjust to investment shocks — the mid-1990s productivity boom being the example where the balance did not fall in lockstep with rising investment. **The pivotal offset here is China: with a saving rate well above the global average, a rising surplus inevitably builds global savings, and on the historical relationship it recovers roughly half the ground lost to AI capex.**

**The key departure from the mid-2000s is structural, not directional — the recycling now runs through different plumbing.** China's share of the Treasury market has shrunk over 15 years, and it is tilting toward outbound FDI in EMs and away from reserve accumulation in Treasuries. So even if surplus capital ultimately finds its way to offset global capex demand, it is less likely to land directly on DM sovereign debt. The consequence is more intermediation friction and a more price-sensitive marginal buyer, meaning the market clears through valuation adjustment and risk premia rather than through a captive official bid.

**Netted out, the balance lands at a modestly bearish equilibrium: a savings-investment balance of 0-0.5pp, sensitivity back to 2-3bp, and persistent upward pressure on long yields — but the incremental damage is contained by the China offset and by disinflation, deregulation, and issuance-mix effects.** For the reader, the practical takeaway is that fiscal supply is becoming a more active driver of the term premium again, and that foreign demand for Treasuries is a less durable backstop than in the last cycle — a regime in which duration is likely to require better compensation.

The note carries a book of active trade ideas across FX and rates (e.g. short USD/EGP, long 10y Gilts vs Bunds, receive KRW 2y IRS, SFRZ6/Z7 steepeners), but these are the desk's standing positions and are not tied to the AI-capex thesis in the text.

subject: US Daily: December FOMC Recap: The Fed Estimates That Job Growth Is Negative
summary:
# Fed Cuts 25bp but Raises the Bar for Further Cuts — While Signaling Employment May Already Be Contracting

**Source:** [REDACTED] — David Mericle
**Focus:** US monetary policy — Federal Reserve
**General comment:** Reads the December FOMC as hawkish in framing but dovish in substance; keeps its below-consensus rate call.

### Context
Recap of the December 2025 FOMC, which delivered a third consecutive 25bp cut to a 3.5-3.75% funds rate. The piece weighs the meeting's mixed signals — a hawkish adjustment to the guidance against Powell's markedly dovish labor-market remarks — and reaffirms the house rate path.

### The case
- **The cut came packaged with hawkish signals that raise the bar for further easing.** The statement borrowed December-2024 language making the "extent and timing" of additional adjustments data-dependent. Powell reinforced this in the press conference, arguing the Fed is "well positioned to wait" after 75bp of cuts since September (175bp since September 2024), and stating six times that the funds rate now sits within the "range of plausible estimates of neutral," if at the "high end." Dissent was unusually broad: two hawkish dissents from voters plus six hawkish soft dissents in the dots, for a record seven total soft dissents.
- **The meeting's most important new information was Powell's estimate that payroll growth is being overstated by ~60k jobs per month — larger than the house's own 30-35k estimate.** On that adjustment, the roughly 40k reported May-September pace would actually be closer to -20k, and Powell flagged "a world where job creation is negative" as something the FOMC must watch "very carefully." Combined with his view that downside risks to employment are "significant" and rising, this framed the labor market as materially weaker than the headline data suggest.
- **Powell's dovish tone drove the market reaction despite the hawkish guidance.** The labor-market comments, his continued confidence on inflation, and the absence of a firmer lean toward a January pause — which some investors expected — produced a dovish reaction in bonds.
- **Where the Committee stops is left genuinely open and likely contentious.** The dot plot showed six different terminal-rate estimates spanning 2.5-2.75% to 3.75-4%, so the stopping point is unsettled even as the base case points to more cuts.

### Implications
- Base case is unchanged: two normalization cuts in March and June 2026 to a 3-3.25% terminal rate, supported by core PCE seen falling to 2.2% by 2025Q4, below the FOMC median of 2.5%.
- The wide dispersion of terminal-rate views is the key risk to that path — the destination, not the near-term direction, is where disagreement concentrates.
- Separately, the Fed will start Treasury purchases on December 12, earlier than expected, to keep reserves ample as the banking system grows.

subject: US Monthly Inflation Monitor: September 2025: Core Goods Inflation Rises but Should Cool in 2026
summary:
# Core Goods Reheat Now, Disinflation Later: Tariff Passthrough Peaks Before a 2026 Fade

**Theme:** Tariff-driven goods pickup masking underlying disinflation toward 2%  
**Markets:** US inflation  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jan Hatzius, 10 December 2025  

### Landscape
- Core PCE rose 0.20% m/m in September; the y/y rate fell to 2.83%, down from a 5.61% peak.
- Core CPI rose 0.23% m/m in September; the y/y rate fell to 3.03%, down from a 6.63% peak.
- Sequential trend-inflation measures decelerated on net in September and have slowed toward their average pre-pandemic pace.
- Core goods prices rose 0.18% in September (from −0.11% in August), running +1.21% y/y in the PCE index versus roughly −0.5% y/y in 2018 when core PCE ran near 2%.
- Core services ex-housing rose 0.22% in September (from +0.32% in August), +3.3% y/y, down from 3.9% in December 2024 but above the 2.5% pace of 2018.
- New-lease rent growth on the best alternative measures ran +0.8% y/y in October (from +0.9% in September).
- Manheim used-car auction prices sat 16% above pre-pandemic levels in early November (depreciation-adjusted), roughly in line with the overall price-level gain since 2019.

### Drivers
- Tariff passthrough is the active goods driver and still building: 58% of tariff costs have reached consumer prices after seven months, with y/y core goods inflation set to accelerate further over the next few months before turning down in 2H 2026.
- Commodities pushed up in November — energy +2.7% m/m, industrial metals +0.9%, precious metals +1.5% m/m and 55% y/y — but are expected to impose only a modest ~5bp average drag on y/y core PCE in 2026.
- Wage pressure is easing: the [REDACTED] wage tracker was +3.9% y/y in Q3 and the composite of business wage-growth expectations ticked down to +3.1% in November.
- Labor-market slack has largely closed the demand side: the jobs-workers gap fell to −0.2mn in November, versus 6mn in early 2022 and 1.3mn on average in 2019.
- Housing is now slowing sequentially and new-lease rent growth is soft, pointing to continued cooling in the largest services component.
- Inflation expectations are normalizing: UMich long-term fell 0.2pp to 3.2% and NY Fed held at 3.0%; short-term measures have partly retraced their tariff-driven spike (UMich 1yr −0.4pp to 4.1%; NY Fed 1yr unchanged at 3.2%). Market-implied CPI declined ~0.1pp to 2.9% for 2025 and 2.4% for 2026–2027.

### Unpacked
The report's central reading is that two forces are moving in opposite directions, and the headline masks the split. **Underlying inflation is already close to target — core PCE net of tariff effects has trended down to about 2.3% and is seen reaching 2% by early 2026 — while tariff passthrough is temporarily holding the reported figure up.** [REDACTED] estimates tariffs have added 0.5pp to y/y core PCE so far and will add another 0.4pp through end-2026, with only a small further rise in the effective tariff rate assumed next year.

On goods, the September rebound reflects tariff costs feeding through faster than the commodity backdrop would otherwise imply. **Core goods inflation is expected to accelerate somewhat more in the near term as passthrough continues, then decline in the second half of 2026 once the tariff impulse has largely worked through.** Autos illustrate the more stable side of the picture: new-car inventories were at 73% of the 2019 average in August, and used-car auction prices have moved sideways, tracking the broad price level since 2019 rather than adding fresh pressure.

Services ex-housing carry the disinflationary thread. **Cooling wages, a labor market roughly back to 2019-style balance, and slowing new-lease rents together point to further easing in the stickiest part of core inflation**, even though the current 3.3% pace remains above pre-pandemic norms. Housing's outsized contribution to y/y inflation is now fading sequentially, reinforcing the direction of travel.

The forecast ties these threads together into a gradual glide down. **[REDACTED] sees core PCE at 3.0% by end-2025 and 2.2% by end-2026, with core CPI easing from 3.0% in September to 2.9% in December 2025 and 2.2% by end-2026** — the 2026 improvement driven by underlying disinflation more than offsetting a tariff effect that peaks and then partially unwinds. The note reports no explicit trade idea and does not lay out formal upside/downside risk scenarios beyond the timing uncertainty around tariff passthrough and the commodity path.

subject: USA: FOMC Lowers Fed Funds Rate by 25bp; Two Hawkish Dissents and One Dovish Dissent; SEP Median Dot Unchanged, With Six Hawkish “Soft Dissents” for 2025
summary:
# FOMC corta 25bp, mas placar dividido e dots inalterados sinalizam Fed cauteloso na sequência

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US monetary policy / Federal Reserve  
**General comment:** Descriptive read of a "hawkish cut" — decision delivered, but dissents and unchanged dots point to a slower path than the easing itself might suggest.

### Context
The FOMC cut the fed funds target range by 25bp to 3.50–3.75% at its December meeting, alongside an updated Summary of Economic Projections (SEP). The comment parses a split decision and a set of forecast revisions to gauge how much further easing the Committee is actually signalling.

### The case
- **The cut came with unusually broad dissent in both directions.** Three officials voted against: Schmid and Goolsbee preferred no cut, while Miran wanted 50bp. The Committee also restored prior language making "the extent and timing" of further adjustments conditional on the data, outlook, and balance of risks — a step back toward meeting-by-meeting optionality rather than a pre-committed path.
- **The projected path is shallow and its median masks a hawkish tilt.** The SEP median shows just one cut in each of 2026 and 2027, reaching a 3.125% terminal rate — unchanged from September — with the longer-run dot steady at 3.0%. Six participants entered "soft dissents" for a higher 2025 rate against only one for a lower rate (likely Miran), and the neutral-rate estimates are near-evenly split (9 above 3%, 10 at or below), underlining that the median understates hawkish sentiment on the Committee.
- **Forecast revisions read as modestly constructive but partly mechanical.** Median GDP growth was revised up across the horizon, most notably +0.5pp to 2.3% in 2026 — an upgrade attributed in part to the mechanical rebound from the government shutdown, estimated at 0.3pp. Core and headline PCE inflation were trimmed for 2025–2026, and unemployment was nudged down 0.1pp in 2027 to 4.2%, leaving a slightly better growth/inflation mix without altering the rate path.
- **A separate operational shift addresses reserve management, not policy stance.** The Fed will begin reserve management purchases on Friday to keep reserves "ample," at roughly $40bn/month per the New York Fed. Combined with $20bn/month of MBS reinvestment into T-bills, this totals about $60bn of bill purchases monthly for the next few months, with the pace expected to slow after April as the Treasury General Account declines.

### Implications
- The bar for further cuts looks higher than the cut itself implies: the restored data-dependent language plus broad hawkish dissent point to a pause-prone, meeting-by-meeting Fed.
- The balance-sheet purchases are a plumbing operation to maintain ample reserves, not a stimulative signal — markets should not read them as QE.

subject: USA: Employment Cost Index Slightly Below Consensus Expectations
summary:
# US: Q3 ECI Slightly Below Consensus, Wages Continue Gradual Deceleration

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius
**Focus:** US labor costs and wages
**General comment:** Descriptive data read; neutral tone, reinforces the narrative of gradual wage moderation

### Context
Comment on the release of the Q3 2025 Employment Cost Index (ECI), the main quarterly measure of US labor costs and a key input into the bank's wage tracker.

### The data
- **The ECI rose 0.8% on the quarter (not annualized), below the median of +0.9% and the prior quarter (+0.9%), in line with the bank's own projection of +0.8%.** The most closely watched underlying measure — private wages excluding incentive-paid occupations — also rose 0.8% (seasonally adjusted by the bank).
- **The sector breakdown shows dispersion.** Compensation growth was led by other services (+1.6%), wholesale trade (+1.6%), and construction (+1.2%); the weakest paces were in professional and scientific services (+0.6%), finance (+0.6%), and leisure and hospitality (+0.6%).
- **The bank's wage tracker stands at 3.8% on an annualized quarterly basis and 3.9% year-over-year in Q3.**

### Implications
- The slightly below-expectations result, combined with the deceleration from the prior quarter, is consistent with ongoing wage moderation.
- The wage tracker levels (around 3.8%–3.9%) remain the reference point for assessing the trajectory of labor costs and its compatibility with the inflation target.

subject: USA: Job Openings Increase in October, Against Expectations and Signals from Alternative Private Sector Data
summary:
# JOLTS Openings Jump in October Even as Private-Sector Data Point Slightly Lower

**Theme:** October JOLTS surprises well above forecast; quits fall to a post-2014 low while alternative data diverge  
**Markets:** US labor market  
**Source:** [REDACTED] (Jan Hatzius), 9 December 2025  

### Definitive impacts
- Job openings rose to 7,670k in October and 7,658k in September, up from an unrevised 7,227k in August — far above the 7,117k median forecast and [REDACTED]'s 7,100k call.
- Openings increased most in retail trade (+142k) and wholesale trade (+52k), and fell most in professional and business services (−114k) and finance and insurance (−69k).
- The job openings rate held at 4.6% in October; the hiring rate fell 0.2pp to 3.2%.
- The layoff rate rose 0.1pp to 1.2%, driven by state and local government (+0.1pp to 0.5%).
- The quits rate fell 0.2pp to 1.8%, the lowest outside Covid since 2014.
- Federal government quits reached 46k in September and 21k in October (vs. a 15k prior three-month average), below the count who signed up for the federal deferred-resignation program.
- Alternative private-sector data through October instead show openings down roughly 15k since August.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] estimates the job-workers gap at −0.2mn in November, from its advance measure blending JOLTS, Indeed, and LinkUp — signaling labor demand still modestly short of supply.

### At issue

- Growth is expected to pick up in 2026, helping stabilize the labor market and shifting the Fed from risk-management mode toward normalization.

### Risks
- Two-sided data risk: the Fed cannot commit to a path because it is "two employment reports out of date," and a January cut could still prove appropriate depending on incoming data — the analyst frames this as the reason the FOMC will avoid boxing itself in.
- Tariffs are the key upside inflation risk: the analyst's 2026 core PCE forecast is 2.2% with tariff effects versus 2.0% without, quantifying the wedge.

### Unpacked
**The base case is a "hawkish cut": the FOMC delivers its third straight 25bp move to 3.5–3.75% while deliberately raising the bar for further easing.** The statement is expected to revive the "extent and timing of additional adjustments" language used a year ago, and Powell is likely to convey that the threshold for future cuts has risen and to explain why some participants opposed this one. The decision is expected to carry two hawkish dissents in the statement and five soft dissents in the dots.

**The updated projections are forecast to show a shallower easing path alongside firmer growth and softer inflation.** The dots are expected to show one cut in 2026 to 3.375% and one more in 2027 to 3.125%. GDP growth is seen revised up for 2025 (+0.4pp to 2%) and 2026 (+0.2pp to 2%), while core inflation is marked down for both years (-0.1pp to 3% in 2025 and to 2.5% in 2026).

**Looking through 2026, the framing shifts from risk management to normalization.** As growth firms and the labor market stabilizes, core PCE is forecast to fall to 2.2% by year-end, at which point the debate turns to the appropriate terminal rate. The expectation is a compromise on two more 25bp cuts, taking the funds rate to 3–3.25%.

**The near-term read hinges on delayed data that will land in a compressed window through late December.** The shutdown pushed JOLTS, the ECI, the trade balance, retail sales, the November employment report (with October payrolls), CPI, and Q3 GDP into a cluster of releases between December 9 and 23, so the Fed is deciding with an unusually stale picture of the labor market.

The disinflation call rests on a methodological point about producer prices: same-month core PPI and core CPI relationships are weak, but aggregating detailed PPI input prices provides a useful lead on specific core PCE items months ahead. That approach underpins the subdued inflation outlook and the 2.0% ex-tariff core PCE forecast for 2026. The note offers no explicit trade idea.

subject: US Daily: What Can the Producer Price Index Tell Us About Inflation?
summary:
# The PPI as an Inflation Signal: Weak Same-Month, Useful a Few Months Out

**Theme:** Whether PPI data can proxy for delayed CPI and forecast the near-term inflation path  
**Markets:** US consumer prices  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Manuel Abecasis, 7 December 2025  

### Key findings
- Same-month core PPI carries little information about core CPI, so the delayed October and November PPI reports offer limited help in reading through the disrupted CPI releases.
- Surprises to consensus core PPI show no meaningful link to core CPI surprises, reinforcing the weak same-month relationship.
- The signal is somewhat stronger at inflation extremes (unusually high or low months) and for core goods categories, as seen in 2020–2022.
- Detailed industry- and commodity-level PPI data does lead inflation by a few months, giving custom intermediate-demand indices useful predictive power for goods categories like appliances, furniture, sports vehicles, and clothing.
- Excluding tariff effects, those indices point to subdued price pressures over the coming months, consistent with continued disinflation into next year.
- Incorporating these signals, plus a smaller assumed 2026 tariff increase, yields a revised forecast of 2.2% year-over-year core PCE inflation for December 2026.

### Method & verdict
[Reasonable] The analysis pairs simple correlation tests — same-month core PPI vs. core CPI, and PPI surprises vs. CPI surprises — with a constructed set of intermediate-demand indices. These are built by aggregating thousands of industry- and commodity-level PPI series for each PCE component according to the BEA input-output tables, selecting the best-performing combination of upstream supply-chain stage and lag per component, and netting out estimated indirect tariff effects to avoid double-counting before feeding them into a bottom-up core PCE model. The approach is careful and transparent about its own limits: the sample for services is short (PPI services indices begin only in 2010, alternate core measures only in 2014), and the lag/stage selection is fitted to historical performance, which invites overfitting.

### Unpacked
The study is a response to a data gap. With the BLS skipping the October CPI and the November print likely distorted by late price collection, the question is whether the PPI — easier to collect retroactively, and thus less affected — can stand in as a read on consumer inflation.

**The direct substitution does not work: outside the sharp swings of 2020–2022, month-over-month core PPI tells you almost nothing about contemporaneous core CPI, and PPI surprises do not map onto CPI surprises.** The relationship is only somewhat useful at inflation extremes and mainly for goods, which limits its value precisely for the routine months in question.

**The payoff comes from a different use of the same report — its granular detail as a leading indicator rather than a coincident one.** The BLS's own intermediate-demand indices lead core CPI by a few months, but they mix in non-consumer purchases (exports, investment, government) and are only available at high aggregation. Building component-specific indices from the underlying commodity and industry series, mapped through input-output tables, sharpens that lead for several goods categories.

**On this basis the near-term signal is disinflationary, tariffs aside, and it has been folded into the forecast where it robustly improves accuracy.** Combined with a smaller assumed tariff increase in 2026, the result is a 2.2% year-over-year core PCE call for December 2026. The note offers no trade idea; it is a forecasting and data-interpretation exercise, and its practical takeaway is how to read the PPI when CPI is missing — not the same month's inflation, but the direction a few months ahead.

subject: US Economics Analyst: December FOMC Preview: Raising the Bar for Further Cuts
summary:
# Third Cut, Higher Bar: [REDACTED] Reads a Hawkish December Cut to 3.5–3.75%

**Theme:** A near-certain third 25bp cut paired with language that raises the bar for further easing  
**Markets:** US monetary policy — Fed funds rate  
**Source:** [REDACTED], David Mericle, 7 December 2025  

### Estimates
- **25bp cut to 3.5–3.75%** expected at the December FOMC — a third consecutive reduction, widely anticipated but likely contentious.
- **"Extent and timing of additional adjustments"** language expected to return to the statement (borrowed from December 2024) to signal a higher bar for further cuts.
- **Two hawkish dissents** expected in the statement (Schmid plus likely one more), and **five participants** projected to register soft dissents via a 3.875% 2025 dot.
- **SEP median GDP growth:** revised up to 2% for 2025 (+0.4pp) and 2% for 2026 (+0.2pp).
- **SEP median core PCE:** revised down 0.1pp to 3% for 2025 and 2.5% for 2026 — the 2026 figure still well above [REDACTED]'s own 2.2% forecast.
- **Dot plot:** expected to show one cut in 2026 to 3.375% and one more in 2027 to 3.125%, unchanged from September (a close call hinging on a single participant).
- **Core PCE net of tariffs** estimated at ~2.3% y/y now (0.5pp tariff impact), seen reaching 2% by 1H 2026; official measure inclusive of tariffs seen at 2.2% by end-2026.

### Outlook
- **The case for a cut is solid**, per [REDACTED]: trend job growth (~40k) is below the ~70k breakeven, unemployment has risen three months running to 4.4%, a 16-measure slack tracker reads softer still, and alternative layoff data are turning up — a new downside risk.
- **The hawkish elements likely add little new information**, in [REDACTED]'s view — the statement language, Powell's press-conference framing, and the dissents are broadly expected and unlikely to surprise the bond market.
- **Two more 25bp cuts to 3–3.25% expected in 2026**, contingent on the labor market stabilizing and inflation falling toward 2%, at which point the Fed shifts from risk-management to normalization mode.
- **Risks skew to more easing:** [REDACTED] sees more downside than upside to the funds-rate path, and its probability-weighted forecast remains more dovish than market pricing.

### Unpacked
The backdrop to this preview is a data-blind Fed: the meeting arrives two employment reports behind schedule, which sharpens the usual uncertainty about January. **That is why [REDACTED] thinks the Committee will resist boxing itself into a strong pause signal — if the labor market is still softening and unemployment pushes above the forecast 4.5% peak, another cut could be warranted.** The result is a "hawkish cut" whose hawkishness lives in tone and language rather than in any hard pre-commitment.

On inflation, the note frames the disinflation story as increasingly clean. Multiple independent estimates — [REDACTED], Fed Board staff, St. Louis Fed, and the Harvard Pricing Lab — now converge on a tariff impact of roughly 0.5pp or a touch more, which strips out to underlying core PCE near 2.3%. **With only a tiny further tariff increase expected next year, even the headline core measure should converge toward 2.2% by end-2026, removing much of the inflation objection to easing.**

The pivot point for 2026 is growth composition: the 2025 tariff drag gives way to a fiscal boost that [REDACTED] estimates peaks in the first half of the year. **The open question — which the note flags as the single most important for 2026 — is whether firmer growth will actually stabilize a labor market where hiring outside healthcare has been negative and where firms are leaning on AI to cut headcount.** This is the hinge on which the dovish tilt rests; the baseline assumes stabilization, but the note treats it as genuinely unresolved.

If stabilization comes, the debate turns to the terminal rate, where participants span a wide range — from those content at 3.5–3.75% to those favoring 2.5–2.75%. [REDACTED]'s best guess is a split-the-difference outcome of two more cuts to 3–3.25%. Going forward, the reader should watch incoming employment data most closely, since the layoff signals in alternative data are what could tip risk management back toward faster easing.

The note offers no explicit trade idea beyond the rate-path view.

# Right Tail Returning: Cuts Anchor the US and UK, Hike Risk Builds Everywhere Else

**Theme:** A split G10 — easing supports US/BoE curves while the rest skews toward the next move up  
**Markets:** Global rates (G10 government bonds)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], George Cole, 5 December 2025

### Landscape
- A 25bp December FOMC cut is 22bp priced, with just 22bp cumulatively priced across the first three meetings of 2026 and 8bp for January.
- 5y US breakevens sit ~15bp below [REDACTED] model fair value (based on oil, cyclical-vs-defensive equities and consensus inflation), decoupling from cyclical equities.
- 10y JGB yields have repriced to multi-decade highs; front-end forwards now fully price a 25bp BOJ hike by January, with end-2027 pricing at 1.4% versus [REDACTED]'s 1.5% terminal forecast.
- Canadian unemployment fell 0.4pp (versus +0.1pp expected); the CAD front-end has removed all cut premium and now prices hike risk as early as April 2026.
- CAD, AUD and NZD curves all now price hikes in 2026; the European front-end has re-steepened to price one hike between Dec-2025 and Dec-2027.
- European 5y HICP sits around 1.8%; UK country risk premia embedded in 10y Gilt yields are 20bp lower since the budget.

### Drivers
- **Central-bank divergence is the organizing force:** the US and UK are supported by expected cuts, while Commonwealth and European curves anticipate the next hike — [REDACTED] expects this configuration to persist.
- **US labor data risk skews dovish near-term:** with three months of jobs data due before January, [REDACTED] sees risks leaning marginally toward further pull-forward of cut pricing on larger jumps in unemployment, though the outlook turns two-way further out as 2026 growth picks up.
- **European cyclical upswing:** forward-looking signals point to improving domestic demand (German GDP tracking the [REDACTED] Current Activity Indicator higher), which [REDACTED] expects to pressure rates more than structural headwinds — the core of its short-Bund view.
- **Fed balance-sheet pressure:** funding conditions have become materially more sensitive to system-liquidity swings; [REDACTED] expects reserve management purchases to begin in January, likely announced at next week's meeting.
- **BOJ normalization maturing:** having been the only G10 hiker in 2025 and set to hike again in December, further belly upside now needs confirmation of sustained wage/inflation cycles — leaving 10y JGB risk-reward more balanced.
- **Gilt risk-premium compression:** post-budget, outsized premia are unwinding and could extend into a likely December BoE cut, with potential dovish spillovers from US data reinforcing lower UK yields.

### Risks
- **Upside (hawkish) US risk, flagged by [REDACTED]:** reiterated FOMC dispersion or dissents against cutting next week could be read as a hawkish signal, though clear data-dependence from Powell should cap more extreme hawkish pricing; leadership change may also mute the usual dot-plot sensitivity.
- **Downside risk to the short-Europe view:** low-inflation outcomes remain the key threat — with 5y HICP near 1.8% and energy prices capping front-end upside, [REDACTED] views the low-inflation tail as elevated.
- **Canadian belly vulnerability:** [REDACTED] calls the CAD selloff somewhat excessive given the gains came mostly from part-time and catch-up youth employment, leaving belly valuations exposed to retracing on softer growth/inflation data.
- **Dovish Fed-composition risk:** uncertainty around the incoming Fed leadership and committee keeps dovish policy-path risks alive, underpinning the case for breakeven hedges.

### Unpacked
The FOMC meeting is framed less around the cut itself than around its choreography. **The market read hinges on the dispersion of committee views, Powell's forward message, and the 2026 dots — front-end rates typically trade with a ~0.2 beta to the dots, but the leadership transition may make terminal pricing less dot-sensitive than usual.** [REDACTED] keeps its preference for steepeners a little further out the curve — Z6/Z7 and conditional 2s10s — rather than betting on the very near term.

On inflation, traded breakevens have stayed under pressure and pulled 5y valuations well below fair value. **The compression makes belly breakevens (5y or 5y5y) the cleaner hedge against a shift in the Fed reaction function**, with dovish risks still live around Fed composition and the policy path; tariff uncertainty and the dampening effect of FOMC divergence on inflation upside are cited as reasons for the recent cheapening.

Money-market plumbing gets specific attention. November month-end pressure was amplified by Thanksgiving timing and heavy settlement, but the underlying signal is greater funding sensitivity to liquidity swings. **[REDACTED] expects reserve management purchases to start in January and be announced next week**, while seeing no strong case yet to adjust IORB or the SRF — EFFR is still setting comfortably below the top of the range and SRF usage over month-end was modest.

Canada is the clearest repricing story. The employment beat took out remaining cut premium and pushed the curve to price hikes from April, tripping the receive-CORU6 recommendation at its stop. **[REDACTED] reads the selloff as overdone given the low-quality composition of the jobs gains, but places it in a global context of visible green shoots — Australia and New Zealand included — that are steepening belly forwards.**

Europe is where [REDACTED] pushes hardest against consensus. Client sentiment has soured on Chinese export competition, weak spot data and German fiscal under-delivery, but **[REDACTED] argues cyclical improvement will dominate structural headwinds for yields, keeping it short core rates outright and versus Gilts.** Curve-point selection is nuanced: 30y yields lag G4 peers and face steepening risk from Dutch pension reform, while a cyclical pickup and wider deficit argue for pressure at the 5y; the very front-end is partly insulated by low cut premium and H1-2026 inflation-undershoot risk, making optionalised front-end longs the preferred hedge against growth disappointment.

The inflation debate in Europe mirrors the US. **With 5y HICP near 1.8%, substantial downside is already priced, and stabilising German labour and manufacturing data skew risks toward higher HICP** — but energy-driven downside caps the front-end, so [REDACTED] prefers front-end receivers and EGB sovereign-credit longs over HICP shorts as inflation hedges. In the UK, post-budget risk-premium compression is expected to continue into a likely December BoE cut, keeping the long-Gilt-versus-Bunds-and-OIS trade in place.

Japan rounds out the picture as the maturing normalizer. **With the next hike now the December baseline and end-2027 forwards approaching the 1.5% terminal forecast, further belly upside needs confirmation of sustained wage and inflation cycles.** [REDACTED]'s spillover framework has Japan exerting upward pressure on global yields at a low beta, leaving USTs wedged between bullish Gilts and bearish Bunds and JGBs — and 10y JGB risk-reward now more balanced. The book stays: short 10y Bunds vs Gilts, long 5y5y AUD vs NZD, belly-led flattening in Japan, and an asymmetric tilt toward lower front-end US yields.
