subject: G10 Inflation Monitor: [REDACTED] Trimmed Core Inflation Ticks Up in Japan, Slows in Euro Area
summary:
# Trimmed Core Splits G10: Firmer Almost Everywhere, Easing Only in the Euro Area

**Theme:** Underlying inflation broadly ticking up on the month, with the Euro area the lone softener; Japan revised higher on a weaker Yen  
**Markets:** G10 core inflation  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Megan Peters, 29 November 2025  

### Landscape
- [REDACTED] trimmed core year-over-year now stands at +3.2% in the UK, +2.8% in Canada, +2.4% in the US, +2.3% in the Euro area, and +1.7% in Japan.
- October sequential (month annualized) trimmed core rose in Japan (2.3% vs. -0.2%), Canada (3.0% vs. 1.8%) and the UK (3.4% vs. 2.4%), but fell in the Euro area (2.2% vs. 2.8%).
- On a 3-month annualized basis, trimmed core edged up in Canada (2.1% vs. 1.6%), the UK (2.7% vs. 2.4%) and Japan (1.3% vs. 1.1%), and slipped in the Euro area (2.4% vs. 2.5%).
- Traditional 3-month core has fallen ~6pp from its peak in the UK, ~5pp in Canada and the Euro area, and ~4pp in the US.
- The share of the headline basket exceeding an 8% annualized pace fell to 3% in the UK and held at 1% in the Euro area, but remains higher in Canada (10%) and Japan (11%).

### Drivers
- Core services are the sticky force, accelerating in Canada (3.9% vs. 2.5%), Japan (2.3% vs. 1.3%) and the Euro area (3.9% vs. 3.2%), and easing only in the UK (3.2% vs. 3.9%).
- Core goods firmed in Japan (2.9% vs. 1.7%), the UK (1.2% vs. 0.9%) and Canada (0.2% vs. 0.1%) but slowed sharply in the Euro area (0.2% vs. 1.3%).
- Rent inflation is diverging: accelerating in Canada (7.8% vs. 6.1%) and the UK (3.8% vs. 3.0%) while slowing in Japan (0.4% vs. 0.7%) and the Euro area (2.8% vs. 2.9%).
- Energy and food inflation slowed across DMs except Japan, where both ticked up.
- The distribution of 3-month inflation rates continues shifting back toward pre-pandemic norms in most economies, but stays more dispersed in Canada.

### Risks
- Upside (US): the analyst forecasts core holding at +2.9% Q4/Q4 as tariff-driven price pressures offset fading shelter and wage impulses — a stall in disinflation rather than continued progress.
- Upside (Japan): the analyst revised end-2025 core up 0.5pp and end-2026 up 0.3pp after the [REDACTED] FX team cut its Yen appreciation path following Ms. Takaichi's surprise election win, adding a currency-driven inflation impulse.
- The analyst notes end-2026 core forecasts sit generally below consensus across G10, implying the analyst sees more disinflation than the market into next year.

### Unpacked
The monthly signal this cycle is a near-uniform firming in underlying inflation, with the Euro area the sole exception. **On every summary gauge — sequential trimmed core, 3-month trimmed core, and the weighted median month-over-month rate — the Euro area softened while the other G10 economies ticked up, most notably Japan.** Japan's sequential trimmed core swung from -0.2% to 2.3%, the sharpest single move in the panel.

The category detail explains the split. **Core services remain the dominant sticky force, reaccelerating everywhere except the UK, while the Euro area's cooling is concentrated in core goods, which collapsed from 1.3% to 0.2% on a 3-month annualized basis.** Rent is the other cross-country fault line, running hot and accelerating in Canada (7.8%) and the UK, but subdued in Japan and the Euro area — a gap the report attributes partly to differences in how each country measures rent changes.

The October data surprised in both directions. **Core inflation came in below expectations in the UK (cultural services and core goods) and the US (a shelter slowdown outweighing firmer core goods), but above expectations in Canada (non-core goods and volatile services) and slightly firm in the Euro area on services.** These surprises align with the breadth picture, where extreme price moves are fading fastest in the UK and Euro area but linger in Canada and Japan.

On the forecast path, year-over-year core is expected to move sideways into year-end in the US (+2.9% Q4/Q4), the UK (+3.4%) and Canada (+3.0%), and to edge down in the Euro area (+2.3%) and Japan (+2.7%). **The only material revision this month was Japan, marked up on the [REDACTED] FX team's call for slower and smaller Yen appreciation after Takaichi's election win.**

A methodological note frames how to read levels across countries. **[REDACTED]'s harmonized core — which strips a consistent item set, including owned housing, from every country's CPI — runs above the central banks' preferred core in the US and Canada because softer owned-housing inflation is excluded, but below the BoJ's preferred measure in Japan, where excluded non-fresh food keeps running hot.** The report offers no trade idea; it is a monitor of where underlying inflation stands and how the [REDACTED] forecast has shifted.

subject: Global Rates Trader: Return of the Macro
summary:
# Global Rates: Data Cycle Resumes, Front-End Tilts Dovish

**Theme:** Return of macro as the driver — too little priced for Q1 cuts, and carry giving way to long-vol hedges  
**Markets:** G10 rates (US, Canada, UK, Euro area, Australia, New Zealand)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], George Cole, 28 November 2025

### Landscape
- December FOMC now close to fully pricing a 25bp cut, but only 27bp of cumulative cuts priced into the January meeting — seen as too little given three payroll prints due before then.
- US 10y has outperformed on the curve recently, leaving belly forwards (5y5y) as the vulnerable point.
- US swap spreads sit generally within 5bp of the February highs, when deregulation expectations peaked.
- UK budget delivered a £22bn headroom buffer (slightly above expectations) but a borrowing path revised ~£9bn higher, with consolidation backloaded; long-end Gilts rallied ~20bp on limited FY2025 issuance.
- EUR implied vol has stabilised at levels not seen outside the zero-lower-bound period.
- AUD and NZD rates jumped this week; AUD–NZD forward spreads (5y5y) sit near record wides.
- Australia October monthly CPI showed trimmed-mean inflation reaccelerating above the RBA's target band.

### Drivers
- **US labor market slack** is the dominant force pulling front-end pricing dovish; with three payroll reports before the January FOMC, the skew favors pulling cuts forward and steepening (SFRZ6/Z7, conditional 2s10s bull steepeners).
- **FOMC division** is the counterweight, restraining dovish pricing and set to remain a key constraint into 2026 under new Fed leadership; reported frontrunner Kevin Hassett as Chair produced only modest front-end rally, curve steepening and wider breakevens — watch for extension if confirmed.
- **US funding strain** persists near-term: a cumulative $138bn of net Treasury settlement Friday–Monday (largest two-day since end-September) puts the effectiveness of the Fed's SRF backstop under scrutiny into the December FOMC. The finalized SLR amendment (effective April 1, 2026, early adoption from January 1) adds up to $5.6tn of balance-sheet capacity but is well-priced.
- **UK disinflation and soft labour data** point toward lower Gilt yields; the DMO's shift away from long-end issuance and a continuing WAM reduction (plus a Bills-market consultation) keep compressing long-end risk premium through Q1 2026.
- **RBNZ near the end of its cutting cycle** — softened easing bias after a 25bp cut plus a Q3 retail sales surge led [REDACTED] economists to drop further cut expectations; both RBA and RBNZ now seen on hold through 1H2026.
- **BoC** judged to be done cutting, though risks skew lower; US and Canadian labour data keep the theme alive (stay long CORU6).

### Risks
- **Downside (US rates):** labor market weakness could upend the low-vol regime and force faster front-loading of cuts — the analyst's central asymmetry.
- **Upside (US belly):** 5y5y vulnerable to cheapening on growth reacceleration, or underperformance if growth deteriorates sharply.
- **Two-sided (vol):** a more divided FOMC and fiscal-policy uncertainty argue against much further vol compression; the analyst sees a weaker risk/reward for outright vol shorts and prefers long-vol hedges over carry.
- **Downside (France/OATs):** a drawn-out 2026 budget process (votes December 12th and 23rd; possible resort to a special law) could delay compression of idiosyncratic risk; new parliamentary elections seen as the main tail but currently contained.
- **Ambiguous (European rates):** a Russia-Ukraine ceasefire is assessed as a contained rates reaction — commodities strategists are skeptical on near-term Russian gas resumption — but points to lower inflation and steepening risk (2s5s, 2s10s).

### Unpacked
**The core call is that the market is under-pricing Q1 Fed cuts even as it converges on December.** Somewhat softer activity data nudged December pricing higher, but with the January FOMC holding just 27bp and three payroll prints landing before it, the asymmetry favors the front end pulling cuts forward. The offsetting force is committee division, which restrains dovish pricing without a labor-market push and stays central next year under new Fed leadership. The reported Hassett candidacy offered a live read on a dovish appointment — front-end rally, mild steepening, wider belly breakevens — but the moves were small, consistent with that perceived restraint. The preferred expressions are steepeners, both in the front end and further out via conditional 2s10s.

**Belly forwards are flagged as the exposed point on the curve.** The recent 10y outperformance, tied partly to growth concerns and risk-sentiment wobbles, leaves 5y5y vulnerable either way — cheapening on reacceleration or underperformance on sharper deterioration.

**Funding markets remain the near-term pressure point despite structural relief on the way.** The finalized SLR amendment adds up to $5.6tn of balance-sheet capacity but is well-priced, and other constraints such as system-wide liquidity will limit how much actually flows into Treasuries and repo; the impact on swap spreads is seen as limited since spreads already embed a forward-looking funding view, sitting within 5bp of February highs. More pressing is the $138bn two-day settlement into a system already showing liquidity strain, making the Fed's backstop a focus into December.

**On volatility, the low-vol regime looks sustainable in the baseline but the risk/reward for shorting it is deteriorating.** Resumed data releases have richened implied vols as macro and policy risks turn two-sided. The baseline — some 1H2026 growth reacceleration plus continued normalization cuts — is consistent with low vol persisting, but labor-market weakness, a more divided FOMC, and fiscal uncertainty (especially for longer-dated vol) argue against further compression. The conclusion is to diversify carry sources and overlay long-vol hedges, using cheap vol to express directional views.

**In the UK, the budget's main service was removing near-term uncertainty rather than resolving the fiscal question.** The biggest positive surprise was near-term supply — limited FY2025 Gilt issuance and a further long-end squeeze — which compressed 30y risk premium and drove a ~20bp long-end rally expected to continue through Q1. The macro impact was backloaded, with no major implication for BoE decisions, and credibility of the backloaded consolidation remains an open risk. With disinflation and soft labour data pointing to lower yields, the recommendation is long 10y Gilts vs Bunds and vs OIS, though the lack of urgency for BoE cuts leaves front-end risks two-sided. The DMO's Bills-market consultation signals continued WAM reduction, justified by long-end yields sitting above equilibrium estimates rather than merely by curve steepness; UK bill share is among the lowest in the G10, implying roughly £160bn of scope to the G10 average.

**Euro-area core rates carry a bearish baseline for Bunds, but with hedges attached.** EUR vol has stabilised near post-crisis lows, leaving little room for further compression and a floor from potential US spillovers; mid-2026 receivers are recommended to hedge core EUR shorts, given disinflation risks — including Chinese export competition — to the 2026 ECB path. A Russia-Ukraine ceasefire is treated as ambiguous: lower inflation and possible risk-premium reduction argue for steepening, but German fiscal support and trade headwinds are seen as better guides into 2026. On France, spread targets were marked to market — **10y OAT-Bund, BTP-Bund and Bonos-Bund now forecast at 75/70/50bp for year-end and 70/75/55bp for end-2026**, with sovereign credit expected to trade well but risks tilted to slight widening.

**The Antipodean trade rests on convergence between two structurally similar economies now diverging cyclically.** Australia's hawkish surprise was inflation-driven (trimmed-mean above target), New Zealand's came from a softened RBNZ bias and a Q3 retail surge that ended the expected cutting path; both are now seen on hold through 1H2026. The NZD curve is meaningfully steeper given its lower policy-rate start and longer normalization path, but with AUD–NZD 5y5y near record wides and NZ's recovery aided by accommodative settings, the call is forward-rate convergence: **receive AUD 5y5y vs pay NZD 5y5y (entry 0.47%, target 0.15%, stop 0.65%).**

subject: Global FX Trader: Beyond The Budget Bounce
summary:
# Dollar Softer, Sterling Vulnerable: The Post-Budget FX Map

**Theme:** Fiscal risk clears in the UK; focus shifts back to soft data and Fed easing  
**Markets:** Global FX (G10 and EM)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Kamakshya Trivedi, 28 November 2025  

### Landscape
- Sterling posted a slight relief rally on Wednesday after the UK Autumn budget landed close to expectations, with realised FX moves undershooting what was priced ahead of the event.
- Implied Sterling vol fell over the week as budget digestion risk proved benign; skew rose.
- The Rupee pushed through 89 versus the Dollar, underperforming even as pro-cyclical, high-carry currencies rallied.
- India's macro backdrop shows Q3 growth of 8.2% and a record-low October inflation print.
- NZD positioning is broadly net short (as of week ending October 14); NZD firmed after the RBNZ meeting and stronger Q3 retail sales.
- FX volatility overall remains very low, held down in part by the still-lagged US data flow.

### Drivers
- **USD, softening:** As the US data backlog clears, [REDACTED] expects it to reveal a softer run rate — especially in labor — clearing the way for more Fed easing and a weaker Dollar into year-end.
- **Foreign pull on the Dollar:** Escalating FX warnings from Japanese officials, the benign UK budget, and another strong CNY fixing are all pulling the Dollar lower and seen as fairly long-lasting.
- **GBP, still pressured:** Softening UK data versus the Euro area and prospects for faster BoE easing remain the key drivers of further Sterling underperformance on European crosses; the budget does not add to those trends. Watch mid-December UK data and the December MPC to reengage at better levels.
- **NZD, turning up:** Q3 retail sales strength plus more hawkish RBNZ guidance meet the bar for turning positive — best expressed short AUD/NZD, the cross most cleanly driven by relative monetary policy.
- **INR, managed drift:** A central bank intervening less heavily and tolerating more volatility catalysed the move past 89; the IMF reclassified the regime as "crawl-like" from "stabilized." No line in the sand, but volatility stays managed and the RBI is expected to rebuild reserves on USD/INR dips.
- **CEE FX, geopolitically bid:** Renewed Ukraine ceasefire discussion has investors focused on CEE upside; [REDACTED] sees limited geopolitical risk premium embedded, as external balances have largely corrected since 2022.

### Risks
- **Upside to USD (downside to the [REDACTED] view):** The economists' baseline sees US growth recovering toward 2–2.5% in 2026, which could sustain Dollar strength; [REDACTED] remains comfortable because risks to the US policy rate are skewed down, and this year's weaker US equity returns owe mostly to strong performance abroad rather than US weakness.
- **INR asymmetry:** [REDACTED] frames the fundamental case as less negative than sentiment implies, but expects it to show up as a more rangebound nominal rate rather than outright appreciation.
- **CEE carry unwind:** To the extent popular EM carry trades face unwind risk, ceasefire developments may keep investors engaged with CEE FX longer.

### Unpacked
On Sterling, the budget mattered mainly for what it avoided: neither a larger-than-expected near-term fiscal contraction nor so little consolidation that a UK fiscal risk premium re-entered the currency. **With that tail risk cleared, the note steers attention back to the macro case for Sterling underperformance — soft UK data and faster BoE easing — which the budget leaves intact.** The economists nudged 2026 GDP up a tenth and left inflation unchanged, and parts of the MPC may read the measures as positive for disinflation. [REDACTED] frames this week's reset in spot and vol as an opportunity to reengage cleaner, pointing to the mid-December data round and December MPC.

The Dollar view rests on convergence: less US outperformance than before should mean less Dollar strength over time. **The main risk to that view is the economists' own baseline of a 2026 US growth recovery, which [REDACTED] acknowledges still sets a "fairly high bar" — but it holds the call given downside-skewed rate risks and the fact that weak US relative equity returns reflect strength abroad, not US weakness.**

NZD is the clearest long. **[REDACTED] argues the burden of proof for NZD strength — some cyclical improvement after a series of RBNZ cuts — has now been met by the retail sales surge and hawkish RBNZ guidance.** The recommended expression is short AUD/NZD, target 1.11, stop 1.17; Australia's upside CPI surprise is not seen as a headwind given the RBA's already hawkish stance. Long NZD/CAD and NZD/USD are flagged as alternatives, though both carry more sensitivity to US 10y yields; the bearish-USD and soft-Canada backdrops support them.

On the Rupee, the message is drift, not collapse. **A less negative fundamental case — solid growth, record-low inflation, growing undervaluation — is more likely to show up in a nominal rate that stabilises than in appreciation, because the RBI is expected to rebuild reserves on dips.** [REDACTED] sees those fundamentals better expressed through Indian equities, which it has upgraded after a year, and through a reversal of recent pressure on bonds.

In CEE, [REDACTED] keeps a short EUR/HUF recommendation initiated last week and prefers HUF over PLN. **The Forint screens cheaper than the Zloty and historically converges to fair value faster, while PLN's underperformance this year reads as payback for 2023–2024 strength rather than a catalyst for renewed outperformance.** Both should react positively to a Ukraine breakthrough. Looking out over the next year, the HUF preference could narrow as the MNB begins cutting (favouring rate receivers in Hungary) and the NBP nears the end of its cycle — but not yet: the MNB stays hawkish despite softer inflation, whereas Poland's softer prints, including October, led [REDACTED] economists to shift their call to a 25bp cut to 4.00% next week.

subject: European Credit Brief: Week ending November 28, 2025
summary:
# November's Concessions and Heavy Supply Should Fade — EUR Spreads Grinding Tighter Into Year-End

**Theme:** Seasonal drop in December supply supports spread tightening
**Markets:** European credit (EUR IG & HY)
**Source:** [REDACTED], Sara Grut, 28 November 2025

### Landscape
- EUR IG issued roughly €90 billion in November, the second-largest month of the year after May; HY issued €8 billion.
- Year-to-date gross supply reaches €780 billion in IG (a record, above the full-year forecast of €775 billion) and €121 billion in HY.
- EUR IG and HY spreads widened 6-7bp in November, a broad move across EUR and USD that reflects more than technicals, including US-specific concerns.
- New issue concessions (NICs) in EUR IG rose above the post-COVID average in November, after spending most of the year below it; USD IG showed a similar rise.
- Weekly flows: EUR IG +$1.7bn and USD IG +$2.3bn (10% and 8% of last year's AUM cumulatively); EUR HY -$0.1bn and USD HY +$1.2bn (4% and 6% of AUM).

### Drivers
- **Supply seasonality:** issuance typically slows sharply in December — the IG forecast was raised to €785 billion, implying only about €5 billion of issuance in December — which has historically been accompanied by spread tightening.
- **Firm inflows:** steady inflows kept secondary spreads and primary pricing firm despite record supply, supporting NIC resilience; the same dynamic holds in USD.
- **Sovereign fiscal premiums:** EUR IG banks remain more sensitive than non-banks to sovereign fiscal risk; the UK and France trade wider, reflecting delayed fiscal consolidation in the UK and ongoing budget debates in France.
- **Elevated common factor in IG:** a single factor explains ~83% of sector spread variation in EUR IG versus ~49% in EUR HY, making sector allocation secondary to the macro call in IG.

### Risks
- **Downside:** the analyst conditions the spread-tightening call on there being no economic shock ("barring an economic shock"); a shock would break the trajectory.
- **Downside:** persistent sovereign fiscal risk in the UK and France could keep bank premiums elevated and limit any further compression in the bank sleeve.
- The note does not quantify probabilities or present a comparable upside risk — the focus is on conditional downside.

### Unpacked
November's supply surge pushed EUR IG to an annual record and above the bank's own forecast, prompting a mechanical revision to €785 billion. **The central read is that, with supply about to dry up seasonally and barring an economic shock, EUR spreads remain well supported and should tighten gradually into year-end.**

On concessions, the usual pattern is that NICs rise when supply is heavy. **The standout feature of 2025 was NIC resilience in EUR despite record supply, attributed to steady inflows — which is why November's pop is seen as transitory.** The operational recommendation is not to wait for primary to add risk, but to seek carry in secondary as well.

In banks, the call is underweight versus non-banks, adopted in September after bank spreads tightened through the index and left little carry. **Since then bank spreads have started tracking the broad market and the outperformance phase has faded, keeping the risk-reward unfavorable given greater sensitivity to fiscal risk.** Within a smaller bank sleeve, the preference is for selective subordination for carry, excluding the UK and France.

The factor structure separates the two markets. In EUR IG, with a common factor explaining 83% of variation, sector allocation is secondary to macro — the priority is duration and beta, not large sector tilts; Media, Technology, and REITs offer only modest diversification. **In EUR HY, the more moderate systemic correlation (49%) leaves room for sector fundamentals and alpha generation via tactical allocation**, with Utilities, Technology, and Diversified Manufacturing less tied to the common factor; the strategy remains underweight Chemicals.

Finally, flows reinforce the picture. **Steadier IG inflows through the year, against more erratic HY flows, indicate that credit is being treated as a yield-first allocation, with carry and quality dominating over spread beta.** USD HY returned to inflows this week, while EUR HY saw a slight outflow.

subject: Weekly Fund Flows: Subdued Foreign Demand for US Equities
summary:
# Foreign Bid for US Equities Stays Muted as Broad Inflows Cool

**Theme:** Slowing equity inflows, resilient bond and EM demand  
**Markets:** Global cross-asset fund flows  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Michael Cahill, 28 November 2025  

### Landscape
- Global equity funds took in +$18bn in the week ending November 26, down from +$26bn the prior week.
- Global fixed income funds held firm at +$20bn, up slightly from +$18bn, spread across Agg-type and government bond funds.
- Money market fund assets rose $29bn on the week.
- Foreign demand for US equities remains well below 2024 levels, with euro area investors having resumed net sales in recent weeks.
- EM equity inflows stayed robust, with very strong net inflows into South Korea and Taiwan.
- Cross-border FX inflows increased, with CNY and ARS the strongest net recipients as a share of AUM.

### Drivers
- Equity inflows slowed on softer G10 demand, led by large net outflows from Japan on the week.
- US equity demand from abroad stays subdued: euro area investors are net sellers again, while rest-of-world demand is only modest.
- EM equity flows are intensifying, concentrated in North Asia tech markets (South Korea, Taiwan).
- Fixed income demand is broadening — high yield turned net positive this week, and EM bond flows were positive across both hard and local currency.
- At the sector level, technology and health care drew the strongest equity inflows while financials saw the largest outflows.
- FX inflows are led by Asia and LatAm, with China and Argentina standing out.

### Unpacked
**The headline is a cooling in equity demand — +$18bn versus +$26bn — driven by weaker G10 flows rather than any broad reversal.** Japan was the notable soft spot, posting large net outflows on the week. The rest of the equity picture is one of rotation rather than retreat: EM remained a strong draw, and at the sector level money moved toward technology and health care and away from financials.

**The persistent story beneath the weekly noise is the muted foreign bid for US equities, still far below its 2024 pace.** Euro area investors have turned net sellers of US equities over the past few weeks, and demand from the rest of the world is only modest — the focus of the note's Chart of the Week. EM equities are absorbing the more active flows, with South Korea and Taiwan seeing very strong inflows.

**Fixed income remains the firmer side of the ledger, and its strength is widening.** Agg-type and government bond funds carried the +$20bn total, high yield flipped to net positive, and EM bond funds drew inflows in both hard and local currency. Alongside a $29bn build in money market assets, the bond side points to steady rather than risk-hungry positioning. On FX, cross-border flows picked up on the back of Asia and LatAm, with CNY and ARS the standout recipients relative to their asset base. The note flags no explicit risks and offers no trade idea.

subject: Global Markets Comment: Post-Budget UK Market Thoughts
summary:
# UK Post-Budget: Why the Market's Relief Rally Is Justified — Gilts, Sterling, and Domestic Equities

**Source:** [REDACTED] — George Cole
**Focus:** UK markets after the Autumn Budget
**General comment:** Constructive read — sees the budget as roughly in line with expectations and validating pre-positioned long-Gilt and pro-domestic-equity views; leans against the gloomy consensus on UK assets.

### Context
The comment responds to the UK Budget, which delivered a smaller and more delayed fiscal consolidation than expected. It enters the debate on whether UK markets had priced in excessive pessimism on fiscal risk and growth.

### The arguments
- **The Budget surprised on the less-tight side, reducing the main event risk.** Headroom against the fiscal rules came in at £21.7bn, above the £15bn expected, helped by a less negative deterioration in the OBR's updated projections. Consolidation is more backloaded, which modestly raises near-term financing needs and gilt issuance, but the measures imply +0.1pp of demand in 2026 and -0.4pp on CPI.

- **Gilts should continue to see risk premium compression, supporting the long 10-year position.** The initial reaction was ambiguous — tension between larger headroom and delayed tightening — but relief prevailed, reinforced by the DMO's decision to shift issuance away from 30-year gilts more than expected. The 30-year-led bull-flattening and the positive correlation between Gilts and sterling indicate that risk-premium compression is the dominant driver, not a change in the expected BoE path. The read is that the market had been pricing excessive risk premium relative to the macro backdrop; with the event past, focus should shift to weak activity and inflation data and to BoE decisions, with disinflation pulling front-end rates lower. Long positions in 10-year Gilts versus Bunds and OIS are maintained, along with year-end forecasts of 4.25% for end-2025 and 4.0% for end-2026.

- **Sterling's neutral reaction is consistent with a balanced Budget, but event risk is not fully behind us.** The slightly less contractionary impulse is a mild positive, and part of the initial rally reflects the unwinding of tactical short positions (the positioning proxy had been modestly short, -0.6 standard deviations). Moves fell short of implied volatility priced in options. Caution stems from a recent pattern: in fiscal events over the past year, the larger FX moves came in the days following the event, not on the day itself — and the broad tax package still needs to be digested. Over the medium term, the macro trajectory remains the main source of sterling weakness: decelerating data and more BoE easing than priced, which the Budget's consolidation does not alter.

- **UK domestic equities are the most favored segment, starting from depressed expectations.** Sentiment was gloomy and positioning light: domestic stocks ([REDACTED]) fell 11% versus the FTSE 100 since July, and the FTSE 250 offers a dividend yield 100bp above the FTSE 100, a historically wide spread — a sign that weak growth and fiscal vulnerability are already well priced in. Since the underperformance of these assets (and of real estate and homebuilders) is strongly correlated with rising Gilt yields, a modest decline in those yields over 6-12 months should support them, in an underweighted segment. Adding to this was relief that there was no extra taxation on UK banks, which trade at 8.6x P/E with positive earnings momentum.

- **ISA reform favors equities in the long run, but with caveats that limit the effect.** From April 2027, £8k of the £20k annual ISA allowance will be earmarked for stocks (for those under 65), addressing the lack of savings directed to higher-return assets — today heavily skewed toward cash. The caveats: a sustained shift in flows depends more on consumer confidence than on the fiscal incentive; there was a 2pp increase in the tax rate on savings income, dividends, and property (dividends are a meaningful share of returns and much is reinvested); and the cap on salary sacrifice for pension contributions is marginally unfavorable. Even so, managers' reaction to the focus on domestic investment was positive.

### Implications
- Reinforces existing positions: long 10-year Gilts (vs. Bunds and OIS) and a favorable bias toward UK domestic equities, real estate, and homebuilders, supported by lower rates ahead.
- Sterling should remain pressured over the medium term by the macro trajectory; the near-term risk is that the larger FX move comes in the days following the announcement, not on the day itself.
- UK banks stand to gain as a cheap segment spared the feared taxation; unlocking flows into equities, however, depends more on consumer confidence than on the ISA fiscal incentive.

subject: USA: Initial Claims Somewhat Below Expectations; Durable Goods Orders Increase
summary:
# US: Initial jobless claims below expectations; durable goods orders rise 0.5% in September

**Theme:** Weekly labor and durable-goods data leave Q3 growth tracking intact  
**Markets:** US economy (labor market, business investment)  
**Source:** [REDACTED] (Jan Hatzius), 26 Nov 2025  

### Definitive impacts
- Initial jobless claims fell 6k to 216k in the week ended Nov 22, below the 225k median forecast; the four-week moving average edged down 1k to 224k.
- Continuing claims rose 7k to 1,960k (week ended Nov 15), in line with consensus, from a prior week revised down 21k to 1,953k.
- Durable goods orders rose +0.5% MoM in September, matching consensus; the increase largely reflects a second straight month of higher defense aircraft orders.
- Durable goods ex-transportation (+0.6%), core capital goods orders (+0.9%) and core capital goods shipments (+0.9%) all came in above expectations in September.
- August was revised up across the board: durable orders +0.1pp to +3.0%, ex-transport +0.2pp to +0.5%, core orders +0.5pp to +0.9%, core shipments +0.3pp to -0.1%.
- State-level initial claims: +3k in California, -2k in both Georgia and Texas ([REDACTED] seasonal adjustment).

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] leaves its Q3 GDP tracking estimate unchanged at +3.7% (QoQ annualized) after the data, with Q3 domestic final sales tracking at +2.6%.

### At issue
Two US data releases published the morning of Nov 26. First, weekly jobless claims from the Department of Labor: initial claims for the week ended Nov 22 and continuing claims for the week ended Nov 15. Second, September durable goods orders, covering headline orders, ex-transportation orders, and the core capital goods orders and shipments components, alongside upward revisions to August.

### Unpacked
**The releases came in marginally firmer than expected but changed nothing material in the growth picture.** Initial claims undershot the forecast, continuing claims matched consensus from a lower base, and durable goods orders landed on the headline expectation while the underlying investment-relevant components — ex-transport, core orders and core shipments — all beat.

The August revisions reinforce this read: every component was revised higher, including core shipments moving from a decline to a smaller one. Because core capital goods shipments feed the equipment-investment input to GDP, these upgrades matter more for tracking than the headline print, which was flattered by lumpy defense aircraft orders.

**Even with the beats, the Q3 GDP tracker held at +3.7%, signalling the data was already broadly consistent with what the model expected.** The note carries no explicit trade idea and no policy-rate call — it is a routine data comment, with the reader's takeaway being simply that Q3 growth tracking remains firm.

subject: US Daily: Distortions to November Data: Weaker Job Growth and Lower Inflation
summary:
# Shutdown and Calendar Distortions Set Up Softer November Payrolls and a Downward-Biased CPI

**Theme:** How the ended government shutdown, DOGE resignations, and a late Thanksgiving distort November jobs and inflation data  
**Markets:** US labor market and inflation  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Ronnie Walker, 26 November 2025  

### Definitive impacts
- **A 25-50k drag on November nonfarm payrolls** from the residual effect of the DOGE deferred resignation program, following a 100k drag in October.
- **Roughly 15k of retail hiring shifted out of November** because the late Thanksgiving (November 27th) delays the start of holiday-season hiring; retail job growth decelerated versus its three-month average in six of the last seven late-Thanksgiving years.
- **October CPI will not be published for hand-collected series**, so November price changes for a large share of the basket — including headline and core — must be read on a two-month (versus September) or year-on-year basis rather than one-month.
- **Fewer prices collected in November** owing to the abridged collection window; after the 2013 shutdown, which also ended mid-month, only about 75% of the normal price count was gathered in the reopening month.
- **The BLS reference week moved back one week**, from Nov. 2-8 to Nov. 9-15, with response collection also starting a week later.

### Opinative impacts
- **[REDACTED] expects only limited shutdown damage to payroll quality**, since most establishment-survey responses are electronic and can be filed anytime; about a third arrive late in a normal month, and December revisions to November payrolls show no consistent bias.
- **[REDACTED] expects limited shutdown impact on the household survey**, arguing the later reference week aligns better with historical norms than the unusually early original week; collection nearer Thanksgiving may modestly lower the response rate, as in 1995.
- **The furlough-driven boost to the November unemployment rate should be smaller than under the original timing**, because most furloughed federal workers returned to work for a couple of days within the new reference week.
- **The unemployment rate could still rise further** beyond September's 4.4%, as alternative slack measures have continued their gradual climb.
- **Late collection could exert as much as a 10-15bp drag on November core CPI**, because prices gathered only in the second half of the month over-capture holiday-sale markdowns that the seasonal factors are not calibrated for.
- **The apparent CPI drag may look milder on a two-month basis and reverse into December**, since a larger share of the usual November-December goods decline lands in November, leaving December inflation commensurately higher.
- **PCE inflation should be less affected than CPI**, [REDACTED] argues, because its other main input, the PPI, can be — and regularly is — reported retroactively.

### At issue
The federal government shutdown has ended and collection and release of federal economic data have resumed. The note assesses how delayed collection, plus other calendar and program effects, distort the November readings for nonfarm payrolls, the unemployment rate, and CPI. Concrete mechanical changes include the BLS pushing its household-survey reference week from Nov. 2-8 to Nov. 9-15, the suppression of October CPI for hand-collected series, a compressed November price-collection window, the tail of the DOGE deferred resignation program, and a late Thanksgiving compressing holiday retail hiring.

### Backdrop
US payrolls come from the establishment survey and the unemployment rate from the household survey, each tied to a defined reference and interview week; CPI is built from prices collected across a full month, some electronically and some by hand, with seasonal factors calibrated to the normal within-month timing of price changes. Not-seasonally-adjusted core goods prices typically fall 1-1½% cumulatively across November and December, split roughly evenly, but with a pronounced intramonth pattern — a sharp mid-November drop as holiday sales begin, then a slight December rebound. PCE draws on both CPI and PPI as source data. These structural features are what make the timing of a shutdown-shortened collection month matter.

### Unpacked
The exercise is essentially a triage: with data flowing again, which November prints can be trusted and which carry artifacts that should not be read as signal. **The verdict is that the two labor surveys survive the shutdown largely intact, while the CPI is the release most compromised — less by outright error than by biased and incomplete collection.**

For payrolls, the reassuring evidence is behavioral: late submissions are routine and, historically, do not differ systematically from on-time ones, so a delayed start to non-electronic collection does not bias the count. **The real softness in November payrolls comes not from the shutdown but from two identifiable, quantified forces — the fading DOGE resignation drag and a calendar-driven delay in holiday retail hiring — that a reader can net out rather than treat as noise.**

The household survey is a story of two offsetting timing effects. Moving the reference week later risks a lower response rate, but it also lands after the shutdown ended, so returning furloughed workers no longer inflate the jobless count the way they would have under the original week. **Even with those distortions stripped out, the underlying drift still points up: slack measures now sit consistent with an unemployment rate above September's 4.4%.**

CPI is where interpretation, not just quality, is at stake. The missing October reading forces much of the basket onto a two-month or year-on-year frame, and the compressed window thins the sample. **The subtler problem is the holiday-sales bias: collecting prices only in the back half of November over-weights markdowns the seasonal factors expect to be spread across the whole month, mechanically pulling core CPI down by an estimated 10-15bp.**

The practical implication is that a soft November core CPI should be discounted rather than extrapolated. **The drag is a timing artifact, not disinflation — it looks smaller on a two-month average and should reverse as a boost to December inflation, while PCE, cushioned by the retroactively reportable PPI, will show less of it.** The note offers no explicit trade idea.

subject: US Economics Analyst: From IT to AI: What Explains US Productivity Outperformance?
summary:
# From IT to AI: The Structural Roots of Persistent US Productivity Outperformance

**Theme:** Why US TFP growth outpaces Europe's, and why AI should extend the lead  
**Markets:** US and Euro area productivity / macro  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Pierfrancesco Mei, 25 November 2025  

### Landscape
- US labor productivity has grown ~2.1% annually since 1995, more than twice the pace of other advanced economies, opening a cumulative ~50% gap over three decades.
- The US-Euro area labor productivity growth gap splits into ~0.55pp from stronger capital deepening (higher US investment) and ~0.35pp from faster TFP growth.
- TFP grew ~0.95% annually in the US versus ~0.6% in the Euro area over 1995-2025.
- US labor quality added ~0.25% per year since 1995 versus near-zero in the Euro area — omitted from the analysis as small relative to capital deepening and TFP everywhere.
- The outperformance is concentrated in IT and IT-intensive sectors such as professional services and finance and insurance.

### Drivers
- **Measurement, overstating the raw gap:** more aggressive US quality adjustments on hardware/software prices added ~0.1pp to annual US TFP since 1995, and understated US hours worked (via declining CPS reported hours) added ~0.2pp since 2019 — together ~30% of the gap, leaving an adjusted 0.25pp.
- **Intangibles (largest structural driver):** heavier US investment in software and R&D contributed ~0.25pp/year to capital deepening (vs <0.1pp in the Euro area) and, via TFP spillovers, ~0.2pp/year (vs ~0.1pp) — the 0.1pp spillover gap explains ~40% of the adjusted gap.
- **Allocative efficiency:** capital and labor flow more to productive firms in the US; matching US-level allocation would lift Euro area TFP growth and cut the adjusted gap by ~0.1pp.
- **Management practices:** performance monitoring, merit pay and merit promotion speed US technology adoption, accounting for ~0.02pp of the adjusted gap.
- **Firm scale:** larger US firms across the lifecycle grow productivity about twice as fast as small ones since 2007; partially credited with the residual ~0.03pp.
- **AI tailwind (forward-looking):** the sectors leading US AI adoption — IT, professional services, finance and insurance — are the same ones that drove past divergence and already carry stronger US momentum.

### Risks
The note frames the outlook as one-directional: the structural drivers plus AI adoption should sustain US outperformance. No explicit downside scenarios or two-sided risks to this baseline are laid out.

### Unpacked
Labor productivity is decomposed into capital deepening, labor quality and TFP. The capital-deepening half of the US-Euro gap is well understood — it reflects higher US investment rates. The TFP half is the puzzle the note sets out to explain, and it does so by first shrinking the puzzle, then attributing what remains.

**The raw 0.35pp annual TFP gap is meaningfully overstated by two measurement artifacts, which together account for about 30% of it.** US price indexes for comparable hardware and software have fallen far more sharply than European ones since 1995, pointing to larger, unharmonized quality adjustments by US statistical agencies; applying Euro-area deflators to US IT products in a counterfactual shows these adjustments added almost 0.1pp to annual US TFP. Separately, US hours worked have been understated recently — chiefly falling reported hours in the CPS used to adjust the statistics — and since output-per-hour rises mechanically when hours are undercounted, this added ~0.2pp since 2019. The residual to be explained is therefore an adjusted 0.25pp per year.

**Intangibles do the heaviest lifting on the adjusted gap.** Using the INTANProd database, US firms invested far more in software, R&D and organizational capital, contributing ~0.25pp/year to capital deepening between 1995 and 2019 against under 0.1pp in the Euro area. Beyond that direct effect, intangibles generate TFP spillovers through externalities in software, R&D and organizational capital; drawing on Corrado and co-authors, these spillovers lifted US TFP by ~0.2pp/year versus ~0.1pp in the Euro area. That 0.1pp spillover differential alone covers roughly 40% of the adjusted gap, consistent with recent Fed work.

**Resource allocation is the second-largest factor, worth about another 0.1pp.** US labor productivity sits ~50% above what random allocation of employment across firms would deliver, versus only ~15-25% in the Euro area, per the Olley-Pakes decomposition applied by Bartelsman, Haltiwanger and Scarpetta. Translated into growth terms via Bun and co-authors, misallocation drags US TFP growth to ~45% of potential and Euro-area growth to ~30%; closing that efficiency gap would narrow the adjusted TFP gap by ~0.1pp.

**The last two factors are smaller and harder to pin down.** Better management practices — performance monitoring, performance-based pay, merit promotion — explain over 20% of firm-level productivity variation across 30,000+ US manufacturing plants and let US firms absorb new technology faster; aligning Euro-area practices to US levels would close 5-10% of the gap, or ~0.02pp. US firms are also larger throughout the lifecycle thanks to more integrated product and capital markets, and larger firms have grown productivity about twice as fast as small ones since 2007. Gains concentrate in frontier "superstar" firms, whose productivity has far outpaced the economy-wide average; while that once raised fears of stalled diffusion, Amiti and co-authors find these firms lift suppliers' productivity through technology spillovers. The difficulty of measuring scale effects across regions means only the residual ~0.03pp is partially attributed here.

**The forward view is that the same structural machinery, now joined by AI, keeps the US ahead.** Echoing the Draghi competitiveness report — which warned Europe missed the late-1990s IT revolution and is again lagging on frontier technologies — the note argues the US is positioned to capture AI gains earlier. The sectors with the highest US AI adoption rates in the Census Business Trends survey are precisely IT, professional services, and finance and insurance, which already show accelerating post-pandemic productivity leads over Europe. No explicit trade idea is offered; this is a structural read, not a positioning call.

subject: USA: Consumer Confidence Declines More Than Expected; Lowering Q3 GDP Tracking to +3.7%
summary:
# US Consumer Confidence Falls Sharply in November; Q3 GDP Tracking Nudged Down to +3.7%

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US consumer confidence and Q3 GDP tracking  
**General comment:** Neutral data note; softer confidence but the GDP tracking mark barely moves, staying above trend.

### Context
A quick read on the November Conference Board consumer confidence release, which came in weaker than expected, combined with same-day updates to core retail sales, PPI, and pending home sales — all fed into [REDACTED]'s running Q3 GDP estimate.

### The case
- **Confidence dropped more than expected, and the weakness was broad.** The headline index fell 6.8pt to 88.7, below the ~93 consensus and [REDACTED]'s own 93.0, landing at its second-lowest level since April after several flat months. Both sub-components declined — expectations by 8.6pt to 63.2 and present situation by 4.3pt to 126.9 — with all five underlying components described as flagging or weak, and the tone of write-in responses slightly more negative than October.
- **The labor market signal softened again after a one-month pause.** The labor differential — jobs "plentiful" (27.6%) minus jobs "hard to get" (17.9%) — edged down 0.6pt to 9.7, resuming its year-to-date decline after October's brief respite. October itself was revised up slightly to 10.3. Inflation expectations 12 months out held at 5.7%.
- **The GDP-relevant data cut both ways, netting to a marginal downgrade.** Core retail sales came in softer than [REDACTED] had assumed, while the GDP-relevant details of the PPI and pending home sales reports were firmer. On balance these offset to a 0.1pp cut in the Q3 tracking estimate.

### Implications
- Q3 real GDP tracking now sits at +3.7% annualized, with domestic final sales at +2.5% — a trim small enough to leave the above-trend growth picture intact.
- The renewed slide in confidence and the labor differential points to a softening consumer backdrop, even as the hard activity data for Q3 remain firm.

subject: USA: Core Retail Sales Below Expectations; Core PPI Below Consensus Expectations; Estimating 0.22% for September Core PCE
summary:
# US: September Data Reinforces Disinflation — Retail Sales Below Expectations and Softer PPI Lead to 0.22% Core PCE Estimate

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius
**Focus:** US activity and inflation (retail sales, PPI, and core PCE)
**General comment:** Descriptive data read, with a slightly dovish tilt — downside surprises in consumption and producer prices.

### Context
Comment on the simultaneous release of September US retail sales and PPI, used to refine the core PCE estimate — the inflation measure tracked by the Fed.

### The arguments
- **Goods consumption came in weaker than expected, with a downward revision to the prior month.** Core retail sales (ex-autos, gasoline, and building materials) fell 0.1% in September, against expectations of a gain, and the August level was revised down by 0.2%. The headline gain (+0.2%) was driven by gasoline (+2.0%), while motor vehicles fell 0.3%. By category, the positive standouts were miscellaneous stores (+2.9%), health and personal care (+1.1%), and food services (+0.7%); the weakest were sporting goods (-2.5%), online retail (-0.7%), and apparel (-0.7%). Combined with the CPI, real core sales are estimated to have fallen 0.4% on the month, but still rose 3.1% annualized on the quarter.
- **The PPI confirmed contained core pressure, despite energy and food.** The headline index rose 0.3% (in line with consensus), driven by energy (+3.5%) and food (+1.1%), but core producer prices rose only 0.1%. The measure excluding food, energy, and trade services rose 0.1%, below consensus, with retail and wholesale margins down 0.2%. Among components relevant to PCE, airfares rose 4.0%, but portfolio management fell 1.2%, leaving the net set a bit softer than projected.
- **Health-care inputs to PCE rose modestly.** Based on PPI data (including interim, seasonally adjusted figures), the PCE health-care services category is estimated to rise 0.12% in September.
- **The net result marginally lowers the core inflation projection.** With the PPI and CPI details, core PCE is estimated at +0.22% for the month (versus 0.24% projected before the PPI), putting the year-over-year rate at +2.85%. Headline PCE is estimated at +0.29% for the month (+2.81% over 12 months) and core market-based PCE at +0.23%.

### Implications
- Weaker consumption and the downward revision suggest a smaller demand impulse than appeared, even as the real quarterly trend remains positive.
- The composition of the PPI points to pressure coming from energy and food, not the core, keeping the underlying disinflation picture intact.
- The revision of the core PCE estimate to 0.22% reinforces a marginally more benign read for the inflation trajectory tracked by the Fed.

subject: Global Views: Looking Beyond December
summary:
# Fed Set for December, But 2026 Is the Open Question

**Theme:** A dovish-leaning Fed cut nearly locked for December, with a wider global rate map behind it  
**Markets:** Global macro & rates  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jan Hatzius, 23 November 2025  

### Landscape
- Core PCE (Fed staff estimate) sat at 2.8% y/y in September, going sideways this year, but underlying inflation is judged near 2% once 50-60bp of tariff pass-through and ~20bp from imputed financial services are stripped out.
- The unemployment rate stood at 4.44% in September; September nonfarm payrolls grew 119k, above expectations.
- China GDP is seen decelerating only modestly from 5% in 2025 to 4.7% in 2027, despite an October data miss.
- UK unemployment rose another 0.2pp to 5.0%, alongside steady progress on wage and price inflation.
- US equity valuations already embed much of the AI upside, with 10-year US equity returns expected to trail both the historical US average and the forward-looking non-US average.

### Drivers
- **Fed easing:** Williams' call for "a further adjustment in the near term" — citing higher downside employment risk and lessened inflation upside — points to a 25bp cut on December 10; with the next jobs report (Dec 16) and CPI (Dec 18) falling after the meeting, nothing on the calendar can derail it.
- **US growth reacceleration:** Reduced tariff drag, tax cuts, and easier financial conditions are expected to lift 2026 growth to 2-2.5%, which underpins the base case of a slower easing pace next year.
- **Labor market weakening:** Underlying job growth trend is only 39k as of September, alternative indicators show renewed October job losses, and Challenger, WARN and Q3 earnings-call layoff signals have risen even as initial claims stay low — watch whether the weakness becomes entrenched.
- **China Shock 2.0:** Export-led growth is set to push China's current account surplus toward a record 1% of global GDP by 2029, weighing on manufacturing output and employment across trading partners.

### Risks
- **Downside to the funds-rate path (more meaningful, per the analyst):** Labor-market weakness could prove too entrenched for a modest growth pickup to reverse, prompting deeper cuts.
- **Downside, college-graduate labor market:** Graduate unemployment is up ~50% (25+, to 2.8%) and ~70% (ages 20-24, to 8½%) from 2022 lows; since this group is 55-60% of labor income, further deterioration — possibly AI-driven — could hit spending and force more easing.
- **Upside to the funds-rate path (limited, per the analyst):** Would require large second-round tariff effects (no signs) or an equity-driven jump in imputed prices.
- The skew is asymmetric — the analyst frames upside risks as limited and downside risks as more meaningful.

### Unpacked
**The December cut is treated as all but decided, and the real question is what the Fed does afterward.** Williams' view is read as consistent with Powell — who almost certainly penciled in three cuts in the September dot plot — and a majority of the 12 voting members, though not necessarily a majority of all 19 participants. The base case has the FOMC slowing in 2026H1: pausing in January, then cutting in March and June to a terminal 3-3.25%.

**The benign inflation read is what keeps upside risk to that path contained.** With tariff pass-through and equity-driven financial-services prices accounting for the gap above 2%, core PCE should recede once pass-through ends in mid-2026 — conditional on no large second-round effects and stable equity markets.

**Against that, the labor-market signals argue the risks lean toward more easing, not less.** The strong headline payroll print masks a weak 39k underlying trend and rising layoff indicators. The graduate-employment deterioration is singled out as particularly notable given its outsized share of labor income and its potential link to AI adoption.

Outside the US, the map splits by central bank. China's pivot to export-led growth to hit its targets drives the record-surplus call and the China Shock 2.0 theme. **Germany gets a cyclical upgrade to 1-1.5% growth as government spending starts, but a downgrade to the prior forecast** — dragged by China Shock 2.0 and a potential-growth estimate cut to just 0.5% on weak demographics and slow reform — though not enough to trigger renewed ECB easing. The Bank of England is the clearest dovish case: Bailey, the MPC swing vote, is thought to have narrowly held off cutting on November 5, and with the disinflationary November 26 budget in view, the forecast is three more 25bp cuts in 2026, meaningfully below market pricing.

**On AI, the economics and the valuations point in opposite directions.** Cumulative AI capex stays well below the incremental capital income AI is likely to generate — a baseline $8trn present value, range $5-19trn — but the equity market has already priced much or all of that in. The 10-year cross-asset forecasts round out the picture: 10-year Treasury yields drifting up to 4½% on fiscal deterioration even as the funds rate settles near 3%, upward pressure on JGB yields but lower Gilt yields on disinflation, large back-loaded appreciation in the yen, RMB and other Asian currencies, and oil falling in 2026 on surplus before Brent recovers to $80/barrel by 2028.

**Markets:** US economic activity

subject: Global Rates Trader: The Wait Goes On
summary:
# US Front-End Still Skewed Dovish, But the Data Signal Hasn't Arrived

**Theme:** Waiting on decisive US data; fiscal events set the near-term tone across the UK, Germany and Japan  
**Markets:** G10 rates (US, Europe, Japan)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], George Cole, 21 November 2025

### Landscape
- Terminal rate pricing steady around 3%, with forward gaps beyond 2026 at historically flat levels.
- September payrolls showed solid job growth offset by a continued drift higher in the unemployment rate — no clear signal, and no further NFP release before the December FOMC.
- TGA balance fell to $900bn at Wednesday's close, $100bn below the end-October highs, as the post-shutdown drawdown begins.
- SFRZ6/Z7 curve at 6bp; UST-OIS swap spreads look fair in the front-end and belly on a forward funding basis but still wide at the long end.
- Japan's supplementary budget came in at ¥17.7tn (2.8% of GDP), larger than expected, with FY2025 bond issuance seen rising more than ¥10tn versus the initial ¥29tn plan.
- German October spending data (first month of the new budget) was inconclusive, though infrastructure over-delivered modestly.

### Drivers
- **US labor slack** is softening and skews front-end risks dovish versus pricing; watch for confirmation, but note no payrolls print lands before December's meeting.
- **TGA drawdown** is now reversing and adds liquidity into year-end; beyond that, a stable Fed balance sheet plus TGA implies a gradual reserve drift lower, with reserve management purchases expected to start in January.
- **German cyclical upswing** should push belly yields higher through 2026, but structural pessimism (China export competition) is a steady headwind; 30y remains the tactical weak point.
- **UK budget** (next week) is the gating event — Gilts are in stasis; a contractionary, non-inflationary budget is expected to green-light lower yields on faster BoE easing.
- **Japanese supply** trajectory stays challenging, keeping the long-end steep and pressuring belly yields; a larger deficit means more JGBs, though much is bill-financed.
- **Global long-end spillovers** are led by German 30y, with JGBs now contributing — a rising, not fading, force.

### Risks
- **Upside (US rates/hawkish):** a reacceleration in underlying activity could open the right tail on forward rates; the analyst sees this as the counter-scenario to the dovish front-end skew.
- **Downside (funding instability):** the analyst flags scope for money-market turbulence around large liquidity events (e.g. the April tax date), suggesting April/July 2026 SERFF steepeners as a hedge.
- **Spillover risk:** sustained upward pressure on global long-ends could seep more clearly into USTs, especially if Fed-path perceptions turn more hawkish; the analyst notes recent JPY spillover has been smaller than the 0.2–0.3 coefficient implies, partly due to cheaper JPY hedging costs.

### Unpacked
The US section is built around a data vacuum. **The September payrolls print settled nothing — solid hiring against a rising unemployment rate — and with no further release before the December FOMC, both doves and hawks retain an argument.** Even so, the read is that very front-end risks, December included, sit dovish relative to market pricing, supported by softening slack measures and recent risk-sentiment wobbles (which stopped out a 5y5y inflation long). The preferred expression is a SFRZ6/Z7 steepener at 6bp (target 20bp, stop 0bp), whose asymmetry works because weaker labor data would front-load cuts and pull terminal pricing below 3% while leaving forwards sticky.

On funding, the TGA drawdown is the near-term relief valve into year-end, but the structural point is that stable Fed and TGA balances still leak reserves lower via growth in other liabilities like currency in circulation. **Given repo volatility and official comments that ample reserves are near, reserve management purchases are seen as prudent from January.** The baseline priced by the market — the Fed ultimately supplying enough liquidity to anchor repo near IORB — still leaves room for instability around big liquidity dates, hence the April/July 2026 SERFF steepener as a hedge.

Swap spreads get a dedicated treatment because the usual valuation lens is misfiring. Spread widening paused this week despite steadier spot funding, and the standard framework increasingly reads spreads as wide versus spot-funding fair value. **Substituting an implied GC-OIS level from SOFR-FF forwards closes most of that gap in the front-end and belly, which look fair, but long-end spreads remain meaningfully wide.** Deregulation expectations and hard-to-isolate flow drivers are the suspected residual.

Europe splits into a rates call and a credit call. On Bunds, the stance stays bearish versus UK and US on a 2026 cyclical upswing, with infrastructure over-delivery a small positive against persistent structural scepticism. The curve steepening since April's lows has run through 5y and 10y outperformance; **higher 5y rates are expected to accompany the cyclical pickup, but until the data confirm it, 30y Bunds remain the tactical weak point and a major source of global spillovers.** The ERH6ERH7 steepener is closed for a small 4bp gain. In sovereign credit, the 2026 outlook is constructive — muted macro uncertainty, an on-hold ECB, less fragmentation, continued NGEU support — with the specific trade being compression of French and Belgian versus Finnish and Austrian spreads, where semi-core fiscal deterioration looks under-priced; Southern Europe stays tight, and Bonos screen less exposed than the recently outperforming BTPs.

Gilts are the clearest event trade. Weak services inflation, retail sales and PMIs barely moved yields beyond cementing a December BoE cut, leaving the market frozen ahead of the budget. **The base case is that Gilts have priced enough event risk premium, and a contractionary, non-inflationary budget clears the way for lower yields as BoE easing expectations build.** The focus is threefold: borrowing roughly £8bn above the Spring figure with matching gilt sales, the credibility and front-loading of revenue measures, and the macro/BoE implications. The book favours long Gilts (e.g. versus Bunds) and adds long 10y Gilt on ASW (entry −52bp, target −44bp, stop −57bp); the 2s5s Gilt steepener is closed for a 10bp gain.

Japan ties the global thread together. The larger-than-expected package lifts issuance materially, though bills absorb much of it and some spending may slip to FY2026. **Friday's long-end flattening and wider swap spreads suggest fiscal uncertainty — not just supply — drove the recent long-end selloff, and the supply path should keep the long end steep and belly yields under pressure.** The watch item is spillover: JGB transmission to USTs has run below its historical coefficient, helped by compressed 30y JGB/UST hedged spreads as JPY hedging costs fell, but the concern is that sustained global long-end pressure eventually reaches the US, particularly if the Fed narrative turns hawkish.

subject: Global FX Trader: Data Rewind, Position Unwind
summary:
# Dollar Firm on Data Vacuum and Position Unwinds, But the Strength Looks Borrowed

**Theme:** Risk-off positioning unwinds and a US data blackout prop up the Dollar, while diminished USD appeal lingers beneath the surface  
**Markets:** Global FX (USD, CNY, EM and Asian FX)  
**Source:** [REDACTED] — Kamakshya Trivedi, 21 November 2025  

### Landscape
- USD/JPY is testing early-January highs, near the 161-162 level that triggered intervention in July 2024, with last Wednesday's 2-big-figure rally overshooting rates.
- USD/CNY fixing has trended lower for over half a year at a very gradual pace, tracking toward the 7.0 year-end view.
- The Dollar firmed over the past week even as both low-yielding havens (CHF, JPY) and high-carry names (BRL, ZAR) sold off — an unusually disjointed move.
- The September US employment report landed but did little to settle the December Fed debate; BLS confirmed further backlogged reports will not arrive before the December FOMC.
- Philippine Q3 GDP printed 4% versus 5.2% consensus, dragged by weak public capex.
- The Shekel briefly traded below [REDACTED]'s 12-month 3.20 forecast earlier this month; ILS no longer screens as undervalued.

### Drivers
- **Positioning unwinds** amid negative risk sentiment are a key force: crowded BRL and, to a lesser degree, ZAR longs have amplified the beta to risk-off as investors brace for backlogged US data.
- **Foreign fiscal developments** are broadly Dollar-supportive — a larger-than-expected Japanese fiscal package, German military spending yet to accelerate, and pre-Budget nerves in the UK.
- **The US data vacuum** carries a hawkish tilt: with no further reports before December, the risk-off tone has a policy element that typically aids the USD.
- **China's external sector** is the CNY engine — export volume forecasts revised up to 5-6% yoy, trade surplus seen at a record USD 1.2trn in 2025 and USD 1.4trn in 2026, with 2026/27 GDP forecasts (4.8%/4.7%) above consensus.
- **The Dollar-VIX correlation** remains a lingering vulnerability even as the Dollar-S&P relationship has normalized; watch whether recent USD strength alongside higher equity vol marks a genuine normalization or just technical positioning noise.

### Risks
- **Downside (USD):** [REDACTED] remains wary of a quick return to a "Dollar down, equities down" regime on any meaningful deterioration in the US outlook, which historically moves FX more than other markets.
- **Upside (USD/JPY):** [REDACTED] flags rising odds of Japanese direct intervention as the rally extends, which would cap near-term upside; verbal pushback has escalated but the full prerequisites are not yet met.
- **Downside (HUF trade):** [REDACTED] notes the main risk to the new short EUR/HUF is continued pressure on risk sentiment as popular positions unwind, though HUF is less "risk-on" than BRL or ZAR.
- **Asymmetric read:** [REDACTED] judges last week's Dollar strength "justified but not durable," implying limited follow-through rather than a durable uptrend.

### Unpacked
**The week's price action is best read as technical rather than fundamental** — a positioning unwind layered on a hawkish data vacuum, not a clean growth shock. [REDACTED] notes the Dollar's firmness was, if anything, underwhelming relative to its typical betas, and that recent [REDACTED] moves mostly bring the USD back in line with other cyclical indicators rather than stretching it. The signature of positioning is visible elsewhere too: non-profitable tech and the most-shorted stocks underperformed, and Fed pricing for end-2026 plus longer-end yields shifted only marginally dovish — far less than a real growth scare would produce.

On China, the constructive case rests less on near-term activity — October data was soft on property and investment — than on the external sector and the 4th Plenum's emphasis on manufacturing competitiveness. **[REDACTED] rolls its USD/CNY path to 6.95, 6.90 and 6.85 (3M/6M/12M), citing still-significant undervaluation and a trade dominance reminiscent of the first China shock, which was followed by large appreciation.** The PBoC is managing the descent tightly in line with forwards, so the pace stays gradual.

Sterling is framed around next Wednesday's Autumn budget. **[REDACTED] expects the negative impulse to come through the standard channel of a contractionary fiscal shift that clears the path for BoE easing, rather than a fiscal risk-premium flare-up** — sensitivity to fiscal headlines has already faded, as the muted reaction to the income-tax U-turn showed. A roughly £25bn net consolidation would support rate-cut-driven underperformance, with market pricing still needing to catch down to the call for three cuts across four meetings. [REDACTED] also argues options are overpricing budget-day vol relative to the following two days, where past events show worse digestion tends to land.

On the Yen, [REDACTED] reiterates that speed matters more than level and that Wednesday's rate-overshooting rally fits the intervention template, even if verbal warnings (FM Katayama's "appropriate action as needed") stop short of "prepared to respond." Crucially, USD/JPY looks less dislocated than it appears — most of the post-Takaichi move traces to higher fiscal premium, mirrored in a tight correlation with JGB curve steepness, which should worry officials less than 2024's unexplained weakness. **With intervention risk rising as the rally extends, [REDACTED] leans toward expressions like short CAD/ZAR over fresh JPY shorts, noting sustained USD/JPY upside would need a return to US outperformance.**

Across Non-Japan Asia, the tech-sensitive low-yielders have lagged despite strong fundamentals. TWD is favored on a current-account surplus rising to 17-18% of GDP, a decade of accumulated USD deposits, and a US-Taiwan FX statement allowing more downside flexibility; KRW hinges on a possible NPS hedging restart; MYR is backed by tech supply chains, data-center FDI and stable policy. **Among high-yielders, [REDACTED] expects PHP to underperform** — typhoon and corruption-protest disruരption plus BSP rate cuts could push USD/PHP above a record 59.0 — while IDR struggles to outperform as Bank Indonesia uses appreciation spells to cut.

In CEEMEA, [REDACTED] initiates a new short EUR/HUF (target 375, stop 390) and revises forecasts to 380/375/375, arguing this week's resolutely hawkish MNB and the gap to the next policy event create a tactical entry; the Virag departure is judged immaterial for policy. ILS tailwinds are fading — no longer undervalued, a Bank of Israel cut expected next week, and election noise possible — with USD/ILS seen ranging 3.20-3.30 absent stronger US tech equities. On EGP, a hawkish "wait-and-see" CBE hold keeps Egyptian real rates among the highest in Frontier/EM HY; **[REDACTED] keeps its short USD/EGP recommendation, tightening the stop to 8.5% and extending the target to 12.5%, expecting carry to drive most of the return even as spot stays range-bound into year-end.**

subject: Weekly Fund Flows: Explaining the Unexplained
