subject: US Daily: Government Shutdown: Much Closer to the End Than to the Beginning
summary:
# US Government Shutdown: Longest and Costliest on Record, but an Exit Nears in Mid-November

**Theme:** Why the shutdown has outlasted expectations, what could end it, and its GDP and data-release consequences  
**Markets:** US fiscal policy and growth  
**Source:** [REDACTED] (Alec Phillips), 2 November 2025

### Definitive impacts
- **-1.15pp to 2025Q4 quarter-on-quarter annualized real GDP growth**, assuming a ~6-week shutdown — driven mainly by federal employee furloughs, with smaller drags on federal investment and government purchases.
- **+1.3pp to 2026Q1 growth**, as furloughed workers return and some Q4 federal investment and purchases shift into Q1; a residual **-0.15pp in 2026Q2** as spending normalizes.
- **Real GDP growth forecasts revised to +1.0% in 2025Q4 and +3.1% in 2026Q1** (quarterly annualized).
- **First missed full paychecks land on fixed dates**: air traffic controllers and airport screeners (Oct. 28, next Nov. 10); House staff (Oct. 31); Senate staff second check (Nov. 5); support staff (Oct. 28, Nov. 10). Military pay was met Oct. 15 and likely Oct. 31, but the Nov. 15 payment is in doubt.
- **November SNAP benefits were withheld** (USDA announcement Oct. 24), reversing its own Sep. 30 contingency plan; two district courts ruled Oct. 31 that contingency funds must cover at least partial benefits, implying either ~60% of normal benefits (~$5bn) or full benefits with transferred funds — in all cases delayed.
- **Public blame skews toward Republicans/Trump**, averaging 43% vs. 35% for Democrats since the shutdown began; Democratic-voter approval of congressional Democrats rose to 58% from 39% in July.
- **Vote math is fixed**: with 52 Republicans backing a clean CR (Sen. Paul excepted), 8 Democrats are needed for 60; only 3 have so far voted for it.

### Opinative impacts
- **[REDACTED] expects the shutdown to end around the second week of November** — its base case, drawn from converging pressure points (missed pay, political milestones passing, the Nov. 7 recess) and prediction markets pricing roughly even odds of reopening by Nov. 15.
- **The more likely reopening path is a Democratic commitment to back the CR in exchange for a post-reopening vote on health subsidies**, rather than more Democrats simply defecting — this lets Democrats keep leverage on ACA subsidies without forcing Republicans to negotiate mid-shutdown.
- **[REDACTED] judges this the most economically damaging shutdown on record** — not only longer than the 35-day 2018-19 episode but far broader, as it is a full lapse in appropriations rather than a partial one.
- **Filibuster abolition to force the CR through is seen as unlikely**, despite Trump's Oct. 30 call: Majority Leader Thune reiterated opposition Oct. 31 and at least four Republicans would object.
- **On data releases**, [REDACTED] expects the September employment report a few days after reopening, the November jobs report on/near Dec. 5 (possibly delayed a week), and a possible one-week slip in November CPI from Dec. 10; how BLS handles missing October data is unresolved, but any October figures would likely come in December alongside November's.

### Backdrop
Every prior shutdown has ended when the party blocking a "clean" continuing resolution — a temporary extension of spending authority with no policy concessions attached — relented under mounting political pressure as consequences accumulated. Most were also narrow, affecting only a few unfunded agencies. Two structural features usually create the pressure: shutdowns interrupt paychecks for federal workers and the military, and they suspend appropriations-dependent programs. Most entitlements (e.g. Medicare) sit outside annual appropriations, but a few, including SNAP, depend on them.

Congressional Democrats' core demand is extension of the enhanced ACA premium subsidies enacted in 2021, which enlarged subsidies for low- and middle-income earners and extended eligibility upward. Those enhancements lapse for 2026 plans, so enrollment opening Nov. 1 exposes buyers to sharply higher, less-subsidized premiums.

### At issue
The partial federal shutdown, now running longer than any prior episode, has resisted the usual pressure to end for two reasons. First, polling blame has fallen on Republicans, so Democrats face little pressure to accept a clean CR without health-care concessions. Second, the administration has stretched to make payments normally barred during shutdowns — paying troops from unspent FY2025 RDT&E funds ($8bn) and leaning on multi-year defense, immigration and air-traffic funding from July's fiscal package — removing pressure points that might otherwise have forced a deal.

Signs of an approaching resolution are now emerging. The AFGE, the largest federal workers' union, called Oct. 27 for a clean CR, pressuring a key Democratic constituency. A cluster of forcing events lands in early-to-mid November: missed air-travel-staff pay (echoing the delays that ended the 2018-19 shutdown), withheld and litigated SNAP benefits, the Nov. 1 ACA enrollment opening, Nov. 4 elections (NJ and VA governors, NYC mayor, California redistricting), and the Senate recess beginning after Nov. 7. The pending CR would fund the government through Nov. 21, though Republican leaders are now eyeing an early-2026 end date, which would need House passage.

### Unpacked
The note's central puzzle is why a shutdown that "should" have ended already has not. **The usual mechanism — blame builds, the blocking party folds — has stalled because the blame is landing on the other side.** With independents blaming Republicans even more lopsidedly and Democratic-voter approval of their own party rising, Senate Democrats have had political cover to hold out for an ACA-subsidy deal rather than accept a clean CR.

The administration's willingness to improvise payments is the second reason, and it cuts both ways. **By paying troops from repurposed funds and drawing on the July package's multi-year appropriations, the White House removed the early pressure points that ended past shutdowns — but the funds it is willing or able to tap are running thin.** It has signaled it cannot pay air traffic controllers, the Nov. 15 military payment is uncertain, and SNAP required a court order to move at all. The pressure the administration deferred is now arriving on a schedule.

That schedule is what underpins the mid-November call. **The tightest analogy is 2018-19, when a second missed controller paycheck and the travel delays around it broke the impasse — the equivalent date this year is roughly Nov. 6, just as the Senate's Nov. 7 recess departure adds its own forcing function.** Layered on top are the passing of Election Day and the ACA enrollment opening, both of which remove reasons for either side to keep holding firm. [REDACTED] reads prediction markets — near-even odds of reopening by Nov. 15, under 20% chance of a shutdown lasting past Thanksgiving — as reinforcing rather than driving its view.

**The likelier off-ramp preserves Democratic leverage rather than surrendering it**: a promise to support the CR in return for a guaranteed post-reopening vote on subsidies, with the CR's Nov. 21 expiry becoming the new deadline. That is cleaner for both sides than either more Democratic defections or the filibuster-abolition route Trump floated, which leadership and at least four Republicans have effectively closed off.

For the reader, the operative consequences are the growth path and the data calendar. **The GDP hit is real but mechanically reversing — a Q4 drag that more than unwinds in Q1 — so the more durable effect is the fog over incoming data.** A mid-November reopening would deliver the delayed September jobs report quickly but leave the November employment and CPI releases at risk of week-long slips, with October data handling still unresolved. There is no explicit trade idea in the note.

subject: Global Rates Trader: Reassessing the Risks, Not the Regime
summary:
# Fed Jolts a Complacent Market, but the Cutting Regime Holds

**Theme:** Reassessing risks around a still-intact easing path, not the regime itself  
**Markets:** G10 rates (US, Canada, Euro area, UK, Japan)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], George Cole, 31 October 2025

### Landscape
- The Fed cut 25bp on Wednesday but Powell's tone was more hawkish than expected, jolting a market that had priced high odds of steady cuts continuing into 2026.
- QT will stop from the start of December, one month later than [REDACTED] expected; the incremental balance-sheet impact is only ~$20bn.
- Early-2026 SOFR-FF pricing (Exhibit 1) already embeds improving liquidity conditions; [REDACTED] sees a normalization of the TGA to $850bn plus one more month of runoff and currency growth worth roughly +$100bn in liquidity and ~5bp lower repo rates.
- The BoC cut as expected and signalled a hold; the market reacted hawkishly, with front-end gaps steepening and the belly underperforming.
- The ECB stayed on hold with 12bp of cuts priced to June, which [REDACTED] does not view as excessive.
- 10y Gilt forecasts lowered to 4.25% end-2025 (from 4.40%) and 4.0% end-2026 (from 4.25%).
- The BoJ held; JPY implied vol has compressed to post-April lows, with 1m30y now trading below realized vol (Exhibit 4).

### Drivers
- **US labor market is the swing factor:** with policy now near longer-run rate estimates, deeper cuts hinge on the data; [REDACTED] still expects a December cut but sees higher yields coming only from stronger growth, with faster/deeper cuts the likely response to labor weakness. Watch next week's ADP, an unusually large potential mover with the shutdown still suppressing official data.
- **Fed balance-sheet shift toward bills:** MBS proceeds will reinvest exclusively into bills from December; [REDACTED] estimates $366bn of Fed bill purchases in 2026 (~2/3 MBS reinvestment, ~1/3 reserve management purchases expected in 2H26), supporting bill demand ahead of next week's refunding.
- **Canada easing skew persists despite the hold:** a wide output gap unlikely to close quickly caps hike risk while softer inflation lifts the odds of further easing, leaving risks tilted to lower 2026 rates.
- **Euro-area growth risks abating:** the ECB judges downside growth risks have receded, supported by recent PMIs and GDP; with two-sided inflation risks flagged, the bar to ease further is high.
- **UK disinflation:** the main force behind Gilt outperformance, calming long-end risk premium and allowing the BoE to cut below market pricing, including next week.
- **BoJ conviction building with time:** Ueda signalled the next hike is in sight; [REDACTED] expects a January hike, pending a shunto in the low-3% range and continued US resilience. The resolution of BoJ and fiscal uncertainty is relieving the long end.

### Risks
- **Downside to Canadian rates:** [REDACTED]'s baseline is that Wednesday's cut ended the BoC cycle, but it flags risks skewed toward lower rates in 2026 — the basis for the CORU6 long.
- **Upside to US yields via QT/funding:** [REDACTED] sees room for more risk premium to be priced for reserve management purchases taking longer than mid-2026 to begin, though seasonal year-end pressures could pull that forward.
- **Two-sided EUR inflation risk:** flagged by Lagarde, keeping the ECB comfortably on hold rather than easing.
- **Supply risk in Canada and Japan:** next week's Canadian budget carries medium-term issuance risk from infrastructure and defense investment; Japan's supplementary budget poses some risk to long-end absorption.

### Unpacked
The core message is a repricing of risks within an unchanged easing regime, not a break from it. **[REDACTED] judged the market's shift toward pricing more risk of a pause or a return to "wait-and-see" as sensible, but sees no strong case for a meaningful reappraisal of the Fed's reaction function.** The asymmetry matters: higher yields should come from more benign growth, while a faltering labor market would bring faster or deeper cuts. With the shutdown still in place, [REDACTED] expects yields to settle back into a fairly narrow range near term. Medium-term it keeps favoring belly-cheapening expressions and inflation longs, while tightening stops on both the belly-cheapening fly and the 5y5y inflation swap after recent performance.

On funding, the extra month of runoff signals some Fed tolerance for recent funding volatility and a baseline that the balance sheet can stay stable for a while. **[REDACTED] reads the liquidity relief priced into early 2026 as reasonable even without balance-sheet expansion, but wants more premium for the risk that reserve management purchases start later** — expressed via SERFFG6/M6 (Feb/Jun 2026) flatteners (entry 1bp, target -2bp, stop 2.5bp). It expects Fed bill buying to take 2–2½ years to bring bill holdings to a market-neutral 20–25% of SOMA Treasury holdings.

The refunding backdrop reinforces this. Favorable bill demand sets up next week's Treasury refunding, where [REDACTED] expects TBAC to reaffirm a preference for shorter-term and belly issuance over the long end. **Coupon auction sizes are seen rising from 2H2026, with gradual front-end and belly growth but stable long-end sizes**; buyback programs are a further focus, with [REDACTED] noting Treasury may emphasize flexibility rather than preemptively adjust.

In Canada, the on-hold signal drew a hawkish reaction [REDACTED] views as overdone in the belly. **It adds CORU6 longs (entry 2.205%, target 2.05%, stop 2.3%),** citing a persistent output gap and softer inflation, while flagging next week's budget as a medium-term issuance risk likely met through across-the-curve bond issuance. The CAD move contrasts with Australia, where a similar pricing-out of cuts looks more justified given a meaningfully lower unemployment rate and thus a higher bar for the RBA to resume easing.

In Europe, [REDACTED] reads the October ECB meeting as largely uneventful but notes the constructive growth judgment sits somewhat at odds with earlier hard data and downbeat sentiment. **It expects no further ECB cut and likes front-end steepeners such as ERH6ERH7 as the cyclical backdrop improves into 2026, while looking for terminal-rate pricing to grind higher over time.** EGB net supply should decline modestly in 2026 as German fiscal expansion is offset by Southern European reductions, with ECB QT a steady headwind; maturity at issuance stays in focus given long-end steepening and Dutch pension reform, though issuance strategies adjust only gradually (Exhibit 3).

On Gilts, **ongoing disinflation is expected to let the BoE cut below market pricing and calm long-end premium, with the Autumn budget's credible deficit-reduction measures improving the fiscal outlook** — together worth around 10–20bp lower yields, though the market has already embedded some of this. The DMO is likely to keep WAM low without further skew away from the long end.

In Japan, [REDACTED] raises conviction on a January BoJ hike and maintains its Oct25/Jan26 OIS steepener, tightening stops to 17bp. **With uncertainty on both BoJ and fiscal policy resolving, and JPY vol compressed to post-April lows, it recommends owning 1m30y receivers (entry 4.7bp, target 10bp, stop 2bp)** to position for further long-end relief in limited-risk form, despite some supply risk from supplementary budget discussions.

subject: US Daily: October [REDACTED]: Freaky Friday
summary:
# October [REDACTED]: Prices Surge Even as Hiring Cracks

**Theme:** Activity holds above trend while employment collapses and price components jump  
**Markets:** US business activity and inflation  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jessica Rindels, 31 October 2025

### Landscape
- The headline [REDACTED] fell 1.9pt to 59.0 in October, still comfortably above the 50 line that signals contraction (and above the ~50 level [REDACTED] reads as trend growth).
- New orders rose 4.9pt to 64.4, while shipments slipped 1.5pt to 60.6.
- The employment component dropped 27.5pt to 31.2, its lowest reading since October 2023.
- Inventories rose 2.7pt to 66.7 and exports jumped 21.4pt to 71.4, the highest since June 2022; the orders-less-inventories gap widened 2.2pt to -2.3.
- Price components surged: materials prices +14.8pt to 77.3, output prices +25.2pt to 80.3, wages +1.4pt to 62.5.
- [REDACTED]'s broader trackers firmed modestly — manufacturing +0.9pt to 51.6, nonmanufacturing +0.3pt to 52.2 — but their employment sub-indices stayed contractionary (manufacturing 48.9, services 46.9).

### Drivers
- Hiring is the clear weak point: the [REDACTED] employment plunge and the sub-50 employment readings across both business survey trackers point to a labor-demand pullback, even as output and orders hold up.
- Pricing pressure is intensifying on both input and output sides, with materials and output-price components jumping sharply — consistent with tariff cost passthrough now working through firms.
- Capex intentions are supportive into 2026: 36% of manufacturing and 39% of services firms in the Philadelphia Fed survey expect higher 2026 capex versus 2025, with another 45% and 41% expecting it roughly flat.
- The government shutdown is a live drag on affected industries, expected to hit revenue or disrupt production for a portion of covered firms.

### Risks
- Downside: analysts flag the government shutdown as likely to cut revenue (40%) or disrupt production (20%) in affected industries, though 40% expect no impact on their sector.
- Upside (idiosyncratic): [REDACTED] insurance analysts note that FEMA being unable to write new policies during the shutdown could lift sales at the insurers they cover.

### Unpacked
**The October [REDACTED] tells a split story: demand and pricing power remain firm, but the labor signal broke down sharply.** New orders and exports strengthened while the employment component fell to a two-year low and the trackers' employment sub-indices stayed in contraction. Activity is still expanding at an above-trend pace, but the hiring impulse behind it has faded.

**Price components moved in one direction — up, and hard.** Output prices jumped more than 25 points and materials prices nearly 15, a signal that firms are both facing and passing through higher costs. This ties directly to the tariff special questions: 66% of surveyed analysts said their sector has faced or will face higher input costs from tariffs, and every one of them expects at least some passthrough to consumers.

**On average, analysts expect consumers to absorb 58% of tariff costs, just below the 60% recorded in the June [REDACTED].** Among those expecting passthrough, 40% said companies had or would raise prices on tariffed goods only, while another 40% said they had or would raise prices on both tariffed and non-tariffed goods — meaning tariffs are lifting prices beyond the directly affected products. A few sectors pass costs through differently: retail hardlines firms are raising prices selectively on items that sell out or are bought infrequently, while insurers expect most property-related products to reprice higher on anticipated future costs.

**The capex signal offers a firmer footing for 2026.** In the Philadelphia Fed special questions, most firms expect capex to rise or hold steady next year. Manufacturers expect increases across every category; services firms expect more software and hardware spending but net declines in energy-saving investment and structures.

The shutdown question rounds out the picture: while 40% of analysts see no sector impact, an equal share expect a revenue hit and 20% expect production disruptions, leaving the balance tilted toward mild negative effects with the insurance-sector FEMA dynamic as the one notable exception. Survey responses were collected October 27–30.

subject: Global FX Trader: Hawkish for a Spell
summary:
# Dollar Downside Intact, But Hawkish Fed and BoE/BoJ Risks Cloud the Near Term

**Theme:** Cross-currency read where domestic policy shocks briefly interrupt a structural weak-Dollar view  
**Markets:** Global FX (G10 and EM)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Kamakshya Trivedi, 31 October 2025  

### Landscape
- USD firmed this week in line with a hawkish Powell press conference, though most recent Dollar strength has come from foreign developments rather than domestic drivers.
- USD/JPY trades back near its January highs, up nearly 5% since October 1, with the Yen the weakest major over the past month.
- USD/CNY fixing has continued lower, with CNY undervaluation now comparable to the mid-2000s "China shock" period.
- Korea's outbound portfolio flows reached USD89bn between January and August, up from USD61bn in all of 2024, weighing on KRW despite strong local equities.
- Argentina's real effective exchange rate sits close to fair value versus its five-year moving average, but the correction of prior overvaluation has been slow; net reserves remain critically low.

### Drivers
- **USD:** The rationale for Fed cuts — a US economy that no longer outperforms as it once did — supports further Dollar downside from a rich starting point (~15% overvalued on [REDACTED]); a December cut is still seen as quite likely.
- **JPY:** Near-term BoJ hike expectations have fallen (rates held in October) and post-Takaichi fiscal risk premium has reset the Yen weaker; watch for a shift in FM Katayama's intervention language toward "prepared to respond to excessive fluctuations" as the trigger signal.
- **CNY:** A clear policy impulse toward gradual appreciation, reinforced by improving US-China trade (possible fentanyl-tariff cut) and raised China growth forecasts, points toward the 7.00 year-end target.
- **KRW:** Outbound flows can reverse as Korea-US rate differentials narrow and the trade/investment deal removes domestic uncertainty (auto tariffs cut to 15% from 25%); outlook shifted from neutral to bullish.
- **GBP:** Softer inflation and wage data keep the dominant driver pointed toward earlier, deeper BoE cuts; the 6 November meeting is close to a binary event, with Breeden speeches on Tuesday and Wednesday as possible clues.
- **CAD:** A slightly hawkish BoC (rate "about the right level," bar for further easing raised) leaves CAD attractive as a low-vol funder given a soft domestic backdrop and trade risks.

### Risks
- **Upside (USD):** AI-led productivity gains could let the Dollar defy its overvaluation and sustain a high valuation, as it has for much of the past decade.
- **Downside (JPY crosses):** Direct FX intervention is a rising risk around any rapid depreciation, which limits USD/JPY upside; the analyst judges it not yet imminent given moves remain broadly in line with fundamentals.
- **Two-sided (JPY):** Growing fiscal premium under the new administration (possible early elections) argues for more Yen weakness on crosses, while intervention risk caps it — the analyst sees less room to press shorts.
- **Upside (ARS):** The midterm result opens a window to float the Peso more freely, with one-off-move costs cushioned by US support, anchored inflation expectations and low pass-through; the currency's bounce has lagged bonds.
- **Skew (EM long-term):** The analyst flags asymmetric total-return upside in high-inflation EM currencies (Brazil, South Africa), noting markets tend to overcompensate for EM drawdown risk after conditions converge.

### Unpacked
The connecting thread is that this week's Dollar strength is a domestic policy interruption, not a change of trend. **Powell's hawkish tone is read as giving voice to a divided Committee rather than signalling a hold, and as individual members speak and more inflation and labour data arrive, markets are expected to converge on a December cut and unwind the week's Dollar gains.** The structural case rests on the US no longer outperforming to the same degree — a point the equity strategists reinforce by framing the case for international diversification as better performance elsewhere rather than US weakness.

On the Yen, the note carefully separates two phases of the move: an initial reset on post-Takaichi fiscal risk premium, then a bumpier grind driven by fading near-term BoJ hike pricing. **Intervention is treated as a real but not-yet-imminent risk — verbal warnings have historically preceded actual operations by months (June 2022 comments, September 2022 action), and officials themselves attribute part of the move to Fed and BoJ fundamentals, usually a precondition against intervening.** The base case is caution on fresh shorts after the recent weakness rather than a call for reversal.

China is the clearest constructive story. **Improving trade relations and above-consensus 2026-27 growth upgrades — led by higher real export growth — combine with deep undervaluation and a strengthening current account to support gradual CNY appreciation toward 7.00.** This policy impulse also matters for Korea, the most CNY-sensitive Asian currency, whose upgrade to bullish rests both on reversible outflows and on the trade deal clearing domestic uncertainty; announced investment commitments are expected to have little FX impact since they can be funded from existing USD assets.

Sterling and the Canadian Dollar sit on the weaker side. GBP faces a near-binary BoE meeting where a 25bp cut is expected to narrowly clear the bar, which given limited priced cut premium would imply meaningful further downside — though near-term caution is warranted after this week's move, with the longer-horizon view still for underperformance on European crosses. **CAD's appeal is structural rather than a directional call: a soft economy, trade risks, and its ability to neutralise risk exposure, improve carry and lower volatility keep it a preferred funder against AUD and high-carry EM such as BRL and ZAR, even without a dovish BoC.**

Two longer-lens sections round out the note. The 2035 forecasts (EUR/USD 1.21, USD/JPY 100, GBP/USD 1.24, USD/CNY 5.17) lean on [REDACTED]'s roughly 20%-per-year convergence to fair value and point to continued Dollar depreciation, with the strongest total returns concentrated in EM real-carry stories. On tactics, the note argues relative value deserves more room while major Dollar pairs sit in narrow ranges under low data visibility. **Relative value crosses — especially same-region pairs — mean-revert, whereas Dollar pairs trend, so RSI signals work well on crosses (better still when overlaid with the [REDACTED] cyclical fair-value model) but not on Dollar pairs.** Preferred expressions are GBP underperformance on European crosses, tactical JPY weakness versus CHF, and PLN weakness versus CZK and HUF.

subject: Weekly Fund Flows: Domestic Japanese Equity Demand
summary:
# Japan Draws the Week's Strongest Equity Demand, Led by Domestic Buyers

**Theme:** Broad-based fund inflows across equities and bonds; Japan the G10 standout  
**Markets:** Global cross-asset fund flows  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Isabella Rosenberg, 31 October 2025  

### Landscape
- Global equity funds took in +$17bn in the week ending October 29, up from +$14bn the prior week.
- Global fixed income funds drew firm demand led by Agg-type funds at +$18bn, versus +$17bn the previous week.
- Money market fund assets rose by $36bn.
- Japanese equity funds saw the largest G10 net inflows as a share of AUM, yet remain in net outflow year-to-date.
- Commodities funds saw the week's largest sector outflows, likely on a gold selloff.

### Drivers
- Equity flows split by benchmark: funds including US equities saw outflows while those excluding US equities took inflows, leaving the aggregate positive.
- Japanese equity demand was led primarily by domestic investors, though the cumulative year-to-date figure stays negative.
- EM equity flows diverged: mainland China saw outflows while Korea drew strong inflows.
- UK equity funds continued their run of net outflows.
- Within fixed income, inflation-protected bond funds saw firm inflows; EM local currency bond funds drew positive flows while hard currency funds saw outflows.
- Cross-border FX flows were firm on broadly positive risk sentiment, with USD, EUR, and JPY the largest G10 net inflows.

### Unpacked
The week's message is resilient, broad-based demand across risk assets, with no single asset class carrying the flow. **Equities and bonds both drew firm inflows, and money market assets still grew by $36bn — demand was additive rather than a rotation out of cash.**

**The equity story is regional dispersion around a positive headline: buyers favored funds that exclude US equities and sold those that include them, so the net figure masks a clear tilt away from US exposure.** Japan is the featured case — it led the G10 in inflows as a percentage of AUM, driven by domestic rather than foreign investors, but the flow remains a partial recovery: the year-to-date cumulative total is still negative, the point made in the Chart of the Week. In EM, Korea's strength stood against mainland China's outflows, and UK funds extended their persistent selling.

**Fixed income demand was concentrated in core Agg-type funds, with supporting inflows into inflation-protected bonds and a hard-versus-local split in EM.** Local currency EM bond funds attracted money while hard currency funds lost it. The commodities outflow, the largest at the sector level, is tied to a gold selloff rather than a broader risk-off signal, consistent with the firm FX flows into USD, EUR, and JPY that point to constructive risk sentiment. The note carries no explicit trade idea.

subject: European Credit Brief: Week ending October 31, 2025
summary:
# European Credit Brief: EUR credit keeps its edge over USD, but tight spreads cap the upside

**Theme:** EUR outperformance holding as attention turns to softer November technicals and widening HY dispersion  
**Markets:** European credit (EUR IG & HY), vs. USD credit  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Sara Grut, 31 October 2025  

### Landscape
- The 5-year EUR/USD spread differential compressed 7bp in October to 10bp, sitting at the 24th percentile relative to post-2010 history.
- EUR IG and HY spreads are back near their tightest levels since early 2018.
- EUR BB and B issuer spread dispersion sits at the 69th and 95th percentiles since 2021, against just the 26th percentile for EUR BBBs.
- EUR IG new-issue concessions have faded toward near zero.
- Since July, the EURO STOXX 600 is up ~7% while EUR IG and HY spreads have tightened by roughly 17bp and 30bp — broadly in line with historical beta.
- EUR IG and HY drew weekly inflows of $0.66bn and $0.54bn, taking year-to-date totals to about 9% and 4.3% of last year's AUM.
- USD HY and USD loans took in just $83mn and $169mn last week, versus $4.4bn into USD IG, and have not recovered from October's outflows.

### Drivers
- EUR outperformance over USD is driven by a US-centric rise in loan default headlines, calmer French policy improving European risk sentiment, and heavier USD supply — including AI-related issuance at ~26% of USD net supply year to date — against subdued EUR supply since summer.
- Seasonality points to heavier EUR IG net supply and modest widening in EUR IG and HY into November, usually reversing in December as issuance slows; USD is the mirror image, with subdued IG net supply into year-end and spreads tending to firm.
- EUR HY dispersion is broadening across issuers and sectors — Chemicals has underperformed year to date — pushed by higher-for-longer funding costs, uneven growth, and competitive disruption from China and AI; expected to stay elevated.
- EUR credit flows favour a diversification move away from US-centric risk, helped by lighter net supply and a stronger cross-currency hedged yield pick-up.

### Risks
- Downside: tight starting spreads leave upside capped and imply slower momentum in November; this year's seasonal pattern is also distorted by April's tariff shock, adding uncertainty to the usual playbook.
- The analyst notes HY dispersion drivers may take time to filter into IG, where subdued dispersion and vanishing concessions mean spreads may not compensate for embedded risks.

### Unpacked
**EUR credit has outperformed USD through October while moving in the same direction, and the note expects that edge to persist even with limited room to rally.** The spread differential is compressing from an already low base, and the case for continued EUR outperformance rests less on spreads going tighter than on a cleaner backdrop — a slightly better growth mix and supply technicals free of the AI issuance overhang weighing on USD.

November is framed as a seasonally softer stretch for EUR credit. The typical pattern is heavier IG supply and modest widening across IG and HY, then a December retracement as issuance slows. The mirror pattern in USD — subdued year-end IG supply and firming spreads — reinforces the divergence, though April's tariff shock has skewed this year's seasonality enough that the tight starting level, rather than the calendar alone, is the reason to expect slower momentum.

**Beneath resilient headline HY spreads, dispersion is the real story.** BB and B dispersion is elevated while BBB dispersion stays contained, and the widening is broad-based across sectors and issuers rather than concentrated in one pocket. With funding costs staying high, growth uneven, and competitive disruption from China and AI ongoing, that dispersion is expected to persist — and on ratings allocation the preference is for B over BB.

**In IG the problem is the opposite: alpha is scarce because everything is tight and calm.** Spreads are compressed, dispersion is subdued, and near-zero new-issue concessions have handed pricing power to issuers. Until HY's dispersion drivers filter through, the stance is to avoid areas that don't pay for their risk, with an underweight in Banks versus Non-Banks on the former's greater sensitivity to sovereign fiscal risk.

**Against equities, EUR credit looks better set up than the raw rally suggests.** Credit's tightening since July has broadly matched its historical beta to a European equity market that has climbed more measuredly than the US, helped by Europe's lighter mega-cap tech footprint. Combined with lighter net supply and a stronger hedged yield pick-up that should support inflows, this leaves EUR credit positioned to capture diversification flows away from US-centric risk — a reading the flow data already echoes, with EUR HY among the largest weekly inflow recipients relative to AUM while USD HY and loans still lag.

subject: USA: Preliminary Data Suggest Initial Claims Decline
summary:
# US: [REDACTED] estimate points to a decline in initial jobless claims during the shutdown

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius
**Focus:** Weekly US jobless claims
**General comment:** Technical estimate note; fills a gap in official data during the shutdown, with no directional thesis.

### Context
With the federal government in shutdown, the Department of Labor (DOL) is not publishing official jobless claims data. The note builds its own estimate from the state-level data that are still released and from the seasonal factors the DOL had pre-released.

### The case
- **Seasonally adjusted initial claims are estimated to have fallen to around 218k in the week ended October 25.** The estimate combines the seasonal factors pre-released by the DOL with the state-level data published on the afternoon of the release — possible because some of the staff who administer unemployment insurance are exempt from the shutdown and continue publishing state data as part of their normal duties. The figure compares with 230k projected by [REDACTED] itself, 229k for the market median, and 231k for the revised prior reading.
- **The absence of three states from the data requires assumptions, and there is a range of uncertainty around the central estimate.** Arizona, Massachusetts, and Washington DC did not appear in the DOL data; their claims are assumed to have been in line with the prior week. Using the lowest and highest levels observed in those states this year, the range runs from 216k to 223k. At the state level, no state would have risen 2k or more, with declines of 4k in Kentucky (after a 4k increase the prior week) and 3k in Tennessee.
- **Continuing claims rose to 1,949k in the week ended October 18,** under the same assumptions, with a likely range of 1,927k to 1,963k — above the median of 1,925k and the revised prior reading of 1,938k.

### Implications
- The estimates are preliminary and may be revised once the DOL resumes official releases after the shutdown.
- They serve as a provisional reference for reading the labor market during the period without official data, keeping the picture of low initial claims intact.

subject: US Daily: October FOMC Recap: Despite a More Hawkish Message, a December Cut Still Looks Likely (Mericle)
summary:
# Um FOMC mais hawkish no tom, mas o corte de dezembro segue como cenário-base

**Source:** [REDACTED] — David Mericle  
**Focus:** Federal Reserve / US monetary policy  
**General comment:** Constructive on a December cut; holds its dovish-leaning baseline against a more hawkish Powell and a more divided market read.

### Context
The FOMC cut the funds rate by 25bp to 3.75–4% at its October meeting and set balance-sheet runoff to end in early December. Powell's press conference read as more hawkish than expected, reopening the debate over whether a third cut follows in December — which this piece pushes back on while keeping its forecast unchanged.

### The case
- **Powell's tone was a genuine hawkish surprise, delivered through three deliberate signals.** He declined to reference the September dot plot (whose median implied a December cut) and instead stressed that policy is "far from" a preset course, that the FOMC holds "strongly different views" with a "growing chorus" favouring waiting a cycle, and that the shutdown's data blackout could itself be a reason for some participants to hold. He was careful not to endorse any of these views himself, noting it will "probably be argued both ways."

- **The hawkish messaging reflects internal opposition Powell chose to voice, not a shift in the baseline.** There is likely substantial resistance on the committee to the risk-management cuts, and Powell judged it important to air those concerns — but the underlying case for cutting remains intact. The September dots showed most participants treating a December cut as the baseline, and the Fed's past risk-management easing packages point to a third and final cut as the default.

- **Incoming labor data are unlikely to be reassuring enough to justify a hold.** The cooling is seen as genuine, and near-term readings will be distorted: DOGE deferred resignations should produce a weak October payrolls print and weigh on November, while the shutdown has disrupted October (and possibly November) data collection, leaving the signal less reliable rather than convincingly stronger.

- **Powell's own framing of policy as modestly restrictive is itself an argument to cut.** He tied the ongoing gradual cooling of the labor market to the restrictive stance. Since the committee does not want further cooling, that logic favours another cut unless the labor market has clearly stabilised by December.

### Implications
- The base case stays a December cut as "quite likely," despite the hawkish press conference and the acknowledged split on the committee.
- The main risk to that call is data-driven and definitional: a clear stabilisation in the labor market by December would strengthen the hold camp; distorted or missing data cuts the other way.
- Markets that read the conference as a hawkish pivot may be overweighting Powell's decision to voice dissent relative to where the committee's median still sits.

subject: G10 Consumer Dashboard: October 2025: Spending Growth Slows Across DMs (Peters)
summary:
# G10 Consumer Dashboard: Fundamentals Still Solid, but Spending and Sentiment Roll Over

**Theme:** Consumer health softening at the margin despite strong balance sheets  
**Markets:** G10 developed-market consumers  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Peters, 29 October 2025  

### Landscape
- Overall consumer health sits above P60 in the Euro area, near P50 in Japan and the US, around P45 in Australia, and near P30 in Canada and the UK — a slight deterioration across DMs since the prior dashboard.
- Household net worth to income runs above P90 in the US and Australia, above P80 in Canada, the Euro area, and Japan, and around P55 in the UK.
- Real net worth growth is soft: around P60 in the Euro area (improved), P40 in Australia, P30 in the UK, and just P10 in Japan.
- Unemployment remains near historical lows in the Euro area (6.3%), Japan (2.6%), and Australia (4.5%), but has risen to ~P60 in the US (4.3%), ~P30 in the UK (4.7%, 3m MA), and ~P10 in Canada (7.1%).
- Real income growth ticked up in Canada (P55) but stayed subdued in the US (P35), UK (P30), and Australia (P25).
- Consumer sentiment sits below its historical average across the G10; it worsened in the US and Australia and edged up elsewhere.
- Debt service ratios are low by historical standards in the US, Euro area, and Japan, but elevated in Canada, Australia, and the UK; house prices broadly moved sideways, still climbing in Australia.

### Drivers
- **Spending is decelerating** across the G10; US PCE data is unavailable because the government shutdown blocked its release. Australia's nominal spending grew at its slowest monthly pace since April.
- **Labor markets are diverging**: still healthy outside Canada and the UK, but unemployment rose in the Euro area, UK, Japan, and Australia and held at an elevated level in Canada.
- **Wage growth is fading** in the UK and Japan. UK private-sector pay slowed to 4.2% in August, expected to undershoot the BoE's 4.6% Q3 forecast; Japan's nominal cash wage growth dropped to 1.5% in August as summer bonuses rolled off, though same-sample basic wages held at 2.4%.
- **Balance sheets remain a support**, with net worth elevated and saving rates still cushioning; the US and Australia saving rates are near/below pre-pandemic norms, while Canada's has declined recently.
- **Mortgage credit stays subdued**: outstanding mortgage debt edged up in the UK, Canada, and Australia, moved sideways in the US and Euro area, and slowed in Japan.

### Unpacked
This is a monthly scoreboard update rather than a thesis, and the through-line is a modest, broad-based softening layered on top of still-solid fundamentals. **The balance-sheet picture remains the anchor of strength — net worth to income is elevated almost everywhere — but the flow variables (spending, income, sentiment, employment) are what turned down this month.**

On spending, the slowdown is general rather than country-specific, and the US read is simply missing: the government shutdown prevented the PCE release, so the US spending percentile carries forward August. Where data exist, the direction is consistent — Australia's monthly nominal spending surprised to the downside, real retail sales moved sideways in Western Europe, and Japanese real retail sales stayed negative. **Goods spending has normalized to pre-pandemic levels in the US, Australia, Italy, and Japan but remains depressed in Germany, France, the UK, and Canada.**

The income and wage detail is where the softening is clearest. **UK private-sector regular pay is set to notably undershoot the BoE's Q3 forecast, and Japanese wage growth fell sharply once the bonus boost dropped out — leaving underlying basic pay flat at 2.4%.** Canada is the one bright spot on income, edging up to P55, though it pairs that with the weakest labor market in the group, with unemployment stuck near P10 at 7.1%.

Sentiment stays the persistent drag: below-average everywhere, and notably still weak among low-income consumers, though that cohort ticked up in Australia. On the financial side, interest expenses remain elevated in Canada and Australia, house prices have mostly stabilized except for continued gains in Australia, and mortgage credit growth is subdued across the board. **Netting it out, the dashboard's percentile framework shows consumer health slipping modestly across DMs even as the underlying wealth position holds up.**

The note flags no explicit trade idea, and none should be inferred — it is a monitoring product reporting the state of play.

subject: USA: FOMC Lowers Fed Funds Rate by 25bp and Announces End of Balance Sheet Runoff
summary:
# Fed Cuts Rates 25bp to 3.75–4% and Ends Balance Sheet Runoff Starting in December

**Theme:** October rate cut with two opposing dissents and the end of balance sheet runoff
**Markets:** US monetary policy
**Source:** [REDACTED] (Jan Hatzius), 29 Oct 2025

### Definitive impacts
- 25bp cut to the fed funds target range, from 4–4.25% to 3.75–4%, decided at the October FOMC meeting.
- Two dissents in opposite directions: Governor Miran preferred a larger 50bp cut, and Kansas City Fed President Schmid preferred no cut.
- Language change in the statement: downside risks to employment "have risen in recent months" (versus "risen earlier"); economic activity continued "expanding at a moderate pace."
- End of balance sheet runoff starting December 1, halting the reduction in reserves.
- MBS principal payments will now be reinvested exclusively in Treasury bills.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] reads the new language on employment as a possible sign that the labor-market indicators still available during the government shutdown remained weak.
- [REDACTED] assesses that reinvesting MBS payments into bills brings the composition of the Fed's Treasury holdings, at the margin, closer to that of the market, since the balance sheet today holds a larger proportion of long-dated securities than the market as a whole.

### Backdrop
The Fed had been reducing its balance sheet (quantitative tightening) by letting part of its holdings mature without fully reinvesting the principal. In parallel, interest rate policy operates in an easing cycle, with the labor market as the main focus of risk. A government shutdown limited the release of official data, leaving the Committee reliant on the remaining set of indicators to calibrate its decisions.

### At issue
At the October 2025 meeting, the FOMC (i) cut the fed funds target range by 25bp, to 3.75–4%, with dissents from Miran (in favor of 50bp) and Schmid (against any cut); and (ii) announced the end of balance sheet runoff on December 1, with MBS payments reinvested only in Treasury bills. Aside from the update on employment and activity risks, the statement saw minimal changes.

### Unpacked
The cut itself was widely expected; what gives the meeting texture are the two dissents in opposite directions, which expose a Committee split between those who see room to ease faster and those already resisting further cuts. **This contrast suggests that consensus around the pace of easing is more fragile than the unanimous-seeming decision would suggest.**

The change in the description of employment risks is the statement's most informative detail. With the shutdown restricting official data, the Committee signals that the indicators still available have not improved — and the read that risks "have risen in recent months" keeps the labor market at the center of the reaction function. **The justification for continuing to cut remains anchored in employment, not inflation.**

The balance sheet announcement has two parts with distinct implications. Ending runoff in December removes a source of quantitative tightening; reinvesting MBS payments into Treasury bills is a composition choice, shortening the duration of purchases and bringing the profile of the Fed's Treasury holdings closer to the market's. **It is a technical composition adjustment, not a resumption of balance-sheet stimulus.**

The note presents no explicit trade idea.

subject: Global Markets Daily: Rising Subprime (Auto) Delinquencies: Limited Risk to Financial Stability (Manohar)
summary:
# Rising subprime auto delinquencies are real, but the channels that made 2008 systemic are absent

**Theme:** Why climbing subprime auto (and low-FICO mortgage) delinquencies are unlikely to produce a 2008-style crisis  
**Markets:** US consumer credit — subprime auto ABS, low-FICO mortgages, banking system  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Arun Manohar, 29 October 2025  

### Definitive impacts
- Subprime auto borrowers now pay roughly 15 points more than prime borrowers, up from a 9-point differential pre-GFC — a wider risk premium built into underwriting.
- Subprime auto ABS annual issuance averages about $40bn in recent years, a fraction of the ~$450bn of subprime RMBS issued each year in 2005–2006; total auto loan origination is about one-third of 2006 subprime mortgage volume.
- 7% of recent mortgage originations carry a FICO below 650, and 58% of those sub-650 loans are FHA-insured — shifting their credit risk to the government rather than to originators, servicers or investors.
- FHA's Mutual Mortgage Insurance Fund capital ratio stood at 11.47% in 2024, about 1.5x its 2006 level.
- Bank Tier-1 risk-based capital ratios are materially higher than pre-GFC across all FDIC-insured size groups.
- Loss coverage ratios (reserves as a share of noncurrent loans) run above pre-pandemic averages, with the largest cushions at consumer and credit card lenders.
- D60+ delinquencies on subprime auto and FHA loans have risen steadily and sit well above pre-pandemic levels, while prime auto and mortgage delinquencies remain low.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] sees a 2008-style systemic event as "highly improbable," arguing subprime auto underwriting is structurally more conservative — high coupons, thick subordination, income/employment verification, and no reliance on collateral appreciation.
- [REDACTED] judges the FHA fund sufficiently capitalized to absorb rising low-FICO mortgage delinquencies without stressing private market participants.
- [REDACTED] expects the financial system to absorb idiosyncratic auto-linked bankruptcies easily, citing higher capital and reserves and generally upbeat Q3 management commentary (Fifth Third, Ally).
- [REDACTED] flags a conditional risk: if fraud proves more widespread than expected, smaller institutions and specialty lenders with concentrated subprime exposure could face greater stress, while large banks — with limited subprime exposure — keep the systemic impact contained.

### Backdrop
The 2008 crisis originated in subprime mortgages underwritten with lax standards — NINJA loans, teaser rates, and expectations of continued home-price appreciation — then amplified through a large RMBS market where credit risk sat with private investors and thinly capitalized banks. That combination of weak underwriting, scale, and private risk-bearing is the reference point against which the current episode is measured.

Post-GFC, mortgage lending standards tightened sharply: average credit scores and their distribution shifted higher, private subprime lending shrank, and most remaining low-FICO origination flows through FHA insurance and GNMA-guaranteed MBS, placing the credit risk with government agencies.

### At issue
Delinquencies on subprime auto loans have climbed steadily and stand well above pre-pandemic levels — a continuing trend, not a new one. What is new is the scrutiny: recent bankruptcies tied to the auto lending industry have prompted market participants to draw comparisons with the run-up to 2008. The note responds to that comparison, extending the analysis to rising delinquencies among low-FICO mortgage borrowers as well.

### Unpacked
The comparison to 2008 is the prompt, and the note's work is to show where the analogy breaks. **The rising delinquency numbers are conceded outright — the disagreement is about transmission, not about the trend.** Higher delinquencies exist; whether they can become systemic depends on how the losses are underwritten, how large the market is, and who ultimately bears the credit risk.

On auto, the argument is that the market was built to expect losses. **Subprime auto lending prices in large losses from the outset — high coupons, thick subordination, verified income, and no bet on the collateral rising in value — the opposite of the pre-GFC mortgage playbook.** The wider risk premium and heavier credit enhancement mean investors are cushioned against exactly the deterioration now showing up, and the market's smaller scale limits how far any stress can propagate.

On mortgages, the key move is that the risk has been socialized. **Because most low-FICO mortgages are FHA-insured and packaged into government-guaranteed MBS, rising delinquencies land on the FHA insurance fund rather than on private originators, servicers or investors** — and that fund carries a capital ratio roughly 1.5x its 2006 level. The credit stress among lower-income borrowers is acknowledged as real and cross-product; the point is where it settles.

The system-resilience leg ties the two together and adds the one live tail risk. Higher bank capital and above-normal reserves, plus reassuring Q3 commentary, support the view that idiosyncratic bankruptcies are absorbable. **The genuine open question is fraud: if invalid loans or misrepresented collateral are more widespread than the isolated cases suggest, concentrated specialty and smaller lenders — not the large banks — are where it would bite.** For a reader, the takeaway is a contained-risk base case with a monitorable fraud tail, and no trade idea attached to the thesis itself.

The note's "Best Trade Ideas Across Assets" list is a standing cross-asset rates/FX/EM section (USD/EGP, SOFR flies, PHP and INR bonds, JPY OIS, and others) unrelated to the subprime discussion; none of the ideas express this credit view.

subject: USA: Consumer Confidence Declines Slightly Less Than Expected
summary:
# US Consumer Confidence Holds Roughly Flat in October as Present Conditions Firm but Job Outlook Softens

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US consumer confidence  
**General comment:** Neutral read of the data; slightly better-than-feared, but flags softer forward-looking sentiment.

### Context
Comment on the Conference Board's October consumer confidence release, which came in at 94.6 versus a [REDACTED] estimate of 93.0 and a median forecast of 93.4 — a smaller decline than expected from an upwardly revised prior.

### The case
- **Confidence moved sideways rather than falling sharply.** The headline index slipped just 1.0pt to 94.6, off an upwardly revised September level (95.6). The composition was mixed: the expectations component fell 2.9pt to 71.5, while the present situation component rebounded 1.8pt to 129.3 from its lowest reading since September 2024. The Conference Board characterized the month as confidence holding "sideways," with present conditions regaining strength but consumers more pessimistic about future job availability and business conditions.
- **The labor differential ticked up off a multi-year low.** The gap between respondents saying jobs are "plentiful" (27.8%, +0.9pp) and "hard to get" (18.4%, +0.2pp) rose 0.7pt to 9.4, recovering from September's lowest level since February 2021 — a modest improvement in perceived labor-market tightness.
- **Inflation remained the dominant concern.** Twelve-month-ahead inflation expectations edged up 0.1pp to 5.9%. Write-in responses were led by prices and inflation as the main topic shaping consumers' economic views. References to tariffs declined further but stayed elevated.

### Implications
- The softer expectations component alongside firmer present conditions points to caution about the forward path rather than the current state of the economy.
- Persistently elevated inflation expectations and still-high tariff references keep price pressure at the center of consumer sentiment.
- The uptick in the labor differential tempers, but does not reverse, recent signals of a cooling jobs market.

subject: US Economics Weekly Update 10/27/2025
summary:
# Fed on track for October and December cuts, with balance-sheet runoff set to end

**Theme:** FOMC easing into a data blackout as the shutdown pauses the flow  
**Markets:** US monetary policy and economy  
**Source:** [REDACTED], David Mericle, 27 October 2025  

### Landscape
- Fed funds seen moving to 3.75–4% at the October meeting via a 25bp cut, with another 25bp cut expected in December.
- September median dot implies three cuts this year, the baseline the FOMC is still expected to follow.
- Core CPI rose 0.23% in September and 3.02% year-over-year.
- Shelter decelerated to 0.21% monthly, below its 0.28% three-month average.
- Headline CPI rose 0.31%, driven by a 1.5% jump in energy and a 0.25% rise in food.
- Core goods rose 0.2%, with tariff-exposed apparel +0.7%, recreation goods +0.4%, and personal care +0.4%.

### Drivers
- Labor-market support is the active rationale for cutting: alternative data have been mixed at best since the August employment report, with the job-growth tracker up from summer lows but alternative job-openings and tightness measures still declining.
- The government shutdown has paused official data, removing any reason to deviate from the September plan and delaying this week's releases including Q3 GDP, durable goods, the advance goods trade balance, the employment cost index, and personal income/spending with PCE.
- December cut logic rests on labor data being distorted by DOGE deferred resignations and shutdown-related collection gaps, making a convincing all-clear signal unlikely by then.
- Shelter disinflation is expected to continue, with the year-over-year rate seen falling another 1pp to 2.6% by end-2026.
- Balance-sheet runoff is expected to end, with an announcement anticipated this week.

### Risks
- Timing risk on 2026 cuts is two-sided, per the analyst: the two penciled-in 25bp cuts (March and June, to 3–3.25%) could come earlier if labor data stay soft or later if the economy looks sturdier and the FOMC waits for inflation nearer 2%.
- Downside data risk: if the shutdown runs through mid-November as prediction markets expect, most delayed releases would slip to December, raising the chance that distortions hit not just October but November data too.

### Unpacked
**The base case is a 25bp cut to 3.75–4% in October and another in December, consistent with the September median dot's three-cut path.** No formal December guidance is expected, but if asked, Powell is seen as comfortable pointing to the September dots, which already imply the third cut. With the data flow paused by the shutdown, there is no reason to abandon the plan to support the labor market.

**The December cut hinges less on strength than on the absence of a clear all-clear.** Labor-market signals have been mixed since the August payrolls report — the job-growth tracker has recovered from its very low summer pace, but alternative gauges of openings and tightness keep falling — and DOGE deferred resignations plus shutdown-impaired data collection make a convincing improvement signal unlikely by year-end.

**On inflation, September core CPI at 0.23% and 3.02% year-over-year showed decelerating shelter alongside firm, tariff-exposed goods.** The 0.21% shelter print likely overstates the underlying slowdown, but the trend still points lower, with year-over-year shelter seen down another 1pp to 2.6% by end-2026. Core goods strength in apparel, recreation, and personal care reflects tariff pass-through.

**Beyond this week's two cuts, the path thins to two more 25bp moves in March and June 2026, to 3–3.25%, with timing contingent on how labor and inflation data evolve.** The FOMC is also expected to announce the end of balance-sheet runoff this week. The larger near-term wildcard is the shutdown: if it lasts through mid-November, delayed releases bunch into December and risk distorting successive months of data.

**A research recap frames small businesses as having a hard year.** Firms under 100 employees make up 35% of the private workforce, churn jobs faster than large firms, are increasingly involved in innovation, and are more exposed to recessions and tight financial conditions given higher average rates and more variable-rate debt. Recently their employment growth has slowed more than at large firms, 2022 rate hikes raised their borrowing costs by more, post-April tariffs lifted input costs and output prices similarly across firm sizes, the recent fiscal bill extended tax cuts and reinstated subsidies (some aimed at capital spending), and they lag badly in AI adoption.

No explicit trade idea is offered.

subject: US Economics Analyst: Small Businesses: Navigating a Challenging Year (Mei/Rindels)
summary:
# US Small Business: Falling Behind on Every Front That Matters

**Theme:** How the most cycle-sensitive slice of the economy is absorbing a slowing labor market, high rates, tariffs, and fiscal changes  
**Markets:** US economy — small businesses (fewer than 100 employees)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Pierfrancesco Mei, 27 Oct 2025  

### Landscape
- Small firms (<100 employees) employ 35% of the private workforce, a share that has trended down over recent decades.
- Small business employment was roughly flat between 2024Q1 and 2025Q1, versus +2% for large businesses (Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages).
- Firms with fewer than 50 employees have shed roughly 125k jobs on net since April, while large firms added about 200k over the same span (ADP).
- Interest payments as a share of revenues for noncorporate businesses rose from below 7% in 2022 to around 8% in 1H2025 — about twice the increase seen by large firms.
- Short-term loan rates paid by small firms have fallen since late 2024 and credit availability is roughly back to pre-pandemic levels (NFIB).

### Drivers
- **Labor demand is contracting fastest at small firms**, concentrated in trade, manufacturing, and tech — sectors that make up nearly 30% of small business jobs; survey data suggest the deceleration has continued through mid-2025.
- **Rate pass-through is easing but still elevated**: small firms carry more variable-rate debt, so the 2022 hiking cycle hit them harder, and Fed cuts are only now beginning to relieve interest burdens.
- **Tariffs have raised input costs and output prices** roughly equally for small and large firms, but confidence swings are larger at small firms in both directions after a spring drop and partial rebound.
- **The 2025 tax bill is a tailwind for capex**: higher Section 179 limits ($1mn→$2.5mn), reinstated 100% bonus depreciation, and extended Section 199A passthrough deductions should support small business capital spending.
- **AI adoption is lagging** — in the five most AI-exposed industries, far fewer small firms have integrated AI into operations, pointing to weaker relative productivity gains ahead.

### Risks
- **Downside — recession sensitivity:** the analyst notes small firms cut investment more sharply and recover more slowly than large firms after downturns and monetary tightening, leaving them more exposed if the labor market weakens further.
- **Downside — AI divide:** persistently lower AI adoption could become a lasting drag on small firms' relative productivity, widening the gap with larger competitors.

### Unpacked
The note is built around five structural facts before turning to five current trends, so it reads as a reference on the sector rather than a single call. **The starting point is that small businesses are a large but shrinking employer, tilted toward leisure and hospitality, construction, and other services, and underweight in education, health, and manufacturing.** This industry mix matters because it shapes how policy and cycle shocks land on the sector.

Two facts frame why small firms swing more than the aggregate. They create and destroy jobs at nearly twice the pace of large firms, with young firms — those under ten years old — employing few workers but accounting for an outsized share of that churn. **They are also structurally more fragile: as noncorporate businesses they cut investment more deeply after recessions and contract more when monetary policy tightens, and their capex takes longer to recover.** On innovation, they punch below their weight — intellectual property investment is under 1% of GDP versus nearly 5% for corporates — though the share of very small firms holding a recent patent has tripled since 1980 to about 0.3%.

Financing is the other structural vulnerability. Small firms pay higher average rates and spend more on interest, and their debt shows a bimodal maturity profile: roughly half is variable rate and reprices quickly, while the other half carries somewhat longer maturities than a typical large-firm term loan. **That variable-rate tilt is the mechanism behind the outsized rate pass-through — interest costs rose about twice as fast for small firms as for large ones since 2022 — and it also means Fed cuts should relieve them faster on the way down.**

On the current picture, the labor slowdown is the sharpest signal: hiring has stalled at small firms while large firms keep adding, concentrated in trade, manufacturing, and tech. Tariffs, by contrast, have hit both size classes similarly on costs and prices, with the main difference being wider confidence swings among small firms; the note cites Boston Fed work linking trade-policy uncertainty to shakier investment and headcount plans among small importers. **Fiscal policy is the clearest offset — the 2025 tax bill's expensing and depreciation provisions point to stronger small business capex — while AI is the clearest longer-term threat, with low adoption suggesting small firms are poorly positioned to capture an AI productivity boost.** Notably, small firms in AI-exposed industries are not planning faster headcount cuts, unlike their larger peers — consistent with them not yet deploying the technology.

The note offers no trade idea; it is a contextual read on the sector, timed to the firm's small business summit.

subject: Global Markets Analyst: FX in 2035—Finding Fair and Getting There
summary:
# FX in 2035: [REDACTED] Sees the Dollar Working Off a 15% Overvaluation, With EM the Big Winner

**Theme:** New 10-year currency forecasts from mean-reverting fair-value estimates — where "fair" sits in 2035 and how currencies get there  
**Markets:** Global FX (developed-market and emerging-market currencies vs USD)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Kamakshya Trivedi, 27 October 2025

### Definitive impacts
- New 2035 point forecasts: EUR/USD at 1.21, USD/JPY at 100, GBP/USD at 1.24, USD/CNY at 5.17.
- The Dollar screens ~15% overvalued now on [REDACTED] fair value; the broad USD TWI is forecast to fall a further 6%–7% over the decade, weighted more toward Asia and EM than the Euro-centric move seen in 2025.
- Current undervaluation signals are largest in JPY, NOK, CNY and CLP; the most overvalued are CZK, GBP and MXN.
- Fair-value drift to 2035 pushes high-inflation-targeting currencies (INR, MXN, ZAR, BRL) weaker and lower-inflation currencies (CHF, CNY, other Asia) stronger; these trends mirror the last decade but are smaller in magnitude.
- Convergence assumptions: 20% per year to fair value for most pairs; a lower 10% per year for USD/CNY and USD/CZK, plus a bespoke path for USD/SGD, reflecting tighter FX management.
- Methodology change (now permanent in [REDACTED]): productivity is projected from GDP forecasts, UN working-age population (15–75) and 2015–2024 employment-ratio trends, replacing the prior regression approach; terms-of-trade sensitivities re-estimated over 2000–2024.
- Applying an inflation-target "slippage" adjustment lowers implied 10-year total returns for most high-carry currencies and cuts the return-vs-inflation R² from ~50% to ~30%.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] expects most forecast currencies to deliver positive total returns vs USD over 10 years, led by LatAm and high-carry names, consistent with harvesting long-term real carry and the documented tendency of markets to overprice EM drawdown risk.
- BRL, COP and ZAR offer the highest potential total returns, mostly from cumulated carry; for BRL and ZAR, [REDACTED] also sees scope for spot appreciation if growth and fiscal risks are addressed, though it flags an unsettled political backdrop.
- The Yen is seen making the largest move to spot on the forecasts, strengthening toward 100 as extraordinary easing (e.g. YCC) is gradually unwound; [REDACTED] argues a renewed "Abenomics" pivot under PM Takaichi would likely be muted given the unpopularity of inflation.
- CNY has a strong appreciation case given deep undervaluation and dominant export/trade-surplus performance, but realization hinges on Beijing relaxing tight FX management — which [REDACTED] does not expect near-term, while noting a decade is long.
- [REDACTED] sees no valuation case for the Euro after 2025's correction; it expects EUR/USD to trade sideways near 1.20, with a stronger move requiring conviction on structural European growth or capital-market outperformance.
- On the Dollar, the main upside risk is a fresh AI-led US productivity/exceptionalism boost; [REDACTED] expects AI to help US productivity but questions whether the gains stay US-confined and whether returns justify lofty tech valuations.
- [REDACTED]'s overriding message: over a 10-year horizon, structural forces most likely move FX toward better balance, and it pays to be imaginative about the trends that could drive markets.

### Backdrop
[REDACTED] has been [REDACTED]'s fair-value workhorse for 30 years. It assumes real exchange rates mean-revert over time — with a half-life of roughly three years, or about 20% convergence per year — while structural drivers (relative productivity via the Balassa-Samuelson effect, and terms of trade) shift the underlying trend. [REDACTED] positions this against the "random walk" view, citing academic support that such models beat it over long horizons. [REDACTED] dominates at long horizons, whereas the complementary [REDACTED] model is more useful at the 12-month cyclical horizon. Fair-value estimates carry wide confidence intervals and have shifted materially over the past decade, mostly on the inflation component, so the projected paths are expected to move over time.

### At issue
[REDACTED] is introducing formal long-term (2035) FX forecasts to sit alongside its economists' long-run projections and support structural investment decisions. The exercise runs in three steps: (1) extend [REDACTED] fair values 10 years forward using inflation forecasts, market-forward terms of trade, and a newly built productivity projection; (2) refresh estimates of how fast currencies converge to fair value; and (3) combine these with 12-month cyclical starting points, embedding 20% annual real convergence from 2027 onward plus currency-specific management adjustments. The note also introduces two methodological updates now baked into [REDACTED] — the new productivity forecast and re-estimated terms-of-trade sensitivities — and an illustrative "inflation slippage" scenario that phases historical central-bank target misses into the inflation path.

### Unpacked
The exercise is aimed at market participants who carry FX risk over very long horizons — multinationals, acquirers, long-term direct investors — for whom structural factors outweigh the cyclical noise that dominates shorter calls. **The entire result set hangs on one starting fact: the Dollar is judged about 15% overvalued today, so the broad direction is Dollar depreciation, front-loaded in the early years before the TWI "catches down."**

The engine behind fair value is relative inflation, productivity and terms of trade, all measured as differentials to the US. Inflation does most of the work: economies that tolerate higher inflation see their anchors drift weaker, while low-inflation economies appreciate. **US productivity strength partly offsets somewhat higher US inflation, which keeps fair value comparatively "pinned" for the Euro and Japan and concentrates the interesting moves in Asia and EM.**

Convergence is the second lever, and it is deliberately uneven. Free-floating, open, well-measured economies converge near the 20% rule of thumb; managed regimes converge slowly or not at all — hence the 10% rate imposed on CNY and CZK. **This is why the Renminbi story is framed as "turning a super tanker": the gravitational pull toward strength is real, but whether it plays out depends entirely on policy willingness to loosen management.**

The headline market takeaway is a clear positive relationship between projected 10-year returns and current inflation, putting LatAm and other high-carry names on top. **Two forces drive it — a risk-premium harvest on "riskier" high-carry currencies, and a gap between [REDACTED]'s modal inflation views and the higher steady-state inflation markets embed in forwards.** Box B tests the second by phasing historical target "slippage" into the forecasts; doing so pulls high-carry forecasts toward the forwards, trims their returns, and weakens the inflation-return fit — a caution that some of the EM upside reflects an inflation assumption markets may not share. Valuation, not just carry, explains the deviations: deeply undervalued CNY and Asian low-yielders (THB, TWD, PHP) screen better than carry alone implies, while GBP, HUF and ILS look expensive alongside the Dollar.

**The through-line is humility about the path and conviction about the direction:** fair values have moved a lot before and will again, the Dollar has defied gravity for a decade and could do so again on AI, but the base case is that structural forces slowly restore balance — with the Yen's normalization the largest single move, China the biggest policy-contingent question, and Brazil and South Africa the largest prizes if growth and fiscal risks are tamed.

subject: Global Week Ahead: October 27– November 02
summary:
# Global Week Ahead: Six Central Banks Meet, US Data Goes Dark in the Shutdown

**Theme:** Forecasts vs. consensus for the week's central-bank decisions and data releases  
**Markets:** Global macro (rates and activity)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jan Hatzius, 26 October 2025

### Landscape
- Six central banks meet — US, Japan, Euro Area, Canada, Colombia, Chile — with [REDACTED] forecasts matching consensus in every case.
- US: 3.875% expected (from 4.125% last), a cut in line with consensus.
- Canada: 2.25% expected (from 2.50%), a cut in line with consensus.
- Japan (0.5%), Euro Area (2.0%), Colombia (9.25%) and Chile (4.75%) all seen on hold at prior levels.
- Most US economic data releases are delayed until the government shutdown ends, thinning the week's US calendar.

### Drivers
- On the six policy decisions, [REDACTED] sits with consensus across the board — the week's rate story is convergence, not surprise, with the only moves being the US and Canada cuts.
- Where [REDACTED] diverges is in the data: it is above consensus on China NBS Mfg. PMI (50.0 vs. 49.6, last 49.8), calling a return to the expansion line versus a consensus still below it.
- [REDACTED] is below consensus on the US Employment Cost Index (0.8% QoQ vs. 0.9%), a modestly softer wage-cost read.

### Unpacked
The week's headline event is the cluster of central-bank meetings, but [REDACTED] carries no differentiated view on any of them — its forecasts equal consensus for the US, Japan, Euro Area, Canada, Colombia and Chile. **The two policy moves both point the same way: a US cut to 3.875% and a Canadian cut to 2.25%, with the other four banks held at existing levels.**

The genuinely out-of-consensus calls — those differing from consensus by at least one historical standard deviation — sit in the data, not the decisions. On the upside relative to consensus, [REDACTED] looks for a stronger US Goods Trade Balance (-78.0bn vs. -90.0bn), firmer Spain GDP (0.7% vs. 0.6%), a hotter Tokyo core CPI ex-fresh food and energy (2.8% vs. 2.6%, last 2.5%), and notably stronger Taiwan GDP (7.3% YoY vs. 6.0%). **The Tokyo inflation call is the one with policy relevance, pointing to underlying price pressure running above what the market expects into the Bank of Japan's hold.**

On the downside, [REDACTED] is below consensus on German HICP (2.0% vs. 2.2%, last 2.4%), consistent with continued disinflation in the Euro Area's largest economy. The remaining key global indicators — US GDP, Australia CPI, Euro Area Core HICP and GDP — are flagged as important but carry no out-of-consensus [REDACTED] view.

The note offers no trade idea; it is a forecast scorecard for the week's calendar. Its practical value this week is narrowed by the US shutdown, which pushes most US releases past the window.

subject: US Week Ahead: October 27 – November 2
summary:
# US Week Ahead: A Shutdown Data Blackout Meets an Expected Fed Cut

**Theme:** Government shutdown postpones the week's key releases as the FOMC is set to cut again  
**Markets:** US macro (activity, inflation, rates)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jan Hatzius, 26 October 2025

### Landscape
- Q3 GDP tracking estimate stands at +3.3% (qoq annualized), down from the +3.8% recorded in Q2, with domestic final sales tracked at +2.4%.
- The preliminary October Current Activity Indicator sits at +2.1%, up from +1.6% in September.
- The US MAP index of economic surprises reads +0.1, essentially neutral.
- Case-Shiller home prices are seen at -0.2% in August, a third soft monthly print after -0.1%.
- Conference Board consumer confidence is forecast at 93.0 for October, easing from 94.2 and just below the 93.4 consensus.
- Core PCE is running near 2.9% year-over-year (2.87% forecast for September), still above the Fed's 2% target.

### Drivers
- The government shutdown is the dominant force this week: durable goods (Mon), the advance goods trade balance (Wed), Q3 advance GDP (Thu) and core PCE (Fri) will almost certainly be postponed if it persists; official jobless claims are also at risk from Thursday, though preliminary state-level data should still be available.
- Monetary policy is easing: the FOMC is expected to cut 25bp to 3.75-4% on Wednesday, consistent with the September dot plot's baseline of three cuts this year, with no official data to justify deviating from support for the labor market.
- Q3 growth is being lifted mechanically by an imports rebound (-6.4% annualized vs. -29.3% in Q2) as tariff-frontloading distortions fade, alongside accelerating consumption (+3.1% vs. +2.5%).
- Residential investment remains a persistent drag, forecast at -8.6% annualized after -5.1% in Q2.
- Labor cost growth is cooling: the Q3 employment cost index is seen at +0.8%, holding the year-on-year rate at 3.6%, as slower wages offset a rebound in benefits.

### Risks
- Downside to visibility rather than to the baseline: the analyst notes the forecasts above are built on limited information and may change by the time reports are actually released.
- On rates, the analyst flags upside to the dovish read — no formal December guidance is expected, but if pressed, Chair Powell is likely comfortable pointing to the September dots, which imply a third cut in December.

### Unpacked
The week is defined less by what will be released than by what won't. **With the shutdown in effect, the flagship reports — durable goods, the goods trade balance, Q3 GDP and core PCE — are all likely to be postponed, and there are no Fed speakers because of the FOMC blackout.** The forecasts below are provided on the information available and are explicitly provisional.

On Monday's durable goods, orders are seen up 1.0% on a jump in commercial aircraft, while the ex-transportation and core capital goods measures are much softer (+0.2% and +0.1%).
