The softness ran through the composition: new business dropped 0.5pt to 53.5 and employment fell 0.4pt to 51.6. Pricing signals were mixed — input prices rose 2.2pt to 62.0 while output prices declined 1.9pt to 56.0.
- **Manufacturing pulled back more sharply from a multi-year high.** The manufacturing PMI fell 1.0pt to 52.0 (forecast 52.2, prior 53.0), down from its highest level since May 2022. Every key component weakened — output -3.2pt to 52.1, new orders -2.4pt to 50.9 (barely above the 50 expansion line), and employment -0.6pt to 52.6. Both price components fell, input -0.3pt to 65.8 and output -4.3pt to 56.5.
- **Tariff costs are getting harder to pass on.** S&P's own commentary framed the month as growth having slowed from its July peak, with companies pulling back on hiring in September. Tariffs were again cited as a driver of higher input costs in both sectors, but the number of firms able to raise selling prices to pass those costs to customers has fallen.

### Implications
- Momentum is cooling into late Q3, with hiring pulling back across both sectors — a softer signal on activity even as headline prints met expectations.
- Weaker pricing power on tariff-driven input costs points to a margin squeeze rather than fuller pass-through into consumer prices.

subject: Global Markets Daily: Why the Back-end of Corporate Spread Curves Keep Flattening (Ali)
summary:
# Why USD IG Long-End Spread Curves Keep Flattening — Technicals, Not a Credit Warning

**Theme:** Flat/inverted back-end IG spread curves reflect supply-demand technicals, not rising cycle risk  
**Markets:** US investment-grade corporate credit  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Shamshad Ali, 23 September 2025  

### Definitive impacts
- The USD IG 10s30s spread differential sits near its flattest level in over a decade, even as the Treasury 10s30s back end is near its steepest in five years.
- 13% of non-financial issuers and 40% of financial issuers now have 30-year bonds trading tight to (inside) their own 10-year bonds on spread, measured with issuer- and seniority-matched pairs.
- Long-dated supply has run at 17% of non-financial issuance this year, below the 21% historical average.
- Flatness has spread up the curve: issuer-matched non-financial 5s10s and 2s10s spread curves stand at 19bp and 39bp — around their flattest 5th percentile of the past 10 years.
- Individual fixed annuity sales have exceeded $75bn per quarter over the past year, feeding insurer demand concentrated at the 10-year point.
- M&A-related USD IG issuance has kept a stable tenor even as the weighted-average maturity of general issuance shortened by nearly five years.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] argues the flatness is a technical phenomenon, not a signal of more acute credit risk — strong long-end demand from insurers and pensions meets anemic 30-year supply, running contrary to standard risk-aversion pricing.
- [REDACTED] sees both the supply and demand technicals as durable: with the market already pricing considerable Fed easing, elevated yields and range-bound spreads should keep pushing back-end curves flatter.
- [REDACTED] views the supply channel — high incremental funding cost deterring 30-year issuance — as the strongest driver of the negative link between flatter rate curves and steeper credit curves.
- [REDACTED] is mixed on the "M&A to the rescue" thesis: historically M&A does not lean on the 30-year point more than other issuance, so the hurdle to large back-end supply stays high while all-in issuer yields make it prohibitive, though elevated upcoming M&A and the recent yield rally could improve duration issuance at the margin.

### Backdrop
Textbook theory holds that corporate spread term structures should slope upward on average, since investors demand more compensation for bearing default risk over longer maturities — the same logic that gives Treasury curves their average upward slope via term premium. Curves flatten or invert mainly when near-term default or growth risk rises sharply, as in downturns or severe risk-off episodes.

The 10s30s spread curve is normally uncorrelated with 10-year spread levels, so a steep back end offers no hedge against tight spreads. There is a typically negative relationship between yield curves and spread curves, more visible over the medium term, driven by the negative rates-spreads correlation and by the inverse link between steeper yield curves and long-dated issuance.

### At issue
This note documents and explains a divergence: the back end of USD IG corporate spread curves has materially flattened in 2025 — modestly inverted for many non-financial issuers — while the Treasury back end has steepened. Using issuer- and seniority-matched 10s/30s pairs to strip out index composition bias, [REDACTED] confirms the flattening holds for both financials and non-financials, then attributes it to technical supply and demand rather than credit-risk repricing, and extends the finding to the belly and front end of the curve.

### Unpacked
The starting question is whether flat and partly inverted long-end credit curves are credit investors flagging doubt about the durability of the cycle. **The answer is no — the shape is a technical artifact, produced by a persistent mismatch between who wants long duration and how little of it is being issued.** Measurement matters to this claim: broad indices mislead because many issuers with 10-year bonds have no 30-year bonds, so the analysis pairs matched bonds within the same capital structure to get a clean read on slope.

On supply, the incremental cost of extending to 30 years has held long-dated issuance below its historical share, removing the steepening pressure that heavy back-end supply would normally create. The natural catalyst for more long-end paper is large cash-funded M&A, but the data undercut that hope: **M&A issuance does not tilt toward the 30-year point more than ordinary issuance, even though its tenor has stayed unusually stable while general issuance shortened its maturity by almost five years.** So long as all-in issuer curves make the 30-year point prohibitively expensive, the supply hurdle remains high.

On demand, corporate long ends have avoided the headwinds hitting long-end sovereigns. Insurers and pensions keep buying long corporate duration despite its thinner spread pickup, and record fixed-annuity sales channel that bid especially into the 10-year, which matches their fixed liabilities. **The combined effect of tight spreads, shorter issuance and steady structural demand has flattened not just the back end but the 5s10s and 2s10s curves too, pushing much of the USD IG complex to decade-flat levels.**

Looking forward, the piece expects the flatness to persist, with only marginal relief possible from a heavier M&A calendar and the recent rally in yields. The report is a Global Markets Daily and carries a broad cross-asset trade-idea list, but it offers no explicit trade tied to this credit-curve analysis beyond the relative-value framing of 10s versus 30s.

subject: US Economics Analyst: The Outlook for Productivity and Potential GDP Growth: Tech Leads the Way (Abecasis)
summary:
# US Potential Growth Reset Higher: Tech-Led Productivity, Even as Immigration Fades

**Theme:** Why potential GDP has risen since 2019 and where it heads through the early 2030s, with tech/AI-led productivity offsetting slower labor-force growth  
**Markets:** US growth and productivity  
**Source:** [REDACTED] (Manuel Abecasis), 22 September 2025  

### Definitive impacts
- Potential GDP growth is estimated at ~2.4% since the pandemic, up from ~1.8% pre-pandemic — driven by both stronger productivity and higher immigration-led labor-force growth.
- After correcting for measurement issues, economywide labor productivity grew ~1.5% last year (vs. 1.0% currently published) and ~1.6% over five years (vs. 1.7% published).
- Three measurement adjustments underlie the revision: pending BLS payroll benchmark revisions (raise productivity), unmeasured AI-related capex of ~0.5% of GDP since 2022, and understated hours worked (productivity data imply hours ~2% below pre-pandemic, largely a CPS proxy-response distortion).
- Labor-force growth peaked at nearly a 1pp boost in 2023 from the 2022–2024 immigration surge; its contribution to potential growth averaged 0.8pp since 2019 (vs. 0.6pp in 2007–2019).
- Nonfarm business productivity grew 2% annually over five years (vs. ~1.5% pre-pandemic), mostly from higher TFP; nonfinancial corporate productivity was stronger at 2.5%.
- Tech and related high-value services (scientific research, engineering, consulting) contributed ~0.3–0.4pp of the productivity acceleration versus pre-pandemic pace, concentrated in within-industry gains rather than cross-industry reallocation.
- Post-pandemic productivity gains are concentrated in services and among larger firms, with widening dispersion between fastest- and slowest-growing firms; the US–G10 productivity gap has widened further since 2019.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] expects labor-force growth's contribution to potential GDP to fall to ~0.3pp over coming years, on tighter immigration policy and aging, partly offset by rising participation among older workers.
- [REDACTED] expects economywide productivity growth to average ~1.7% through 2029 and ~1.9% in the early 2030s as AI adoption raises capital per worker and efficiency.
- [REDACTED] forecasts potential GDP growth of ~2.1% in 2025–2029, accelerating to ~2.3% in the early 2030s as AI lifts productivity further.
- [REDACTED] attributes the tech-sector productivity outperformance at least partly to AI, while calling it premature to ascribe the full acceleration to AI.
- [REDACTED] sees AI adding ~0.4% to GDP over the next few years and ~1½% cumulatively long term, expecting an investment-led boost first (as in the 1990s), then a later TFP gain.
- [REDACTED] estimates tariffs, deregulation and fiscal incentives net to a ~0.1pp/year drag on productivity over five years — smaller than initially feared because foreign retaliation has been limited and capex incentives offset part of the drag.
- [REDACTED] flags two-sided risks: upside from faster AI adoption or a path to AGI; downside from weaker AI capex, sharper population slowdown, or slower technological progress.

### Backdrop
Potential growth is the sum of labor-force growth and labor-productivity growth. Before the pandemic, labor-force growth was on a gradual decline as fertility fell, life expectancy rose, and an aging population lowered average participation. Productivity is usually tracked through nonfarm business output per hour because it is easier to measure; economywide productivity runs about 20% lower, mainly because government-sector productivity is assumed to be zero. Productivity itself decomposes into capital deepening, labor quality, and total factor productivity (TFP), the last treated as the contribution of technological innovation.

### At issue
This is a forecasting exercise, not a single event: [REDACTED] assesses the outlook for US productivity and potential GDP, reworking the current data and projecting through the early 2030s. It corrects the published productivity statistics for three distortions — the coming BLS payroll benchmark revision (through March 2025, partly reflecting exclusion of unauthorized immigrants from UI records), AI capex the BEA books as intermediate inputs rather than investment, and CPS hours understated by proxy responders — and it decomposes the post-pandemic productivity gain by sector, firm size, and country to locate its source.

### Unpacked
The exercise starts from a puzzle in the official numbers: the US economy looks like it has shifted to a higher potential growth rate since 2019, but the productivity statistics are noisy enough that the true pace is unclear. **Cleaning up three measurement problems lifts last year's productivity read from 1.0% to about 1.5%, which matters because it changes whether the recent slowdown is real or an artifact of mismeasured hours and uncounted AI investment.**

The two engines of potential growth are moving in opposite directions. Immigration did most of the work in 2022–2024, but its boost was never one-for-one with headcount because new arrivals — especially unauthorized workers — cluster in lower-productivity, below-average-wage jobs. **With immigration set to slow under tighter policy, the labor-force contribution is expected to collapse from 0.8pp to about 0.3pp, so the whole case for sustained potential growth now rests on productivity.**

On that front, the analysis traces the gains to a specific place rather than a broad rebound. The acceleration is within-industry, not reallocation across sectors; it sits in services, in tech and adjacent high-value professional fields, and it is stronger among larger firms — the same "superstar firm" dynamic seen last cycle. **The tell is the tech sector holding fast real-output growth while employment growth slows sharply, a pattern consistent with an early AI effect even if it is too soon to attribute the whole move to AI.** This same concentration in information and professional services explains why the US keeps pulling away from other G10 economies.

Looking forward, the mechanism is expected to run in the familiar 1990s sequence: capital per worker rises first — helped by AI investment and a temporary bump in frictional unemployment as adoption displaces some workers — and TFP gains arrive later. **Netting AI's lift against a modest ~0.1pp drag from tariffs and related policy, potential GDP is projected around 2.1% now and 2.3% in the early 2030s, with the risks genuinely two-sided rather than skewed.** The note offers no trade idea; it is a macro framework piece.

subject: Global Week Ahead: September 22-28
summary:
# Central Banks in Focus: Sweden the Lone Dovish Call in a Broadly In-Line Week

**Theme:** Week-ahead forecast map — where [REDACTED] sits versus consensus

**Source:** [REDACTED], Jan Hatzius, 21 September 2025

### Landscape

- Key data releases due: US PCE and durable goods, European PMIs, and Australian CPI.
- [REDACTED] holds only one out-of-consensus call above the one-standard-deviation threshold this week — Sweden's rate decision; all other views are within normal ranges.

### Drivers
- **Sweden:** [REDACTED] looks for a cut to 1.75%, versus consensus and the prior rate both at 2.0% — the week's single notably dovish call.
- **Switzerland:** [REDACTED] and consensus align at 0.0% (unchanged).

- **Inflation:** [REDACTED] is marginally above consensus on Australia CPI (3.0% yoy vs 2.9%, up from 2.8%).

### Unpacked
**The only meaningful gap between [REDACTED] and the market this week is Sweden, where [REDACTED] expects a 25bp cut to 1.75% against a consensus for no change at 2.0%.** The other four decisions — Switzerland held at zero, Mexico cutting to 7.5%, Hungary at 6.5%, and the Czech Republic at 3.5% — carry no daylight between the [REDACTED] forecast and consensus.

On the data side, the divergences are small and do not clear the one-standard-deviation bar [REDACTED] uses to flag a genuinely out-of-consensus view. [REDACTED] reads the European activity picture slightly softer than consensus, with both the German and UK composite PMIs edging lower, and looks for a sharper drop in US durable goods orders than the market. The one point where [REDACTED] sits above consensus is Australian CPI, seen ticking up to 3.0% year on year.

**[REDACTED] explicitly states it holds no notably out-of-consensus forecasts for any other indicator this week** — the report is a scoreboard of where its calls line up with the market rather than a set of contrarian bets.

subject: US Week Ahead: September 22 – September 28
summary:
# US Week Ahead: Core PCE and Durable Goods Headline a Fed-Heavy Calendar

**Theme:** A light data week dominated by Fed speakers, with core PCE (Fri) and durable goods (Thu) the only major releases  
**Markets:** US inflation, activity and Fed policy  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jan Hatzius, 21 September 2025  

### Estimates

- **Core PCE +0.21% m/m** in August (consensus +0.2%, last +0.3%), taking the **y/y rate to +2.92%** (consensus +2.9%, last +2.9%).
- **Headline PCE +0.25% m/m** in August (consensus +0.3%, last +0.2%), or **+2.72% y/y** (consensus +2.7%, last +2.6%).
- **Personal income +0.4%** and **personal spending +0.4%** in August (income consensus +0.3%; spending consensus +0.5%, last +0.5%).
- **Durable goods orders -1.5% m/m** in August preliminary (consensus -0.3%, last -2.8%), on lower commercial aircraft orders.
- **Durable goods ex-transportation flat**, **core capital goods orders flat** (consensus -0.1%, last +1.1%), **core capital goods shipments +0.3%** (consensus +0.2%).
- **Q2 GDP third release +3.4% q/q ann.** (consensus +3.3%, last +3.3%), a 0.1pp upward revision; **personal consumption revised to +1.9%** (from +1.6%). Coincides with the 2025 annual update to the National Economic Accounts.
- **Advance goods trade balance -$92.0bn** in August (consensus -$96.0bn, last -$102.8bn), on lower gold and Southeast Asian imports.
- **Initial jobless claims 230k** (consensus 235k, last 231k); continuing claims consensus 1,938k.
- **New home sales -1.5%** (consensus -0.3%); **existing home sales -2.5%** (consensus -1.3%, last +2.0%).
- **S&P Global September flash PMIs:** manufacturing 51.7 (last 53.0), services 53.9 (last 54.5).
- **UMich consumer sentiment 55.0** final (consensus 55.4); **5-10yr inflation expectations 3.8%** (last 3.9%).

### Outlook

- The forecast frames the September FOMC cut as a **"risk management cut,"** in Powell's words, against a labour market that is softening but that the Fed does not want to soften further.
- Fed commentary is **split on the balance of risks:** Miran and Musalem stress downside labour-market risks and policy sitting well above neutral, while Schmid and Bostic flag sticky services inflation and tariff pass-through as reasons for caution on further easing.
- Q3 activity tracking is steady: **GDP tracking +2.2% q/q ann.**, domestic final sales +1.3%, the preliminary September Current Activity Indicator at +2.1%, and the US MAP surprise index at +0.3.

### Unpacked

The week carries little top-tier data, so the read comes mostly from Friday's PCE report and a dense schedule of Fed appearances, headlined by Powell on Tuesday and Williams on Monday. **The central inflation call is benign at the margin — core PCE at +0.21% m/m — but the year-over-year rate edges up to +2.92%, keeping core inflation stuck near 3% rather than converging toward target.** Personal income and spending are both seen holding at +0.4%, consistent with a consumer that is cooling gradually rather than stalling.

Thursday's durable goods report looks weak on the headline (-1.5%) but the softness is concentrated in commercial aircraft; the ex-transportation and core capital goods measures are essentially flat, with the forecast noting possible payback after an outsized prior-month jump against improving manufacturing-survey orders components. **Stripping out the aircraft noise, the underlying capex signal is steady rather than deteriorating.** The same day brings the third Q2 GDP release, revised up to +3.4% on stronger consumption, investment and net exports, alongside the annual National Economic Accounts update that folds in more complete source data and methodological changes — a reason to watch for revisions beyond the headline.

**The real content this week is the Fed chorus, and it is audibly divided on how much further to cut.** On the dovish side, Miran argues policy is "quite restrictive" and warns the longer it stays there the greater the risk of missing on employment, while Musalem sees downside labour-market risks rising. On the cautious side, Schmid worries about cutting into an inflation "mentality" running closer to 3% than 2%, and Bostic expects tariff effects on consumer prices to build over months rather than fade. Powell's own framing — a softening labour market the Fed does not want to soften further, met with a risk-management cut — sits between the two camps.

Looking ahead, the tension the reader should track is between a labour market that most officials agree is losing momentum and inflation that is not yet clearly on a path to target, with tariff pass-through the wild card that could keep services prices firm. The activity trackers — GDP around +2.2%, CAI at +2.1%, surprises modestly positive — describe an economy still growing near trend, which gives the Fed room to move gradually rather than urgently.

subject: Weekly Fund Flows: Slower Foreign Demand for US Equities
summary:
# Foreign Bid for US Equities Cools as Domestic Buyers Drive the Rally

**Theme:** Domestic-led US equity inflows; softening foreign demand  
**Markets:** Global equity and fixed income fund flows  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Isabella Rosenberg, 19 September 2025  

### Landscape
- US equity funds saw a sharp domestic-buyer swing to +$68bn, up from -$10bn the prior week.
- Global fixed income inflows slowed slightly to +$15bn from +$17bn, staying positive.
- Money market fund assets fell by $5bn on the week.
- Foreign net purchases of US equities continued but at a slower pace than in prior weeks.
- Euro area equity inflows remained positive but have turned more subdued in recent weeks.

### Drivers
- Domestic demand is the dominant force behind US equity inflows, more than reversing the prior week's outflow.
- Foreign appetite for US equities is fading at the margin — still net positive, but decelerating, with the Euro area bid softening (the report's Chart of the Week).
- Within equities, cyclicals outpaced defensives, and industrials, financials and telecom led sector inflows while consumer goods and technology saw the largest outflows.
- In EM, flows concentrated into mainland China and global EM benchmark funds; Taiwan saw outflows driven by local investors.
- In fixed income, agg-type funds led, followed by high yield and government bonds; EM hard currency bonds drew inflows while local currency bonds saw outflows.
- Cross-border FX flows stayed firm, with GBP the strongest net inflow in G10.

### Unpacked
**The headline is a rotation in who is buying US equities, not whether they are being bought.** Domestic investors swung hard into US stocks, from a small net sale to +$68bn, while foreign investors kept buying but at a slower clip. The report frames the cooling foreign bid — and specifically a more subdued Euro area contribution — as the development worth tracking, singling it out in its Chart of the Week.

**Beneath the strong equity headline, sector and style flows were mixed rather than uniformly risk-on.** Cyclicals drew more than defensives, and the sector leaders were industrials, financials and telecom, while consumer goods and technology saw the largest outflows. The pattern points to selective positioning rather than a broad chase.

**In G10 outside the US, direction diverged: the UK saw larger equity outflows while the Euro area took in moderate inflows.** EM flows were narrow, concentrated in mainland China and global EM benchmark funds, with Taiwan an outflow driven by local investors.

**Fixed income held up but lost a little momentum.** Inflows eased to +$15bn, led by agg-type funds ahead of high yield and government bonds. The EM split — hard currency bonds in, local currency bonds out — echoes the more cautious tone, while money market assets dipped $5bn. On the currency side, cross-border FX flows stayed firm and GBP led G10 inflows.

The note carries no explicit trade idea; it is a flows scoreboard rather than a positioning call.

subject: Global Rates Trader: September Deja Vu
summary:
# September Déjà Vu: A First Fed Cut That Markets Read Hawkishly, Again

**Theme:** Risk-management easing across G10 — belly cheapening, inflation longs, and divergent central-bank paths  
**Markets:** Global rates (US, Canada, Euro area, UK, Scandinavia, Japan)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], George Cole, 19 September 2025

### Landscape
- The Fed delivered its first 25bp cut of the expected series; a dovish dot shift and softer statement language sparked only a short-lived rally before longer forwards sold off, echoing September 2024.
- US funding pressure set at year-to-date highs, with SOFR and TGCR at or just above the top of the target band around mid-month settlements and corporate tax payments, but with scant SRF uptake and a quick Tuesday reversal.
- The BoC cut 25bp to leave one more move expected to a 2.25% terminal rate; CORRA has fixed persistently above target since month-start.
- The ECB is on hold with Euro-area inflation at target; German Q4 issuance was revised up €15bn (following +€19bn for Q3), ~€5bn of it in Bills.
- The BoE held Bank Rate; markets price the first full cut by April, and [REDACTED] pushed its next-cut call to February.
- Norges Bank cut to 4.0% but signalled a slower path; [REDACTED] lifted its terminal forecast to 3.25% and dropped its 2025 cut call. The Riksbank is expected to deliver a final cut next week.
- The BOJ held, but two hike dissents plus small ETF sales pushed October-hike pricing to roughly 50/50 (14bp vs 8.5bp pre-meeting).

### Drivers
- **US growth risk-management** is the pivot: with the Fed more attentive to labour-market downside and [REDACTED] baselining firmer 2026 growth, meaningful yield richening likely needs actual growth weakness — the first cut in a series has historically capped the rally in long forwards.
- **Fed easing is compressing rates vol** across the surface, leaving valuations cheap to macro models; the benign baseline favours carry-friendly gamma-selling with long-vega hedges rather than outright long-vol.
- **US liquidity drainage** is making secured funding increasingly sensitive to reserve shifts — now at a level beyond which effective fed funds has historically started ticking up in the range; the quarter-end turn and October funding will decide whether QT ends at the next meeting.
- **German fiscal easing** is the main European catalyst: supply grinds — not spikes — higher, so Bund spread tightening slows, and spending evidence should only start accruing in Q4.
- **French political risk** keeps OATs choppy, with resistance to pension and wealth-tax compromise; [REDACTED] still sees an eventual resolution and a 70bp year-end 10y OAT-Bund spread.
- **BoJ cycle longevity**, not the next hike's timing, is the durable source of long-end risk-premium relief; clearer wage momentum into year-end is the signal to watch.

### Risks
- **Downside (US):** a sharper labour-market slowdown could force 50bp cuts and trigger a vol spike, given how cheap implied vol now sits — though the analyst notes valuation alone has been an unreliable vol-selling predictor.
- **Upside (US funding):** effective fed funds becoming sensitive to liquidity and drifting up in the range is flagged as an increasingly live risk; more acute strains may be needed before the Fed shifts on QT.
- **Downside (France):** fresh parliamentary elections remain a key risk; the analyst judges an OAT move to ~85–90bp (matching 2024 stress episodes) as too pessimistic given how much idiosyncratic risk is already priced.
- **EUR vol:** the analyst sees the hurdle as low for realised vol to outperform what is priced on short expiries, with implied now below realised.
- **Japan:** the analyst views the pull-forward in October-hike pricing as somewhat overdone given fiscal, tariff and wage-cycle uncertainty before year-end.

### Unpacked
The central US read is a rerun of last year: a dovish Fed reduced perceived downside risks further out the curve, so longer forwards backed up even as the front end got its cut. **The valuation case for a deeper rally without fresh fundamental weakness is weak, and a Fed leaning against near-term labour downside alongside firmer 2026 growth is instead read as supportive for traded inflation.** On a beta-weighted basis the 5y5y point looks cheap to nominals, so the note adds a long in 5y5y inflation swaps against a 0.2x long in 5y5y nominal swaps (entry 1.66, target 1.8, stop 1.6).

On the belly, the preference is to fade richness selectively rather than aggressively. **Resolution of labour-market uncertainty — whether via front-loaded cuts or the fading of downside risk embedded in terminal pricing — can see the belly underperform, and the carry-to-vol profile favours expressing it forward.** The note recommends paying the belly on the 1y-forward 2s5s30s fly (entry -40bp, target -20bp, stop -50bp), while keeping low-strike 2s5s bull-steepening exposure as insurance against faster cuts.

US money markets drew attention without real stress: funding costs pressed the top of the band but SRF uptake stayed scant and pressure reversed quickly, which likely leaves officials comfortable for now. **This raises the risk to the standing call that the Fed ends QT at its next meeting — more durable strains, rates setting further outside the range or heavier SRF use, may be needed to force the shift.** In Canada, benign inflation cemented the BoC cut, and persistently firm CORRA fixings point to liquidity operations — overnight and term repo first, then a gradual ramp in bill purchases later in Q4 — to steady system liquidity ahead of late-2025 and early-2026 maturities.

In Europe, German fiscal expansion is framed as slow but persistent, and the market is seen as underpricing its eventual macro impact; the 10y Bund forecast stays at 3.0% for end-2025, with rising net supply and ECB QT slowing the pace of spread tightening. **OAT spreads are expected to hold their range — 70bp at year-end — because the hurdle for deficit or growth expectations to deteriorate against already-low market pricing is high.** EUR vol is judged to have fallen about as far as fundamentals justify at the front, while long-end vol stays elevated on global long-end uncertainty and Dutch pension reform, and should keep trading directionally with the curve.

In the UK, the BoE's wait-and-see stance pushed the next expected cut to February, but the case for lower terminal rates after a contractionary autumn budget keeps the note long 2s5s Gilt steepeners; the 10y Gilt forecast is nudged up 20bp to 4.4% for year-end. **The slower QT pace and skew away from long-end active sales gave no marginal lift to the long end — subsiding inflation risk is seen as the key to long-Gilt outperformance.** Scandi divergence is sharpening: Norges Bank turned hawkish while the Riksbank is expected to cut again, and the note flags scope for a further 10-15bp of NOK-vs-SEK 1y1y widening tactically, with balanced risk-reward beyond that as the spread sits near historical wides.

In Japan, the hawkish tilt came from two hike dissents and unexpected ETF sales, but the reprice toward a coin-flip October hike is seen as premature given fiscal, tariff and wage uncertainty before year-end. **The note recommends Oct25/Jan26 OIS steepeners for their asymmetry (entry 10.8bp, target 23bp, stop 5bp), since a pause keeps January hike pricing high while an October hike would still leave some pricing further out.** Belly forwards cheapened and the long end saw relief, consistent with the view that conviction on the hiking cycle's longevity — reinforced by clearer wage momentum into year-end — is the more powerful driver of risk-premium relief.

subject: Global FX Trader: Range Break Head Fake
summary:
# Dollar's Risk Relationship Shifts as the Fed Turns Toward Neutral

**Theme:** A "risk-management" Fed cut leaves USD soft, with EUR emerging as the new risk-off substitute  
**Markets:** Global FX  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Kamakshya Trivedi, 19 September 2025

### Landscape
- USD ends the week roughly flat after the selloff stalled on Powell's "risk-management cut" framing, and remains firmly in the trough of the "smile" on relative US growth.
- USD/CNY spot at its strongest levels of the year, converging down to a fix that stalled in September after a rapid August move.
- USD/JPY slightly higher on the week despite briefly breaking below 146 on Tuesday for the first time since late July.
- USD/BRL below 5.40 — a level last seen in mid-2024 — with the Real down nearly 15% year-to-date.
- Within CEE, HUF and CZK have appreciated versus the Euro and traded through the 3-month forecasts, while EUR/PLN stays range-bound.
- Norges Bank delivered a 25bp cut with hawkish guidance; NOK lagged the rest of the European complex over the week.

### Drivers
- The Fed's shift toward employment as its primary mandate concern keeps downward pressure on USD versus "good carry" names (BRL, ZAR, HUF, MXN); direction now hinges on slack data, with the baseline a further modest labor-market loosening.
- Lower US policy rates change hedging costs and are expected to catalyze a new leg of diversifying and FX-hedging flows on existing Dollar assets, ahead of annual portfolio reviews.
- The Dollar's relationship to risk has shifted: EUR now acts as the next-best risk-off substitute after CHF and JPY, especially when risk-off is US-policy-driven — evidenced by Tuesday's price action and USD weakness despite better relative US equity returns.
- China's external sector stays resilient (exports +5.9% over eight months, trade surplus seen topping USD 1trn in 2025) even as domestic activity and property weaken; deep CNY undervaluation supports gradual strengthening.
- BRL total returns underpinned by BCB's "resolute hawkishness" — restrictive policy for "a very prolonged period" — alongside high real rates.
- CEE appreciation supported by central bank hawkishness (CNB, MNB on hold) and a stronger Euro backdrop, though that hawkishness is largely priced in.

### Risks
- Upside USD risk: investors are increasingly focused on a potential US reacceleration, which runs against the baseline of continued labor-market softening.
- Downside JPY (upside USD/JPY): tactical risk into the October 4 LDP election — if Takaichi, who favors a consumption tax cut and fiscal easing, gains ground, markets may reprice fiscal sustainability worries.
- HUF vulnerability: heavy carry-driven positioning and pre-election inflows leave the Forint exposed to political noise ahead of the 2026 vote.
- NOK downside asymmetry: the analyst notes NOK reliably depreciates versus EUR on sharp equity drawdowns while gains on equity upside are more mixed, and is asymmetrically exposed to lower oil — making the EUR/NOK drift-lower base case more finely balanced.
- The risk skew on USD is tilted toward continued depreciation under the baseline, with reacceleration the main two-sided counter.

### Unpacked
The framing note is that the Dollar's soft tone is not really about this week's cut, which markets had already discounted after the early-August payrolls report. **[REDACTED] reads the FOMC communication as confirming that employment risk now drives policy, which removes the basis for the Dollar's prior overvaluation and keeps it in the trough of the growth "smile."** The delivery of cuts matters less for its immediate rate impact than for what it does to hedging economics and to the signal longer-term investors and policymakers take from an actual rate change — both pointing toward more hedging of existing Dollar exposure into the annual portfolio-review window.

The more structural observation is a change in how the Dollar trades around risk. Tuesday looked like a classic negative growth shock — CHF and JPY up, AUD and NZD down — except the US currency clusters underperformed rather than led. **EUR was the second-best performer on the day, suggesting it is now the preferred risk-off substitute after CHF and JPY, particularly when the stress originates in US policy.** This is not a claim that EUR has become a safe haven — it remains a more open cyclical economy and has tracked the [REDACTED] models — but the marginal preference for holding Dollars, especially among European investors, has fallen, and USD has weakened even as relative US equity returns improved.

On China, the picture stays bifurcated: soft August domestic and property data against a resilient external sector. The forecasts roll forward but hold the year-end USD/CNY target at 7.00 (in 3m), with a push toward 6.90 in 6m and 12m, supported by deep undervaluation and an extending US-China détente after the Trump-Xi call and a possible APEC meeting.

Japan is a near-term caution despite a constructive medium-term view. **Recent JPY price action has tracked fundamentals closely, and the notable absence of a political risk premium after Ishiba's resignation leaves scope for tactical USD/JPY upside into the October 4 election.** The preference is therefore to express Dollar shorts elsewhere — EM carry and cyclicals like SEK, NOK and AUD — and to fade any USD/JPY strength via options once the event risk passes, since lower hedging costs, CNY appreciation and elevated recession risk still favor a stronger Yen.

Brazil is presented as having room to run. Most of the 15% YTD move is explained by the cyclical fair-value model, with only ~3% outperformance versus a 10%+ underperformance in 2024 — implying a remaining valuation buffer. **High real rates from a hawkish BCB, even paired with loose fiscal policy, are expected to keep supporting BRL total returns toward the 3-month forecast of 5.20**, an equilibrium acknowledged as unsustainable long term but supportive for now.

Within CEE, the earlier CZK-ahead, HUF-catch-up, PLN-behind ranking has played out. With CNB and MNB hawkishness now priced, monetary policy limits both downside and upside; CZK skews to further gains on higher EUR/USD and German growth outperformance given supply-chain links, while HUF's outperformance rests on a less demanding valuation but carries positioning and election risk. Forecasts roll to EUR/CZK 24.20/24.00/23.90 and EUR/HUF 390/385/380 over 3/6/12 months.

Sterling stays a funder against European peers even though the drivers have changed. **[REDACTED]'s economists dropped the November BoE cut call on sticky inflation and hawkish signals, so UK policy is no longer seen as the key source of GBP underperformance — but labour-market vulnerability, Autumn-budget consolidation, cyclical risk and a poor structural valuation still point to a gradual EUR/GBP drift higher.** Norway rounds out the note: the hawkish-tilted cut gave NOK a small bullish impulse, but recent decoupling from rate differentials, oil softness and the Krone's equity-drawdown asymmetry — set against the Euro's new safe-haven quality — leave the EUR/NOK lower base case more finely balanced.

subject: European Credit Brief: Week ending September 19, 2025
summary:
# European HY Dispersion Persists as Spreads Hit Records; M&A and Issuance Stay Subdued

**Theme:** Decompression within record-tight credit — quality dispersion, LME-driven defaults, and thin deal flow  
**Markets:** European corporate credit (EUR IG & HY)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Sara Grut, 19 September 2025  

### Landscape
- The HY/IG average spread ratio sits around the 82nd percentile of its post-Covid range, near the high end despite record-tight absolute spreads (Exhibit 1).
- The median HY/IG spread ratio sits near the low end of the same post-Covid range, and the widening gap versus the average reflects elevated HY dispersion against still-low IG dispersion (Exhibits 1–2).
- The 12-month issuer-weighted default rate stands at 3.74% in EUR HY and 1.9% in leveraged loans; excluding LMEs, both fall sharply to 1% and 0.6% (Exhibits 3–4).
- The value-weighted HY default rate reached a record 8.62%, a record gap versus the issuer-weighted rate, driven by Altice France (€7.5bn, June) and Thames Water Utilities (€5.1bn, February).
- European M&A volumes are tracking roughly in line with last year and well below the 2020–2022 jumbo-deal average, in contrast to the US (Exhibit 5).
- M&A-related EUR IG issuance is at the low end of its historical range at €6.6bn year to date, just 1% of total gross supply (Exhibit 6).
- The issuer-matched EUR IG non-financial 5s10s curve has steepened to roughly 25bp this year even as index spreads tightened (Exhibit 7).
- EUR IG funds saw a $10mn outflow this week, the first since mid-April, against a ~$2bn weekly inflow average since then; EUR HY took in $90mn, below its ~$500mn weekly average (Exhibit 9).

### Drivers
- Lower-quality issuers keep HY dispersion elevated through a mix of higher refunding costs, tariff headwinds, and macro uncertainty; the analyst expects this to persist.
- Liability management exercises now make up a record share of restructurings, inflating headline default rates well above the "clean" ex-LME rate; the phenomenon mirrors the USD market.
- Weak M&A and elevated funding costs are suppressing debt-funded deals, keeping M&A-related IG supply minimal; cash and alternative financing are expected to dominate.
- Duration extension within EUR IG has drawn investors wary of the macro outlook and reluctant to move down in quality, steepening the 5s10s curve even as spreads tighten.
- Flows turned pro-risk this week — inflows to EUR HY and equities, outflows from money markets — broadly mirroring the US (Exhibit 10).

### Risks
- Downside: the analyst remains cautious on EUR CCCs as a group given elevated idiosyncratic risk, and reiterates a 4% year-end forecast for the 12-month issuer-weighted default rate.
- Downside to the constructive growth call: the weak European deal tape challenges the view that higher government spending and stronger growth will feed corporate investment; the analyst notes a more favorable operating environment is a prerequisite.

### Unpacked
The report frames a market where record-tight spreads coexist with unusually wide internal dispersion in high yield. **The average HY/IG ratio near its post-Covid high, set against a median near the low, is the signature of a two-track market — most issuers priced calmly while a distressed tail drags the average.** IG shows no comparable split, and the expectation is that HY dispersion holds as weaker names absorb refunding, tariff, and macro pressure.

**The default picture is almost entirely a story of liability management exercises and a few large capital structures, not broad-based deterioration.** Strip out LMEs and default rates collapse toward 1% and below, while Altice France and Thames Water alone push the value-weighted rate to a record 8.62% — a gap that says more about deal size than systemic stress. The caution on CCCs and the 4% year-end default forecast follow from this idiosyncratic, rather than cyclical, read.

**On M&A, the European tape is underwhelming and directly undercuts the thesis that fiscal expansion and better growth would lift corporate investment.** Volumes merely match a soft prior year, jumbo deals lag the 2020–2022 norm, and M&A-linked IG supply at €6.6bn is a rounding error in gross issuance. With funding costs high, any pickup is expected to lean on cash and alternative financing rather than new debt.

**The duration trade within IG is presented as a yield play, not a spread hedge.** The 5s10s steepening to ~25bp alongside tighter index spreads makes curve extension appealing for those avoiding lower quality, but the low correlation between 5s10s and the index (Exhibit 8) means it offers weak protection in a broad selloff. With a constructive European growth view and an expectation of Bund curve steepening, the stated preference is to stay neutral duration versus the index.

**The single-week IG outflow is explicitly downplayed as noise rather than a turn.** It is the first since mid-April, but EUR IG remains on track for a record annual inflow pace; the base case is a slower but still-positive run rate, consistent with the week's pro-risk flow pattern.

subject: Global Markets Daily: Hedging Dollar Assets—What We Know and What We Think (Cahill/Kanter)
summary:
# Dollar Hedging Has Turned, But the Shift Is Small — and It's a Symptom, Not the Cause

**Theme:** Pension-fund FX hedge ratios as a read on US Dollar appetite  
**Markets:** US Dollar / global FX  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Michael Cahill, 19 September 2025  

### Landscape
- Danish Insurance & Pension Funds cut unhedged Dollar exposure from a February peak of 37% to 29.6% in July, just above their 2015–2020 average, with the July print ticking up slightly from recent lows.
- Finnish funds lowered their open currency position from an average of 30.3% to 25.6% over H1 2025, roughly halfway back to their long-run average.
- Sweden's AP1 cut open exposure from 23.6% to 15.5% and was the only AP fund to explicitly report more hedging; AP2, AP3 and AP4 all reported higher currency exposure.
- Australia's Superannuation funds, whose hedge ratio has fallen in recent years, ticked up in Q2 to a little above 30%.
- Canadian funds trimmed USD: CPP took net USD exposure from 63% to 61% (Q1→Q2), CDPQ from 22% to 21%, while OTPP cut USD by ~CAD 51bn and raised EUR/CHF exposure.
- The Dollar entered 2025 with allocations near highs and hedge ratios near lows; both have cooled somewhat.

### Drivers
- FX hedging is turning modestly higher across reporting funds, with the biggest adjustments concentrated in late Q1 and early Q2; the move has since stalled, with Danish and Finnish exposure stabilizing and Denmark's July reading nudging back up.
- The shift is being driven partly by genuine hedging decisions and partly by regional reallocation out of Dollar assets — [REDACTED] reads Sweden AP2's rising exposure as a rotation out of (fully hedged) US assets into other regions, not fresh USD bulls.
- The Dollar's changing correlation with risk is the structural force: if USD exposure now amplifies rather than dampens portfolio variance, allocators have an ongoing reason to keep hedging, which [REDACTED] expects to persist into next year.

### Risks
- The report frames these hedging flows as a headwind to the Dollar at most, not a decisive driver; [REDACTED] judges the direct price impact of the transactions themselves to be relatively limited.
- Interpretation risk runs in both directions: reported hedge ratios can move for reasons unrelated to USD views — currency mix, asset-allocation drift into equities, EM/DM country mix, and snapshot timing — so the topline figures may overstate or understate actual USD hedging.

### Unpacked
The data come from a handful of regular, relatively timely reporters — the Swedish AP funds (bi-annual), Danish pension funds (monthly), Finnish funds (quarterly), plus Australian and Canadian disclosures. Swedish AP1–4 operate under a 40% maximum currency-exposure mandate (AP6 at 10%), and for years most had drifted toward higher exposure as hedging weighed on liquidity and returns. **The interim reports confirm that funds did hedge some Dollar exposure in H1 2025, but the shifts were consistent and small — in Denmark and Finland they merely brought ratios back near long-term averages, and most moves were smaller still.** FX valuation was a drag on performance across the board despite these tactical adjustments.

Canada offers the most granular picture: OTPP raised total FX derivatives by ~CAD 40bn while cutting USD, CPP and CDPQ trimmed net USD exposure, and OMERS cited active hedging including a ~30bp lift from USD hedges added at end-2024. **Even here, the disclosures cannot separate a durable strategy shift from reallocation away from Dollar assets or ordinary spot transactions** — a snapshot on the last day of a period tells you the level, not the intent.

The caveats are the analytical core of the note. Funds hold different hedge ratios per currency — AP2, for instance, was near-fully hedged on USD but near-fully unhedged on INR, TWD, JPY and KRW at end-2024 — so shifting regional allocation alone moves the topline. **A reported hedge-ratio change can reflect asset mix rather than any Dollar decision: DM fixed income is almost fully hedged while DM equity is only partly hedged, so a passive drift into equities lowers the ratio, and a move into EM (structurally less hedged) does the same.** These effects appear limited in H1 based on the sampled reports, but interim disclosures rarely break them out.

**[REDACTED]'s central point is that the flows are a lens, not the engine: shifting hedge ratios, cross-border fund flows, and cross-asset correlations are best read as observable proxies for the thing that actually matters — global appetite for Dollar assets.** Investors who repatriate some US holdings and hedge others are unlikely to be adding with prior enthusiasm. FX flows alongside cyclical variables like rate differentials (in [REDACTED]'s [REDACTED] framework) explain much of this year's FX performance, but the note argues it is not the transactions doing the work. The US current-account deficit still needs foreign funding; 2025's price action is consistent with international investors demanding a lower price to provide it — via higher yields and a weaker Dollar.

The note carries a standing book of trade ideas across FX, rates and equities (including short USD/JPY, short USD/EGP, short EUR/CHF, and several EM rate and bond trades), but these are portfolio recommendations listed alongside the piece rather than a trade derived from the hedging analysis itself.

subject: US Daily: Finding a Job Takes Longer in a Low-Turnover Labor Market (Mei)
summary:
# Job Search Lengthens as Low Labor-Market Churn Locks Out Younger Workers

**Theme:** Decomposing worker turnover into reallocation vs. churn to explain longer unemployment spells  
**Markets:** United States  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Pierfrancesco Mei, 18 Sep 2025  

### Key findings
- Churn — worker flows between existing jobs — now sits well below 2019 levels and accounts for nearly all the decline in total turnover since the pandemic, answering what is driving the low-hire, low-fire pattern.
- The turnover drop is mostly cyclical, not structural: churn is highly procyclical and tracks labor-market health, while the secular fall in job reallocation has slowed over the past decade.
- The decline in churn is broad-based across industries and states, but sharpest in construction, leisure and hospitality, professional services and retail — historically the highest-transition sectors.
- Workers who lose jobs in industries and states with larger churn declines now face longer unemployment spells, evidence of a "locking-out" effect on re-entry.
- The burden falls mainly on younger workers: in states with the biggest churn drops, those aged 16–35 take about 12 weeks to find work versus 10 in 2019 — a real but modest deterioration.

### Method & verdict
[Reasonable] The note decomposes total turnover into job reallocation (from Business Employment Dynamics data, latest 2024Q4) and churn, cross-checked against JOLTS hiring, quits and layoffs rates and the job-finding rate. It then exploits cross-sectional variation in churn declines by industry and by state, and links that to unemployment-spell duration measured from individual Current Population Survey records, restricting the sample to workers unemployed no more than one year. The design is transparent and the correlation between churn decline and spell length is consistent across both the industry and state cuts, but it rests on associations rather than causal identification, uses lagged BED data, and the estimated effects are small.

### Unpacked
The starting worry is concrete: with hiring and quits below pre-pandemic norms yet layoffs steady, the unemployed — new graduates especially — may be getting shut out. A year earlier the low hiring rate looked benign, simply the mirror image of fewer quits leaving fewer slots to backfill. **That reassurance no longer holds cleanly, since the job-finding rate has trended down for three straight years.**

To see what changed, total turnover is split into two parts that move for different reasons. Job reallocation — the creation and destruction of jobs — has drifted down since the late 1990s for structural reasons such as a shift toward larger, older firms and better worker-firm matches, but that drift is slow and steady. **Churn, the flow of workers between existing jobs, is what actually swings the cycle, and it has done almost all the work in pulling turnover down since 2019 after spiking in 2022.** Because churn closely tracks overall labor-market health, the recent softening reads as cyclical rather than a new structural break.

The distributional question is where the note adds most. Churn has fallen almost everywhere, but hardest in the sectors where job-hopping is normally most frequent. **Using the cross-section, workers displaced from industries and states with the steepest churn declines take measurably longer to find new work — the signature of a labor market where fewer open positions mean slower re-entry.** Sorting by age narrows the incidence further: the cost lands mostly on the 16-to-35 group, both entrants and the previously employed.

For the reader, the takeaway is calibrated rather than alarming. The lengthening of unemployment spells is another sign the labor market has softened, concentrated among the young, but two extra weeks — 12 versus 10 — is a modest shift, not evidence that the unemployed are being durably locked out. The note offers no explicit trade idea.

subject: USA: Jobless Claims Below Expectations; Philly Fed Well Above Expectations
summary:
# US: Jobless Claims Below Expectations; Philly Fed Well Above

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US labor market and manufacturing data  
**General comment:** Neutral read of a data release; net-positive surprise, with caveats on data noise.

### Context
Comment on two US data prints for the week: weekly jobless claims (initial and continuing) and the September Philadelphia Fed manufacturing survey. Both came in stronger than expected, but each carries composition and seasonal-adjustment caveats.

### The case
- **Initial claims fell 33k to 231k, below the 240k median, but part of the move is a partial unwind of noise rather than genuine labor-market strength.** Texas claims dropped 13k, reversing much of the prior week's spike that the Texas Workforce Commission confirmed was driven by fraudulent filings — yet Texas remains ~10k above its level of two weeks earlier. Michigan and Connecticut normalized back to their early-to-mid August levels after recent jumps. Seasonal adjustment around Labor Day can distort the series: in 2014, the last year with a comparable calendar, claims rose 11k then fell 36k across the same two weeks. Continuing claims fell 7k to 1,920k, also slightly below consensus.
- **The Philadelphia Fed manufacturing index jumped 23.5pt to +23.2, far above the +1.7 median, with a mixed-to-strong composition.** New orders (+14.3pt to +12.4) and shipments (+21.6pt to +26.1) rose, while employment edged down (-0.3pt to +5.6). The forward-looking six-months-ahead business conditions index rose 6.5pt to +31.5. On prices, both paid (-20.0pt to +46.8) and received (-17.3pt to +18.8, lowest since December 2024) declined, pointing to easing cost and pricing pressure.

### Implications
- Labor data are consistent with a still-firm claims trend, but the Texas fraud episode and Labor Day seasonality argue for discounting the headline improvement.
- The Philly Fed beat, led by orders and shipments alongside softer prices, points to firmer manufacturing activity with less pricing pressure — though the soft employment component tempers the read.

subject: US Daily: September FOMC Recap: On Track for an October Cut (Mericle)
summary:
# Fed on a Path, Not a Pause: Why September's Cut Is Likely the First of Several

**Source:** [REDACTED], David Mericle  
**Focus:** US Federal Reserve monetary policy  
**General comment:** Reads the September FOMC as the opening of a cutting cycle; stays slightly more dovish than market pricing.

### Context
The FOMC cut the funds rate by 25bp to 4-4.25% at its September 2025 meeting and signalled another cut is very likely in October. The piece reads the meeting for evidence on whether this is a one-off adjustment or the start of a series, and argues for the latter.

### The case
- **The Fed's own projections turned more dovish than expected.** The median dot showed three cuts this year, by a narrow 10-9 margin, above the expectation of two. The Fed leadership is very likely in the majority, which suggests a meaningful number of participants were strongly swayed by the softer recent labor market data.
- **The statement echoed the language that preceded the 2024 cutting cycle.** Its description of the labor market — job gains slowing and the unemployment rate edging up but remaining low — was almost identical to September 2024, when the Fed delivered the first of three consecutive cuts. The added lines that "downside risks to employment have risen" and that the cut reflected "the shift in the balance of risks" show the broader committee was comfortable with the dovish framing Powell used at Jackson Hole.
- **Powell's read of the labor market emphasized weakness beyond the headline.** He described the market as "really cooling off" and argued that, although labor supply has fallen with lower net immigration, the rise in unemployment points to demand slowing more. He flagged that minority and young workers are faring worse, that part of the drop in participation is probably cyclical, and stressed the Fed doesn't want further softening — the same message it sent when it cut three times a year ago.
- **Framing the move as "risk management" implies more cuts to follow.** Powell called it a risk management cut against downside labor-market risks. Such insurance cuts have historically come in consecutive packages, acting quickly rather than skipping meetings.
- **Powell tied the cut's effectiveness to delivering the whole path.** Asked whether a single 25bp cut meaningfully supports the economy, he said "you have to look at the whole path" — the market pricing in a series of future cuts is what provides the support, which in turn creates pressure on the Fed to follow through.

### Implications
- Base case remains 25bp cuts in October and December, then two more in 2026 to 3-3.25%, with a 50bp move possible if the labor market weakens faster than expected.
- The probability-weighted path stays a bit more dovish than market pricing, leaving room for rates to fall further than markets currently discount.
- Because the support comes from the expected path rather than any single cut, the Fed is effectively committed to delivering on it — raising the cost of an early pause.

subject: USA: FOMC Lowers Fed Funds Rate 25bp; SEP Median Projects Three Cuts for 2025, One Each in 2026 and 2027
summary:
# FOMC Cuts 25bp to 4–4.25%; Dot Plot Now Pencils In Three 2025 Cuts and a Lower 3.125% Terminal Rate

**Theme:** September rate cut, softened forward guidance, and a more dovish dot plot against firmer growth and inflation forecasts  
**Markets:** US monetary policy  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jan Hatzius, 17 September 2025  

### Definitive impacts
- Target range lowered 25bp to 4–4.25% at the September meeting, with Governor Miran the sole dissenter, who preferred a 50bp cut.
- Forward guidance dropped the prior reference to "the extent and timing" of further cuts; the statement now flags that "downside risks to employment have risen" while inflation "has moved up."
- SEP median moved to three 2025 cuts (from two in June), decided by a narrow 10-9 margin, with one cut each in 2026 and 2027 unchanged.
- Terminal rate median lowered to 3.125% (from 3.375% in June); longer-run neutral dot unchanged at 3.0%, with the split shifting to 9 participants above 3% and 10 at or below (vs. 8 and 11 in June).
- GDP growth revised up across the horizon: +0.2pp to 1.6% (2025), +0.2pp to 1.8% (2026), +0.1pp to 1.9% (2027).
- Unemployment median unchanged for 2025 but 0.1pp lower in 2026 (4.4%) and 2027 (4.3%).
- Core and headline inflation medians unchanged for 2025, 0.2pp higher in 2026 (to 2.6%), and unchanged in 2027.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] reads the removal of "the extent and timing" language as signaling less Committee uncertainty about continuing to cut at future meetings.

### At issue
The FOMC cut the fed funds target range by 25bp to 4–4.25% at its September 2025 meeting, its statement reweighting risks toward employment even as it acknowledged inflation had moved up. The accompanying SEP shifted the 2025 median to three cuts and lowered the projected terminal rate to 3.125%, while raising growth and 2026 inflation forecasts and trimming out-year unemployment.

### Unpacked
**The cut itself was widely anticipated; the information sat in how the Committee framed what comes next.** By striking the "extent and timing" qualifier from its forward guidance, the FOMC removed a hedge it had used to keep future moves conditional — a small edit that leans toward a continued easing path rather than a one-off adjustment.

The dot plot underscores how thin the consensus is. The three-cuts-in-2025 median rests on a single vote (10-9), so the central projection could flip with one participant's revision. The neutral-rate distribution is similarly balanced, with the group nearly evenly split around 3%, even as the median longer-run dot held steady.

**The forecast mix is unusual for an easing decision: the Committee cut while marking up growth and near-term inflation.** Higher GDP across the horizon and firmer 2026 core and headline inflation would ordinarily argue against faster cuts, so the pivot rests on the labor-market side of the mandate — slower job gains, an edging-up unemployment rate, and rising downside employment risks. That tension is the note's real signal: the path lower is being driven by employment concern rather than by inflation returning to target.

For the reader, the takeaway is a Fed that has committed more firmly to easing while lowering where it expects to stop, but on a fragile internal majority and against data that are not uniformly cooperative. The note offers no explicit trade idea.

subject: USA: Housing Starts Below Expectations
summary:
# US Housing Starts Undershoot in August as Permits Hit a Five-Year Low

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US residential construction data  
**General comment:** Neutral read-through of a soft housing print; weak headline but no change to the growth outlook.

### Context
This note comments on the August US housing starts and building permits release from the Department of Commerce, gauging whether the softer-than-expected figures shift the near-term growth picture.

### The case
- **Housing starts fell much more than expected, but the underlying trend is less weak than the headline.** Starts dropped 8.5% MoM to 1,307k (SAAR), versus a median forecast of -4.4% and the [REDACTED] call of -3.0%. Offsetting this, the prior two months were revised up (July to 1,429k, August's earlier reading to 1,382k). The decline was broad across segments — multi-family -11.7%, single-family -7.0% — and regionally mixed, with gains in the Northeast (+9.2%) and West (+30.4%) but sharp falls in the Midwest (-10.9%) and South (-21.0%).
- **Building permits, a forward-looking signal, were the weaker element.** Permits fell 3.7% to 1,312k (SAAR) — the lowest since June 2020 — against consensus for a small rise. The softness spanned both multi-family (-6.4%) and single-family (-2.2%) permits and most regions, the West (+9.5%) being the exception. The permits reading points to continued weakness in the construction pipeline.
- **The growth read-through is nil.** Despite the miss, the Q3 GDP tracking estimate is left unchanged at +2.2% (QoQ annualized), with Q3 domestic final sales at +1.3%.

### Implications
- A soft print with no change to the growth call: the housing weakness is real but not large enough to move the Q3 tracking estimate.
- Permits at a five-year low signal a still-contracting construction pipeline, a downside risk for residential investment ahead.

subject: USA: Industrial Production Increases in August, Against Expectations; Boosting Q3 GDP Tracking Estimate to +2.2%
summary:
# US: Industrial production surprises to the upside in August, lifting Q3 GDP tracking to +2.2%

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius
**Focus:** US industrial activity and GDP tracking
**General comment:** Constructive data read, marginally above consensus expectations.

### Context
Commentary on August industrial production data released by the Federal Reserve, combined with the same morning's retail sales report, to update the Q3 GDP growth estimate.

### The arguments
- **Industrial production surprised to the upside, though with a downward revision to the prior month.** Industrial production rose 0.1% in August, against an expected decline ([REDACTED] and median at -0.1%), but the July figure was revised down 0.3pp, to -0.4%. Manufacturing rose 0.2%, also above expectations (-0.2%), with July revised down 0.1pp to -0.1%. Capacity utilization was unchanged at 77.4%, starting from a downwardly revised July level.
- **The components relevant to GDP tracking were mixed.** Vehicle assemblies rose 6.0%, to 11.0 million units, supporting the positive read. In the opposite direction, the utilities component — which enters as a consumption input in GDP accounts — fell 2.0%, and the business equipment category, sensitive to capex, declined 0.1%.
- **The tracking revision was driven mainly by retail sales, not industry.** The retail sales report's details came in significantly stronger than the prior tracking assumptions. Combined with the mixed industrial production result, this led to a net 0.6pp upward revision in the estimate.

### Implications
- The Q3 GDP tracking estimate rises 0.6pp, to +2.2% (quarterly annualized), signaling firmer activity than previously assumed.
- Q3 final domestic sales also rise 0.6pp, to +1.3%, indicating the boost comes from underlying demand rather than just volatile factors.

subject: USA: Retail Sales Above Expectations and Revised Up; Core Import Prices Slightly Above Expectations; Estimating +0.21% for August Core PCE
summary:
# US Data: Firmer Consumer Spending and Import Prices Nudge the August Core PCE Estimate Higher

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US August retail sales and import prices, PCE inflation tracking  
**General comment:** Descriptive data read, mildly hawkish on inflation and constructive on consumer demand; in line with consensus framing.

### Context
A same-day reaction to the August US retail sales and import prices releases, used to update [REDACTED]'s tracking estimates for consumer spending, inflation (core PCE), and GDP.

### The case
- **Consumer spending came in clearly stronger than expected, with upward revisions.** Core retail sales (ex-autos, gasoline, and building materials) rose 0.7% in August against a 0.3% [REDACTED] forecast and a 0.4% median, and the July level was revised up 0.1%. Headline sales rose 0.6%. Strength was led by nonstore retailers (+2.0%), sporting goods (+0.8%), and food services (+0.7%), while miscellaneous retailers (-1.1%) and department stores (-0.8%) were soft. Adjusting for prices using the CPI report, real core retail sales rose 0.6% in August and a strong 6.3% on a three-month annualized basis.
- **Import prices ran hotter than expected, with a broad-based gain.** Headline import prices rose 0.3% (vs. -0.2% expected) and the ex-petroleum measure rose 0.2%. Increases spanned consumer goods (+0.7%), capital goods (+0.5%), industrial supplies (+0.4%), and autos (+0.2%), offset only by food and beverages (-2.1%). The international airfares component — source data for the foreign travel piece of core PCE — jumped 4.5%.
- **These inputs lift the August core PCE tracking estimate marginally.** Core PCE is now seen at +0.21% for the month (up from +0.20% before the import prices data), or +2.92% year-over-year. Headline PCE is estimated at +0.25% month-over-month and +2.72% year-over-year, with market-based core PCE at +0.16%.
- **GDP tracking is left open.** The retail details were stronger than prior assumptions, but the GDP estimate is not revised here — that update is deferred to later mid-morning data.

### Implications
- Consumer momentum entering the second half looks solid, with real spending running well above trend on a three-month basis.
- The inflation read is a touch firmer than expected but modest in size — core PCE still tracks near 2.9% year-over-year, with the import prices surprise adding only about a basis point to the monthly estimate.
- The stronger retail details point to upside for GDP tracking, though the piece stops short of quantifying it.

subject: Global Markets Daily: G10 Rates—Dovish Relief... For Now (Cole/Marshall)
summary:
# G10 Rates: Dovish Relief Buys the Long End Time, But the Bearish Duration Story Still Has Legs

**Theme:** US dovish repricing has balanced risk-reward, but the global 30y selloff has staying power — the pressure now migrates to the belly.  
**Markets:** G10 rates  
**Source:** [REDACTED], George Cole, 15 September 2025

### Landscape
- US front-end now prices terminal firmly below 3%, broadly matching the [REDACTED] Fed baseline, with some mass on a lower terminal.
- ~45bp of cuts priced from April 2026 to April 2027, with the post-Powell forward curve staying inverted despite the near-term rally.
- 30y yields are up on the year across G4, with Germany and Japan — not the US or UK — showing the biggest rises.
- Long-end curve steepness looks modestly excessive versus the cycle on [REDACTED] valuation frameworks.
- US long-end carries little unique risk premium versus the rest of the world, implying Fed-independence concerns are largely unpriced.
- French idiosyncratic risk is priced near its wides versus other EGBs; [REDACTED] sees OAT-Bund near 70bp at year-end.
- UK weighted average maturity of Gilts has fallen substantially as the DMO reshapes issuance toward demand.

### Drivers
- Dovish US repricing on weaker labor data has lowered long-end risk premium, but cross-asset growth pricing is resilient — cuts are being added cumulatively, not pulled forward, so richening from here needs fresh growth weakness.
- Large, sticky deficits plus shifting demand for very long duration keep the clearing price for the long-end stock of bonds lower (higher yield) even as issuance dynamics improve.
- In Germany and Japan the term-premium channel is nearing its limit; further 10y rises should come from an upward repricing of policy paths — better German growth, a more sustainable Japanese tightening cycle.
- Reduced Japanese life-insurer demand for super-long JGBs (>15y) leaves the long-end exposed, compounded by political uncertainty.
- UK long-end relief hinges on disinflation and confidence the BoE can cut; the 26 November budget is the gating event, with cross-market Gilt outperformance unlikely to unlock before it.
- French relief from a new PM, plus compressed EUR credit spreads, skews OAT-Bund toward tightening.

### Risks
- Upside (yields): the largely unpriced US long-end premium for Fed-independence concerns is flagged as a potential source of risk the market has navigated too calmly.
- Downside (Gilt yields): [REDACTED] expects deeper BoE cuts than priced, but warns supply-side responses alone cannot deliver sustained outperformance without fundamental tailwinds.
- Two-sided (France): tail risks such as early Presidential elections may warrant extra premium, though [REDACTED] does not expect near-term uncertainty to materially move the 2025-26 deficit or growth path.
- [REDACTED] notes EUR spread compression is likely near its floor — end of ECB tightening, bottoming EUR vol, and possible core-rate pressure argue for stability rather than further tightening.

### Unpacked
The early-September duration wobble has faded, and the episode is read as a reminder that inflation relief and room to cut can offset a higher term premium. **With the US front-end now priced close to the [REDACTED] Fed baseline and terminal below 3%, risk-reward there is judged relatively balanced — sustaining this pricing requires weaker growth, which would itself argue for more front-loading than the market's drawn-out cutting path implies.** On that logic, 2y1y is seen as too rich and 2H26-vs-2H27 gaps too flat, though it may take a clearer macro picture for belly-cheapening trades to work. The rally is framed as a dovish repricing rather than a growth scare: recession pricing has not built, and the post-Powell forward curve stays inverted, showing cuts added cumulatively rather than pulled forward.

**The rise in 30y yields is treated as a durable, global story, with Germany and Japan — not the fiscally scrutinized US and UK — as the most consistent sources of bearish spillover.** Large deficits, residual inflation upside, and a structural shift in long-duration demand should keep the clearing yield elevated even as issuance improves. The notable absence of unique US long-end premium is highlighted both as evidence of how calmly markets have handled Fed-independence questions and as an under-priced risk.

**Gilts stay in the spotlight on their high absolute level rather than as an origin of shocks.** DMO issuance realignment and BoE attentiveness to dysfunction have helped, but supply responses alone are seen as insufficient. [REDACTED] expects disinflation and BoE cuts to eventually deliver, favoring UK 2s5s steepeners and 30y Gilt outperformance versus USTs and Bunds — but only closer to or through the 26 November budget.

**For Germany and Japan, the key call is that the driver of higher 10y yields shifts from term premium to policy-rate repricing, putting the 5y point in the lead.** This underpins a rotation preference toward 2s5s and 2s10s steepeners over the previously successful 5s30s and 10s30s. In France, compressed EUR credit and a marginally reassuring new PM skew OAT-Bund toward tightening around 70bp by year-end, with Italy's fiscal outlook cited as a positive surprise, even as broader EUR spread compression looks close to exhausted.

**Across the rest of G10, [REDACTED] economists see the BoC delivering its final two cuts to the bottom of neutral faster than priced**, though risk-reward on receivers is less compelling before month-end inflation data. The RBA sits near baseline with downside skew leaving 1y1y room to richen, and RBNZ forwards only just reach the expected terminal, keeping 1y1y longs attractive as positive-carry front-end carry. The note carries an explicit trade sheet, including Gilt 2s5s steepeners and a range of cross-asset positions.

subject: USA: Empire Manufacturing Well Below Expectations
summary:
# US Factory Activity Contracts Sharply as Empire Index Misses Badly

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US manufacturing survey data

The September Empire State manufacturing survey came in at -8.7, a sharp miss versus the median forecast of a positive 5.0 reading and down from 11.9 in August. The note assesses what the release signals about the state of US factory activity.

subject: US Economics Weekly Update 9/15/2025
summary:
# Fed Set for a September Cut, First of Three as Labor Market Softens

**Theme:** Cutting cycle begins with jobs as the Fed's priority; inflation a two-part tariff-plus-trend story  
**Markets:** US economy and monetary policy  
**Source:** [REDACTED], David Mericle, 15 September 2025  

### Landscape
- Core CPI rose 0.35% in August and 3.11% over the past year, with airfares, hotels, and owners' equivalent rent the largest upside surprises.
- August core PCE is forecast at 0.20%, tracking toward a modest rise in core PCE inflation to 3.2% year-over-year by December.
- Q3 GDP tracking sits at 1.6% annualized, above the 0.7% domestic final sales forecast; full-year 2025 Q4/Q4 GDP growth is put at 1.3%.
- Underlying trend job growth is estimated at just 25k/month, below the 70k breakeven rate, with the unemployment rate seen rising to 4.5% by Q4.
- The preliminary benchmark payrolls revision for April 2024–March 2025 was -911k, broad-based across industries, though viewed as likely exaggerated.

### Drivers
- A softening labor market is the decisive force: rising unemployment over the last two months and job growth below breakeven make supporting jobs the Fed's top priority, driving the expected cutting path.
- Inflation is a two-part story — a growing tariff bump layered over a falling underlying trend — netting to a modest rise in core PCE; tariff passthrough evidence is mixed (apparel firmer, household furnishings and recreation goods softer) and will be reassessed after PCE prices.
- Consumer spending is fading: core retail sales are forecast up 0.3% in August (vs. 0.4% consensus) on slower card spending, with soft 2025H2 spending as weaker jobs and rising tariffs slow real income growth.
- GDP support comes from an expected rebound in inventory accumulation after the Q2 import-frontloading drawdown, plus a narrowing trade deficit as tariffs cut imports while exports hold up on dollar depreciation and limited foreign retaliation.

### Risks
- Downside to jobs: the analyst estimates the BLS birth-death model is still overstating payroll growth by ~30k/month, and up to 35k/month with non-response bias and seasonal adjustment issues, implying trend job growth may be weaker than headline prints.
- Statistical mismeasurement flagged around AI: the analyst estimates AI's true GDP boost at $160bn (0.7%) since 2022 versus only $45bn (0.2%) measured, a gap that understates actual output.

### Unpacked
**A 25bp cut at the September FOMC is expected to be the first of three this year, with further 25bp moves in October and December and two more in 2026, taking the funds rate to 3–3.25%.** The FOMC statement is not expected to nod toward an October cut, though Powell may hint softly at consecutive cuts in the press conference. The dot plot is projected to show two cuts in 2025 to 3.875% (by a narrow 10-9 majority), two more in 2026 to 3.375%, one in 2027 to 3.125%, no change in 2028, and an unchanged 3% neutral rate.

**The near-term data calendar frames the decision: core retail sales are forecast up 0.3% in August against 0.4% consensus, with headline up 0.2% held back by lower auto sales.** The August core CPI print carried upside surprises in airfares, hotels, and owners' equivalent rent, but these are seen as having minimal implications for the forward inflation trend.

**The payrolls picture is the analytical core of the update.** The -911k preliminary benchmark revision, though judged exaggerated, points to still-overstated job growth; combined with the birth-death and other adjustments, this leaves underlying trend job growth at roughly 25k/month — well below the 70k breakeven — and supports the call for unemployment to reach 4.5% by Q4.

**On growth, the gap between the 1.6% Q3 GDP track and the 0.7% domestic final sales forecast is explained by inventory rebound and a narrowing trade deficit** rather than firmer end demand, with tariffs reducing imports while exports are cushioned by a weaker dollar and the absence of major retaliation.

The update closes with an AI accounting point: because GDP statistics treat semiconductors and in-house cloud services as intermediate inputs, investment used to train AI models is not counted as final demand until embodied products are sold. This leaves the measured AI boost ($45bn, 0.1pp annualized) far below the estimated true impact ($160bn, 0.3pp annualized) since 2022.

subject: Global Week Ahead: September 15-21

# Week Ahead: Nine Central Bank Meetings, Almost All On-Consensus — Fed and BoJ in Focus

**Theme:** Central bank week with forecasts largely tracking consensus  
**Markets:** Global rates and macro data
