### Landscape
- Nine central banks meet this week: the US, Japan, UK, Canada, Norway, Brazil, South Africa, Indonesia, and Ghana.

**The single dovish deviation is South Africa, where [REDACTED] looks for a 25bp cut to 6.75% against a consensus and prior of 7.0%** — and the same dovish lean shows up in its below-consensus South Africa CPI print. The other sub-consensus data calls, UK core CPI and US core retail sales, are marginal rather than material.

# Fed Cut Locked, No Dovish Tilt Expected; Retail Sales Seen Cooling

**Theme:** A 25bp September cut with unchanged guidance, alongside softening consumer and factory data  
**Markets:** US macro (consumer, industrial activity, monetary policy)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jan Hatzius, 14 September 2025  

### Estimates

subject: US Economics Analyst: September FOMC Preview: Supporting the Labor Market (Mericle)
summary:
# September FOMC: First of Three Consecutive Cuts to Defend a Softening Labor Market

**Theme:** Labor-market deterioration makes supporting employment the Fed's top priority — a 25bp cut this week, with the debate over whether the Fed signals a consecutive series  
**Markets:** US monetary policy / Fed rate path  
**Source:** [REDACTED] (David Mericle), 14 September 2025  

### Estimates
- **25bp cut expected at the September meeting**, to 4.00–4.25%, driven by labor-market softening now seen as the Fed's urgent priority.
- **Median 2025 dot: two cuts total, to 3.875%**, by a narrow 10-9 margin — not the three-cut dot that would openly flag an October cut.
- **Median dot path beyond 2025:** two more cuts in 2026 to 3.375%, one cut in 2027 to 3.125%, no change in 2028, and an unchanged longer-run/neutral rate of 3%.
- **Trend job growth ~25k/month**, down sharply and below the ~70k breakeven rate that would stabilize unemployment; risks still tilt to further negative revisions (August likely revised up).
- **Unemployment rate 4.3%**, up 0.1pp in each of the last two months; the broader slack tracker implies slightly more softening than that.
- **SEP economic projections (2025) little changed:** 1.4% GDP growth, 4.5% unemployment, 3.1% core PCE — all near [REDACTED] forecasts.
- **Core inflation seen rising to 3.2% by December**, netting a growing tariff effect against a falling underlying trend.
- **[REDACTED] Fed path:** consecutive 25bp cuts in September, October and December, then two more in 2026 to a terminal 3–3.25% — a bit more dovish than market pricing on a probability-weighted basis.

### Outlook
- **This is likely the first of three consecutive cuts**, per [REDACTED], but the September statement will only acknowledge labor softening — no change to the durable policy guidance and no explicit nod to October.
- **Powell may hint softly at more cuts** in the press conference; framing the cut as labor-market support could be read as signaling October, since "insurance cuts" have historically come as a consecutive series.
- **A 50bp cut is possible in October or December** if the labor market deteriorates faster than assumed; at least one September dissent in favor of 50bp is likely.
- **Balance-sheet reduction expected to end at the October meeting**, so no change to the QT sentence in September; Powell may note it was discussed.
- **Below-potential growth in 2025H2** should push unemployment to 4.5%; [REDACTED] expects a 2026 rebound as tariff effects fade and fiscal support kicks in, but the Fed will not wait, fearing labor weakness could compound.

### Unpacked
The note frames September as a pivot forced by data. **The decisive change since late July is a labor market that "now looks very different"** after weak July and August employment reports and a large negative preliminary benchmark revision. [REDACTED]'s trend job-growth estimate has collapsed to about 25k, well under the 70k breakeven, while unemployment has ticked up to 4.3% and the broader slack composite suggests even a touch more weakening. That combination is what makes a cut close to certain and reframes the Fed's priority away from inflation and toward employment.

Inflation is cast as a two-part story that does not block easing: a growing but moderate tariff effect layered on an underlying trend still drifting toward target, netting to a modest rise in core PCE to 3.2% by December. **Officials differ on how much to worry about the tariff bump, but with the labor market now the more urgent problem, it is unlikely to stop the cut.** The growth picture reinforces the same conclusion — below-potential growth into year-end argues for action now rather than betting on the 2026 rebound that fading tariffs, the fiscal bill and easy financial conditions should deliver.

The live question is signaling, not the cut itself. **[REDACTED] expects the statement to note softer job growth — perhaps echoing September 2024 language — but to keep the durable policy guidance intact and avoid any explicit gesture toward October.** The subtler tell would be the dot plot: a three-cut 2025 median would openly flag consecutive moves, but [REDACTED] sees the median landing at two cuts (3.875%) by a razor-thin 10-9, judging that Fed leadership anticipates three cuts yet will not push participants to show it. The June projections are described as "prescient" and largely unchanged; [REDACTED] discounts the Atlanta Fed's 3.1% GDPNow read as distorted by tariff frontloading, expecting the staff forecast handed to participants to be lower.

Looking forward, the reader should watch Powell's press conference for a soft steer, the dot-plot margin, any 50bp dissent, and the October signal on ending balance-sheet runoff. **[REDACTED] holds to three straight cuts into December and a 3–3.25% terminal rate, leaving its probability-weighted path modestly more dovish than the market** — with a faster-than-assumed labor deterioration the trigger that could force a 50bp move. The note offers no explicit trade idea, only the rate-path view.

subject: US Daily: What Do the Preliminary Benchmark Revisions to Payrolls Tell Us About the Economy? (Abecasis)
summary:
# US payrolls revised down 911k; underlying job growth now ~25k/month, below the ~70k breakeven

**Theme:** What the preliminary benchmark revision and new QCEW data reveal about a materially softer labor market, and their knock-on effects on productivity, income and GDP  
**Markets:** US labor market and macro data  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Manuel Abecasis, 13 September 2025  

### Definitive impacts
- Payroll growth for April 2024–March 2025 cut by 911k jobs (−76k/month), lowering the average pace from 147k to 71k/month — the largest annual downward benchmark revision since at least 2000, if it holds.
- Revision broad-based across sectors, down in every industry except transportation and utilities; largest cuts in leisure and hospitality, professional and business services, manufacturing and trade, while education and healthcare and government saw only modest cuts.
- Job growth weakest for small- and medium-sized businesses (year-over-year pace near zero) versus 1.7% at large businesses.
- Seasonally adjusted QCEW job gains decelerated to about 40k/month in 2025Q1 even after adding back the average benchmark revision, versus 111k currently in the payroll survey.
- Nonfarm productivity growth likely to be revised up to 1.7% year-over-year and 1.9% annualized since 2019Q4 (from 1.2% and 1.8%); nonfinancial corporate productivity to 2.9% and 2.7% (from 2.3% and 2.6%) — well above the ~1.2–1.3% pre-pandemic decade average.
- Personal income and GDI: only modest revisions expected, since QCEW compensation growth closely matched the establishment survey; GDP effect very small (under 5bp).
- JOLTS hiring, layoffs and quits rates, and job openings, will likely be revised as they are benchmarked to the establishment survey; direction clearer with November's BEDs data.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] estimates the BLS birth-death model is currently overstating payroll growth by a little under 30k jobs/month, based on its own higher-frequency model of business formation and bankruptcies.
- It adds a further 3–5k/month overstatement from non-response bias and concurrent-seasonal-adjustment difficulties, while cautioning this rests on few annual observations and is volatile.
- Underlying job growth is judged to have slowed to about 25k/month, below the estimated ~70k breakeven rate needed to hold the unemployment rate steady — the ~50k pace over the last six months is roughly consistent with the observed 0.2pp rise in unemployment.
- The reported 911k could overstate the true revision: the QCEW has been revised up in nearly every quarter since 2019, and it likely excludes many unauthorized immigrants (though the latter matters less given slowing immigration).
- [REDACTED] reads a broad set of immigration-insensitive tightness indicators as confirming the labor market has softened materially and now sits well below pre-pandemic levels.

### Backdrop
Each February the BLS re-benchmarks its monthly establishment survey — a sample of roughly 630k establishments covering about 47 million workers — to unemployment-insurance tax records covering over 95% of US jobs across 12.2 million establishments, published quarterly as the QCEW. Two structural gaps drive the annual revisions: the monthly survey cannot observe hiring at newly opened firms, so the BLS imputes net job creation through its birth-death model; and firms that respond to the survey may hire differently from those that do not, a growing concern as response rates fall. Since 2011 the average absolute annual revision has run about 0.15%, or roughly 20k jobs/month.

### At issue
On 9 September 2025 the BLS announced a preliminary benchmark revision of −911k to payroll growth over April 2024–March 2025, alongside new QCEW data through 2025Q1. This is a preliminary figure; the final revision arrives with the January employment report in February 2026, which will also revise April–December 2025 using updated seasonal factors and birth-death estimates. Separately, in the February 2025 benchmark the BLS introduced a new method that lets the pace of job growth for continuing businesses inform the birth-death contribution, improving real-time capture of turning points. That method is not yet applied to monthly estimates because of processing constraints, though the BLS is researching how to do so.

### Unpacked
The note reads the preliminary benchmark less as a one-off data quirk than as confirmation of a labor market that was weaker all along than the monthly prints suggested. **The headline 911k cut reframes the past year's job growth from a solid 147k/month to a soft 71k, and the new QCEW detail lets [REDACTED] push that logic into the present, where it lands on an underlying pace of just 25k jobs/month — comfortably below the breakeven rate.**

Much of the analysis is a careful attempt to separate signal from mechanical noise. The revision could be overstated, because the QCEW itself tends to be revised up and excludes many unauthorized immigrants; but the birth-death model and survey non-response bias cut the other way, and [REDACTED]'s own model puts the current combined overstatement at a little over 30k jobs/month. **The upshot is that the note trusts the direction of the message — a genuine, broad-based slowdown concentrated in small and medium firms — even while flagging that the precise magnitude will shift in the final benchmark.**

The February 2025 methodology change is treated as the reason the revision was not even larger. By letting continuing-business trends feed the birth-death estimate, the BLS avoided revising up the birth-death contribution through late 2024; the divergence between the two surveys instead widens later, in early 2025. **That timing matters: it locates the real deterioration in 2025Q1 rather than spreading it evenly, which is why the "underlying pace now" conclusion carries weight.**

For the reader, the second-order effects are as important as the payroll number itself. **Because compensation growth in the QCEW tracked the establishment survey, income, GDI and GDP are largely spared — so the same downward revision that weakens the jobs story simultaneously raises measured productivity by about half a point, a genuinely different narrative for the supply side of the economy.** Fewer workers producing roughly unchanged output implies a faster productivity trend than any pre-pandemic decade, even as the labor demand signal turns clearly softer. The note offers no explicit trade idea; its value is in recalibrating the reader's read of the jobs data and its cross-checks ahead of the November BEDs release and the February final benchmark.

subject: US Daily: A Primer on the Impact of AI on the GDP Statistics (Peng/Briggs/Dong)
summary:
# AI's Contribution to US Growth: Big in Revenue, Small in the GDP Statistics

**Theme:** How AI spending flows through the national accounts, and true vs. measured GDP impact  
**Markets:** United States  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Elsie Peng, 13 September 2025  

### Key findings
- AI has added roughly $160bn (0.7%) to *true* US real GDP since 2022 — about 0.3pp annualized — far less than the $400bn revenue surge at AI-infrastructure firms would suggest.
- Official statistics capture only about $45bn (0.2%) of that, roughly 0.1pp annualized, because the BEA's methodology misses most of the real activity.
- The headline 39% annualized jump in information processing equipment investment in 2025H1 overstates AI's role: the goods were mostly imported (a GDP offset) and the surge largely reflects one-time frontloading ahead of tariffs.
- Nearly half the $400bn revenue gain came from margin/price expansion and foreign sales of equipment produced abroad, leaving ~$220bn of real US domestic demand — and ~$60bn of that was imported.
- The measured impact is dragged down because semiconductors are treated as intermediate inputs: their rising imports subtract from GDP while the offsetting investment (chips used to build in-house AI models) goes uncounted, making the semiconductor channel a net negative for measured GDP.
- About $75bn of cloud spending on AI model development and enterprise solutions also goes unmeasured in investment statistics.
- Measured AI contribution was 0.2pp in 2023 but negligible since, as the capex boost was offset by an import drag.

### Method & verdict
[Reasonable] The estimate builds up from revenue at US public companies exposed to AI infrastructure ($400bn since 2022, cross-checked against ~$368bn of projected 2025 hyperscaler capex), then nets out margin/price effects, foreign sales produced abroad, and imported inputs using company balance-sheet data to isolate real domestic output. AI's four GDP channels — equipment, structures, intellectual property, and net exports — are mapped against BEA accounting treatment, with the semiconductor-as-intermediate-input distinction driving the gap between true and measured impact. The approach is transparent and internally consistent, but rests on judgmental splits (e.g., how much revenue growth is price vs. quantity, what share of foreign sales is produced abroad) and on identifying which firms and flows are "AI-related," so the point estimates carry meaningful uncertainty.

### Unpacked
The starting puzzle is a mismatch: revenue at US AI-infrastructure providers has jumped $400bn since ChatGPT's launch, and equipment investment lines in the accounts have spiked, yet headline GDP growth has not obviously reflected an AI boom. **The note's purpose is to reconcile the eye-catching spending figures with what actually lands in GDP, and to separate AI's true economic footprint from what the statistics record.**

The gap opens in two stages. First, much of the apparent AI spending never adds to US output: about half the $400bn is price/margin expansion or foreign sales of equipment made abroad, and a further slice of genuine domestic demand is met by imports, which offset the investment. **Stripping these out leaves a true GDP boost of roughly $160bn, or 0.7% since 2022 — real, but a fraction of the gross revenue number.** The 2025H1 equipment-investment surge is a cautionary example: driven by imported servers and inflated by pre-tariff frontloading, it flatters AI's contribution rather than measuring it.

The measured impact is smaller still because of how the accounts are built. **The BEA treats semiconductors as intermediate inputs, counted in final demand only when the finished product they enable is sold — but today's high-performance chips are used to train in-house AI models, an intangible asset whose output value is not yet capitalized or measured.** So the ~$42bn rise in US semiconductor demand, met entirely by imports, subtracts from measured GDP without any offsetting investment credit, turning the chip channel net-negative. Add ~$75bn of unmeasured cloud spending on model development, and official statistics capture only about $45bn of the true $160bn effect.

For the reader, the takeaways are twofold. **AI is contributing to growth, but its measured contribution is understated by current statistical conventions and has been roughly nil in recent years once the import drag offsets the capex boost.** It also means the broader capex and net-export categories overstate AI's specific role, since they sweep in non-AI hardware and software — a reason to treat headline "AI-driven growth" claims from the GDP data with caution until measurement catches up with intangible AI capital.

subject: Global FX Trader: The Stall Before the Fall
summary:
# Dollar Poised to Resume Its Decline as Fed Cuts Approach

**Theme:** Dollar stalled but set to fall again, with Asia FX and quality carry taking the lead  
**Markets:** Global FX (G10 and EM)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Kamakshya Trivedi, 12 September 2025  

### Landscape
- The Dollar is roughly flat over recent months on DXY, the broad TWI, and total returns, ending a period of stalled depreciation.
- Recent Dollar weakness has come mainly against high-carry EM currencies (BRL, ZAR, MXN), not broadly.
- EUR/USD has stalled near the 1.17 3-month target after a faster-than-expected earlier rally.
- The Yen ended the week near its September 5 close despite Ishiba's September 7 resignation, with little political risk premium priced ahead of the October 4 election.
- CAD is the worst-performing G10 currency in September, while AUD and NZD have recovered from earlier underperformance.
- TCMB gross reserves are back above $180bn, fully reversing the mid-March TRY selloff decline; Lira depreciation has slowed to ~1.3%/month from 2%/month in mid-July.
- The Argentine Peso has fallen more than 30% since the float began, with a ~4% drop after the Buenos Aires election pushing it toward the upper band.

### Drivers
- Impending Fed cuts should catalyze fresh Dollar downside: the US economy no longer outperforms as before, undercutting the Dollar's overvaluation; the front-end rally has not yet reignited broad depreciation, but delivered cuts plus labor-market concerns should.
- Falling hedging costs should push Asian investors to trim USD exposure, mirroring the European reallocation that drove first-half FX performance.
- A policy bias in the CNY fixing mechanism is a "policy push" that can support broader Dollar weakness.
- European asset-allocation shifts away from the Dollar are expected to continue, though some reallocation is already done, leaving less room to run for EUR.
- Higher gold prices are a growing FX force: a terms-of-trade tailwind for CHF, a strong driver lifting THB (+10% gold over the month), and a support for TRY reserves.
- In Canada, a softer domestic backdrop drove CAD weaker; the latest employment report raised BoC cut expectations and deepened terminal-rate pricing, with a 25bp cut expected next week and two more this year.

### Risks
- **Downside (ARS):** Political volatility — corruption allegations, the Milei party's provincial defeat, and the approaching October 26 midterms — could pressure already-low reserves, which recently missed mid-June IMF targets; the analyst sees forecast risks skewed to a weaker Peso.
- **Downside (IDR):** Sri Mulyani's replacement raises fiscal-discipline concerns; the analyst expects macro investors to stay focused on fiscal fears until a credible plan emerges.
- **Downside/volatility (TRY):** The September 15 hearing on the CHP national congress annulment could reinstate prior leadership and spark forward volatility; positive summer current-account seasonality is now behind.
- **Upside (JPY):** A Takaichi win or a low-probability opposition PM adds political uncertainty, keeping the analyst wary of tactical Yen longs near term.
- **Two-sided (EUR):** Continued reallocation supports the Euro, but the analyst is skeptical EUR/USD can exceed 1.25 without clearer EA fiscal strength or further US slippage.

### Unpacked
The central call is that the Dollar's multi-month stall ends as the Fed actually delivers cuts. **The motivation for easing — a US economy that no longer outperforms — is itself the reason the Dollar should shed its overvaluation.** Until broad depreciation resumes, quality carry currencies remain a preferred holding, and G10 Dollar-short positions are better expressed through options. The composition of this year's move matters: an early decline against the Euro and its satellites on European fiscal-spending expectations, a broad post-Liberation Day selloff, and more recently weakness against good-carry names like BRL, ZAR, and MXN.

On the Euro, the forecast path is rolled forward to 1.20, 1.22, and 1.25 at 3, 6, and 12 months (from 1.17, 1.20, 1.25), with the year-end 1.20 target kept. **The early European reallocation out of the Dollar cuts both ways — it confirms the appetite to reduce USD dominance, but also means less room left to run.** The next leg of Dollar weakness is expected to come from Asian currencies, chiefly CNY and JPY, rather than the Euro.

For the Yen, the near-term stance is patient. Political noise around the October 4 election is judged to have limited fundamental impact, but the thin risk premium priced argues against tactical longs. **High-beta FX (AUD, SEK, BRL, ZAR) is expected to outperform JPY over the coming weeks as long as US data stay benign**, while the longer-term Yen and Asia FX bull case rests on lower hedging costs. The next BoJ hike is not seen as imminent, with no change expected in September and low October odds. The preferred expression is long JPY via options.

CAD forecasts are revised weaker to 1.38, 1.37, and 1.36 (from 1.35, 1.34, 1.32), reflecting a softer domestic backdrop that has moved USD/CAD against the prior 3-month call. **Low volatility and underperformance make CAD an attractive funder or tactical short versus AUD and NZD**, though it should still benefit modestly from broader Dollar weakness longer term. Tuesday's August inflation report is flagged as a risk to next week's BoC decision.

The Franc remains favored versus the Dollar, with USD/CHF forecasts lowered to 0.78, 0.76, and 0.74 (from 0.81, 0.79, 0.76) and EUR/CHF kept flat at 0.93. **CHF has in fact outperformed its typical relationship to gold since mid-August**, consistent with the view that it is moving back in line with its drivers and closing the gap to [REDACTED] fair value. Expected EUR upside should keep EUR/CHF rangebound.

Across the EM bullets, gold and politics dominate. In Indonesia, the new finance minister's arrival triggered an IDR and bond selloff and BI intervention; a plan to shift IDR 200trn (~USD 12bn, ~2.2ppt of system deposits) to state banks to boost lending is a liquidity positive, but fiscal credibility is the swing factor, with BI seen holding at 5% on September 17. In Thailand, a change of government did little to dent a strong THB, which tracked the gold rally; **as long as gold climbs and the BoT lacks credible measures to break the correlation, THB is unlikely to underperform despite weak fundamentals** — the short THB/KRW trade was closed for a ~3.5% loss.

For Turkey, spot stability masks rising political risk, visible in forwards moving on the CHP congress rulings even when spot held. **The long-TRY trade is no longer exceptional, with carry now comparable to peers like the Egyptian Pound, which is preferred**, and the TCMB's de-emphasis of real FX appreciation adds to the caution; USD/TRY forecasts are rolled to 43, 45, 50 (from 42, 44, 48). In Argentina, the float has delivered a large depreciation with limited inflation pass-through so far, but the October 26 midterms and thin reserves dominate the outlook. **Forecasts are revised sharply weaker to 1,515/1,560/1,650 (from 1,250/1,350/1,500), along the upper band**; forwards price a break of the regime (~1,595/1,693/1,905), but the authorities' willingness to intervene is read as commitment to the float, with risks skewed to a weaker Peso.

subject: European Credit Brief: Week ending September 12, 2025
summary:
# European credit withstands fiscal risk as compression returns to HY

**Theme:** Spreads shrug off UK/France sovereign risk; compression and cyclicality lead HY
**Markets:** European corporate credit (EUR/GBP IG and HY)
**Source:** [REDACTED], Sara Grut, September 12, 2025

### Landscape
- EUR and GBP corporate credit spreads returned to post-Covid lows versus USD peers (Exhibit 1).
- French IG issuers in EUR — chiefly financials — continue to lag the index, even as a subset trades below OATs (Exhibit 3).
- UK-domiciled issuers make up about 9% of the EUR HY benchmark and French issuers about 18%; French credit has been firm year-to-date and the UK has lagged (Exhibit 5).
- In EUR IG primary, about €30 billion was issued in the first two weeks of September, in line with the four-year seasonal average (~€27 billion); HY totaled ~€6.4 billion, versus a historical average near €2 billion (Exhibit 11).
- Cumulative gross issuance stands at ~€585 billion in IG and ~€85 billion in HY, on a record pace for the year.
- YTD flows: EUR IG at $61.6 billion (~9% of last year's AUM) and EUR HY at $4.4 billion (~4%), with weekly inflows of $1.1 billion in IG and $0.16 billion in HY (Exhibits 13 and 14).

### Drivers
- Favorable technicals and strong expected German growth momentum support EUR and GBP IG despite UK and France fiscal risk (Exhibits 1 and 2).
- Negative net supply in GBP IG — for a second straight year — plus comparatively cheap starting valuations contain the sovereign beta of UK issuers (Exhibits 2 and 4).
- In HY, positive UK net supply this year contrasts with negative net supply from France and the EUR HY index; combined with a difficult UK macro mix, this weighed on vulnerable balance sheets and widened spread dispersion (Exhibits 6 and 7).
- Compression has returned to EUR HY, with B/BB spreads narrowing versus July's highs, reflecting firmer growth expectations (Exhibit 8).
- Cyclical rotation in EUR HY: Supermarkets, Retail, and Autos lead year-to-date, while Healthcare, Utilities, and Food & Beverage lag (Exhibit 9).
- Supply absorption is solid: new-issue concessions in EUR IG have risen but remain well below the post-2017 average (Exhibit 12).

### Risks
- Downside: persistent underperformance of French IG issuers, chiefly financials — the analysis expects this to continue.
- Limited upside: in GBP IG, the resilience of UK issuers should persist, but the analysis sees no room for them to outperform the index.
- Upside: in EUR HY UK, given very cheap valuations versus the index, the analysis assesses that most of the underperformance is already behind it.
- In IG, richer starting valuations and idiosyncratic factors — including tariff risk — limit performance in select sectors.

### Unpacked
The EUR and GBP IG indices absorbed the UK and France fiscal noise without ceding ground. **Beneath the surface, though, dispersion by domicile matters: French issuers continue to lag the index even as some trade below OATs, and that gap is expected to persist.** In GBP, the resilience of UK names stems from negative net supply and cheap valuations that have contained sovereign beta — resilience expected to continue, but without an outperformance premium.

In high yield, the country picture flips relative to IG. **French credit has been firm versus the EUR HY index this year, while UK issuers have lagged — a move rooted in technicals, not fundamentals.** Positive UK net supply, against negative supply from France and the EUR HY aggregate, concentrated pressure on more fragile balance sheets and widened dispersion. As UK issuer valuations in EUR HY are very cheap versus the index, the read is that most of the adjustment has already happened.

The compression theme has re-emerged clearly in HY and less so in IG. **The "down-in-quality" bias is clear in EUR HY, with B/BB narrowing since July's highs, but IG remains rangebound, with A vs. BBB barely moving.** At the sector level, HY shows a defined cyclical rotation (Supermarkets, Retail, Autos ahead; Healthcare, Utilities, Food & Beverage behind), whereas in IG the pattern is mixed — Chemicals and Utilities outperforming, Retail and Healthcare lagging.

The read is that cyclical and lower-quality leadership in HY reflects firmer growth expectations, while in IG richer valuations and idiosyncratic noise, tariffs included, limit specific sectors. **The stance remains overweight B vs. BB, sought mainly for extra carry rather than expectation of significant further compression.**

On the supply side, September started strong and was well absorbed, with IG and HY heading toward new gross issuance records. **The projection is for strong momentum through year-end, reaching around €725 billion in IG and €125 billion in HY, with record gross prints but net supply close to historical norms.** On the demand side, EUR IG inflows remain consistent and HY resumed positive flows after two weeks of outflows; the pace is attributed to the search for geographic diversification and a backdrop of firmer European growth, trends expected to persist.

subject: Global Rates Trader: Room to Cut, Less to Rally
summary:
# G10 Rates: Room to Cut, Less to Rally — Cut Pricing Is Rich, Term Premia Sticky

**Theme:** Duration's valuation cushion thins as front-ends price easing; long-ends stay steep to cyclicals  
**Markets:** G10 rates (US, Euro area, UK, Sweden, Japan)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], George Cole, 12 September 2025  

### Landscape
- Over 70bp of Fed cuts are priced for 2025 with terminal-rate pricing near ~2.8%, on the richer side of the recent range heading into the FOMC.
- US 5s10s has flattened 6bp and 10s30s over 7bp since before the prior Friday's payrolls, pushing 10s toward multi-year lows on the 5s10s30s fly.
- US 5s10s and 10s30s each remain ~20-30bp steep versus spot fair value despite the recent long-end outperformance.
- SOFR has set within +/-1bp of IORB since 2 September, versus an average 5.5bp below IORB through August, signalling lingering funding pressure.
- NY Fed custody holdings of USTs have fallen a further $54bn over the past month.
- ECB left policy unchanged and described it as in a 'good place'; almost all 2025 EUR cut pricing has now been removed.
- Markets price ~8bp of BOJ hikes for October and 17bp by year-end.

### Drivers
- US terminal-rate pricing is richening and cut pricing pulling forward, driven by softer-but-muddy labor data (higher initial claims, larger benchmark revisions) alongside close-to-consensus inflation that translates favorably to core PCE (0.2% expected for August) — watch next week's FOMC SEP and Powell for confirmation of the easing path's character.
- Greater conviction on near-term cuts and a lower endpoint is boosting long-end appeal, with the migration of richening from 5s to 10s; the long-end starts steep to cyclical factors, but global-yield and US-fiscal forces keep the term-premia reset intact.
- Funding-market tightness is building into Monday 15 September, when September tax collections coincide with $78bn of net coupon settlement; a ~$150bn liquidity drain is modelled as worth 4-5bp of upward SOFR pressure — watch the speed of normalization for signs of underlying tightness.
- Euro-area easing risk is fading as growth downside diminishes, flattening the EUR front-end (ERZ5Z7); a 2026 growth pickup and inflation bottoming should eventually re-steepen it.
- France is tentatively stabilising: a quickly named PM and resumed centre-left budget talks point to a small deficit improvement (5.4% in 2025 to 5.2% in 2026), supporting OATs.
- Riksbank easing continues on softer Swedish CPI and labour data, but SEK front-end remains tethered to the Euro area and flattened with Bunds on the ECB's hawkish tone.
- BOJ is on hold with the next hike expected January, contingent on wage-momentum signals; front-end short conviction is rising while further-out forwards (5y5y) have yet to participate.

### Risks
- Downside (yields): the analyst notes meaningfully lower US yields require labor-market news that more convincingly opens up left-tail worries — absent that, the rally is hard to sustain.
- Upside (yields): the belly is seen as more vulnerable to underperformance on a sharp shift in the macro outlook, and larger, more sustained funding spikes could visibly widen swap spreads, with the front-end more exposed than the belly.
- The analyst frames US front-end risk as asymmetric: a downside UK inflation surprise is flagged as the asymmetric outcome for UK front-end pricing after four consecutive misses.
- OAT rating actions are assessed as a manageable risk given idiosyncratic risk is already near the wides of its range.
- The analyst views ~8bp of BOJ October hike pricing as slightly overdone given the political calendar, while 17bp by year-end does not look excessive.

### Unpacked
In the US, the softer labour picture has been enough to sustain richening in terminal-rate pricing and some pull-forward of cuts, even without definitive evidence of a sharper slowdown. **With front-end rates now below the baseline expectation for the 2026 Fed path, the valuation case for duration longs is diminished, and further rally likely requires clearer evidence of economic slowing.** The recommendation for long SFRZ5 vs short ERZ5 is closed for a potential 23bp profit, driven by both the US pull-forward and the EUR repricing toward a no-cut baseline.

The FOMC is the week's focal point. An unchanged 2-cut 2025 median could read hawkish, though the market may discount it if paired with dovish language or lower 2026/2027 dots; a 3-cut median with a lower terminal rate would lower the bar to further front-loading on labour weakness. **Whether the FOMC frames easing as 'normalization cuts' or shows genuine concern about labour downside will dictate how much mass the market places on the left tail.** The preferred expression is low-strike conditional bull steepeners in 2s5s.

On the long end, the stronger fundamental catalyst, cheaper valuations, and positioning have combined to support outperformance and the shift of richening out toward 10s. **The read is a case against the long-end leading selloffs from here, rather than an argument for extended bull flattening, since global-yield and fiscal factors still support the term-premia reset.** The belly's low-vol, carry-friendly properties make its richness hard to unseat, but leave it exposed in the tails.

Funding dynamics warrant close monitoring: a pullback in tri-party volumes, a sustained rise in TGCR, and richening bills suggest money funds may be terming out ahead of cuts. Attention centres on Monday's combined tax and coupon-settlement draw, with Treasury due to pay down about $50bn in bills the next day. Swap spreads have been resilient to the funding move, consistent with some risk premium already embedded, but sustained spikes would likely bite. QT is still expected to end in October, and balance-sheet or SRF discussion at the FOMC will be watched.

In Europe, the further reduction in EUR cut pricing is judged justified, and the resulting front-end flattening should eventually reverse as 2026 growth improves and inflation risk bottoms — **the upward pressure in 2y2y rates is seen as the driver of sustainably higher Bund yields over time, with the 10y Bund forecast held at 3% for end-2025.** France's incremental improvement supports a maintained 70bp end-2025 target for 10y OAT-Bund, with scope for foreign buyers to return.

For the UK, the Gilt long-end rode the US-led rally, but next week's inflation print is the key domestic input after four consecutive misses and MPC concern over second-round effects. **With BoE policy-rate forecasts 60bp below market pricing to mid-2026, the recommendation remains long 2y vs 5y Gilts**, and UK CPI priced in line with the US out to 5y alongside activity weakness argues for a lower terminal rate than priced. Separately, QT is expected to slow from £100bn to £70bn, implying a modest rise in active sales from £13bn to £21bn with a skew away from long-end sales; the estimated 1-2bp swap-spread tightening per pp of free float points to only modest 30y compression. Durable Gilt outperformance would require renewed disinflation, BoE cuts, and modest fiscal tightening at the November budget.

In Japan, the BOJ is expected to hold and signal little urgency, with the next hike seen in January pending wage-momentum leading indicators. **Belly forward gaps (1y1y, 2y1y) have edged back toward prior cycle highs on rising short conviction, but further-out forwards like 5y5y have not yet followed** — a move expected to take time and hinge on wage signals, with resolution of political uncertainty a potential tailwind to both the hiking cycle's sustainability and long-end risk-premium compression.

subject: Weekly Fund Flows: Commodities Drive Cyclical Sector Inflows
summary:
# Cyclical Tilt Holds: Commodities Lead, Equities Turn to Net Selling

**Theme:** Risk appetite intact beneath a one-off US equity outflow; cyclicals still beating defensives  
**Markets:** Global fund flows (equities, fixed income, FX)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Isabella Rosenberg, 12 September 2025  

### Landscape
- Global equity funds swung to net outflows of -$10bn in the week ending September 10, down from +$18bn the prior week.
- Global fixed income funds took in +$17bn, slower than the prior week's +$22bn but still positive.
- Money market fund assets rose by $66bn.
- Commodities funds drew the largest sector inflows, with cyclical funds continuing to outpace defensive funds.
- In FX, CAD led G10 inflows as a share of AUM, while foreign flows into Asia slowed and demand for LatAm rose broadly.

### Drivers
- The equity reversal was driven mainly by an idiosyncratic domestic outflow from US equity funds; other G10 flows stayed positive but subdued.
- EM equity flows were mixed — global EM benchmark funds saw inflows while dedicated mainland China equity funds saw outflows.
- The fixed income slowdown came from smaller inflows into government and Agg-type bond funds; short-duration and inflation-protected funds kept attracting money while long-duration funds saw outflows.
- Within FX, Asia inflows were dragged by CNY outflows, offsetting broad-based LatAm demand.

### Unpacked
**The headline equity outflow overstates any shift in risk appetite: the -$10bn print was concentrated in a single domestic US equity outflow the report characterises as idiosyncratic, while the rest of G10 stayed positive.** Beneath the aggregate, the cyclical-over-defensive tilt persisted and commodities funds led all sectors, consistent with a risk-on posture rather than a defensive rotation.

**EM flows split by geography — global EM benchmark funds gained while dedicated mainland China equity funds lost — showing selective rather than uniform EM demand.** This divergence carried into FX, where CNY outflows slowed the broader foreign bid for Asia even as LatAm demand strengthened across the region.

**In fixed income, the composition points to defensive duration positioning within a still-positive flow picture:** money left long-duration bond funds while short-duration and inflation-protected funds kept drawing inflows, and the overall slowdown traced to lighter buying of government and Agg-type funds. Money market assets rose a further $66bn.

The note offers no explicit trade idea; it is a positioning and flows snapshot.

subject: USA: UMich Consumer Sentiment Declines; Long-Term Inflation Expectations Well Above Expectations
summary:
# US Consumer Confidence Slips as Long-Run Inflation Expectations Jump Unexpectedly

**Source:** [REDACTED], Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US consumer sentiment and inflation expectations  
**General comment:** Neutral data read-through; flags an upside surprise in long-run inflation expectations against a softening confidence backdrop.

### Context
A quick reaction to the University of Michigan's preliminary September 2025 consumer survey, which came in weaker than expected on sentiment and hotter than expected on longer-term inflation expectations.

### The case
- **Headline sentiment fell more than forecast, driven by expectations rather than current conditions.** The index dropped 2.8pt to 55.4, below both the [REDACTED] estimate (57.4) and consensus (58.0). The decline was concentrated in the forward-looking expectations component, which fell 4.1pt to 51.8, while current economic conditions were roughly flat, down just 0.5pt to 61.2. The survey ties the weakness to consumers seeing multiple vulnerabilities — risks to business conditions, labor markets, and inflation — with tariffs still front of mind, cited unprompted by about 60% of respondents, little changed from the prior month.
- **Near-term inflation expectations held steady, but the long-term measure surprised sharply to the upside.** One-year expectations were unchanged at 4.8%, matching consensus. The 5–10-year measure rose 0.4pp to 3.9%, well above both the [REDACTED] (3.4%) and median (3.4%) forecasts and up from a 3.5% prior — the notable divergence in the report.

### Implications
- The split signals softening confidence anchored in expectations, not in households' assessment of present conditions.
- The upside miss on long-run inflation expectations is the key watch item, as de-anchoring at that horizon carries more weight for policy than a steady near-term reading.
- Tariffs remain a persistent, salient driver of consumer concern.

subject: Top of Mind: Data (un)reliability
summary:
# US data reliability under strain: costs of lost trust fall on TIPS and the Dollar

**Theme:** Whether recent revisions and political interference threaten the reliability of US and global economic data — and what it costs if trust breaks  
**Markets:** US economic data, TIPS, US Dollar  
**Source:** [REDACTED] (Allison Nathan), 11 September 2025  

### Definitive impacts
- Large downward revisions to May and June US payrolls, cutting the previously reported pace of job growth for those months.
- A downward revision to the level of US employment in the BLS annual benchmark review, lowering the recorded employment base.
- TIPS are directly exposed, since their payoffs are mechanically tied to official inflation statistics; any loss of confidence in those figures hits the instrument directly.

### Opinative impacts
- Global economic data mostly remain reliable for now, per [REDACTED]'s Joseph Briggs — the immediate concern is the future trajectory, not present-day quality.
- The future of US data is at risk, argue Erica Groshen (former BLS Commissioner) and Harvard's Alberto Cavallo, tied partly to recent actions by the Trump Administration, including the dismissal of the BLS Commissioner.
- The opposite view, from Arthur Laffer: the Administration's actions should help secure data reliability going forward, not undermine it.
- The economic costs of losing trust in official data could be significant, [REDACTED] concludes, with the Dollar liable to weaken further as a consequence.

### Backdrop
Official statistics — payrolls, inflation, employment levels — are produced by government agencies such as the BLS and used as the reference point for policy, markets, and inflation-linked contracts. Their value rests on being seen as accurate and free from political interference. Revisions are a routine feature of the process as more complete source data arrives, but the credibility of the institution producing them is what lets markets treat the numbers as trustworthy. This edition of Top of Mind gathers competing expert views on how solid that credibility is, in the US and globally.

### At issue
A sequence of events has raised doubts about US data quality: substantial downward revisions to May and June payrolls; the subsequent dismissal of the BLS Commissioner; and a large downward revision to the level of employment in the BLS's annual benchmark review. The note frames these against the broader question of global data quality, noting such concerns are neither new nor unique to the US, and canvasses views from Groshen, Laffer, Cavallo, and [REDACTED] economists Briggs and Walker.

### Unpacked
The trigger is a run of bad news about US statistics arriving in close succession, capped by the removal of the official responsible for producing them. **The central question the note poses is not whether today's data are wrong, but whether the machinery that produces them can still be trusted tomorrow.** That reframing matters because it separates a technical issue — revisions, which are normal — from an institutional one — political interference, which is not.

**The expert panel splits precisely on that institutional axis:** Groshen and Cavallo read the Administration's actions as a threat to future data integrity, while Laffer reads the same actions as corrective. Briggs supplies the anchoring point that, for all the noise, the data themselves remain broadly reliable at present — locating the problem in expectations about the future rather than in the current numbers.

**The market conclusion is concrete: eroded trust carries a real economic price, lands directly on TIPS, and points to a weaker Dollar.** The TIPS channel is mechanical — the instrument settles against official inflation prints, so doubt about those prints is doubt about the asset. The Dollar channel is broader, reflecting confidence in US institutions overall. The note offers analysis and directional market implications rather than an explicit trade recommendation.

**→ Read in full:** the substance sits in the individual expert interviews (Groshen, Laffer, Cavallo, Briggs/Walker) and the detailed market analysis behind the TIPS and Dollar conclusions, none of which is reproduced here beyond its headline direction.

subject: Global Markets Daily: Macro Pricing Suggests Two Risks to a Friendly Baseline (Chang)
summary:
# Fed Pricing Has Overtaken Growth Fears — Two-Sided Risk to a Benign Baseline

**Theme:** Market prices resilient growth plus a dovish Fed; both recession and hawkish-repricing risks sit around the baseline  
**Markets:** US macro (equities and rates)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Vickie Chang, 11 September 2025

### Landscape
- US equities have made new highs over the past month, with the recovery since April built on confidence that soft growth is a one-off tariff adjustment.
- US 10y yields have fallen more than 30bp since end-July.
- The market now prices nearly three Fed cuts in 2025 and three more in 2026.
- Implied market pricing of forward US growth sits near 1.6% — slightly above [REDACTED] forecasts for the next four quarters but below its 1.8% Q4/Q4 2026 forecast.
- Equity implied volatility has declined, particularly at short tenors.

### Drivers
- The dominant recent move is a dovish reassessment of the Fed's reaction function, not a change in growth pricing; a slowing labor market is read as loosening the constraint that tariff-inflation uncertainty had placed on the Fed.
- Growth pricing has stayed resilient and stable: the weaker-than-expected July payrolls print triggered an initial 30–40bp growth downgrade, but that was short-lived and reversed.
- The market treats spot labor-market weakness as having limited read-through to the 2026 outlook, anchoring instead on a gradual reacceleration toward potential.
- Growth momentum is not yet turning sharply lower — data surprises are roughly neutral on average and survey-based indicators have turned more positive — but the next few months are the period of "maximum risk" as the tariff drag works through; watch the unemployment rate as the key trigger.

### Risks
- **Downside:** a sharper rise in unemployment turns the labor-market slowdown into a recessionary dynamic; because growth pricing is currently resilient, the analyst sees equities as vulnerable, cushioned only partly by the prospect of faster Fed easing.
- **Upside/hawkish:** if growth simply holds, the market may conclude it has priced too much easing; with little recession fear currently in the price, good news is more likely to reverse the dovish policy shock than to lift growth pricing, pushing rates up in a way less supportive of equities than in 2024.
- **Upside/bull case:** the analyst notes the market could still upgrade its growth view and/or expect an even more dovish 2026 FOMC, which would extend the friendly path for risk assets.

### Unpacked
The framework here decomposes joint moves in equities and yields into "growth" and "policy" shocks, assuming both markets price a single consistent narrative. **The reading it produces is that the apparent tension between record equities and falling yields resolves into one story — resilient growth plus a more dovish Fed — rather than two markets pricing different economic realities.** The note is explicit that this synchronization is an assumption requiring judgment: it is possible equities and rates are in fact pricing different views, so the narrative is offered as plausible, not certain.

**That narrative sits roughly on top of [REDACTED]'s own baseline — a gradual reacceleration toward potential in 2026 with the Fed cutting at the three remaining 2025 meetings and twice more in 2026 — an inherently benign setup.** Historical work on past cutting cycles supplies the key conditional: when cuts arrive without recession, equities have tended to keep rising after the first cut. The benign outcome therefore depends on one condition holding — that the market stays able to look through current weakness as temporary and contained.

**The two risks are the two ways that condition breaks, and the note frames them as roughly symmetric around the baseline.** On the downside, the unemployment rate is the pivotal indicator, both as the Fed's guide amid uncertainty over the true pace of job growth and the breakeven rate, and as a driver of risk premia through the link between job loss and risk aversion. On the hawkish side, the contrast is drawn against September 2024: then, recession fears had risen sharply, so reassuring growth news let the market relax and supported equities even as yields rose. This time growth worry is limited, so the same kind of good news is more likely to unwind priced easing than to lift growth expectations.

**The hedging structure maps directly onto the two-sided risk rather than expressing a single trade idea.** With equity vol depressed, the note points to equity calls to express long views and puts for protection. In rates, front-end receivers protect against a negative growth shock, since the market still has room to pull the cutting cycle forward; against a hawkish shock, the more exposed points are later-2026 cut pricing and terminal-rate pricing further out toward the belly of the curve. The accompanying cross-asset trade list (FX, rates and equity ideas across USD/EGP, USD/JPY, SOFR flies, EM bonds and more) is a standing menu rather than an expression of this note's thesis.

subject: Fed Chatterbox: September Edition (Mei)
summary:
# Fed leans toward a cut: labor market outweighs inflation in the reaction function

**Theme:** Consensus favors cutting in September, with dissenters worried about inflation
**Markets:** US monetary policy (Federal Reserve)
**Source:** [REDACTED] (Pierfrancesco Mei), September 11, 2025

### Landscape
- [REDACTED] base case: three consecutive 25bp cuts in 2025 (September, October, and December), plus two more 25bp cuts in 2026, taking the terminal rate to 3-3.25%.
- Most participants classify current policy as "modestly restrictive"; Powell estimates the rate is 100bp closer to neutral than a year ago.
- Waller places the rate 1¼-1½ points above neutral, using the FOMC's June long-run median (3%) as the reference.
- Governors Bowman and Waller already voted for a cut at the July meeting.
- Core inflation remains about 1 percentage point above the 2% target, according to Musalem; Williams estimates tariffs will raise prices by 1 to 1.5% in total, with the effect lasting through mid-2026.

### Drivers
- Labor market weakening pulls the committee toward a cut: Powell points to "rising downside risks to employment"; Waller warns conditions "could deteriorate quickly and sharply" and sees private job creation near "stall speed."
- Convergence around Jackson Hole: several participants adopted Powell's framing that "policy in restrictive territory" justifies adjusting the stance toward neutral.
- Dominant tariff thesis — a one-time level shock: Bowman, Waller, Williams, and Daly expect a temporary effect, with inflation expectations anchored; the next battle is confirming whether the services "uptick" is noise or signal.
- Stable, not growing, hawkish undercurrent: Hammack and Schmid maintain that a "modestly restrictive" stance is still needed because "inflation remains too high"; Musalem and Collins see risk of a "larger and more persistent" tariff impact.
- Divergence on the labor diagnosis: Williams, Barkin, Bostic, and Schmid read the market as "in balance," against the camp (Waller, Bowman, Cook, Daly, Musalem) emphasizing downside risks — the data to watch are unemployment, layoffs, openings, and hires rates.

### Risks
- Downside (employment): Powell and Daly warn that if downside risks materialize, the labor market "falls fast and hard," with layoffs and unemployment rising abruptly — the central reason to cut preemptively.
- Upside (inflation): Musalem cautions that giving excessive weight to employment risks over-easing, with curve steepening, a higher term premium, and de-anchored expectations; Bostic does not rule out a new inflationary "flare-up."
- Tariff persistence: Collins, Bostic, Kashkari, and Goolsbee flag that tariffs may not be "one and done"; Goolsbee describes them as having a "stagflationary component" and Kashkari admits the effects may take "quarters or a year" to become clear.
- Asymmetry: the balance of risks has shifted toward employment — Bowman says upside risks to price stability "have diminished," while downside risks to labor have gained weight in the committee's reaction function.

### Unpacked
Since the July meeting, **the FOMC's center of gravity has clearly shifted toward a September cut**, anchored in Powell's Jackson Hole remarks that policy in restrictive territory, combined with the shift in the balance of risks, may justify adjusting the stance. Waller is the most explicit: he wants to "get ahead" of the labor market and would support 25bp in September, signaling 100-150bp of cuts over the next 3-6 months, with the pace — every meeting or every other meeting — data-dependent. Bostic converges on "around 25bp" for the rest of the year, and Williams acknowledges it will become appropriate to move the rate toward neutral.

The debate's axis is the labor market, and that's where views diverge. **One camp emphasizes that the current balance is fragile and could break quickly**; Powell describes a "curious balance," resulting from simultaneous slowing in labor supply and demand, which raises downside risks to employment. Waller, Cook, and Daly reinforce the idea that when the market stumbles, it "falls fast and hard." On the other side, Williams, Barkin, Bostic, and Schmid see a market "in balance" and resist reading too much into the payrolls slowdown — Goolsbee notes that immigration, labor supply, and participation distort the aggregate numbers, and prefers to look at unemployment, layoffs, openings, and hires rates.

On inflation, **most treat the tariff effect as a one-time level shock that policy should "look through,"** as long as expectations remain anchored. Waller sums up the logic: it makes no sense to raise rates for a level effect expected to end in about six months. Williams reinforces that he sees no amplification or second-round effects, with short- and medium-term expectations back within pre-pandemic ranges. The caveat comes from services: Goolsbee wants to confirm whether the recent "uptick" is a "blip" or a more ominous signal, and describes the current tariffs as having a "stagflationary component," since they were not "one and done."

The hawkish dissent is a minority, but firm. **Hammack and Schmid maintain that inflation remains too high and that a modestly restrictive stance is still needed**; Schmid notes that equity prices near highs and credit spreads near lows do not suggest policy that is very restrictive. Musalem and Collins occupy the middle ground, accepting the cut but warning of a potentially more persistent tariff impact. Kashkari admits two cuts in 2025 are reasonable, but prefers to adjust and, if needed, pause or reverse, rather than wait for full clarity on tariffs.

On restrictiveness, **there is broad agreement that policy is only "modestly restrictive" — the disagreement is over what to do about it**. Bowman and Waller want to move proactively toward neutral to avoid unnecessary erosion of employment, and Daly judges policy "probably too restrictive for where the economy is heading." Hammack, at the other extreme, sees the rate a "very small distance" from neutral and calls for caution in removing restriction. The document carries no explicit trade recommendation beyond [REDACTED]'s own rate call: three cuts in 2025 and a terminal rate of 3-3.25% in 2026.

subject: USA: Core CPI in Line With Expectations; Initial Jobless Claims Higher Than Expected; Estimating 0.20% for August Core PCE
summary:
# US: Core CPI In Line, but PCE Components Weaker and Claims at Highest Level Since 2021

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US inflation and labor market data (August 2025 CPI and weekly jobless claims)  
**General comment:** Descriptive data read; broadly dovish tilt — reads the softer PCE-relevant components and rising claims as consistent with cooling inflation and a weakening labor market.

### Context
Reaction to the August 2025 US CPI print and the weekly jobless claims release. The core question is what these reports imply for the Fed's preferred gauge (core PCE) and for the trajectory of the labor market.

### The case
- **Core CPI met expectations, but the strength was concentrated and partly volatile.** Core rose 0.35% MoM (YoY up to 3.11%). Volatile airfares (+5.9%) and used cars (+1.0%) together added 8bp. Shelter rose 0.44%, driven by a reacceleration in rent (+0.30%) and OER (+0.38%) above their recent three-month averages, plus a 2.6% jump in hotel prices after prior declines and a start-of-school-year rise in housing at school. The rent/OER strength was concentrated in small Southern cities, where OER posted its fastest sequential pace on record. Apparel added 2bp, helped by a record 5.5% rise in jewelry and watches.

- **The components most relevant for core PCE came in softer than the headline core CPI suggested.** Dental care fell 0.7% (after +2.6%), recreation goods were flat, and computer software — which carries a larger weight in core PCE than in core CPI — dropped 5.7%. Because of this, the August core PCE estimate is cut to 0.20% (from 0.30% expected pre-CPI), a 2.92% YoY rate, with market-based core PCE estimated at just 0.16%.

- **Jobless claims rose sharply, but the spike is partly a Texas and seasonal-adjustment story.** Initial claims jumped 27k to 263k, above forecasts, with roughly three-fourths of the increase concentrated in Texas (+21k). Labor Day timing can distort the reading — 2014, the last year with a comparable calendar, saw a similar initial spike that was later revised down and reversed. That caveat is stated openly rather than dismissed.

- **Even allowing for the noise, the labor market trend is softening.** Claims have risen steadily over recent weeks to their highest level since 2021, and other indicators, including payroll growth, have weakened in recent months. Continuing claims, however, were unchanged at 1,939k, slightly below consensus — leaving the deterioration concentrated in new claims rather than in the pool of ongoing recipients.

### Implications
- The lower core PCE estimate points to a milder read on the Fed's preferred inflation gauge than the core CPI headline implies, supporting a more dovish interpretation of the data.
- Rising initial claims at a multi-year high, alongside softer payrolls, reinforce a cooling-labor-market narrative — though the Texas concentration and holiday distortion argue against over-reading a single week.
- Watch next week's claims for a reversal, as occurred in the comparable 2014 calendar, before treating the jump as a clean trend signal.

subject: USA: PPI Below Expectations in August; Estimating +0.30% for Core PCE
summary:
# US PPI Undershoots in August, but Core PCE Still Tracking +0.30%

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US inflation data (August PPI and core PCE read-through)  
**General comment:** Neutral, technical read; headline PPI surprised soft, but the components that feed core PCE were slightly firmer, leaving the inflation trajectory little changed.

### Context
The note reacts to the August PPI release, which came in below expectations, and translates the report into an updated estimate for core PCE — the Fed's preferred inflation gauge — ahead of the next day's CPI print.

### The case
- **Headline and core PPI fell in August despite expectations for a rise, and the prior month was revised down.** PPI declined 0.1% (vs. +0.3% median) and PPI ex-food and energy also fell 0.1% (vs. +0.3% median), with July revised lower to +0.7%. The headline drop reflected weaker energy (-0.4%) and a 1.7% decline in retailer and wholesaler margins, while food rose 0.1%. The softness was concentrated in the volatile trade-services (margins) component rather than in underlying prices.
- **Stripping out that noise, the firmer measures held in line.** PPI ex-food, energy, and trade services rose 0.3%, matching expectations, and the 'old methodology' core PPI (finished goods ex-food and energy) also rose 0.3%. Core intermediate prices gained 0.4%, while crude materials ex-food and energy fell 0.5%.
- **The categories that actually map into core PCE came in slightly firmer than expected.** Passenger airfares rose 1.0% and portfolio management prices rose 2.0%. Medical care categories relevant to PCE increased on net, implying an estimated 0.23% month-over-month rise in PCE medical care services. On balance these inputs offset the soft headline.

### Implications
- The read-through keeps the core PCE estimate essentially unchanged: +0.30% in August (up marginally from +0.29% pre-report), a +3.01% year-over-year rate — i.e., a weak PPI headline does not signal cooler underlying inflation.
- The estimate is preliminary and will be revised after the CPI report, which carries additional core PCE inputs.

subject: Global Markets Analyst: The Rising Tide of Government Interest Costs (Cole)
summary:
# G10 Interest Costs Keep Rising Even as Policy Rates Fall

**Theme:** Modelling how refinancing, WAM and rate cuts reshape sovereign interest burdens  
**Markets:** Developed markets (G10)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], George Cole, 10 September 2025  

### Key findings
- Government interest costs are still climbing across G10 even after policy-rate peaks, because high existing debt stocks are being refinanced at rates above their current average — the peak-rate turn does not relieve the budget.
- Marketable-debt interest spending is projected to rise by an average of 0.5pp of GDP by 2029, with France, Japan and the US facing the largest increases given their deficit paths, debt levels and the forward curve.
- Shortening the weighted-average maturity (WAM) does little to contain the burden: a two-year cut yields only small savings, largest for Japan (0.24pp) and the UK (0.13pp) — falling short as a fix.
- Cutting front-end rates below market pricing helps more than shortening WAM, but only genuinely reduces costs if lower rates are justified by lower inflation rather than weaker growth; a 100bp extra cut saves most in the US (0.51pp), Japan (0.43pp) and Italy (0.28pp).
- As a rule of thumb, shortening WAM by one year is worth ~3bp, lowering front-end rates ~19bp, and cutting the deficit by 1pp ~13bp (with the deficit effect compounding over time via a smaller debt stock).
- Spending is set to stay inelastic — non-discretionary health and social protection sit near historical highs and planned defence increases add to them — while elevated revenue-to-GDP ratios (especially in Europe) leave little room to close deficits through tax and correlate with lower growth.
- The pressure is already priced: term premia keep climbing, 30y yields have reached multi-decade highs, curves are steep despite high front-end rates, and fiscal events carry outsized market volatility.

### Method & verdict
[Reasonable] The note builds a projection model for sovereign interest costs from three inputs — current forward rate curves, official deficit paths, and each country's debt term structure and existing WAM — then runs two stylized ceteris paribus scenarios (a two-year WAM reduction, and front-end cuts of 100bp at 2y / 50bp at 5y with 10–30y held constant) to isolate policy levers. It is grounded in observable market and IMF/OECD data across the G10 and is transparent about its assumptions, but the scenario results depend on holding macro variables fixed — an acknowledged simplification, since the conditions that lower rates (e.g. weaker growth) would often also widen deficits — and lean on official deficit forecasts the note itself flags as prone to slippage.

### Unpacked
The study starts from an apparent puzzle: central banks are past their rate peaks, yet the interest bill governments pay keeps growing. **The resolution is refinancing — debt issued cheaply in the post-GFC and pandemic years now rolls over at higher rates, so the marginal cost of debt sits well above the average cost still embedded in the stock.** Because deficits in most developed markets are wide by historical standards, fresh borrowing compounds the effect. WAM governs the speed of this pass-through: short-WAM issuers like the US feel it fast, while longer-WAM markets are insulated for longer.

**Whether rising interest costs actually signal fiscal deterioration hinges on the real rate relative to real growth, not the headline number.** If higher costs reflect stronger inflation or growth, sustainability is unaffected; if they reflect a higher real rate or a risk premium demanded against fiscal risk, the outlook worsens. This framing is what lets the note separate benign from damaging rate rises.

The two policy levers are tested against that baseline. **Shortening WAM captures some saving from steeper curves but delivers little, and buys that saving at the cost of higher funding-cost volatility and greater rollover risk** — and countries with already-short WAMs, like the US and Canada, have limited room to shorten further. **Cutting front-end rates works better, but the note is careful that it only truly lowers the burden when driven by genuinely lower inflation; a cut unjustified by the data risks pushing long-end yields up on inflation-risk premium.** The rule-of-thumb figures make the ranking concrete: deficit reduction beats WAM shortening and compounds over time.

The spending backdrop is what makes these levers matter. **With non-discretionary health and social protection near record shares of GDP, defence spending set to rise, and European revenue already so high that further tax increases are both hard and growth-negative, budgets are structurally inelastic on both sides.** The implication for the reader is a rates view rather than a discrete trade: terminal rates settling high, curves staying steep on elevated long-end premium, fiscal events driving volatility, and — the one directional call — 30y Gilts outperforming Bunds over time as UK inflation eases and European cyclical pressure builds.

subject: US Economics Weekly Update 9/9/2025
summary:
# Fed on track for three cuts as labor market softens and tariffs keep core PCE elevated

**Theme:** August CPI/jobs read — softening labor market, sticky-but-declining core inflation, three 2025 cuts  
**Markets:** US inflation, labor, and monetary policy  
**Source:** [REDACTED], David Mericle, 9 September 2025  

### Landscape
- Nonfarm payrolls rose just 22k in August, with the unemployment rate up 8bp to 4.3%.
- Underlying job growth is estimated at 41k after modestly negative net revisions — below the 80k breakeven rate.
- Average hourly earnings rose 0.3% in the month and 3.7% year-on-year.
- Core PCE inflation stands at 2.9% year-on-year; core services inflation is 3.5%, above its 2.75% pre-pandemic pace when core PCE was last at 2%.
- Q3 GDP is tracking +1.6% annualized; 2025 Q4/Q4 real GDP is forecast at 1.3%, about 1pp below a no-policy-change baseline.

### Drivers
- Labor demand is cooling: underlying job growth of 41k sits below breakeven, and the preliminary benchmark revision implies an 911k downgrade over April 2024–March 2025 — though this is seen as likely exaggerated.
- Tariffs are pushing inflation up: they add an estimated 0.14pp to August core CPI in exposed categories and are expected to lift core PCE from 2.9% to 3.2% later this year.
- Core services disinflation has stalled — slowing only 0.2pp over the year — as easing housing and labor-intensive prices are offset by firmer healthcare, transportation, and financial services.
- Shelter should keep slowing: catch-up effects are done, apartment supply growth is strong, and demand has softened (primary rent forecast +0.25%, OER +0.26% in August).
- The August payroll print is expected to be revised up, consistent with the recent seasonal pattern; for other months, revisions are seen as more likely negative.

### Risks
- The benchmark revision is judged too large on two grounds: QCEW source data has persistently been revised up, and it likely excludes unauthorized immigrants initially captured in payrolls.
- Uncertainty over the breakeven rate — and what pace of job growth is "good enough" given the immigration slowdown — makes the unemployment rate an unusually important signal, per the analyst.
- Firmer categories pose upside inflation risk: healthcare catch-up to pandemic cost spikes could persist, and transportation is directly exposed to auto-parts tariffs.

### Unpacked
For August CPI, the forecast is a 0.36% rise in core prices (vs. 0.3% consensus) and 3.13% year-on-year, driven by used cars (+1.2%), new cars (+0.2%), car insurance (+0.4%), and airfares (+3%, partly seasonal distortion, partly firmer underlying fares). Shelter is expected roughly steady. Headline CPI is seen at +0.37% on higher food (+0.35%) and energy (+0.6%), consistent with a **0.29% rise in core PCE for the month.**

On the labor benchmark, the model of net job gains from firm births and deaths points to a downward revision of 550k, or 45k per month — smaller than the reported cut. **This implies monthly job growth over the period was closer to 100k than the initially reported 147k, but not as low as the 71k pace the revisions suggest.** The BLS birth-death adjustment was probably too generous in 2024H2, but the overstatement is estimated to have narrowed to about 10k jobs/month, so extrapolating from the benchmark is cautioned against. The revision covers the year ending March 2025 and says little about the current state of the labor market, which is still judged to have softened materially.

**The soft payrolls and higher unemployment rate raised confidence in three consecutive 25bp cuts in September, October, and December**, followed by two more quarterly cuts in 2026 to a 3–3.25% terminal rate.

On the inflation path, core services inflation is still seen returning toward the 2% target despite recent slow progress. **PCE core services inflation is forecast at 3.2% by December 2025 and 3.0% by July 2026.** Tariffs are expected to raise overall core PCE to 3.2% later this year, but core PCE excluding tariff effects should keep falling from 2.6% now to 2.3% by December and 2.0% by July 2026 — the disinflation trend continuing beneath the tariff bump.

subject: USA: BLS Estimates 911k Downward Revision to Payroll Employment in March 2025
summary:
# BLS's 911k payroll revision overstates how much US job growth was really inflated

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US labor market — annual payroll benchmark revision  
**General comment:** Reads the headline revision skeptically; argues the true overstatement was smaller and stresses the data is backward-looking.

### Context
The BLS released its preliminary benchmark revision for payroll growth over April 2024–March 2025 at -911k (-76k/month), the largest such downward revision since at least 2000 and at the top of [REDACTED]'s own -550k to -950k range. This piece pushes back on reading that headline at face value as a measure of how weak hiring actually was.

### The case
- **The -911k figure likely overstates the true overcount, because the QCEW source data systematically undercounts and gets revised up.** The QCEW draws on unemployment-insurance records, so it misses many unauthorized immigrants who added materially to employment in recent years (though this matters less going forward given slower immigration). Separately, the QCEW has been revised upward in every quarter since 2019 except 2020H1, and the preliminary benchmark has come in below the final revision in each of the last five years — by 119k on average. This upward-revision tendency is why the BLS benchmarks to the QCEW only annually and with a long lag.

- **[REDACTED]'s own firm birth/death model implies a smaller correction of about -550k (-45k/month), not -911k.** Net job gains from business formation and closure are the main source of monthly uncertainty that benchmarking exists to fix. Using higher-frequency business-formation and bankruptcy data plus the BED program, [REDACTED] estimates true job growth over the period was closer to 100k/month than the 71k implied by the revision — above the reported 147k only in the sense that it, too, was overstated, but by less than the headline suggests.

- **The overstatement was concentrated in time and has since faded.** The BLS's birth-death adjustment was probably too generous in 2024H2, but [REDACTED] estimates the excess has narrowed to roughly 10k jobs/month now — a caution against extrapolating the large benchmark number to the present.

- **By sector, weakness clustered in a few areas.** Revisions were largest in leisure and hospitality, professional services, retail and wholesale trade. Taken at face value, the estimates imply outright contraction in professional services (-18k/month), manufacturing (-14k), information (-7k), retail (-7k), wholesale (-5k) and mining (-1k).

### Implications
- The revision says little about the labor market now: it covers a distant window and does not touch the household survey (unemployment rate) or other current indicators.
- The final, incorporated revision won't land until the January 2026 employment report in February 2026 — and history suggests it will be smaller than -911k.
- Despite discounting the headline, [REDACTED] still holds that the labor market has softened materially.

subject: US Economics Analyst: Services Inflation: Are We Still on Track? (Peng)
summary:
# Core Services Inflation: Progress Stalled at 3.5%, but [REDACTED] Still Sees a Path to 2%

**Theme:** Whether slower core-services disinflation derails the return of core PCE to target, examined category by category  
**Markets:** US inflation  
**Source:** [REDACTED] (Elsie Peng), 8 September 2025  

### Definitive impacts
- Year-on-year core services inflation fell just 0.2pp to 3.5% over the past 12 months, versus the 2.75% pace it ran at when core PCE was last at 2% pre-pandemic.
- Shelter's three-month annualized rate has slowed to 3.3% (in line with the pre-pandemic 2%-core pace), while the year-on-year rate remains 4% because earlier catch-up-driven readings are still in the lookback window.
- Official shelter prices have now fully caught up to market rents in level terms, exhausting the catch-up effect.
- Alternative new-lease rent growth measures have fallen to 1.6% (multifamily) and 2.1% (single-family) year-on-year, both below pre-pandemic averages.
- Wage growth in labor-intensive services has cooled from a peak above 8% to about 3% in recent months.
- Financial services inflation rose to 5.5% year-on-year, driven largely by the 2024H2 equity rally.
- Healthcare inflation accelerated from 2.3% to 2.7% year-on-year, with current prices still below the pandemic-era spike in input costs.
- Wholesale auto-parts prices from domestic producers rose notably following auto and country-level tariffs, lifting inflation in motor-vehicle maintenance and car-rental services.
- Current core PCE is 2.9% year-on-year; excluding tariff effects it is 2.6%.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] sees core services inflation declining to 3.2% year-on-year by December 2025 and 3.0% by July 2026, led by housing, labor-intensive services, and financial services.
- [REDACTED] expects core PCE ex-tariffs to keep falling — to 2.3% by December and 2.0% by July 2026 — while tariffs temporarily lift headline core PCE from 2.9% to 3.2% later this year as a one-time, mostly-goods effect.
- Shelter inflation is expected to slow to a 2.9% annualized pace by December and 2.6% by mid-2026, with the year-on-year rate reaching 3.4% by year-end and 2.8% by July 2026, on softer demand (reduced immigration) and strong multifamily completions.
- Labor-intensive inflation is seen easing from 3.2% (July) to 3.0% by December as a soft labor market pressures wages.
- [REDACTED] argues the sharp immigration slowdown will not materially threaten this disinflation, because the labor market is now in balance — unlike the tight 2022 backdrop — and immigration shifts move wages little under balanced conditions.
- Financial services inflation is expected to slow to 4.7% by December as last year's equity gains exit the lookback window.
- Healthcare is seen staying firm at roughly 2.7% through 2025 and edging to 2.8% in 2026, kept ~1pp above its pre-pandemic rate by slow, contract-lagged catch-up to pandemic cost increases.
- Transportation services inflation is expected to stay above 3% year-on-year in December, with tariff-driven input costs adding about 0.4pp in 2025.

### Backdrop
Returning core PCE to the Fed's 2% target has historically meant core services running somewhat hot (near 2.75%) offset by mildly negative core goods inflation. For roughly three years, the disinflation engine has been labor-market rebalancing and the fading of pandemic-era catch-up inflation. Core services is not a monolith: shelter and labor-intensive categories respond to rents and wages, financial services tracks equity markets with a lag, and healthcare adjusts slowly because of long contract cycles. Shelter indexes blend existing and new leases, so official measures lag market rents by design.

### At issue
