Progress on core PCE has stalled recently, even before new tariffs took effect, and core services inflation has barely moved — down only 0.2pp to 3.5% over the past year. The note decomposes that stall: disinflation in housing and labor-intensive sectors has been largely offset by firmer healthcare, transportation, and financial services. It then re-examines each component's outlook to test whether the underlying trend is still on track to 2%.

### Unpacked
The trigger is a credibility question about [REDACTED]'s own forecast. If the underlying trend is really converging on target, why has the most tariff-insulated part of the index — core services — refused to fall much over a full year? **The answer the note lands on is compositional: the trend is intact, but a rotation in which categories are hot has masked continued progress underneath.**

On the disinflating side, the housing story is the linchpin. **The catch-up of official shelter to market rents is now declared fully exhausted, which removes the mechanical drag that kept the year-on-year rate elevated and clears the way for softening new-lease rents to pass through.** Reduced immigration and heavy multifamily supply do double duty here — cooling demand while rental vacancies rise — and the same immigration slowdown is pre-empted as a wage risk, on the argument that labor supply shocks matter far less when the market is already balanced.

The offsetting categories are where the forecast leans hardest on interpretation. **Financial services disinflation is nearly mechanical — a lookback-window effect as the 2024 equity rally rolls off — but healthcare and transportation are expected to stay firm for structural reasons that also make them slow to reverse.** Healthcare's long contracts mean prices are still climbing toward pandemic-era costs, a source of persistent upside; transportation carries a genuine tariff footprint through auto-parts input costs, the one place where the "tariffs are goods-only" framing bleeds into services.

For the reader, the practical payoff is the split forecast: headline core PCE ticks up to 3.2% on a one-time tariff bump, while the ex-tariff series is claimed to reach 2.0% by July 2026. **The whole note is an argument for looking through the tariff-driven acceleration to an underlying trend [REDACTED] insists is still landing on target — the same read the Fed leadership holds.** The note offers no explicit trade idea; it is a forecast-maintenance piece.

subject: Global Views: Still Softening
summary:
# US Labor Market Softens Enough to Lock In a September Fed Cut

**Theme:** Cooling jobs data confirms a below-breakeven pace, validating a gradual easing path even as tariff-driven inflation rises  
**Markets:** US monetary policy (with Euro area, China and EM growth context)  
**Source:** [REDACTED] (Jan Hatzius), 8 September 2025

### Definitive impacts
- Nonfarm payroll growth slowed to 22k in August, while [REDACTED]'s broader trend estimate (moving averages of the establishment and household surveys) edged up to 41k on stronger household employment.
- The unemployment rate rose to 4.32%, a new cycle high, consistent with the payroll signal.
- [REDACTED]'s summary measure of labor-market tightness (unemployment, openings, quits, business and consumer surveys) has resumed declining and now sits clearly below its pre-pandemic level.
- China's August exports grew 4.4% year-on-year in nominal dollar terms despite a 33% year-on-year drop in exports to the US, as producers redirected to other markets.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] sees a 25bp cut as sealed for the September 16–17 FOMC, followed by 25bp cuts at both remaining 2025 meetings (October and December) and two more quarterly cuts, leaving the funds rate at 3–3¼% by June 2026; market pricing has converged toward this but stays a bit above [REDACTED]'s probability-weighted path.
- [REDACTED] expects underlying job growth to stay below its 80k "breakeven" rate near-term, given a below-potential 1.3% Q4/Q4 2025 GDP estimate, and pencils in an upward revision to the August payroll figure next month.
- [REDACTED] argues the Fed should look through the tariff-driven rise in core PCE (seen reaching 3.2% by Q4), treating it as a one-off price-level shock akin to a VAT hike that fades in 2026–2027, barring second-round effects — especially with the employment mandate calling for a more neutral stance.
- [REDACTED] expects the US economy to reaccelerate toward a solid ~2¼% potential in 2026 as the tariff drag abates, fiscal policy turns expansionary and easing continues, with AI-driven productivity a growing support.
- [REDACTED] sees the ECB as done easing (2% deposit-rate baseline, risks skewed lower) and expects European growth to pick up, helped by Germany's Q4 fiscal boost; the French political crisis is judged manageable, with wider spreads offset by slower deficit reduction.
- Strategy views: rates strategists expect the Fed/ECB spread to narrow more than priced and a steeper UK gilt curve; FX strategists expect renewed dollar weakness on overvaluation and current-account deficit; equity strategists see modest positive returns; commodity strategists favor gold on Fed easing, reserve diversification, and Fed-independence and geopolitical concerns.

### At issue
The August US employment report is the trigger. Payrolls rose just 22k and unemployment ticked up to 4.32%, confirming a material softening of the labor market. [REDACTED] reads this as removing any doubt about a September rate cut and pushing market pricing for later meetings closer to its own forecast. The note is [REDACTED]'s weekly global macro round-up, so it also folds in updated reads on Europe, China and emerging markets alongside the US call.

### Unpacked
**The core message is that softening is real but orderly — loose enough to justify cuts, not weak enough to signal contraction.** Heightened uncertainty around both the true pace of hiring (falling survey response rates, large revisions) and the breakeven rate (volatile immigration) has raised the weight [REDACTED] places on the unemployment rate relative to payrolls. This month the two agreed, which strengthens confidence in the softening signal rather than leaving it ambiguous.

**The rate call rests on separating a price-level shock from genuine inflation.** Tariff pass-through is expected to lift core PCE further, but [REDACTED] frames it as a one-time step akin to a VAT hike whose impact recedes over 2026–2027. An inflation-targeting central bank looks through such shocks, and with the labor side of the mandate now arguing for a more neutral setting, the note treats above-target inflation as no barrier to easing.

**The optimism about 2026 hinges on productivity outrunning the hit from lower immigration.** Real GDP per hour has grown 1.8% annualized in nonfarm business and 2.6% in the nonfinancial corporate sector since 2019Q4, and a growing AI contribution is expected to sustain or lift that. This is what lets [REDACTED] pair a weak near-term jobs picture with a reacceleration toward ~2¼% potential.

**Outside the US, the through-line is resilience feeding into a "done easing" stance abroad and steady EM growth.** Europe's Q3 tracking disappointed but the trade drag is fading and German fiscal support is due in Q4, supporting the view that the ECB has finished cutting. China's export strength despite US tariffs has nudged [REDACTED]'s 2025 growth forecast up to 4.7% with upside risks, part of a broader pattern of EMs holding near 4% while advanced economies wobble.

The note offers no explicit standalone trade idea; the actionable content is the strategy stance embedded in the opinative impacts (narrower Fed/ECB spread, steeper UK curve, weaker dollar, long gold).

subject: US Daily: August CPI Preview (Rindels/Walker)
summary:
# August CPI: Core at 0.36%, a Tick Above Consensus on Autos, Airfares, and Tariffs

**Theme:** Tariff pass-through and firm goods prices push core CPI slightly above consensus, even as underlying trend inflation cools  
**Markets:** US inflation  
**Source:** [REDACTED] (Jessica Rindels), 8 September 2025  

### Estimates
- **+0.36% m/m core CPI** for August, above +0.3% consensus.
- **3.13% y/y core CPI**, versus +3.1% consensus.
- **+0.37% m/m headline CPI**, above +0.3% consensus, on higher food (+0.35%) and energy (+0.6%) prices.
- **2.90% y/y headline CPI**, in line with +2.9% consensus.
- **+0.29% m/m core PCE** implied by the CPI forecast, to be updated after this week's PPI and CPI.
- **+1.2% m/m used car prices**, on rising auction prices; **+0.2% new car prices**, on lower dealer incentives.
- **+0.4% m/m car insurance**, per online premium data.
- **+3% m/m airfares**, on seasonal distortions plus higher underlying fares from online price tracking.
- **+0.14pp tariff contribution to core**, spread across furniture (+0.8%), motor vehicle parts (+0.6%), apparel (+0.3%), recreation (+0.5%), personal care (+0.5%), communication (+0.2%), and education (+0.2%).
- **Shelter roughly flat on net**: rent +0.25% (vs +0.26% in July), owners' equivalent rent +0.26% (vs +0.28%).
- **~0.3% m/m core CPI over coming months**, sustained by tariffs.
- **December 2025: +3.1% y/y core CPI and +3.2% y/y core PCE** (both +2.3% excluding tariff effects).

### Outlook
- Tariffs will keep boosting monthly inflation over the next few months, with the sharpest goods-price increases in consumer electronics, autos, and apparel given their import reliance, and limited near-term impact on core services.
- Underlying trend inflation should fall further this year, as contributions from housing rents and the labor market shrink — the tariff and non-tariff forces pull in opposite directions.
- Car insurance increases should return to a sustainable, pre-pandemic pace now that most of the gap between premiums and costs has closed.

### Unpacked
The August forecast sits a touch above consensus across headline and core, and the gap is built from identifiable component moves rather than a broad reflation. **Used cars are the largest single swing, up 1.2% on higher Manheim auction prices, with new vehicles adding a smaller lift as dealers pull back incentives.** Airfares contribute a seasonal 3% jump, and car insurance adds a steady 0.4% as insurers finish passing through cost increases that regulators had delayed.

Tariffs are the through-line. **They account for +0.14pp of core this month, concentrated in import-exposed goods — furniture, vehicle parts, apparel, recreation, personal care, communication, and education — and are expected to keep monthly core running near 0.3% in the months ahead.** The mechanism is specific to goods: the note sees acute pressure in electronics, autos, and apparel, but little spillover into core services for now.

**Beneath the tariff noise, the disinflationary trend is still intact — shelter is essentially flat on net, and rent and OER are both decelerating slightly from July.** Stripping out tariffs, both core CPI and core PCE would land at 2.3% by December rather than the 3.1%/3.2% headline path, which frames the central tension for the reader: a genuine cooling in the rent- and labor-driven core, masked by a policy-driven goods shock.

Watch this week's PPI and CPI releases, which will drive the analyst's update to the +0.29% core PCE estimate, and the coming months' goods categories for the pace at which tariff pass-through actually shows up.

subject: Global Markets Daily: Q&A on Stablecoins and Financial System Implications (Zu)
summary:
# Stablecoins Add Treasury Demand but Threaten a Smaller, Costlier Banking System

**Theme:** How stablecoin adoption reshapes bank funding, deposits, and demand for USTs — and why foreign "dollarization" demand may be self-limiting  
**Markets:** US financial system, Treasuries and bank funding  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Bill Zu, 8 September 2025

### Definitive impacts
- At an individual bank, a customer withdrawing deposits to buy a stablecoin mechanically reduces that bank's reserves and deposits; a reserve-constrained bank must then liquidate securities or loans to meet the outflow.
- At the system level, the initial effect on aggregate deposits is roughly neutral: the deposit moves from the buyer's bank (A) to the T-Bill seller's bank (B), while the stablecoin issuer ends up holding the T-Bill and the buyer holds the stablecoin.
- Foreigners hold roughly half of USD physical currency in circulation, about $1tn as of Q1 2025 (Fed estimate) — the pool that could convert into stablecoins.
- Any foreign private access to USD stablecoins still requires an offsetting FX transaction as an on-ramp, so the foreign currency is ultimately converted into USD through traditional FX channels.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] sees the neutral-deposit outcome as an unstable equilibrium: the T-Bill seller (B) now earns uncompetitive deposit rates versus bills, forcing either higher deposit rates or rotation into money funds/repo/FHLB notes — the latter producing some incremental UST demand.
- Over the longer run [REDACTED] expects meaningful stablecoin growth to leave banks with more expensive, less deposit-heavy funding, compressing net interest margins and ultimately shrinking the aggregate bank balance sheet and credit intermediation.
- The risk falls hardest on smaller banks and those with concentrated or flight-prone (corporate rather than retail) deposit bases, since they rely more on deposit funding and interbank frictions can block timely liquidity redistribution — an SVB-like dynamic in extreme cases.
- [REDACTED]'s banks team views liquidity regulation as the most binding constraint going forward — given proposed SLR relaxation and lower CET1 requirements from this year's CCAR — which would raise the relevance of the stablecoin liquidity channel over time.
- Conversion of foreign-held physical cash into stablecoins is judged a net short-term boost to Treasury demand, but one [REDACTED] thinks could be offset long-term by a smaller Fed balance sheet.
- [REDACTED] is skeptical that foreign "dollarization" demand can grow substantially: genuinely incremental demand comes only from foreigners currently blocked by capital controls, and the resulting FX pressure would likely prompt those governments to extend similar controls to stablecoins.
- The note's core view on foreign demand: the advantage of stablecoins reduces to a regulatory arbitrage between how stablecoins and traditional capital-flow channels are treated abroad — nothing intrinsic to the instrument.

### Backdrop
Outside zero-lower-bound periods, bank deposits typically pay much less than T-Bills and other money-market instruments (Exhibit 1), so the relative yield on where short-term cash sits drives whether it stays as deposits or rotates elsewhere. Banks differ sharply in their reliance on deposit funding: smaller banks fund a larger share of assets with deposits (Exhibit 2), making them more exposed to deposit migration. The uneven distribution of reserves across banks — and the difficulty of redistributing liquidity quickly when interbank markets seize — is a standing policy challenge, not one created by stablecoins.

Foreign demand for USD comes in distinct forms already: official-sector holders have full access to USD assets (and their demand has been declining), while some foreign private holders hold physical USD cash and others are shut out of USD entirely by capital controls.

### At issue
This Daily answers three recurring investor questions following [REDACTED]'s earlier work on payment-stablecoin adoption and its implications for the US financial system, safe-asset demand, and Treasury issuance. The questions: (1) how stablecoins actually displace deposits when issuer asset purchases seem to recycle funds back into the system; (2) how bank heterogeneity changes those dynamics; and (3) whether foreign "dollarization" via stablecoins is a genuine tailwind for Treasuries. No new event or data release — this is a clarification of an existing thesis.

### Unpacked
The piece exists to rebut a specific pushback: if a stablecoin issuer spends deposit outflows on T-Bills, the seller receives a deposit, so nothing leaves the banking system. **[REDACTED] concedes the accounting is correct at a single point in time but argues it cannot hold as an equilibrium, because the swap leaves one party — the former T-Bill holder — earning deposit rates well below what bills pay.** That yield gap is the engine of the whole thesis; without it, stablecoins would simply reshuffle claims and nothing would change.

**The resolution of that gap runs two ways at once: banks pay up to keep funding, and some money rotates into money funds, repo and FHLB paper — which is where the incremental Treasury demand comes from.** The same force that generates extra UST demand is what erodes bank economics, so the two effects the note flags are two sides of one adjustment, not independent stories. In the near term it shows up as margin compression; over time, as a structurally smaller and costlier deposit base. [REDACTED] notes banks can defend themselves, for instance by offering tokenized deposits.

**Heterogeneity turns a gradual repricing into a potential stress channel:** deposit flight from banks that are already liquidity-tight or hold few safe assets forces asset sales rather than orderly funding substitution, and interbank frictions can stop reserves reaching the banks that need them. This is layered onto a regulatory backdrop the banks team reads as shifting toward liquidity rules as the binding constraint, which is why the concern is framed as rising in relevance rather than immediate.

**On foreign demand, the argument narrows a broad bullish story down to a single genuinely incremental channel — and then questions its durability.** Conversion from existing USD assets is unlikely on yield grounds; conversion from physical cash is real but potentially offset by a smaller Fed balance sheet; only foreigners locked out by capital controls represent demand that would not otherwise exist. Even there, the required FX on-ramp generates the same exchange-rate pressure that motivated capital controls in the first place, so the benefit ultimately rests on a regulatory gap that foreign governments can close. The practical takeaway for a UST investor: the stablecoin demand tailwind is real but conditional and probably modest, while the banking-sector consequences are the more durable structural shift to watch. The note carries no trade idea tied to this thesis; its listed trade ideas are a separate cross-asset book unrelated to the stablecoin analysis.

subject: [REDACTED] FX Morning Notes: The Push and Pull on the Yen
summary:
# JPY Shrugs Off Ishiba's Exit as Global Factors Take Over

**Theme:** Why the Yen's selloff on Japanese political uncertainty was unexpectedly muted, and how the news reshapes [REDACTED]'s broader FX views  
**Markets:** Global FX; Japan politics and rates  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Michael Cahill, 8 September 2025  

### Definitive impacts
- JPY sold off only ~0.75–1.0% versus other cyclical assets at today's open — roughly half the 1.5–2.0% underperformance seen in [REDACTED] models ahead of the summer Lower House election — and has since recovered part of that move.

### Opinative impacts
- **Bearish tilt on JPY from the resignation, but modest:** [REDACTED] reads Ishiba's exit as opening political uncertainty and a path to more expansionary fiscal policy, both currency-negative — yet sees limited follow-through because the outcome was foreseeable since the election and a sharp policy shift now looks less likely given gradually improving LDP polling.
- **Global factors, not politics, should drive JPY medium-term:** [REDACTED] holds this as fundamentally correct and notes the dimmer global macro backdrop after two soft US employment reports; it is nonetheless "somewhat surprised" by how limited the initial reaction was and flags it is early.
- **Express JPY longs via options rather than spot:** [REDACTED] prefers options formats to hedge against a sharper-than-baseline rise in recession risk, citing elevated uncertainty and carry costs.
- **Supportive for CHF and, less so, EUR:** Japanese political uncertainty plus US growth worries and sequential Fed cuts should benefit both, per [REDACTED].
- **Procyclical FX are the clearest winners of easier Fed policy:** [REDACTED] favors ZAR, SEK and AUD under its baseline, consistent with the broad Dollar reaction to Friday's payrolls.
- **CNH stays a top conviction long:** Unlike JPY, [REDACTED] sees policy as a supportive factor, with global and local signals aligned.

### At issue
Japanese Prime Minister Ishiba resigned. [REDACTED] frames the move as a clear possibility ever since the LDP's narrow Lower House election loss earlier in the summer, so the potential policy steps are already well understood by the market.

### Unpacked
The note's puzzle is a reaction that didn't happen. Heading into the summer election, the Yen and JGBs underperformed on fears of political instability and looser fiscal policy; the same script should, in principle, have applied to Ishiba stepping down. **Instead the open brought only about half the expected weakness, and even that partly reversed — the market treated the resignation as old news.**

[REDACTED] offers two reasons. The resignation was telegraphed by the election result, so the associated policy paths were already priced, and improving LDP opinion polls make a dramatic policy break look less probable. At the same time, **the global backdrop has softened since July after two weak US payrolls prints, reinforcing [REDACTED]'s long-standing claim that global macro — not domestic politics — is the dominant medium-term driver of the Yen.** The muted price action, in that reading, is the thesis working rather than failing.

The trade construction reflects the residual risk. **[REDACTED] still wants to be long JPY but in options rather than spot, to keep exposure while hedging against a recession shock larger than its baseline and to sidestep the carry drag on a long-Yen position.** The same Fed-easing and US-slowdown logic then fans out across the book: defensively into CHF and EUR, procyclically into ZAR, SEK and AUD, and — separately from the Yen story — into CNH, which [REDACTED] holds as one of its strongest views because global and local signals point the same way.

subject: AI Adoption Tracker: 2025Q3: AI Hardware Investment Remains Strong; Adoption Progress Slows (Dong/Briggs)
summary:
# AI Hardware Spend Stays Hot While Firm Adoption Cools and Labor Impact Stays Narrow

**Theme:** Investment momentum diverging from a slowing adoption curve; labor effects still concentrated  
**Markets:** US AI hardware, software, and labor market  
**Source:** [REDACTED] (Sarah Dong), 8 September 2025

### Landscape
- Semiconductor firm revenues are expected to grow 38% from current levels by end-2026, per equity analyst estimates.
- Since ChatGPT's late-2022 release, analysts have raised end-2025 semiconductor revenue forecasts by $203bn (0.7% of US GDP) and AI hardware-enabler forecasts by $123bn (0.4%), the latter up from $105bn last quarter.
- 9.7% of US firms now use AI to produce goods or services, up from 9.2% in Q2 — a slower pace of gain.
- AI-related job openings stand at 28% of all IT postings and 1.5% of all job postings.
- Tech's employment share has fallen below its long-run trend, the clearest labor-market signal in the data.

### Drivers
- Capital investment is intensifying, led by semiconductors and cloud service providers, both still seeing strong upward revenue revisions.
- US AI-related hardware and software investment picked up in Q2, likely aided in part by tariff frontloading — a temporary boost to watch for reversal.
- Manufacturers' shipments of AI-related components rose and stayed elevated in the US, Japan, and Canada.
- Firm adoption is broadening unevenly: finance, insurance, and real estate posted the largest gains while educational services declined; broadcasting and publishing expect the biggest six-month increase.
- Adoption ticked down among large (250+) and medium (100-249 employee) firms in Q2, though their expected future adoption stays firm — a divergence between current and planned use.
- Productivity uplift where generative AI is deployed remains large: ~27% in academic studies and ~31% in company anecdotes.

### Risks
- Downside to adoption: per the analysts, data security, quality, and availability remain the top barriers cited in recent industry surveys, capping near-term uptake.
- Labor-market skew: the analysts assess broad AI employment effects as still small and statistically insignificant, but flag concentrated headwinds in marketing, graphic design, customer service, and especially tech, with eventual displacement of 6-7% of all workers after full adoption.

### Unpacked
**The report's central tension is a widening gap between money committed to AI and AI actually in use.** Investment signals are uniformly strong — semiconductors, other hardware enablers, and cloud providers all continue to see revenue forecasts revised upward — while the share of firms putting AI into production is rising only marginally. The Q2 investment pickup carries a caveat: part of it reflects tariff frontloading rather than underlying demand, so the strength may not fully persist.

**Adoption is advancing fastest exactly where it is easiest to apply.** Computing, publishing, and web search remain the highest-adoption subsectors, and adoption stays strongly correlated with a subsector's exposure of work tasks to AI automation. The quarter's rotation — gains in finance, insurance, and real estate against a decline in educational services — fits that pattern, as does the expectation that broadcasting and publishing will lead over the next six months. The dip among larger firms alongside firm forward expectations suggests a pause rather than a retreat.

**The labor-market footprint is real but still narrow.** Across most industries the effect of AI exposure on broad outcomes remains small and statistically insignificant, yet payroll growth is underperforming in the specific occupations where anecdotes point to AI — marketing, graphic design, customer service, and tech, whose employment share has now dropped below trend. Since the last update AI was named in corporate layoffs affecting 10,375 employees, but the unemployment rate for AI-exposed roles still tracks that of less-exposed ones. Rising AI job intensity — 28% of IT postings — shows the technology creating demand even as it displaces it. The eventual 6-7% displacement estimate frames this as an early stage, not a settled outcome.

**Where AI is deployed, the productivity gains are consistently large** — roughly 27-31% across studies and company accounts — which is what keeps the investment case intact despite the slow adoption curve.

subject: Global Week Ahead: September 8-14
summary:
# Central Banks Hold Steady on Easing Path as US CPI Headlines a Data-Heavy Week

**Theme:** Six central-bank decisions plus a global inflation calendar, with [REDACTED] in line with consensus on every policy call  
**Markets:** Global macro — rates and inflation  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jan Hatzius, 7 September 2025  

### Landscape
- All six scheduled policy decisions have [REDACTED] forecasts matching consensus exactly: Turkiye 41.0% (from 43.0%), Russia 16.0% (from 18.0%), Peru 4.25% (from 4.5%), Chile 4.75% (unchanged), and Ukraine 15.5% (unchanged).
- Euro Area seen on hold at 2.0% — [REDACTED], consensus, and the prior rate all aligned, implying no further ECB move this meeting.
- US Headline CPI forecast at 0.37% MoM, above the 0.3% consensus and up from 0.2% last; US Core CPI at 0.36% MoM versus 0.3% consensus.
- US UMich 5-10yr inflation expectations forecast at 3.4%, below the 3.5% consensus and prior reading — [REDACTED]'s most below-consensus US call.
- Brazil IGP-DI seen at 2.99% YoY, under the 3.16% consensus but above the 2.91% prior.
- India CPI forecast at 2.3% YoY (vs 2.2% consensus, 1.55% last) and Russia CPI at 8.4% YoY (vs 8.3% consensus, 8.79% last) — both above consensus but showing base effects in opposite directions.

### Drivers
- Regional easing cycles remain in motion: Turkiye, Russia and Peru are all expected to cut, extending disinflation-driven normalization, though each cut is fully consensus-anticipated with no [REDACTED] divergence.
- US inflation momentum is the week's live driver — [REDACTED] sits above consensus on both headline and core CPI, pointing to firmer sequential prints that bear directly on the Fed's near-term reaction function.
- Where [REDACTED] breaks from consensus, the gaps are outside rate decisions entirely: South Africa's current account (+0.1% vs -0.8% of GDP), UK GDP (-0.1% vs +0.1% MoM), and the softer US long-run inflation expectation.

### Unpacked
This is a calendar note, not a thesis piece: its content is [REDACTED] Economics' forecasts for the coming week's central-bank meetings and data releases, flagged against Bloomberg consensus. **The defining feature of the policy calendar is agreement — [REDACTED]'s forecast equals consensus for every one of the six central banks meeting (Turkiye, Russia, Peru, Euro Area, Chile, Ukraine), so no rate decision this week is expected to surprise.** The interest sits in the direction of travel: cuts in Turkiye (41.0% from 43.0%), Russia (16.0% from 18.0%) and Peru (4.25% from 4.5%), against holds in the Euro Area (2.0%), Chile (4.75%) and Ukraine (15.5%).

**The genuine divergence is concentrated in the US inflation data, where [REDACTED] forecasts firmer CPI than the market on both headline (0.37% vs 0.3% MoM) and core (0.36% vs 0.3% MoM).** That above-consensus read is the note's most policy-relevant signal, cutting against a softer US UMich 5-10yr inflation expectation forecast of 3.4% versus 3.5% consensus — near-term prices running hotter than expected while longer-run expectations tick down.

Elsewhere the out-of-consensus calls (defined as differing from consensus by at least one standard deviation of the historical surprise) fall outside the inflation and policy space: [REDACTED] is most above consensus on South Africa's current account, projecting a small surplus (+0.1% of GDP) against a -0.8% consensus deficit, and most below on UK GDP, seeing a -0.1% MoM contraction versus +0.1% expected. EM inflation prints in India (2.3% YoY) and Russia (8.4% YoY) both run marginally above consensus, though India's is a sharp rise off a 1.55% base and Russia's a continued deceleration from 8.79%.

The note offers no trade idea and no editorial view — it is a scoreboard of forecasts, with the underlying detail carried in the regional week-ahead publications it points to.

subject: US Week Ahead: September 8 – September 14
summary:
# CPI the Week's Main Event, Plus a Big Benchmark Payroll Markdown

**Theme:** August core CPI seen firm at 0.36% m/m on cars, airfares and tariffs; large downward payrolls benchmark revision due  
**Markets:** US inflation and labour market  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jan Hatzius, 7 September 2025  

### Estimates

**August CPI (Thursday, Sep 11)**
- **+0.36% m/m core CPI (SA)**, vs consensus +0.30% and +0.3% prior — leaves y/y unchanged at 3.1% ([REDACTED] +3.13%, consensus +3.1%, prior +3.06%).
- **+0.37% m/m headline CPI**, vs consensus +0.3% and +0.2% prior; y/y +2.90% (consensus +2.9%, prior +2.70%).
- Component drivers within core: used cars +1.2%, new cars +0.2%, car insurance +0.4%, airfares +3%, primary rent +0.25%, OER +0.26%; tariffs add +0.14pp.
- Headline extras: food +0.35%, energy +0.6%.
- Read-through: consistent with **+0.29% m/m core PCE** in August (to be updated post-CPI).

**August PPI (Wednesday, Sep 10)**
- **+0.2% m/m final demand**, vs consensus +0.3% and +0.9% prior.
- **+0.3% m/m ex-food and energy** (consensus +0.3%, prior +0.9%); ex-food, energy and trade +0.3% (prior +0.6%).

**Payrolls benchmark revision (Tuesday, Sep 9)**
- **Downward revision on the order of 550–950k** to the March 2025 payroll level (≈45–80k/month over Apr 2024–Mar 2025), based on QCEW; [REDACTED] flags the preliminary print could overstate the markdown by as much as 400k.

**Other releases**
- Initial jobless claims **230k** (consensus 234k, last 237k); continuing claims consensus 1,950k (last 1,940k).
- U. Michigan sentiment (Sep prelim) **57.4** (consensus 58.0, last 58.2); 5–10yr inflation expectations **3.4%** (consensus/last 3.5%).
- NY Fed 1yr inflation expectations last 3.1%; NFIB optimism consensus 100.5 (last 100.3).

### Outlook
- **Tariffs remain an active upward force on core inflation**, contributing +0.14pp this month concentrated in exposed categories (communication, household furnishings, recreation).
- **Shelter is roughly neutral on net** this print, with rent and OER both near +0.25%.
- **Fed silent this week** — officials are in the blackout period ahead of the September FOMC, so no policy commentary is expected.
- **Activity tracking is soft but positive**: Q3 GDP tracking +1.6% q/q ann. (domestic final sales +0.7%), Current Activity Indicator +2.0% in August (down from +2.3% in July), MAP surprise index flat.

### Unpacked
The week's calendar is front-loaded around two very different signals. **The August CPI is the headline event, and at +0.36% core m/m the estimate sits a touch above the +0.30% consensus while holding the year-over-year rate at 3.1%.** The build-up runs through the auto complex — auction prices lifting used cars, thinner dealer incentives nudging new cars, and online premium data pushing car insurance — alongside a seasonal and underlying boost to airfares.

Tariffs are the recurring cross-current. **The +0.14pp lift penciled into core comes from categories most exposed to import costs, keeping trade policy a live contributor to the inflation path rather than a one-off.** Against that, shelter — usually the dominant core driver — is expected to be broadly flat on net this month, so the surprise risk is concentrated in the goods and travel components rather than housing.

The other set-piece is the preliminary benchmark payrolls revision. **A downward mark of 550–950k would materially recast the strength of the labour market over the past year, but the note cautions the preliminary figure could itself overstate the cut by up to 400k**, with the final revision only landing with the January 2026 report next February. Read together with a soft-but-positive growth backdrop — Q3 GDP tracking at 1.6% and the activity indicator easing to 2.0% — the picture is one of cooling momentum rather than contraction, into an FOMC the Fed is now entering in silence.

subject: Global Rates Trader: Steep Learning Curve
summary:
# Global Rates: The Rally's Cheap Fuel Runs Low, Long-Ends Stay Fragile

**Theme:** Front-end richness near fair value; long-end steepness driven globally by fiscal aversion  
**Markets:** G10 rates (US, Canada, Euro area, UK, Japan)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], George Cole, 5 September 2025  

### Landscape
- US terminal rate pricing sits around 2.75%, with more than 25bp priced for September — now closely aligned with [REDACTED] economists' probability-weighted Fed path.
- 1y4y inflation swaps price about 2.5%, consistent with headline CPI returning to modestly above-target PCE once the tariff boost fades.
- 5s30s has steepened 25-30bp over the past three months; [REDACTED] attributes only 5-10bp of that to a dovish shift in the perceived Fed reaction function.
- Canada's policy rate has been held at 2.75% since March, mid-range of the BoC's 2.25-3.25% neutral band; terminal rate pricing is around 2.3%, with September cut ~75% priced.
- 30y Gilts hit multi-decade highs this week; European 10s30s has steepened steadily with little pullback since January.
- ECB policy rate at 2%; end-2025 easing still partly priced despite [REDACTED] view the cutting cycle is over.
- JGBs price ~7.5bp for the October BOJ meeting versus [REDACTED] economists' call for the next hike in January 2026.

### Drivers
- **US labor softening** is the dominant force, strengthening the case for sequential Fed cuts and lowering sensitivity to inflation upside, but the trajectory does not yet signal the deeper deterioration needed for a large additional rally.
- **Perceived Fed reaction-function shift** — Fed officials signaling openness to cuts despite inflation risk, plus political pressure and expected dovish future leadership — supports terminal-rate outperformance and 2H26 inversion, though inflation risk premia remain contained.
- **Vol compression** continues across the surface, with short-gamma Sharpe ratios above the 90th percentile; the only interruptions were the two soft NFP prints. Falling vol reduces the convexity benefit of holding long-term bonds, undercutting long-end demand globally.
- **Global long-end spillovers** — large moves in German and Japanese long rates — are the main source of higher 30y yields, including the Gilt sell-off, rather than country-specific fundamentals.
- **Japan fiscal/political risk** intensified on reports that LDP Secretary-General Moriyama, a fiscal conservative, may resign, raising the odds of more aggressive fiscal expansion; market aversion to fiscal uncertainty remains high.
- **Improving euro-area growth** — EU-US trade deal and German fiscal boost — should lift ECB growth projections and push terminal-rate pricing up; watch survey data confirming the 2026 growth pickup.
- **Canada easing tailwinds** — milder inflation and removal of retaliatory tariffs on USMCA-compliant goods — reduce a source of BoC caution.

### Risks
- **Upside to yields (bear steepening):** [REDACTED] flags the curve as vulnerable to steepening if the market perceives greater risk of an excessively dovish Fed path; belly and long-end have limited room to fall further absent sharper fundamental deterioration.
- **Downside to yields (bull steepening):** cuts could be pulled forward on weaker data, or a V-shaped forward curve could emerge — [REDACTED] sees the relative flatness priced from 2H26 through 2027 as vulnerable.
- **Europe long-end:** [REDACTED] judges risks to the curve as increasingly balanced after a strong run in short-vol and steepener strategies; higher European terminal-rate pricing could add 5y-segment volatility.
- **UK:** investor doubts on budget consolidation ahead of the 26 November budget suggest ongoing Gilt premium versus peers, which [REDACTED] expects to reverse into an entry opportunity closer to the budget.
- **Japan:** near-term risks skewed toward further political uncertainty weighing on sentiment; [REDACTED] does not expect a swift BOJ hawkish pivot.

### Unpacked
The US section frames the current juncture as a tradeoff between front-loading and deeper cuts. **The August jobs report reinforced the softer labor trend and strengthens the argument for sequential Fed cuts, but with the market already pricing most of this, risk/reward on further front-end richening has deteriorated.** [REDACTED] closes its 1m2y receiver for a potential 8bp profit and tightens the stop on its long SFR vs ERZ5 position. The route to meaningfully lower belly and long-end yields now depends on conviction in faster cuts, which in turn requires sharper fundamental deterioration.

On the reaction function, the decoupling of front-end pricing from inflation forwards points to a shift in how the market reads the Fed, linked to dovish official signaling and political pressure. **Yet neither terminal-rate pricing nor inflation risk premia look extreme: terminal pricing below the [REDACTED] baseline is defensible once elevated recession risk and a more growth-sensitive Fed are accounted for.** [REDACTED]'s regression work attributes only 5-10bp of the recent 5s30s steepening to the perceived dovish shift, implying most of the move has other sources.

In volatility, compression has been broad, with short-gamma strategies richly rewarded except around the soft payroll prints. **Belly tails have cheapened even as outright belly yields richened, signaling market conviction on the eventual Fed endpoint** — but [REDACTED] sees a valuation case for hedging belly cheapening risk via 1y5y payers or conditional curve flatteners should terminal pricing richen further, and favors long-vega as a carry-friendly hedge against short-gamma risk in a growth drawdown. [REDACTED] still prefers low-strike bull steepeners as a cost-effective expression.

Canada mirrors the US setup. Jobs data, milder inflation, and the removal of retaliatory tariffs all support further BoC easing, with 50bp of room to cut before policy turns accommodative. **With terminal pricing already near 2.3%, [REDACTED] closes its receive-September-BoC recommendation for a potential 9bp profit, judging tactical risk/reward less compelling ahead of the next inflation report,** even as economists now see a 2.25% terminal rate via cuts in September and October.

In the euro area, [REDACTED] expects the ECB to reiterate that policy is in a good place, with the trade deal and German fiscal boost lifting growth projections but leaving the HICP path little changed. **The easing cycle is treated as over, so [REDACTED] expects end-2025 cut pricing to decay and maintains its ERZ5 short against the US,** while arguing the recent ERZ5Z7 flattening has run its course as the front-end should slope upward on a 2026 growth pickup.

The European long-end, by contrast, is called increasingly precarious after a remarkable run in 10s30s steepeners. **[REDACTED] stresses the steepening is global, making it premature to blame the Dutch pension transition, and judges curve risks now more balanced given stretched vol valuations and strong short-vol performance.** Sustaining core yields above current levels likely needs firmer growth expectations as the German fiscal impulse accumulates.

The Gilt sell-off is framed as "blameless but buyer-less": UK fundamental news was limited beyond the 26 November budget date, and the G4 spillover framework attributes most of the 30y rise to German and Japanese moves. **A supply response — lower issuance maturity and slower BoE QT sales — may not be enough; long-end Gilts likely need both lower inflation and credible budget consolidation.** [REDACTED] expects continued premium into the budget but sees widening Gilt-UST spreads as an opportunity closer to it, and continues to recommend 2s5s steepeners on the view the front-end has priced out too much.

Japan closes the note. Long-end JGBs remain a source of bearish global pressure, with political risk back in focus on the possible resignation of a fiscally conservative LDP figure that could open the door to more aggressive expansion. **Front-end rates have crept higher on better global sentiment, and greater conviction in a higher BOJ endpoint could relieve long-end steepness even without an imminent hawkish turn** — [REDACTED] economists still see the next hike in January 2026 — though near-term risks tilt toward political uncertainty weighing on sentiment.

subject: Global FX Trader: Back to Fall(ing)
summary:
# Dollar Turns Cyclical: A Broad-Based Downtrend Led by Asia

**Theme:** Weaker USD spreads across FX as the Fed resumes cutting  
**Markets:** Global FX (G10 & EM)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Kamakshya Trivedi, 5 September 2025

### Landscape
- **USD sold off broadly on Friday's weak August payrolls** — the decline was notably wider than the historical norm for a payrolls disappointment, with high-beta EM (BRL, ZAR) moving on par with safe havens.
- **Q3 US GDP tracker improved to 1.6%**, up from 1.0% a month earlier.
- **CNY was one of the best-performing EM currencies in August on a volatility-adjusted basis**, even as the USD/CNY fix held stable near recent lows while DXY recovered pre-payrolls.
- **Sterling was the worst major on Tuesday** as UK Gilts joined a global bear-steepening, with long-end Gilt yields at decade highs; GBP/USD risk reversals repriced lower by more than the spot move implied.
- **Gilt yields have since more than fully retraced Tuesday's spike.**
- **ZAR remains among the most undervalued EM currencies** in both trade-weighted and bilateral terms, though it has traded a tighter range over recent months.

### Drivers
- **USD depreciation on fading exceptionalism** — a less exceptional economy warrants a less overvalued currency and struggles to attract the foreign inflows funding the current-account deficit; the labour-market slowdown confirms the challenge. Shifting hedging behaviour should let the Dollar underperform rate differentials as the Fed cuts.
- **The Dollar is trading more cyclically this year**, broadening the sell-off beyond the usual safe-haven response to weak data — a pattern seen in both July and August payrolls and expected to persist.
- **Gradual CNY appreciation as a policy impulse** — slow but steady, anchored by large export-share gains, a surging current-account surplus, and undervaluation comparable to the mid-2000s "China shock"; forecast to drift to USD/CNY 7.0 in 6M.
- **UK fiscal risk as recurring premium, not a 2022-style event** — bouts of pressure into the 26 November Autumn budget, reinforced by labour-market vulnerability, BoE terminal-rate downside, and stretched Sterling valuation, skew EUR/GBP higher.
- **Asian FX becoming a bigger participant in Dollar weakness** as Fed cuts lower hedging costs, notably for JPY.
- **Watch next week's SA GDP and current-account data** ([REDACTED] forecasts above consensus) and Monday's LDP vote on replacing PM Ishiba (a tactical JPY headwind).

### Risks
- **Downside to JPY longs (tactical):** an Ishiba resignation or a vote to call an election could lift USD/JPY on rising fiscal-easing expectations — [REDACTED] expects the impact to be short-lived and dominated by the JPY-positive macro backdrop.
- **Downside to GBP (contained):** UK fiscal stress could resurface, but [REDACTED] expects premium bouts rather than a full crisis; risks to EUR/GBP are skewed to the upside.
- **Downside to INR:** larger-than-expected US tariffs (25% reciprocal + 25% ad valorem) would drag on the external sector; with the RBI seen unlikely to spend heavily defending the rupee, [REDACTED] flattened its USD/INR path.
- **Downside to IDR:** political uncertainty after last week's protests may restrain appreciation despite a favourable external backdrop.
- **Elevated US recession risk** with the economy at "stall speed" keeps tactical JPY and CHF hedges valuable, and [REDACTED] expects US data — payrolls especially — to drive greater FX volatility through year-end, with USD/JPY and USD/CHF the largest movers.

### Unpacked
The through-line is a Dollar that is weakening for cyclical rather than crisis reasons. **[REDACTED] reads the labour-market slowdown as confirmation that US economic outperformance is fading, which should pull the currency toward a less overvalued level and reduce its pull on the foreign capital that funds the current-account deficit.** The August payrolls print is treated as the trigger that pushes the market toward the baseline of sequential Fed cuts and broader FX participation. The one offset is the modest activity pickup — the Q3 GDP tracker rising to 1.6% — which leaves room for cyclical currencies like SEK and AUD and for EM carry to run alongside the core Dollar-down view.

**The CNY story is about durability, not speed:** appreciation has been frustratingly slow, but that is the nature of a managed, steady currency, and [REDACTED] sees a policy impulse plus strong fundamentals — export-share gains, a rising current-account surplus, and deep undervaluation — sustaining it as an anchor for the wider Dollar call. Equity strategists see further upside in the Chinese stock rally despite soft domestic demand.

**Sterling's problem is framed as "a tantrum, not a tempest":** the Tuesday sell-off and outsized skew repricing reflect bearish positioning around decade-high Gilt yields and cabinet changes, but yields have already retraced and rates strategists expect a more benign Gilt backdrop. The conviction on a EUR/GBP grind higher rests less on fiscal risk than on the breadth of supporting drivers — labour-market softness, BoE terminal-rate downside, global cyclical risk, and Sterling's stretched valuation after a strong run.

**On the Yen, [REDACTED] keeps a short USD/JPY with a 142 target and 152 stop**, arguing the recent USD/JPY outperformance on its [REDACTED] model is already dissipating and that falling hedging costs plus recession risk favour the Yen — which outperformed post-payrolls. Monday's LDP leadership vote is flagged as a near-term headwind that should prove short-lived.

The Rand carries several supports: deep undervaluation, high sensitivity to both a stronger Yuan and lower US yields, and an improving domestic backdrop (growth seen reaching 2.5% medium-term, a credible debt-stabilisation path). [REDACTED] notes ZAR returns historically correlate negatively with front-end rate differentials, so a deeper cutting cycle need not undermine the currency, and sees YTD precious-metal gains more than offsetting tariff drag on exports. **ZAR stays a preferred EM carry long alongside BRL and HUF.**

In non-Japan Asia the message is fine-tuning within a constructive frame: KRW is the top pick on its high beta to the broad USD and USD/CNY, aided by equity inflows and pre-positioning for WGBI inclusion (March 2026); TWD appreciation is trimmed after its Q2 surge and subsequent correction; THB has outperformed on record gold prices, drawing BoT attention to "non-fundamental" drivers. **The biggest change is a flatter USD/INR path (87.5 / 87.0 / 86.0) on the tariff shock, while PHP is the preferred high-yielder on Q4 remittance seasonality and lighter reliance on US and Chinese growth.**

Finally, the payrolls post-mortem crystallises the cyclical-Dollar thesis: the currencies that led (CHF, JPY, SEK) are the usual beneficiaries of a double survey miss, but the breadth of the move — with BRL and ZAR matching safe havens — is what marks this cycle as different, while growth-sensitive MXN and CAD lagged as usual (CAD also hit by its own weak jobs data).

subject: Weekly Fund Flows: Cyclicals Supported
summary:
# Cyclical Rotation Broadens as Equity and Bond Inflows Hold Firm

**Theme:** Cyclical demand widens beyond tech; commodities inflows unusually strong  
**Markets:** Global fund flows (equities, fixed income, FX)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Isabella Rosenberg, 5 September 2025  

### Landscape
- Global equity funds took in +$18bn in the week ending September 3, up marginally from +$17bn the prior week.
- Global fixed income inflows held firm, led by Agg-type funds at +$22bn versus +$19bn the previous week.
- Money market fund assets rose by $52bn on the week.
- Technology funds saw the largest net equity inflows at the sector level.
- Commodities fund inflows were especially elevated relative to their own history.
- Euro area inflows into US equity funds have risen on average and are back closer to 2024 levels.

### Drivers
- Equity inflows broadened across G10: US inflows shrank but stayed positive, while Western Europe turned net positive.
- EM equity flows shifted similarly — mainland China inflows slowed while flows elsewhere turned modestly positive.
- Cyclical demand widened beyond tech: cyclical ex-tech flows strengthened alongside stronger tech demand, so tech is not the sole driver (Chart of the Week).
- Within fixed income, short-duration bond funds outpaced long-duration; EM bond flows were positive across both hard and local currency.
- Cross-border FX flows increased on stronger foreign inflows into G10 and Asia.

### Unpacked
**The week's signal is breadth rather than magnitude: inflows into both equities and bonds were roughly steady week-over-week, but the composition shifted toward a wider set of cyclical exposures.** Equity flows spread more evenly across G10, with the US giving up its dominant share as Western Europe turned positive, and a parallel move in EM as China cooled and other markets picked up modestly.

**The cyclical rotation is the note's central observation — tech is leading, but not alone.** Cyclical ex-tech flows have firmed in step with tech demand, and commodities funds stand out with inflows unusually large by historical standards, reinforcing the tilt toward cyclically sensitive segments.

**In fixed income, the preference for shorter duration and the positive tone across EM hard and local currency bonds sit alongside firm Agg-type inflows and a sizable $52bn build in money market assets.** On the FX side, cross-border flows strengthened on foreign demand into G10 and Asia, with euro area buying of US equity funds recovering toward 2024 averages. The note is a flows scoreboard and carries no explicit trade idea.

subject: USA: Payroll Employment Below Expectations, Unemployment Rate Rises to 4.3%
summary:
# US Payroll Growth Stalls at 22k as Unemployment Ticks Up to 4.3%

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US August 2025 employment report  
**General comment:** Reads the report as confirming a softening labor market; supports a September rate cut, in line with market consensus.

### Context
A reaction to the August 2025 US jobs report, which came in well below forecasts and fed the debate over whether the Fed cuts rates in September.

### The case
- **Headline job growth was much weaker than expected and the recent trend is soft.** Nonfarm payrolls rose only 22k versus a 75k median forecast. July was revised up 6k to 79k but June was revised down 27k to -13k, pulling the three-month average to 29k. Government employment fell 16k (mostly a 15k drop in federal jobs). Gains were concentrated in healthcare (+47k), leisure and hospitality (+28k) and other services (+12k), while durable goods (-19k), professional services (-17k) and wholesale trade (-12k) contracted.
- **The rise in unemployment reflects labor supply outpacing demand, not just weak hiring.** The jobless rate rose 8bp to 4.32% as a 288k gain in employment was outstripped by a 436k increase in the labor force. Participation edged up to 62.3%. Broader slack widened too: the U6 underemployment rate rose 0.2pp to 8.1% and the job-finding rate for the unemployed fell 2.1pp to 24.7%.
- **Wage growth held steady and continues to ease on a yearly basis.** Average hourly earnings rose 0.27% month over month, in line with expectations, with the year-over-year rate slipping 0.19pp to 3.69%.
- **The estimated underlying pace of job growth is running around +41k**, blending the payroll and household surveys.
- **Sectors exposed to policy shifts are showing strain.** Industries most exposed to immigration-policy changes lost jobs on a three-month average basis through July (-13k, versus +27k on average in 2024). Tariff-exposed industries showed little movement either way (+2k for the negatively exposed, -4k for the positively exposed).

### Implications
- Reinforces the case for a September Fed rate cut, the report being read as evidence of a cooling labor market.
- Rising slack — a higher U6 rate and a falling job-finding rate — points to a genuine loss of demand momentum, not just noise around a low headline print.
- Policy-sensitive segments, particularly immigration-exposed industries, bear watching as an early source of continued weakness.

subject: US Economics Weekly Update 9/4/2025
summary:
# Payrolls Set to Undershoot, Tariffs Face Court Limbo, and Jackson Hole Takeaways

**Theme:** August jobs preview, tariff legal risk, and structural research reads  
**Markets:** US macro / labor, trade, and payments  
**Source:** [REDACTED] (David Mericle), 5 September 2025  

### Landscape
- Q3 GDP tracking estimate stands at 1.6%.
- Job openings fell 176k to 7,181k in July, with turnover measures still low.
- Personal income rose 0.4% and consumer spending 0.5% in July, leaving the saving rate at 4.4%.
- Core capital goods shipments rose 0.7% in July.
- Construction spending fell 0.5% in real terms in July; new single-family home sales fell 0.6%.
- The trade deficit widened in July on higher gold imports and imports from China.

### Drivers
- Labor demand is cooling: payroll growth is forecast at 60k for August (80k private, offset by a 20k federal decline as a lifted injunction unblocks layoffs), with unemployment ticking up to 4.3%.
- Low hiring and turnover is the key friction — soft flows risk locking out the unemployed and new graduates even without mass layoffs.
- Tariff policy is the swing factor: an appeals court largely affirmed the block on IEEPA tariffs, which account for 8pp of the effective tariff rate increase to date.

### Risks
- Downside (data): the analyst sees future revisions to prior-month job growth as more likely negative than positive.
- Technical downside on August print: initial August payrolls have carried a consistent negative bias over the past decade — underperforming trend by ~40k on average — driving the below-consensus 60k call versus 75k consensus.
- Policy two-sided: even if the Supreme Court strikes the IEEPA tariffs, the analyst notes the president retains substantial alternative authority (Section 122, Sec. 301, sectoral tariffs), limiting the downside to the effective tariff rate.

### Unpacked
The August payroll call sits below consensus mainly for technical reasons. **Big data indicators firmed relative to prior months but stayed soft, and the decisive factor is a well-documented negative bias in initial August prints — seasonal adjustment factors suited to the final print misfire on the first read.** The federal drag is specific: an injunction that had been blocking layoffs was lifted, so the government component should fall more than in recent months.

On trade, the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit largely affirmed an earlier ruling against the IEEPA tariffs but delayed effect until Oct. 14, or — if the administration appeals — until the Supreme Court declines review or rules. **If the Supreme Court takes the case, the affected tariffs could stay in place as late as June 2026, and whatever the outcome, the president keeps ample fallback authority through Section 122 (up to 15% for up to 7 months), Sec. 301, or sectoral measures.**

The note recaps four Jackson Hole papers. **Nakamura argues central banks raised rates less than the Taylor rule implied during the pandemic surge yet kept inflation expectations anchored thanks to their credibility, and maps when that restraint is the optimal choice.** Auclert contends population aging will lift asset demand enough by 2100 to hold interest rates stable even at a 250% debt-to-GDP ratio. Foschi reads the 50-year decline in US inter-state migration as reduced incentive to move rather than workers being "stuck" — they still relocate after local shocks, undercutting the mortgage lock-in story. Goldin ties falling global fertility to greater female autonomy unmatched by shared childcare within couples or public support, and expects the trend to persist absent policy change.

A research recap covers digital money. **Stablecoin volumes remain very small versus global payments and skew toward cross-border uses — saving in a more stable currency or cheaper remittances — rather than domestic retail.** Only the Bahamas, Nigeria, and Jamaica have fully launched central bank digital currencies, all with low adoption. Public fast-payment systems have gone furthest where card networks are less entrenched: in Brazil and Thailand they are now the main non-cash method, while developed markets lag.

subject: US Economics Analyst: The Evolving Landscape of Digital Money and Payments (Abecasis)
summary:
# Digital Payments: Network Effects Keep Incumbents Ahead, with Traction Mostly in EMs

**Theme:** Why stablecoins, CBDCs, and public fast payment systems have gained ground abroad but face steep incumbency barriers, especially in DMs  
**Markets:** Global digital money and payments  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Manuel Abecasis, 4 September 2025  

### Landscape
- Stablecoin market capitalization reached about $270bn in August, dominated by Tether (USDT) and USD Coin (USDC), with over 95% of value pegged to the dollar.
- Stablecoin transaction volume rose to just under $1tn in August — about 0.5% of global payments — while retail-sized (<$250) transactions were around $6bn, or just 0.01% of retail payments.
- Only three countries run live CBDCs — the Bahamas, Jamaica, and Nigeria — all with low adoption, while the US and others have abandoned or ruled out projects.
- Public fast payment systems have become the leading non-cash method in Brazil (Pix) and Thailand, with India (UPI) and Costa Rica (SINPE Móvil) also achieving widespread adoption; DMs have lagged.
- A single exchange, Bitso, processed about $7bn of US-to-Mexico stablecoin remittances in 2024, roughly 10% of that corridor's total.

### Drivers
- Network effects dominate payments and favor incumbents: an efficient new technology is worthless unless enough people accept it, while an inefficient incumbent survives on universal acceptance — the central obstacle for all three innovations.
- Stablecoins settle instantly and cheaply on-chain, but adoption is capped by limited direct acceptance, forcing costly "on/off-ramping" to traditional rails, plus FX costs across currencies.
- Stablecoin demand concentrates where fiat is weak or restricted — Turkiye (high inflation), and countries near sanctions or with capital controls — and in cross-border flows (over 60% cross-region), pointing to saving and remittances rather than retail payments.
- Public fast payment adoption is driven mainly by broad bank and nonbank participation, not settlement speed; Brazil and Thailand mandated bank acceptance, while India and Costa Rica achieved voluntary participation.
- Entrenched card networks slow adoption in DMs: higher credit card penetration correlates with lower fast-payment uptake, as consumer rewards funded by merchant fees lock users into incumbents.

### Risks
- The report frames outcomes as structural rather than as scenario risks, and flags no explicit upside/downside risk set.

### Unpacked
Payments involve two distinct tools: the asset used (cash, bank deposits, stablecoins, CBDCs) and the payment rail that moves it. A new rail can be built without a new asset — the public fast payment systems do exactly that, running existing deposits or cash over new infrastructure. **The note treats stablecoins and CBDCs as new digital assets and public fast payment systems as new rails, and judges each by how well it overcomes the same network-effect barrier.**

Stablecoins are privately issued; under the GENIUS Act, US issuers must back them one-for-one with safe assets like T-bills, deposits, or reserves, and follow KYC/AML/CFT rules — so users share identity with issuers, though transactions stay invisible to the government unless the provider discloses them. CBDCs, by contrast, are a direct central-bank liability, and some give the government visibility into individual transactions. **The efficiency case for stablecoins — instant, cheap on-chain settlement — is undercut in practice because few merchants accept them directly, so most use still requires converting to and from regular money on traditional rails.**

That conversion friction matters more in the US because domestic rails are already fast and cheap: RTP and the Fed's FedNow (launched July 2023) run instantly and 24/7 at low cost, Zelle over same-day ACH is often free for individuals, and fintechs like Wise and Remitly handle low-cost cross-border transfers. **Where stablecoins do fit is international flows into weaker-currency or restricted economies — a use case existing DM rails do not serve well.** Turkiye shows the largest purchases relative to GDP amid high inflation, and countries near sanctions or with capital controls also see heavy volumes, consistent with research from the Fed, IMF, and FSB.

The consumer-versus-business split explains why incumbents are so hard to dislodge. Consumers use expensive credit and debit cards heavily, generating the bulk of provider revenue despite being smaller than the B2B ex-cards segment, where businesses favor cheap, pre-arranged ACH transfers. **Card networks sustain their lead through a two-sided pricing structure: generous consumer rewards financed by high merchant fees, which merchants absorb rather than lose card-paying customers.** This lock-in is precisely what a newcomer must break to win consumer payments.

CBDCs have largely failed to clear that bar. Most central banks are researching or piloting, but the three live launches all show limited take-up despite governments routing payments through them, and abandonments — including the US — stem from low adoption, trust and privacy concerns, or existing rails already meeting the need, especially in DMs. **Public fast payment systems are the clearest success story, and the note attributes it to design: the winners let users sign up and pay many ways — QR codes, usernames, bank or fintech apps, tap-to-pay — are free for consumers and cheap for merchants, and interoperate with other financial tools.** Pix lets the unbanked register through a provider and deposit cash via ATMs or agents; India subsidizes account-opening costs for UPI; Costa Rica eased account requirements for SINPE. Mexico's CoDi failed largely because few banks joined, compounded by a large unbanked population and weak interoperability.

Adoption timing underscores how long network effects can suppress a useful technology. Brazil and Thailand saw fast uptake after mandating bank acceptance, while Costa Rica's SINPE only took off in 2020 when Covid lockdowns forced the switch — a reminder that a clear catalyst can be needed to trigger change. **A cross-sectional test finds bank and nonbank participation are the dominant drivers of adoption, with settlement speed far less important — again pointing to network reach, not technical performance, as what decides success.** The overall read: these technologies gain traction mainly in EMs, where cards are less entrenched and financial inclusion gains are large, while DM adoption would need incentives strong enough to pull consumers off existing networks — and even sizeable incentives may not overcome the incumbency advantage.

subject: US Daily: August Payrolls Preview (Walker/Rindels)
summary:
# August Payrolls: [REDACTED] Sees +60k, Below Consensus on Government Drag and the Perennial August Undershoot

**Theme:** Firmer big-data private hiring offset by a federal-payroll decline and August's recurring first-print bias  
**Markets:** US labour market  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Ronnie Walker, 4 September 2025  

### Estimates
- **+60k** nonfarm payrolls in August, below consensus of +75k but above the three-month average of +35k.
- **+80k** private payrolls, versus consensus of +75k.
- **−20k** government payrolls, split between a −20k federal decline and unchanged state and local.
- **−3k** drag from newly striking workers, per the BLS strike report.
- **+81k** average reading across the alternative "big data" employment indicators tracked for August.
- **4.3%** unemployment rate on a rounded basis, edging up from an unrounded 4.248% in July.
- **+0.3% m/m** average hourly earnings (seasonally adjusted), reflecting slightly positive calendar effects.

### Outlook
- [REDACTED] sees a genuine risk the print lands soft on August's well-documented first-print bias: since 2010, the initial August vintage has decelerated from the prior three-month trend every year (median −39k) and been revised higher later (median +61k), and it has missed consensus in 10 of the last 15 years.
- The federal hiring freeze — extended from 15 July to 15 October — plus resumed layoffs after the Supreme Court struck down a blocking injunction in early July are expected to keep weighing on federal payrolls; federal JOLTS layoffs already rose from 5k in June to 10k in July.
- On the unemployment rate, [REDACTED] flags two offsetting forces: continued easing in other slack measures argues for upward pressure, while payback from July's outsized spike in new-entrant unemployment argues for downward pressure.
- Employer survey signals (manufacturing 48.7, services 48.4, both contractionary) were discounted, as post-pandemic survey data has been a poor and at times misleading guide to payrolls.

### Unpacked
The forecast sits between two opposing forces. **On the constructive side, the alternative data firmed sequentially — still soft, but better than recent months — averaging 81k and supporting the above-trend private-payroll call.** Working the other way is the structural quirk of August: because seasonal factors are calibrated on final vintages, the first print systematically understates hiring, with the softness concentrated in information, professional services, manufacturing, and retail. A sharp drop in those industries' contribution on Friday would be read as evidence the bias is at work again.

Government hiring is the clearest drag. Job openings in Washington DC have fallen 17% since the inauguration-day federal freeze, and the lifting of the injunction that had paused layoffs opens room for federal separations to accelerate. State and local payrolls, by contrast, are assumed flat.

**The report frames August as an early read on how three policy channels are filtering into the labour market.** Tariffs are pressuring factory jobs, with manufacturing employment down 12k per month over the past three months versus −9k in 2024. Federal reduction-in-force efforts are cutting federal employment by 14k per month since February, though feared spillovers into state and local government, healthcare, and education have not yet materialised — hiring there stays elevated. And tighter immigration shows up in the most exposed industries, where job growth slid to 4k in Q2 from a 2024 average of +27k.

The broader backdrop is one of gradual cooling rather than rupture. Jobless claims and the JOLTS layoff rate are steady, but announced layoffs rose to 86k in August and the Conference Board labour differential fell to +9.7, its lowest since February 2021 and far below the 2019 average of +33.2. Openings across several measures have moved sideways. **The watch items on Friday are the industry composition — for signs of the August bias — and the federal government line, for how fast the resumed layoffs are landing.**

subject: USA: ISM Services Somewhat Above Expectations; S&P Services PMI Revised Down
summary:
# ISM services firmed in August while tariffs came to dominate business decisions

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US August services activity surveys  
**General comment:** Neutral read-through of the data; notes a modestly firmer ISM but flags tariffs as the overwhelming driver of activity and pricing behavior.

## Context
A same-day comment on the August US services surveys: the ISM services index and the final S&P Global services PMI, released amid ongoing debate over how far tariffs are feeding into activity and prices.

## The data
- **ISM services beat, with strong internals.** The headline rose 1.9pt to 52.0, above the 51.0 median and [REDACTED]'s 51.5. The gain was broad: business activity (+2.4pt to 55.0) and new orders (+5.7pt to 56.0) both climbed, and employment ticked up (+0.1pt to 46.5) though it stayed below 50. Supplier deliveries edged down to 50.3. Imports jumped sharply (+8.7pt to 54.6, NSA) while new export orders slipped to 47.3.
- **Tariffs now dominate respondent decision-making.** The press release tied part of the pickup in activity and imports to firms getting ahead of further price increases and stocking up for the holiday peak season. Tariff mentions rose to 14 (from 11 in July, 9 in June, 5 in January). Respondents said they are starting to see tariff costs in imported goods, that "all decision making is currently dominated by tariff considerations," and that holding the line on not passing costs through is "getting harder as this goes on." Prices paid eased slightly to 69.2 but remained near its highest since October 2022.
- **S&P Global services PMI sent a softer signal.** The final August reading was 54.5 — revised up 0.9pt from the preliminary print, but below the 55.4 median and prior. Within it, new business, employment, input prices, and output prices were all revised down from the flash reading.

## Implications
- Services momentum looks resilient into late summer, but part of the strength may be pull-forward — imports and activity front-loaded ahead of expected tariff-driven price rises — rather than durable underlying demand.
- Pricing pressure remains elevated even as it eases at the margin; the growing difficulty of absorbing tariff costs points to a rising risk of pass-through to consumers.
- The two surveys diverge — ISM firmer, S&P's internals softer — leaving the underlying pace of services somewhat ambiguous.

subject: Global Markets Daily: The FX Playbook for NFP (Fishman/Jenkins)
summary:
# NFP tomorrow: below-consensus payrolls may still trade like a "beat" if unemployment holds

**Theme:** How FX behaves on payroll surprises, and why a soft headline with steady unemployment could still support cyclical currencies  
**Markets:** Global FX around US labor data  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Karen Reichgott Fishman, 4 September 2025  

### Definitive impacts
- On historical "beats" (since Sep 2010, 98 observations), the Dollar strengthened almost across-the-board, most against JPY, CHF and EUR, with equities up and US 2y yields higher; high-beta EM FX was the exception, and cyclicals (KRW, CAD, NZD, AUD) outperformed.
- On historical "misses" (80 observations), the Dollar broadly weakened, especially versus the havens, MXN and EUR, with equities lower and yields down.
- When both the establishment and household surveys disappointed together (19 episodes over 15 years), moves were larger: even greater demand for havens and EUR, and Dollar strength against growth-exposed CAD and MXN.
- Intraday (30-minute windows, past year), beats again showed broad Dollar strength with cyclical outperformance; miss patterns differed for the havens — JPY and CHF actually weakened against the Dollar over the four disappointing releases before August 1, partly a small-sample/short-window effect.
- Over the last three reports, realized moves ran larger versus JPY, CHF and EUR and smaller versus high-beta currencies than the 2010–2024 average, tracking each currency's beta to the S&P 500.
- Roughly 25bp of Fed easing is priced for September and about 60bp through December.
- The April 4, 2025 report is excluded from all samples as markets were reacting to the April 2 tariffs.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] sees limited market impact from its own forecast (60k jobs, unemployment rounding up to 4.3%), and thinks FX may trade it like a "beat" — a weak headline with a steady unemployment rate keeps Fed cuts on track and recession fears contained, supporting cyclical currencies and crosses such as AUD/JPY.
- [REDACTED] expects a downside surprise — especially if payrolls and unemployment both disappoint — to bring Dollar weakness and volatility similar to the August 1 report, most against JPY, CHF, EUR and possibly high-carry EM.
- [REDACTED] expects a beat to produce broad Dollar strength (again led by JPY, CHF, EUR) but relative outperformance of cyclical crosses as equities rally.
- [REDACTED] attributes the outsized FX reaction to the July report partly to the Dollar's more cyclical, risk-correlated behavior in response to US data.
- Trade idea: stay short USD/JPY (opened Aug 1 at 147.69, target 142, stop 152), reflecting downside-skewed labor risks and a dovish Fed view.

### Backdrop
The note builds on [REDACTED]'s earlier finding that, so far in 2025, FX has delivered larger returns and higher volatility in NFP weeks than in other weeks. The Fed's current focus on the labor market raises the stakes for each release, and the unemployment rate — rather than the headline job count — is the variable most likely to drive tomorrow's reaction. A relevant precedent is August 2024: technically a consensus "miss," but markets read it as reducing the odds of a 50bp cut because the unemployment rate fell.

### At issue
Ahead of tomorrow's US jobs report, the note reviews how FX has historically moved on payroll surprises — daily (Thursday close to Friday close since September 2010) and intraday (30-minute windows, focused on the past year) — across 13 USD crosses, the S&P 500, the [REDACTED] Cyclicals-vs-Defensives ratio, and US 2y yields, all vol-adjusted. [REDACTED]'s economists expect 60k job gains and unemployment rounding up to 4.3%, below consensus on job growth.

### Unpacked
The exercise is framed around an apparent contradiction: [REDACTED]'s own forecast is soft, yet it argues the market may not treat it as bad news. **The reconciling logic is the split between the two surveys — a weak headline print paired with a steady unemployment rate would confirm the easing path already priced without stoking recession fears, which is why FX could react as though the number beat.**

The historical work establishes the base case that the Dollar rises on beats and falls on misses, with the sharpest moves against low-beta havens and the euro. **What has changed in 2025 is the Dollar's character: it now trades more like a cyclical, risk-correlated asset, so its data sensitivity has concentrated against JPY, CHF and EUR while high-beta currencies have become relatively "risk-neutral" to payrolls.** The August 1 report is the live illustration — an outsized FX reaction that dwarfed moves in other assets.

The asymmetry to watch is a joint disappointment. **A simultaneous downside surprise in payrolls and the unemployment rate is the scenario [REDACTED] flags as most likely to reproduce August 1's magnitude of Dollar weakness**, with the euro and the havens the main beneficiaries and high-carry EM possibly joining. The short USD/JPY position, targeting 142, is the direct expression of that skew.

Beyond the NFP thesis, the note carries [REDACTED]'s standing cross-asset trade list (THB/KRW, USD/EGP, the SOFR fly, PHP bonds, Colombia IBR, EUR/CHF, and others), included as a running book rather than as arguments developed here.

subject: USA: Productivity Growth Revised Up; ADP Employment Below Expectations; Trade Deficit Widens in July; Lowering Q3 GDP Tracking to +1.6%; Initial Jobless Claims Somewhat Above Expectations
summary:
# US Data: Firmer Productivity but Soft Labor Signals Nudge Q3 GDP Tracking Down to +1.6%

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US macro data release round-up  
**General comment:** Neutral read-across; incremental softening keeps [REDACTED] below consensus on payrolls and growth  

### Context
A same-day compilation of several US data releases on 4 September 2025 — Q2 final productivity and unit labor costs, the ADP employment report, the July trade balance, and weekly jobless claims — ahead of Friday's nonfarm payrolls. The note updates [REDACTED] forecasts in light of each print.

### The case
- **Q2 productivity was revised up and unit labor costs down, easing the cost-side inflation signal.** Nonfarm productivity was revised up 0.9pp to +3.3% annualized (year-over-year +1.5%, up 0.2pp), while unit labor costs — compensation divided by output — were revised down 0.6pp to +1.0% annualized (year-over-year +2.5%). Since 2019Q4 productivity has grown at a 1.8% annualized pace. Compensation per hour was revised up to +4.3% annualized; the [REDACTED] wage tracker stands at +3.9% annualized and +3.7% year-over-year.
