The sheer size of foreign holdings, combined with US-specific risks, is what lends durability to the relative repricing.

Next week's Quarterly Refunding is a near-term event. The base case is unchanged nominal coupon sizes, modest TIPS increases, and retention of the "at least the next several quarters" guidance — softening it without an offset could revive term-premium concerns. **The working assumption is that nominal auction sizes begin rising in 3Q26, later than the prior 1Q26 call**, consistent with the bills share staying modestly above 20%, though the timing hinges on the deficit path and Fed balance-sheet policy.

Europe is framed as an ECB-anchored, sovereign-credit story rather than a terminal-rate one. Front-end risk-reward is roughly balanced, and appetite for longs beyond the next three ECB meetings is limited by the chance of a more gradual domestic slowdown, better global risk sentiment, and an eventual fiscal-expansion focus. **The setup favors sovereign credit longs: any growth weakness draws an ECB response, while ECB caution means an upside growth surprise is unlikely to bring a hawkish surprise.** German swap spreads are the cleaner risk expression — their widening reflected safe-haven flow, and a further easing of risk would point to renewed, front-end-led tightening, even if slower than the H2 pace.

The Eurex EU bond future, planned for September 10, is a structural footnote. A derivatives contract can help build and hedge exposure and thus support liquidity, but its mere existence guarantees neither popularity nor liquidity — low open interest on ICE EU and Bonos futures makes the point. **In the near term the growing stock of EU debt is expected to outweigh any liquidity benefit, keeping EU bonds wide to their rating**, with longer-term improvement possible if common defence funding and eventual ECB structural purchases help.

The UK case rests on the inflation constraint easing. This week's data gave little signal — PMI weakness offset by stronger retail sales — and lower yields mostly reflected fading tariff stress. With a May cut essentially confirmed and talk turning to faster easing, the risk skews toward lower yields, but front-end pricing and the growth factor already embed a large growth hit while spot data holds up. **The long-end still looks cheap versus other curve points and peers, with an unusually large deviation from its typical G4 relationship**, so the eventual payoff is long-end outperformance as the inflation constraint relaxes — not yet.

Japan carries the note's one new trade. The global selloff was unusual: USTs underdelivered as the dominant risk-off hedge and the rest of G4 outperformed their US beta, with the belly the relative winner — most strongly in Japan, even though near-term growth and inflation undercut the case for a dovish BOJ pivot. Long-end rates lagged that outperformance, and **JGB 30s were the clear underperformer, an overshoot the note expects to revert as liquidity stabilizes and as explicit BOJ QT plans add flattening pressure ahead of the June tapering review.** The recommendation is to add 10s30s JGB flatteners (entry 1.36; target 1.1; stop 1.5).

subject: Global FX Trader: Art of the Repeal
summary:
# The Dollar's Structural Downtrend Has Further to Run, With European FX and Yen as the Cleanest Expressions

**Theme:** USD overvaluation unwinding as allocators diversify; tariff-driven recession risk keeps high-beta FX on edge  
**Markets:** Global FX  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Kamakshya Trivedi, 25 April 2025  

### Landscape
- The Dollar has fallen swiftly in recent weeks, with moves outstripping [REDACTED]'s short-term [REDACTED] models even as structural positioning remains very long.
- European FX (the Euro and satellites) has clearly outperformed the Dollar in the [REDACTED] framework year-to-date, and especially since April 2nd.
- Within the Scandis, SEK outperformed during the March European fiscal re-rating while NOK has underperformed notably since April 2nd; EUR/NOK screens well above fair value and near the top of its range, NOK/SEK near its historical low.
- Oil sits roughly 20% below its January highs despite a recent recovery, with commodity strategists seeing downside risk.
- CAD has already reached [REDACTED]'s 12-month forecast; the latest Canada payrolls report was possibly the first sign of the trade war hitting hard data outside the US.
- The Ruble has appreciated sharply year-to-date on peace-deal optimism, and real rates sit close to 10%.

### Drivers
- Global allocators shifting toward more diversified portfolios compress the Dollar's high valuation as US asset returns look less exceptional — the core structural force, expected to be persistent but not as fast or high-conviction as the last month's move.
- US policy recalibration is pushing the other way: less DOGE-related uncertainty, hinted US-China tariff de-escalation, pressure on other countries to restrict China, and Trump's assurance he won't remove the Fed chair — all aimed directly at [REDACTED]'s key concerns, though investors will take time to be convinced.
- Still-large planned and actual tariff increases plus high uncertainty keep US businesses and consumers potentially frozen, sustaining recession watch and keeping high-beta currencies on edge.
- Rates as a USD/JPY headwind have become less reliable amid shifting correlations and perceived institutional risks; watch next week's US employment report for labor-market slowdown that would raise risks of deeper, earlier Fed cuts.
- Canada's April 28 election is a fiscal fork: a Liberal (Carney) win points to more expansionary spending that offsets tariff drag and lets the BoC ease less, on net supporting CAD.
- COP is dragged by high oil beta and domestic fiscal slippage risk; a more prudent BanRep has stabilised COP carry, cushioning returns but not enough to fully curtail weakness if oil falls further.

### Risks
- Upside to the Dollar (downside to the short-USD view): continued market-friendly policy shifts or resilient hard data in upcoming releases — [REDACTED] flags this as the main risk to tactical short AUD/JPY and to the broader Dollar-decline call.
- Downside for COP: on a dovish BanRep surprise next week, USD/COP would move more since a hold is priced; the rate decision is a close call per [REDACTED].
- Downside for RUB: a ceasefire acting as a negative demand shock would prompt faster CBR cuts than priced, and unwinding capital controls would release trapped foreign capital, pressuring the currency lower.
- [REDACTED] notes the Dollar's structural repricing is "not a sure thing" and cannot continue at the pace seen over the past month.

### Unpacked
**The central call is that the Dollar's overvaluation unwinds as global allocators diversify, and [REDACTED] pushes back on two common objections.** Worries about positioning are misplaced because the whole point is that structural positioning is still very long; evidence that some investors have sold or hedged Dollar assets is read as confirmation they will not add with the same enthusiasm, not as a "stock" of unhedged assets needing correction. The focus is on the shift in future allocations, which historically drove large, persistent exchange-rate moves. Recent US policy recalibrations are acknowledged as directly targeting [REDACTED]'s concerns, but conviction is tempered by the frequency of policy changes and still-large tariffs.

**Short USD/JPY is framed as the best recession hedge, but with visible limits.** It generally worked across recent key periods except around the late-March auto tariffs announcement, when higher yields let USD/JPY rise even as equities fell. With rates now a less obvious headwind, and with the Dollar expected to move from over- to undervalued, USD/JPY is seen falling to 135 over 12 months — risks skewed to reaching or breaching that earlier. Because equities remain vulnerable near-term and the Dollar sell-off leaves it prone to swings, the preferred tactical expression is short AUD/JPY, and a dovish BoJ next week is not viewed as a barrier to Yen strength.

**On CAD, the currency's path is a function of fiscal policy.** A Liberal win likely brings larger spending increases that offset US-tariff growth headwinds; since the BoC has placed the onus of offsetting the trade war on fiscal policy, more fiscal support could mean less BoC accommodation and a slightly stronger currency. [REDACTED] stays optimistic on CAD versus USD but expects its US linkages to weigh on the crosses, revising forecasts to 1.36, 1.35 and 1.34 at 3, 6 and 12 months (from 1.40, 1.39, 1.38).

**COP is expected to underperform its peers despite room for tactical catch-up.** The case rests on high oil beta with downside oil risk, plus domestic fiscal slippage from pre-agreed spending and likely overestimated tax revenue, with a higher bar to adjust spending than in 2024. A more prudent BanRep has stabilised carry, but an on-hold stance is unlikely to fully offset weakness if oil falls and fiscal risks persist. The preferred LatAm long remains BRL for its value, carry and limited trade exposure; the long BRL/MXN recommendation from the prior week is kept, with the stop tightened to 3.40 to protect gains.

**In the Scandis, model dislocations are cleanest on relative-value crosses rather than EUR/USD, where large directional flows blur the signal.** Both short EUR/NOK and long NOK/SEK screen attractive, but NOK/SEK is preferred for its lower sensitivity to global risk, since NOK strength is most threatened by weaker risk sentiment via a deeper Norges Bank cutting path and lower oil. The recommendation is to buy 3-month 0.9450/0.9700 NOK/SEK call spreads.

**On RUB, the currency is judged stronger than fundamentals warrant.** With oil down ~20% from January highs and external buffers now thinner — a small current account surplus relative to oil, partly due to expansionary fiscal policy — the exchange rate is expected to act as the main shock absorber. Even with attractive ~10% real-rate carry, the path hinges on the timing and sequencing of sanction removal and capital-control withdrawal; USD/RUB is forecast to grind up to a 12-month 110, a larger depreciation than forwards imply.

subject: Weekly Fund Flows: Flows to US Treasuries Remain Positive
summary:
# Flows into Treasuries stay firm while credit loses traction

**Theme:** Rotation into governments and non-US equities; risk improves at the margin  
**Markets:** Global fund flows (equities, fixed income, FX)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Isabella Rosenberg, 25 April 2025  

### Landscape
- Global equity funds drew +$9bn in the week ending April 23, up slightly from +$8bn the prior week.
- Global fixed income funds saw a small net outflow of -$0.8bn, far shallower than the -$21bn of the previous week.
- Money market fund assets rose by $33bn.
- Cross-border FX flows turned positive, favoring USD, EUR, GBP, and CNY.

### Drivers
- The equity improvement came from less negative US equity outflows, while inflows into Western European equity funds slowed.
- Within EM, mainland China equity flows turned positive and Taiwan continued to see strong net inflows.
- The bond outflow was concentrated in credit — Agg-type, IG, and high yield funds led net redemptions — while government bond funds kept drawing inflows.
- US Treasury bond funds have been supported mainly by US investors, with European investors also participating.
- Duration preference stayed tilted to short-duration over long-duration bond funds.
- Sector equity flows were subdued, with health care, financials, and energy funds seeing the largest net outflows.

### Unpacked
**The week's signal is a shift toward safety within fixed income rather than a wholesale retreat from it:** overall bond outflows nearly disappeared, but the composition split sharply, with credit products bleeding while government bonds and, in particular, US Treasuries kept attracting money. The persistence of Treasury inflows despite the broader macro backdrop is the report's featured point, highlighted as the Chart of the Week.

**What stands out on the demand side is that Treasury buying is not solely a US phenomenon** — while US investors have driven the strong flows, European investors have joined in. The continued lean toward short-duration over long-duration funds suggests the appetite is for safety and carry near the front end rather than a duration-extension call.

**On equities, the modest headline gain masks a rotation away from the US and toward parts of EM.** The improvement was mechanical — US outflows simply grew less negative — even as Western European inflows cooled, while mainland China flipped positive and Taiwan stayed strong. Sector flows were quiet, with health care, financials, and energy the notable laggards. FX flows turning positive, spread across USD, EUR, GBP, and CNY, rounds out a picture of incrementally better risk appetite. The report flags no explicit risks and offers no trade idea.

subject: Global Markets Daily: Drivers of and Risks to Foreign Demand for USTs (Marshall)
summary:
# Foreign Demand for USTs: Little Sign of Active Selling, but a Durable Cheapening Looks Warranted

**Theme:** Why foreign appetite for Treasuries is shifting, and what would be needed to keep clearing the market  
**Markets:** US Treasuries / foreign demand  
**Source:** [REDACTED], William Marshall, 25 April 2025  

### Definitive impacts
- Foreign ownership of the UST market rose from ~20% (1990) to nearly 60% by the late 2000s, then fell back — the decline driven mainly by a smaller foreign official footprint.
- Since the start of 2020, foreign official net UST purchases total just $140bn, versus $2.12tn of foreign private net buying.
- Foreign official holdings have been roughly flat in notional terms for about a decade, reflecting slower reserve accumulation and gradual dollar diversification.
- Flows show private foreign investors rotating along the curve — away from longer maturities toward the front end — rather than exiting outright.
- US Treasuries have grown as a share of the Bloomberg Global Treasury Aggregate index outstanding.
- Treasury free float as a share of domestic GDP is higher than for Bunds and Gilts, and US swap spreads are correspondingly tighter; all three markets currently sit somewhat cheap to the common swap-spread/free-float pattern (Japan an outlier due to large central-bank ownership and limited foreign presence).

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] sees little compelling evidence that active foreign divestment has driven recent price action; the higher risk premia and weaker dollar look instead like the adjustment normally needed to attract future demand.
- [REDACTED] judges a passive drop in foreign appetite as still consequential, given the large foreign footprint and the price-insensitivity of official holders — a retreat by official buyers would shift the clearing burden onto more price-sensitive private and domestic investors, requiring a greater yield concession.
- The US inflation-versus-growth tension is viewed as a near-term headwind to USTs relative to markets with easier policy trade-offs (e.g. the euro area), justifying a relatively steeper UST curve; [REDACTED] expects this to be shorter-lived rather than persistent.
- [REDACTED] frames rising global safe-asset supply — as Europe expands fiscally and the ECB and BoJ shrink their footprints — as a longer-term drag on valuations across all core markets, not USTs uniquely.
- However, US fiscal-sustainability and institutional-credibility questions are seen as UST-specific challenges that could reduce the appeal of the marginal unit of Treasury supply.
- [REDACTED] argues a weaker dollar can absorb part of the needed risk-premium build, but because the marginal buyer also cares about yield/spread, the cheapening in USTs should show at least some durability.

### Backdrop
The US, as long as it runs a current-account deficit, must remain a net exporter of financial assets to the rest of the world — an accounting identity. But the mix of those assets and the compensation required to induce absorption are fluid. Official and private foreign buyers respond to different signals: official demand tracks global reserve accumulation and dollar performance (USD strength typically coincides with weaker official buying via rebalancing), making officials — aside from the Fed — the least price-sensitive holders. Private foreign demand instead responds to relative yield pick-up, hedge value (the UST-equity correlation), and relative scarcity of safe duration.

For much of the post-GFC decade USTs offered a consistent positive yield pick-up versus JGBs, Bunds and Gilts on both an outright and FX-hedged basis, while constrained supply abroad (flat German and Japanese free float relative to GDP) reinforced their relative scarcity — conditions that sustained foreign appetite.

### At issue
No single event: the note is a framework piece responding to a cluster of developments — trade tensions, slowing US momentum, progress on a fiscal package, and President Trump's escalating pressure on the Fed — that together sharpened focus on whether foreign demand for USTs can hold up. Recent bouts of higher yields, tighter swap spreads and a weaker dollar had fuelled fears of large foreign selling. The note's assessment: the data show rotation within the curve, not active liquidation.

### Unpacked
The question that prompts the analysis is whether the past month's move in Treasuries reflects foreigners heading for the exits. **The answer offered is no — the evidence points to repositioning rather than divestment — but the more important point is that outright selling was never required for the story to matter.** A passive cooling of foreign appetite, consistent with the FX team's "marginal" allocation case for dollar weakness, is enough to move prices when the holders in question are as large and as price-insensitive as the official sector.

The mechanism runs through who has to clear the market next. **As official demand fades, the marginal buyer becomes progressively more economically motivated — first foreign private investors, then domestic ones — and each step down that ladder is more price-sensitive than the last, so the same supply needs a bigger yield or spread concession to be absorbed.** That is why a shift in the composition of demand, even without net selling, carries a valuation cost.

Two distinct pressures sit on top of that. **The near-term one is the Fed's unusually sharp inflation-versus-growth bind, which dulls Treasuries' hedge value at a time when peers face cleaner policy trade-offs** — a cyclical headwind [REDACTED] expects to ease as inflation returns toward target. The longer-term one is structural: the global pool of safe assets is set to widen as Europe borrows more and the ECB and BoJ retreat, lifting risk premia everywhere. Treasuries are not singled out by that tide, but fiscal-sustainability and credibility questions are the part that is specific to them.

**The resolution need not fall entirely on yields — a weaker dollar can carry some of the adjustment — but because the buyers now doing the marginal absorbing care about yield and spread, the cheapening in USTs should prove at least somewhat durable rather than snapping back.** Current swap spreads, cheap to the common free-float pattern shared with Bunds and Gilts, are read as broadly consistent with that supply picture.

The note carries a Global Markets Daily trade-idea list (KRW steepeners, INR NDOIS receivers, BRL/MXN longs, a 30y TIPS-versus-nominals position, among others), but these are standing book recommendations, not conclusions of this analysis, which offers no explicit trade idea of its own.

subject: USA: Existing Home Sales Below Expectations; Lowering Q1 GDP Tracking to -0.2%
summary:
# US: Existing Home Sales Disappoint, Pull Q1 GDP Tracking Down to -0.2%

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius
**Focus:** US housing data and GDP tracking
**General comment:** Factual data-tracking note; marginally revises down the Q1 growth projection.

### Context
Comment on the March release of US existing home sales, combined with the details of the same morning's durable goods report, used to recalibrate the Q1 GDP tracking estimate.

### The data
- **Existing home sales fell well more than expected.** They declined 5.9% in March, to 4.02 million units (SAAR), below [REDACTED]'s projected -3.0% and the -3.1% consensus, reversing the prior month's upward-revised +4.4% gain. The decline was led by single-family homes (-6.4%), while condos and co-ops were stable. All regions declined: West (-9.4%), South (-5.7%), Midwest (-5.0%), and Northeast (-2.0%).
- **Prices eased at the margin, but the supply-demand imbalance improved.** The median price of all existing homes fell 0.9% on the month (seasonally adjusted by [REDACTED]), up +2.8% year-over-year. Available supply rose 0.3 month, to 4.5 months — still above the 2019 average of 3.9 months.
- **The combination of the two reports lowered GDP tracking.** The durable goods details point to somewhat weaker inventory accumulation than assumed, and home sales fell more than expected. On net, the Q1 GDP tracking estimate was cut by 0.3pp, to -0.2% (quarter-over-quarter annualized).

### Implications
- The growth projection moves into slightly negative territory in Q1, pressured by inventories and housing.
- The improvement in the housing supply/demand relationship signals market accommodation, with prices already easing at the margin.

subject: Global Markets Daily: Hedge with JPY—vs AUD Short-Term and vs USD Long-Term (Fishman/Jenkins)
summary:
# Yen Hedge: Against AUD in the Short Term, Against the Dollar in the Long Term

**Theme:** why short USD/JPY remains a recession hedge, but short AUD/JPY is tactically preferable
**Markets:** developed-market FX (JPY, USD, EUR, AUD)
**Source:** [REDACTED], Karen Reichgott Fishman, April 24, 2025

### Definitive impacts
- Across the four periods delimited between March 26 and the present, USD/JPY fell (the short "worked") in all of them, with the exception of March 26-27, when the yen weakened as yields rose following the auto tariffs, more than its rate beta would have predicted.
- At the peak of stress, the VIX topped 52 on April 8, the period in which USD/JPY posted its most pronounced decline.
- On April 10-11, during the most acute phase of Treasury market stress, the yen underperformed the euro — atypical for a risk-off episode.
- In March 2020, dollar funding pressures pushed the USD higher against other reserve currencies; in that scenario, buying yen against a high-beta currency (such as AUD) outperformed short USD/JPY.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] prefers short AUD/JPY tactically: with risks in equities still skewed to the downside and a dollar whose rapid decline leaves it vulnerable to tactical swings, being long yen against a cyclical currency maximizes protection.
- [REDACTED] sees USD/JPY falling to 135 over 12 months, with risk of reaching (or breaking through) that level well before then, underpinned by the thesis that the dollar should unwind its overvaluation and likely turn undervalued.
- For the yen to outperform the euro, [REDACTED] argues the market needs to price a higher probability of US recession and deeper Fed cuts; without that, EUR/JPY could rise even amid falling risk appetite, given the reallocation of flows toward Europe.
- The rates-FX correlation should keep oscillating between positive and negative while doubts about institutional credibility persist, but [REDACTED] expects dollar weakness to continue.
- [REDACTED] sees the probability of a dollar liquidity crisis as low, even lower after reports of possible tariff and policy rollbacks.
- An eventual dovish shift by the BoJ would not, in [REDACTED]'s view, be a barrier to yen appreciation.
- Main risk to the trade: policy continuing to shift in a market-friendly direction, or hard data proving resilient in upcoming releases; pre-tariff front-loading may be masking weakness in activity.

### Backdrop
The yen has historically high sensitivity to both US yields and equities, which makes short USD/JPY one of the most effective FX hedges against negative growth shocks: when risk appetite falls and demand for traditional havens rises, the yen tends to outperform. The classic exception is a dollar funding crisis — as in March 2020 — when the dollar itself appreciates against all currencies, including other havens, and the USD/JPY hedge fails. Buying yen against a high-beta currency protects against that left tail.

Normally, the only regime in which the hedge fails is one of rising yields, since the yen tends to lag even as equities fall. The current regime, marked by unstable correlations and heightened perceptions of institutional risk, makes rates a less obvious obstacle to this hedge, at least while those concerns persist.

### At issue
The note assesses the recent performance of short USD/JPY as a hedge in light of price action over the past month, split into four periods: March 26-27 (auto tariffs), April 2-4 (reciprocal tariffs), April 7-11 (the following week, with Treasury market stress and the 90-day postponement on April 9), and April 14 to the present. The operational conclusion: keep short USD/JPY as the structural portfolio hedge, but express the protection tactically via short AUD/JPY. The short AUD/JPY trade appears on the idea list, opened on March 17 at 94, with a revised target of 85.0 and a revised stop of 91.5, trading at 91.19.

### Unpacked

The starting point is a practical question that April itself raised: whether short USD/JPY, the recession hedge preferred by so many managers, still delivers protection when stress intensifies. The note's answer is nuanced — **it worked most of the time, but two episodes expose its limits: the perverse reaction to yields in late March, and the underperformance versus the euro precisely during the most acute phase of Treasury stress.**

These two stumbles are not random; they point to the same underlying theme. **What is changing the regime is the combination of doubts about US institutional credibility with the reallocation of flows out of the dollar and toward Europe**, which supports the euro even in moments of lower risk appetite. That is why EUR/JPY can rise atypically, and why the yen only outperforms the euro if the market starts pricing US recession and deeper Fed cuts.

The choice between the two hedge expressions follows from that. **Short USD/JPY is the structural bet — anchored in the thesis that the dollar unwinds its overvaluation and falls to 135 over 12 months — while short AUD/JPY is the tactical expression, which protects better in the short term by being dollar-neutral and by capturing the Australian dollar's cyclical beta.** AUD/JPY tends to show among the highest volatility-adjusted returns in equity selloffs, and also offers additional protection against the tail of a dollar funding crisis — a tail currently seen as unlikely, but fresh in memory after the signs of cracks in Treasuries.

The cost of this choice is well known: shorting high-beta currencies tends to be more expensive than shorting the dollar, whose carry remains relatively elevated. **For the reader, the practical takeaway is twofold: keep short USD/JPY as the long-horizon hedge and use short AUD/JPY as tactical protection while equity risks skew to the downside and the dollar remains vulnerable to rallies.** The trade unwinds if policy keeps shifting toward a market-friendly tone or if hard data comes in resilient — a relevant caveat, since pre-tariff front-loading may be temporarily masking weakness in activity.

subject: USA: Durable Goods Orders Above Expectations But Core Orders Softer; Initial Claims Rebound in Line With Expectations
summary:
# US: Durable Goods Orders Surprise on the Headline, but Core Remains Weak

**Source:** [REDACTED], Jan Hatzius
**Focus:** US durable goods orders and jobless claims, March/April 2025
**General comment:** Descriptive data comment; headline beat is largely mechanical, underlying signal is soft.

### Context
Comment on the March release of durable goods orders and weekly jobless claims in the US, current inputs for tracking activity and Q1 GDP.

### The case
- **The 9.2% rise in total durable goods orders is almost entirely mechanical, not a sign of demand strength.** The number came in well above consensus (median +2.0%) and the house's own projection (+5.0%), but was driven by a $26bn jump in new orders for nondefense aircraft and parts. Excluding transportation, the measure was flat on the month, slightly below expectations — that is, underlying demand did not keep pace with the headline.
- **The core, the cleaner indicator of business investment, shows a weak pace.** Core capital goods orders rose only 0.1% (in line with consensus) and shipments 0.3% (slightly above). In addition, February data were revised down by 0.1pp across each series — durable goods orders to +0.9%, core orders to -0.3%, and core shipments to +0.7% — lowering the starting point.
- **Jobless claims remain contained.** Initial claims partially recovered, rising 6k to 222k, in line with consensus, and the four-week moving average fell 1k, to 220k. Continuing claims declined 37k, to 1,841k, slightly below expectations. There is no sign of labor-market deterioration in these data.

### Implications
- The details point to somewhat weaker inventory accumulation than assumed, which tends to weigh on Q1 GDP tracking; the estimate will be updated after the mid-morning data.
- For the reader, the headline beat should be discounted: the flat core plus the downward revisions suggest tepid business investment, not acceleration.

subject: Global PMI Monitor: New Export Orders Fall in the US, UK, and Japan (Dong)
summary:
# Developed-Market Momentum Cools as Export Orders Buckle Under Tariff Uncertainty

**Theme:** April flash PMIs — services-led slowdown, new export orders rolling over in the US, UK, and Japan  
**Markets:** Developed-market growth and inflation  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jan Hatzius, 23 April 2025

### Landscape
- The DM composite flash PMI fell -1.1pt to 50.7, still in expansion but its weakest reading of recent months.
- Manufacturing edged up +0.2pt to 49.3 (still contractionary), while services slipped -1.6pt to 50.8.
- US manufacturing rose +0.5pt to 50.7; UK manufacturing fell -0.9pt to 44.0.
- US services dropped -3.0pt to 51.4 and UK services -3.6pt to 48.9, the latter into contraction.
- The composite employment PMI fell in most major DMs, -0.7pt to 50.8 in the US and -0.8pt to 46.3 in the UK.
- New export orders declined notably for both manufacturing and services in the US, Japan, and the UK, but held steady in France and Germany.

### Drivers
- Services momentum is fading across DMs and driving the composite lower, with the UK falling into contraction and the US decelerating sharply — the clearest downward force this month.
- Manufacturing is stabilizing rather than accelerating: the DM factory index ticked up but stayed below 50, and the forward-looking orders-to-inventories ratio rose only marginally, +0.01 to 1.03.
- Export demand is weakening asymmetrically — orders falling in the US, UK, and Japan while the Euro-area core (France, Germany) holds — pointing to a differentiated hit rather than a uniform global slowdown.
- Services forward expectations are deteriorating: the future activity component fell -2.6pt to 57.2, signaling the services softness may persist.
- Price pressures are mixed: input price PMIs eased slightly (manufacturing -0.5pt to 59.7, services -0.5pt to 59.8) while output price PMIs rose (manufacturing +1.4pt to 56.3, services +0.8pt to 54.1), consistent with firms passing costs through even as input inflation cools. The UK stands out, with manufacturing output prices up +5.2pt to 60.5.

### Unpacked
The report is a modular scoreboard of the April flash PMIs, moving from aggregate DM trends to country detail to the activity and inflation components. **The headline is a services-led loss of momentum: the DM composite fell to 50.7, held above 50 only by a marginal improvement in manufacturing, while services softened broadly.** The DM aggregate is a GDP-weighted composite of the US, Euro area, UK, Australia, and Japan.

**The most notable cross-country signal is the drop in new export orders in the US, UK, and Japan, contrasted with steady orders in France and Germany** — a split that separates the economies most exposed to the current trade backdrop from the Euro-area core. At the country level, the US showed a manufacturing/services divergence (factory PMI up to 50.7, services down to 51.4), while the UK weakened on both fronts, with services falling into contraction at 48.9 and manufacturing sliding further to 44.0.

**Forward-looking components lean negative, particularly for services, where the future activity index fell to 57.2 and employment readings softened across most DMs.** Early US business surveys cited alongside the flash data pointed to mixed-to-negative manufacturing signals and negative services signals for April, reinforcing the PMI picture rather than contradicting it.

On inflation, the components send a two-sided message. **Input price pressures eased slightly while output prices rose, suggesting firms are still lifting selling prices even as cost inflation moderates** — with the UK the standout on output-price acceleration. Manufacturing suppliers' delivery times lengthened marginally (DM average +0.3pt to 49.3), a modest sign of supply friction. The note is a data monitor and offers no explicit trade idea or baseline risk scenarios of its own.

subject: What's Top of Mind in Macro Research: Tariff-induced US recession risk, China's slower growth outlook, US copper tariffs
summary:
# Tariff recession still underpriced; China slows and copper enters the radar

**Theme:** Tariff hit to US growth as the through-line across markets, hedging, China and Germany  
**Markets:** Global macro (US growth & rates, China, commodities, Europe)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jenny Grimberg, 23 April 2025  

### Landscape
- US recession probability put at an elevated 45% over the next 12 months.
- Soft data already showing signs of a significant slowdown ahead, while hard data has stayed fairly solid — likely reflecting purchase front-loading before tariffs.
- China Q1 GDP and March activity came in stronger than expected, but the strength is read as export front-loading rather than underlying momentum.
- Gold sits at what is described as an attractive entry point; longer-dated USTs and Dollar longs have failed to act as effective hedges.
- Germany still expected to contract in 2025 for a third straight year.

### Drivers
- Tariffs are the dominant drag on US growth; hard data expected to start weakening around mid-to-late summer, consistent with past growth slowdowns — the key window to watch for confirmation.
- Market comfort from Trump's remarks that China tariffs "will come down substantially" and his walk-back of threats to fire Fed Chair Powell has pushed markets to again underprice recession risk relative to the forecast.
- China facing a significant forward tariff drag; policymakers expected to intensify easing across fiscal, monetary, housing and credit, with the April Politburo meeting the near-term catalyst — but easing seen as insufficient to fully offset the drag.
- US Section 232 copper investigation expected to produce a 25% import tariff by mid-2025, a probability the market is not currently pricing.
- German coalition agreement delivers investment incentives and electricity tax cuts, but leaves the tax and social-security burden largely unreformed — limiting the growth lift.

### Risks
- Downside (US): a full-blown recession is the central risk scenario the analyst flags — modeled as S&P 500 near 4,600, HY spreads above 600bp, front-end yields below 3%, a steeper curve, material damage to commercial real estate (residential relatively insulated), and some further downside to US natural gas even though it already prices recession.
- Downside (China): the analyst expects sequential GDP growth to slow sharply in Q2 and stay low through H2, with the risk that policymakers prioritize employment stability over GDP.
- Skew: the note frames US risks as asymmetric — markets are underpricing recession, leaving them vulnerable to any sign it is materializing, with no comparable upside case developed.

### Unpacked
**The central call is that a sizable tariff-induced hit to US growth is coming, and that markets have again grown too comfortable to price it.** The gap between soft and hard data is the crux: surveys are already softening while activity holds up, a divergence attributed to front-loaded purchases. History from prior event-driven recessions — the 1973 and 1990 oil spikes, the 1979–80 rate increases, and the 2001 dot-com crash — shows soft data turning first and hard data following only a few months later, which underpins the mid-to-late-summer timing for visible weakening. Uncertainty is stressed as very high, with hard data, soft data and global trade flows the series to watch for the true scale of the damage.

**Because the usual portfolio hedges have stopped working, the note redirects investors toward alternative recession protection.** Longer-dated USTs and Dollar longs failed as hedges, so the preference shifts to the Yen, the Swiss Franc and gold, the latter seen at an attractive entry point. Shorter-maturity USTs and curve steepeners are still viewed as protective — but conditional on the Fed cutting decisively, which is the expected response if a recession does materialize.

**China is watched less for its recent upside surprise than for the tariff drag still ahead.** The strong Q1 print is discounted as front-loading, and the expected policy response — easing across fiscal, monetary, housing and credit, with the April Politburo meeting the key event — is judged too small to offset the hit, partly because employment stability may be prioritized over the growth target. The result is a sharp sequential slowdown in Q2 and subdued growth through the second half.

**On copper, the note pairs a specific policy forecast with a positioning view:** a Section 232 investigation seen leading to a 25% import tariff by mid-2025, a risk the market is underpricing, which motivates a newly initiated long in the Dec-25 COMEX-LME copper arbitrage — the one explicit trade recommendation in the note.

**Germany rounds out the radar as a story of reform that fell short of the need.** Investment incentives and electricity tax reductions should help, but only limited income-tax relief, an unfinished broader tax reform, and no cut to employee social-security contributions leave the core burden intact. The economy is still expected to contract in 2025 before recovering to 1.1% growth in 2026 and 2.0% in 2027, carried by higher infrastructure and defense spending.

subject: USA: S&P Services PMI Declines; Manufacturing PMI Edges Up; Lowering Q1 GDP Tracking Estimate to +0.1% on Weaker Real Construction
summary:
# US Q1 GDP Tracking Trimmed to +0.1% as April PMIs Soften and Tariff-Driven Prices Climb

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US April flash PMIs, new home sales, and Q1 GDP tracking  
**General comment:** Cautious read of the April data flow — softening activity with tariff-driven price pressure, prompting a downward GDP revision.

### Context
A same-day review of April preliminary S&P Global PMIs and March new home sales, feeding into a marginal cut to the Q1 GDP tracking estimate. It sits within the debate over how tariffs are simultaneously pressuring prices and weighing on activity.

### The case
- **Services activity slowed and its composition weakened.** The services PMI fell 3.0pt to 51.4, below consensus for a smaller decline, with both new business (-1.0pt to 52.7) and employment (-0.8pt to 51.0) softening. S&P attributed the slowdown to weaker demand, notably in export-facing segments such as travel and tourism. Input prices eased (-2.2pt to 58.0) even as output prices rose (+1.7pt to 54.2).
- **Manufacturing edged up but is broadly stagnating, with prices at multi-year highs.** The manufacturing PMI rose 0.5pt to 50.7, above consensus, as output (+1.6pt to 50.2) and new orders (+0.3pt to 51.5) gained while employment slipped (-0.2pt to 49.7). Input (+0.9pt to 66.9) and output (+2.0pt to 60.8) prices reached their highest in over two years; S&P linked the price increases to rising import costs tied to tariffs and higher labor costs. Any tariff benefit is described as offset by economic uncertainty, supply-chain concerns, and falling exports.
- **New home sales beat, but the construction deflator did the work in the GDP revision.** March new home sales rose 7.4% to a 724k annualized rate, well above the ~1% expected, and February was revised up to +3.1%; gains concentrated in the South (+58k) and Midwest (+2k), with declines in the Northeast (-8k) and West (-2k). The offsetting factor was the price index for new homes under construction: after rising 2.7% and 2.1% in January and February (versus roughly flat through 2024), the expected March payback in the construction deflator came in smaller than assumed, weighing on real construction.

### Implications
- The net effect is a 0.3pp cut to the Q1 GDP tracking estimate, to +0.1% quarter-over-quarter annualized — the stronger nominal home-sales figure outweighed by weaker real construction from the deflator.
- The PMI mix points to stagflationary pressure: cooling demand and softer employment alongside the highest input and output price readings in over two years, with tariffs cited as the driver of the price side.

subject: Global Rates Notes: 2Q25 Treasury Refunding Preview
summary:
# Treasury to Hold Coupon Sizes; [REDACTED] Pushes First Increase to August 2026

**Theme:** Unchanged nominal coupon auctions and steady guidance, with the first size hike delayed to Aug 2026 on higher term premium  
**Markets:** US Treasury issuance / rates  
**Source:** [REDACTED], William Marshall, 23 April 2025  

### Estimates
- **Nominal coupon auction sizes unchanged** at the April 30 refunding statement (8:30am), with guidance of stable nominal auctions "for at least the next several quarters" left intact.
- **+$1bn each** to the 10y TIPS reopening and new issue, plus **+$1bn** to the 5y TIPS reopening — the only auction-size changes expected.
- **Q2 net marketable borrowing revised up to ~$750bn** (from $123bn), assuming an $850bn end-quarter TGA; released Monday April 28 at 3pm. Of the revision, **$445bn** simply replenishes the TGA from end-March levels.
- **3Q25 marketable borrowing projected at $875bn**, with an $850bn end-of-quarter cash balance.
- **Net privately held coupon issuance of $495bn (2Q25) and $467bn (3Q25)** — about **$230–235bn of 10y-equivalent duration supply** per quarter, held stable by unchanged coupon sizes.
- **First coupon size increases now expected at the August 2026 refunding** (prior: February 2026), keeping the bills share steady around 22%.

### Outlook
- **Guidance change is unlikely**, per the analyst: updated deficit projections let Treasury hold current coupon sizes for several more quarters if it accepts a bill share a couple points above 20%, and the recent term-premium rebuild argues against adding duration supply now.
- **A lower steady-state TGA target and/or larger buybacks are risks, not the base case.** Either could be a short-term positive for duration and spreads, but the analyst sees no formal shift announced next week.
- **Any TGA-target cut has no long-term yield implications**, and even short-term positives could be diluted if a lower balance lets the Fed shrink its balance sheet further.
- **Buybacks unlikely to be formalized as a flexible liquidity tool next week**, though the analyst wouldn't rule out an eventual adjustment; the impact would likely be limited in true market stress.
- **The debt-limit path could drive large TGA deviations**: depending on resolution timing, the balance may fall into the low hundreds during Q3 before rebuilding to $850bn by November.

### Unpacked
The near-term call rests on a market environment and medium-term funding uncertainty that make strong conviction on the timing of coupon increases difficult. **The recent reset higher in term premium is the central reason for pushing the first size hike out to August 2026 — it argues for a more cautious approach to adding duration supply now.** With deficit projections supporting stable sizes for several more quarters, the bills share settles around 22%, a couple of points above the 20% anchor.

The mechanics of next week's borrowing revision are almost entirely a debt-limit artifact. **The jump in Q2 borrowing to roughly $750bn reflects a much lower-than-projected end-Q1 cash balance, with $445bn of the revision simply rebuilding the TGA — and the $850bn target again assumes a debt-limit raise or suspension, leaving it vulnerable to an undershoot.** Depending on when the limit is resolved, the cash balance could dip into the low hundreds during Q3 before rebuilding by November.

Two structural questions sit behind the headline numbers. **A lower steady-state TGA could delay the urgency to raise coupon sizes by a few months and ease concerns about near-term duration supply, but it carries no long-term implications for equilibrium yields** — and any short-term benefit could be offset if it enables further Fed balance-sheet shrinkage. Reinforcing the later-hike view, the analyst expects eventual Fed Treasury purchases (to offset MBS runoff after QT and later to grow reserves) to skew toward the front end, easing pressure on Treasury to term out.

The second question is buybacks. **Liquidity conditions have been challenging, but there are no clear signs of dislocation in the off-the-run complex, so proactive liquidity-support buybacks remain a possibility rather than a plan.** The small starting scale leaves room to lean on them if dislocations emerge, though doing so could pull forward the need to raise coupon sizes, and the benefit would likely be limited in genuine stress. The reader should watch the April 30 statement for any signal on TGA stance or a more flexible buyback role — both framed as risks, not the base case.

subject: Global Markets Daily: The Copper Tariff Trade (Dinsmore/Waltham/Forcellese)
summary:
# Copper's 25% Tariff Gap: Long the COMEX-LME Arbitrage Before the S232 Lands

**Theme:** A Section 232 copper tariff is underpriced; the COMEX-LME arbitrage should widen toward full tariff pricing.  
**Markets:** US copper / global metals trade policy  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Eoin Dinsmore, 23 April 2025

### Definitive impacts
- **The Dec-25 COMEX-LME arbitrage sits at $1,707/t (an 18% premium over LME), versus $2,287/t if a 25% tariff were fully priced** — a gap of ~$580/t at the current LME price.
- **Copper markets are pricing under 60% probability of a 25% import tariff by May**, per the arbitrage forward curve (Exhibit 1).
- **US refined-copper import reliance has roughly doubled, from 25% in 2010 to nearly 50% in 2024** — about 725kt or $7bn of net imports, mostly from Chile, Canada and Peru.
- **US domestic refined-copper production has fallen ~20% since 2010**, driven by higher processing costs and permitting challenges, while global output rose ~40% over the same period (over 90% of that growth from China).
- **US share of global refined-copper output has dropped below 4%** (Exhibit 2), and the US has raised exports of scrap and concentrates since 2010, with China a top destination.
- **The S232 investigation was initiated 25 February 2025**; a tariff decision must legally be made by December, the anchor for the Dec-25 trade horizon.

### Opinative impacts
- **[REDACTED] recommends going long the Dec-25 COMEX-LME copper arbitrage**, judging the market is not pricing a high enough likelihood of the tariff it expects; the trade would be closed once the arbitrage reflects the ~22.5% probability-weighted tariff.
- **[REDACTED] expects a 25% tariff on copper imports by mid-2025**, on par with existing S232 steel and aluminium tariffs, and assigns it a 90% subjective probability (versus 10% for no refined-copper tariff, and effectively nil for a 10% tariff, which it sees as hard to rationalise).
- **Baseline timing is a tariff by end-June (55% probability)**, 125 days after initiation and consistent with a March 26 press report citing action "within weeks"; a 30% probability is assigned to a slower 180-day path pushing implementation to after June but by early September (Exhibit 3).
- **[REDACTED] argues the tariff will persist as a real COMEX premium** because the US must keep importing refined copper to meet demand even as domestic output slowly rises — so it expects a ~25% COMEX premium over LME.
- **[REDACTED] sees tariffs lifting US self-sufficiency only over time** — 2-3 years for import reliance to shift materially via recycling, a smelter/refinery restart and lower semis exports, with fast-tracked mine permitting adding supply by the early 2030s.
- **[REDACTED] flags that the market is right to discount Trump tariff threats generally** — given recent reversals on "reciprocal" tariffs — but treats metals as an exception where the commitment is firm.

### Backdrop
Section 232 lets the US impose tariffs on national-security grounds, the same mechanism behind existing 25% duties on steel and aluminium. Copper is central to that framing: it is the second most-used material by the US Defense Department and underpins power distribution, energy-transition equipment and AI infrastructure. Copper was excluded from the baseline 10% universal tariff already in place, which is part of why an intermediate 10% copper rate is viewed as unlikely.

Refined copper can be produced via three routes — electrowinning of leached ore, primary smelting/refining of concentrates, and secondary smelting/refining of scrap — which shapes how tariffs would ripple through US recycling and smelter economics.

### At issue
On 25 February 2025 the Trump Administration opened a Section 232 investigation into US copper imports. Its stated aim is to strengthen "national security, economic strength and industrial resilience" by encouraging domestic production and cutting import reliance. The investigation is ongoing; no tariff has yet been set. The note's central call is that it will conclude with a 25% tariff on copper imports, most likely by mid-2025.

### Unpacked
The trade rests on a probability gap, not a forecast of copper's outright price. **The market and [REDACTED] largely agree on the mechanics of a tariff — a 25% duty would translate into a ~25% COMEX premium over LME — but disagree on how likely and how soon it is, and that disagreement is what the arbitrage position monetises.** At current LME levels the Dec-25 arbitrage would need to move from $1,707/t to $2,287/t to fully reflect the tariff, so the position pays off as the market converges toward [REDACTED]'s higher assumed probability.

The structural case for the tariff is a two-decade slide in US self-reliance: production down ~20% since 2010 on cost and permitting, demand rising, and the gap filled by imports from Chile, Canada and Peru while China captured the bulk of global refining growth. **That shift — the US exporting raw scrap and concentrate while importing finished refined metal, increasingly to and from China — is the vulnerability the Administration is invoking, and it is durable enough that a tariff would bite rather than be quickly engineered around.**

Timing is the main open variable. **[REDACTED]'s fair-value tariff is 22.5% — a 90%/10% blend of the 25%-versus-no-tariff outcomes — and that number, not the trade entry itself, defines the exit: once the curve prices it, the position is closed.** The base case is implementation by end-June, but a 180-day Commerce timeline, matching the recent critical-minerals investigation, could delay it into early September; the trade is structured on the December contract precisely because a decision is legally required by then regardless of the exact date.

The note's own copper-industry counterpoint is worth holding in view: in the no-refined-tariff scenario, the Administration would instead tariff semi-finished and finished products and directly incentivise new mines — closer to what producers actually want. [REDACTED] assigns that only 10% weight, but it is the scenario in which the arbitrage trade underperforms.

subject: Global Market Views: Along the Knife Edge
summary:
# Recession Risk Underpriced as the Dollar's Structural Reset Begins

**Theme:** Defensive positioning through a high but unrealized US recession risk; a durable rotation out of Dollar assets  
**Markets:** US and global macro — equities, rates, credit, FX  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Kamakshya Trivedi, 22 April 2025  

### Landscape
- US economics team puts recession probability at 45% over the next 12 months, unusually high but not a base case.
- After the April 9 tariff pause reversed part of the growth downgrade, cross-asset pricing sits close to the non-recessionary baseline — leaving little cushion against recession risk that [REDACTED] still views as underpriced.
- Only short-dated equity volatility and skew reached recessionary levels during the turmoil; most assets never came close to pricing a full recession.
- Treasury yields rose sharply and the curve steepened on April 7–8 as illiquidity edged toward dysfunction — a much smaller safe-haven rally than in the August 2024 or March 2023 growth scares.
- The Dollar has weakened beyond what interest-rate differentials imply, with the 10-year forward EUR/$ appreciating alongside spot — a sign of structural, not cyclical, repricing.

### Drivers
- Tariffs remain substantial and disruptive even after the pause; a reversal below the 10% baseline looks unlikely, keeping an inflationary drag on US consumption and investment.
- Policy uncertainty stays very high, giving countries, firms and consumers strong incentives to defer trade concessions and new investment — markets risk extrapolating too optimistically from early "deals."
- Financial conditions have eased from peak tightness but remain tighter than two months ago, and fragilities exposed in Treasury markets could resurface.
- For the US, tariffs plus Dollar weakness create an offsetting inflationary impulse that constrains the Fed; for the rest of the world the trade war is a cleaner negative growth shock, and lower energy prices open room for G10 and EM central banks to ease.
- Foreign demand for US assets is being re-evaluated — the shift is led by private investors (not official reserve managers), with room for hedge ratios to rise even absent outright selling.
- Watch the hard data: front-loaded purchases may flatter March–April spending, and weak hiring rather than mass firing makes jobless claims a softer-than-usual signal; the true damage may not be visible until mid-May or early June.

### Risks
- Upside (near-term): with the largest part of the tariff shock likely behind, an absence of fresh bad news, further tariff reductions, or a China trade deal could fuel relief and re-risking.
- Downside: any data pointing to rising recession risk leaves markets vulnerable; [REDACTED] estimates a full recession would take the S&P 500 to ~4600, HY spreads above 600bp and short-maturity yields below 3%.
- Downside (structural): renewed concerns over US fiscal sustainability, a change in Fed leadership, and weaker foreign demand at upcoming auctions could keep the Treasury back end under pressure.
- Skew: [REDACTED] reads risk as tilted to the downside relative to current pricing, and says it would add to downside exposures if markets relax on near-term resilience.

### Unpacked
The April 9 pause pulled the US back from the edge of a clear recessionary slide, but the reprieve has been brief — continued trade-policy concerns and pressure on Fed leadership have pushed US asset prices lower again. **The core judgement is that markets are still underpricing recession risk, so a defensive and diversified stance across equities and credit remains warranted.** The April 2 tariffs were hawkish relative to expectations and, had they held, would almost certainly have forced a recession; the 90-day pause is a stay of execution, not a resolution, leaving the economy on "recession watch" for at least the next two or three months.

On rates, the message is a steeper curve over time. **[REDACTED] sees value in the front and belly of the Treasury curve (2s and 5s), expecting the Fed to cut decisively — perhaps 200bp in a recession, far more than priced though less than a typical downturn — once unemployment turns up.** The back end is treated differently: term-premium reset, structural questions about foreign UST demand, fiscal sustainability worries and Fed-independence concerns should keep long yields elevated and sensitive to any sign of weaker foreign demand. The April 7–8 spike, tied more to levered unwinds and swap-spread moves than to confirmed foreign selling, was the first hint of illiquidity tipping toward dysfunction.

The Dollar view is the note's most emphatic structural call. **Broad, unilateral tariffs make US businesses and consumers the price-takers, so the Dollar itself may need to weaken — reversing the usual logic that a strong Dollar absorbs tariff adjustment.** The tariff reversals arguably ease the path lower by pushing away the left tail of the "Dollar Smile" — the panic rush into Dollars — so investors can hold shorts comfortably when the outlook looks weak but not catastrophic. The move has outrun cyclical factors, and safe G9 currencies (JPY, CHF, EUR) have strengthened, pointing to a genuine desire to cut US allocations.

That reallocation is framed as durable rather than a reserve-currency crisis. **The Dollar's reserve share has been falling for years and is likely to retain its dominant status absent a more dramatic shock; the real shift is private foreign investors — who piled into US equities and bonds for yield and quality — now reassessing, in something resembling the unwind of an "EM-style carry trade."** With a historic USD overweight, high valuations and a large current-account financing need, and with room for hedge ratios to rise even without selling, the process has room to run.

Outside the US the policy tradeoff is easier, and China is pivotal. **If China leans on fiscal, monetary, housing and credit easing rather than a weaker CNY, EM currencies stay anchored and EM local rates should keep outperforming; a smaller, domestically oriented echo of the post-2009 stimulus could also support local and EM equities and Europe.** Redirecting trade via a weaker CNY would be more problematic given competition concerns elsewhere.

Hedging has become harder and more expensive. **With Treasuries and USD longs having failed as equity hedges and implied vol still high, the safest step is simply right-sizing and diversifying exposures.** [REDACTED] points to German and, to a lesser extent, UK bonds as more effective protection than Treasuries through April, alongside JPY, CHF and gold, USD shorts against the G10, and short-maturity Treasuries plus curve steepeners for recession outcomes. The near-term path stays complicated: relief rallies are possible on quiet news or trade progress, but direction should increasingly be set by the data — and until the limits of the damage are visible, markets may struggle to find a firm floor.

subject: US Economics Weekly Update 4/22/2025
summary:
# Survey data first, hard data by late summer: reading the tariff slowdown before it shows

**Theme:** Why weak surveys precede weak hard data — and the timeline to watch  
**Markets:** US macro / growth and labor  
**Source:** [REDACTED], David Mericle, 22 April 2025  

### Landscape
- Q1 GDP tracking estimate raised 0.2pp to +0.4% last week.
- Core retail sales rose 0.4% in March, with January and February growth revised up.
- Industrial production fell 0.3% in March, but manufacturing production rose 0.3% and business equipment rose 1.7%.
- Housing starts fell 11.4% in March, on declines in both single- and multi-family.
- Import prices fell 0.1% in March; March core PCE inflation forecast left at 0.08%.
- Empire manufacturing index rose 11.9pt to -8.1, while the Philly Fed index fell 38.9pt to its lowest since April 2023 — its second-lowest reading outside recessions.

### Drivers
- **Consumer spending** is expected to slow as rising prices eat into disposable income, probably within 2-3 months of tariff implementation, best tracked through core retail sales.
- **Capital spending** should begin slowing this quarter and slow most in H2; surveys flag this faster (1 month) than hard data (5 months) — watch Thursday's durable goods report for the first read on trade-war effects on business investment.
- **Labor market** weakness shows first in jobless claims, then in the unemployment rate and job-finding rate after 2-3 months; low hiring may matter more than high layoffs this cycle.
- **Survey vs hard data lag:** in past shock-driven recessions, survey expectations weakened within a month and current conditions shortly after, but hard data took four months — implying hard data likely only starts to weaken by mid-to-late summer.

### Risks
- **Downside (net employment):** [REDACTED]'s read of the research literature is that tariffs are a net drag on US jobs — a ~100k boost to protected manufacturing employment against a ~500k drag on downstream jobs from higher input costs.
- **Downside (policy):** Powell set a seemingly higher bar for rate cuts than in the first trade war, putting more weight on inflation, which limits Fed support if growth slows.

### Unpacked
The note's central argument is methodological: the survey data deserve a second chance despite a poor recent record. **In past recessions triggered by clear shocks, business-survey expectations components weakened within a month and current-conditions components shortly after, while the hard data took a full four months to turn in real time.** On that pattern, the current soft-survey signal should not be dismissed, and the hard data would only begin to roll over around mid-to-late summer. The timeliest past indicators were the Philly Fed manufacturing and ISM services indices, initial jobless claims, and — perhaps surprisingly — the unemployment rate.

**Thursday's durable goods report is the near-term test.** [REDACTED] expects total durable goods orders up 5% (consensus +1.5%), driven by a sharp jump in commercial aircraft, but core capital goods orders down 0.2% (consensus +0.1%), reflecting the March drops in the new-orders and shipments components of manufacturing surveys — an early glimpse of trade-war effects on business investment.

On policy, Powell called the White House tariffs significantly larger than expected and, like other recent Fed speakers, leaned harder on inflation than at the March FOMC press conference. **He framed the tariff shock as a possible conflict between the Fed's maximum-employment and price-stability goals**, saying the FOMC would weigh how far the economy sits from each goal and over what horizon each deviation would close.

The research recap quantifies the employment tradeoff. Studies suggest a 10pp tariff increase raises employment in protected industries by 0.2-0.4%, while each 1pp rise in tariff-driven costs cuts employment by 0.3-0.6%. **Scaled to the US, that implies roughly 100k of added manufacturing jobs from protection against about 500k lost downstream to input-cost pressure — a negative net effect.** The note offers no explicit trade idea; it is a framework for reading the incoming data.

subject: US Economics Analyst: When Will Growth Slow, and When Will We Know? (Abecasis)
summary:
# When Growth Slows, Which Indicators Flag It First — and When

**Theme:** Real-time indicator timing around growth slowdowns; where tariff drag will show up  
**Markets:** United States (developed markets)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Manuel Abecasis, 22 April 2025

### Key findings
- GDP growth is expected to slow from 2½% in 2024 to just 0.5% in 2025 (Q4/Q4), driven by higher tariffs, tighter financial conditions, and elevated policy uncertainty.
- Among 45 indicators tested for real-time accuracy, initial jobless claims, the Philly Fed manufacturing and ISM services indices, and the unemployment rate flagged past slowdowns most timely — answering which datapoints to watch first.
- In recessions with an identifiable catalyst, hard data took about four months to weaken in real time while survey expectations components turned about one month after the shock — so soft data leads.
- Tariff-driven price increases should appear within the next two or three inflation reports, based on the 2018-19 trade war where most sequential inflation hit within 2-3 months of implementation.
- Core retail sales is the best real-time hard signal of consumer spending around slowdowns, ahead of the personal income and spending releases.
- Capex hard data (e.g. capital goods orders) took about five months to weaken and was noisier than soft data in past capex-led slowdowns; broad measures like manufacturing production give a better real-time read than narrow capex gauges. The expected drag on capex growth peaks at ~5½pp in 2025H2.
- Labor market so far shows no deterioration: WARN layoff notices and Indeed job openings remain healthy; hard weakness is expected around mid-to-late summer.
- The current episode so far tracks prior "event-driven" slowdowns — expectations sharply down, other soft data lower, hard data not yet weakening — but the data are too limited to draw strong conclusions.

### Method & verdict
[Reasonable] The note builds a daily dataset of 45 indicators with real-time vintages, regressing each on a Current Activity Indicator to rank real-time accuracy around slowdowns (defined as a ≥1.5pp drop in the CAI's 3-month centered average). Event-driven episodes are studied via first principal components of hard data, survey current-conditions, and survey-expectations, using back-cast series for the 1970s-80s cases. The scoring rewards higher-frequency, less-revised, earlier-released data. The design is transparent and well-suited to timing questions, but the authors flag real limits: false positives are not penalized (only true slowdowns are sampled), some indicators rest on few events, back-casting and methodological changes add noise, and manufacturing gauges are less representative than they once were.

### Unpacked
The study is motivated by a specific forecasting problem: growth is expected to fall sharply this year for a clear reason — tariffs and their knock-on effects on financial conditions and uncertainty — yet the hard data have not yet confirmed it. **The practical question is not whether growth slows but when the official statistics will show it, and which series will show it first.**

Historically, the earliest reliable warnings come from business surveys and labor data — jobless claims, the Philly Fed and ISM services indices, and the unemployment rate. When a slowdown has a discrete catalyst, the pattern is consistent: expectations components move within about a month because respondents anticipate the hit, while hard data lags roughly four months, partly because it is released late and revised often. **That lag is why the current sharp drop in survey expectations should not be dismissed even though soft data has cried wolf for several years.** Two things make the surveys more credible now than in 2022-23: the deterioration reflects more respondents expecting outright declines rather than a rise in "unchanged" answers, and several post-pandemic distortions have faded — though surveys still tend to overshoot around politically charged events.

The note then traces where the drag lands. On consumption, tariffs raise prices, prices erode real disposable income, and spending follows; the 2018-19 experience and VAT-hike analysis both point to inflation showing up within a few months, so the effects should surface in the next two or three CPI reports. **Core retail sales is singled out as the timeliest hard read on spending**, with vessel-tracking import proxies giving a noisier high-frequency view — those have softened only modestly so far. Added drags include slower hiring in healthcare, government and education, and a roughly ¼pp negative wealth effect from lower equities peaking around Q3.

On capex, tighter conditions and uncertainty are expected to bite this quarter and peak in the second half. Here the hard data is especially unhelpful in real time — noisy and lagging about five months — so manufacturing production is a better cyclical signal than narrow capex measures, and survey capex expectations have already fallen sharply. On labor, claims are timeliest but could mislead this cycle if uncertainty depresses gross hiring more than it lifts layoffs; the unemployment rate and job-finding probability turn later but signal more reliably, and payrolls should capture the government/education/healthcare slowdown well, with a notable hit expected in late summer as deferred-resignation exits land in September.

**The bottom line for the reader is a timeline: continued soft-data weakness now, with hard data expected to confirm around mid-to-late summer — and, so far, an evolution consistent with past event-driven slowdowns rather than a false alarm.** The authors are careful to note the dating of the catalyst (they use March 4) is subjective and the evidence base is still thin. The note offers no explicit trade idea; it is a monitoring framework for when the forecast slowdown becomes visible.
