### Definitive impacts
- Import-weighted average rate of **18.2%** under the announced policy — about 3pp above what [REDACTED] expected.
- Increase in the effective rate of only **~12.5pp**, because roughly **1/3 of imports ($1.1 trillion)** are exempt, being subject to sector-specific tariffs (implemented or pending): steel, aluminum, autos, copper, lumber, pharmaceuticals, semiconductors, critical minerals, and energy.
- Two-part structure: a **10% base tariff** on imports from all countries except Canada and Mexico (effective April 5), plus an **additional tariff** equal to half the ratio of the US bilateral deficit to imports from the country (effective April 9).
- Asian rates above expectations: **China 34%** (includes Hong Kong and Macau) added to the 20pp already imposed in Feb/Mar; **Vietnam 46%, Taiwan 36%, Thailand 36%, Indonesia 32%** — a result of the USTR's simplified methodology.
- Canada and Mexico: the exemption for **USMCA**-compliant goods from the 25% tariff was maintained. If the exemption ends, compliant goods and energy remain tariff-free; non-compliant goods pay **12%** (energy and potash exempt).
- The new reciprocal rates apply only to the **non-US content** of a good, if at least 20% of the content is of US origin.
- **De minimis** (exemption for personal shipments under $800) maintained, except for **China**, whose exemption was revoked by a separate order.

### Opinative impacts
- For the full year, [REDACTED] estimates the announced tariffs raise the effective rate by **18.7pp** — above the **15pp** built into its economic forecast.
- [REDACTED] assumes **negotiations will lower reciprocal rates** below the announced levels, but sees **greater upside risk** than the 15pp, from retaliation, escalation, and a high probability of new sector-specific tariffs.
- The split into two components suggests the **10% base is unlikely to be negotiated down**, while the additional portion tends to fall after negotiation.
- The broader-than-expected exemption exists **because new sector-specific tariffs appear likely**, and these will add to the effective rate once they take effect, probably still this year.
- Canada and Mexico received **better-than-expected treatment** ([REDACTED] had expected at least an incremental increase); the 12% ceiling may signal the upper bound for both.
- Excluding US content would matter more for Canada and Mexico and is **unlikely to be a material factor** for imports overall.

### At issue
On April 2, 2025, President Trump announced by executive order a two-tier "reciprocal" tariff policy: a universal 10% base tariff (effective April 5) and a country-specific additional tariff (effective April 9), calculated as half the ratio of the US bilateral trade deficit to imports from the country. The order excludes products already subject to, or candidates for, sector-specific tariffs (Sec. 232) and energy, exempts USMCA-compliant goods from Canada and Mexico, limits the levy to non-US content when at least 20% of the content is of US origin, and — in a separate order — revokes de minimis treatment for shipments from China.

### Unpacked
[REDACTED] went into this release expecting something milder: it had anticipated an auto exemption, incremental — not status quo — treatment for Canada and Mexico, and China falling within the reciprocal scope on top of existing tariffs. **The announcement came in harsher on the nominal rate (18.2% average) while, at the same time, narrower on the effective rate, because the sectoral exemption covered about a third of imports.** That apparent contradiction is the note's central point.

**The broad exemption is not relief — it is deferral.** The products that escape the reciprocal tariff do so because they are already, or will soon be, under their own sector-specific investigations and tariffs. As those measures take effect over the course of the year, the effect that does not show up in the effective rate today will be added later, pushing the number up rather than down.

Reading the structure matters for calibrating negotiation expectations. Because they are separate components, the 10% base functions as a floor that is unlikely to be negotiated down, while the additional portion — mechanically tied to the bilateral deficit — is what can retreat in bilateral deals. The same simplified methodology explains the surprisingly high Asian rates: countries with large surpluses versus the US, such as Vietnam and Taiwan, appear at the top by construction of the formula, not by case-by-case decision.

**The balance of risks is skewed to the upside.** [REDACTED]'s working assumption is relief via negotiation, but retaliation from partners, subsequent escalation, and the queue of pending sector-specific tariffs leave the effective rate with more room to exceed than to fall short of the 15pp assumed in the economic forecast — the difference between that figure and the estimated 18.7pp is the margin the reader should monitor as sector-specific measures are announced.

subject: Global Markets Daily: How Far Away Is the Left Tail of the “Dollar Smile”? (Rosenberg)
summary:
# The Dollar Smile's Left Tail Is Still Far Off — Sentiment Has Overshot

**Theme:** How weak US growth would have to get before the Dollar's safe-haven "left tail" activates  
**Markets:** US Dollar / G10 FX  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Isabella Rosenberg, 2 April 2025  

### Definitive impacts
- The Dollar has weakened in recent weeks as markets reprice US exceptionalism, with the move larger than the shift in economic consensus implies — placing priced expectations closer to the distribution's "trough" than consensus estimates, which still sit on the right-hand side of the smile.
- In the empirical framework, Dollar strength tracks *relative* not absolute US growth: most G10 currencies strengthen on strong domestic growth and weaken on soft growth, and there is no fixed growth or unemployment level that mechanically triggers the Dollar's left tail.
- During the initial US growth shock of 18–28 February, FX performance matched the clustering framework's typical negative-shock pattern — the Dollar and other safe havens outperformed, cyclical currencies weakened — a concrete instance of the Dollar's safe-haven behavior.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] sees Dollar sentiment as too negative, largely because the market has already priced much of the expected slowdown and its baseline carries some tariff-driven Dollar support.
- On the baseline forecast, [REDACTED] judges the left tail is still "some distance away"; if consensus fell to that baseline it would sit at the trough, not the recessionary tail.
- If US growth slows more sharply and idiosyncratically than expected, [REDACTED] argues history shows the left tail remains far off — leaving room for further Dollar weakness before safe-haven demand takes over.
- [REDACTED] flags an upside risk for the Dollar: if rest-of-world data soften once tariffs are applied, the relative growth picture could turn more Dollar-favorable than markets have priced; rising recession risk and policy uncertainty could also drive tactical risk-off episodes of Dollar strength, as in late February.

### Backdrop
The "Dollar smile" describes how the Dollar tends to strengthen at both extremes of the global growth cycle — when the US strongly outperforms (right side) and when a severe global downturn drives safe-haven demand (left side) — while weakening in the middle, when US growth merely softens without spilling over abroad. The critical distinction is that USD outperformance on weak US growth requires *deep relative* US underperformance plus fears of spillovers to the rest of the world; ordinary US softening simply weakens the Dollar like any other currency.

### At issue
Markets have begun questioning the durability of US exceptionalism, and the Dollar has fallen. The note assesses where current growth expectations place the Dollar on the smile. Consensus 1-year-ahead growth still favors the US (right side), but recent price action suggests investors have marked down US exceptionalism further than consensus has — consistent with the trough. Contributing factors: policy uncertainty weighing on US growth expectations, and upward revisions to European growth that narrow the scope for US outperformance.

### Unpacked
The note reframes a fashionable bearish-Dollar narrative as a question of *degree*: how far the growth backdrop would have to deteriorate before the Dollar stops falling and starts rallying on safe-haven flows. **The answer is that the two regimes — a softening that hurts the Dollar and a shock that helps it — are separated by a wide gap that current conditions do not bridge.**

The analytical spine is the relative-growth reading of FX. Because Dollar direction depends on the US position *versus* others rather than on any absolute threshold, the recent European growth upgrades matter as much as US softness: they compress the room for US outperformance and, importantly, would cushion any negative spillover, keeping the world away from the left-tail scenario. **The market has arguably already done the repricing work, pulling out more US exceptionalism than the economists have — which is precisely why [REDACTED] reads sentiment as overshooting.**

Tariffs are the pivotal caveat and cut in the Dollar's favor. **They anchor the baseline's Dollar support and could tilt the relative-growth distribution toward the Dollar if rest-of-world data weaken once tariffs bite** — a channel markets have not fully priced. The February episode serves as the working proof of concept: even with diminished US-exceptionalism expectations, rising recession risk produced a clean bout of Dollar strength, showing the safe-haven reflex is intact and can reassert itself tactically well before any true left-tail outcome.

The practical takeaway is two-sided. Being far from the left tail means further Dollar weakness is possible if US growth disappoints sharply and idiosyncratically; but the same distance, combined with tariff support and an already-repriced market, is why [REDACTED] leans against the prevailing bearishness. On the Dollar itself the note offers a view, not an explicit trade; the "Best Trade Ideas" list appended to the daily is a standing cross-asset roster unrelated to this analysis.

subject: USA: Factory Orders Roughly in Line With Expectations
summary:
# US: February Factory Orders Unsurprising, No Impact on Q1 GDP

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius
**Focus:** US factory orders (February)
**General comment:** Neutral, descriptive read on a data point essentially in line with consensus; no change to the scenario.

### Context
Comment on the release of February 2025 factory orders, a data point tracked as an input for first-quarter GDP growth tracking.

### The case
- **The data came in essentially in line with expectations, with marginal revisions.** Factory orders rose 0.6% in February (versus [REDACTED] +0.3% and median +0.5%), and January's gain was revised up 0.1pp, to 1.8%. Within the components the revisions offset each other: core capital goods orders rose 0.1pp (to -0.2%) while core capital goods shipments fell 0.1pp (to 0.8%); durable goods orders were revised up 0.1pp (to 1.0%) and the ex-transportation measure was unchanged at 0.7%. Factory inventories rose 0.1%.
- **The result does not change the activity read.** Given no material surprise in the data, the Q1 GDP tracking estimate was kept at +0.3% (quarter-over-quarter, annualized).

### Implications
- No sign of either reacceleration or deterioration in industry: the data simply confirms the scenario already in place.
- No forecast revision follows from the release; GDP tracking remains at +0.3%.

subject: USA: ADP Employment Above Expectations
summary:
# ADP Surprises to the Upside, but Doesn't Move the Payroll Forecast

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius
**Focus:** US labor market
**General comment:** Constructive read, aligned with consensus; the strong data confirms, but does not change, the expectation of solid job creation.

### Context
Comment on the March 2025 ADP private employment report, released ahead of the official payroll figure. The question at stake is whether the pace of job creation remains firm and what the data signals for the official number.

### The case
- **Private employment came in above expectations, with broad-based composition.** ADP registered +155k in March (seasonally adjusted), above consensus, with February revised up (+7k, to +84k). The gain was driven by services (+132k), led by professional and business services (+57k) and financial services (+38k); goods-producing sectors added +24k, of which +21k in manufacturing. Median pay for job-stayers rose 4.6% year-over-year, 0.1pp below February.
- **Other alternative measures confirm the picture.** Other tracked job-creation indicators also point to a solid pace in March, reinforcing rather than contradicting the ADP read.

### Implications
- The March payroll forecast of +150k was maintained, slightly above the consensus of +140k — the strong data confirms, but does not change, the expectation.
- On the US surprise map, the result registers as slightly positive (ADP +3), consistent with a still-resilient labor market.

subject: USA: ISM Manufacturing Index and Job Openings Below Expectations; Nominal Construction Spending Increases in February; Boosting GDP Tracking to +0.3%
summary:
# US activity data softens as ISM manufacturing contracts and job openings fall, yet a construction beat nudges Q1 GDP tracking up

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US macro data (ISM manufacturing, JOLTS, construction spending)  
**General comment:** A read-through data note; on-balance soft activity signal with rising tariff-driven price pressure, partly offset by a construction beat.

### Context
A same-day comment on three US data releases — the March ISM and S&P Global manufacturing surveys, February JOLTS job openings, and February construction spending — used to refresh the firm's Q1 GDP tracking estimate amid growing attention to tariff effects.

### The case
- **ISM manufacturing fell back into contraction with a weak internal composition.** The headline dropped 1.3pt to 49.0, slightly worse than expected, and the decline was broad-based across the components that matter most: new orders (-3.4pt to 45.2), production (-2.4pt to 48.3), and employment (-2.9pt to 44.7) all moved deeper into contractionary territory. Inventories rose (+3.5pt to 53.4) and supplier deliveries eased.
- **Tariffs are the dominant theme and are pushing prices sharply higher.** The prices-paid index jumped 7.0pt to 69.4, its highest since July 2022, and the release carried 18 mentions of tariffs, with respondents citing pressure on gross profits and a challenging, uncertain business environment. The signal is one of rising input-cost pressure coinciding with weakening demand.
- **The S&P Global PMI told a marginally firmer story.** In contrast to the ISM, the final March S&P Global manufacturing PMI was revised up 0.4pt to 50.2, with new orders and employment revised higher even as output was nudged down — leaving the two surveys somewhat at odds on the sector's momentum.
- **Labor demand is cooling but the market is not loosening abruptly.** Job openings fell 194k to 7,568k from an upwardly revised January level, led by declines in trade/transportation/utilities and financial activities and partly offset by professional and business services. The openings rate slipped to 4.5%, but quits, hiring, and layoff rates were unchanged. On the JOLTS/Indeed/LinkUp composite, the job-workers gap narrowed only modestly to 0.5mn. A higher federal government layoff rate is consistent with an expected ~25k drop in federal payrolls.
- **Construction spending beat, but the strength is nominal, not real.** Nominal spending rose 0.7% in February, above consensus, led by private residential (+1.3%). However, with construction costs up 0.9%, real spending actually fell about 0.2% — so the beat reflects price growth rather than added volume.

### Implications
- The Q1 GDP tracking estimate was raised 0.1pp to +0.3% (q/q annualized) and Q1 domestic final sales to +1.3%, driven by the construction beat despite the softer activity surveys.
- The combination of contracting manufacturing demand and a multi-year high in prices paid frames a stagflationary risk from tariffs — the central watch-point flagged by respondents.
- Labor-demand cooling remains gradual, keeping attention on Friday's employment report, where federal job losses are expected.

subject: Global Markets Daily: Lowering Yield Forecasts on a More Severe Tariff Baseline (Cole/Marshall)
summary:
# US Growth Downside to Dominate: [REDACTED] Cuts Yield Forecasts on Harsher Tariff Baseline

**Theme:** More severe tariff baseline pulls G4 yields lower and curves steeper, led by US growth risk  
**Markets:** Developed-market rates (US, Euro area, UK, Japan)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], George Cole, 1 April 2025  

### Definitive impacts
- YE25 US 2y yield forecast cut to 3.30% from 3.95%, and 10y to 4.00% from 4.35% — a bull-steepening revision.
- YE25 10y Bund forecast lowered 20bp to 2.80% from 3.00%.
- YE25 10y JGB forecast lowered to 1.50% from 1.60%.
- YE25 10y Gilt forecast unchanged at 4.25%.
- Forecasts for YE26 and beyond left mostly unchanged.
- 2025 core PCE forecast set at 3.5% y/y, driven by a cumulative 15pp rise in the effective tariff rate.
- Recommendation to go long JPY 3m 10y A/A+25bp payer spreads closed, for a potential 1bp gain.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] expects US growth downside to outweigh inflation, producing lower yields and a steeper curve this year; the Fed is seen delivering three consecutive 25bp cuts from July to a 3.50–3.75% terminal rate, triggered by labor-market weakness rather than preemption.
- [REDACTED] sees the belly (5y) as the best risk/reward for longs, since inflation may constrain how much the very front-end can richen and could delay cuts.
- [REDACTED] expects the ECB to cut three more times to 1.75%, with growth risks outweighing modest inflation upside; front-end EUR yields drift slightly lower while Bunds stay near current levels because tariff damage reinforces expectations of German fiscal expansion.
- [REDACTED] expects UK yields to track US yields lower absent domestic direction, with 10y Gilts remaining the curve's weak point due to heavy belly issuance.
- [REDACTED] argues elevated US recession risk skews BoJ pricing dovish and the JPY stronger; a slowdown short of recession would delay, not derail, the eventual move higher in Japanese rates.
- [REDACTED] sees further US–Europe and US–Japan front-end spread compression but judges spreads not yet too tight to fade.
- [REDACTED] flags a de-anchoring of long-term inflation expectations as the more challenging risk, with the curve outcome hinging on whether the Fed leans against inflation (later, deeper cuts) or growth (sharper steepening, larger inflation risk premia).

### Backdrop
Rates markets sit at the intersection of two opposing tariff impulses: tariffs weigh on growth but push up near-term inflation, complicating every G4 central bank's reaction function. The revision follows a downgrade to the economics team's tariff baseline, which lifts the 2025 US inflation path and forces a rethink of how quickly policy can ease. In Europe, the added variable is prospective German fiscal loosening, which underpins medium-term growth and steep EUR curves even as near-term growth risk dominates ECB policy. In Japan, the wage-price cycle remains the anchor for the BoJ's gradual tightening path, alongside ongoing QT.

### At issue
[REDACTED]'s economists adopted a more severe tariff baseline — a cumulative 15pp increase in the 2025 US effective tariff rate — prompting the rates team to revise G4 yield forecasts. US 2y/10y, Bund and JGB forecasts were cut; Gilt and longer-dated (YE26+) forecasts held. European growth forecasts for 2025 and 2026 were downgraded with only a modest inflation boost. The note also closes the JPY payer-spread trade and reaffirms a set of expressions: staying tethered to terminal-rate pricing (2y1y forwards, 5s spot), selling 1x2 cap spreads on the 2s10s curve, and owning 5y TIPS beta-weighted versus nominals.

### Unpacked
The core tension is sequencing. Inflation running toward 3.5% core PCE means the Fed cannot cut preemptively against growth risk; instead it must wait for clear labor-market softening, which [REDACTED] places around mid-year. **Until that weakness shows through, inflation risks cap how far the very front-end can rally, which is why the belly rather than the front-end carries the constructive view.** Once softening arrives, the case for faster cuts strengthens and bull steepening takes over.

**The trade construction follows directly from that path: keep longs tethered to terminal-rate pricing to balance cyclical exposure against scenarios where inflation pushes cuts further out the curve.** Outright front-to-belly steepeners are awkward given the current curve shape and news sequence, so the deep-tail expression is owning the right side of the distribution via 1x2 cap spreads on 2s10s, complemented by beta-weighted 5y TIPS.

**Europe splits into a near-term and a medium-term story that pull yields in different directions.** Front-end EUR yields drift lower on ECB cuts, but Bunds hold near current levels because tariff-driven growth damage strengthens — rather than weakens — the case for German fiscal expansion into 2026–2027, keeping curves steep. The UK is largely a follower of US yields, with 10y Gilts structurally soft on issuance.

**Japan is the clearest recession-risk proxy: tighter global financial conditions and a stronger yen both argue for lower JGB yields, with tradables inflation the key transmission channel.** The domestic wage-price cycle remains the backstop — as long as it holds, a non-recessionary US slowdown only delays the move higher in Japanese rates, while QT keeps front-end forwards biased steeper and 2s10s flatter over time.

The longer end of the forecast horizon is deliberately left alone. **[REDACTED] expects the near-term bullish, US-driven pressure to uncoil as recession is avoided and terminal-rate views hold steady, though tariff revenue flattening the debt trajectory could temper the eventual rise in yields.** The main asymmetric risk to the whole framework is inflation expectations de-anchoring, where the curve outcome depends entirely on how the Fed chooses to respond.

subject: Q4 2024 COFER Data: Headline Share of Dollar Reserves Ticks Up
summary:
# Q4 2024 COFER: Headline Dollar Reserve Share Edges Up, but Valuation-Adjusted Picture Is More Mixed

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Lexi Kanter  
**Focus:** Global FX reserve currency composition  
**General comment:** Descriptive read of the latest IMF reserve data; broadly consensus, notable for flagging why the raw figures overstate the yen's rise.

### Context
The IMF released its Q4 2024 COFER data on the currency composition of official FX reserves. This note reads the numbers on two measures — the headline share and a share adjusted for FX valuation moves — and draws out where the two tell different stories.

### The case
- **The dollar's direction depends on which measure you use.** Its headline reserve share ticked up in Q4, recovering off the low reached in Q3, but the valuation-adjusted share fell. The same divergence applies to the euro in reverse: its headline share slipped slightly while its valuation-adjusted share posted the largest gain since Q3 2022. In both cases the valuation adjustment implies reserve managers were leaning against currency market moves rather than actively reallocating.

- **The yen's apparent gains are overstated by the data's construction.** JPY reserves were stable on the headline measure but rose on a valuation-adjusted basis — and over the past several years yen holdings have grown more than any other currency on that measure. Much of this likely reflects purchases of Japanese securities on an FX-hedged basis for yield enhancement, not a genuine shift toward the yen as a reserve currency. Because COFER counts only the cash asset, the yen share is inflated whenever managers hedge, so the figure should not be read as rising conviction in the currency.

- **The renminbi continues to drift lower.** Both measures of CNY reserves were stable in Q4, but allocated renminbi holdings have fallen by roughly $90bn since end-2021. Among countries that report a geographic breakdown, most now hold a smaller CNY share than in Q1 2022, with Brazil and Israel showing the largest declines over the quarter. The other major reserve currencies — GBP and CHF — were roughly stable.

### Implications
- The gap between headline and valuation-adjusted shares matters more than either level alone: this quarter's moves look driven by managers offsetting price swings, not deliberate rebalancing away from the dollar.
- Read the yen's rise with caution — hedged security purchases, not reserve-status demand, explain much of it.
- The renminbi's multi-year, broad-based decline continues, undercutting the diversification-away-from-dollar narrative on the currency most often cited for it.

subject: Global Economics Analyst: Foreign Boycotts Imply a Modest Incremental Headwind to US Growth (Briggs/Peters)
summary:
# Foreign Boycotts of US Products: A Small, Tourism-Led Drag on 2025 US Growth

**Theme:** Sizing how anti-US sentiment and boycotts feed through to US GDP, via two independent methods  
**Markets:** US growth; global trade and tourism  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Joseph Briggs, 31 March 2025

### Definitive impacts
- Foreign arrivals to the twelve largest US airports fell 11% yoy through 25 March, against +5% for returning US citizens.
- Canadian resident return trips from the US fell 13% yoy by air and 23% yoy by automobile in February, roughly a 20% overall decline; OAG bookings from Canada point to a 70% shortfall over the following six months.
- Tesla net favorability dropped sharply: -31pp in Canada, -27pp in France, -24pp in the UK, -13pp in Germany. Declines for most other US brands stayed within normal historical volatility.
- US alcohol exports to Canada face a ~$1.5bn hit as provincial monopolies pull US products (Ontario alone sold nearly C$1bn of US alcohol last year); Canadian food retailers report a 10% uptick in domestic-product sales.
- Foreign tourism equals ~0.7% of US GDP, with the EU and Canada together spending ~$50bn a year (0.2% of GDP).
- Mechanical GDP sensitivities: a 10% tourism pullback = 7bp drag, 25% = 18bp; a 10% pullback in food & beverage, autos, or other consumer goods = 2-3bp each.
- US-owned multinationals' foreign production is separately exposed: auto gross output for local consumption of $20bn (Canada), $13bn (UK), $8bn (Germany); food manufactures $21bn, $15bn, $11bn respectively.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] estimates a ~0.1% bottom-up drag on US GDP from boycotts, assuming Canadian tourism falls 25%, other-country tourism 5-10%, and other exposed goods ~5%.
- Its top-down method — a panel regression over 21 countries (2002-2019) where a 1pp favorability decline maps to a 0.3% drop in US imports — implies a larger 0.2-0.3% drag.
- [REDACTED] frames this as one more reason US GDP should undershoot consensus in 2025, on top of tariffs and retaliation already in its forecast.
- The revenue hit to US multinationals is judged larger than the GDP hit, since demand also falls for US brands made abroad (which do not show up as lost US exports).
- [REDACTED] is skeptical the 70% Canadian booking shortfall will fully materialize.
- The offsetting boost to other economies is seen as moderate only in Canada (~0.4% GDP: 0.2% domestic tourism + 0.2% food & beverage) and 0.1% or less elsewhere; top-down estimates are larger if boycotts broaden.

### At issue
US tariff announcements and a more confrontational posture toward traditional allies — including comments on the sovereignty of Canada and Greenland — sharply lowered global sentiment toward the US in early 2025. Declines were broad-based and largest in Canada and the Nordics; only Russia and China grew more favorable. This prompted widely reported consumer boycotts of US products: 53% of Canadians and about a third of French consumers report boycotting to some degree, and several governments (UK, Germany) issued cautionary guidance on travel to the US. The note quantifies the resulting hit to US GDP.

### Unpacked
**The concern the note tests is whether a soft, sentiment-driven phenomenon — people choosing not to buy or visit — is large enough to matter for the US macro outlook.** The answer is qualified: it matters, but modestly, and almost entirely through tourism rather than through goods.

The bottom-up and top-down methods are built to check each other. Aggregating anecdotes risks missing the diffuse, interrelated ways aversion spreads, so the statistical approach — anchored to the Iraq war and Trump's first term, when a 10pp favorability drop cut a country's US import share by 0.5-0.9pp — serves as an upper-bound cross-check. **That the top-down figure (0.2-0.3%) runs two to three times the bottom-up figure (0.1%) is itself the signal: the headline is a range whose top depends on boycotts broadening beyond today's evidence.**

**Two facts keep the goods channel small: consumers have not soured on most US brands, and the products they have soured on most — Tesla vehicles — are largely made abroad, so lost demand does not subtract from US exports.** The damage there lands on multinationals' revenue, a corporate rather than a national-accounts problem, which is why the note separates the two.

**Tourism is the real transmission channel because it is a large, purely domestic US export that foreigners can withdraw from immediately and visibly.** The airport and border data already show the pullback underway, and its timing — stepping down after each tariff escalation in February and March — is what lets the note attribute it to voluntary avoidance rather than to tighter immigration policy alone. For the reader, the practical takeaway is directional: another modest, tourism-weighted reason to sit below consensus on 2025 US growth, with the mirror-image boost concentrated in Canada.

subject: G10 Inflation Monitor: Inflation Surprises to the Upside in Canada, Japan and the US (Peters)
summary:
# Tariffs Split the G10: US Core Inflation Re-accelerating While Peers Keep Normalizing

**Theme:** February upside surprises in the US, Canada and Japan against a broad disinflation backdrop — tariffs the wedge  
**Markets:** G10 core inflation  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jan Hatzius, 31 March 2025  

### Landscape
- [REDACTED] trimmed core (monthly annualized) rose in the US to +3.2% (from +2.1%) and the Euro area to +2.1% (from +1.6%), but fell in the UK (+2.9% vs +4.9%), Japan (+1.1% vs +2.0%) and Canada (+3.2% vs +3.4%).
- On a 3-month annualized basis, trimmed core ticked up only in the US (+2.6% vs +2.2%), eased in the UK (+3.5%) and Japan (+1.6%), and held at +1.9% (Euro area) and +3.3% (Canada).
- Year-over-year, [REDACTED] trimmed core stands at +3.5% in the UK, +3.1% in Canada, +2.4% in the US, +2.2% in the Euro area and +1.5% in Japan.
- Inflation breadth (share of headline basket above 4%, six-month annualized) kept rising in the UK to 57% (from 49%) and the Euro area to 21% (from 18%), but fell in the US to 22% (from 33%), Canada to 36% (from 43%) and Japan to 26% (from 30%).
- Traditional core has moderated from its cyclical peak by 5.4pp (UK), 4.6pp (Euro area), 3.1pp (US PCE) and 2.9pp (Canada) on a 3-month basis; Japan's new core is only 2.6pp below peak.

### Drivers
- Tariffs are the dominant force lifting the US path: [REDACTED] forecasts year-over-year core PCE accelerating to +3.5%, of which 1.4pp is a direct tariff boost — the clear outlier against expected moderation elsewhere.
- Core goods (3-month annualized) turned up in the US (+2.2pp to +2.2%), Canada (+2.1pp to +2.2%) and the Euro area (+0.1pp to +0.8%), while slowing in the UK (-1.8pp to +1.4%) and Japan (-0.7pp to +5.8%).
- Core services firmed in most economies, led by Canada (+3.3pp to +3.9% after a soft January), but decelerated in Japan (-0.1pp to +0.8%).
- Rent inflation is fading in most markets — largest declines in Canada (-1.1pp to +2.1%) and the UK (-1pp to +6.9%) — but still ticking up in the US (+3.8% vs +3.6%).
- Energy accelerated only in the US (PCE +16.5% vs +16.1%) and slowed elsewhere; food eased in Japan (-5.3pp to +9.2%), the US and the UK, but rose in the Euro area and Canada (the latter reflecting the end of the sales-tax holiday in mid-February).
- The cross-item distribution of 3-month inflation rates keeps shifting back toward pre-pandemic norms, most clearly in the US and Euro area, while Canada and the UK stay more dispersed.

### Risks
- Upside (US): [REDACTED] flags that its own tariff baseline has moved twice in 30 days and could move again; each revision has raised the end-2025 core PCE path (now 3.5%), so the balance of risk to the US forecast is tied to further tariff escalation.
- Upside (Euro area/Canada): retaliatory tariffs are an active upward channel — EU retaliation drove a +0.1pp revision to the Euro area forecast, and tariff news plus a firmer February print lifted Canada by +0.3pp.
- The skew described is asymmetric to the upside and tariff-driven; the report flags no comparable downside scenario to the baseline.

### Unpacked
The report is a scoreboard, not a thesis, and its organizing fact is divergence. **Underlying inflation is still normalizing across most of the G10, but the US is pulling in the opposite direction, and tariffs are the reason.** February brought year-over-year core upside surprises in Canada, Japan and the US (PCE); the Euro area printed broadly in line and the UK came in below consensus.

**[REDACTED] end-2025 forecasts sit generally above consensus specifically because of more aggressive tariff assumptions.** Core PCE is seen accelerating to +3.5% in the US, while core inflation moderates to +3.1% in the UK, +2.5% in Japan, +2.3% in Canada and +2.1% in the Euro area. The US revision path is the story of the month: the effective tariff-rate assumption was first raised from 4–5pp to 10pp (adding 0.5pp to the year-end core PCE forecast, to ~3%), then lifted again to a 15pp increase with a more aggressive reciprocal tariff, taking end-2025 core PCE to 3.5%. The Euro area's year-end core forecast is unchanged at 2.1% on net — a +0.1pp tariff/retaliation revision offset an earlier cut on softer final HICP details — while Canada was raised 0.3pp.

Beneath the headlines, the category mix explains some apparent noise. **Canada's numbers are distorted by the sales-tax holiday: its end in mid-February pushed food inflation up (+2.2pp to +1.8%), and the earlier holiday depressed food, alcohol and tobacco enough to skew the central bank's own preferred core lower.** This is why the [REDACTED] harmonized core — which strips a consistent item set across countries — runs substantially above the Bank of Canada's statistical measure on a 3-month basis. Japan sits at the other end: its new core CPI excludes only energy and fresh food, so rice-based food items that the harmonized basket excludes stay in, leaving Japan's harmonized core lower than the official reading.

The note gives no trade idea; its value is the like-for-like comparison and the tariff-revision trail. **→ Read in full:** only if you need the harmonized-core cross-country adjustment tables to reconcile Canada's and Japan's official readings against a common basket — that methodology-dependent detail cannot be reproduced from this summary and directly affects how you read those two prints.

subject: Tariffs Preview: Markets and Economics ahead of April 2nd
summary:
# Tariffs Preview: What April 2nd Could Bring for Markets, the Fed, and Growth

**Theme:** Positioning and macro implications ahead of the April 2nd tariff announcement  
**Markets:** US trade policy — cross-asset (equities, FX, rates)  
**Source:** [REDACTED] (Alec Phillips), 31 March 2025  

### Estimates
- This item is an audio discussion; the transcript provided contains no point estimates, forecast paths, or numerical figures. The specific tariff assumptions and revised forecasts referenced sit in the linked written notes, not in this text.

### Outlook
- The discussion is framed around three questions: what additional tariffs may be announced on April 2nd, how markets are currently positioned for them, and the implications for the Fed and the broader economy. The direction of the analysts' view — higher tariff assumptions, weaker growth, and lower earnings — is signalled by the accompanying research titles rather than stated with figures here.
- Linked notes indicate the house view has moved toward a further increase in tariff assumptions, reduced S&P 500 earnings estimates and return forecasts, and a judgement that fiscal policy will not offset the drag from tariffs. These conclusions are pointers to the related written research, not claims substantiated within this transcript.

### Unpacked

subject: US Daily: March [REDACTED]: March Sadness (Rindels)

# [REDACTED] Falls to Five-Year Low as New Orders Collapse, Even as Employment Holds Up

**Theme:** Business activity cools sharply in March; policy uncertainty weighs more than demand or hiring  
**Markets:** US business activity / macro  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jessica Rindels, 31 Mar 2025

### Definitive impacts
- 9.5pt drop in the [REDACTED], to 40.9 in March — the lowest level since May 2020.
- New orders component fell 10.1pt to 33.4 and shipments fell 10.3pt to 36.1 — both at their lowest since May 2020.
- Employment component rose 6.8pt to 54.0, in contrast with the rest of the composition.
- Inventories plunged 34.3pt to 24.6, the lowest level since January 2010; the orders-less-inventories gap widened 8.8pt to 24.2.
- Export component advanced 22.9pt to 66.7.
- Materials prices fell 12.1pt to 57.1 and wages fell 4.0pt to 63.6, while selling (output) prices rose 7.1pt to 61.3.
- Survey trackers pulled back modestly: manufacturing -0.6pt to 51.7 and non-manufacturing -0.5pt to 52.6; employment components were nearly unchanged (manufacturing 50.2; services 49.9).
- In the Philadelphia Fed surveys, uncertainty constrained operations at 93% of services firms and 79% of manufacturing firms during the quarter; 29% and 24%, respectively, rated it a "significant" constraint, and most expect it to worsen next quarter.
- In the [REDACTED] special questions: 58% of analysts do not expect hiring cuts from tariffs or federal spending cuts; 84% see 2025 demand equal to or greater than 2024; 42% report that firms raised their estimated probability of a recession in 12 months.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] classifies the index composition as "mixed-to-weak" — the rise in employment does not offset the collapse in orders and shipments, which pulls the headline to its post-pandemic low.
- The bank reads the drop in inventories combined with the widening orders-less-inventories gap as a potentially constructive signal for future production, despite headline weakness.
- According to [REDACTED], elevated uncertainty has not yet meaningfully affected investment decisions: 2025 capex intentions have changed little versus 2024 in both sectors.
- The bank highlights specific sectors as points of demand fragility — restaurants and digital advertising, due to deteriorating consumer confidence — and lists investment banks, biotech, and non-alcoholic beverages among those that raised their perceived recession risk.

### Backdrop
The [REDACTED] is [REDACTED]'s monthly index built from responses by its sector analysts, covering both services and manufacturing. The headline uses weights of 30% for new orders, 25% for sales/shipments, 20% for employment, 15% for materials prices, and 10% for inventories — replicating the pre-2008 ISM methodology, with the materials price index in place of supplier deliveries. As with ISM readings, 50 is the theoretical boundary between expansion and contraction, though [REDACTED] assesses that a [REDACTED] of 50 is more consistent with trend growth than with stagnation.

### At issue
Release of the March 2025 [REDACTED] reading, with responses collected between 24 and 27 March. Beyond the usual components, this edition includes special questions to analysts on the effects of tariffs, federal spending cuts, and policy uncertainty on hiring, demand, and recession risk, and incorporates the special questions from the Philadelphia Fed surveys on how uncertainty constrained operations in Q1 and is expected to constrain them in Q2.

### Unpacked
The March reading brings together two movements pointing in opposite directions. **The headline sinks to its post-pandemic low, but the source of the decline is concentrated in orders and shipments, not the labor market** — the employment component not only held up but rose, and the employment trackers from the manufacturing and services surveys were essentially flat around 50.

The backdrop analysts point to is policy uncertainty, not organic demand weakness. **Firms report that uncertainty is already constraining operations and expect it to weigh even more going forward, but that constraint has not yet migrated into hiring or investment decisions** — most analysts do not foresee hiring cuts, and 2025 capex intentions have changed little versus 2024. The transmission channel, for now, is current activity and risk perception, not capital spending.

The more forward-looking signal lies in tail-risk perception: roughly half of analysts report that firms raised the probability they assign to a recession over the next 12 months, concentrated in consumer- and cycle-sensitive sectors — restaurants, digital advertising, investment banks, biotech, and beverages. **For the reader, the picture is one of deteriorating current order flows with employment still firm, in an environment where policy uncertainty is the central variable to monitor.** The note does not present an explicit trade idea.

# Tariff Shock Deepens: [REDACTED] Lifts Recession Odds to 35% as Reciprocal Tariffs Loom

**Theme:** Escalating tariff assumptions reshaping the growth, inflation, and Fed path  
**Markets:** US macro (growth, inflation, labor, monetary policy)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], David Mericle, 31 March 2025  

### Landscape
- Effective tariff rate assumption raised again, from +10pp to +15pp, built from a projected 15% average reciprocal tariff (+9pp after exemptions) plus tariffs already imposed and expected sectoral measures.
- Conference Board consumer confidence at its lowest since January 2021; Michigan sentiment down sharply, with its expectations component the weakest since July 2022.
- Conference Board one-year inflation expectations up 0.4pp to 6.2%, the highest since April 2023; Michigan 1-year at 5.0% and 5-10-year at 4.1%, the highest since February 1993.
- Personal spending rose less than expected in February, with January revised down; durable goods orders up 0.9% but core capital goods orders down 0.3%; new home sales up 1.8%.

### Drivers
- A 25% tariff on autos and key parts is the near-term escalator: light vehicles from April 3, key parts by no later than May 3, other parts within 90 days — expected to add 2.2pp to the effective rate by July, with USMCA-compliant US content and parts initially excluded.
- Deteriorating confidence and rising inflation expectations are the transmission channel from tariffs to demand, though the Michigan surge is partly distorted by partisanship and the shift to online collection.
- Federal spending cuts, DOGE-related layoffs, and reduced hiring are dragging on growth and employment, with spillover risk to state & local government, healthcare, and education.
- The coming payrolls report is the key data point to watch for early policy effects — on manufacturing (tariffs), government-adjacent sectors (spending cuts), and the household survey (immigration crackdown).

### Risks
- Downside (fiscal): the Republican tax package — mainly an extension of existing cuts with limited new ones — is unlikely to offset the tariff hit to GDP, and may slip from late July/August to September or later.
- Downside (fiscal mechanics): a harder-to-avoid shutdown at the Sep. 30 deadline, Treasury likely exhausting borrowing room by September, and DOGE cuts weighing on growth.
- The note frames risks as skewed to the downside; the raised 35% recession probability reflects lower growth, falling confidence, and White House statements signaling willingness to tolerate economic pain.

### Unpacked
**The core revision is a broad markdown of the outlook to reflect a heavier tariff assumption:** core PCE inflation raised 0.5pp to 3.5% at end-2025, Q4/Q4 GDP growth cut 0.5pp to 1%, and the unemployment rate raised 0.3pp to 4.5% at end-2025. The 12-month recession probability moves from 20% to 35%.

**On the Fed, the call is now three consecutive "insurance cuts" in July, September, and October, reaching a 3.5-3.75% terminal rate.** With inflation and inflation expectations elevated, the bar for cutting is higher, so a rising unemployment rate is expected to be the important justification for easing.

**For March payrolls, the forecast is a slightly above-consensus 150k, lifted by special factors** — solid big-data indicators, a 15k boost from returning strikers, and a rebound in weather-sensitive hiring after a cold winter, partly offset by a 25k drag from the federal government. The unemployment rate is seen unchanged at 4.1% and average hourly earnings up 0.3% on positive calendar effects, while JOLTS openings are estimated to have fallen to a below-consensus 7.5mn in February.

On the growth data, last week's flow was weaker on net: softer personal spending with a downward January revision, and a goods trade deficit that narrowed by less than expected — most of the narrowing tied to lower industrial-supplies imports, likely gold, which is excluded from GDP.

**Theme:** Higher assumed US tariffs drive below-consensus growth downgrades and a more dovish Fed path  
**Markets:** US and Euro-area growth, inflation and rates  
**Source:** [REDACTED] — Stuart Jenkins, 31 March 2025

### Definitive impacts
- Assumed average US tariff rate for 2025 raised to +15pp, from +10pp previously.
- 2025 Q4/Q4 US growth cut by 0.5pp to 1.0%; Euro-area growth cut by 0.3pp to 0.5% — both stated as notably below Bloomberg consensus.
- 2025 US unemployment forecast raised to 4.5%, from 4.2%.
- 2025 US core PCE forecast raised to 3.5% Y/Y, from 3.0%.
- Italy March flash inflation came in three-tenths above consensus; national German HICP tracking around 2.4% Y/Y, in line with consensus.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] raised its US recession probability to 35%, from 20%, reflecting the heavier tariff drag.
- [REDACTED] now expects three consecutive Fed cuts — July, September and November — to an unchanged terminal rate of 3.5%–3.75%.
- [REDACTED] equity strategists downgraded both the 3-month and 12-month S&P 500 targets (revised levels not stated).

### At issue
[REDACTED]'s economists lifted their assumed 2025 US tariff increase to 15pp and rebuilt the US and Euro-area macro forecasts around it. The result is lower growth for both regions, higher US unemployment and core inflation, a higher recession probability, and a Fed now seen cutting three times in the second half of 2025. Separately, March flash inflation surprised to the upside in Italy while German regional prints pointed to slight Y/Y moderation.

### Unpacked
**The single change doing the work is the tariff assumption: moving the expected US tariff increase from 10pp to 15pp is what pushes growth down, unemployment and core PCE up, and recession odds from 20% to 35%.** Everything else in the US forecast follows from that one input.

**The rate view is dovish on timing but not on destination** — three back-to-back cuts in July, September and November bring policy to a terminal 3.5%–3.75% that is left unchanged, so the Fed is seen moving sooner rather than deeper. Higher forecast core PCE of 3.5% alongside those cuts implies a Fed weighting growth and labour-market risk over sticky inflation.

**The framing is that [REDACTED] now sits markedly below consensus on 2025 Q4/Q4 growth for both the US and the Euro area**, which is the note's main signalling point: this is a call that the market has not yet fully priced the tariff drag. The European inflation data is a side observation — mixed, with an Italian upside surprise against softer German prints — and carries none of the forecast weight of the US revisions. The note offers no explicit FX or other trade idea.

# US Week Ahead: ISM and Payrolls Bracket a Tariff Announcement

**Theme:** Softening activity surveys and a still-solid jobs print, framed by Wednesday's expected new tariff rollout  
**Markets:** US labour market, US activity, and monetary policy  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jan Hatzius, 30 March 2025  

### Estimates
- **+150k** nonfarm payrolls in March (consensus +138k, last +151k); private payrolls **+160k** (consensus +130k, last +140k).
- **4.1%** unemployment rate in March, unchanged on a rounded basis (consensus 4.1%); participation held at 62.4%.
- **+0.3%** average hourly earnings m/m in March (consensus +0.3%, last +0.3%), helped by positive calendar effects.
- **49.5** ISM manufacturing in March, down 0.8pt (consensus 49.5, last 50.3).
- **52.5** ISM services in March (consensus 53.0, last 53.5).
- **7,500k** JOLTS job openings in February (consensus 7,680k, last 7,740k).

- **16.4mn** lightweight motor vehicle sales in March (consensus 16.0mn, last 16.0mn).
- Tracking: Q1 GDP at **+0.2%** q/q AR, domestic final sales at +1.2%; March Current Activity Indicator at +1.2% (vs +2.0% in February); US MAP surprise index at -0.3.

### Outlook
- The March payroll composition is mixed: returning strikers add a net 15k and weather-sensitive hiring should rebound, while federal reduction-in-force actions subtract an assumed 25k, partly offset by positive state and local hiring (+15k).
- Both ISM readings are seen softening in March, consistent with sequential weakening in the survey trackers, with residual seasonality a tailwind for manufacturing but a headwind for services.
- Fed messaging is characterised as patient and somewhat dovish: Powell's post-March comments treated tariffs as delaying inflation progress into 2026 rather than derailing it, and officials describe policy as well positioned to hold.

### Unpacked
The week is bracketed by two hard data points — Tuesday's ISM manufacturing and Friday's payrolls — but the pivotal event is political. **President Trump is expected to announce new tariff policies on Wednesday, and the surrounding uncertainty is already threading through the Fed commentary and the activity surveys.** Tracking estimates paint a soft near-term picture: Q1 GDP is running at just +0.2% annualised and the Current Activity Indicator has decelerated to +1.2% from +2.0% a month earlier.

The Fed speaker slate is unusually heavy, and the through-line is caution. **The central question officials keep returning to is whether tariffs deliver a one-time lift to the price level or a persistent lift to the inflation rate** — Barkin says he is "open to" the one-time view but does not start there, wary that inflation expectations have "loosened" after the recent episode. Waller frames the Fed's scope to cut this year as contingent on isolating tariff effects, while Kugler flags that goods inflation has turned positive again, removing a factor that had capped total inflation.

**The labour market read is still constructive despite the crosscurrents**, with big-data indicators pointing to solid job creation and the unemployment rate holding at 4.1%. The drags — federal workforce reductions and cooler public-sector hiring — are real but modest in the estimate, leaving the headline near trend.

For the reader, the watch list is clear: the ISM prints for confirmation of the survey-based softening, the Wednesday tariff announcement for the policy shock, and Powell's Friday speech for whether the "delay, not derail" framing on tariff inflation still holds. As a Week Ahead calendar preview, the note carries no trade idea.

subject: US Economics Analyst: A Further Increase in Our Tariff Assumptions (Walker / Phillips / Mericle)
summary:
# [REDACTED] Raises Tariff Baseline Again: Core PCE to 3.5%, Growth to 1.0%, Recession Odds to 35%

**Theme:** Second tariff-assumption upgrade in a month and its cascade through inflation, growth, unemployment, and the Fed path  
**Markets:** US economy, trade policy, and monetary policy  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Ronnie Walker, 30 March 2025  

### Definitive impacts
- Baseline average US tariff-rate rise for 2025 raised to 15pp (from 10pp), matching the prior "risk case"; almost all the revision is a more aggressive reciprocal-tariff assumption.
- Reciprocal tariffs assumed to average ~15% across trading partners (import-weighted) on the April 2 announcement, but expected to net down to about a 9pp addition to the effective rate after country and product exclusions.
- Yearend 2025 core PCE inflation forecast lifted 0.5pp to 3.5% y/y (peak), up from 3.0% under the prior assumption and 2.8% in February — consistent with the rule of thumb that each 1pp of tariff adds ~0.1pp to core PCE.
- 2025 GDP growth cut 0.5pp to 1.0% Q4/Q4 (and 0.4pp to 1.5% annual average), 0.7pp below consensus; peak tariff drag on y/y growth now 1.3pp versus 0.8pp before.
- Combined fiscal, immigration, and tariff policy estimated to subtract 1.2pp from GDP growth over the next year, with likely tax changes not enough to offset.
- Yearend 2025 unemployment-rate forecast raised 0.3pp to 4.5%.
- 2025 real income growth expected at just 1.4%, down sharply from +4.6% in 2023 and +2.2% in 2024.
- Trump's stated $600bn–$1trn tariff revenue target implies an 18%–30% effective rate on current import volumes, well above [REDACTED]'s baseline.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] sees the new baseline as a likely negative surprise to markets, noting its survey found the average investor expects only a ~9pp rise and just 4% expect 15pp or more.
- [REDACTED] raises its 12-month recession probability to 35% (from 20%), citing the lower growth baseline, collapsing household and business confidence, and White House signals of tolerance for near-term weakness; it is less willing than before to dismiss soft data because fundamentals are weaker.
- [REDACTED] now expects three 2025 Fed cuts (July, September, October), pulling forward the lone 2026 cut, with the terminal rate unchanged at 3.5–3.75%.
- [REDACTED] views a package of 2019-style "insurance" cuts as the modal outcome, while seeing less room for "normalization" cuts.
- [REDACTED] argues rising inflation expectations raise the bar for cuts, making a higher unemployment rate the key justification the Fed would need; the timing of cuts depends on when labor-market data show sufficient weakness.

### At issue
[REDACTED] raised its tariff assumptions for the second time in under a month, ahead of Trump's expected April 2 "reciprocal" tariff announcement. The central expectation: reciprocal tariffs averaging ~15% (import-weighted) across all trading partners, added on top of tariffs already in place (20% on China, plus steel/aluminum and the newly announced 25% auto tariff) and expected sectoral tariffs (a further 1–2pp). The estimated net effect lifts the average effective US tariff rate by 15pp in 2025.

The ~15% reciprocal headline is expected to translate into roughly a 9pp addition to the effective rate for four reasons: exclusion of smaller partners and deficit countries (~13% of imports); replacement of the current Canada/Mexico tariffs (which add only ~0.6pp given USMCA compliance); product carve-outs, notably autos being handled under the separate 25% auto tariff rather than stacked; and eventual negotiated rate reductions and industry-specific exclusions, as seen with China in the first Trump term.

### Backdrop
[REDACTED]'s framework routes tariffs into GDP through four channels: the tax-like hit to real disposable income and consumer spending, tighter financial conditions as markets react, weaker business investment under trade-policy uncertainty, and a small offset from a narrower trade deficit. On implementation, reciprocal tariffs are assumed to take effect within days to weeks of announcement, while other product-specific measures would likely wait until Q3 because they require new Section 232 investigations that take months.

The "insurance cut" reference is to 2019, when the Fed eased pre-emptively against downside risks rather than in response to a realized downturn — the template [REDACTED] now treats as most likely.

### Unpacked
This is the second upgrade in under a month, and the framing is deliberate: **[REDACTED] believes the market has consistently under-priced the April 2 risk**, with its own survey showing almost no investors positioned for a 15pp move. The note is as much about that expectations gap as about the tariffs themselves — the baseline is now set where the prior "risk case" sat.

The mechanics are largely arithmetic. A headline reciprocal rate near 15% sounds severe, but the chain of exclusions — smaller and deficit partners, USMCA-compliant Canada/Mexico goods, autos diverted to their own tariff line, and later negotiated carve-outs — pares the effective addition to roughly 9pp. **The gap between the announced rate and the realized rate is where most of the forecasting judgement lives**, and [REDACTED] flags real uncertainty in both timing and coverage, including whether autos get a separate lower reciprocal rate or a full substitution.

From there the forecasts move together. The inflation revision follows mechanically from the 0.1pp-per-1pp rule; the growth downgrade combines the larger tariff drag with an already-soft Q1 tracking estimate of 0.2%; and weaker growth feeds directly into the higher unemployment path. **The through-line is real income: growth of just 1.4% this year, down from 4.6% and 2.2%, is what makes [REDACTED] treat the collapse in sentiment as signal rather than noise.** In prior years strong fundamentals let the team dismiss soft-data weakness; that cushion is thinner now.

The Fed section carries the sharpest tension. **Higher inflation expectations cut against cuts, so the case for easing rests on the labor market weakening enough to justify insurance moves** — which is why [REDACTED] leans on the unemployment rate as the trigger and pencils in three consecutive cuts from July. The terminal rate is unchanged because the 2026 cut was simply pulled forward, not added. For the reader, the actionable watch-item is the labor data: the timing of the first cut hinges on when it turns, and [REDACTED]'s probability-weighted path sits dovish relative to market pricing.

The note offers no explicit trade idea beyond these forecast and probability shifts.

subject: Global Economics Comment: Introducing Our US Government Activity Tracker (Dong)
summary:
# Government Downsizing: Real-Time Signals Visible, Macro Footprint Still Small

**Theme:** Early data check on Trump-era federal cuts — measurable at the margins, limited in aggregate  
**Markets:** US macro / federal government activity  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jan Hatzius, 30 March 2025  

### Landscape
- RIF mandates have hit an estimated 49.3k federal employees so far — 1.6% of all federal employment — including roughly 21k probationary staff.
- Federal job growth slowed to 0.7% year-over-year in February.
- Initial unemployment claims from federal employees rose in late February and early March, then pulled back slightly in the two most recent reports.
- Indeed.com job postings for Washington DC sit 11% below the start of the year.
- Total operating cash withdrawals from the Treasury General Account remain close to historical levels across federal organizations.
- Federal grant awards have stagnated at a below-trend level since Inauguration Day, while monthly contract awards ticked down in February but stayed within normal ranges.
- DC Metrorail weekday ridership has surged to a post-pandemic high, tied to the return-to-office mandate.
- The [REDACTED] basket of government-exposed companies is down 9.3% since Inauguration Day, versus 6.9% for the S&P 500.

### Drivers
- Reduction-in-force mandates are the active lever on employment, concentrated so far in probationary staff; further cuts have been reported at Veterans Affairs, Defense, and the IRS, so the headcount tally is likely to grow.
- Spending restraint is showing selectively — operational and discretionary outlays are undershooting at the Department of State and FCC and grants have flattened — while overall Treasury withdrawals track prior-year norms.
- The return-to-office mandate is a distinct, opposite-direction force: it is lifting local transit demand even as headcount falls.
- Company-reported weakness in government travel has not yet dented actual airline supply; DC-area flight capacity shows no impact so far — a gap worth watching.

### Risks
- Downside: reported further RIFs at VA, Defense, and the IRS could push the affected total materially above 49.3k and broaden the labor-market signal, though the analyst judges the current employment and activity impact small.
- The analyst's baseline view is explicitly limited macroeconomic impact from the spending cuts; the note frames the data as confirming that view rather than challenging it.

### Unpacked
On employment, the tracker reads the downsizing through several independent signals. **The hard data confirms a real but contained reduction in force — 49.3k affected, about 1.6% of federal employment, with roughly 21k probationary — against a backdrop of federal job growth still positive at 0.7% year-over-year in February.** Federal-employee jobless claims rose then eased, and DC job postings are down 11% on the year, consistent with hiring cooling faster than separations are spiking.

Spending tells a more muted story. **Aggregate Treasury cash withdrawals remain roughly on-trend, with the visible cuts confined to specific pockets — State and the FCC on operations, and federal grants, which have stagnated below trend since Inauguration Day.** Contract awards dipped in February but stayed inside the range of normal volatility, so the contracting channel shows no clear break yet.

The travel and mobility indicators pull in opposite directions. Companies in airlines and hospitality have flagged softer government travel, yet DC-area flight capacity across the three major airports is unchanged, meaning the anecdotes have not translated into supply cuts. **Metrorail weekday ridership hitting a post-pandemic high underscores that the return-to-office mandate is currently a bigger, and opposing, force on local activity than the layoffs.**

On sentiment and markets, confidence among government employees has fallen since January, sharpest among those in the immediate DC metro. Government-exposed equities have underperformed — the [REDACTED] basket down 9.3% versus 6.9% for the S&P 500 since Inauguration Day — though this reflects positioning rather than realized fundamentals. **Notably, some IT software, defense, and DC-exposed REIT names have struck a cautiously optimistic tone, framing efficiency-driven cuts as a potential tailwind rather than a threat.** The overall read: modest real-time effects on employment and discretionary spending, but limited growth implications and an unchanged expectation of relatively contained macro impact.

subject: Global FX Trader: Drawbacks of the Clawbacks
summary:
# Dollar's Reprieve Rests on Tariffs Being Seen as Negotiable, Not Permanent

**Theme:** Tariffs as one force among many — and not the one moving the Dollar  
**Markets:** Global FX (G10, EM Asia, LatAm)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Kamakshya Trivedi, 28 March 2025  

### Landscape
- The broad Dollar sits 2% above its pre-election level even though DXY is flat on the year — most of the year-to-date decline is the Euro after the German fiscal surprise, not tariffs.
- [REDACTED]'s non-manufacturing survey tracker has fallen 3pts since December while manufacturing surveys improved on net — the opposite pattern to a tariff-driven slowdown.
- In the University of Michigan survey, ~50% of respondents cited government policy as bad for business but only 1% cited the trade deficit, versus ~8% in 2018-2019.
- Canadian business sentiment (CFIB) hit its lowest in 25 years, and [REDACTED]'s Canada CAI fell from above 2% in Q4 to -1%.
- NOK and SEK were the two best-performing G10 currencies over the past two months.
- INR bested Asian FX peers in March, moving back to a 4-5 vol currency after trading near a quasi-peg through Q3 2024; Indian equities drew ~$3bn inflows in two weeks after 13 straight weeks of selling and ~$30bn of outflows over five months.
- China's Q1 real GDP is tracking slightly above 5% despite +20pp of tariff increases this year; USD/CNY fix held near 7.17 since inauguration day.

### Drivers
- A more hawkish US trade agenda should be Dollar-positive over time, but the near-term signal is dominated by growth concerns — Friday's payrolls may matter more for direction than the April 2 tariff announcement.
- Markets treat tariffs as less durable than other policy shifts; economists expect a high headline, a long implementation period, and a final tariff below the initial proposal ("negotiation is a feature, not a bug").
- US soft data are weakening (softer sentiment, a personal-spending miss), raising the odds hard data follow and keeping risks skewed to a downside US growth surprise — watch ISMs, claims and NFP next week.
- Scandi outperformance is partly European growth optimism priced too fast, plus a genuine defense-spending tailwind; Norges Bank stayed on hold on hot inflation and economists raised the odds of a hawkish path.
- India's improvement rests on a services surplus outweighing the goods deficit and a bottoming domestic cycle; the RBI is expected to cut 25bp in April and keep injecting liquidity, prioritizing the cycle over the currency.
- CNY stability, backed by resilient Chinese growth and the PBoC's revealed FX-stability preference, is the anchor for the rest of USD/Asia.
- 25% auto tariffs (autos from April 3, parts by May 3) hit Mexico, Korea and Canada hardest by share of activity, but USMCA content exemptions and possible further Canada carve-outs have muted the near-term FX response.

### Risks
- **Downside (USD):** Markets are vulnerable to a negative tariff surprise, though the bar to deliver one next week is high and depends more on the implementation period than initial "sticker shock."
- **Upside (short AUD/JPY trade):** Better US data next week that challenge rising-recession-odds narrative — but momentum and the balance of risks point the other way.
- **Downside (GBP):** A sharp global duration sell-off could revive fiscal-based pressure on Sterling, with gilt yields near January highs; the analyst sees this as well appreciated and bearish sentiment as overdone.
- **Downside (SEK, CZK, HUF):** A tariff hit to euro-area growth weighs on SEK ("Euro-squared"), while auto tariffs threaten CE3 — the analyst sees attractive asymmetry in short CZK and HUF, with HUF also exposed to fiscal slippage.
- **Downside (CAD):** Difficult budget process, weaker growth, and US knock-on effects could force the BoC to ease more than it prefers; risk skew stays bearish but slightly less so.
- **Downside (MXN):** Limited scope for sustained tariff relief before USMCA negotiations, with carry falling as Banxico cuts.

### Unpacked
The through-line is that 2025's tariff escalation is not happening in a vacuum. **The Dollar's year-to-date softness owes more to the German fiscal surprise, DOGE-related shifts, fiscal-restraint talk and idiosyncratic US growth worries than to trade policy itself** — a mix that would normally weigh on the Dollar regardless of tariffs. [REDACTED] still expects a hawkish trade stance to be Dollar-supportive over time, but concedes the data are mixed and that next week's activity prints could dominate the tariff headline for near-term direction.

On the Yen, positioning into April 2 is hard because it is unclear whether an aggressive tariff outcome would hurt US growth expectations most or instead erode optimism elsewhere, such as in Europe; anything short of immediate implementation could even bring relief. **With markets more exposed to a downside US growth surprise, [REDACTED] keeps its open short AUD/JPY recommendation targeting 90.5 and frames long JPY as the most attractive equity hedge in a long time.** The March 28 shift in relative rates looked larger than the USD/JPY move, implying room for further downside; better US data is the main threat.

Sterling is expected to "muddle through" a tough fiscal backdrop. The Spring Statement landed close to expectations, and the government's responsiveness to fiscal concerns underpins a constructive view. **A supportive and somewhat distinctive feature is GBP's relative resilience when tariff risk is priced — the realised correlation between EUR/GBP and tariff-sensitive pairs like USD/CAD and USD/MXN has fallen sharply this year** — and a tariff delivery in line with expectations should push EUR/GBP tactically lower.

The Scandi case rests on structure. Both currencies may have run too far on European growth optimism that could still disappoint, but **their outsized industrial concentration means a coordinated European defense-spending response would benefit them disproportionately**, with Norway's aerospace and defense market cap standing out. Because tariffs should weigh more on SEK (its "Euro-squared" behavior), [REDACTED] sees NOK/SEK moving higher over the medium term.

India's return to genuine two-way volatility is read as healthy, backed by better fundamentals and returning flows. **The Rupee is not yet clear of risk: India runs among the highest tariff differentials with the US and remains exposed on reciprocal tariffs, while below-target inflation means the RBI will favor the domestic cycle over the currency.**

In North America, the Dollar-weakness tailwind plus a domestic shift — tariff focus moving away from Canada, USMCA exemptions, possible auto-tariff easing, and greater fiscal-spending optimism from both candidates — has firmed CAD. **[REDACTED] trims its USD/CAD forecast to 1.44 at 3, 6 and 12 months (from 1.46), while keeping a bearish lean given budget, growth and US-spillover risks.** For Mexico the backdrop has turned tougher: Banxico cut 50bp with dovish guidance signalling another similar move, lowering the policy-rate path and eroding carry. **USD/MXN should keep tracking US growth pricing, and with carry falling and US growth risks skewed weak, the total-return case for MXN longs is clearly less attractive than earlier in the year — though CAD/MXN shorts carry lower beta to US growth news.**

Across non-Japan Asia, the complex stays anchored by a steady Renminbi. Korea's 2025 GDP forecast was cut 0.3ppt to 1.5% and the Won was the weakest Asian currency last week on auto exposure, though the complexity of Korean exports makes them hard to substitute. Within ASEAN, Thailand screens most vulnerable, followed by Singapore and Malaysia on electronics, with Indonesia and the Philippines less exposed. **On autos, [REDACTED]'s economists expect the 25% tariffs to persist, but USMCA content exemptions leave Mexico's effective exposure closer to Korea's, and the FX adjustment may take longer to arrive** — with the CE3 (CZK, HUF) carrying little priced-in tariff risk premium, hence the short-CZK, short-HUF asymmetry.

subject: Global Rates Trader: Bracing for Impact
summary:
# Bracing for Impact: Tariffs and Payrolls Set a Pivotal Week for Global Rates

**Theme:** Growth-vs-inflation tension across G4 as tariffs and US jobs data approach; central banks lean toward protecting growth  
**Markets:** G10 rates (US, Euro area, UK, Japan)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], George Cole, 28 March 2025  

### Landscape
- US front-end inflation has reset lower this week after choppy tariff headlines, now better aligned with the baseline path for the next year.
- Rates volatility has normalized from its recent peak alongside stabilizing risk sentiment, despite still-elevated uncertainty.
- Reserves plus RRP balances rose ~$370bn as Treasury cash balances declined since mid-February, pushing reserve balances close to June 2024 levels; ON-RRP uptake hit year-to-date highs into quarter-end.
- Swap spreads screen mildly cheap versus fair value across the curve after tightening this week.
- EUR 2025 rate pricing richened this week as the market braced for tariffs; front-end pricing now judged fair at current valuations.
- Euro area sovereign spreads sit close to historic tights, with the 10y BTP-Bund, OAT-Bund and Bonos-Bund targets held at 120bp, 70bp and 60bp.
- 10y JGB yields have brushed the end-2025 forecast of 1.60%, with 5y5y JGB yields near 2%; 10y JPY real rates now around 0% while 5y real rates hover at the low end of the BOJ neutral-rate range.
- The DMO set the lowest long-end Gilt issuance share on record; total 2025-26 Gilt sales came in at £299.2bn versus the £305bn expectation, though likely to be revised higher.

### Drivers
- Tariffs: the April 2 announcement is the near-term catalyst, with [REDACTED] economists seeing risks skewed more negative than the market expects; unless the phase-in is short, the signal may matter less than payrolls for US rates.
- US payrolls (two days after the tariff news): seen as the larger volatility event — a firm print erodes conviction in near-term cuts, a downside surprise pivots focus to growth and steepens the curve. Watch next week's print.
- ECB reaction function: expected to prioritize downside growth risks over inflation, supporting April and June cuts and a steeper EUR curve.
- Fiscal/supply: US fiscal policy unlikely to offset the tariff hit this year given timing and magnitude; elevated EUR debt supply and rising EMU-4 debt levels push toward wider spreads; higher EU issuance keeps EU bonds wide versus their AAA rating.
- UK issuance mix: the record-low long-end Gilt share and new "programmatic tenders" for off-the-run Gilts signal more active curve management, a force expected to compress long-end risk premium over time — but not yet, given upside issuance risk and a large unallocated share.
- Japan domestic inflation: March Tokyo CPI surprised to the upside (rice prices plus broader services), supporting higher yields, partly offset by tariff risk to growth that is softened by auto tariffs being broad-based rather than Japan-specific.

### Risks
- Downside (US rates): a weaker-than-expected payrolls print, which the analyst sees as a volatility-positive outcome given current pricing and likely to steepen the curve.
- Downside (Euro area growth): larger-than-baseline tariffs could cost roughly 0.5% of Euro area growth, mapping to about 15-20bp lower in 10y Bund yields.
- Upside (EGB spreads): rising EMU-4 debt levels skew risks toward wider sovereign spreads, with clearer asymmetry toward widening in France on political constraints to deficit consolidation.
- Upside (US swap spreads): the analyst flags that improved bank buyback economics could divert capital to higher shareholder returns rather than balance-sheet growth, a risk to the deregulation-driven spread-widening narrative.
- Upside (UK issuance): the analyst notes upside risk to Gilt issuance and the large unallocated share that historically skews toward more long-end supply.

### Unpacked
In the US, the very front-end is likely to stay anchored while the growth-versus-inflation tension is unresolved, absent clearer growth weakness or a more hawkish inflation tone. **Next week's payrolls is cast as the point of resolution — determining which risk the market prioritizes — and as a bigger vol event than the tariff announcement itself.** The preferred long positions are 5s and greens (2y1y), which historically benefit from a flattening inflation curve while insulating against front-end inflation widening propagating further out. Further out, the baseline range is seen as tighter, with steepening skew in the tails; the note keeps selling ATM to buy 2x OTM curve caps on 2s10s, and tightens the stop while raising the target on its long 5y beta-weighted TIPS to 1.6% and 1.75%.

**The vol backdrop matters because the post-rally starting point for front-end inflation raises the bar for a tariff-driven vol shock, while current pricing leaves clearer room for a downside payrolls surprise to lift vol.** The fundamental vol model treats higher inflation and lower growth as roughly equally vol-positive per 1pp. Under a baseline of moderate slowdown, implied vol is expected to reset somewhat lower once tariff clarity arrives.

On funding and spreads, the TGA drawdown has eased reserves, but proximity to quarter-end and record ON-RRP usage point to balance-sheet pressures, even without a material DVP/tri-party spread widening that would signal severe intermediation strain. The SOFR-fed funds futures curve has shifted lower, and a flatter July-August slope implies the market sees a less concentrated debt-limit x-date around August — consistent with the economists' view that the limit is likely raised by early August. **Swap spreads tightened more than the repo move implies, plausibly reflecting LDI rebalancing after the equity selloff and more attractive bank price-to-book, and screen mildly cheap versus fair with regulatory progress seen as ultimately supportive.**

In Europe, focus has moved from medium-term deficits to near-term tariff-driven growth risk, keeping EUR front-end risks skewed lower. **The tension between 2026-27 fiscal-stimulus-led growth and near-term risk, plus heavy supply, argues for a steep EUR curve rather than outright front-end longs at fair valuations** — with 5s10s box BTP-Bund steepeners preferred to monetize BTP carry and hedge gradual spread widening. A meaningful tariff-driven rally would be used to add shorts in belly forwards; the end-25 Bund forecast stays at 3%. On EU bonds, generic credit risk explains their underperformance poorly, pointing to liquidity and idiosyncratic factors; higher issuance should aid liquidity but will dominate near term, keeping EU bonds wide versus ratings until they operate more "sovereignly" and potentially benefit from ECB purchases.

In the UK, the spring budget update brought only fleeting relief, with attention shifting to potential future budget revisions rather than the reduced long-end skew. **The durable reduction in weighted-average maturity at issuance is expected to support the long end eventually, but the 10s30s flattening recommendation was stopped out and is closed.** The combination of gradual cuts and a DMO more responsive to weak long-end demand is still seen compressing Gilt risk premium over time.

In Japan, yields have drifted higher and 2s10s has re-steepened toward multi-year highs. **The note keeps 1y1y/2y1y steepeners and short positions further out via payer spreads, but now also sees value in being short 5s** — 5y real rates still sit at the low end of the BOJ neutral range even as 10y real rates reach roughly 0% and 5y5y approaches 2%, a repricing viewed as sustainable.

subject: CEEMEA in Focus: CEEMEA’s US Export Exposures, Bilateral Trade Balances, and Effective Tariff Differentials
summary:
# Reciprocal tariffs: Hungary, Israel and South Africa most exposed in CEEMEA; Turkey faces the widest tariff gap
