### Drivers
- Goods prices reheating: the projected rise in core reflects used cars (+1.5%), new cars (+0.5%), and auto insurance (+0.75%), while shelter moderates slightly (OER +0.31%, rent +0.27%).
- Seasonal factors revised by the BLS (using 2024 data) tend to smooth monthly fluctuations — last year core CPI ran 10bp above average in Q1 and 14bp below between May and July.
- Consumption losing traction: core retail sales projected at +0.2% (vs. consensus +0.3%), with a possible drag from colder weather; headline at -0.2% on more expensive gasoline and fewer auto sales.
- End of the immigration surge: net immigration fell from a peak annualized pace of 3.5-4mn in late 2023 to 1.7mn in December 2024, with a projected drop to 750k/year under tighter policy — which will reduce labor force and payroll growth over the course of the year.
- Trade policy as an active source of uncertainty: imminent "reciprocal" tariffs and the announced rise in aluminum tariffs (to 25%) and steel already weighing on expectations.

### Risks
- Upside (inflation): the analyst notes that including VATs in the calculation of reciprocal tariffs would raise the effective tariff by an additional ~10pp — a risk scenario, with no current indication that policy will include this.
- Upside (unemployment): a crackdown on unauthorized immigrants is an upside risk to the unemployment rate, offsetting the natural downward trend flagged by the analyst.
- Downside (activity/inflation): a scenario in which unauthorized immigrants — 4-5% of the total labor force and 15-20% in some sectors — stop working out of fear would be highly disruptive and carry a larger inflationary impact, according to the analyst.

### Unpacked
The "reciprocal" tariffs Trump intends to announce would raise US tariff rates to match those imposed by trading partners, at either the product or country level. **The product-level version would raise the average US tariff by about 2pp, and the country-level version somewhat less.** The sensitive point is the treatment of non-tariff barriers: including VATs in the calculation would add another ~10pp to the effective tariff, though there is no sign policy is heading in that direction.

There is a reading that the measure could reduce uncertainty at the margin, since Trump appears to view it as an alternative to a universal 10-20% tariff. **Even so, further tariff announcements remain likely** — as already illustrated by the revocation of exclusions to the 2018 steel tariffs (25%) and aluminum, with the latter rising to 25%, adding 0.4pp to the effective tariff rate. The monetary backdrop: at the January FOMC, Powell described the rate as "meaningfully restrictive" and policy as in "wait and see" mode until there is clarity on the new administration, but indicated that, once that clarity arrives, the bar for a further cut is low. Since then, new tariffs have arrived along with a jump in University of Michigan inflation expectations, with respondents citing tariffs. Powell testifies before Congress on Tuesday and Wednesday.

On immigration, the base case has a limited economic impact. **The extra boost to the labor force, currently 40k above normal, should return to normal in early 2026**, and lower immigration would subtract 30-40bp from potential GDP growth versus 2023-2024 — but just 5bp versus the pre-pandemic norm. With the labor market back in balance, the effect on wages and inflation tends to be modest, except in the risk scenario of an abrupt loss of workers.

The January payroll report also brought broad annual revisions, in line with expectations. **The household survey now correctly reflects the immigration surge for the first time**, meaningfully raising the cumulative employment growth reported over recent years. The 7bp drop in unemployment, added to December's 15bp, already fulfills the entire reduction projected for the year in the bank's 2025 Outlook. The acceleration in hourly earnings is discounted as possibly weather-related — hours fell — and by the continued deceleration in other wage measures. The report does not present an explicit trade idea.

subject: [REDACTED] FX Morning Notes: Limited FX Impact from the Metals Tariffs
summary:
# Metals tariffs raised to 25%, but only a modest Dollar impact expected

**Theme:** Why the new steel and aluminum tariffs carry limited FX consequences  
**Markets:** USD and global FX; US trade policy  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Stuart Jenkins, 11 February 2025  

### Definitive impacts
- Steel and aluminum tariffs raised to 25%, removing all country- and product-specific exemptions, effective March 12th.
- Faster implementation timeline than a fresh Section 232 process would allow, because the proclamation relies on the January 2018 investigation rather than commissioning a new one.
- ~0.5pp rally in USD/CAD and USD/MXN on Sunday's open, with limited further FX reaction after the tariffs were confirmed.
- University of Michigan 5-10y inflation expectations at 3.3% in the preliminary February release — the highest in the survey's history — while other measures (5y5y breakevens, NY Fed survey, the Fed's Index of Common Inflation Expectations) show no comparable rise.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] expects only a modest Dollar impact from the metals tariffs, because they add little to the US effective tariff rate.
- [REDACTED] sees a smaller FX response as justified because commodity strategists expect limited pass-through to global metals prices but significant pass-through to domestic US prices — foreign producers can pass on the cost.
- [REDACTED] flags that tariffs on other critical goods, such as pharmaceuticals and semiconductors, would likely have a larger effect on both the effective tariff rate and the Dollar.
- [REDACTED] notes tariff policy has shifted toward economic aims and away from extracting non-trade concessions; if reciprocal and metals tariffs substitute for broad across-the-board increases, that is a downside risk to its baseline.
- [REDACTED] expects Chair Powell, testifying to Congress, to reiterate the FOMC is in no hurry.

### Backdrop
Section 232 tariffs normally require a fresh Department of Commerce investigation into the imports in question. In the last trade war, steel and aluminum tariffs were implemented unevenly, with country- and company-specific delays and exemptions and varying retaliation from US trading partners. That history is what makes the impact and timing of the current measures uncertain.

### At issue
President Trump signed proclamations raising tariffs to 25% on steel and aluminum and stripping out all existing exemptions, effective March 12th. Reports suggest an exemption for Australia is under consideration and that other countries may seek to renegotiate. Separately, Trump has signaled "reciprocal tariffs" to be announced today or tomorrow. A range of Fed, ECB and BoE speakers are due, including Powell's congressional testimony; BoE's Mann has explained her push for more activist policy after her dovish dissent last week.

### Unpacked
**The core logic is that a tariff's FX consequence tracks its effect on the effective tariff rate, and metals move that rate only slightly.** The market has already priced this: beyond the initial half-point pop in USD/CAD and USD/MXN at Sunday's open, confirmation of the measures barely registered.

**What determines the muted Dollar call is who ultimately bears the cost.** With global metals prices expected to hold but domestic US prices to rise, the burden falls on US buyers rather than forcing foreign currencies to adjust — so the FX channel stays narrow. The larger risk lies elsewhere: tariffs on pharmaceuticals or semiconductors would bite harder, and the pending reciprocal tariffs mark a shift toward using tariffs for economic rather than diplomatic ends.

**The open question is whether these targeted measures replace broader increases or come on top of them** — if they substitute, [REDACTED]'s baseline faces downside. Powell's testimony and the inflation-expectations picture are the near-term watch items: the record Michigan reading stands alone for now, unconfirmed by breakevens or other surveys, leaving it ambiguous whether expectations are genuinely de-anchoring or the survey is an outlier.

subject: US Daily: What Might Reciprocal Tariffs Look Like? (Phillips/Peng)
summary:
# Reciprocal Tariffs: Likely a ~2pp Rise, but VATs Are the Tail Risk

**Theme:** How a promised "reciprocal tariff" could be designed, the range of possible impacts, and its legal basis  
**Markets:** US trade policy / effective tariff rate  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Alec Phillips, 11 February 2025  

### Definitive impacts
- **+~2pp to the US weighted-average tariff rate** if reciprocity is applied product-by-product per country, matching each foreign product-specific rate.
- **Less than +1pp** if applied at the country level (one uniform add-on per country), with no effect on free-trade-agreement partners such as Mexico, Canada and Korea.
- **A further +10pp** to the average effective rate only in the risk scenario where foreign VATs are folded into the calculation.
- **+~0.4pp to the average effective rate and ~4bps to core prices** from the separate Feb. 10 move rescinding 2018 steel/aluminum exclusions and raising the aluminum tariff to 25%, affecting roughly $50bn of imports.
- **No additional tariff on a large share of US imports**, including China, whose average US tariff already exceeds China's average rate after successive Sec. 301 rounds; some individual partners could still face increases above 10pp but represent small import shares.

### Opinative impacts
- **[REDACTED] does not expect VATs to be included**, despite Trump's criticism of them: VATs apply to domestic and imported goods alike and resemble a sales tax, and the 2020 USTR trade-barriers report did not generally treat them as barriers.
- **Reciprocal tariffs could incrementally reduce trade-policy uncertainty**, since Trump appears to frame them as an alternative to a 10–20% universal tariff; matching foreign rates would cap how far US tariffs rise absent retaliation.
- **They could lead to lower tariffs over time**, as some partners cut their own rates — [REDACTED] notes the EU already appears to be readying a cut to its 10% auto tariff — potentially bringing commensurate US reductions.
- **A hybrid design is seen as plausible**: mostly country-level but with selected product equalization, most likely on autos aimed at the EU ([REDACTED]'s baseline already assumes new US tariffs on EU autos).
- **The reprieve is not durable**: [REDACTED] stresses this is only the fourth week of the term and expects many further tariff announcements regardless, with no guarantee against a later broad tariff.
- **Implementation may be slower than recent tariffs**, in [REDACTED]'s view, given administrative complexity — especially for product-level or NTB-inclusive versions.

### Backdrop
The US average effective tariff rate is the reference metric throughout, and its baseline already reflects earlier action: multiple Sec. 301 rounds that pushed the average US rate on Chinese goods above China's average rate on US goods, and 2018 Sec. 232 tariffs on steel (25%) and aluminum (10%) that had accumulated product exclusions. The US also has free-trade agreements with 20 countries — including Mexico, Canada, Korea, Australia and Israel — under which reciprocity would generally add nothing.

Trump has long backed a "Reciprocal Trade Act" — during his first term and the 2024 campaign — that would let the president match, product by product, the tariff a country applies to the same US good. A new version was recently introduced in Congress. This note assumes any unilateral plan resembles that concept.

### At issue
- **Reciprocal tariff announcement.** On Feb. 9 Trump said he would announce reciprocal tariffs on Feb. 11 or 12, raising US tariffs to match exporting countries' rates (with no assumption US rates fall to match lower foreign ones). The note lays out three possible designs — country-level, product-level-by-country, and a version incorporating non-tariff barriers — plus a possible hybrid. Legal authority is unsettled: [REDACTED] expects reliance on IEEPA (used for the recent China tariffs and delayed Canada/Mexico tariffs) or the never-used Sec. 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, which allows up to 50% tariffs against discriminatory trade practices. Neither requires a formal investigation.
- **Steel and aluminum.** Separately, on Feb. 10 Trump rescinded prior exclusions to the 2018 steel and aluminum tariffs and raised the aluminum rate to 25%.

### Unpacked
The note is written before the fact: Trump has flagged an announcement but not specified its form, so the exercise is to bound the plausible outcomes rather than describe a decided policy. **The central message is that design choice, not the headline of "reciprocity," determines the size of the shock** — from under 1pp for a simple country-level add-on to around 2pp for product-level matching.

The analysis turns on one distinction that carries most of the risk. **The gap between a manageable ~2pp increase and a severe one is whether the policy treats VATs as trade barriers** — an inclusion that would add roughly 10pp and, because VATs are economically closer to a sales tax than a tariff, would be far less likely to prompt reciprocal foreign cuts. [REDACTED] treats this as a genuine risk flagged by Trump's rhetoric while judging it unlikely, since there is no current indication VATs are in the calculation and the administration's own past trade-barrier reporting did not classify them as such.

The framing of reciprocity as a *substitute* for a universal tariff is what makes the note read, on balance, as a possible de-escalation. **If matching foreign rates genuinely replaces a 10–20% flat tariff, the ceiling on US tariffs is set by others' existing rates rather than by open-ended discretion** — and could ratchet down if partners like the EU cut auto tariffs to pre-empt US action. That optimism is deliberately hedged: the same discretion that could cap tariffs could also be abandoned later, and the very early point in the term argues for treating any single announcement as provisional.

The legal discussion matters for timing and durability rather than magnitude. Because both IEEPA and Sec. 338 avoid a formal investigation, action can be fast in principle, but the administrative load of a per-product, per-country schedule — still heavier if NTBs are estimated — argues for slower rollout than the near-immediate Canada/China/Mexico tariffs. The steel and aluminum move is offered as concrete evidence that the "critical imports" track is advancing in parallel, independent of whatever reciprocal design emerges.

subject: US Daily: January CPI Preview (Rindels/Walker)
summary:
# Core CPI +0.34% in January, a Touch Above Consensus — Cars, Insurance, and Annual Revisions in Focus

**Theme:** Above-consensus core print, with used cars, car insurance, and communications the swing components, plus annual seasonal-factor and weight updates  
**Markets:** US inflation  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jessica Rindels, 10 February 2025  

### Estimates

**January core CPI**
- **+0.34% m/m** core CPI, vs. +0.3% consensus.
- **3.19% y/y** core CPI, vs. 3.1% consensus.
- **+0.40% m/m** core services ex-rent and OER.
- **+0.32% m/m** core PCE translation for January (to be updated after CPI and PPI).

**January headline CPI**
- **+0.36% m/m** headline CPI, vs. +0.3% consensus, on +0.4% food and +0.6% energy prices.
- **2.96% y/y** headline CPI, vs. 2.9% consensus.

**Key components**
- **+1.5% m/m** used car prices, up from +1.2% in December, on higher auction prices.
- **+0.5% m/m** new car prices, as dealer incentives fell 12% sequentially.
- **+0.75% m/m** car insurance, up from +0.40% in December.
- **+0.5% m/m** communications, vs. flat in December and -1.0% in November, on seasonal distortions and a postage increase.
- **+0.31% m/m** owners' equivalent rent (vs. +0.33% in December); **+0.27% m/m** rent (vs. +0.33%).

**Forecast path**
- **~0.25% m/m** core CPI over the next few months.
- **+2.8% y/y** core CPI and **+2.6% y/y** core PCE by December 2025.

### Outlook

- Further disinflation is in the pipeline over the coming year, driven by rebalancing in the auto, housing rental, and labor markets — but partly offset by catch-up inflation in healthcare and by an escalation in tariff policy.
- Tariffs are the decisive swing factor for 2025: absent them, core CPI would slow to +2.3% y/y by December; including them, the forecast is +2.8%.
- Car insurance inflation is seen returning sustainably to its pre-pandemic pace this year, as most of the gap between premiums and costs has now closed; an early read on February points to a slightly larger rise than January.

### Unpacked

The January estimate sits modestly above consensus across both core and headline, with several component-level stories doing the work. On autos, higher used-car auction prices lift used vehicles to +1.5%, while a 12% sequential drop in promotional dealer incentives points to another increase in new-car prices. **Car insurance is set to accelerate to +0.75% as insurers continue passing through higher car, repair, medical, and litigation costs — a pass-through that lags because premium increases must be negotiated with state regulators, and one that is now largely complete.** Communications is expected to jump to +0.5%, breaking from its usual deflationary trend on seasonal distortions and a postage price increase, though that boost could be tempered by this month's seasonal-factor revisions. Elsewhere, airfares should soften and shelter moderates slightly.

**This report also carries two annual updates — new seasonal factors and new expenditure weights — that could reshape the recent inflation pattern.** The seasonal-factor revision pulls monthly readings toward the annual average: over the past decade about 20% of a month's initial relative strength has typically been revised away in the first annual revision. That matters because last year's core CPI ran 10bp above the 2024 average in Q1 and 14bp below in May–July, so the strong early-2024 prints are candidates to be revised down. The weights update, reflecting 2023 spending shares, is not expected to move components meaningfully since the largest post-pandemic consumption shifts were already in place by 2022.

**A subtler effect is the possible resumption of seasonal adjustment for components dropped during the pandemic.** The BLS stopped adjusting categories worth roughly 16% of the basket in early 2021 and has not resumed for many; seasonal patterns now appear to have reemerged for some, such as consumer electronics. Because these components carry larger weights in PCE than in CPI, any resumption would matter more for PCE — but with only the prior two months revised per PCE release, the full impact likely waits for the NIPA annual revisions in September.

Beyond the print, the medium-term picture is a tug-of-war: disinflation from auto, rental, and labor-market rebalancing against offsets from healthcare catch-up and tariffs. The tariff assumption is what separates a benign +2.3% core path from the +2.8% baseline, making trade policy the key variable to watch through year-end.

subject: [REDACTED] FX Morning Notes: Broadening Out of Tariff Targets
summary:
# Steel, Aluminium and Reciprocal Tariffs Mark a Shift Toward Durable Dollar Support

**Theme:** Trump's next tariff round moves from political-leverage tariffs to protectionist "economic" tariffs, with a more lasting USD impact than the market prices  
**Markets:** US Dollar and trading-partner FX  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Stuart Jenkins, 10 February 2025  

### Definitive impacts
- US imports of iron, steel and aluminium total ~$50bn — modest relative to larger critical-industry categories, so a 25% metals tariff would only marginally lift the US effective tariff rate.
- Exposure is concentrated in Canada, the Euro area, Mexico, Korea and Brazil, which supply a larger share of US metal imports and would face the more disruptive effect.
- On Sunday's open the Dollar strengthened while CAD, MXN and EUR underperformed; other currencies with larger metals-tariff exposure did not clearly differentiate.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] sees the two tariff sets as a shift from "negotiation" tariffs (aimed at political concessions) to "economic" tariffs (protecting US industries and narrowing bilateral deficits), a category already in its economists' baseline as 10% additional tariffs on a broader set of critical imports.
- [REDACTED] expects a more durable Dollar impact than the market currently prices, because economic tariffs are less contingent on bilateral political negotiations and therefore less likely to be unwound.
- [REDACTED] flags that the market's key uncertainty on reciprocal tariffs is scope — matching a country's overall effective rate versus matching rates good-by-good — with the granular approach likely requiring a longer legislative process.

### Backdrop
Steel and aluminium tariffs were a central feature of the 2018-2019 trade war. Despite periods of country-specific exemptions for key partners, those tariffs were ultimately enacted. Recent tariff activity had been dominated by the "negotiation" type — threats used to extract political concessions — rather than measures aimed at trade or industrial protection.

### At issue
Over the weekend President Trump said he plans to announce two new tariff sets this week: 25% tariffs on steel and aluminium on Monday, and reciprocal tariffs — matching the rates trading partners apply to the US — on Tuesday or Wednesday.

### Unpacked
The note reads the weekend announcements as a change in kind, not just degree. **The move from leverage-driven threats to structural protection is what makes this round matter for the Dollar, because tariffs justified on economic grounds are harder to bargain away.** The metals tariffs themselves are small in dollar terms, so their significance is less about the direct hit to the US effective rate and more about what they signal.

The reciprocal-tariff design is the open question. Whether the administration matches a partner's aggregate effective rate or moves good-by-good determines both the economic reach and the timeline, since the granular route drags in a slower legislative process. That ambiguity is left unresolved here.

**[REDACTED]'s central claim is a pricing gap: because these economic tariffs sit in its baseline and are less reversible, it expects a more durable Dollar impact than the market has discounted.** Friday's price action fits only partially — the Dollar rose and North American partners plus the Euro underperformed, but currencies most exposed to metals tariffs did not clearly separate, suggesting the market has not yet mapped the exposure. The note offers no explicit trade recommendation.

subject: US Economics Analyst: The End of the Immigration Surge (Peng / Mericle / Phillips)
summary:
# The End of the US Immigration Surge: Modest Macro Hit in the Base Case, a Labor-Supply Shock in the Tail

**Theme:** How far immigration slows under the new enforcement regime and what it does to labor supply, growth, and inflation  
**Markets:** US economy — labor supply, growth, inflation  
**Source:** [REDACTED] (Elsie Peng), 9 February 2025  

### Definitive impacts
- Net immigration had already fallen by more than half from its late-2023 peak of 3.5–4mn annualized to ~1.7mn by December 2024, driven by unauthorized inflows dropping from ~2.8mn to ~0.8mn.
- Gross unauthorized inflows fell from 3.5–4mn at the year-ago peak to ~1.4mn in December, still above the pre-pandemic ~0.7mn average; gross outflows ran at ~0.6mn.
- Net authorized immigration is running at ~0.9mn per year — above the first Trump administration's pace but in line with the period before it.
- Immigration's boost to labor-force growth has fallen from ~100k/month above normal at the peak to ~40k above normal now.
- The breakeven pace of payroll growth that holds unemployment steady has dropped to ~150k.
- Unauthorized immigrants make up 4–5% of the total US workforce and 15–20% in crop production, food processing, and construction; the median unauthorized worker earns ~20% less than other non-supervisory workers in the same industry.
- The unemployment rate is down ¼pp over the past two months to 4.0%.
- Real-time immigration trackers carry a ~1.5-month lag; voluntary departures surface only with a one- to two-year lag via DHS airline-manifest estimates.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] expects net immigration to slow further to 750k/year — 750k net authorized plus zero net unauthorized, with ~500k deportations offsetting ~500k asylum seekers and illegal entrants — citing budget, enforcement-capacity, legal, and court-backlog limits that cap a larger crackdown.
- Deportations are seen running at or slightly above the historical 200–450k/year range, not into the millions.
- Macro consequences of the baseline are judged limited: the 750k pace subtracts 30–40bp from potential GDP growth versus 2023–2024 but just ~5bp versus the pre-pandemic pace, with the immigration boost to labor supply back to normal by early 2026.
- Wage and inflation effects are expected to be modest now that the labor market is back in balance; the 2022 disinflationary effect of the surge was itself modest, secondary, and roughly inflation-neutral once offsetting rent pressure is counted.
- The breakeven payroll rate is seen falling to ~90k by end-2025, and [REDACTED] expects unemployment to keep drifting down on healthy labor demand.
- The main risk is not mass deportation but a "fear" climate in which unauthorized workers stay home or employers stop hiring them — potentially causing serious, localized inflation via supply bottlenecks in dependent industries, echoing the pandemic lesson that acute shortages push prices up sharply.
- [REDACTED] flags that such a shock might not show cleanly in official data, since frightened workers may also stop answering the household survey; on the evidence so far it sees no dramatic break — the job-finding rate has dipped, but participation, unemployment, and survey response for recent immigrants have been broadly stable through December.
- No explicit trade idea is offered.

### Backdrop
For most of the pre-pandemic period, US net immigration ran near a trend of about 1mn per year, and the breakeven pace of job growth needed to hold unemployment steady was correspondingly higher. From 2022 to 2024 that trend broke: net immigration surged well above 1mn, peaking at a 3.5–4mn annualized rate in late 2023, overwhelmingly through unauthorized channels — a diverse group spanning asylum seekers, parolees, Temporary Protected Status holders, and people entering illegally. That surge lifted labor-force growth and, arriving when the labor market was the tightest in US history, likely helped cool especially hot low-wage wage growth.

Because new immigrants often only enter the workforce in their second or third year, the labor-supply boost lags the inflow itself — so the contribution to labor-force growth keeps running above normal for a time even after inflows fall, then unwinds with a delay.

### At issue
Two developments are analysed together. First, the inflow surge has already reversed sharply on its own, more than halving by December 2024. Second, in its first two weeks the new administration has moved on three fronts to cut the unauthorized population: reducing new inflows (tighter border security, reinstated "Remain in Mexico," ending several humanitarian parole programs); rolling back protections for those already present (TPS set to expire for several hundred thousand people in 2025, which would strip work permits — though courts may block non-renewal, especially for long-tenured immigrants); and raising deportations, particularly of those with criminal records, via more expedited removals and an expected Congressional allocation of at least $100bn for enforcement later this year. Enforcement capacity, detention space, and court throughput remain binding constraints.

### Unpacked
The note is framed as a Q&A that reappraises a story already in motion: the immigration surge peaked over a year ago and had substantially unwound before the new administration took office. **The central message is that the incremental policy tightening, on the baseline, formalizes a slowdown that was already happening rather than engineering a new shock — pushing net immigration to 750k, a large break from recent years but only a touch below the pre-pandemic norm.** That distinction is what keeps the macro estimates small: growth loses 30–40bp against the 2023–2024 pace but almost nothing against the 1mn trend the economy operated on for years.

The mechanics matter because timing is counterintuitive. Inflows fell first, but the labor-supply contribution declines only with a lag as prior arrivals mature into the workforce, which is why the boost is still ~40k above normal today and does not normalize until early 2026. **The same lag is quietly reshaping the labor market's speed limit: the breakeven payroll rate is collapsing from ~150k toward ~90k, meaning steady or even soft-looking job numbers are consistent with falling unemployment.** This underpins the call that unemployment keeps drifting down despite slower hiring.

**The real tail risk is not deportations but chilling effects** — a climate where unauthorized workers, 4–5% of the workforce and up to a fifth in agriculture, food processing, and construction, stay home or lose employers willing to hire them. An abrupt withdrawal there could produce pandemic-style bottlenecks and sharp, localized price spikes, a qualitatively different outcome from the benign baseline. The inflation asymmetry is the point: the baseline is roughly neutral for prices, but the tail is one-sided to the upside in specific supply chains.

Much of the note is devoted to how to tell which world is unfolding, and it is candid about the limits. **Immigration trackers built from court cases, DHS border data, and ICE arrests lag by ~1.5 months and, crucially, cannot capture voluntary departures in real time — so labor-market data on recent immigrants' participation, unemployment, job-finding, and even survey-response rates are the better early-warning system.** The catch is reflexive: if fear keeps workers from their jobs, it may also keep them from answering the survey, so the very shock most worth detecting could partly hide itself. So far the trackers show no dramatic break through December, with a soft job-finding rate the only wobble — too noisy to read as a signal yet. The practical takeaway is a monitoring checklist, not a call to action: watch the immigrant sub-samples and the unauthorized-heavy sub-industries for the first genuine break from trend.

subject: US Week Ahead: February 10 - February 16
summary:
# CPI Preview: Core +0.34% m/m as Refreshed Seasonal Factors Reshape the January Print

**Theme:** January CPI holds near 3.2% core y/y, with new BLS seasonal factors and updated weights as the wildcard; Powell testimony in focus  
**Markets:** US inflation and US macro data  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jan Hatzius, 9 February 2025  

### Estimates
**January CPI (Wed, Feb 12)**
- **Core CPI +0.34% m/m** (consensus +0.3%, last +0.2%) — leaves the y/y rate unchanged on a rounded basis at 3.2%.
- **Headline CPI +0.36% m/m** (consensus +0.3%, last +0.4%), on higher food (+0.4%) and energy (+0.6%).
- **Core CPI +3.19% y/y** (consensus +3.1%, last +3.2%).
- **Headline CPI +2.96% y/y** (consensus +2.9%, last +2.9%).
- **Core PCE +0.32% m/m** implied for January; forecast to be updated after CPI prints.

**January retail sales (Fri, Feb 14)**
- **Headline −0.2% m/m** (consensus −0.1%, last +0.4%) — higher gasoline prices offset by lower auto sales.
- **Core (control group) +0.2% m/m** (consensus +0.3%, last +0.7%).
- **Ex-auto +0.3%** (consensus +0.3%, last +0.4%); **ex-auto & gas +0.4%** (in line, last +0.3%).

**Other releases**
- **PPI final demand +0.4% m/m** (consensus +0.3%, last +0.2%); ex-food & energy +0.2%; ex-food, energy & trade +0.2%.
- **Initial jobless claims 215k** (consensus 217k, last 219k).
- **Industrial production +0.1%** (consensus +0.3%, last +0.9%); manufacturing −0.1%; capacity utilization 77.6%, unchanged.

### Outlook
- **The refreshed seasonal factors are the key swing risk to the January print.** The BLS will publish recalculated factors reflecting 2024 price movements plus updated weights; annual revisions tend to pull monthly readings toward the year's average, so 2024's elevated Q1 (10bp above average) tends to revise lower and the weak May–July stretch (14bp below) tends to revise higher. Historically about 20% of a month's initial core strength is revised away in its first annual revision.
- **The Fed remains in no hurry to cut, per the analyst's read of Powell.** Powell still views the funds rate as "meaningfully restrictive," but the bar is "not high" for another cut once the new administration's policy is clearer. Bowman leans hawkish (policy may be near neutral, not very restrictive); Williams sees inflation moving toward 2% with the labour market in balance; Bostic puts neutral around 3–3.5%.
- **Activity tracking stays solid.** Q1 GDP tracking is +2.3% (q/q annualized), the January Current Activity Indicator is +2.4% (down from +3.2% in December), and the US MAP economic-surprise index is +0.6.
- The note offers no explicit trade idea.

### Unpacked
The January core forecast is built from a handful of moving parts on the goods side. **Autos and insurance do the heavy lifting: used car prices are seen up 1.5% on firmer auction prices, new cars up 0.5% as incentives fade, and car insurance accelerating 0.75% based on online premium data.** Seasonal distortions plus a postage increase are expected to lift communications to +0.5%, a sharp swing from flat in December and −1.0% in November.

**The offset comes from shelter, where both major components are seen cooling slightly** — OER +0.31% versus +0.33% in December, and primary rent +0.27% versus +0.33%. That modest moderation is what keeps the rounded y/y core rate steady rather than ticking up, even as the monthly figure runs above consensus.

The larger interpretive question this month is methodological rather than fundamental. **Because the annual seasonal-factor revision mechanically drags high prints down and low prints up, the "clean" signal from January's number is harder to read than usual** — a point worth holding in mind before extrapolating any surprise into the Fed path or the PCE read-through.

On the consumer, the headline retail sales dip masks steadier underlying demand: card-spending measures point to middling growth, colder-than-usual weather is a potential drag, and the headline decline is largely a gasoline-versus-autos composition story. The same cold snap cuts two ways in industrial production, boosting utilities output on heating demand while weighing on autos and mining.

**The week's bigger event risk is Powell's two days of semi-annual Congressional testimony, alongside a dense Fed speaking calendar spanning Hammack, Bowman, Williams and Bostic** — the venue where any shift in tone on the timing of the next cut would land, against a backdrop of still-solid growth tracking.

subject: US Monthly Inflation Monitor: January 2025: Ending 2024 On a Softer Note (Rindels)
summary:
# US Inflation Ends 2024 Softening Back Toward 2%, With Tariffs the Main Thing Standing in the Way

**Theme:** Disinflation on track ex-tariffs; expected tariffs delay but don't derail the return to target  
**Markets:** US inflation  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jessica Rindels, 9 February 2025  

### Landscape
- Core PCE rose 0.16% m/m in December, with the y/y rate down 0.03pp to 2.79% — off a 5.65% peak but above June's 2.63% low.
- Core CPI rose 0.23% m/m, y/y down 0.05pp to 3.25%, versus a 6.64% peak.
- Sequential underlying-trend measures ticked up slightly in December but have slowed toward their pre-pandemic average pace.
- Core goods PCE fell 0.24% m/m and −0.1% y/y, softer than the −0.5% y/y average seen in 2018 when core PCE ran near 2%.
- Core services ex-housing PCE rose 0.28% m/m and 3.5% y/y, above the 2.5% pace of 2018.
- New-lease rent growth ran +0.2% annualized in December, a 2.1% y/y pace.
- Energy prices sat at 129% of pre-pandemic levels and industrial metals at 140% in January.

### Drivers
- **Shelter, transportation services and other regulated prices are the residual overshoot** — market rents and input costs spiked then slowed, and consumer prices are now in a lagged catch-up that should gradually fade as the price-cost gap closes.
- **Labor-market cooling is easing services inflation**: the [REDACTED] wage tracker fell to 3.9% y/y in Q4, wage-expectation surveys held at 3.4%, and the jobs-workers gap stayed at 0.8mn (vs 6mn in early 2022, 1.3mn in 2019).
- **Used cars remain a disinflationary force with more to give**: Manheim auction prices are 18% above pre-pandemic (depreciation-adjusted) versus 33% in the PCE, so consumer prices still have room to normalize — though a wider-than-historical gap may persist.
- **Supply chains are still healing but slowly**: ISM production-material lead times fell to 83 days from a 100-day peak, still ~10 days above the pre-pandemic trend.
- **Commodities turn into a modest drag**, expected to shave ~5-10bp off y/y core PCE on average across 2025.
- **The "January effect" should be smaller this year** — moderated price pressures and higher seasonal-factor bars leave less scope for an outsized start-of-year jump.

### Risks
- **Upside — tariffs beyond the baseline**: the analyst notes Trump has proposed additional large tariffs that, if implemented, would give a larger (though still one-time) boost; permanent Mexico/Canada tariffs could push inflation above 3%.
- **Upside — de-anchoring of expectations**: the baseline tariff effect, or even a universal tariff, is judged too small on its own to unanchor expectations, but survey measures could jump if tariff-driven price hikes draw outsized media attention. UMich already shows respondents linking expectations to anticipated tariff policy.
- The skew is explicitly to the upside; no comparable downside scenario is flagged.

### Unpacked
Excluding tariffs, the bottom-up model has core PCE slowing from 2.8% y/y in December 2024 to 2.1% by end-2025 (and 2.0% by end-2026), with core CPI falling from 3.2% to 2.3% (then 2.1%), driven by shrinking shelter and transportation-services contributions. **The clean read is that disinflation is largely on autopilot — the remaining overshoot is lagged catch-up in housing, health care and car insurance, not a live supply-demand imbalance.**

**Tariffs are the wedge between that clean path and the realized number.** The baseline assumes higher tariffs on China imports, EU autos and critical imports, lifting the effective rate 4.7pp and adding ~0.5pp to core PCE — leaving it at 2.6% at end-2025 and core CPI at 2.7%. The effect is framed as moderate and one-time: enough to keep inflation moving sideways near 2.6% through 2025, not enough to prevent the eventual return to target.

On the Fed's likely response, the base case is that policymakers mostly look through tariff-driven price increases. The caveat comes from the last trade war, when Fed staff flagged that looking through would not be appropriate if inflation expectations rose — which is why the expectations channel, rather than the direct price effect, is the variable to watch.

The expectations picture is already mixed and diverging by source. Long-term UMich rose 0.1pp to 3.3% while the NY Fed 5yr measure fell 0.2pp to 2.7%; short-term UMich jumped a full point to 4.3% while the NY Fed 1yr held at 3.0%. Market-implied 2025 CPI rose 0.1pp to 2.6%, with pricing implying a 32% chance of headline CPI topping 3% over the next five years. Business expectations, by contrast, have fallen back to the top of their pre-pandemic range.

subject: Global Rates Trader: Tariff Teaser
summary:
# Tariff Risk Keeps a Flattening Bias in US Rates; [REDACTED] Shifts to Outright Receiving June ECB

**Theme:** Tariff uncertainty has repriced vol more than yields; regulatory hopes now sit in swap spreads; G10 divergence with JGBs the lone bear.  
**Markets:** Developed-market rates (US, Euro area, UK, Japan)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], George Cole, 7 February 2025  

### Definitive impacts
- Front-end inflation markets still price below [REDACTED]'s revised tariff baseline, even while embedding somewhat more underlying inflation stickiness.
- Long-end SOFR-UST swap spreads have widened to levels modestly rich versus fair value, while front-end spreads remain cheap to the spot funding picture.
- Implied rates vol has richened across the curve since tariff news broke on 29 January, with shorter expiries outperforming; the move held even after Canadian and Mexican tariffs were delayed.
- Treasury's refunding left nominal coupons and FRNs unchanged; 5y and 10y TIPS auction sizes rose $1bn each, 30y TIPS unchanged, and "next several quarters" guidance was kept intact.
- Gilts are the best-performing 10y market of the past few weeks; JGBs the sole G10 underperformer, selling off during a global rally.
- BoE cut 25bp and raised its near-term inflation projection to 3.7% while still guiding toward further cuts. ECB confirmed a 1.75-2.25% neutral-rate range and de-emphasised its usefulness for policy.
- 5y JGB real rates around -0.9%, only slightly above the lower end of the BOJ's estimated neutral range.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] favors a flattening bias in US rates given vulnerability to tariff escalation, but tightens stops on its SFRZ5/Z6 flattener (to -4bp) and 2s5s CAD steepener/USD flattener (to +5bp) after the week's moves.
- [REDACTED] reads recent long-end spread widening as the market now pricing potential future regulatory relief, but sees back-end widening as increasingly vulnerable since the underlying capacity and demand picture has not actually shifted and nominations remain open.
- [REDACTED] thinks a higher inflation starting point limits the Fed's ability to front-load cuts into tariffs, capping how much the front-end can out-deliver the built-in vol premium — unlike 2018-19.
- [REDACTED] now expects coupon auction size increases to begin one quarter later (from the February 2026 refunding) and QT to end later — Treasury runoff halting end-June, balance-sheet shrinkage stopping end-September — implying $135bn more runoff and more bill supply.
- On Europe, [REDACTED] sees further downside to Bund yields (up to 25bp from the growth hit, 30-35bp under broad-based tariffs, peak impact at 5y) and shifts from ERM5Z5 flatteners to outright receiving June 2025 ECB OIS (Entry 2.03%, Target 1.90%, Stop 2.10%).
- [REDACTED] reads the BoE's stance as slightly more dovish with a higher inflation hurdle, expects continued decline in Gilt risk premium, and stays in 10s30s Gilt flatteners despite a possible near-term pause.
- [REDACTED] stays paid 10s on a 5s10s30s weighted fly in JGBs, expecting the low level of real rates to sustain 10s30s flattening; stops tightened to -0.38%.

### Backdrop
US rates sit against a Fed that can afford patience: the data support waiting for clearer disinflation and policy clarity before easing further. Swap spreads are shaped by Treasury's issuance mix (bills versus coupons), the debt-limit-driven easy funding conditions, and bank balance-sheet constraints tied to the leverage ratio and G-SIB surcharge — the levers regulatory reform could loosen. In Europe, the ECB is easing toward a confirmed neutral range while the BoE eases into an inflation upswing, and the BOJ is the outlier, hiking as wage and inflation data firm.

### At issue
Friday's US payrolls reinforced the case for Fed patience. Alongside it, the week brought a step-up in tariff uncertainty (with Canadian and Mexican tariffs announced then delayed), Treasury's quarterly refunding, and Fed Governor Bowman's speech flagging possible amendments to the leverage ratio and G-SIB surcharge to preserve dealer balance-sheet capacity. In Europe, [REDACTED]'s baseline now embeds EU auto and critical-industry tariffs, with broad-based 10% EU tariffs at 40% probability; the BoE cut 25bp; and the ECB published its neutral-rate study.

### Unpacked
The week's central puzzle is that a clear jump in tariff uncertainty left a surprisingly light mark on outright yields, even as it repriced volatility durably. **The market broke the usual co-movement between growth and inflation, treating the far end of the curve as a hedge against growth risk while the front end absorbs the near-term complication to the Fed path.** That the vol richening survived the tariff delays — unlike the yield move — is the tell that uncertainty, not a changed central case, is doing the work.

The swap-spread story is separate but ran the same week. Treasury's unchanged guidance calmed fears of faster terming-out of bills, and Bowman's regulatory comments gave the belly and long end a second leg of support. **[REDACTED]'s read is that long-end spreads now embed a bet on future regulatory relief that may take a long time to arrive, leaving that part of the widening exposed if free-float and funding fundamentals reassert themselves.** The nuance matters for positioning: front-end spreads still look cheap to spot funding, so the vulnerability is concentrated in the back end.

Europe is the cleaner directional trade. With the growth hit from tariffs — 50bp in the baseline, up to 1ppt under broad-based tariffs — mapping to 25-35bp of Bund downside centered on the 5y, and an ECB unconstrained by its own neutral estimates, **the setup argues for receiving front-end euro rates outright rather than via a curve spread, which is why [REDACTED] rotates out of the ERM5Z5 flattener into receiving June ECB.** The UK and Japan round out a deliberately divergent G10 book: long Gilt risk premium into a dovish-leaning BoE, and paid JGBs where domestic inflation and BOJ hikes keep pushing yields higher against the global grain.

For the reader, the actionable frame is that near-term US direction is a tariff-headline function best expressed through flatteners and vol, while the more durable convictions sit offshore — lower European front-end yields and higher Japanese belly-and-long yields.

subject: Global FX Trader: From Tariff-fied to Tariff-fried
summary:
# Dollar Floored by Tariffs and Firm Data — G10 and EM Read Through Trade War Two

**Theme:** How tariff escalation is repricing FX, currency by currency  
**Markets:** Global FX (G10 and EM)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Kamakshya Trivedi, 7 February 2025

### Landscape
- The broad Dollar appreciated about 1.2% in response to weekend tariff headlines, even with onshore CNY closed for Lunar New Year and markets pricing only a small probability of lasting tariffs.
- The Yen has been one of the best-performing currencies globally since the January BoJ meeting, with outperformance building over the most recent trading days.
- USD/MXN sits back near the middle of its range of the last few months after a 25% US tariff was delayed at the last minute on Monday.
- USD/CAD has weakened back to mid-December levels following the delay of Canada tariffs.
- Sterling was the best-performing G10 currency early in the week after the safe havens (USD, JPY, CHF).
- Rupee implied and realised vol has moved back toward the 4–5 range as the RBI allows the currency to weaken.

### Drivers
- Tariffs are the dominant force and still building: [REDACTED] economists now expect Trade War Two to be roughly three times the size of the first trade war by effective tariff rate, up from a prior estimate of twice the size, and separate negotiating-leverage threats from genuine tariffs aimed at reshoring and narrowing the trade deficit.
- FX is now clearly responding to tariff risk in both directions — recent event studies map the Dollar outperforming, the Euro underperforming, and the Yen as the marginal safe haven — settling the earlier debate over whether tariffs were already "priced in."
- US economic strength is putting a floor under the Dollar; the solid payrolls report means much of recent Dollar strength reflects shifting macro outcomes rather than tariff expectations alone.
- Yen strength is driven mainly by falling US long-end real yields and higher JGB yields on stronger wage data, now amplified by speculation over a possible US–Japan currency deal and the upcoming GPIF strategy review — though watch next week's US CPI, as a firm print plus easing tariff risk could trigger a tactical reversal.
- Banxico is easing into the volatility, delivering a larger 50bp cut with dovish forward guidance, which will erode MXN carry over time.
- The RBI has shifted its revealed preference toward easing domestic liquidity, running daily repo auctions since mid-January and letting the Rupee weaken.

### Risks
- **Downside to the Dollar view (analyst-flagged):** tariff under-delivery and more balanced global economic performance remain the key risks to the bullish forecasts; repeated walk-backs should also shrink the market's initial reaction to each headline over time.
- **Downside to JPY:** the analyst sees a risk the growth drag from tariffs proves smaller than anticipated (the FCI response has so far been muted), shifting focus to inflation upside and weakening the Yen, particularly versus CHF.
- **Two-sided for GBP:** the analyst flags risks from a BoE over-delivery of cuts and softer UK growth data, plus tactical fiscal-headline sell-offs into the Spring budget, but judges these more of a longer-term headwind than a near-term negative.
- **Asymmetric CAD mispricing:** the analyst assesses tariff risk on Canada near 40%, versus options-implied probabilities of about 25% (Monday's highs) and 10% (1.50), implying markets have unwound too much tariff premium.

### Unpacked
The through-line is that this is a landscape being reshaped by tariff repricing, and the note works currency by currency rather than around a single call. **On the Dollar, the central message is that the past two weeks resolved the "is it priced in" question: the currency does still respond forcefully to tariff news, which makes FX the preferred asset class for cross-asset investors hedging trade risk.** The caveats matter, though — ongoing negotiations, the fentanyl framing, and post-holiday shipping lags mean the higher effective rate takes weeks to bite, and there is a somewhat higher risk of a smaller CNY response this time.

**On the Yen, the recommendation leans against the recent momentum: near-term the currency should keep outperforming on tariff escalation while markets price a growth hit and flatten the rates curve, but the setup favors a tactical reversal if CPI is firm and tariff risk eases.** Skepticism runs through the two bullish narratives — a US–Japan currency deal is complicated by the administration's desire for easier financial conditions and the possibility Japan would have to sell Treasuries, and the GPIF question turns on whether reallocation means foreign bond sales or simply more FX hedging.

**On Mexico, a range-bound USD/MXN is the base case, which makes MXN longs attractive for carry, though large Banxico cuts will erode that carry over time.** With tariffs hard to price ahead of time and a premium likely to persist through the USMCA review, the note pairs this with a tariff-neutral idea: vol-adjusted CAD/MXN shorts, on the view that CAD's tariff premium has unwound too far.

**That CAD view is the note's clearest expression of mispricing — long USD/CAD is favored as a hedge because options markets are underpricing a tariff risk the economists put near 40%, with the political transition making Canada's path riskier than Mexico's.** Sterling remains a bullish-on-crosses call, but for a shifted reason: last year's thesis rested on GBP benefiting from rallying equities and falling yields together, and with both themes more at risk, the support now comes from relative resilience to tariff escalation (relevant given likely EU tariffs), a risk-friendly backdrop, and more two-sided UK growth risks than in the Euro area.

**Finally, India illustrates the cost of a policy transition: the attempt to move the Rupee from a peg to a "stable port" has been more destabilizing than expected, and bonds now look better than the currency near-term.** Q4 interventions coincided with a domestic cyclical soft patch, tightening liquidity at an untimely moment; policymakers have since pivoted to easing, and the note has initiated a recommendation to receive INR 2Y NDOIS ahead of a deeper easing cycle. The high yield-to-vol appeal of Indian government bonds explains why the RBI cut only cautiously, and the Rupee stays at risk until the cyclical picture improves.

subject: USA: Payroll Growth Somewhat Below Expectations but Prior Months Revised Up; Unemployment Rate Declines to 4.0%; UMichigan Inflation Expectations Jump
summary:
# US Labor Market Holds Firm on Upward Revisions as UMichigan Inflation Expectations Spike

**Theme:** January jobs data plus annual benchmark revisions; consumer inflation expectations jump on tariff fears  
**Markets:** US labor market and inflation  
**Source:** [REDACTED] (Jan Hatzius), 7 February 2025  

### Definitive impacts
- Nonfarm payrolls rose 143k in January, below the 175k median forecast, but November and December were revised up by 49k and 51k, lifting the three-month average to 237k.
- The unemployment rate fell 0.1pp to 4.0%; the participation rate held at 62.6%.
- Average hourly earnings rose 0.48% MoM (4.1% YoY), above the 0.3% expected, alongside a 0.1-hour drop in average weekly hours to 34.1 — the lowest since March 2020.
- Establishment-survey benchmark revisions subtracted 610k from the December 2024 payroll level, driven by a 589k downward revision through March 2024 from QCEW source data; of that, only 256k is attributable to the birth-death model.
- Household-survey revisions raised the population level by 2.9mn, the labor force by 2.1mn, and household employment by 2.0mn, incorporating updated Census estimates that capture recent immigration.
- The re-benchmarking added 11bp to the participation rate and 1bp to the unemployment rate through a composition effect, and narrowed the household-payroll employment gap to 1.5mn from 3.7mn.
- UMichigan consumer sentiment (preliminary) fell 3.3pt to 67.8, below expectations, with both current-conditions and expectations components down.
- One-year inflation expectations jumped 1.0pp to 4.3%, the highest since November 2023; the 5–10-year measure rose 0.1pp to 3.3%, which would be the highest since June 2008 if it holds.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] puts the underlying pace of job growth at 239k and underlying wage growth at 4.3%, after adjusting for what it sees as the official statistics' undercounting of immigration.
- [REDACTED] argues much of the establishment revision was misleading because the QCEW excludes most unauthorized immigrants outside the unemployment-insurance system; it had estimated the "true" downward revision closer to 300k (25k/month), a view it says the BLS breakdown supports.
- [REDACTED] treats the household-survey revisions as validating its prior calls that population controls had understated the 2022–2024 immigration surge, noting the outcomes matched its estimates.
- UMichigan attributes the sentiment decline in part to consumers' fear that high inflation will return and a perception that it may be too late to avoid the impact of tariff policy.

### At issue
The January 2025 US employment report, released 7 February, carried three developments at once. First, the monthly data: soft headline payrolls offset by upward prior revisions, a lower unemployment rate, and firm wages held down partly by weather-affected hours. Second, the annual benchmark revisions to both the establishment survey (down 610k) and the household survey (population and employment levels revised sharply up to reflect immigration). Third, the same day's preliminary February UMichigan survey, in which sentiment dropped and inflation expectations rose sharply, with the survey period ending 4 February.

### Unpacked
The report matters less for its headline than for what the annual revisions did to the reading of the labor market. **The two benchmark revisions pull in opposite directions but resolve a long-standing measurement puzzle: payroll employment was marked down while household employment was marked up, and together they cut the gap between the two surveys from 3.7mn to 1.5mn.** [REDACTED] frames both moves as confirmation of a thesis it had argued repeatedly — that official statistics were mismeasuring the immigration surge, overcounting establishment-survey jobs the QCEW never captured and undercounting the household-survey population.

Beneath the surface the labor data read firmer than the 143k print suggests. The household survey was strong, the job-finding rate recovered to its September level, and the payrolls diffusion index stayed near its 2019 norm. The wage beat is complicated by the drop in hours, which the note ties to bad weather rather than genuine acceleration.

**The sharper signal is the jump in near-term inflation expectations, which UMichigan links explicitly to tariff anxiety.** A 1.0pp leap in one-year expectations to 4.3% and a 5–10-year reading that would be a 17-year high sit awkwardly against an otherwise solid labor backdrop, and they arrive while consumers are already souring on current conditions. For the reader, the combination — resilient employment, contained but revised data, and rising inflation expectations driven by policy fears — is the tension worth carrying forward.

subject: [REDACTED] FX Morning Notes: More Vol from Payrolls
summary:
# January Payrolls: A High-Vol Wildcard, With [REDACTED] Above Consensus at 190k

**Theme:** January payrolls are historically among the highest-vol US data releases; annual revisions and weather/wildfire distortions complicate the signal  
**Markets:** US labour market, USD FX  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Stuart Jenkins, 7 February 2025  

### Estimates
- **190k** headline nonfarm payrolls for January, above consensus of **175k**.
- **4.1%** unemployment rate, essentially flat versus **4.09%** currently.
- **~−20k** drag on the headline from the LA wildfires and colder-than-usual January weather combined.
- **+4bp** modest net upward impact on the unemployment rate from updated population controls, even as those revisions lift population, labor force, and household-survey employment materially.
- Recent-history reference point: January prints have averaged a **~+280k** upside surprise to Bloomberg consensus over the past three years.

### Outlook
- Modest FX impact expected on the modal forecast, per the analysts, since a 190k print sits only slightly above consensus.
- Skew toward Dollar strength on the release: 1-day USD TWI moves have historically been larger for January payrolls than for any other reference month, and have on average shown clear USD appreciation.
- That directional bias is caveated by evolving seasonal factors — as the BLS seasonal adjustment "learns" to expect fewer layoffs and higher net job growth, the recent pattern of large upside surprises should fade over time.
- The signal from this print may be unusually noisy, given annual revisions to both the establishment and household surveys land alongside it, and the analysts flag building concerns about a more challenging labour-market environment in coming months.

### Unpacked
**January is singled out because it stacks several sources of uncertainty on top of each other:** large and hard-to-pin seasonality, weather effects, and the annual revisions to both the establishment and household surveys. That combination has made it one of the most unpredictable releases of the year, and this January adds the LA wildfires as a further distortion — worth roughly 20k off the headline together with the cold weather.

The recent track record frames why markets are wary. **Over the past three years January prints have surprised consensus to the upside by around 280k on average**, driven in part by a slower pace of layoffs than the BLS seasonal factor was trained to expect. The note's own economists expect that effect to erode as the seasonal factor adapts to lower layoffs and higher net job growth, so the historical upside bias is not something to lean on mechanically.

On the population controls, the update is expected to revise population, labor force, and household-survey employment sharply higher, yet net out to only a +4bp move in the unemployment rate — a reminder that large-looking revisions need not shift the headline signal much.

**For FX, the setup is a modal call with a fat tail:** the central forecast implies little more than a modest move, but January payrolls have historically produced the largest 1-day USD TWI moves of any reference month, skewed toward Dollar strength. Against a backdrop where FX has been whipsawing on tariff headlines, the release is a candidate for another burst of volatility. Watch the interaction between the raw print, the revisions, and the seasonal-factor caveat — together they could muddy the immediate read and feed concerns about a softer labour market ahead.

subject: USA: Productivity Growth in Line With Expectations; Initial Claims Slightly Higher Than Expected
summary:
# US: Q4 productivity in line, jobless claims a bit above expectations

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US productivity data, labor costs, and jobless claims

### Context
Comment on the preliminary release of Q4 productivity (quarterly annualized) and unit labor costs, together with weekly jobless claims data for the week ended 1 February.

- **Unit labor costs below expectations, but wage pressure still visible.** Unit labor costs — compensation divided by output — rose 3.0% in Q4, a bit below [REDACTED] (+3.4%) and consensus (+3.4%); the year-on-year rate rose 0.5pp, to +2.7%. subject: US Daily: January Payrolls Preview (Walker/Rindels)
summary:
# January Payrolls: [REDACTED] Sees +190k, Above Consensus — Wildfires and Cold Weather Trim the Print

**Theme:** Solid underlying job creation partly masked by LA wildfires and cold weather; landmark benchmark and population-control revisions land alongside  
**Markets:** US labour market  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Ronnie Walker, 6 February 2025  

### Estimates
- **+190k** nonfarm payrolls for January, above consensus of +170k and the three-month average of +170k.
- **+160k** private payrolls, vs consensus +140k.
- **4.1%** unemployment rate, unchanged and in line with consensus.
- **62.5%** labour force participation, up 0.1pp.
- **+0.3% m/m** average hourly earnings, which would lower the y/y rate to 3.7%.
- **−20k each** assumed drag from the LA wildfires and from colder-than-usual weather.
- **−818k** preliminary benchmark revision to cumulative payroll growth over April 2023–March 2024 (BLS estimate), of which [REDACTED] sees 300–500k as an inappropriate exclusion of unauthorised immigrants.
- Updated population controls: **+3.5mn** to the population level, **+2.5mn** to the labour force, **+2.3mn** to household employment — the largest upward revisions on record — with modest upward pressure on participation (+0.11pp) and unemployment (+0.04pp) via composition.

### Outlook
- Risks look two-sided but the note leans to a firm underlying pace: alternative "big data" measures averaged +216k and layoffs sit at historically low levels, arguing for strength, while wildfires, cold weather, and sideways job-openings measures argue the other way.
- [REDACTED] reads the headline benchmark revision as partly misleading — the 818k markdown likely wrongly drops 300–500k unauthorised immigrants captured in payrolls but absent from state UI/QCEW records; the remainder reflects appropriate birth-death model corrections (an estimated ~25k/month overstatement in 2023).
- The population-control update is framed as a one-off catch-up to the immigration surge, not a signal of labour-market deterioration — the small rise in the unemployment rate is compositional.

### Unpacked
**The estimate rests on evidence that hiring stayed healthy even as one-off shocks clipped the January count.** Alternative employment gauges pointed to an average +216k, though ADP and the firm's own layoff tracker are historically less sensitive to weather and disasters, so those readings may modestly overstate the month. Low end-of-year layoffs are the other pillar: because January seasonal factors expect a large start-of-year drop, unusually few layoffs translate into strong seasonally-adjusted gains — a boost expected again this month, if a smaller one, since the fully-revised seasonal factors should increasingly anticipate the softer layoff pattern.

**Two identifiable shocks pull the other way and account for the assumed 40k combined drag.** Roughly 0.5% of California's population, about 90k payroll jobs, fell under evacuation orders, but with the fires starting 7 January and most workers paid biweekly or longer, many still worked at some point in the reference week and count as employed — hence a contained 20k hit. The coldest January in recent history adds another 20k drag, concentrated in construction, leisure and hospitality, and other services. Alongside, job-availability signals have gone sideways: JOLTS openings fell 0.6mn to 7.6mn in December, and the Conference Board labour differential dropped 6.0pt to +16.2, still well below its 2019 average of +33.2. Employer survey components are treated as near-neutral, given their weak post-pandemic signal.

**The bigger story tomorrow is the twin set of revisions, which [REDACTED] argues largely reflect measurement rather than a true change in the labour market.** On the establishment side, the −818k benchmark is discounted because 300–500k unauthorised immigrants were captured in initial payrolls but excluded from the QCEW; the rest is read as a legitimate birth-death correction. On the household side, December's revision to Census immigration methods raised net immigration for July 2021–July 2024 by 3.5mn, close to [REDACTED]'s own estimates, and feeds record upward revisions to population, labour force, and employment. The resulting nudge higher in participation and unemployment is compositional — the point to hold onto when the revised levels print.

subject: Global Rates Notes: 1Q25 Treasury Refunding Recap
summary:
# Treasury Refunding: Why Standing Pat on Guidance Points to a Higher-for-Longer Bill Share

**Source:** [REDACTED] — William Marshall  
**Focus:** US Treasury issuance and quarterly refunding  
**General comment:** Interpretive read of the February refunding; broadly aligned with the market's dovish-on-long-end-supply reaction but more balanced, and pushes back its own coupon-increase call.

## Context
The piece reacts to Treasury's February (1Q25) quarterly refunding decision, which kept nominal coupon auction sizes unchanged and left its forward guidance intact. It enters the debate over when Treasury will begin raising coupon auction sizes and how heavily it will lean on bills in the meantime.

## The case
- **The issuance decisions were largely expected, but retaining the guidance was the real surprise.** Treasury held nominal coupon and FRN sizes flat, raising only 10y TIPS reopening and 5y TIPS new-issue sizes by $1bn each. The notable outcome was the unchanged language that it "anticipates maintaining nominal coupon and FRN auction sizes for at least the next several quarters." A meaningful risk had been seen that this would be watered down given uncertainty over future borrowing needs — and a November start to coupon increases would have stretched "at least the next several quarters" to its limit. The choice to leave 30y TIPS unchanged for a fourth straight year fits the same reluctance to add long-end supply, leaving 30y at roughly 7.5% of gross TIPS supply versus about 10% in FY2021.

- **Two readings explain why the guidance survived, and they are not mutually exclusive.** One is that Treasury's deficit assumption implies lower funding needs, buying patience on the timing and size of eventual coupon increases. The other is that Treasury is simply comfortable letting the bill share run slightly higher for longer — under the piece's deficit profile, delaying coupon increases to February would lift the bill share to around 22% from a mid-year trough near 20%. The market clearly favored the bill-leaning read: the nominal curve flattened and swap spread curve steepened, consistent with pricing in less long-end supply.

- **The market's read has merit but is worth resisting as the sole explanation.** The reset in term premia and curve steepening since mid-last year reduce the advantage of terming out — on both spot and expected interest-expense grounds — which argues for being deliberate about issuance. But caution is warranted on jumping fully to the bills interpretation, because Treasury's own borrowing estimates seem to imply a smaller FY25 deficit than the firm's economists project. The first-quarter FY25 deficit of $711bn already runs above the prior two years' pace (roughly $510bn at the same point in FY2024). April tax receipts — seasonally high and unusually variable — are flagged as the key near-term test; a weak print could shift Treasury's "projected borrowing needs" assessment.

- **The fiscal package is the larger medium-term swing factor, and Treasury's baseline may not reflect it.** Full extension of the expiring 2017 tax cuts plus other measures is expected, leaving the primary deficit roughly steady as a share of GDP. It is unclear whether Treasury's "current projected borrowing needs" already embed such a deal; assumptions closer to current law (as CBO uses) would be vulnerable to reassessment if the eventual package lands near this baseline.

## Implications
- The baseline for the first coupon auction size increase is pushed from November 2025 to February 2026, reflecting greater tolerance for a higher bill share — though timing confidence is low given uncertainty over funding needs and strategy.
- Under this later start, the bill share stays around 21.5% through 2026 before declining to 20% by mid-2027.
- April tax receipts and the shape of the fiscal deal are the two triggers that could force Treasury — and this view — to be reassessed.

subject: Top of Mind: High bond yields: here to stay?
summary:
# 10-year Treasury yields after the reset: three drivers, three destinations

**Theme:** Why G10 bond yields rose despite rate cuts, and whether they stay high  
**Markets:** US rates (G10 government bonds)  
**Source:** [REDACTED] (Allison Nathan), 5 February 2025  

### Definitive impacts
- G10 bond yields have reset higher over recent months, led by the US, even as central banks began long-awaited easing cycles — the reversal of the usual direction is the note's starting fact.
- The reset traces to three identifiable drivers: a reassessment of the inflation/Fed outlook, a higher neutral rate, and a higher term premium.
- The 10y Treasury has traded within a 3.5–5% range, and the current level sits toward the upper part of that band.

### Opinative impacts
- Peters (PGIM) sees 10y yields supported near the top of the 3.5–5% range, arguing persistently above-target inflation keeps them elevated.
- Marshall ([REDACTED]) expects yields to end the year around or modestly below current levels, resting on the further disinflation Mericle ([REDACTED]) forecasts.
- Caballero (MIT) argues 10y rates could eventually settle well below current levels, on the view that the future neutral rate may prove lower than many assume.
- [REDACTED] judges the near-term risks skewed toward higher rates, and on that basis examines what a renewed yield surge would mean for risky assets and portfolios.

### At issue
The note collects competing explanations for why long-end G10 yields, led by US Treasuries, have risen since central banks started cutting — behavior it calls unusual. It weighs how much of the move reflects each of the three drivers, and asks whether tariff and broader economic developments will keep yields elevated. Contributors span a range of views on both the causes and where 10y rates head from here.

### Unpacked
The puzzle is the direction: policy rates are falling, yet the long end has climbed. **The disagreement is less about whether the reset happened than about which of the three drivers is doing the work — and that choice dictates where each contributor thinks yields land.** If it is above-target inflation, elevated yields persist; if it is disinflation still in train, they drift back; if it is a mis-estimated neutral rate, the long-run anchor is lower than the market currently prices.

The three horizons stack rather than conflict. Peters and Marshall differ over the coming year — sticky inflation versus continued disinflation — while Caballero speaks to a longer settling point below today's levels. **The practical takeaway is the skew: even where contributors expect yields to ease, [REDACTED] frames the near-term risk as tilted upward, which is why the note turns to portfolio implications of another surge rather than to a directional rates call.**

No explicit trade idea is offered. The note is a survey of views on drivers and destinations, with the actionable content being the risk framing for risky assets should yields rise again.

subject: Global PMI Monitor: US Manufacturing Hiring Bounces Back (Dong)
summary:
# US Manufacturing Turns the Corner as Services Momentum Cools

**Theme:** Manufacturing firming and hiring rebounding, offset by softer services  
**Markets:** Global PMIs (manufacturing, services, prices, employment)  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jan Hatzius, 5 February 2025  

### Landscape
- Global composite PMI at 51.8, down -0.8pt in January, as a manufacturing gain (+0.5pt to 50.1) was outweighed by a services drop (-1.6pt to 52.2).
- US manufacturing PMI (avg. ISM/S&P Global) rose +1.7pt to 51.0, back above the 50 expansion line.
- US manufacturing employment component jumped +3.0pt to 51.1, moving into positive territory, while China's kept contracting (-1.5pt to 47.1).
- Euro area manufacturing PMI rose +1.5pt to 46.6, still in contraction; China's fell -0.7pt to 49.6 (avg. Caixin/NBS).
- Services PMI fell across all three majors — US -2.5pt to 52.9, China -1.5pt to 50.6, Euro area -0.3pt to 51.3.
- Composite PMI rose in the Euro area (+0.6pt to 50.2) but fell in North America (US -1.7pt to 52.7, Canada -0.6pt to 51.6).

### Drivers
- Manufacturing is firming globally: the forward-looking orders-to-inventories ratio ticked up +0.01 to 1.02, and the sector's PMI crossed back above 50.
- The rebound is US-led, most visibly in factory hiring; China remains the drag, with both its manufacturing activity and employment components still contracting.
- Services momentum is fading from a high base: the future-activity component slipped -0.7pt to 62.4, though services hiring rose +1.0pt to 51.6 even as manufacturing employment fell -0.9pt to 48.5.
- Price pressures are edging up on both sides: global manufacturing input prices +0.1pt to 54.5 (output +0.2pt to 51.5) and services input prices +1.0pt to 57.7 (output +0.8pt to 53.5), keeping services costs the firmer of the two.
- Supply chains loosened marginally, with manufacturing suppliers' delivery times lengthening slightly (+0.3pt to 49.6).

### Unpacked
**The month's signal is a rotation within the cycle rather than a broad shift in level: manufacturing is healing while services come off the boil.** The global composite eased, but the composition matters more than the headline — the manufacturing component pushed to the 50 line as services gave back some of their lead. The divergence is clearest in the United States, where the factory PMI moved into expansion and the manufacturing employment component posted its standout move, a +3.0pt jump to 51.1.

**The regional split runs Europe up, North America down.** The Euro area composite crossed back above 50 and its manufacturing reading improved, even if it remains in contraction at 46.6. The US and Canadian composites both fell, with the US decline driven by its services side rather than manufacturing. On a three-month basis the composite has risen in most major economies but fallen in China, the UK, and the US, framing the North American softening as recent rather than entrenched.

**China stays the persistent laggard.** Both its manufacturing and services PMIs fell in January, and its manufacturing employment component continued to contract, a counterpoint to the US hiring rebound that anchors the note's title.

**On prices, the pressure sits with services.** Input and output price components rose across both manufacturing and services, but services input prices are the firmest at 57.7, a reminder that the cost impulse is now more services- than goods-led. Supplier delivery times lengthened at the margin globally; at the country level they worsened in Colombia and Brazil but eased in India, and on a three-month view have improved in China, India, and Switzerland.

The note carries no explicit trade idea and flags no scenario risks — it is a monthly scoreboard, supported by the economics team's country-level PMI write-ups for the US, China, India, Mexico, Brazil, Europe, and CEE.

subject: USA: ISM Services Below Expectations; S&P Global Services PMI Revised Up

# US Services: Softer ISM, Firmer S&P Global — a Mixed Read on Early-2025 Momentum

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US services activity (January 2025 ISM and S&P Global PMIs)  
**General comment:** Neutral data read; softer ISM headline but a mixed, not decisively weak, picture.

### Context
Reaction to the January 2025 services surveys: the ISM services index came in below expectations while the final S&P Global services PMI was revised up from its preliminary reading, leaving the two gauges pointing in slightly different directions.

Business activity (-3.5pt to 54.5) and new orders (-3.1pt to 51.3) drove the decline, but employment rose (+1.0pt to 52.3) and new export orders gained (+1.9pt to 52.0). Slower supplier deliveries (+0.5pt to 53.0) also nudged the composite up.
