Confidence in timing is explicitly low: even a disinflation-plus-healthy-labor baseline would not make cutting an obvious choice, and tariffs complicate the Fed's read. **Despite that uncertainty, market pricing of Fed paths is still seen as too hawkish, even after the recent move lower in yields.** The rest of G10 diverges around this — ECB, BoE, BoC and Riksbank easing at their own pace, the BoJ tightening — with the BoC path most sensitive to whether Trump follows through on Canada tariffs.

On Trump, the through-line is that markets have under-priced tariff risk in two places at once. **FX has unwound too much of the tariff premium, so implementation should ultimately support a stronger Dollar, while equities embed little retaliatory- or universal-tariff risk and are exposed if those materialize.** The deferred-resignation program is a minor fiscal item — up to $25bn, slightly under 0.1% of GDP.

Also on the radar is Germany's fiscal position: a funding gap of up to €23bn a year (0.5% of GDP) over 2025-2028, with the next government expected to open space via debt-brake reform and a defense fund. **The near-term growth lift is modest, but a more material spending increase could raise medium-term growth more substantially.**

subject: US Daily: January [REDACTED]: Nearly Frozen (Rindels)
summary:
# January [REDACTED]: Activity Flatlines Near the Top of Its Range as Firms Fixate on Policy

**Theme:** A near-frozen activity read, with immigration and federal policy as the emerging swing factors  
**Markets:** US business activity and inflation  
**Source:** [REDACTED] (Jessica Rindels), 30 January 2025

### Landscape
- The headline [REDACTED] rose just 0.4pt to 60.2 in January, a near-flat reading that stays well above the 50 line.
- New orders jumped +8.6pt to 67.7, while shipments slipped -1.0pt to 61.1 and exports fell -6.2pt to 43.8 (into contraction).
- Inventories dropped -13.3pt to 50.0, widening the orders-less-inventories gap by +17.7pt to +21.9 — a forward-positive signal for activity.
- The employment component rose +3.0pt to 51.0; the wages component fell -4.0pt to 61.8.
- Materials prices fell -8.3pt to 62.5 while output prices rose +3.8pt to 61.0.
- [REDACTED]'s manufacturing survey tracker rose +3.8pt to 53.4 (led by a 55pt jump in the Philadelphia Fed index), while the nonmanufacturing tracker fell -1.5pt to 54.2.
- Employment components of both external trackers stayed in contraction: manufacturing +1.1pt to 49.9, services -0.4pt to 49.6.

### Drivers
- New orders are the month's engine, more than offsetting softer shipments and a drop into contraction on exports; the widening orders-less-inventories gap points to activity holding up near term.
- Price pressure on inputs is easing (materials prices down) even as firms nudge output prices higher — Philadelphia Fed firms broadly expect cost disinflation across nearly all categories in 2025 versus 2024.
- Hiring is stabilizing slightly below 2019 norms: 42% of manufacturers and 49% of services firms report currently hiring, roughly flat versus July 2024, with hiring impediments becoming less widespread.
- Wage-cost expectations are moderating unevenly — manufacturers see only a modest slowdown in wage growth (-0.1pp to +2.7%), services a sharper one (-0.7pp to +2.4%) — but softer immigration is a countervailing force pushing the other way (see Risks).

### Risks
- Upside risk to wage costs (analyst view): half of surveyed [REDACTED] analysts expect weaker immigration or increased deportations to hit companies in their sector or suppliers, and all but one of that group expect the effect to push wage costs higher.
- Policy risk cuts both ways and dominates firm outlooks (Dallas Fed): manufacturers flag the business regulatory environment (56%) and international trade (48%) as most important, while services firms cite regulation (48%), monetary policy (53%), and corporate taxes as key — leaving the outlook heavily exposed to federal policy shifts.

### Unpacked
The [REDACTED]'s message this month is stasis at a firm level: **a 0.4pt move to 60.2 leaves the index essentially where it was, with a mixed-to-stronger composition rather than a clear directional turn.** Beneath the flat headline, the internals lean constructive — new orders surged and inventories fell sharply, so the orders-less-inventories gap widened to +21.9, the kind of configuration that usually supports activity in the following months. The offsetting weakness sits in shipments and especially exports, which slid into contractionary territory.

On prices, the picture is one of easing inputs meeting still-positive pass-through. **Materials prices fell while output prices rose, and Philadelphia Fed firms across both manufacturing and services expect cost disinflation in 2025 relative to 2024 in nearly every category** — the lone exception a slight uptick in expected health-benefits inflation among services firms. Manufacturers expect health-benefits cost growth to fall most; services firms expect raw-materials inflation to decline most. When setting prices, both groups put strength of demand first, followed by protecting margins and covering labor costs, and rated supply-chain problems and the cost of capital as less important.

The labor read is one of settling rather than tightening. **Dallas Fed firms report hiring drifting slightly below 2019 rates even as impediments to hiring become less widespread.** The binding constraints are skills and applicant availability — lack of technical skills (53%) and lack of applicants (35%) for manufacturers, applicant availability (47%) for services — with a meaningful minority (40% of manufacturers, 35% of services) citing applicants seeking more pay than offered. Those shares are at or slightly below July 2024 levels. Expected wage growth moderates modestly for manufacturers (+2.7%) and more clearly for services (+2.4%).

Two policy threads frame the outlook. **The special [REDACTED] questions surface immigration as a fresh cost risk: half of surveyed analysts expect softer flows or more deportations to touch their sector or suppliers, and nearly all of those see it lifting wage costs** — a force that runs counter to the broader wage-moderation trend. Separately, the Dallas Fed's special questions show firms rank federal policy on regulation, trade, and corporate taxes — plus monetary policy for services — as the factors mattering most to their operations and outlook, underscoring how much of the current read hangs on decisions yet to be made rather than on demand conditions today.

The report notes no explicit trade idea. Methodologically, the headline [REDACTED] weights new orders 30%, sales/shipments 25%, employment 20%, materials prices 15%, and inventories 10%, mirroring the ISM's pre-2008 practice; a reading of 50 is judged more consistent with trend growth than with no growth. Responses were collected January 26–29.

subject: Global Markets Analyst: The Deal with Currencies: Cross-Border M&A and FX Markets (Jenkins/Trivedi)
summary:
# The FX Footprint of Cross-Border M&A: Small, Brief, and Skewed Toward the Target Currency

**Theme:** Estimating how large cross-border deals move the acquirer/target FX cross, and whether the reverse holds  
**Markets:** Global; mainly G10 currency pairs vs USD, with EM read-across  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Stuart Jenkins, 30 January 2025

### Key findings
- Deal size lifts the target currency against the acquirer's — a positive, statistically significant beta of roughly 2.8bp of excess return per $1bn in Dollar pairs against EUR, GBP, JPY, CNY and CAD — answering whether announcements leave an FX imprint.
- The effect is short-lived: the beta peaks around 5–7 days after announcement and fades to zero within two to three weeks.
- Impact is negligible for small deals (<$1bn) in large, liquid pairs, where daily OTC volumes above $10bn absorb the flow; only larger deals produce a visible move (e.g. ~1pp in EUR/USD one week out).
- Market positioning into the announcement shows no significant effect on the size of the response, so it matters less than prevailing liquidity.
- No reliable reverse causality: currency moves do not robustly drive M&A flows once relative equity performance is controlled for — equity valuations dominate, consistent with prior literature.
- Net M&A flows are persistent by currency (USD and most G10 trend in one direction; EUR is more balanced), so a single month's change is best read against the structural trend rather than in isolation.
- Structural driver identified: higher national saving rates are associated with larger net M&A outflows, especially across EM, plausibly linked to demographics.
- A naïve average-impact approach gives a misleading negative long-horizon signal — an artifact of deals flowing developed-to-EM while EM currencies trend weaker on higher inflation.

### Method & verdict
[Reasonable] The study uses Bloomberg data on cash-settled cross-border deals of $100mn or more from January 2010 to November 2024, measuring excess FX returns versus forwards at announcement and regressing them on deal size, after excluding pegged currencies and same-currency pairs. It cross-checks the M&A beta against MoF USD/JPY intervention data, where transaction size and timing are observable, as a plausibility anchor. The design is sound and the currency-controlled beta is more credible than the raw average, but the authors are candid about limits: financing choice (spot FX vs debt/equity issuance) and the actual timing of the FX transaction are unobservable, so flow and FDI effects cannot be cleanly separated, and beta magnitudes across pairs are sensitive to the estimation window and to deal count per pair.

### Unpacked
The work is motivated by a 2025 dealmaking backdrop the firm's equity strategists expect to strengthen — a projected 25% Y/Y rise in US deals above $100mn under a second Trump administration — and by the premise that cross-border M&A, roughly a third of total M&A volume, matters for FX both as durable FDI and as fast, directional flow. **The question is whether that flow is large enough to see, and the answer is: only sometimes.**

The central result is a modest but genuine directional beta once the analysis controls for which currencies are being measured. **The target currency appreciates against the acquirer's at about 2.8bp per $1bn, peaking within a week and gone within three.** The intervention cross-check is instructive: MoF USD/JPY interventions move the pair about 4.2bp per $1bn — more than twice the M&A beta — which the note attributes to interventions coinciding with overstretched positioning, carrying a forward-looking policy signal, and having a known transaction date, none of which cleanly apply to deals whose FX leg may occur before, after, or never as a single spot trade.

Alongside the announcement effect sits a slower-moving story. **Net M&A flows persist by currency, so the informative signal is a shift relative to a country's own norm, not the monthly number itself** — the note flags that US inflows ran unusually light in 2024, making a 2025 normalization a marginal Dollar positive, while stronger-than-average flows into Canada and Japan leave those exposed to reversal. On what drives the flows, exchange rates largely drop out once equity performance is included, while saving rates (and behind them, demographics) emerge as a structural explanator, particularly in EM.

For the reader, the practical takeaways are asymmetric by size and liquidity. **Corporates doing sub-$1bn deals in liquid pairs can essentially ignore the FX footprint; those doing larger deals should hedge, use debt/equity financing in the target currency, or wait two weeks and spread purchases to limit impact.** Investors gain most in smaller, less liquid pairs, where tracking large announcements helps explain flow and price action, and in reading structural flow shifts for the majors. The net directional call is deliberately muted: a lighter regulatory backdrop could lift M&A spending, but elevated trade uncertainty under Trump's tariff agenda is a countervailing drag on cross-border FDI, so the two roughly offset for the currencies — chiefly EMs — that typically see net inflows.

subject: USA: Q4 GDP Rises 2.3% on Strong Consumption and Despite Inventory Drag; Initial Claims Below Expectations
summary:
# US Q4 GDP: Headline Misses but Composition Is Stronger, with Consumption Doing the Heavy Lifting

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US Q4 GDP, inflation, and jobless claims  
**General comment:** Constructive read of a soft headline; sees underlying demand as healthier than the top-line number suggests

### Context
A same-day reaction to the advance Q4 2024 US GDP release (plus the latest jobless claims), which came in below consensus on the headline but with a very different internal composition than the number alone implies.

### The case
- **The 2.3% headline understates underlying demand because the miss is concentrated in volatile line items, not final demand.** GDP printed 2.3% annualized — below the 2.6% consensus though above [REDACTED]'s own 1.8% forecast. The weakness came largely from inventories, which subtracted 0.9pp this quarter. Consumption, the core of final demand, grew 4.2% — a full 1pp above consensus — making the composition stronger than the headline suggests.
- **The remaining components were mixed but net supportive.** Business fixed investment fell 2.2%, dragged by a 7.8% drop in equipment (lower transportation and information-processing equipment). Offsetting this, housing investment rose 5.3% and government spending rose 2.5% (federal +3.2%, state and local +2.0%) — both above expectations.
- **The inflation read was benign and left the forecast unchanged.** Core PCE prices rose 2.50% annualized, in line with expectations; the GDP price index rose 2.2%, slightly below expectations. On the back of the report, January sequential core and headline PCE estimates were held at 0.16% and 0.26% (2.80% and 2.56% year-over-year).
- **The labor market signal stayed firm despite a known distortion.** Initial claims fell 16k to 207k, against expectations for a small rise, even with an ongoing lift from the Southern California wildfires. Continuing claims dropped 42k to 1,858k, mostly retracing the prior week's increase.

### Implications
- The composition matters more than the headline: with consumption strong and the shortfall in inventories, the piece reads the quarter as healthier than 2.3% implies.
- No change to the near-term inflation path — the report does not shift the January PCE trajectory.
- Q1 GDP tracking will be launched after the next day's personal income and spending details.

subject: [REDACTED] FX Morning Notes: Business as Usual for the ECB
summary:
# ECB on Autopilot: Fourth Straight Cut Expected as Euro Area Growth Disappoints Again

**Theme:** A well-telegraphed ECB cut against widening US–Euro area growth divergence  
**Markets:** Euro area / US macro and FX  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Stuart Jenkins, 30 January 2025  

### Landscape
- Euro area Q4 flash GDP came in flat on the quarter, missing both consensus and ECB expectations.
- Spanish January flash headline HICP beat consensus by a tenth, with Belgium also on the firmer side.
- [REDACTED] economists sit above consensus on both the remaining national inflation prints and Monday's area-wide flash, aided by a 15bp sequential "January effect" on price resets.
- US Q4 GDP is tracked at 1.8% q/q annualized by [REDACTED], eight-tenths below the Bloomberg consensus — though that consensus is likely stale, pre-dating yesterday's trade and inventory data.
- The US–Euro area growth and labour-market surprise gap ([REDACTED] MAP indices) has narrowed over the past two months as Euro area activity stabilized at low levels.

### Drivers
- ECB easing on a "gradual regular path": a fourth consecutive 25bp cut is expected and well flagged, with Lagarde likely to repeat that "the direction is very clear" — the meeting should deliver little new to markets.
- Euro area growth underperformance is reinforced by today's weak hard data plus softer forward-looking surveys, arguing for further divergence this year.
- US demand remains firm beneath a soft headline: [REDACTED] expects Q4 consumption growth of 3.3% q/q even as the top-line print undershoots consensus.
- US trade policy is a watch item — the ECB's read on the macro risk to Europe is a key focus for today's communication.
- Near-term US data: today's GDP inflation detail lets [REDACTED] back out an estimate of tomorrow's December core PCE, benchmarked to their 0.16% m/m call.

### Risks
- Downside (near-term, relative pricing): the analyst flags that a soft US Q4 GDP print poses clear risks to relative growth pricing, even though [REDACTED] forecasts imply the growth divergence widens more than consensus expects this year.

### Unpacked
**The ECB meeting is set up as a non-event: a fourth straight 25bp cut that officials have already telegraphed, delivered with the same cautious guidance seen in recent communication.** Lagarde's tone is expected to echo her Davos remarks — policy direction "very clear," the path "gradual regular" — so the interest lies less in the decision than in how the Governing Council characterizes the incoming data and the risks from US trade policy.

That data mix is genuinely mixed. **Growth disappointed — area-wide Q4 GDP was flat, below both consensus and the ECB — while inflation surprised to the upside, with Spain beating and [REDACTED] economists tracking above consensus into Monday's area-wide flash.** The inflation firmness is partly mechanical, carrying a 15bp sequential lift from a January price-reset effect, which tempers how hawkish the surprise should read.

**The through-line is transatlantic divergence: Euro area activity has stabilized but only at low levels, and [REDACTED] sees this year's growth gap with the US widening more than consensus expects.** The surprise-index gap had actually narrowed over the past two months as Euro area data steadied, making today's flat GDP and softer surveys a reassertion of the underperformance story.

**The near-term wrinkle is on the US side.** [REDACTED] tracks Q4 GDP at 1.8% annualized, well below a consensus they view as stale, but with solid internals — 3.3% consumption growth — suggesting the softness is in the headline rather than in demand. The report also serves as a read-through to tomorrow's December core PCE, against a 0.16% m/m estimate. The main tactical caveat is that a weak US print could pressure relative growth pricing in the very near term, even as the medium-term divergence view points the other way.

subject: US Daily: January FOMC Recap: Not March, but Maybe Later (Mericle)
summary:
# January FOMC: Not Done Cutting, Just Not Yet — Waiting on the New Administration Before the Next Move

**Source:** [REDACTED], David Mericle  
**Focus:** US monetary policy — the Federal Reserve  
**General comment:** Constructive read of a hold; sees cuts still coming and treats the bar for resuming them as low, roughly in line with a patient-but-easing consensus.

### Context
The FOMC held the funds rate at 4.25–4.5% at its January 2025 meeting and made only minor statement edits. This recap reads Powell's press conference to gauge whether the pause signals an end to cuts or just a delay, and to judge the odds of a March move.

### The case
- **The Fed is not done cutting.** Powell still calls the policy stance "meaningfully restrictive" and above every Committee member's estimate of the longer-run neutral rate, saying "our eyes are telling us that our policy is having effects on the economy." That framing implies rates remain above where the Fed thinks they should ultimately settle, leaving room to ease further.
- **A March cut is unlikely because the Fed is waiting on the new administration.** Powell said five times the FOMC is not "in a hurry," and stressed it is "waiting to see what policies are enacted." The hesitation is not about the economy weakening but about policy uncertainty — tariffs, fiscal and other measures — that the Fed wants clarified before moving again.
- **Once that uncertainty clears, the bar to resume cutting looks low.** Powell downplayed the removal of the word "progress" from the statement as "language cleanup" and noted the last two inflation readings were good. The key metric is the 12-month inflation rate (which strips out residual seasonality), and the example he gave — further disinflation in housing services — is seen as an easy hurdle, since catch-up effects in that category are fading in a more predictable way than other components. Moderate tariffs might not, on their own, block a cut.
- **Whether the Fed would cut mid-year with tariffs freshly in place is left open.** Powell gave no strong signal on the specific scenario of falling inflation plus reduced policy uncertainty but newly-implemented moderate tariffs. His remark that "policies affect it at the margin" hints he may agree such changes won't decisively alter the economy's path — but he did not commit.
- **On the framework review, Powell defended the 2020 conclusions.** The 2025 review began in January and wraps by late summer; the 2% target is off the table. He rejected two Jackson Hole critiques: that a tight labor market alone justifies preemptive hikes (he still thinks that insight holds), and that flexible average inflation targeting made the Fed hike too late. On the latter, he argued the make-up strategy simply proved irrelevant this cycle — the delay in hiking came from reading the initial inflation surge as transitory, not from the framework.

### Implications
- Base case unchanged: two more 25bp cuts in 2025 (June and December) and one in 2026, with March effectively ruled out.
- The path hinges on year-over-year core PCE falling meaningfully — projected from ~2.80% in December to ~2.55% by March and lower thereafter — enough to build the "confidence" Powell wants; the main swing factor is which tariffs actually take effect.
- Policy-change uncertainty, not incoming inflation data, is the binding constraint on the near-term rate path.

subject: US Daily: Q4 GDP Preview (Rindels/Walker)
summary:
# Q4 GDP: [REDACTED] at 1.8%, a Full 0.8pp Below Consensus

**Theme:** Advance Economic Indicators report forces a sharp downgrade; strong consumption and housing offset by weaker trade, capex and inventories  
**Markets:** US growth  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jessica Rindels, 29 Jan 2025  

### Estimates
- **+1.8% annualized** — Q4 real GDP growth; 0.8pp below consensus (+2.6%) and 0.5pp below Atlanta Fed GDPNow, and below the +2.6% average pace over 2024Q1–Q3.
- **+3.3%** — Q4 personal consumption, contributing +2.2pp to GDP; supported by strong retail sales and auto sales at 16.5mn SAAR (highest since 2021Q2).
- **+4.3%** — Q4 residential fixed investment, a sharp rebound from -4.3% in Q3 and above GDPNow's +3.9%; December multifamily starts jumped 61.5%.
- **-0.2pp** — net exports contribution (vs -0.6pp average over 2024Q1–Q3): imports -0.7% (vs +8.1% average over the first three quarters), exports -3.0% (vs +9.6% in Q3); trade deficit widens from $1,069bn to $1,083bn.
- **+1.6%** — Q4 business fixed investment (vs +4.1% 2024Q1–Q3 average, GDPNow +1.7%): structures -0.7% (vs -5.0% in Q3), equipment +1.4% (vs +10.8% in Q3).
- **-0.8pp** — inventory accumulation contribution, partly reflecting hurricane and strike disruptions and a 0.5% December wholesale inventories decline.
- **+2.49% annualized** — Q4 core PCE (+2.80% y/y), from +0.16% m/m in December.
- **+2.4% annualized** — 2025Q1 and 2025 full-year GDP; Q1 net exports -1.1pp offset by inventories +1.1pp.

### Outlook
- **Growth reaccelerates to +2.4% in 2025**, per the analyst, on healthy consumption backed by solid real income and job gains, continued residential strength, and an equipment investment rebound.
- **Tariff front-loading is the key Q1 swing factor:** strong imports growth expected from front-loading ahead of potential January–February tariff increases, offset by a rebound in inventory accumulation and normalizing auto inventories.
- **Severe weather nets to roughly neutral in Q1**, with rebuilding after Hurricanes Helene and Milton balancing the drag from the Los Angeles wildfires.
- No explicit trade idea is offered.

### Unpacked
The 1.8% call is the product of a volatile tracking history. **The estimate fell from an initial 2.6% to 2.3–2.4% through December on hurricane drags, climbed back to +2.7% over the following two weeks on upside surprises, then was cut 0.9pp the morning of publication when the Advance Economic Indicators report came in far weaker than expected.** GDPNow took the same 0.9pp hit, but consensus barely moved (-0.1pp to +2.6%), leaving [REDACTED] well below the field — a gap that rests heavily on how much weight to place on that single morning's trade and inventories data.

Beneath the headline, the composition tells a two-sided story. **Consumption and housing are the strength — resilient retail, post-hurricane replacement auto demand, and a multifamily homebuilding recovery — while the drag comes from trade, capex and inventories, much of it traceable to Boeing.** Aircraft exports fell 35% in Q4 as the machinists strike hit production, dragging exports to -3.0%, and the same normalization in Boeing shipments pulls equipment investment down to +1.4% after a Q3 ramp. Import swings add noise: goods imports dropped in October on the short-lived port strikes, then rebounded, with a 19% December jump in industrial supplies that may signal tariff front-loading.

Looking into 2025, the moving parts are expected to largely cancel. **Q1 sees strong imports from continued tariff front-loading (net exports -1.1pp) offset by an inventory rebound (+1.1pp), while hurricane rebuilding balances wildfire damage** — leaving underlying momentum, not these transitory swings, as what the reader should track into the release.

subject: USA: FOMC Statement Notes Solid Labor Market Conditions Amid "Somewhat Elevated" Inflation
summary:
# Fed holds rates and adjusts its language: labor market "solid," inflation still "somewhat elevated"

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** Federal Reserve / US monetary policy  
**General comment:** Neutral, descriptive read of the decision; notes a slightly less dovish tone adjustment in the language, in line with consensus.

### Context
Immediate comment on the January 2025 FOMC meeting, which held the rate steady and revised the statement text following the prior cutting cycle.

### The case
- **The FOMC held the fed funds target range at 4.25–4.50%**, unchanged at the January meeting.
- **The description of the labor market turned firmer.** The statement now states that the unemployment rate "has stabilized at a low level" and that the labor market remains "solid," removing the prior reference to labor market conditions easing.
- **The language on inflation pulled back from the previous, more constructive read.** The Committee dropped the clause stating that inflation had "made progress" toward the 2% target and kept the assessment that it remains "somewhat elevated."

### Implications
- The combination — solid employment and the omission of inflation progress — signals less urgency for further cuts, without indicating a change in the rate path.
- The decision and the language adjustment were in line with expectations, with limited near-term market implications.

subject: USA: Trade Deficit Widens and Wholesale Inventories Decline by More Than Expected in December
summary:
# US goods trade deficit hits a record on likely tariff front-loading, as inventories fall

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US December trade and inventories data  
**General comment:** Neutral data readout; flags import front-loading ahead of tariffs, deficit and inventory draws both worse than consensus.

### Context
A reaction to the December Advance Economic Indicators Report. The goods trade deficit and wholesale inventories both came in weaker than expected, with the numbers read partly through the lens of potential tariff increases.

### The case
- **The goods trade deficit widened to a record $122.1bn, well beyond forecasts ([REDACTED] -$104.0bn, median -$105.5bn, prior -$103.5bn).** If it holds in the final trade balance report, it would be the largest goods trade deficit in history. The widening came from both sides: imports rose $10.8bn to $289.6bn while exports fell $7.8bn to $167.5bn.
- **Import strength likely reflects front-loading ahead of possible tariff increases.** The import gain was concentrated in industrial supplies (+$10.6bn), with smaller increases in consumer goods (+$2.2bn) and capital goods (+$1.4bn), partly offset by declines in autos (-$2.2bn) and food (-$0.3bn). Exports fell across all categories, led by industrial supplies (-$2.9bn).
- **Inventories drew down more than expected.** Wholesale inventories fell 0.5% in December against consensus for a 0.2% rise (-0.5% durables, -0.3% nondurables). Retail inventories declined 0.3%, driven by a 1.2% drop in autos, while retail ex-autos rose 0.2%.

### Implications
- Both the record deficit and the inventory drawdown feed directly into Q4 GDP tracking; the note defers its updated estimate to a forthcoming Q4 GDP preview.
- The import surge is presented as possible pre-tariff front-loading rather than confirmed, leaving open whether it unwinds in later months.

subject: Global Markets Daily: Pricing Macro Uncertainty in FX Implied Volatility (Rosenberg)
summary:
# FX Implied Vol Has Fallen Below What Macro Uncertainty Justifies

**Theme:** How much of FX option-implied volatility is explained by macroeconomic uncertainty, and what that gap implies for tariff hedging  
**Markets:** EUR/USD volatility; US and Euro area macro uncertainty  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Isabella Rosenberg, 29 January 2025

### Definitive impacts
- Across single-factor regressions, US CPI-forecast dispersion has the strongest explanatory power for EUR/USD 1-year implied vol, with Euro area policy uncertainty a close second.
- In a multivariate setting, most other factors (US and Euro area GDP, Euro area CPI, US policy) lose their explanatory power, driven by the high correlation among the uncertainty measures.
- US uncertainty measures generally outperform their Euro area counterparts; adding a US–Euro area interaction term does not improve the fit over US measures alone.
- Decomposing recent moves, rising inflation uncertainty since roughly mid-2024 accounts for most of the increase in EUR/USD implied vol.
- The relationship between macro uncertainty and FX implied vol is positive: wider forecast dispersion on growth or inflation coincides with higher implied vol, a link visible in EUR/USD over the past two decades.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] sees current EUR/USD implied vol as having fallen further than the decline in macro uncertainty would justify, suggesting the market has priced out part of the direct FX impact of tariffs.
- [REDACTED] expects trade-policy and tariff risk to keep inflation uncertainty elevated over the medium term, sustaining FX volatility going forward.
- [REDACTED] argues long FX vol expressions can be a useful hedge against tariff risk, alongside USD calls and long USD/CAD positions.
- The models are treated as diagnostic, not prescriptive: [REDACTED] notes they explain moves in implied vol but do not indicate the correct level.

### Backdrop
FX option-implied volatility tends to rise when the macroeconomic outlook becomes more uncertain. The note proxies that uncertainty with the cross-forecaster standard deviation in Consensus Economics surveys for year-ahead GDP, inflation, and monetary policy in the US and Euro area — wider dispersion meaning more disagreement about outcomes. These measures are heavily correlated both across variables within a country (a variable US GDP outlook usually comes with a variable inflation outlook) and across regions (Euro area and US GDP dispersion tend to move together), which is why individual factors compete for the same explanatory role in a joint model.

### At issue
Recent weeks have seen sharp swings in FX implied vol, rising across major currencies exposed to tariffs. To quantify how much of this is macro-driven, [REDACTED] regresses EUR/USD 1-year-ahead implied vol on the US and Euro area GDP, CPI, and policy uncertainty measures, then uses the fitted model to decompose the moves of recent months.

### Unpacked
The starting point is a market observation — implied vol jumping on trade-policy headlines — and the analytical question of whether that jump reflects genuine macro uncertainty or something else. Tariffs hit FX directly, but also indirectly by unsettling growth, inflation, and policy expectations, so the note tries to separate the macro-uncertainty channel from the rest.

**The headline finding is that inflation uncertainty, specifically US CPI-forecast dispersion, does most of the work in explaining both the level and the recent rise in EUR/USD implied vol.** Euro area policy uncertainty matters too, but the other candidate drivers largely drop out once correlations are accounted for — a statistical artifact of the measures moving together rather than evidence that growth uncertainty is irrelevant.

**The more actionable point is the gap: implied vol has come down by more than the model's macro inputs would imply, meaning the market has partly unwound the tariff premium even as inflation uncertainty stays high.** [REDACTED] reads this as vol looking cheap relative to the macro backdrop, which frames the trade rationale — if uncertainty persists and vol is under-pricing it, long FX vol is an attractive tariff hedge, complementing USD calls and long USD/CAD.

The note carries an explicit trade view: long FX vol, USD calls, and long USD/CAD as tariff hedges. The broader cross-asset trade-idea list appended to the daily is a standing menu, not tied to this analysis.

subject: [REDACTED] FX Morning Notes: A Flurry of Central Banks
summary:
# Central Banks in Focus: Dovish Pivots Broaden Across G10 as the Fed Holds

**Theme:** A single-day cluster of policy decisions, with disinflation opening the door to faster easing  
**Markets:** Global FX and rates  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Stuart Jenkins, 29 January 2025  

### Landscape
- Q4 Australian inflation printed below expectations across measures, including a one-tenth miss on the RBA's preferred trimmed-mean series, with sequential headline and underlying inflation now more comfortably inside the 2-3% target range.
- Markets price ~48bp of Fed cuts for 2025, now matching the December dot plot's two-cut projection.
- Australian markets price ~61bp of RBA cuts through the August meeting, versus the 100bp in [REDACTED] economists' updated call.
- Brazilian markets price close to 200bp of additional BCB hikes beyond the March meeting, on top of the guided 100bp moves in January and March.
- Core inflation has fallen across G10 economies over the past year, with Japan the sole exception.

### Drivers
- **Disinflation is broadening across G10**, pulling former hawkish holdouts — the RBA, Norges Bank, and BoE — toward dovish pivots as Australia, Norway, and the UK catch down toward peers.
- **The RBA timeline has accelerated**: on the soft Q4 print, [REDACTED] economists now expect back-to-back cuts in Feb/April/May then Aug, replacing the prior quarterly-cut path.
- **The Riksbank has shifted emphasis from inflation to growth**, delivering an expected 25bp cut while reiterating December guidance that implies no further cuts as its modal view; [REDACTED] still expects growth disappointment to force additional easing in March and June.
- **Tariff and government-policy uncertainty dominates the Fed outlook** — the path of macro data and policy, not the reaction function, is the live variable, and limited guidance is expected today.
- **The BoC faces two-sided pressure**: rates at the top of the neutral range, bottoming growth, and above-target spot inflation on the hawkish side; an intact negative output gap and tariff risks on the dovish side.

### Risks
- Downside for AUD (analyst view): a dovish RBA reassessment could weigh on AUD on crosses, though [REDACTED] expects China tariff risks and USD/CNY moves to be the larger determinant.
- Downside for SEK (analyst view): eventual over-delivery of Riksbank cuts versus market pricing is one channel for broader SEK weakness, given its outsized exposure to tariffs and trade uncertainty.
- Near-term downside for USD/CAD (analyst view): a more hesitant BoC tone on the pace of cuts could pressure the pair, even as [REDACTED] keeps long USD/CAD as a preferred tariff expression.

### Unpacked
The RBA sits at the center of the day's Australian story. **The Q4 miss has already prompted [REDACTED] economists to pull forward the easing path to consecutive cuts in February, April and May, then August — a materially faster pace than the ~61bp the market prices through August against their 100bp call.** [REDACTED] had flagged AUD as vulnerable to a sharper dovish pivot than markets anticipate; the muted currency reaction overnight leaves room for that reassessment to act as a crosses headwind, but China tariffs and USD/CNY are expected to matter more for the currency.

The Riksbank delivered its expected 25bp cut while formally signalling it may be done, yet the statement's tilt from inflation toward growth — with noted early signs of an activity rebound from a weak base — leaves the door open. **[REDACTED] reads growth disappointment as likely to warrant further easing in March and June, and expects that over-delivery versus pricing to feed broader SEK weakness through the krona's heavy tariff and trade exposure.**

On the Fed, the expected cautious hold matters less than the framing. **The real uncertainty lies in the path of upcoming data and government policy — tariffs above all, but also tax and immigration — rather than in the Fed's current reaction function.** A higher-volatility run of January data, plus Q4 GDP and the ECI, arrives in the coming weeks, and Powell's stated refusal to "guess, speculate, or assume" policy outcomes argues for limited guidance. Fed speakers who have addressed tariffs generally see only a limited inflation impact, consistent with the Fed's ex-post read of the Trump 1.0 experience.

The BoC decision hinges on signalling rather than the cut itself. **With a 25bp move expected, the pace guidance is the CAD driver, and [REDACTED] sees the balance of risks favouring a cautious message given tariff uncertainty** — while flagging that a more hesitant tone could pull USD/CAD lower near term. Over the medium term, [REDACTED] stays comfortable with a below-consensus neutral rate estimate and keeps long USD/CAD as a preferred way to capture tariff risk.

Brazil is the day's outlier on direction. **The BCB is expected to hike 100bp, having already guided to another 100bp in March, so the question is whether it signals anything beyond March, where markets still price close to 200bp of further tightening.** This is also the first meeting of the Galipolo-led MPC. With real rates above their long-term average and political noise in a seasonally quieter phase, [REDACTED] has been recommending shorts in EUR/BRL as its preferred EM carry long.

subject: USA: Trump Administration Announces Payment Pause and Federal Employee "Deferred Resignation"
summary:
# US: federal payments pause reaches up to $600bn, but the direct effect on GDP should be small

**Theme:** Scope and macro impact of the federal payments pause and the "deferred resignation" program  
**Markets:** US fiscal policy / federal spending  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Alec Phillips, 28 Jan 2025  

### Definitive impacts
- Up to roughly $600bn (2% of GDP) in annual payments could be subject to the pause, though the actual amount could be much smaller. Estimated composition: up to $300bn in grants to states (excluding Medicaid and income-support programs), $120bn to NGOs and universities, up to $140bn in direct loans and up to $90bn in guaranteed loans.
- Practically all "mandatory" spending projected for FY2025 ($4.6 trillion) would be exempt, assuming that "other similar programs" refers to income-security programs like those already excluded (Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid, food stamps, small business and farm loans, rental assistance).
- Small impact on the discretionary portion: a reduced fraction of the ~$900bn in non-defense spending and very little of the ~$900bn in defense spending, since federal employee salaries and contracts for goods/services do not appear to be covered by the pause.
- A federal court suspended implementation of the pause on 28 January until a hearing scheduled for 3 February; the measure could still take effect after that ruling.
- On the "deferred resignation" program: if 10% of federal employees opt in, the reduction in compensation costs would be up to ~$25bn/year (just under 0.1% of GDP), starting in Q4. Compensation for non-defense federal employees totals $260bn.

### Opinative impacts
- [REDACTED] assesses that, unlike a shutdown — which directly reduces the government's contribution to quarterly GDP because employees stop working — the *timing* of these payments should have a small direct effect on economic data, provided the pause is not larger than expected and is resolved quickly.
- [REDACTED] assumes "other similar programs" covers income-support programs analogous to those explicitly exempted; the note acknowledges the scope is not yet entirely clear, and the figures are presented as ceilings ("no more than").
- The bank notes the pause could create complications for state/local governments, universities, and entities expecting to receive payments, with possible second-order effects — without quantifying them.

### At issue
Two Trump administration announcements, both in January 2025:

- **Payments pause.** A freeze on grants, loans, and federal assistance programs potentially affected by the prior week's executive orders. The initial scope was confusing, generating reports that major programs could stop payments; subsequent guidance narrowed the scope, explicitly excluding Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid, food stamps, small business and farm loans, rental assistance, and "other similar programs." OMB instructed agencies to review all programs by 10 February, which could allow payments to resume.
- **"Deferred resignation."** A program allowing certain federal employees to resign effective 30 September 2025, receiving salary and benefits until then. Military, national security, immigration, and postal staff are excluded. Press reports cite the administration's expectation of 5–10% uptake.

### Unpacked
The note's starting point is the gap between the headline and the fiscal mechanics. **The pause announcement was read by the market as a threat to major programs, but the structure of the federal budget sharply limits what can actually be frozen.** Nearly all mandatory spending — the bulk of the budget — is protected by the exemptions, and most discretionary spending consists of salaries and contracts that do not appear to be covered. What remains is the layer of grants, direct loans, and guaranteed loans, from which the $600bn ceiling is drawn.

The key distinction for the reader is between a *pause* and a *shutdown*. **A shutdown cuts government output and drags down quarterly GDP; a pause merely shifts the timing of payments that remain owed, with a small direct effect on the data — provided it stays short and contained.** The relevant risk is not aggregate but cash-flow: states, universities, and entities dependent on these disbursements could face strain, with second-order effects the note flags without sizing.

The picture remains fluid on two fronts. **The pause is judicially suspended until 3 February, and the OMB review due 10 February could either release or formalize the freezes — the outcome determines whether the figures are theoretical ceilings or actual losses.** "Deferred resignation," meanwhile, is a separate fiscal lever of modest magnitude: even at 10% uptake, the savings stay below 0.1% of GDP and only begin in Q4, contingent on the acceptance rate.

The note offers no explicit trade idea; it is a read on scope and magnitude to calibrate the macro risk.

subject: USA: Consumer Confidence Somewhat Below Expectations

# US: Consumer confidence declines in January, slightly below expectations

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US consumer confidence (Conference Board)  
**General comment:** Descriptive read of a marginally weaker-than-consensus print; no directional bias of its own.

### Context
Comment on the January 2025 release of the Conference Board consumer confidence index, which came in below both [REDACTED]'s forecast and the market median.

### The points
- **The index fell to 104.1 in January, a decline of 5.4 points and below expectations.** The reading came in below [REDACTED]'s forecast (105.0) and the median (105.7). The decline was broad-based: both the expectations component (-2.6 pt, to 83.9) and the present situation component (-9.7 pt, to 134.3) fell. The move came from both ends: fewer respondents see the labor market as tight, and more see it as difficult.

### Implications
- A marginally weaker signal on consumer perceptions at the start of 2025, without materially changing the level picture.
- The employment differential remaining persistently below its pre-pandemic level reinforces the read of a less-heated labor market from the household perspective.

subject: USA: Core Durable Goods Orders Above Expectations in December; Boosting Q4 GDP Tracking to +2.7%
summary:
# US Q4 GDP Tracking Nudged to +2.7% After a Firmer December Core Capital Goods Print

**Source:** [REDACTED] — Jan Hatzius  
**Focus:** US December durable goods orders and Q4 GDP tracking  
**General comment:** A routine data read-through; headline miss but firmer underlying capex signals lift the growth estimate marginally.

### Context
The note reacts to the December durable goods report. Headline orders fell 2.2%, defying consensus expectations for an increase, but the underlying capital goods detail came in stronger than the market and [REDACTED] had assumed, prompting a small upward revision to Q4 growth tracking.

### The case
- **The headline decline is a transport-driven distortion, not a signal of weaker capex.** Durable goods orders fell 2.2% in December against consensus for a gain, but roughly $7bn of the drop came from a decline in nondefense aircraft orders. Stripping out transportation, orders rose 0.3%, in line with expectations, indicating the underlying picture was not weak.
- **Core capital goods — the cleaner gauge of business investment — beat across both orders and shipments.** Core capital goods orders rose 0.5% and shipments 0.6%, each above the roughly 0.2–0.3% consensus and [REDACTED]'s own estimates. November was also revised up on both measures (orders +0.5pp to +0.9%, shipments +0.1pp to +0.4%), reinforcing the firmer trend even as headline November orders were revised down.
- **The combined data feed lifts Q4 growth tracking.** The headline miss was roughly in line with [REDACTED]'s own forecast, while the inventories data pointed to slightly stronger Q4 inventory accumulation and both core capital goods and aircraft shipments ran ahead of prior GDP tracking assumptions. Together these raised the estimate.

### Implications
- Q4 GDP tracking and domestic final sales estimates were each raised by 0.1pp, both to +2.7% (quarter-over-quarter annualized).
- The stronger core capital goods and shipments detail — rather than the negative headline — is the input that matters for reading business investment momentum into the quarter.

subject: Global Rates Notes: 1Q25 Treasury Refunding Preview
summary:
# Treasury Refunding Preview: Coupon Sizes On Hold, But "Several Quarters" Guidance At Risk

**Theme:** Nominal coupons unchanged now, but deficit and debt-ceiling uncertainty threaten the "stable for several quarters" pledge; TIPS keep rising  
**Markets:** US Treasury issuance / rates  
**Source:** [REDACTED], William Marshall, 28 January 2025  

### Estimates
- **No change to nominal coupon or FRN auction sizes** at the February 5 refunding statement (8:30am), consistent with prior guidance.
- **TIPS 30y +$1bn** in February and **TIPS 5y +$1bn** in April, each over the prior new-issue size — continued gradual growth.
- **$931bn of Q1 net marketable borrowing** projected, vs Treasury's prior $823bn estimate, holding the end-of-quarter TGA target at $850bn (financing estimates due Monday, February 3, 3pm).
- **$194bn of Q2 net marketable borrowing** under baseline (TGA held constant, Treasury QT ceasing end-Q1).
- **Coupon auction size increases begin at the November 2025 refunding**, phased over four quarters, adding a cumulative ~$290bn/quarter to gross issuance.
- **Deficits of $1.8tn / $2.05tn / $2.1tn** for FY25/26/27.

### Outlook
- **Meaningful risk Treasury dilutes its forward guidance** that it won't need to raise nominal coupon sizes "for at least the next several quarters"; the analyst's preferred rewording points to language about current sizes providing "sufficient capacity" for near-term needs.
- **Bill share to drift back toward ~20% of outstanding debt by late 2026** via the gradual coupon ramp, rather than a rapid terming-out — supported by the higher reset in term premia and an upward-sloping curve that means faster terming-out would not lower current interest expense.
- **Debt ceiling is the key near-term swing factor** for bill supply and the TGA. A protracted impasse could cut 1H borrowing estimates by a cumulative $450-500bn, with cash balances near $250-300bn at end-Q1 and $350-400bn at end-Q2; the analyst's most likely case is resolution near the x-date, estimated around mid-Q3.
- **Fed QT baseline:** Treasury runoff halts end-March, balance sheet stops shrinking end-June, MBS proceeds reinvested into Treasuries from July, reserve management purchases from early 2026. If instead Treasury assumes runoff continues at $25bn/month, that adds ~$75bn to Q2 privately held net borrowing.
- **No explicit trade idea** is offered; the note is a positioning/expectations preview.

### Unpacked
The February 5 statement is the first refunding of the year and of the new administration, and the analyst expects it to change little in near-term issuance while offering hints on how Treasury will handle the larger questions ahead. **The central tension is between a rising deficit path and elevated uncertainty on several inputs to borrowing needs, which together put real pressure on the credibility of the "several quarters" pledge on stable coupon sizes.** A precedent cuts both ways: the February 2017 statement under the first Trump administration was nearly unchanged and stayed stable until November, whereas February 2021 saw substantial revisions — though that reflected pandemic-era funding volatility rather than today's steadier backdrop.

**The debt ceiling dominates the near-term picture, driving both the size of the borrowing estimates and the eventual liquidity drain when it resolves.** The analyst suspects Monday's financing estimates will, as in 2021 and 2023, assume a relatively quick suspension or increase that permits TGA normalization. A drawn-out impasse would instead depress cash balances and lower 1H borrowing estimates materially. Congress could address the limit alongside a March spending package, but given the year-end stalemate, a deal near the deadline looks more likely, with the x-date somewhere in Q3.

**Fed balance-sheet policy is the other major input, and its endgame is now entangled with debt-limit politics.** The baseline has the Fed sizing reserves to the "ample" range of 12-13% of bank assets under a steady-state $850bn TGA. The risk is that the Fed instead calibrates off observed funding pressures — which could push the end of QT later, while compressing the window between runoff and renewed balance-sheet growth. A lower steady-state TGA could in turn give the Fed room to shrink further.

Beyond the fiscal outlook, which will not be resolved next week, several structural questions loom. New Treasury leadership's approach to debt composition is untested, but the analyst expects only a gradual move toward a ~20% bill share, with the weighted average maturity of debt staying broadly steady rather than a rapid shift. Cash management is another open item: the "steady state" TGA has risen with the larger deficit and rollover needs, and while the 2015 framework could be revisited, any change would likely follow a formal strategic review first. **The most intricate question is how Treasury interacts with the Fed's eventual SOMA composition, since the Fed starts from a below-market bill share and longer WAM, making short-maturity-skewed purchases likely.** A heavily bill-tilted Fed could drain the supply of short-term safe assets the market wants; Treasury could accommodate a front-end Fed skew by delaying or dampening its coupon-increase path, but that would erode the role of bills as shock absorbers to unexpected swings in issuance needs.

For the near term, watch Monday's financing estimates for the embedded debt-limit and QT assumptions, and Wednesday's statement for exactly how the "several quarters" language is reworded — refunding days have historically coincided with swap-spread volatility, so the wording carries weight.

subject: G10 Inflation Monitor: Firmer in Japan (Peters)
summary:
# G10 Inflation: Broad Disinflation Intact, but Japan Firms and the UK Stays Sticky

**Theme:** Underlying inflation still cooling across most of the G10, with Japan the outlier turning firmer  
**Markets:** G10 core inflation  
**Source:** [REDACTED], Jan Hatzius, 28 January 2025  

### Landscape
- December [REDACTED] trimmed core (month-over-month annualized) softened in the UK (+2.8% vs. +5.1%), Euro area (+1.9% vs. +2.1%) and Canada (+3.1% vs. +3.2%), but ticked up in the US (+2.2% PCE forecast vs. +1.4%) and Japan (+1.9% vs. +1.5%).
- On a 3-month annualized basis, trimmed core eased in the UK (+4.0%) and Euro area (+2.2%), held at +2.0% in the US, and edged up in Japan (+1.8%) and Canada (+3.2%).
- Year-over-year trimmed core stands at +3.5% in the UK, +2.8% in Canada, +2.5% in the US, +2.4% in the Euro area and +1.3% in Japan.
- The share of the headline basket running above 4% (six-month annualized) rose in the UK for a third straight month to 42% (vs. 35%), with smaller upticks in Canada (35%), the Euro area (20%) and Japan (25%), and a dip in the US (26%).
- Extreme moves are fading: the share of the headline CPI basket above an 8% annualized pace runs at 2% in the Euro area, 6% in the US, 10% in Japan and the UK, and 14% in Canada.
- December year-over-year core came in below consensus in the UK and US, and in line in the Euro area, Japan and Canada.

### Drivers
- Core services inflation (3-month annualized) firmed in most economies — Euro area +2.7%, UK +4.0%, Canada +3.5%, Japan +2.4% — while easing only in the US (-0.4pp to +3.6%), leaving services the main sticky component outside the US.
- Core goods inflation edged up in the UK but softened elsewhere, notably the US (CPI -0.5pp to +1.6%) and Canada (-0.4pp to -0.4%); Japan stayed high at +4.7%.
- Rent inflation was broadly sideways: slowing in Japan (+0.2%) and the Euro area (+2.8%), flat in the UK (7.6%), and firming modestly in the US (+3.3%) and Canada (+5.8%).
- Energy inflation accelerated across all DMs covered, while food inflation generally ticked down — except in Japan, where rice inflation continued to climb and is pulling Japanese food and core measures higher.
- The distribution of 3-month inflation rates keeps moving back toward pre-pandemic norms in most economies, with Canada the most dispersed laggard.

### Risks
- The note frames no explicit upside/downside scenario risks; its forward view is expressed through forecast revisions rather than a risk skew. [REDACTED] nudged up end-2025 core forecasts in the Euro area (+0.2pp) and UK (+0.1pp) and lifted headline in both by 0.3pp, while trimming the US end-2025 headline PCE forecast by 0.2pp.

### Unpacked
The report is a scoreboard rather than an argument, and its through-line is that the disinflation of the past two years is still intact but no longer uniform. **Traditional core inflation has fallen sharply from its cyclical peak — around 5.9pp in the UK, 5.3pp in the Euro area, 5.2pp in Canada and 4.5pp in the US (PCE) on a 3-month average annualized basis — but Japan has retraced only 2.2pp, marking it as the economy moving against the grain.** On a year-over-year basis the same ranking holds: core is down 3.9pp in the UK, 3.4pp in Canada, 3.0pp in the Euro area and 2.8pp in the US, versus just 1.9pp in Japan.

Beneath the aggregates, the composition is the story. Goods disinflation is doing much of the work outside Japan, while services remain the sticky piece almost everywhere the US is not. **The US is the mirror image of the group — goods and services both cooling there even as they firm across Europe, Canada and Japan — which is why US core sits mid-pack despite a December uptick in the trimmed measure.**

Japan's firmness traces to specific, identifiable pressures rather than a broad reacceleration. **Rice-driven food costs are the visible culprit, feeding into a core-goods rate still running at +4.7% and into breadth measures that keep drifting up.** This also matters for cross-country comparison: Japan's official core CPI excludes only energy and fresh food, so rice-based food items that [REDACTED] strips out of its harmonized basket stay inside the headline Japanese figure.

That harmonization point recurs through the note. **[REDACTED]'s harmonized core — which removes a consistent set of items across countries — sits below central banks' preferred measures everywhere except the UK, with the US and Canada gaps driven mainly by owned-housing costs that Euro-area and UK baskets never include.** The practical read is that headline national core figures overstate underlying pressure in the US and Canada relative to a like-for-like basis.

Forecasts round out the picture and lean slightly dovish versus consensus. **[REDACTED] year-end core projections are +2.4% in the US, +2.1% in the Euro area and Japan, +3.0% in the UK and +2.0% in Canada — generally a touch below consensus — with the past month's revisions nudging Europe and the UK higher and the US headline lower.** The UK remains the highest-core outlier of the group at every horizon, consistent with its still-elevated services and 7.6% rent print.
